valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Oxymercuration-demercuration with alcohol solvent. Markovnikov regioselectivity. Trifluoroacetate Hg salt used for less reactive alkenes.
valid_transformations.conditions: Step 1 (oxymercuration): RT; aqueous ROH or ROH/THF; Hg(OAc)₂ or Hg(OCOCF₃)₂; Markovnikov regioselective addition. Step 2 (demercuration): RT; NaBH₄; NaOH(aq) → replace Hg with H. Overall: anti-Markovnikov? No — Markovnikov: OH (as OR) at more-substituted C, H at less substituted. No rearrangements. Gives mixed ether (ROH as nucleophile in oxymercuration).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

reagents: conc HX (HI > HBr, acidic conditions, SN1 or SN2 depending on R)
valid_transformations.note: For mixed ArOR ethers: ArO-C bond breaks to give ArOH + RX (weaker bond breaks; ArO-C is stronger due to resonance stabilization of ArO).
valid_transformations.conditions: Conc HX (HI > HBr >> HCl) or excess H₂SO₄; reflux. Mechanism: H⁺ protonates ether O → oxonium ion → SN1 (3° or 2° with HI/HBr) or SN2 (1° ethers, X⁻ attacks) → alkyl halide + alcohol → further halogenation of alcohol. HI cleaves fastest (I⁻ best nucleophile). Aryl ethers (PhOR): Ar-O cleaved → PhOH + R-X (aryl C-O too strong for SN on ring). Excess HI: PhOH → PhI ultimately.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.conditions: PCl₅; RT to mild heat; anhydrous. R-O-R' + PCl₅ → RCl + R'Cl + POCl₃. Both C-O bonds cleaved. Compare with HX cleavage (gives one alcohol + one halide initially). PCl₅ is more reactive than HX; both C-O bonds broken. Less commonly used; HX is the standard ether cleavage.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: BF₃ activates ether O → R⁺ (or tight ion pair) → CO insertion → acylium → captures R'O⁻ → ester.
valid_transformations.conditions: BF₃·Et₂O (Lewis acid catalyst); CO (1–3 atm); RT to mild heat; anhydrous. Mechanism: BF₃ activates ether O → oxocarbenium (R⁺-O-R') → CO insertion → acylium → ester product. Koch reaction variant. Uncommon in lab; industrial interest for carbonylation of ethers. BF₃ is essential Lewis acid.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.conditions: AlCl₃ (Lewis acid); RT; anhydrous CH₂Cl₂ or CS₂. R''COCl + AlCl₃ → acylium (R''CO⁺) → attacks ether O → cleaves one C-O bond → ester + R'X. Friedel-Crafts-like mechanism on ether. Anhydrous conditions required.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.conditions: AlCl₃; RT to mild heat; anhydrous. (R''CO)₂O + AlCl₃ → acylium attacks ether → both C-O bonds eventually cleaved → two esters. Similar to acid chloride cleavage above.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Old/stored ether accumulates hydroperoxides at alpha-C. Heating is EXPLOSIVE. Must check for peroxides before distilling ether.
valid_transformations.conditions: O₂ (air); RT, slow process; radical chain, alpha-C selectivity. Radical initiator (trace): ether stored in air slowly forms alpha-hydroperoxide. Alpha C-H abstraction by RO₂• → alpha radical → O₂ → hydroperoxide. HAZARD: ether peroxides accumulate in stored diethyl ether/THF → explosive on evaporation or heating. Always check peroxide level before distilling aged ether. Remove peroxides: ferrous sulphate, copper mesh, alumina.
valid_transformations.notes: Radical mechanism: initiation required (hν or ROOR). Chain process — omitting any propagation step loses marks in mechanism questions.

valid_transformations.conditions: Cl₂/hν or Cl₂/NBS; RT; radical alpha-C-H substitution. Similar selectivity to alkane halogenation but alpha-C (adjacent to O) is most reactive (O lone pair stabilises radical → alpha selectivity). Product: alpha-halo ether (R-O-CHX-R'). Used as alkylating agents (alpha-halo ethers are reactive electrophiles).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.to: acetate ester (R-OAc, +42 Da per OH) — Acetylation
valid_transformations.note: MW trick: No. of OH groups = ΔMW / 42
valid_transformations.conditions: Acetic anhydride (Ac₂O) or acetyl chloride (AcCl); RT to mild heat (Ac₂O) or 0°C (AcCl); base (pyridine or Et₃N) to neutralise HCl from AcCl. Each OH group adds 42 Da (CH₂CO contribution = 42.04). MW increase = 42 × n(OH). Used to determine n(OH) by MW measurement. Acylation is O-selective; N-acylation also occurs for amines. Pyridine is both base and catalyst (via DMAP-like mechanism for Ac₂O).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'II'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Reactivity order: R-COOH > Ph-OH > R-OH toward CH₂N₂
valid_transformations.conditions: CH₂N₂ (diazomethane); RT; anhydrous ether solvent; rapid O-methylation. Mechanism: proton abstraction from R-OH by CH₂N₂ → methyl diazonium → SN2 by RO⁻ → R-OCH₃ + N₂. Selectivity of CH₂N₂: RCOOH >> ArOH > ROH (pKa order). Phenol methyl ethers easy (rate: PhOH reacts at RT; ROH requires slight warming or longer time). Hazard: CH₂N₂ is toxic and explosive gas.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Fastest CH₂N₂ reaction; R-COOH > Ph-OH > R-OH selectivity
valid_transformations.conditions: CH₂N₂ (1 equiv); RT; Et₂O or MeOH as co-solvent; immediate O-alkylation of COOH. Fastest substrate for CH₂N₂ (pKa ~5, most acidic). Product: methyl ester (R-COOCH₃). Quantitative at RT, no workup needed (N₂ evolution drives reaction). Excess CH₂N₂ methylates phenols too. Used for carbodiimide-sensitive carboxylic acids where Fischer esterification would cause racemisation.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: NH₂ more nucleophilic than OH toward acylating agents → N over O selectivity
valid_transformations.conditions: Ac₂O (1 equiv); RT; aqueous or EtOH; no catalyst needed. Selective N-acetylation: N-nucleophilicity >> O-nucleophilicity for acylation (amine lone pair less delocalized than phenol lone pair). 1 equiv Ac₂O → N-acetyl product (paracetamol = 4-acetamidophenol, not the 2-isomer). 2 equiv → O,N-diacetyl. Pyridine unnecessary at RT. Paracetamol synthesis: p-aminophenol + Ac₂O → paracetamol.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.conditions: HONO (HNO₂, in situ from NaNO₂ + HCl); 0–5°C; aqueous-alcoholic. Mechanism: N-protonated HNO₂ → NO⁺ (nitrosonium) → O-attack by alcohol → alkyl nitrite R-ONO. Primary and secondary alcohols. Alkyl nitrites are esters of nitrous acid (HO-N=O); volatile, fragrant, vasodilating (amyl nitrite = 'poppers'). Distinguish from nitro compounds R-NO₂: different functional group.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Mechanism E1; Saytzeff (more substituted alkene) is major
valid_transformations.conditions: Conc H₂SO₄; >170°C (>443K); E1 mechanism. Mechanism: H⁺ protonates OH → oxonium → loss of H₂O → carbocation → loss of β-H → alkene. Saytzeff product (more substituted alkene). Rearrangements possible. Order of ease: 3°ROH > 2°ROH >> 1°ROH. Temperature critical: >170°C for alkene (vs 110–170°C for ether, <110°C for sulphate).
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.note: Intermolecular dehydration; works only with 1° alcohols
valid_transformations.conditions: Conc H₂SO₄; 110–140°C (110°C < T < 170°C); SN2 bimolecular mechanism (not E1 — too cool for elimination). Oxonium ion formation → 2nd ROH attacks C → ether + H₂O (SN2). Works best for 1° alcohols (2° may give mixed results; 3° → only alkene). Industrial production of diethyl ether uses 140°C.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.conditions: Conc H₂SO₄; <110°C (<383K); direct esterification of OH by H₂SO₄. Product: alkyl hydrogen sulphate (monoester of H₂SO₄, R-OSO₃H). No dehydration at this low temperature. Reversible on warming. Used industrially (e.g., ethyl sulphate from ethanol + H₂SO₄ cold). At higher T: ether (110–170°C) → alkene (>170°C).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.conditions: Al₂O₃ (alumina); >300°C; gas-phase or solid-liquid contact; E2 mechanism (base-like behaviour of Al₂O₃ surface). Saytzeff alkene. No rearrangements (no carbocation). Milder than H₂SO₄ at same T. Used for primary alcohols that would require very high T with H₂SO₄. Industrial: ethylene from ethanol/Al₂O₃/300°C.
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.conditions: POCl₃ + pyridine; 0°C to RT (or mild heat); anhydrous. Mechanism: POCl₂ ester formed from ROH → pyridine (base) deprotonates β-H → E2 → alkene (Saytzeff). No rearrangements (concerted E2). Mild conditions (no carbocation). Excellent for sensitive substrates. Pyridine serves as both base and solvent.
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.note: ONLY dehydrating agent that gives Hofmann (least substituted) product
valid_transformations.conditions: ThO₂ (thorium dioxide); Δ (350–500°C); gas phase; E2 or E1cb mechanism. Unique property: ThO₂ is the ONLY dehydration agent that gives Hofmann product (least substituted alkene, anti-Zaitsev). All other dehydration agents (H₂SO₄, Al₂O₃, POCl₃, KHSO₄, H₃PO₄) give Saytzeff. Temperature: very high (>350°C).
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.conditions: KHSO₄ (potassium bisulphate); Δ (100–200°C); melt or solution; mild acid dehydration. E1 mechanism (acid-catalysed): KHSO₄ protonates OH → oxonium → loss of H₂O → carbocation → E1 → Saytzeff. Milder than H₂SO₄ (lower acid concentration). Gives Saytzeff product.
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.conditions: ZnCl₂ (Lewis acid); Δ; neat or in HCl. ZnCl₂ coordinates to OH (Lewis acid-base) → activated leaving group → elimination. E1-like. Less common dehydration agent. Also used in Lucas test (ZnCl₂/conc HCl): tests for 1°/2°/3° alcohols by speed of turbidity development.
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.conditions: Δ (heat alone, 200°C); intramolecular esterification. The two COOH groups (1,2-adjacent on ring) can easily cyclise to anhydride by loss of H₂O. Entropy neutral (intramolecular). No acid catalyst needed for 1,2-diacids (and some 1,4-diacids forming glutaric anhydride). Product: phthalic anhydride (used in Friedel-Crafts acylation, dye synthesis, plasticisers).
valid_transformations.notes: EAS: product regiochemistry determined by existing substituent(s). Check for conflicting or cooperating directors before assigning major product.

valid_transformations.from: tert-butyl ester of pivalic acid (Me₃C-COOH + MeOH/H₂SO₄)
valid_transformations.to: t-BuOMe (tert-butyl methyl ether) + CO — AAc1 trap
valid_transformations.note: Classic JEE trap: pivalic acid + MeOH → ether NOT ester; -CO extrusion is key
valid_transformations.conditions: Conc H₂SO₄ + MeOH; RT. AAc1 (acid, acyl, unimolecular acyl-O cleavage): H⁺ protonates C=O → tetrahedral intermediate → acylium R-CO⁺ → loses CO → t-Bu⁺ (very stable 3°) → MeOH → t-BuOMe + CO. Only works for pivalate (2,2-dimethylpropanoate) and other very hindered esters where acyl C is inaccessible to nucleophile. CO evolution is diagnostic. Normal esters go AAc2.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.to: mesityl carboxylic acid + MeOH — BAL2 hydrolysis
reagents: BAL2: OH⁻ attacks CH₃ (SN2) due to steric bulk on acyl
valid_transformations.note: Normal BAc2 impossible due to extreme steric bulk → forced BAL2
valid_transformations.conditions: NaOH (aq, excess); reflux. BAL2 (base, alkyl-O, bimolecular): steric bulk of 2,4,6-trimethylbenzoyl group completely blocks OH⁻ attack on carbonyl C (normal BAc2 path). Instead: OH⁻ attacks methyl C (SN2) → mesityl carboxylate + MeOH. ¹⁸O label (in NaOH) ends up in MeOH, not in carboxylate — proves O-C(alkyl) cleavage. Diagnostic of extremely sterically hindered esters.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

reagents: BAc2, most common basic hydrolysis, IRREVERSIBLE
valid_transformations.conditions: NaOH (aqueous, 1–2 mol/L); reflux (80–100°C); BAc2 mechanism (base, acyl, bimolecular). Mechanism: OH⁻ attacks ester C=O → tetrahedral intermediate → breakdown → carboxylate + R'OH. Irreversible (carboxylate is resonance-stabilised, does not re-esterify under basic conditions). Used for soap manufacture (triglyceride + NaOH → soap + glycerol). ¹⁸O in NaOH ends up in carboxylate product (acyl-O cleavage).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: R > 12C → fat = oil, product = soap; reaction = saponification
valid_transformations.conditions: Conc NaOH (aq, excess, 30–40%); heat (80–100°C) or steam pressure; saponification (BAc2). Triglyceride + 3 NaOH → 3 RCOONa (soap) + glycerol. Salting out: add NaCl to precipitate soap (less soluble). Hard soap (NaOH) vs soft soap (KOH). Industrial: also enzymatic saponification. Product: long-chain carboxylate Na salt (soap) + glycerol.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'II'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.conditions: Cold (0–5°C), dilute KMnO₄ (Baeyer's reagent, alkaline, ~1%); aqueous NaOH or neutral; syn addition. Mechanism: K₂MnO₄ cyclic ester intermediate (like osmate ester) → syn delivery of two OH. Permanganate decolorised (violet → colourless) = positive Baeyer's test for unsaturation. Gives syn diol. Hot KMnO₄ → oxidative cleavage.
valid_transformations.notes: Stereochemistry: syn-diol from OsO₄ or cold KMnO₄; anti-diol from epoxide then H₂O/base. Specify workup conditions explicitly in answers.

valid_transformations.conditions: OsO₄ (cat. or stoichiometric); NMO (N-methylmorpholine-N-oxide) as cooxidant (Upjohn); aqueous acetone or t-BuOH/H₂O; RT. Cyclic osmate ester → syn addition. NaHSO₃ (aqueous, stoichiometric OsO₄) → workup → syn diol. Highly stereospecific (both OH syn). More reliable than cold KMnO₄ for complex substrates.
valid_transformations.notes: Stereochemistry: syn-diol from OsO₄ or cold KMnO₄; anti-diol from epoxide then H₂O/base. Specify workup conditions explicitly in answers.

valid_transformations.note: Anti diol via epoxide; compare syn from KMnO₄/OsO₄
valid_transformations.conditions: Step 1: mCPBA (or peracetic acid, CH₂Cl₂, RT) → epoxide. Step 2: H₃O⁺ (dil H₂SO₄, RT) or NaOH(aq, RT) → trans-diaxial opening (SN2, anti) → anti diol. Two-step process required for anti diol. Contrast: KMnO₄/OsO₄ → syn. Acid opening of epoxide: more substituted C attacked; base opening: less hindered C.
valid_transformations.notes: Stereochemical outcome critical: syn addition (mCPBA), then ring-opening gives anti-addition overall. Track face selectivity carefully.

valid_transformations.note: Industrial route; Ag catalyst gives epoxide, then ring-opening
valid_transformations.conditions: Step 1: Ag catalyst, O₂ (air), 200–300°C, 10–20 atm → ethylene oxide (industrial). Step 2: H₂O/H⁺ (dilute H₂SO₄, 60°C) or H₂O/base → ethylene glycol. Industrial production of ethylene glycol (antifreeze). Also: Cl₂ + H₂O → chlorohydrin → Ca(OH)₂ → ethylene oxide → glycol.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.conditions: Cu catalyst; 300°C; air/O₂; catalytic oxidative dehydrogenation. HOCH₂CH₂OH → OHC-CHO (glyoxal) + 2H₂O. Industrial. Alternatively: KMnO₄ (mild, partial oxidation stops at aldehyde before carboxylic acid if carefully controlled). Also: HIO₄ cleaves 1,2-diols → 2 HCHO (not glyoxal, since vicinal diol cleaved).
valid_transformations.notes: Stereochemistry: syn-diol from OsO₄ or cold KMnO₄; anti-diol from epoxide then H₂O/base. Specify workup conditions explicitly in answers.

valid_transformations.conditions: KMnO₄ (hot, acidic, excess); reflux. Hot acidic KMnO₄ cleaves vicinal diol → 2 HCOOH (formic acid from primary OH → HCOOH by overoxidation). Contrast: periodic acid (HIO₄) also cleaves 1,2-diols to aldehydes/ketones/HCHO (milder, no overoxidation). KMnO₄ overoxidises HCHO → HCOOH → CO₂ at extreme conditions.
valid_transformations.notes: Stereochemistry: syn-diol from OsO₄ or cold KMnO₄; anti-diol from epoxide then H₂O/base. Specify workup conditions explicitly in answers.

valid_transformations.conditions: Conc HNO₃ (oxidising acid); heat; vigorous conditions. HNO₃ oxidises ethylene glycol completely → oxalic acid (ethanedioic acid, HOOC-COOH). HNO₃ is strong oxidant in this context. Compare: glycerol + conc HNO₃/H₂SO₄ → nitroglycerin (esterification, not oxidation — different reaction).
valid_transformations.notes: Stereochemistry: syn-diol from OsO₄ or cold KMnO₄; anti-diol from epoxide then H₂O/base. Specify workup conditions explicitly in answers.

valid_transformations.note: Unusual: diol dehydration gives aldehyde via unstable enol intermediate
valid_transformations.conditions: Conc H₃PO₄; Δ (200–300°C); dehydration. HOCH₂CH₂OH → H₂C=CHOH (vinyl alcohol, enol) + H₂O → tautomerism → CH₃CHO (acetaldehyde). High-temperature dehydration; acid-catalysed. Enol formed first (thermodynamically unfavourable) → rapid keto-enol tautomerism → acetaldehyde.
valid_transformations.notes: Stereochemistry: syn-diol from OsO₄ or cold KMnO₄; anti-diol from epoxide then H₂O/base. Specify workup conditions explicitly in answers.

valid_transformations.conditions: Step 1: PI₃ (phosphorus triiodide): PhOH + P/I₂ in situ → PI₃ → SN2 on primary OH → ICH₂CH₂I. Step 2: Zn + EtOH (or Mg/dry ether) → dehalogenation (loss of I₂) → CH₂=CH₂. Net: diol → diiodo → alkene. This is a roundabout route; more direct: glycol → acid dehydration.
valid_transformations.notes: Stereochemistry: syn-diol from OsO₄ or cold KMnO₄; anti-diol from epoxide then H₂O/base. Specify workup conditions explicitly in answers.

valid_transformations.conditions: Step 1: LiAlH₄ (dry ether, 0°C, anhydrous) → allyl alcohol (selective 1,2-reduction of C=O; LiAlH₄ does not reduce C=C without catalyst). Step 2: Cold KMnO₄ (dil, alkaline) or OsO₄/NMO → syn dihydroxylation of C=C → glycerol (1,2,3-propanetriol). Two-step synthesis of glycerol from acrolein.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

reagents: ① Cl₂/500°C (allylic radical substitution) → allyl chloride
valid_transformations.conditions: Step 1: Cl₂/500°C (allylic radical chlorination, high-temp gas phase; selectivity: allylic C-H over vinylic, 600:1 at 500°C) → allyl chloride. Step 2: Aq NaOH (SN2) → allyl alcohol. Step 3: KMnO₄/OH⁻ (cold, dilute) → glycerol. Industrial route to glycerol from propene via allyl chloride.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Classic test: glycerol + KHSO₄ → acrolein detected by smell; 1,2-diol portion dehydrates first
valid_transformations.conditions: KHSO₄ or conc H₂SO₄; Δ (strong heat, >200°C); double dehydration (loss of 2 H₂O). Step 1: dehydration at C-2 → enol → propenediol intermediate. Step 2: 2nd dehydration → acrolein (CH₂=CH-CHO, prop-2-enal). Pungent, lachrymatory aldehyde. Characteristic smell of burning fat (triglyceride pyrolysis → glycerol → acrolein).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: All 3 OH → ONO₂; explosive; called Nobel's oil or Black oil
valid_transformations.conditions: Conc HNO₃ + conc H₂SO₄ (mixed acid, 1:2 ratio by vol); 0°C (CRITICAL — below 5°C, above → explosive decomposition); O-nitration of all 3 OH groups → glyceryl trinitrate (nitroglycerin). H₂SO₄ acts as dehydrant/proton source for NO₂⁺ generation. Temperature strictly <5°C. Product: oily liquid, highly sensitive to shock and heat. Alfred Nobel stabilised with kieselguhr → dynamite.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'II'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.conditions: Red phosphorus + excess HI; heat (Δ, reflux); exhaustive dehalogenation. Step 1: HI (or PI₃) replaces OH → 1,2,3-triiodopropane. Step 2: excess HI → reduces C-I bonds → propane. Proof of glycerol structure (historically). HI: red P + I₂ → PI₃ → SN2 on primary OH. Complete reduction.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: 1° OHs (positions 1,3) esterified selectively over 2° OH (position 2)
valid_transformations.conditions: Acetic acid (2 equiv) or Ac₂O (2 equiv carefully); RT to 60°C; no special catalyst. 1° OH groups (C-1, C-3) are less hindered than 2° OH (C-2) → preferential esterification at positions 1 and 3. Selective under mild conditions. Can also use enzymatic acylation for strict regioselectivity.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.conditions: PI₃ (excess, from P + I₂); heat; SN2 on primary OH. Glycerol + PI₃ → 1,2,3-triiodopropane → elimination (HI + alkali or Zn) → allyl iodide (or propene with excess HI). Phosphorus halides substitute OH with I via phosphite ester intermediate → SN2. Primary OH reacts faster than secondary.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Two products: pyrazoline (N₂ heterocycle) and cyclopropane (via N₂ loss)
valid_transformations.conditions: UV light (hν); or room temperature; CH₂N₂ (diazomethane, gas); [3+2] (1,3-dipolar) cycloaddition. Step 1: CH₂N₂ (1,3-dipole) + alkene → Δ²-pyrazoline (4,5-dihydropyrazole). Step 2: hν or Δ → N₂ evolution → cyclopropane. For alkyne: [3+2] → pyrazole (aromatic, 6π-electron, major product). Diazomethane is explosive above 0°C in concentrated form; handle in ether at RT.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Aromatic pyrazole is major product due to 6π aromaticity; non-aromatic isomer minor
valid_transformations.conditions: RT; ether or hexane solvent; CH₂N₂ (diazomethane). [3+2] cycloaddition of CH₂N₂ to triple bond → Δ²-pyrazoline intermediate → aromatic pyrazole (6π, tautomers 1H-pyrazole and 2H-pyrazole). More stable aromatic product (pyrazole) is overwhelmingly major vs cyclopropene from cycloaddition. Pyrazole is aromatic (follows Hückel 4n+2 with n=1).
valid_transformations.notes: EAS: product regiochemistry determined by existing substituent(s). Check for conflicting or cooperating directors before assigning major product.

valid_transformations.note: 1°: red → colorless (oxidized to aldehyde); 2°: stays red (ketone)
valid_transformations.conditions: CAN test: (NH₄)₂[Ce(NO₃)₆] in 2N HNO₃; RT; aqueous. Ce⁴⁺ (yellow-orange) + alcohol → intense RED complex. 1° and 2° alcohols → RED. 3° alcohol → some sources say red-brown or immediate orange — less clear result. Phenols: NEGATIVE (Ce⁴⁺ oxidises phenol → quinone, no stable complex forms). Ethers: NEGATIVE. Distinguishes: 1°/2° ROH from 3° ROH and PhOH.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['III', 'IV'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.conditions: Victor Meyer test step by step: (1) P + I₂ → alkyl iodide; (2) AgNO₂ (silver nitrite, SN2) → 1° nitroalkane R-CH₂-NO₂; (3) HNO₂ (NaNO₂ + HCl, 0°C) → nitrolic acid R-C(=NOOH)=NOH (aci-form, from primary nitro with 2 α-H); (4) NaOH → red solution (nitrolic acid sodium salt soluble, bright RED). Mnemonic: 1°=Red, 2°=Blue, 3°=Colourless (RBC).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.conditions: Victor Meyer: (1) P + I₂ → 2° alkyl iodide; (2) AgNO₂ → 2° nitroalkane R₂CH-NO₂ (one α-H); (3) HNO₂ → pseudonitrole R₂C(NO)(NO₂) (blue oily liquid, from 2° nitro with 1 α-H); (4) NaOH → INSOLUBLE (blue oil remains, pseudonitrole insoluble in NaOH). 2°=Blue/insoluble. 3°: no α-H → no reaction with HNO₂ → COLOURLESS unchanged.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Markovnikov addition; X goes to more substituted carbon
valid_transformations.conditions: RT or 0°C; neat or polar aprotic solvent; HX (HCl, HBr, HI) ionic addition. Step 1: H⁺ adds to less-substituted C (Markovnikov) → carbocation. Step 2: X⁻ attacks. Reactivity: HI > HBr > HCl. Rearrangements possible for certain skeletons. For iodination (HI): often cleanest Markovnikov; anti-Markovnikov: HBr + peroxides.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: NBS = N-bromosuccinimide; radical allylic bromination; no ionic addition
valid_transformations.conditions: Radical allylic bromination: NBS (N-bromosuccinimide), hν or AIBN initiator; CCl₄ solvent; reflux or heat. Mechanism: Br• abstracts allylic H (weakest C-H due to radical stabilisation) → resonance-stabilised allylic radical → Br₂ (from NBS) → allylic bromide. Wohl-Ziegler reaction (NBS). Selectivity: allylic position only (not vinylic). Succinimide radical regenerated.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Kharasch effect; ROOR reverses regioselectivity; Br goes to less-substituted C
valid_transformations.conditions: Radical addition: HBr + peroxide (ROOR) or hν; non-polar solvent; RT. Peroxide → RO• → abstracts H from HBr → Br•; Br• adds to less-substituted C (anti-Markovnikov, avoids steric at Br; secondary radical intermediate more stable) → C-radical → abstracts H from HBr → anti-Markovnikov product. ONLY HBr (not HCl or HI) gives anti-Markovnikov radical addition.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Markovnikov; X on more substituted vinyl carbon
valid_transformations.conditions: Electrophilic addition (ionic): HX (1 equiv); RT; polar aprotic or neat. Markovnikov addition: H adds to terminal C → vinyl halide with halide at internal C. Mechanism: H⁺ adds to terminal C → vinyl cation (or π-complex) → X⁻ attacks. Rate: HI > HBr > HCl. For Markovnikov vinyl halide from terminal alkyne.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Two additions of HX; both X end up on same carbon
valid_transformations.conditions: Excess HX (2 equiv); RT to reflux; ionic electrophilic addition (two-step). Step 1: 1 equiv HX → vinyl halide (Markovnikov). Step 2: 2nd HX adds to C=C of vinyl halide (Markovnikov again → X at same C) → geminal dihalide (1,1-dihalide). Two Markovnikov additions give gem-dihalide. Alternative: X₂ excess → 1,1,2,2-tetrahaloalkane.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Inversion of configuration; SOCL2 without pyridine gives retention; PCl3 gives retention
valid_transformations.conditions: PCl₅ (phosphorus pentachloride); anhydrous; RT or mild heat; no solvent or dry CCl₄. Mechanism: ROH + PCl₅ → R-O-PCl₄ (chlorophosphorane intermediate) → SN2 by Cl⁻ on C → R-Cl + POCl₃ (phosphoryl chloride) + HCl. Inversion of configuration (SN2 mechanism). Primary and secondary alcohols react well; tertiary can give E2.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Retention via chlorosulfite intermediate (SNi-like pathway)
valid_transformations.conditions: PCl₃ (phosphorus trichloride); anhydrous; 0°C to RT. Mechanism: ROH + PCl₃ → R-O-PCl₂ → then intramolecular delivery of Cl from same face → R-Cl + H₃PO₃ (phosphorous acid). Retention of configuration (front-side intramolecular delivery). Less commonly used; PCl₅ preferred for primary. Useful when stereochemical retention required.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: SNi mechanism: intramolecular Cl delivery from chlorosulfite → retention
valid_transformations.conditions: SOCl₂ (thionyl chloride) WITHOUT pyridine; anhydrous; RT. SNi mechanism (substitution nucleophilic internal): ROH + SOCl₂ → R-O-SO-Cl (chlorosulphite ester) → front-side intramolecular delivery of Cl (concerted Sni, [4-membered TS] or [6-membered TS via ion pair]) → R-Cl + SO₂ + HCl. Retention of configuration. Compare: SOCl₂ + pyridine → SN2 → inversion.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Pyridine deprotonates the chlorosulfite; external Cl⁻ now attacks → SN2 → inversion
valid_transformations.conditions: SOCl₂ + pyridine; anhydrous; RT. Pyridine: (1) neutralises HCl; (2) forms acylpyridinium chloride → Cl⁻ attacks C backside (intermolecular SN2) → inversion. Without pyridine: SNi (retention). With pyridine: SN2 (inversion). Both routes give R-Cl from R-OH but with opposite stereochemistry.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Phenol + PCl5 gives poor yield of ArCl; ArOH resonance makes O less nucleophilic
valid_transformations.conditions: PCl₅; anhydrous; RT to mild heat. PhOH + PCl₅ → PhCl + POCl₃ + HCl (slow, poor yield). Aryl C-O bond has partial double bond character (resonance donation of O lone pair to ring) → harder to cleave than aliphatic C-OH. Chlorobenzene (ArCl) better made via Balz-Schiemann (ArN₂⁺BF₄⁻ → ArF) or Sandmeyer (ArN₂⁺ + CuCl → ArCl). PCl₅ on phenol is mostly a mechanistic curiosity.
valid_transformations.notes: EAS: product regiochemistry determined by existing substituent(s). Check for conflicting or cooperating directors before assigning major product.

valid_transformations.note: Two products: R-Cl via SN2 at smaller alkyl (inversion) + R'-Cl at larger (retention/SN1)
valid_transformations.conditions: PCl₅; anhydrous; RT to gentle heat. R-O-R' + PCl₅ → R-Cl + R'-Cl + POCl₃. Both C-O bonds cleaved. Contrast: HI cleavage of ethers (one C-O at a time, gives R-OH then R-I with excess HI). PCl₅ gives both halides directly. Less selective; used mainly for specific halide syntheses.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Two pathways: acyl path (acylium intermediate → RCOC1) + alkyl path (SN2/SN1 at R' → R'Cl)
valid_transformations.conditions: PCl₅; anhydrous; RT to mild heat. RCOOR' + PCl₅ → RCOCl (acyl chloride) + R'Cl + POCl₃. Both O-C bonds cleaved: acyl-O gives RCOCl, alkyl-O gives R'Cl. Useful for converting esters to acyl chlorides without going through the free acid. Clean for primary R'.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Ring-opening; anti addition; trans-dihalide from trans-epoxide
valid_transformations.conditions: HX (1 equiv); aqueous or anhydrous; acid opens epoxide at more substituted C (Markovnikov for SN1-like) → anti addition of H and X. Alternatively: X₂ opens epoxide via halonium. Product: trans (anti) vicinal dihalide from cyclic epoxide. Compare: diol from H₂O opening, amino alcohol from amine opening.
valid_transformations.notes: Stereochemical outcome critical: syn addition (mCPBA), then ring-opening gives anti-addition overall. Track face selectivity carefully.

valid_transformations.note: C=O converted to gem-dihalide (CX2); SF4 gives gem-difluoride specifically
valid_transformations.conditions: PCl₅; anhydrous; RT to gentle heat. R-CHO + PCl₅ → R-CHCl₂ (geminal dichloride) + POCl₃. R-CO-R' + PCl₅ → R-CCl₂-R' + POCl₃. Converts C=O to CCl₂. Product: geminal dihalide. Used to make gem-dihalides; reverse: gem-dihalide + base → alkyne or ketone (via dichlorocarbene or direct).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Borodine-Hunsdiecker: radical mechanism, -CO2; rate 1° > 2° > 3° (opposite carbocation!)
valid_transformations.conditions: Hunsdiecker reaction: Step 1: RCOOH + AgOH (or Ag₂O) → RCOOAg (silver carboxylate). Step 2: RCOOAg + Br₂/CCl₄ → R-Br + CO₂ + AgBr. Reflux; anhydrous CCl₄; dark. Mechanism: radical. One fewer C than acid (decarboxylation). Iodide: 1:1 Ag salt:I₂ → R-I. Ester: 2:1 Ag salt:I₂ → R-OOC-R (ester). Kochi: Cu²⁺ variation.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

reagents: I2/heat (1:1 molar ratio Ag salt : I2)
valid_transformations.note: Birnbaum-Simonini: 1:1 ratio → R-I major
valid_transformations.conditions: Hunsdiecker (Iodide variant): RCOOAg + I₂ (1:1 molar); anhydrous CCl₄; reflux; dark (light-sensitive). Mechanism: radical chain. AgI precipitates (insoluble) → drives equilibrium. Product: R-I (1 fewer C, decarboxylation). Primary carboxylates give primary iodides.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

reagents: I2/heat (2:1 molar ratio Ag salt : I2, excess Ag)
valid_transformations.note: Birnbaum-Simonini trap: EXCESS Ag salt (2 mol per mol I2) → ESTER major, not R-I
valid_transformations.conditions: Hunsdiecker (Ester variant): 2 RCOOAg + I₂ (2:1 molar); anhydrous CCl₄; reflux. The second equivalent of Ag salt captures the carboxyl radical/cation → ester R-OOC-R (symmetric ester). Mechanism: first Ag salt reacts with I₂ → acyloxy radical → loses CO₂ → alkyl radical → reacts with 2nd Ag salt instead of I₂ → ester. Ratio of Ag salt:I₂ = 2:1 → ester; 1:1 → alkyl iodide.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Finkelstein: NaI soluble in acetone; NaCl/NaBr insoluble → precipitate drives equilibrium; SN2→inversion
valid_transformations.conditions: Finkelstein reaction: NaI; dry acetone; reflux. NaCl or NaBr (products) insoluble in acetone → precipitate → drives equilibrium toward R-I. SN2 mechanism (inversion). Primary > secondary >> tertiary. Must use DRY acetone (NaI slightly soluble in wet acetone → equilibrium not driven). Used to convert chlorides/bromides to more reactive iodides for subsequent reactions.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

reagents: AgF or Hg2F2 or CaF2 or CoF3 or SbF3 / heat
valid_transformations.note: Swart reaction: best method for R-F; SN2, gives inversion of configuration
valid_transformations.conditions: Halide exchange with fluoride source: AgF, Hg₂F₂, CaF₂ (industrial) or SbF₃ (antimony trifluoride, Swarts reaction); heat (Δ). Swarts reaction: RCCl₃ + SbF₃ → RCCF₃ (trifluoromethyl). AgF: SN2 on primary. SbF₃/SbCl₅: industrial halogen exchange. Ionic: F⁻ poor nucleophile in polar protic; use dry polar aprotic + F⁻ source (KF/18-crown-6, or CsF in DMF).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Best method for CHCl3; products: CHCl3 + HCOONa (sodium formate)
valid_transformations.conditions: NaOH (aq, 10%); RT or gentle warm (50°C). Chloral (trichloroacetaldehyde, CCl₃CHO) + NaOH → CHCl₃ + HCOONa. Mechanism: OH⁻ adds to C=O of chloral → CCl₃-CH(OH)(O⁻) → CCl₃⁻ carbanion departs (stable because 3 Cl stabilise carbanion by induction) → CHCl₃ + formate (HCOONa). This is the basis of the haloform reaction: any methyl ketone or CH₃CHO gives haloform; chloral gives it with NaOH + water alone (no halogen needed, already fully chlorinated).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

reagents: Cl2/hv (progressive chlorination of CH4), or 2[H] (reductive path)
valid_transformations.note: Progressive chlorination: CH4 → CH3Cl → CH2Cl2 → CHCl3 → CCl4 with increasing Cl2/hv
valid_transformations.conditions: Progressive chlorination of CH₄: Cl₂/hν, stepwise radical chlorination CH₄→CH₃Cl→CH₂Cl₂→CHCl₃→CCl₄ — stopping at CHCl₃ stage by controlling Cl₂:CH₄ ratio. OR: 2[H] reductive path: CCl₄ + Fe/H₂O → CHCl₃ + HCl. Industrial: chlorination of methane at 400°C with excess methane → CHCl₃. Lab: reductive methods (Zn/EtOH or H₂/Pd for CCl₄→CHCl₃).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Why CHCl3 stored in dark bottles filled to brim; phosgene 'extremely poisonous'
valid_transformations.conditions: O₂ + hν (sunlight/air); slow oxidation. CHCl₃ in air and light → CCl₂ (dichlorocarbene) → O₂ → COCl₂ (phosgene) + HCl. HAZARD: phosgene is highly toxic (WWI chemical weapon). This is why chloroform must be stored in dark bottles with stabiliser (ethanol, 1%) to prevent phosgene formation. Industrial phosgene: CO + Cl₂/activated C → COCl₂.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: 1% EtOH added to CHCl3 storage: phosgene scavenged → harmless diethyl carbonate
valid_transformations.conditions: 2 EtOH + COCl₂ → EtOCOOEt + 2 HCl; base (Et₃N or pyridine) to neutralise HCl; anhydrous; RT. Phosgene reacts with two alcohols sequentially → diethyl carbonate (carbonate ester). Highly toxic — handle in fume hood. Alternatively use dimethyl carbonate (DMC) as safer phosgene equivalent.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: CCl3⁻ carbanion adds to acetone C=O; product Chloretone = sleep-inducing drug
valid_transformations.conditions: Acetone + NaOH (base); RT; CCl₃⁻ (carbanion from CHCl₃/base) adds to acetone C=O → CCl₃-C(CH₃)₂-O⁻ → protonation → chloretone (2,2,2-trichloro-1,1-dimethylethanol). Mechanism: CHCl₃ + NaOH → :CCl₂ (dichlorocarbene) → hydration? Or CHCl₃ → CCl₃⁻ (carbanion) → nucleophilic addition to acetone. Product: sedative/hypnotic.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: CCl3⁻ + NO2⁺ → CCl3NO2; chloropicrin = insecticide + war gas
valid_transformations.conditions: CHCl₃ + conc HNO₃; heat. HNO₃ oxidises CHCl₃ → CCl₃NO₂ (trichloronitromethane, chloropicrin). Lachrymatory, used as pesticide. Mechanism: electrophilic nitration of C-H followed by oxidation, or direct reaction with N₂O₅/NO₂. Also: CCl₃CHO + conc HNO₃ → CCl₃NO₂ + CO₂ + H₂O.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Hydrolysis under forcing basic conditions; CHCl3 → CCl3⁻ → H-C(OH)3 (orthoformate) → HCOONa
valid_transformations.conditions: NaOH (aqueous, excess); reflux. CHCl₃ + 4 NaOH → HCOONa + 3 NaCl + 2 H₂O. Mechanism: NaOH converts CHCl₃ → :CCl₂ (carbene) → OH⁻ adds → Cl₂CH-OH → base → Cl₂C=O (dichlorocarbonyl) → OH⁻ → Cl-CO₂H → decarboxylation → formate? Actually: multiple OH⁻ substitutions of Cl → C(OH)₄ → H-COOH → HCOONa.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: CHCl3 + 3 NaOEt → HC(OEt)3 + 3 NaCl; triethyl orthoformate
valid_transformations.conditions: NaOEt (sodium ethoxide); heat (reflux in EtOH). CHCl₃ + 3 NaOEt → HC(OEt)₃ (triethyl orthoformate) + 3 NaCl. Mechanism: NaOEt displaces Cl (SN2) three times on CHCl₃ → HC(OEt)₃. Anhydrous conditions. Orthoformate used as formyl-equivalent, protecting group, and in synthesis.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Radical chlorination of CHCl3 replaces the remaining H
valid_transformations.conditions: Cl₂/hν; RT. CHCl₃ + Cl₂ → CCl₄ + HCl. Radical chain halogenation. Full chlorination of CHCl₃. Industrial: direct chlorination of methane or chloroethylene. Can also be made by CS₂ + 3Cl₂ → CCl₄ + S₂Cl₂.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Haloform reaction (alkaline): rate γ1<γ2<γ3; RDS is C-H breaking (proved by KIE: R-CO-CD3 slower)
valid_transformations.conditions: Haloform reaction: X₂ (Cl₂, Br₂, or I₂) + NaOH (aq, excess); RT to mild heat. Step 1: base deprotonates α-H → enolate → halogenation → repeat ×3 → CX₃ group on methyl. Step 2: NaOH attacks CX₃-CO-R → CX₃⁻ + RCOO⁻ (tetrahedral intermediate → collapse). CX₃⁻ → CHX₃ (haloform). Positive haloform test (yellow CHI₃ precipitate with I₂/NaOH): methyl ketone, acetaldehyde, ethanol, secondary methyl alcohol (CH₃CHOH-R).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Haloform in acidic medium: rate γ1>>γ2>>γ3; STOPS at mono-halogenation; enol mechanism
valid_transformations.conditions: X₂ + sodium acetate (CH₃COONa) buffer; acidic conditions (AcOH); RT. Mono-halogenation stops at monosubstitution under acidic catalysis (unlike base: base-catalysed → trihalomethyl). Mechanism: enol formation (acid-catalysed tautomerism) → halogen attacks enol → mono-halo ketone + HX (neutralised by NaOAc). Product: single α-halo ketone.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: α-C already has Cl; iodination gives CHClI2 not CHI3 — JEE trap (mixed trihalomethane)
valid_transformations.conditions: I₂ + NaOH (excess); RT. Haloform on chloroacetone: the CH₂Cl group is alpha → iodination → CI₂ group → NaOH → carbanion CI₃⁻? More likely: NaOH acts on CH₃CO- group → iodoform pathway on methyl → CHI₂Cl (mixed haloform) + acetate. Or: iodination of alpha-Cl carbon too, giving CHClI₂ as mixed haloform + acetate.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['II', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Haloform on α-keto acid: CI3-CO-COOH → CI3⁻ + ⁻OOCCOO⁻ (oxalate) + CHI3
valid_transformations.conditions: I₂ + NaOH (aq); RT. Pyruvic acid (CH₃COCOOH) contains CH₃CO- group → haloform test positive. NaOH deprotonates COOH → carboxylate; then iodination of CH₃ group → CI₃ group → collapse → CHI₃ (iodoform, yellow precipitate) + COO⁻-COO⁻ (oxalate). Positive iodoform test confirms methyl ketone/acetaldehyde functionality.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Ring ketone: triiodination at α-C then ring-opening by OH⁻ → CHI3 + -(CH2)4-(COO⁻)2 (adipate)
valid_transformations.conditions: I₂ + NaOH (aq, excess); RT. Cyclohexanone: does NOT have CH₃CO- directly → NaOH opens ring? No: cyclohexanone oxidised by NaOI → 6-iodohexan-2-one chain? Actually: NaOI (in situ from I₂/NaOH) oxidises cyclohexanone → ring-opened dicarboxylic acid (adipic acid monosodium salt) + iodoform. The mechanism involves oxidative ring opening by iodine/base.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['II', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Both CH3 and benzylic CH2 get triiodinated → two independent haloform cleavages → 2 CHI3
valid_transformations.conditions: I₂ + NaOH (excess); RT. Both terminal groups (PhCH₂- and CH₃CO-) participate: (1) PhCH₂CO- → PhCOO⁻ + CHI₃; and (2) remaining fragment → CHI₃ + acetate? Wait: PhCH₂-CO-CH₃ has only one CH₃CO- group. The CH₂ group adjacent to phenyl is benzylic — NaOH/I₂ gives oxidative cleavage? Actually: 2 mol CHI₃ because both CH₃CO and PhCH₂CO can undergo haloform (PhCH₂CO- → PhCHI₂ → CHI₃ after further degradation + benzoate).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['II', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.note: Diol oxidized to diacetyl (CH3COCOCH3) → haloform on both methyl ketones → 2 CHI3
valid_transformations.conditions: I₂ + NaOH (excess, aq); RT. 2,3-Butanediol: each CHOH is secondary; NaOI oxidises each CHOH → CO group → CH₃COCH₃ (acetone) fragments or pinacol→pinacolone-like? Actually: 2,3-BDO → oxidation to 2,3-butanedione (diacetyl) under I₂/NaOH → each CH₃CO undergoes haloform → 2 CHI₃ + oxalate (C₂O₄²⁻ from the two carbons).
valid_transformations.notes: Stereochemistry: syn-diol from OsO₄ or cold KMnO₄; anti-diol from epoxide then H₂O/base. Specify workup conditions explicitly in answers.

valid_transformations.note: Oxidized to phenylglyoxal (PhCOCHO); CHO carbon has 1H → triiodinated → PhCOO⁻ + CHI3
valid_transformations.conditions: I₂ + NaOH (excess); RT. PhCH(OH)CH₂OH → PhCHO-CH₂OH via oxidation? The PhCHOH is secondary → NaOI → PhCO-CHO (phenylglyoxal) → haloform on PhCO-CH= ? Alternatively: NaOH/I₂ oxidises CH₂OH → then the adjacent PhCHOH → PhCO → iodoform from CH₃ group? The product benzoate + CHI₃ means: PhCO-CHI₃ intermediate → PhCOO⁻ + CHI₃.
valid_transformations.notes: Stereochemistry: syn-diol from OsO₄ or cold KMnO₄; anti-diol from epoxide then H₂O/base. Specify workup conditions explicitly in answers.

valid_transformations.note: Ester itself is -ve haloform; but OH⁻ saponifies to give EtOH → EtOH gives iodoform (2-step)
valid_transformations.conditions: I₂ + NaOH (aq, excess); reflux. First: saponification of ethyl acetate (NaOH, reflux) → ethanol + acetate. Then: ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) undergoes iodoform test positive (CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃CHO → CH₃CO- → CHI₃ + formate) — or NaOI oxidises EtOH → acetaldehyde → CH₃CO- → CHI₃. Net: ethyl acetate → acetate (from saponification) + iodoform (from ethanol fragment).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['II', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.conditions: resonance delocalization
valid_transformations.mechanism: C=O lone pair delocalizes into ring giving 6pi-electron tropylium-like cation
valid_transformations.notes: Tropone is aromatic; C=O stabilized by resonance into the 7-membered ring

valid_transformations.conditions: double deprotonation, base
valid_transformations.mechanism: Loss of 2 protons gives 4-membered ring dianion with 2pi electrons (n=0, Huckel); aromatic
valid_transformations.notes: Squarate dianion is a rare 2pi aromatic species in a 4-membered ring

valid_transformations.conditions: base removes acidic sp3 H; 1/2 H2 evolved
valid_transformations.notes: Na deprotonates cyclopentadiene; Cp- is 6pi aromatic

valid_transformations.conditions: reduction adds 2 electrons
valid_transformations.notes: Antiaromatic -> aromatic by 2e- reduction; sigma_BMO->pi*ABMO

valid_transformations.conditions: reduction adds 2 electrons
valid_transformations.notes: COT + 2K -> COT2- 10pi aromatic + 2K+; classic JEE reaction

valid_transformations.conditions: no reagent; spontaneous if 2-degree more stable; concerted via bridged T.S.
valid_transformations.notes: H migrates as H- (hydride) with its electron pair; 3-center 2-electron bridged T.S.; driving force = more stable C+

valid_transformations.to: tertiary carbocation (3 degree) via 1,2-hydride or 1,2-methyl shift
valid_transformations.conditions: spontaneous; 1,2-H- shift or 1,2-CH3- shift; driving force = stability increase
valid_transformations.notes: 1,2-methyl shift: CH3 migrates as carbanion-like (with electron pair); analogous to H- shift; same bridged T.S. concept

valid_transformations.from: cyclopropylcarbinyl cation (C+ adjacent to cyclopropane ring)
valid_transformations.conditions: sigma resonance (dancing resonance); Walsh orbital donation; equilibrium
valid_transformations.notes: Cyclopropane Walsh orbitals (high p-character) overlap with empty C+ p orbital; more stable than allyl cation; B.B. notation = bisected bicyclopropylcarbinyl

valid_transformations.conditions: spontaneous; 1,2-methyl shift (CH3 migrates with electron pair); huge stability increase 1° → 3°
valid_transformations.notes: Classic neopentyl rearrangement; methyl migrates as carbanion-like (with e- pair); concerted bridged T.S.

valid_transformations.to: 1-methyl-1-phenylpropan-2-ylium (CH3)2C+-CH2Ph (3 degree) via 1,2-phenyl shift through phenonium ion
valid_transformations.conditions: Ph pi electrons donate into C+; forms bridged phenonium ion (spiro cyclopropane-benzene); then ring opens
valid_transformations.notes: 1,2-Aryl shift; NOT concerted; goes through isolable phenonium ion intermediate; Ph migrates as pi donor

valid_transformations.from: exocyclic carbocation on cyclohexane ring system
valid_transformations.to: endocyclic carbocation (C+ moves into ring) via 1,2-H shift in ring system
valid_transformations.conditions: 1,2-H shift within or at junction of cyclic system; C+ enters more stable ring position
valid_transformations.notes: Ring rearrangements: exo→endo, or ring expansion/contraction via 1,2-methyl or 1,2-ethyl shift

valid_transformations.from: cyclobutylcarbinyl cation (cyclobutane ring with exocyclic C+)
valid_transformations.to: cyclopentyl cation (C+ inside 5-membered ring) via 1,2-bond shift ring expansion
valid_transformations.conditions: 1,2-bond shift: C-C sigma bond of cyclobutane ring migrates into exo C+; ring expands 4→5; driven by ring strain relief
valid_transformations.notes: Ring expansion: smaller ring C-C bond migrates into adjacent C+, ring grows by 1 carbon. 4→5 expansion very favorable (cyclopentane less strained than cyclobutane)

valid_transformations.from: cyclopentylcarbinyl cation (cyclopentane ring with exocyclic C+)
valid_transformations.to: cyclohexyl cation (C+ inside 6-membered ring) via 1,2-bond shift ring expansion
valid_transformations.conditions: 1,2-bond shift: cyclopentane C-C bond migrates into exo C+; ring expands 5→6; driven by formation of most stable (strain-free) 6-ring + more stable endo C+
valid_transformations.notes: Classic ring expansion to cyclohexane; 6-ring is most stable; 5→6 expansion very common in JEE

valid_transformations.to: cyclobutyl cation (C+ inside 4-ring) in equilibrium with allyl cation
valid_transformations.conditions: rapid equilibrium at room temperature; cyclopropylcarbinyl 48%, cyclobutyl 47%, allyl 5%; all in dynamic equilibrium via sigma resonance and ring opening/closure
valid_transformations.notes: Famous 3-way equilibrium: cyclopropylcarbinyl=48%, cyclobutyl=47%, allyl=5%. Cyclopropylcarbinyl chloride and cyclobutyl chloride give SAME solvolysis product mixture

valid_transformations.from: cycloheptyl carbocation (7-membered ring with exocyclic C+)
valid_transformations.to: cyclohexyl carbocation (6-membered ring, endocyclic C+) via 1,2-bond shift ring contraction
valid_transformations.conditions: ring contraction 7→6; 1,2-bond shift where one ring C-C bond migrates into adjacent exo C+; cyclohexane ring is thermodynamic sink
valid_transformations.notes: Ring contraction is the reverse of ring expansion; 7→6 driven by ring strain relief (cyclohexyl more stable than cycloheptyl)

valid_transformations.to: methyl radical CH3 dot + chlorine radical Cl dot
valid_transformations.conditions: homolytic bond cleavage; one electron to each fragment; free radical chain initiation
valid_transformations.notes: Homolytic cleavage: each fragment gets 1 electron. C-Cl BDE ~ 84 kcal/mol; requires UV light energy

valid_transformations.conditions: resonance stabilization by adjacent pi system (allyl, benzyl) or sp hybridization; NOT by hyperconjugation (XX does not apply)
valid_transformations.notes: Carbanion stability: benzyl > allyl > sp > sp2 > sp3; +M destabilizes; -M stabilizes

valid_transformations.from: carboxylic acid derivative (benzoic acid) with ortho substituent G
valid_transformations.conditions: ortho substituent G ≠ NH₂; any ortho group increases acidity via SIR effect (COOH twisted out of conjugation → conjugate base less stabilized by ring → A⁻ relatively more stable) or chelation (intramolecular H-bond forming 6-membered ring with COOH stabilizes A⁻)
valid_transformations.notes: Exception: G = NH₂ does NOT increase acidity. For NO₂: ortho >> para > meta. For CH₃: ortho > benzoic > meta > para. For OH: ortho > meta > benzoic > para.

valid_transformations.from: nitrene R-N: (singlet or triplet, 6e- on N, neutral electrophile)
valid_transformations.to: nitrene insertion product or rearrangement product
valid_transformations.conditions: Nitrene (R-N:) formed by loss of leaving group from R-NH₂ under harsh conditions; singlet nitrene inserts directly into C-H or adds to pi bonds (concerted); triplet behaves as biradical (stepwise); neutral electrophile like carbene
valid_transformations.notes: Nitrene: 6e- total around N, neutral, electrophile, octet incomplete; singlet/triplet same dichotomy as carbene

valid_transformations.from: dicarboxylic acid (oxalic, malonic, succinic, glutaric, adipic) — first ionization
valid_transformations.to: mono-carboxylate anion (first conjugate base); Ka1 order O > M > S > G > A
valid_transformations.conditions: Ka₁ decreases as chain length increases: oxalic (no CH₂) > malonic (1 CH₂) > succinic (2 CH₂) > glutaric (3 CH₂) > adipic (4 CH₂). Reason: the second -COOH acts as a -I EWG stabilizing A⁻; as distance increases, -I effect decreases. pKa₁ values: 1.27, 2.86, 4.21, 4.34, 4.41 respectively.
valid_transformations.notes: Ka₁ order is straightforward: more distant second COOH = less -I stabilization of first ionization product

valid_transformations.to: dicarboxylate dianion; Ka2 order O > G > A > S > M (malonic LEAST acidic second ionization)
valid_transformations.conditions: Ka₂ reversal: malonic acid (1 CH₂) has SMALLEST Ka₂ (pKa₂ = 5.70) due to 5-membered intramolecular chelate ring formed in the mono-anion (OOC-CH₂-COOH forms 5-ring H-bond, stabilizing monoanion → harder second ionization). Oxalic has largest Ka₂ (pKa₂ = 4.27). pKa₂ values: O=4.27, M=5.70, S=5.64, G=5.27, A=5.28. Ka₂ order: O > G > A > S > M.
valid_transformations.notes: Ka₂ order is NOT the same as Ka₁ order: malonic is LEAST acidic second ionization (not most), due to chelation

valid_transformations.conditions: Terminal alkynes (pKa=25) are acidic enough to react with Na metal. R-C≡CH + Na → R-C≡C⁻Na⁺ + ½H₂. Cyclopentadiene (pKa=16) also reacts with Na similarly.
valid_transformations.notes: Na reacts with any compound more acidic than R-NH₂ (pKa ~35); alkynes (25), phenols (10), alcohols (~16) all react. Aliphatic alkanes (pKa 43) do NOT react with Na.

valid_transformations.conditions: Phenol (pKa=10) is MORE ACIDIC than water (pKa=15.7) → PhOH + NaOH → PhONa + H₂O proceeds forward. NaOH reacts with phenols and more acidic compounds (R-COOH, R-SO₃H, picric acid, etc.).
valid_transformations.notes: NaOH does NOT deprotonate aliphatic alcohols (pKa 16-18 > H₂O pKa 15.7). Only phenols and stronger acids react with NaOH.

valid_transformations.conditions: Carboxylic acids (pKa ~1-5) are MORE ACIDIC than H₂CO₃ (pKa₁ = 6.35) → NaHCO₃ can deprotonate them → CO₂ effervescence is the visual test. CO₂ bubbles = RCOOH present. This distinguishes RCOOH from phenols (PhOH pKa=10 > H₂CO₃ pKa=6.35 → no reaction with NaHCO₃).
valid_transformations.notes: CO₂ gas evolution = diagnostic test for RCOOH. Sulfonic acids (R-SO₃H) also react. p-Nitrophenol (pKa≈7.2) does NOT react with NaHCO₃ even though it's more acidic than regular phenol.

valid_transformations.to: cyclopropylcarbinyl cation (cyclopropyl-CH₂⁺) + X⁻ [fastest ionization with AgNO₃]
valid_transformations.conditions: Cyclopropylcarbinyl cation is stabilized by homoaromatic interaction (Walsh orbital overlap between the cyclopropane ring and the empty p orbital on CH₂⁺) → 4 equivalent resonance-like structures → extremely stable carbocation → fastest AgNO₃ precipitation (SN1 ionization). Rate: cyclopropylcarbinyl-X > benzyl-X > secondary allylic-X > secondary-X.
valid_transformations.notes: AgNO₃ in EtOH tests ionization rate (SN1). Faster ionization = more stable carbocation formed. Cyclopropylcarbinyl cation is homoaromatic (2π electrons in a bicyclic system) → rate order 1>2>3>4 (cyclopropylcarbinyl > benzyl > 7-ring > open-chain 2°).

valid_transformations.conditions: Sulfonic acids (R-SO₃H, pKa ≈ -1 to 1) are much MORE ACIDIC than H₂CO₃ (pKa₁ = 6.35) → NaHCO₃ can deprotonate them → CO₂ gas evolved. R-SO₃H is even stronger acid than carboxylic acid (RCOOH, pKa ~1-5). Both sulfonic acids and carboxylic acids react with NaHCO₃ with CO₂ evolution.
valid_transformations.notes: NaHCO₃ reacts with: R-SO₃H (pKa~-1), picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol, pKa~0.4), squaric acid (pKa~1.5), 2,4-dinitrophenol (pKa~4.1), R-COOH (pKa~1-5). Does NOT react with: plain phenol (pKa=10), o-NO₂-phenol (pKa~7.2), p-NO₂-phenol (pKa~7.2).

valid_transformations.conditions: 0°C to room temperature, non-aqueous solvent (DCM)
valid_transformations.mechanism: nucleophilic attack of alcohol O on electrophilic S of MsCl → tetrahedral intermediate → Cl⁻ leaves → R-O-SO₂CH₃ (mesylate ester). Et₃N deprotonates the O-H. Stereochemistry at R is RETAINED (O-H bond broken, C-O bond intact). Mesylate ester is activated toward SN1/SN2 with OMs⁻ as excellent leaving group.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.conditions: -78°C to 0°C, anhydrous conditions
valid_transformations.mechanism: Alcohol O attacks electrophilic S of Tf₂O → forms triflate ester with retention at C. OTf⁻ is the BEST sulfonate leaving group (three F atoms: -I effect of CF₃ makes CF₃SO₃H the strongest sulfonic acid → conjugate base OTf⁻ is most stabilized → best LGA). Triflate esters are extremely reactive toward SN1/SN2.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.conditions: 0°C to room temperature
valid_transformations.mechanism: Tosylation: alcohol O attacks S of TsCl, Cl⁻ leaves. C-O bond at R is intact → stereochemistry RETAINED at R. OTs⁻ (4-methylbenzenesulfonate) is an excellent leaving group: LGA: OTf⁻ > ONs⁻ > OBs⁻ > OTs⁻ > OMs⁻. Tosylate ester is a synthetic equivalent of R-X for SN2 reactions with nucleophiles.
valid_transformations.notes: EAS: product regiochemistry determined by existing substituent(s). Check for conflicting or cooperating directors before assigning major product.

valid_transformations.to: R-Nu (substitution product via SN2 with nucleophile)
reagents: Nu⁻ (nucleophile: NaN₃, NaCN, NaI, NaSR, NaOR, LiAlH₄, etc.)
valid_transformations.conditions: polar aprotic solvent (DMSO, DMF, acetone) for SN2; rate: OTf > ONs > OBs > OTs > OMs
valid_transformations.mechanism: SN2 back-side attack of Nu⁻ on C bearing the sulfonate LG. Sulfonate LG ability: OTf⁻ >> OMs⁻ (no ring), OTs⁻ (p-CH₃, +I), OBs⁻ (p-Br, -I), ONs⁻ (p-NO₂, -I+-M). The -I/-M substituents on the arylsulfonate stabilize the sulfonate anion → weaker base → better LG. INVERSION of configuration at stereocenter (Walden inversion).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.conditions: 0-5°C (ice bath essential: aliphatic diazonium is unstable at higher temperature)
valid_transformations.mechanism: DIAZOTIZATION: (1) NaNO₂ + HCl → HNO₂ (nitrous acid, generated in situ) + NaCl. (2) HNO₂ + H⊕ → H₂O + NO⊕ (nitrosonium ion = electrophile). (3) R-NH₂ + NO⊕ → R-NH₂⊕-N=O → -H⊕ → R-NH-N=O (N-nitrosoamine). (4) Proton transfer → R-N=N-OH (diazoic acid) → R-N=N-OH + H⊕ → R-N=N-OH₂⊕ → -H₂O → R-N≡N⊕ (diazonium ion). IUPAC: alkyldiazonium salt. Unlike aryldiazonium (stable), aliphatic diazonium immediately loses N₂ at any temperature above ~0°C.
valid_transformations.notes: Temperature critical: 0–5°C for stable arenediazonium. Aliphatic diazonium decomposes immediately. Coupling requires alkaline medium.

valid_transformations.conditions: Aqueous medium; aliphatic diazonium → instant N₂ loss even at 0°C (unlike aryl diazonium)
valid_transformations.mechanism: N₂ is THE BEST leaving group (leaves as stable inert dinitrogen gas, pKa of H-N₂⁺ = very negative, extremely thermodynamically favorable). R-N₂⁺ → R⊕ (carbocation) + N₂↑ (gas, drives reaction forward by Le Chatelier). H₂O attacks R⊕ → R-OH₂⊕ → -H⊕ → R-OH. Because R⊕ is formed, rearrangements and racemization can occur. This is NOT a useful preparative route for pure primary alcohols (SN1 via unstable 1° carbocation leads to rearrangements). More useful for tertiary R-N₂⁺ or as a conceptual route for the LGA of N₂.
valid_transformations.notes: Carbocation intermediate: check for rearrangement (1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shift) if a more stable cation is accessible.

reagents: H₂SO₄ (conc. sulfuric acid) or H₃PO₄ or HF
valid_transformations.conditions: Acid-catalyzed; converts poor LG (OH⁻) into decent LG (H₂O)
valid_transformations.mechanism: OH⁻ (pKa of water = 15.7) is a POOR leaving group. Protonation: R-OH + H⊕ → R-OH₂⊕. Now the leaving group is H₂O (pKa of H₃O⁺ = -1.7) — a MUCH better LG. R-OH₂⊕ then undergoes SN1 (form carbocation) or SN2 (direct backside attack by nucleophile). This is why alcohols require acid catalysis for substitution reactions (e.g., R-OH + HBr → R-Br requires HBr as both proton source and nucleophile). Key: cannot do R-OH + NaBr (neutral conditions) → R-Br because OH⁻ won't leave.
valid_transformations.notes: Carbocation intermediate: check for rearrangement (1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shift) if a more stable cation is accessible.

valid_transformations.to: R-OH (alcohol) via diazotization and N₂ loss
valid_transformations.conditions: 0-5°C; two-step sequence: diazotization then aqueous workup
valid_transformations.mechanism: R-NH₂ + NaNO₂/HCl(0-5°C) → R-N₂⁺ (diazonium) → R⊕ + N₂↑ → H₂O capture → R-OH. Overall: converts amine functional group to alcohol via N₂ as driving force. Synthetic utility limited for aliphatic (SN1 → racemization and rearrangements); more useful for Ar-NH₂ → Ar-N₂⁺ (stable) → many synthetic applications.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.to: cyclohexanol via ring-expansion through diazonium and 1,2-C shift
valid_transformations.conditions: 0-5°C diazotization; SN1 ring expansion; aqueous workup
valid_transformations.mechanism: STEP 1: cyclopentyl-CH₂-NH₂ + NaNO₂/HCl(0-5°C) → cyclopentyl-CH₂-N₂⁺ (diazonium, shorthand: R-NH₂ + NO⁺ → R-N₂⁺). STEP 2: -N₂ → cyclopentylcarbinyl cation (cyclopentyl-CH₂⁺, primary carbocation — highly unstable). STEP 3: 1,2-alkyl shift (ring expansion): C-C bond of cyclopentane ring migrates to adjacent carbocation center → 5-membered ring → 6-membered ring → cyclohexyl cation (secondary, more stable). STEP 4: H₂O attacks cyclohexyl cation → -H⁺ → cyclohexanol. NET: cyclopentylmethylamine → cyclohexanol. Ring expansion = 5-ring homologated to 6-ring via carbocation rearrangement. Driving force: N₂ (best LG) release + rearrangement from 1° to 2° carbocation.
valid_transformations.notes: Temperature critical: 0–5°C for stable arenediazonium. Aliphatic diazonium decomposes immediately. Coupling requires alkaline medium.

valid_transformations.from: R-L (alkyl halide or sulfonate, primary or secondary)
valid_transformations.to: Nu-R (substitution product) with INVERSION of configuration via SN2
reagents: Nu⁻ (strong nucleophile: NaI, NaCN, NaN₃, NaSR, NaOR, LiAlH₄, etc.)
valid_transformations.conditions: Polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, acetone) preferred; strong nucleophile; primary substrate best; secondary possible; tertiary = no rxn
valid_transformations.mechanism: SN2 = Bimolecular Nucleophilic Substitution. MECHANISM: single concerted step — Nu⁻ attacks from BACK FACE (180° to leaving group) while L simultaneously departs. TRANSITION STATE: trigonal bipyramidal pentavalent C [Nu---C(R₁R₂R₃)---L]‡ with partial bonds to both Nu and L. Nu-C bond forms as C-L bond breaks in concert. NO intermediate carbocation. RATE LAW: Rate = k[R-L][Nu] (second order; first order in each). Molecularity = 2. STEREOCHEMISTRY: 100% inversion of configuration (Walden inversion): R→S or S→R. STERIC EFFECT: Rate ∝ 1/steric crowding: CH₃-L >> 1° > 2° >> 3° (no rxn). CONDITIONS FOR SN2: (1) Strong Nu; (2) Polar aprotic solvent; (3) Primary substrate preferred; (4) Good LG (R-I > R-Br > R-Cl >> R-F).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: R-Cl or R-Br (alkyl chloride or bromide, primary or secondary)
valid_transformations.conditions: Acetone (SPECIFICALLY — not DMF, DMSO, or other polar aprotic). DRIVING FORCE: NaCl and NaBr are INSOLUBLE in acetone (precipitate out) while NaI is SOLUBLE in acetone. Precipitation of NaCl/NaBr by Le Chatelier drives equilibrium toward R-I. Room temperature to mild heating.
valid_transformations.mechanism: SN2: I⁻ (nucleophile) attacks C-Cl or C-Br from back face → inversion → R-I + NaCl↓ (or NaBr↓). The precipitation of NaCl/NaBr from acetone solution is the thermodynamic driving force — it removes the product salt from solution, shifting the equilibrium entirely toward R-I. In DMF: NaCl and NaBr remain dissolved → back reaction occurs → equilibrium mixture, no clean product. Named: FINKELSTEIN REACTION (halide exchange, R-Cl/R-Br → R-I). IUPAC: This is a halide metathesis via SN2.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: HO-(CH2)n-Cl (omega-chloro alcohol, n=4 for 5-chloro-1-pentanol or n=3 for 4-chloro-1-butanol)
valid_transformations.to: Cyclic ether (tetrahydropyran for n=4; tetrahydrofuran for n=3) via intramolecular SN2
reagents: Na (sodium metal) or NaH or K₂CO₃ to generate alkoxide
valid_transformations.conditions: Base deprotonates -OH → alkoxide -O⁻ → intramolecular backside attack on C-Cl → ring closure. 5-chloro-1-pentanol (n=4) forms 6-membered ring (tetrahydropyran/oxane). 4-chloro-1-butanol (n=3) forms 5-membered ring (tetrahydrofuran/oxolane). KEY: intramolecular SN2 is faster than intermolecular SN2 due to effective concentration effect and reduced entropy penalty.
valid_transformations.mechanism: 1. Na converts -OH → -O⁻Na⁺. 2. The alkoxide O⁻ is tethered to the C-Cl by the carbon chain. 3. INTRAMOLECULAR SN2: O⁻ attacks the C bearing Cl from back face (180°) → forms TS where the oxygen and Cl are on opposite faces of the C → Cl⁻ leaves → cyclic ether formed. Ring size = (number of atoms in chain from O to C-Cl, inclusive) = determines whether THP (6) or THF (5) or other ring forms. Intramolecular rxns are FASTER THAN INTERMOLECULAR rxns (key principle, double-underlined in notes).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.to: R-Nu with NET INVERSION of configuration via 2-step sequence: tosylation then SN2
reagents: Step 1: TsCl (4-methylbenzenesulfonyl chloride) + pyridine → R-OTs (RETENTION at C)
Step 2: Nu⁻ + R-OTs → R-Nu (SN2, INVERSION) in polar aprotic solvent (DMSO, DMF, DMA)
valid_transformations.conditions: Two discrete steps. Step 1 (tosylation) proceeds with RETENTION of configuration at the C-O bond (O attacks S, C-O bond intact — established in RM lec1). Step 2 (SN2 on R-OTs) proceeds with INVERSION. Net result: RETENTION × INVERSION = OVERALL INVERSION. Nu can be: CH₃O⁻ (methoxide, → ether), CN⁻ (→ nitrile), SH⁻ (→ thiol), I⁻ (→ iodide), N₃⁻ (→ azide), etc.
valid_transformations.mechanism: This 2-step sequence converts an alcohol to a product with INVERTED configuration without ever forming a carbocation — useful when SN2 on R-OH is not direct (OH⁻ is too poor a LG for direct SN2 displacement). STEP 1: R-OH + TsCl/py → R-OTs: the O lone pair attacks S of TsCl (S-Cl bond breaks), forming R-O-Ts; the C-O bond is NOT broken at any point → configuration at C is RETAINED. STEP 2: Nu⁻ + R-OTs → R-Nu: I⁻ (or any Nu) attacks C from back face (OTs⁻ is excellent LG) → SN2 → INVERSION at C. OVERALL: retention (step 1) then inversion (step 2) = NET INVERSION. IUPAC: the tosylate ester is an alkyl 4-methylbenzenesulfonate.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: R-L (secondary or tertiary alkyl halide or sulfonate)
valid_transformations.to: R-OH (alcohol, racemic or partially inverted) via SN1 hydrolysis
reagents: or aq K₂CO₃ (mild base, OH⁻ as Nu)
valid_transformations.conditions: Polar protic solvent required (H₂O, R-OH, R-COOH). Secondary or tertiary substrate (2° gives mix of SN1 and E1; 3° gives SN1 predominantly). Weak/moderate nucleophile, dilute. High dielectric constant solvent accelerates. Temperature: moderate to high. STEREOCHEMICAL OUTCOME: near-racemic (50% inversion + 50% retention in ideal SN1; real SN1 = ~60% inversion + ~40% retention due to ion pair). Rate = k[R-L] (first order, unimolecular, independent of [Nu]).
valid_transformations.mechanism: SN1 = Substitution Nucleophilic Unimolecular. TWO STEPS: STEP 1 (SLOW = RDS): Heterolytic C-L bond cleavage → R⁺ (carbocation, flat/sp2) + L⁻. Rate determines = ionization step. L⁻ departs to solvent which stabilizes both R⁺ (by solvation of +) and L⁻ (by H-bonding in protic solvent). STEP 2 (FAST): Nu (e.g., H₂O) attacks the PLANAR R⁺ from either face (50/50 in ideal) → R-Nu + H⁺ (if H₂O is Nu, proton transfer to give alcohol). REAL SN1: Ion pair (R⁺ L⁻) forms first → L⁻ still shields one face slightly → ~60% inversion + ~40% retention. RATE LAW: Rate = k[R-L]¹ (first order only in substrate; [Nu] doesn't appear because Nu attacks AFTER the slow step). Molecularity = 1 (only R-L in slow step). ENERGY PROFILE: Two humps (two TS), one valley (carbocation intermediate). First hump (TS1 = ionization) is HIGHER than second (TS2 = Nu capture).
valid_transformations.notes: Carbocation intermediate: check for rearrangement (1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shift) if a more stable cation is accessible.

valid_transformations.from: R-X (alkyl halide, any substitution pattern, even primary)
valid_transformations.to: R-OH + AgX↓ (silver halide precipitate) via AgNO3-assisted SN1 ionization
valid_transformations.conditions: AgNO₃ in aqueous solution (polar protic). Ag⁺ ion dramatically accelerates ionization by coordinating to the departing X⁻ → forms AgX↓ (AgCl, AgBr, AgI are all insoluble). Rate r₁ (with Ag⁺) >>> r₂ (water alone) [triple inequality in notes]. The precipitation of AgX is the thermodynamic driving force. Even substrates that normally don't ionize readily (e.g., secondary chlorides) react with AgNO₃. Product: alcohol R-OH (from H₂O as nucleophile). DIAGNOSTIC USE: AgNO₃/EtOH test distinguishes alkyl halides — 3° reacts immediately, 2° slower, 1° slowest, aryl/vinyl don't react. Rate of AgX formation: R-I fastest (AgI↓), R-Br medium (AgBr↓), R-Cl slowest (AgCl↓); R-F essentially no reaction.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Ag⁺ acts as a Lewis acid that coordinates to the halide X⁻ in the substrate → forms a [R---Ag---X] complex → this weakens/breaks the C-X bond → carbocation R⁺ forms → nucleophilic capture by H₂O → R-OH + AgX↓. The Ag-X bond formation provides the thermodynamic driving force for ionization. Mechanism: R-X + Ag⁺ → [R⁺···AgX] → R⁺ + AgX↓ → R⁺ + H₂O → R-OH₂⁺ → R-OH + H⁺. Rate is dramatically enhanced by Ag⁺ compared to simple hydrolysis (water alone).
valid_transformations.notes: Carbocation intermediate: check for rearrangement (1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shift) if a more stable cation is accessible.

valid_transformations.from: Cyclobutylcarbinyl halide (cyclobutane ring with exocyclic C-X)
valid_transformations.to: Cyclopentanol or cyclopentyl ether (ring-expanded product, MAJOR) via SN1 with 1,2-C shift
reagents: aq KOH or H₂O or polar protic solvent
valid_transformations.conditions: SN1 conditions (polar protic, weak Nu or H₂O). The cyclobutylcarbinyl C⁺ (primary, exocyclic to cyclobutane) undergoes rapid 1,2-C shift (ring expansion) → cyclopentyl C⁺ (secondary, inside ring) → relieved ring strain (cyclobutane angle strain ~26 kJ/mol) drives the rearrangement. Product: cyclopentanol derivative (MAJOR). Minor: unrearranged cyclobutylcarbinol.
