valid_transformations.mechanism: Cyclobutyl-CH₂-X → SN1 ionization → cyclobutyl-CH₂⁺ (1°, primary carbocation, very unstable) → IMMEDIATE 1,2-C shift: one of the cyclobutane ring C-C bonds adjacent to the exocyclic C⁺ migrates → ring opens to give cyclopentyl C⁺ (2°, inside ring, less strained). Driving force: (1) 1° → 2° carbocation stability gain; (2) cyclobutane (4-membered ring, highly strained) → cyclopentane (5-membered, minimum strain) = ring strain relief. Ring expansion of 4→5-membered is highly favorable. H₂O or Nu captures → cyclopentyl alcohol/ether.
valid_transformations.notes: Carbocation intermediate: check for rearrangement (1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shift) if a more stable cation is accessible.

valid_transformations.from: Triarylmethyl carbinyl chloride with mixed aryl groups (e.g., Ph₂C(p-OMe-Ph)-CH₂Cl or triphenyl-type with EDG/EWG aryl)
valid_transformations.to: Rearranged tertiary alcohol via SN1 with selective 1,2-aryl shift (p-OMe-Ph migrates preferentially)
valid_transformations.conditions: SN1 in aqueous base. Primary C⁺ forms first → unstable → 1,2-aryl migration. Selectivity: the aryl with the strongest EDG (p-OMe > H > p-NO₂) migrates preferentially because it best stabilizes the TS for migration (partial positive charge develops on the migrating aryl π system — EDG stabilizes this).
valid_transformations.mechanism: R-CH₂-C(Ar₁)(Ar₂)(Ar₃) → (-Cl⁻, SN1) → R-CH₂-C⁺(Ar₁)(Ar₂)(Ar₃) (primary) → 1,2-aryl shift: the most electron-rich aryl (p-OMe-Ph >> Ph >> p-NO₂-Ph) migrates to the primary C → R-CH₂(Ar_migrated)-C⁺(Ar₁)(Ar₂) (now 3°, tertiary benzylic = stable) → OH⁻ captures → product. MIGRATION TS: the migrating aryl bridges both carbons partially (bridged phenonium-like TS) → EDG on the aryl ring stabilizes the partial + in this bridge → EDG aryl migrates fastest. This is aryl anchiomeric assistance.
valid_transformations.notes: Carbocation intermediate: check for rearrangement (1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shift) if a more stable cation is accessible.

valid_transformations.from: Chiral alcohol R-OH (primary or secondary, optically pure)
valid_transformations.to: Alkyl chloride R-Cl with RETENTION of configuration via SNi (thionyl dichloride, no base)
reagents: no base (no pyridine, no Et₃N, no R₃N)
valid_transformations.conditions: Neat or in inert solvent. NO amine base present. SOCl₂ converts R-OH to chlorosulfite ester (R-O-S(O)-Cl) first; then Cl is delivered intramolecularly via a 4-membered cyclic transition state (SNi) to the SAME FACE as O → RETENTION. Byproducts: HCl(g) and SO₂(g) — both gases escape, driving reaction forward. Best method for ROH → RCl conversion (Clayden). IUPAC: reaction proceeds via alkyl chlorosulfite intermediate with concerted intramolecular Cl transfer = SNi.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Step 1: R-OH (O: lone pair) attacks S of SOCl₂ → R-O-S(δ+)(=O)(Cl) tetrahedral intermediate → first Cl⁻ departs → chlorosulfite ester (R-O-S(O)-Cl) + HCl↑ (H⁺ from O-H and Cl⁻ from SOCl₂). Step 2: SNi = 4-membered cyclic TS: the Cl on S attacks C from the SAME FACE as the C-O bond (because C, O, S, Cl form a 4-membered ring → concerted bond-making (C←Cl) and bond-breaking (C-O and S-Cl) in pericyclic-like TS). Net: Cl comes from same side as O was attached → RETENTION. SO₂ gas leaves. Product: R-Cl (same config) + HCl(g) + SO₂(g). NOTE: this is a pericyclic (concerted cyclic) mechanism.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Chiral alcohol R-OH (primary or secondary, optically pure)
valid_transformations.to: Alkyl chloride R-Cl with INVERSION of configuration (thionyl dichloride + amine base)
reagents: pyridine OR Et₃N (triethylamine) OR any R₃N amine base
valid_transformations.conditions: SOCl₂ with amine base present. The base intercepts the HCl generated in step 1 → forms pyridinium·Cl (or R₃NH⁺·Cl⁻) → releases free Cl⁻ into solution. This Cl⁻ attacks C from the BACK FACE (SN2) before the intramolecular SNi can occur → INVERSION. Same overall stoichiometry (R-OH → R-Cl + SO₂ + amine·HCl byproduct) but OPPOSITE stereochemistry from the no-base condition.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Step 1: R-OH + SOCl₂ → chlorosulfite ester (R-O-S(O)-Cl) + HCl. Step 2: amine base + HCl → ammonium·Cl⁻ salt → free Cl⁻ released. Step 3: Cl⁻ (external, in solution) attacks C at the face OPPOSITE to the O-S(O) group (SN2, backside) → C-O-S bond breaks heterolytically → R-Cl (INVERTED config) + SO₂ + Cl⁻. Mechanism = SN2 by external Cl⁻ on the chlorosulfite ester intermediate. Pyridine version: pyridine also attacks S of SOCl₂ → different intermediate (acyl sulfinyl pyridinium) → Cl⁻ even more available → same inversion result. Net: amine base DIVERTS SNi to SN2 → INVERSION.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: ω-Hydroxyaldehyde (open-chain form: HO-(CH₂)n-CHO, n=3 or 4) in equilibrium
valid_transformations.to: Cyclic hemiacetal (lactol: tetrahydrofuranyl-OH for n=3, tetrahydropyranyl-OH for n=4) via ring-chain tautomerism
reagents: no reagent — intramolecular acid/base catalysis in equilibrium
valid_transformations.conditions: Ring-chain tautomerism. The terminal OH oxygen attacks the aldehyde C=O intramolecularly → 5-membered or 6-membered lactol (cyclic hemiacetal). Thermodynamically FAVORED for 5-membered (tetrahydrofuranyl) and 6-membered (tetrahydropyranyl) rings. Equilibrium lies predominantly on the CYCLIC HEMIACETAL side. IUPAC names: 5-membered ring lactol = tetrahydrofuran-2-ol derivative; 6-membered = tetrahydropyran-2-ol derivative. These tautomers are interconvertible under mild acidic or basic conditions.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Intramolecular nucleophilic addition: O (of terminal OH) attacks C of aldehyde (C=O) → tetrahedral intermediate → ring closure gives hemiacetal C(OH)(OR) inside ring → LACTOL. 5-exo-trig or 6-exo-trig ring closure (both favored by Baldwin's rules). Equilibrium constant >> 1 for 5- and 6-membered rings (favorable ΔG). SIGNIFICANCE: glucose exists predominantly as cyclic hemiacetal (pyranose/furanose), not open-chain aldehyde. This is ring-chain tautomerism, classified as a tautomeric equilibrium.
valid_transformations.notes: Protecting group strategy: acetal stable to base/LiAlH₄; removed by dilute acid. Ensure the protecting group is compatible with all subsequent steps.

valid_transformations.from: Alcohol R-OH (primary) treated with hydrogen halide HX (HI, HBr, HCl)
valid_transformations.to: Primary alkyl halide R-X via SN2 on protonated alcohol (R-OH₂⁺ intermediate)
valid_transformations.conditions: Primary alcohols (R-CH₂-OH) react with HX via SN2: acid protonates OH → R-CH₂-OH₂⁺ (water becomes the leaving group, pKa ~−1.7 for H₃O⁺ LG, excellent LG). Then X⁻ (from HX) attacks from the back face (SN2) → R-CH₂-X + H₂O. UNREARRANGED product only (SN2 = no C⁺ intermediate = no rearrangement). Rate: HI >> HBr > HCl >> HF (does not react). HF is excluded because: (1) HF is a weak acid (Ka ~6.8×10⁻⁴) → insufficient protonation; (2) F⁻ is a poor Nu in polar protic media. Stoichiometry: 1:1. Note: for 2° and 3° alcohols, the same HX gives SN1 instead (C⁺ intermediate).
valid_transformations.mechanism: Step 1: R-CH₂-OH + HX → R-CH₂-OH₂⁺ + X⁻ (acid-base, fast). Step 2: X⁻ attacks R-CH₂-OH₂⁺ from back face of C (SN2, concerted) → R-CH₂-X + H₂O. Product: primary alkyl halide with INVERSION at C (if chiral center). No rearrangement since no carbocation intermediate.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Secondary or tertiary alcohol R-OH treated with hydrogen halide HX (HI, HBr, HCl)
valid_transformations.to: Alkyl halide R-X (possibly rearranged) via SN1: protonation → C⁺ → X⁻ capture
valid_transformations.conditions: 2° and 3° alcohols react with HX via SN1: protonation of OH → oxonium → -H₂O → carbocation (C⁺) → X⁻ captures from both faces → racemic R-X (or rearranged if C⁺ undergoes 1,2-shift). 3° faster than 2° (more stable C⁺). Rate: HI > HBr > HCl >> HF (same trend as 1°). HF excluded (weak acid + F⁻ poor Nu). REARRANGEMENT: if the initial C⁺ is secondary and an adjacent C has H/alkyl that can migrate to give a 3° C⁺ → 1,2-shift occurs → rearranged product. Product may be unrearranged + rearranged alkyl halides. Since SN1: racemization (or partial racemization) at new C.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Step 1: R-OH + H⁺ (from HX) → R-OH₂⁺. Step 2: R-OH₂⁺ → R⁺ + H₂O (SN1 RDS, ionization). Step 3 (optional): R⁺ → rearranged R'⁺ via 1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shift (if more stable C⁺ accessible). Step 4: X⁻ + R⁺ → R-X (fast, from both faces). Racemic product unless one face blocked (bridged/cyclic cases).
valid_transformations.notes: Carbocation intermediate: check for rearrangement (1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shift) if a more stable cation is accessible.

valid_transformations.to: (1-Bromopropyl)benzene (Ph-CHBr-CH₂CH₃, benzylic bromide) via SN1 with two sequential 1,2-hydride shifts [JEE Mains Jan 2024]
valid_transformations.conditions: JEE Mains Jan 2024 problem. The primary alcohol is 3 carbons from Ph. HBr protonates OH → primary C⁺ forms (terminal C⁺, 3 C from Ph). This undergoes two sequential 1,2-H shifts: (1) 1,2-H shift → secondary C⁺ (1 further from terminal); (2) second 1,2-H shift → benzylic C⁺ (Ph-C⁺H-CH₂CH₃) — stabilized by phenyl resonance. Br⁻ captures → Ph-CHBr-CH₂CH₃ (benzylic bromide). This is the MAJOR product. Driving force: 1° → 2° → benzylic C⁺ (each step thermodynamically favorable). Product is (1-bromopropyl)benzene (formerly named α-bromopropylbenzene). IUPAC product: (1-bromoethyl)benzene? No, Ph-CHBr-CH₂-CH₃ = (1-bromopropyl)benzene.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Ph-CH₂-CH₂-CH₂-OH + H⁺ → Ph-CH₂-CH₂-CH₂-OH₂⁺ → (-H₂O) → Ph-CH₂-CH₂-CH₂⁺ (1°) → 1,2-H shift → Ph-CH₂-C⁺H-CH₃ (2°) → 1,2-H shift → Ph-C⁺H-CH₂-CH₃ (benzylic, stabilized by Ph resonance) → Br⁻ → Ph-CHBr-CH₂-CH₃. Two shifts needed to reach the benzylic position because Ph is at the far end of the chain.
valid_transformations.notes: Rearrangement step: product carbon skeleton differs from substrate. Always verify whether migration occurs before assigning product structure.

valid_transformations.from: Spiro compound with OH at spiro junction (spiro[4.4]nonan-1-ol or similar, with unequal ring sizes e.g., 4+5 ring spiro)
valid_transformations.to: Bicyclic bromide (bridged or fused bicycle) via SN1 with 1,2-C shift ring expansion at spiro junction
valid_transformations.conditions: Spiro compound where OH is at the spiro carbon (the quaternary C joining two rings). HBr protonates OH → spiro-OH₂⁺ → -H₂O → C⁺ at spiro junction. This is a tertiary-like C⁺ (at quaternary-turned-tertiary spiro C). However, the SMALLER ring (e.g., cyclobutane if 4+5 spiro) can donate a C-C bond via 1,2-C shift → ring expansion (4-membered → 5-membered) → bridged bicyclic C⁺ (both rings now equal size, e.g., bicyclo[2.2.1] or fused 5+5). This bridged C⁺ is more stable → Br⁻ captures → bridged bicyclic bromide = MAJOR product. Driving force: relief of cyclobutane ring strain (1,2-C shift) + C⁺ stability.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Spiro[3.4]octan-1-ol (example) + H⁺ → spiro-OH₂⁺ → C⁺ at spiro C → the cyclobutane ring C-C bond adjacent to C⁺ migrates (1,2-C shift) → the 4-membered ring opens and the 5-membered ring expands → fused or bridged bicyclic 5+5 C⁺ (two equivalent structures, '=' in notes) → Br⁻ → bicyclic product. The two representations of the intermediate C⁺ are equivalent (non-classical/bridged character). Product: bridged bicyclic bromide.
valid_transformations.notes: Carbocation intermediate: check for rearrangement (1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shift) if a more stable cation is accessible.

valid_transformations.to: Alkyl chloride R-Cl via Lucas Test (HCl + anhydrous ZnCl₂), rate depends on class: 3°=instant, 2°=5-10min, 1°=only on heating
valid_transformations.conditions: Lucas Test: HCl + anhydrous ZnCl₂. ZnCl₂ is a Lewis acid that coordinates with OH of alcohol → activates C-O bond (better LG) → SN1 for 2°/3° or SN2 (with heat) for 1°. Product R-Cl is insoluble in HCl/ZnCl₂ medium → white turbidity. Diagnostic: INSTANT turbidity = 3° (fast SN1); 5-10 min turbidity = 2° (slower SN1); NO turbidity at RT = 1° (no SN1); turbidity on HEATING = 1° (SN2 needs activation energy). EXCEPTIONS: cyclopropylcarbinol (primary) → INSTANT (cyclopropylcarbinyl C⁺ unusually stable); α-cyano alcohol (-C(OH)-(CN)) → NO turbidity even if 2° (EWG CN destabilizes C⁺). IMPORTANT: methanol = no turbidity even on heating (no SN1, SN2 too slow with ZnCl₂).
valid_transformations.mechanism: R-OH + ZnCl₂ → R-O(H)→ZnCl₂ complex → R⁺ (SN1, for 2°/3°) + [ZnCl₂-OH]⁻ → R⁺ + Cl⁻ → R-Cl (insoluble, precipitates = white turbidity). For 1° + heat: SN2 pathway: Cl⁻ backside attacks R-O-ZnCl₂ type complex → R-Cl + ZnCl₂·OH⁻.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.to: Alkyl halide R-X with INVERSION of configuration via reaction with phosphorus trihalide (PX₃)
reagents: PCl₃ (phosphorus trichloride) OR PBr₃ (phosphorus tribromide) OR PI₃ (phosphorus triiodide)
valid_transformations.conditions: Stoichiometry: 3R-OH + PX₃ → 3R-X + H₃PO₃ (phosphorous acid). Each PX₃ converts 3 molecules of alcohol to 3 alkyl halides (3 P-X bonds each react with 1 ROH). Stereochemistry: INVERSION of configuration (mechanism involves SN2 on a phosphite ester intermediate). Mechanism: R-OH attacks P of PX₃ → R-O-PX₂ (alkyl phosphorodichloridite) + HX; X⁻ then attacks C from backside (SN2 at C-O bond) → R-X (inverted) + O=PX type. Net: INVERSION at C. Contrast with SOCl₂ alone (RETENTION via SNi). PX₃: INVERSION, SOCl₂ alone: RETENTION, SOCl₂+base: INVERSION.
valid_transformations.mechanism: R-OH + PX₃ → [R-O-P(X)₂] + HX (first step: O attacks P, one X⁻ leaves). Then: X⁻ (from HX generated in situ or from P-X bond) attacks C at the face OPPOSITE to C-O-P → SN2 → R-X (inverted) + [HPO₂ or H₂PO₃ species]. Repeat twice more for remaining P-X bonds. Products: 3R-X + H₃PO₃.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Alcohol R-OH or carboxylic acid R-COOH or ester R-COOR' (any oxygen-bearing functional group)
valid_transformations.to: Alkyl/acyl chloride via phosphorus pentachloride (PCl₅): R-OH→R-Cl; R-COOH→R-COCl; R-COOR'→R-COCl+R'Cl; R-O-R'→R-Cl+R'Cl
valid_transformations.conditions:
PCl₅ reacts with ALL oxygen-containing functional groups by replacing C-O bonds with C-Cl bonds. SUBSTRATE-SPECIFIC OUTCOMES:
1. R-OH + PCl₅ → R-Cl + HCl + POCl₃ (phosphoryl trichloride). Stereochemistry: INVERSION (SN2 at C by Cl⁻).
2. R-COOH + PCl₅ → R-COCl (acyl chloride) + HCl + POCl₃. The -OH of COOH is replaced by -Cl.
3. R-COOR' (ester) + PCl₅ → R-COCl (acyl chloride) + R'-Cl + POCl₃. BOTH C-O bonds cleaved.
4. R-O-R' (ether) + PCl₅ → R-Cl + R'-Cl + POCl₃. Both ether C-O bonds cleaved.
5. Ph-OH (phenol) + PCl₅ → Ph-Cl + HCl + POCl₃ (SLOW — aryl C-O bond hard to cleave by SN2; requires different mechanism).
Byproduct: POCl₃ = phosphoryl trichloride (IUPAC: phosphorus(V) oxytrichloride), a useful reagent itself.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Mechanism for R-OH + PCl₅: R-OH attacks PCl₅ at P (displacing Cl⁻) → R-O-PCl₄ species + HCl (or as ionized [R-O-PCl₄⁻] + H⁺ + Cl⁻). Then Cl⁻ attacks C of R-O-P from BACK face (SN2) → R-Cl (inverted) + [O=PCl₃⁻] → POCl₃ released. For RCOOH: the acyl C undergoes nucleophilic acyl substitution (addition-elimination at C=O) → RCOCl. For ester: acyl substitution + SN2 on R'-O-P.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Dialkyl ether R-O-R' (any combination of primary, secondary, tertiary alkyl groups)
valid_transformations.to: Alkyl halide(s) + alcohol (or 2 alkyl halides with excess HX) — cleavage depends on substitution pattern
valid_transformations.conditions:
ETHER CLEAVAGE WITH HX:

STEP 1: Protonation of ether O → oxonium ion R-O⁺H-R' (fast)
STEP 2: C-O bond cleavage — MECHANISM DEPENDS ON SUBSTITUTION:

IF any C is 3° (tertiary): → SN1: the 3° C-O bond breaks → 3° C⁺ → X⁻ captures → 3° R-X. Other fragment = alcohol.
   - 3°/3°: SN1 at either 3° C (racemic/statistical mixture)
   - 2°/3°: SN1 at 3° C → 3° alkyl halide + 2° alcohol
   - 1°/3°: SN1 at 3° C → 3° alkyl halide + 1° alcohol

IF no 3° (both 1° and/or 2°): → SN2: X⁻ attacks at LESS HINDERED C
   - 1°/2°: SN2 at 1° C → 1° alkyl halide + 2° alcohol
   - 1°/1°: SN2 at either 1° C (symmetric: same product both ways)
   - 2°/2°: SN2 at 2° C (slower; competition, may give some SN1 at elevated T)

PRODUCT WITH EXCESS HX: The alcohol product from first cleavage reacts further with HX → 2nd alkyl halide. Net: R-O-R' + 2HX (excess) → R-X + R'-X + H₂O (both alkyl groups converted to halides, no alcohol in final product).

ANHYDROUS HX: ALWAYS follows SN2 (no water to stabilize C⁺ for SN1) → X⁻ attacks at less hindered C regardless of tertiary character.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Step 1: H⁺ + R-O-R' → R-O⁺(H)-R' (oxonium, the O becomes a better LG). Step 2a (SN1): C-O bond of more substituted C breaks heterolytically → R⁺ (3° C⁺) + R'-OH fragment. Cl⁻/Br⁻/I⁻ captures R⁺ → R-X (3° alkyl halide). Step 2b (SN2): X⁻ attacks the less hindered C of the oxonium from the back face → C-O breaks at that C → R-X (from smaller C) + HO-R' (larger alcohol). With excess HX: the alcohol HO-R' produced in step 2 is further converted by HX → R'-X (second halide).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Isopropyl methyl ether ((CH₃)₂CH-O-CH₃, 2-methoxypropane) — ether with 2° and 1° alkyl groups
valid_transformations.to: Bromomethane (CH₃Br) + propan-2-ol ((CH₃)₂CHOH) via SN2 at methyl (less hindered)
valid_transformations.conditions: No 3° groups in ether → SN2 pathway. Oxonium formed: (CH₃)₂CH-O⁺H-CH₃. Br⁻ attacks at CH₃ (1°, less hindered than isopropyl 2°) from BACKSIDE → CH₃-Br (bromomethane) + (CH₃)₂CH-OH (propan-2-ol). Selectivity: SN2 at 1° vs 2° → strongly favors 1° (less steric hindrance). Product: CH₃Br (IUPAC: bromomethane) + (CH₃)₂CHOH (IUPAC: propan-2-ol).
valid_transformations.mechanism: (CH₃)₂CH-O-CH₃ + HBr → (CH₃)₂CH-O⁺H-CH₃ → Br⁻ → SN2 at CH₃ (backside) → CH₃Br + (CH₃)₂CHOH. The oxonium intermediate shows H⁺ on O with both C-O bonds labile; the less sterically hindered methyl C gets Br⁻ via SN2.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: tert-Butyl isopropyl ether ((CH₃)₃C-O-CH(CH₃)₂) — ether with 3° and 2° alkyl groups
valid_transformations.to: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane ((CH₃)₃CBr) + propan-2-ol ((CH₃)₂CHOH) via SN1 at tertiary C
valid_transformations.conditions: One group is 3° (tBu) → SN1 pathway. Oxonium: (CH₃)₃C-O⁺H-CH(CH₃)₂ → the 3° C-O bond breaks (heterolytic ionization) → (CH₃)₃C⁺ (tertiary butyl carbocation, very stable) + HO-CH(CH₃)₂ (isopropanol fragment). Br⁻ captures (CH₃)₃C⁺ → (CH₃)₃CBr (2-bromo-2-methylpropane). Other fragment: (CH₃)₂CHOH (propan-2-ol, the 2° alcohol). RULE: whenever 3° C is present in ether → SN1 at 3° C → 3° alkyl halide is the halide product, alcohol comes from the other fragment.
valid_transformations.mechanism: (CH₃)₃C-O-CH(CH₃)₂ + H⁺ → (CH₃)₃C-O⁺(H)-CH(CH₃)₂ → (CH₃)₃C-O bond breaks (ionization) → (CH₃)₃C⁺ (stable 3° C⁺) + (CH₃)₂CHOH. Br⁻ + (CH₃)₃C⁺ → (CH₃)₃CBr. Net: 3° alkyl gets Br; 2° alkyl remains as alcohol.
valid_transformations.notes: Carbocation intermediate: check for rearrangement (1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shift) if a more stable cation is accessible.

valid_transformations.from: Aryl alkyl ether Ph-O-R (phenyl ether with any alkyl group R = 1°, 2°, or 3°)
valid_transformations.to: Phenol (Ph-OH) + alkyl halide (R-X); Ar-O bond never breaks, only alkyl C-O cleaves
valid_transformations.conditions: ARYL ETHER CLEAVAGE RULE [IIT JEE 2010]: The Ar-O bond (Ph-O) is NEVER broken by HX because the phenyl ring's lone pair on O donates into the ring (resonance) → partial C=O double bond character → Ar-O bond is much stronger than ordinary C-O. ONLY the alkyl C-O bond is cleaved. Products: ALWAYS phenol (Ph-OH) + alkyl halide (R-X). MECHANISM ON R SIDE: if R is 3° → SN1 (3° C⁺ → X⁻ captures); if R is 2° or 1° → SN2 (X⁻ backside attack on R). Examples: Ph-O-CH₃ + HI → Ph-OH + CH₃I (SN2); Ph-O-C(CH₃)₃ + HI → Ph-OH + (CH₃)₃CI (SN1, tBu-I); Ph-O-C₂H₅ + HBr → Ph-OH + C₂H₅Br [IIT JEE 2010] (SN2). Rate: HI > HBr > HCl (same as for alcohols).
valid_transformations.mechanism: Ph-O-R + HX → Ph-O⁺(H)-R (protonated ether, O becomes oxonium). The two possible C-O bonds are: (a) Ph-O: aromatic, resonance-stabilized, very strong → does NOT break. (b) R-O: aliphatic, normal C-O bond → BREAKS. For SN1 (3°): R-O bond ionizes → R⁺ (3° C⁺) → X⁻ → R-X + Ph-OH (phenol formed from Ph-O⁻ + H⁺). For SN2 (1°/2°): X⁻ attacks R-C from back → R-X + Ph-O-H. In BOTH cases: Ph-OH is always formed.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Cyclic aliphatic ether (ring containing O; e.g., tetrahydrofuran, tetrahydropyran, oxacycloalkane) treated with HI
valid_transformations.to: α,ω-diiodoalkane (or ω-iodoalcohol with 1 equivalent, diiodide with excess HI)
valid_transformations.conditions: Cyclic ether ring opening with HI: 1 equiv HI → ring opens at one C-O bond → ω-iodo alcohol (HO-(CH₂)n-I, a linear chain with OH at one end and I at the other). This is the half-opened intermediate. With EXCESS HI: the ω-iodo alcohol OH is converted to I in a second step → **diiodoalkane** I-(CH₂)n-I (no alcohol in final product). General rule: x equivalents of HI needed = number of C-O bonds × 1 (for OMe ethers: 1 per OMe group + 1 per resulting OH if using excess). For a simple cyclic ether: 1 HI for ring opening + 1 HI to convert OH → I = 2 HI total for fully converted product.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Cyclic ether + H⁺ → protonated ether (ring O becomes O⁺H) → I⁻ attacks the LESS HINDERED ring C (SN2) → one C-O bond breaks → linear ω-iodoalcohol (HO at one end, I at the other). With excess HI: the terminal OH + HI → R-I + H₂O (SN2 or SN1 at the OH-bearing C) → diiodoalkane.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: 1,3-Benzodioxole (methylenedioxybenzene, the O-CH₂-O bridge on catechol) or 1,4-benzodioxane (O-CH₂CH₂-O bridge on catechol)
valid_transformations.to: Catechol (1,2-benzenediol) + diiodoalkane (CH₂I₂ or ICH₂CH₂I) via cleavage of 2 C-O bonds with 2 equiv HI
valid_transformations.conditions: Methylenedioxy (benzodioxole) or ethylenedioxy (benzodioxane) compounds contain an -O-CH₂-O- or -O-CH₂CH₂-O- bridge between the two oxygens of catechol. With 2 equivalents of HI: BOTH aliphatic C-O bonds of the bridge are cleaved (one per HI equivalent) → catechol is liberated (both phenolic O-H groups freed) + diiodoalkane (ICH₂I = diiodomethane from benzodioxole, or ICH₂CH₂I = 1,2-diiodoethane from benzodioxane). The Ar-O bonds (Ph-O bonds of catechol moiety) remain intact during cleavage (Ar-O bond resonance stabilization → doesn't break); only the alkyl C-O bonds (C of the CH₂ or CH₂CH₂ bridge) are cleaved by I⁻. x=2 equivalents of HI consumed.
valid_transformations.mechanism: For 1,3-benzodioxole: Ph(-O-)₂CH₂ + 2HI → {First HI: I⁻ (SN2) on CH₂ → opens one ring C-O → gives catechol-O-CH₂I (one OH freed as phenol-OH, one O still attached to CH₂I)} → {Second HI: I⁻ (SN2) on remaining C-O of CH₂I-O-Ph → second C-O breaks → catechol-OH (both OHs freed) + CH₂I₂}. Net: catechol + diiodomethane + no HX byproduct consumed (2 HI → 2 C-O bonds → catechol + CH₂I₂). Similarly for benzodioxane: 2 HI → catechol + 1,2-diiodoethane.
valid_transformations.notes: Stereochemistry: syn-diol from OsO₄ or cold KMnO₄; anti-diol from epoxide then H₂O/base. Specify workup conditions explicitly in answers.

valid_transformations.from: Simple dialkyl ether R-O-R' (both R and R' are simple alkyl groups, no aryl) treated with dilute H2SO4 or H3O+
valid_transformations.to: NO REACTION — ethers are completely resistant to hydrolysis under dilute acid conditions
valid_transformations.conditions: CRITICAL NO-REACTION RULE: Ethers (R-O-R') do NOT hydrolyze with dilute acid or water. Unlike esters (RCOOR' + H2O → RCOOH + R'OH, which hydrolyze readily), ethers require CONCENTRATED HX (HI, HBr) at elevated temperature to cleave the C-O bond. Under dilute acidic conditions (dil H2SO4, dil HCl, H3O+): ZERO reaction occurs. The ether C-O bond is too stable (BDE ~360 kJ/mol) and water is too poor a nucleophile at ambient conditions to break the C-O bond. Students often confuse ethers with esters (which ARE hydrolyzed under acidic conditions). For ether cleavage: always need concentrated HI > HBr > HCl (not dilute). An ether can be used as a SOLVENT in many acidic reactions because it is so inert to dilute acids.
valid_transformations.mechanism: H+ (from dilute acid) can protonate the ether O to form R-O+H-R' (oxonium). However, under dilute conditions: (a) the oxonium concentration is negligible (pKa of protonated ether ≈ -3, very weak base), (b) H2O is a very poor nucleophile (much worse than Cl-, Br-, I-) — it cannot displace R-O in an SN2 step under dilute conditions, (c) for SN1: only if R+ is an extremely stable carbocation (allylic, benzylic, or 3°) will ionization occur under dilute acid. Net: no C-O bond cleavage with dilute acid for typical simple ethers.
valid_transformations.notes: This transformation is deliberately marked as a failed/blocked reaction — a common JEE trap where students predict a product when none forms.

valid_transformations.from: Dialkyl ether R-O-R' treated with concentrated H2SO4 at high temperature OR with H3O+ under vigorous conditions (NOT dilute acid)
valid_transformations.to: Two alcohols: R-OH + R'-OH (complete ether hydrolysis to both component alcohols)
valid_transformations.conditions: When ether hydrolysis DOES occur (harsh conditions): R-O-R' + H+ → R-O+H-R' (protonation) → C-O bond breaks → two alcohols R-OH + R'-OH. The mechanism depends on R/R' structure: if R or R' is 3° or 2° → SN1 at the more substituted carbon (forms C+ → H2O attacks → alcohol); if both are 1° → SN2 (H2O as nucleophile, slow but possible under forcing conditions). Products: ALWAYS two alcohols from complete ether hydrolysis. Note: this is different from HX cleavage (which gives alcohol + alkyl halide), not two halides. In ether hydrolysis with water: the nucleophile is H2O → products are alcohols. With HX: nucleophile is X- → product is alkyl halide + alcohol.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Step 1: H+ protonates ether O → oxonium R-O+H-R'. Step 2 (SN1 path for 3°/2°): C-O ionizes → R+ (or R'+) + R'-OH → H2O attacks R+ → R-OH2+ → deprotonate → R-OH. Step 2 (SN2 path for 1°/1°): H2O (Nu) attacks less hindered R-C from behind → R-OH2+ + R'-O-H → deprotonate → R-OH + R'-OH. Both paths give R-OH + R'-OH as final products.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Triarylmethyl (trityl) ether Ph3C-OR (central C bears three aryl or aryloxy groups) in acidic aqueous conditions
valid_transformations.to: Triphenylmethanol Ph3C-OH + ROH via SN1 at the highly stabilized triarylmethyl carbocation
valid_transformations.conditions: Trityl (triphenylmethyl) ethers R-O-CPh3 are EXCEPTIONALLY reactive toward acid hydrolysis by SN1, despite ethers normally being resistant to dilute acid. REASON: Ph3C+ (trityl cation) is one of the most stable organic carbocations (delocalized over 42 p-orbital positions in 3 phenyl rings, often exists as an isolable salt Ph3C+ BF4-). The ionization Ph3C-OR + H+ → Ph3C+ + ROH is highly favorable. Rate of SN1 hydrolysis is proportional to STABILITY of the triarylmethyl carbocation formed. SUBSTITUENT EFFECTS ON RATE: p-OMe groups on the phenyl rings DRAMATICALLY increase the rate by additional resonance stabilization (the OMe lone pair donates through the ring to the + center — the 4-methoxybenzyl/anisyl stabilization). Ranking: Ph3C-OR << (p-MeO-C6H4)(C6H5)2C-OR << (p-MeO-C6H4)2(C6H5)C-OR << (p-MeO-C6H4)3C-OR (malachite green / crystal violet type). Answer to JEE Q21: (C) two p-OMe groups = fastest because two anisyl groups give more stable C+ than one anisyl or none.
valid_transformations.mechanism: SN1: H+ protonates OR group → Ph3C-O+H-R → Ph3C+ (stabilized) + ROH → H2O → Ph3C-OH2+ → Ph3C-OH. The RDS is formation of Ph3C+. More stable Ph3C+ = faster hydrolysis. p-OMe group on one Ph ring: OMe lone pair → ring → empty p orbital on central C+ (resonance: C+=CH-...=C+-OCH3) → OXOCARBENIUM-type stabilization → very effective. Two p-OMe groups: double the resonance donors → even more stable → even faster.
valid_transformations.notes: Carbocation intermediate: check for rearrangement (1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shift) if a more stable cation is accessible.

valid_transformations.from: Phenyl cyclopentyl ether (cyclopentyloxy)benzene with 18O-labeled oxygen [Ph-18O-cyclopentyl] under acidic hydrolysis H3O+
valid_transformations.to: Phenol (Ph-18O-H, LABELED) + cyclopentanol (unlabeled 16O-H from water); 18O label STAYS on phenol, proving Ar-O bond never breaks
valid_transformations.conditions: 18O ISOTOPE LABELING MECHANISTIC PROOF for aryl ether cleavage rule: Ph-[18O]-cyclopentyl + H3O+ → SN1 at cyclopentyl (secondary, benzylic-adjacent). Mechanism: H+ protonates [18O] → Ph-18O+(H)-cyclopentyl → cyclopentyl C-O bond breaks (NOT Ph-O bond per aryl ether rule) → cyclopentyl+ C+ + Ph-[18O]- (phenoxide with 18O label) → H2O (unlabeled 16O) attacks cyclopentyl+ → cyclopentanol with 16O-H (unlabeled) + Ph-[18O]H (labeled phenol). 18O ENDS UP IN PHENOL. If instead Ph-O bond had broken: phenol would be unlabeled (16O from water), cyclopentanol would be 18O-labeled = OPPOSITE. The observed 18O in phenol CONCLUSIVELY PROVES that the alkyl C-O (cyclopentyl-O) bond breaks, NOT the Ar-O (Ph-O) bond. This is the definitive isotope labeling experiment for the aryl ether rule.
valid_transformations.mechanism: H3O+ → Ph-18O+(H)-Cp (Cp = cyclopentyl) → ionization: Cp-O bond breaks (alkyl C-O, weaker than Ar-O) → Cp+ (2° carbocation; cyclopentyl is 2°, somewhat stable) + Ph-18O- → H2O: attacks Cp+ → Cp-16OH (cyclopentanol, 16O from water) + Ph-18OH (phenol from Ph-18O- + H+). Net: labeled O in phenol, unlabeled O in cyclopentanol.
valid_transformations.notes: EAS: product regiochemistry determined by existing substituent(s). Check for conflicting or cooperating directors before assigning major product.

valid_transformations.from: Alkyl halide R-X (primary or secondary) + KCN (potassium cyanide, free CN- anion)
valid_transformations.to: Alkyl nitrile R-CN (alkyl cyanide; C-attached product, chain lengthened by 1 carbon)
valid_transformations.conditions: AMBIDENT NUCLEOPHILE — CN- FROM KCN ATTACKS VIA CARBON: KCN dissociates in polar solvents to give the free CN- anion. In CN-, both C and N have lone pairs, but the C-end is the kinetically preferred nucleophile (carbon is softer, better HOMO match for SN2 with R-X; also C-end has more electron density in the anion). Mechanism: SN2, backside attack at R-C by :C=N- → inversion, R-CN product. IUPAC products: alkyl nitrile (if R=CH3: acetonitrile; R=C2H5: propanenitrile; R=C6H5CH2: phenylacetonitrile). Chain is lengthened by 1 carbon (CN adds one C). R-CN on hydrolysis gives carboxylic acid R-COOH; on reduction gives amine R-CH2-NH2. For primary R-X: clean SN2. For secondary R-X: SN2 competes with elimination (use polar aprotic to favor SN2). For tertiary R-X: SN2 not possible → must use other methods.
valid_transformations.mechanism: SN2: CN- (C-end as nucleophile) attacks R-C from backside → [C≡N...C-R...X]‡ transition state → R-CN + X-. The C-end of CN- donates into the σ* of C-X → forms new C-C(N) bond. Result: nitrile group (-C≡N) on the alkyl chain. No ambiguity with KCN: product is ALWAYS the nitrile (C-attached), not the isonitrile.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Alkyl halide R-X (primary or secondary) + AgCN (silver cyanide, Ag covalently bonded to C-end)
valid_transformations.to: Alkyl isocyanide R-NC (isonitrile; N-attached product, carbylamine / isocyanide functional group)
valid_transformations.conditions: AMBIDENT NUCLEOPHILE — AgCN: Ag OCCUPIES C-END, N IS THE FREE DONOR: In silver cyanide (AgCN), the Ag atom forms a covalent bond to the CARBON (Ag-C≡N, confirmed by structure). This is because Ag+ is a soft metal ion and preferentially bonds to the softer carbon. Therefore, the NITROGEN lone pair is the only available donor. R-X reacts with the N-end → R-NC (isocyanide / isonitrile, N-C linkage). Mechanism: N of Ag-C≡N attacks R-X → R-N+=C-Ag intermediate → AgX precipitates (AgX is insoluble halide salt, driving force) → R-N+=C- (zwitterionic resonance) = R-NC (isonitrile). Products are characterized by R-N≡C (with formal +/- in full ionic resonance: R-N+=C:-). IUPAC names: R-NC = alkyl isocyanide (also called alkyl carbylamine, alkyl isonitrile). Example: CH3NC = methyl isocyanide.
valid_transformations.mechanism: N (free lone pair in Ag-C≡N) acts as nucleophile → R-X + Ag-C≡N → R-N+(=C:)(Ag) intermediate → -AgX (insoluble AgX precipitates, irreversible removal of Ag and X) → R-N+=C:- = R-N≡C (isonitrile). The product has N bonded to R (N is the connector to the organic group in isonitrile, unlike nitrile where C is the connector).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Alkyl halide R-X + KNO2 (potassium nitrite, free ONO- / NO2- anion, O attacks)
valid_transformations.to: Alkyl nitrite R-ONO (O-nitroso ester; O-attached to R, the ester of nitrous acid HNO2)
valid_transformations.conditions: AMBIDENT NUCLEOPHILE — NO2- FROM KNO2 ATTACKS VIA OXYGEN: Nitrite ion (NO2- = O-N=O-) is ambident: it can attack from either O or N. With KNO2 (free nitrite anion), the O-end attacks R-X preferentially → gives ALKYL NITRITE R-ONO (also written R-O-N=O). The product is an ester of nitrous acid (HO-N=O). IUPAC: alkyl nitrite (e.g., methyl nitrite = CH3-O-N=O; ethyl nitrite = C2H5-O-N=O; amyl nitrite = used medicinally as vasodilator). Alkyl nitrites are volatile, flammable, and have distinct smell. NOT the same as nitroalkane! R-ONO (nitrite ester) vs. R-NO2 (nitroalkane = nitro compound) is the KEY distinction.
valid_transformations.mechanism: K+ O--N=O (nitrite) → O-end lone pair acts as nucleophile in SN2 on R-X → R-O-N=O + KX. The O lone pair on nitrite (the :O: terminal oxygen of O=N-O-) attacks R-C backside → forms R-O-N=O (alkyl nitrite). Note: the O end of nitrite is harder and less polarizable than the N end → under soft electrophile R-X conditions (primary alkyl halides), actually the harder O often attacks when using K+ (solvated free nitrite). This gives R-ONO (alkyl nitrite).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Alkyl halide R-X + AgNO2 (silver nitrite, Ag bonded to O-end, N is the free donor)
valid_transformations.to: Nitroalkane R-NO2 (nitro compound; N-attached, with nitro group -NO2 = -N+(=O)O-)
valid_transformations.conditions: AMBIDENT NUCLEOPHILE — AgNO2: Ag OCCUPIES O-END, N IS FREE DONOR: In silver nitrite (AgNO2), Ag is covalently bonded to the OXYGEN (Ag-O-N=O, structure verified). This leaves the NITROGEN lone pair free. R-X reacts with the N-end → R-NO2 (nitroalkane = nitro compound). Mechanism: N of Ag-O-N=O attacks R-X → R-N+(=O)(O-Ag) intermediate → AgX precipitates (driving force) → R-N+(=O)O- (zwitterionic nitro group) = R-NO2 (nitroalkane). Products: primary nitroalkanes R-NO2 from primary R-X. IUPAC: nitroalkane (e.g., CH3NO2 = nitromethane; C2H5NO2 = nitroethane). Note: nitroalkanes have alpha-H acidity (pKa ~17) and can be deprotonated to give ambident carbanions. They are used as explosives (TNT, RDX via nitro groups on aromatic rings via EAS, NOT SN).
valid_transformations.mechanism: N (free lone pair in Ag-O-N=O) attacks R-X → R-N+(=O)(O-Ag) intermediate → -AgX (AgX precipitates) → R-N+(=O)O- = R-NO2. The nitro group in the product: N is bonded to R AND to two O atoms (one via double bond N=O, one via single bond N-O-). The formal charges: N+ and one O-. Standard representation: R-NO2 with N+ bonded to R and one O double bond and one O-.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Alkyl halide R-X + moist Ag2O (silver oxide with water present)
valid_transformations.to: Alcohol R-OH via SN1 (Ag+ assists ionization, AgX precipitates, OH- attacks carbocation)
valid_transformations.conditions: MOIST Ag2O → ALCOHOL: Moist Ag2O in the presence of water: Ag2O + H2O ⇌ 2AgOH (equilibrium). AgOH provides: (a) Ag+ which coordinates with X in R-X → weakens C-X bond → SN1 ionization → AgX precipitates (drives reaction to completion); (b) OH- which then attacks R+ → R-OH. OR alternatively: AgOH acts directly as nucleophile with its O-end → R-O-Ag intermediate → hydrolysis → R-OH. PRODUCT: R-OH (alcohol). The reaction goes by SN1 mechanism (Ag+ assists halide removal, labeled 'SN1' in notes). AgX is insoluble → precipitation is the thermodynamic driving force.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Ag2O + H2O → 2AgOH → Ag+ + OH-. R-X + Ag+ → R+...Ag-X (Ag coordinates to X, weakens C-X) → R+ + AgX↓ (SN1: Ag assists ionization). R+ + OH- → R-OH (or R+ + H2O → ROH2+ → -H+ → ROH). Net: R-X + moist Ag2O → R-OH + AgX↓. This is a 'silver-assisted' SN1.
valid_transformations.notes: Carbocation intermediate: check for rearrangement (1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shift) if a more stable cation is accessible.

valid_transformations.from: Alkyl halide R-X + dry Ag2O (silver oxide WITHOUT water, anhydrous conditions)
valid_transformations.to: Symmetrical ether R-O-R (Williamson-type; both R groups come from R-X; 2 moles R-X per 1 mole Ag2O)
valid_transformations.conditions: DRY Ag2O → SYMMETRICAL ETHER: In anhydrous (dry) Ag2O (= Ag-O-Ag, both Ag atoms bonded to the O), NO water is present so AgOH cannot form → no alcohol product. Instead, both Ag atoms in Ag-O-Ag each react with one molecule of R-X: one R-X reacts with one Ag end → R-O-Ag-X; simultaneously (or sequentially) the other Ag end reacts with another R-X → R-O-Ag-X + R-X → the O bridges both R groups → R-O-R + 2AgX↓. PRODUCT: R-O-R (symmetrical ether, Williamson type but with same R on both sides). 2 equivalents of R-X are consumed per 1 equivalent Ag2O. Products: dialkyl ether (e.g., 2 CH3I + dry Ag2O → CH3-O-CH3 = dimethyl ether + 2AgI↓).
valid_transformations.mechanism: Dry Ag-O-Ag: both Ag atoms on either side of O. Each R-X reacts with one Ag → R-X + Ag-O-Ag + X-R → R-X...Ag-O-Ag...X-R → (both AgX leave as precipitates) → R-O-R. The O from Ag2O becomes the ether oxygen. Net: 2 R-X + Ag2O → R-O-R + 2 AgX↓.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Unsymmetrical epoxide (one tertiary C, one primary C adjacent to O) in acidic conditions (H+, HA)
valid_transformations.to: Trans-diaxial diol or amino alcohol product with nucleophile (Nu) at the MORE substituted (3 degree) carbon and OH at the LESS substituted (1 degree) carbon
reagents: any HA Bronsted acid with nucleophile Nu-
valid_transformations.conditions: ACIDIC EPOXIDE OPENING — 3 KEY RULES: (1) SN1-TYPE MECHANISM: H+ protonates epoxide O → protonated epoxide (C-O+=H) → C-O bond at the MORE SUBSTITUTED (3°) carbon elongates (partial C+ develops at 3° C) → SN1-like character. (2) NO REARRANGEMENT: despite partial C+ character at 3° C, the three-membered ring geometry prevents migration (ring is rigid); unlike a free 3° carbocation, no 1,2-shifts occur. (3) Nu ATTACKS MORE CROWDED (MORE SUBSTITUTED) ATOM: the nucleophile attacks the 3° C (more C+-like, better electrophile despite being more hindered). The 1° C retains the OH from the epoxide O. PRODUCT: Nu at 3° C + OH at 1° C. STEREOCHEMISTRY: inversion at the attacked C (Nu approaches from opposite face of the O departure) but selectivity is lower than pure SN2 because of SN1-like character. CONTRAST: basic epoxide opening = Nu attacks LESS substituted C (SN2, less hindered path).
valid_transformations.mechanism: Epoxide + H+ → protonated epoxide: the O becomes +OH → the C-O bonds are polarized; the C-O bond at the 3° C is weaker (breaking gives more stable partial C+) → 3° C develops C+ character. Nu:- attacks 3° C+ from opposite face → forms bond → ring opens → product: Nu(3°C)-C1°C-OH (trans/anti relationship due to backside attack). The 1° C retains the O (as -OH after proton transfer). Summary: H+ activates O → Nu attacks most substituted C.
valid_transformations.notes: Stereochemical outcome critical: syn addition (mCPBA), then ring-opening gives anti-addition overall. Track face selectivity carefully.

valid_transformations.from: Symmetrical epoxide (e.g., cyclohexene oxide / 1,2-epoxycyclohexane) with 18O-labeled oxygen under acidic aqueous conditions (H3O+/H2O)
valid_transformations.to: Two enantiomeric trans-diols: one with 18O from epoxide on C1 and unlabeled 16O (from water) on C2; the other with 18O on C2 and 16O on C1; cis-diol (syn-addition product) is NOT formed
valid_transformations.conditions: 18O ISOTOPE LABELING IN ACIDIC EPOXIDE OPENING (symmetrical substrate): H3O+ protonates the labeled 18O → bridged protonated intermediate [C-18O+H-C (epoxide with labeled O protonated)]. H2O (unlabeled, 16O) attacks from ANTI face (backside of the 18O bridge) → forms new 16C-O bond from water, releases 18C-O as 18OH group on the other C. Since the substrate cyclohexene oxide is SYMMETRIC (C2 symmetry), H2O can attack EITHER C with equal probability: attack on C1 → 18O ends up as 18OH on C2 (labeled from original epoxide), unlabeled 16OH on C1 (from water). Attack on C2 → 18O ends up as 18OH on C1, 16OH on C2. The two resulting products are ENANTIOMERS (since the labeled-O and unlabeled-O positions are exchanged). SYN-ADDITION PRODUCTS (cis-diol) are NOT formed (anti addition is required for proper orbital overlap). Net: 2 products (enantiomers of trans-diol with mixed 18O/16O labeling), zero syn products.
valid_transformations.mechanism: H3O+ + 18O-epoxide → C-18O+H-C (protonated epoxide, SN1-like character at both C's since symmetric). H2O: attacks from anti → opens ring → trans-diol. 18OH from original epoxide O; 16OH from water. Anti addition obligatory: the two OH groups are trans (diaxial in chair conformation of cyclohexane product).
valid_transformations.notes: Stereochemical outcome critical: syn addition (mCPBA), then ring-opening gives anti-addition overall. Track face selectivity carefully.

valid_transformations.from: Unsymmetrical epoxide (3 degree C and 1 degree C adjacent to O) under basic or neutral conditions with nucleophile Nu-
valid_transformations.to: Product with Nu at the LESS substituted (1 degree) carbon and O- (alkoxide) at the MORE substituted (3 degree) carbon; ANTI (trans) addition of Nu and O- across the epoxide
valid_transformations.conditions: BASIC/NEUTRAL EPOXIDE OPENING — 2 KEY RULES: (1) SN2 MECHANISM: Nu:- attacks directly (no protonation step). (2) Nu ATTACKS LESS SUBSTITUTED (LESS CROWDED) CARBON: SN2 prefers less steric hindrance → attacks at 1° C (primary C next to O). The 3° or more substituted C gets the O- (alkoxide). Reason: ANGLE STRAIN drives ring opening; SN2 at less hindered C is kinetically favored. ANTI ADDITION: Nu comes from OPPOSITE face of O departure → Nu and OH are trans in product. Products: Nu at less hindered C (1°) + O- at more hindered C (3°) in TRANS (anti) relationship. CONTRAST WITH ACIDIC: Acid → Nu at MORE substituted (3° C) + OH at 1° C (Markovnikov-type for Nu). Base → Nu at LESS substituted (1° C) + O- at 3° C (anti-Markovnikov-type). EXAMPLE: cyclohexene oxide + NaOCH3/MeOH → trans-2-methoxycyclohexan-1-ol (NaOCH3 is Nu = MeO at 1° C, OH at 2° C, TRANS to each other in product).
valid_transformations.mechanism: Nu:- attacks C1° from BACK of the epoxide (SN2, anti to O) → forms new Nu-C1° bond → C1°-O bond breaks → O remains on C3° as alkoxide (O-) → after workup: O-H → OH. Product: C3°-OH is anti to C1°-Nu = trans diol derivative. In cyclic epoxides: trans-diaxial product (both OH and Nu are equatorial or axial depending on ring). The 'angle strain' reason: the 3-membered ring is opened at the less hindered end (less energy cost for the developing transition state at 1°).
valid_transformations.notes: Stereochemical outcome critical: syn addition (mCPBA), then ring-opening gives anti-addition overall. Track face selectivity carefully.

valid_transformations.from: Substrate with beta-thioether (R-S-) neighboring group and leaving group on adjacent carbon (alpha-LG compound), in anti (trans) relationship
valid_transformations.to: Episulfonium bridged intermediate → product with RETENTION of configuration via double inversion (two enantiomers if symmetric episulfonium)
valid_transformations.conditions: NGP FROM THIOETHER (-SR, -SAr): The sulfur lone pair (S is large, polarizable, excellent NGP donor) attacks the adjacent carbon bearing the leaving group from the ANTI face (intramolecular backside SN2, step 1) → forms EPISULFONIUM intermediate (3-membered ring C-S+(R)-C, with positive charge on S). This is STEP 1 (FIRST INVERSION at the LG carbon). Then external Nu (H2O, AcO-, etc.) attacks either carbon of the SYMMETRIC episulfonium from OUTSIDE (anti to the S bridge, SECOND INVERSION, step 2) → opens the 3-membered ring. NET STEREOCHEMICAL RESULT: two inversions = OVERALL RETENTION of configuration at the original reaction center. If episulfonium is symmetric: Nu can attack either C with equal probability → two products that are ENANTIOMERS. QUANTITATIVE RATES: PhS-CH2CH2-Cl reacts 600× FASTER than simple CH3CH2Cl in water (due to episulfonium formation from PhS NGP). The long C-S bond length reduces ring strain in 3-membered episulfonium.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Step 1 (NGP, intramolecular SN2): S lone pair → attacks C-LG from anti → C-S-C bridge forms (episulfonium, 3-membered ring, S+ charged) + LG departs. Step 2 (opening by Nu): external Nu- attacks one C of episulfonium from outside (anti to S) → C-S bond breaks (one of the two) → product with S on one C and Nu on the other. NET STEREOCHEMISTRY: double inversion = retention at the carbon that bore the LG originally.
valid_transformations.notes: Stereocentre created or destroyed. Track all chiral centres through the transformation. Specify whether product is racemic, chiral, or meso.

valid_transformations.from: Substrate with beta-OR or beta-OH neighboring group and leaving group, where the OR can form a 5- or 6-membered cyclic intermediate (NOT 3- or 4- or 7-membered)
valid_transformations.to: Cyclic oxocarbenium/epoxide/ether bridged intermediate then product with retention of configuration; 4000x rate enhancement when O forms 5 or 6-membered ring NGP
valid_transformations.conditions: NGP FROM -OR OR -OH GROUP (RING SIZE CONSTRAINT): Oxygen can act as a neighboring group ONLY when the resulting cyclic intermediate is 5 or 6-membered. Ring size preference for -OR NGP: 3-membered: XXX (strongly disfavored — too strained for O; oxiranium is not stable unlike episulfonium); 4-membered: X (disfavored — oxetanium is strained); 5-membered: ✓ (favored — tetrahydrofuranium type); 6-membered: ✓ (favored — tetrahydropyranium type); 7-membered: X (disfavored — entropy cost too high). RATE ENHANCEMENT: when -OMe can form a 5 or 6-membered cyclic intermediate with the LG → up to 4000× FASTER than simple SN2 without NGP. CONTRAST WITH METHOXY AT BETA: beta-methoxy (MeO-CH2-CH2-LG) would form a 3-membered ring (if LG on adjacent C) → 3 mem = XXX → NO NGP → instead, slightly SLOWER due to -I inductive effect of O (MeO-CH2CH2-Cl is 4× SLOWER than CH3CH2Cl). Also: -O-C(=O)-R (ester) at beta position forms 5-membered dioxolanium (cyclic acyloxonium) in NGP.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Step 1: O lone pair (from -OR or -OH) attacks adjacent C-LG (SN2 intramolecular, anti to LG) → forms cyclic O-bridged intermediate (oxetanium, tetrahydrofuranium, etc. depending on ring size) + LG departs. Step 2: external Nu attacks the cyclic intermediate → opens ring → product. NET: double inversion = retention at the original reaction center. If the cyclic intermediate is symmetric → 2 products (enantiomers). Example: trans-2-hydroxycyclohexyl tosylate + AcO- → O (of OH) attacks C-OTs from anti → cyclic epoxide intermediate → AcO- opens from outside → trans-2-acetoxycyclohexanol.
valid_transformations.notes: Stereochemical outcome critical: syn addition (mCPBA), then ring-opening gives anti-addition overall. Track face selectivity carefully.

valid_transformations.from: Alpha-bromo carboxylic acid (2-bromoalkanoic acid, with COOH and Br on adjacent or same carbon) treated with Ag2O/H2O/NaOH (silver oxide + water + base)
valid_transformations.to: Alpha-hydroxy carboxylic acid with RETENTION of configuration (via carboxylate NGP forming cyclic lactone intermediate, then H2O opens with second inversion = overall retention); contrast: conc. NaOH gives INVERSION (simple SN2)
valid_transformations.conditions:
CARBOXYLATE NGP IN ALPHA-BROMO ACIDS — TWO DIFFERENT MECHANISMS:

PATH 1 — conc. NaOH / SN2: OH- attacks C-Br directly (backside) → INVERSION of configuration at the alpha-bromo C. Product: alpha-hydroxy acid with INVERTED configuration.

PATH 2 — Ag2O/H2O/NaOH (SN NGP): (a) NaOH deprotonates COOH → COO- (carboxylate, the NGP group). (b) Ag+ (from Ag2O) coordinates to Br- → assists ionization (makes Br a better LG). (c) The COO- oxygen attacks C-Br intramolecularly from the ANTI face → forms a cyclic intermediate (alpha-lactone: 3-membered cyclic ester O-C(=O)-C, or beta-lactone: 4-membered, depending on substrate). (d) H2O opens the strained lactone from outside (anti to the C=O oxygen) → second inversion → net RETENTION. Product: alpha-hydroxy acid with RETAINED configuration. Ag+ drives the initial ionization of Br (AgBr precipitates) enabling NGP from COO-.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Step 1: COOH + NaOH → COO- (carboxylate anion). Step 2: Ag+ from Ag2O coordinates to Br → weakens C-Br. Step 3: COO- (O lone pair) attacks C-Br from ANTI → 1st INVERSION → cyclic lactone + Br- (as AgBr). Step 4: H2O (as nucleophile) attacks lactone C-O from ANTI → 2nd INVERSION → lactone opens → net RETENTION. Full circle: two inversions = retention. Note: if using only conc. NaOH (no Ag), direct SN2 by OH- → INVERSION only (one step, one inversion).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Exo-norbornyl brosylate (or tosylate), a bicyclo[2.2.1]heptyl derivative with LG at the exo position (anti to C1-C6 bridge bond)
valid_transformations.to: Exo-norbornyl acetate product via bridged norbornyl cation (sigma-NGP = anchimeric assistance from the C1-C6 sigma bond of the bridge), 140,000 times faster than endo-norbornyl tosylate
valid_transformations.conditions: NORBORNYL (BICYCLO[2.2.1]HEPTYL) SIGMA-NGP: The exo-norbornyl tosylate reacts 140,000 times FASTER than endo-norbornyl tosylate in AcOH. REASON: The C1-C6 SIGMA BOND (the C-C bond of the norbornane bridge) is ANTI to the exo-OTs leaving group (backside geometry) → C1-C6 bond does sigma-NGP (intramolecular SN2-like: the C-C sigma bond electrons push into the C-OTs) → forms the BRIDGED NON-CLASSICAL NORBORNYL CATION (the famous Winstein non-classical ion: a bicyclic C+ where the positive charge is delocalized between C1 and C2 via the C-C bridge). This bridged cation is more stable than the simple secondary carbocation it would be without bridging. AcO- then attacks one of the bridged C's → exo-acetate product. The endo-OTs has NO sigma-NGP (C1-C6 bond is NOT anti to endo-OTs) → slower SN1 without anchimeric assistance. Rate ratio exo/endo = 140,000 (also cited as ~350× in some sources; the 140,000 number reflects additional contributions).
valid_transformations.mechanism: Exo-norbornyl OTs: C1-C6 sigma bond (backside of OTs) → electrons push into C2 (the C bearing OTs) from C1 direction (sigma-NGP) → OTs departs → bridged norbornyl cation [C1(+)...C2 bridge via C6] forms. AcO- attacks: can attack at C1 (original) or C2 (rearranged). Both give exo-acetate (the non-classical cation is symmetric in terms of attack). Product: exo-2-acetoxyortho-norbornane or 2-exo-norbornyl acetate (the product depends on which C AcO attacks).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['III', 'IV'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Substituted benzene ring at beta position doing pi-NGP (phenonium ion formation) with leaving group; G-substituent on phenyl ring controls rate
valid_transformations.to: Phenonium ion (spiro-bicyclic bridged cation where phenyl ring bridges two carbons) + product from external nucleophile opening the phenonium; rate proportional to electron donation by G: -OMe(30x) > -Me(11x) > H(1x) > Cl(0.3x)
valid_transformations.conditions: PI-NGP FROM PHENYL RING (PHENONIUM ION FORMATION): When a phenyl group is beta to a leaving group (Ph-CH-CH-LG), the phenyl pi electrons can act as the NGP group (pi-NGP = pi-system anchimeric assistance). Step 1: The phenyl ring's pi electrons attack the C-LG from anti (the 'benzene ring as nucleophile') → forms a PHENONIUM ION (also called 'spiro-carbocyclic intermediate' or 'bridged arene cation'): the phenyl ring bridges the two C's, with C+ delocalized in the ring → spirocyclic structure. Step 2: External Nu attacks one of the bridged C's → opens the phenonium. HAMMETT CORRELATION FOR RATE: The rate of phenonium formation depends on how electron-rich the phenyl ring is (EDG = faster pi-NGP, EWG = slower): G=-OMe: 30x; G=-Me: 11x; G=H: 1x; G=Cl: 0.3x. This is a rho-negative Hammett correlation (positive charge builds up in the aromatic ring during the phenonium formation = EDG stabilizes the transition state).
valid_transformations.mechanism: Ph(G)-CH(LG)-CH2-Z + base → [Ph pi electrons → C-LG (SN2 from pi)] → LG departs → phenonium ion [bicyclic: Ph ring with + charge, C1 and C2 bridged via C1'-C2' of the ring] → Nu:- attacks at C1 or C2 from outside the bridge → ring opens → product. Rate = k[substrate][Nu]; rate increases with EDG on phenyl (G=-OMe fastest). Products from both C1 and C2 attack = two possible products (retention at one C, inversion/rearrangement at other C).
valid_transformations.notes: EAS: product regiochemistry determined by existing substituent(s). Check for conflicting or cooperating directors before assigning major product.

valid_transformations.from: Substrate with C-C sigma bond bearing EWG substituents (CF3) at the participating carbon, doing sigma-NGP (anchimeric assistance from C-C sigma bond), compared to substrate with H substituents
valid_transformations.to: Dramatically reduced sigma-NGP rate when EWG (CF3) replaces H on the participating C-C bond; rate drops from 14 x 10^12 (R1=R2=H) to 1 (R1=R2=CF3) — a 10^13 range
valid_transformations.conditions: SIGMA-NGP RATE DEPENDENCE ON SUBSTITUENTS (CF3 EFFECT): A bicyclic/bridged compound with an OMOS (arenesulfonate) leaving group and a C-C sigma bond positioned for NGP. The substituents R1, R2 on the participating C-C bond (the bond that acts as the sigma-NGP donor) dramatically affect the rate: R1=R2=H: rate = 14 x 10^12 (fastest; the C-C sigma bond is electron-rich = excellent sigma-NGP donor). R1=H, R2=CF3: rate = 15 x 10^6 (intermediate; one CF3 withdraws electron density from C-C sigma bond = partial inhibition of sigma-NGP). R1=R2=CF3: rate = 1 (slowest/reference; two CF3 groups completely deplete electron density from C-C sigma bond = sigma-NGP impossible = only normal SN1/SN2 pathway). PHYSICAL BASIS: Sigma-NGP requires the C-C sigma bond to donate electrons to the developing cationic center. CF3 (strongly EWG by induction) withdraws electron density from C-C bond → less able to donate → less sigma-NGP → slower rate. This is quantitative evidence that sigma-NGP is real (the 10^13 rate variation cannot be explained without invoking sigma-NGP).
valid_transformations.mechanism: Normal C-C sigma bond (no EWG): high electron density in sigma MO → excellent HOMO for donation into sigma* of C-LG → sigma-NGP occurs (C-C sigma bond assists LG departure) → rate 14 x 10^12. With CF3 groups: CF3 strongly withdraws from C-C sigma bond → depleted HOMO → cannot effectively donate into sigma* of C-LG → sigma-NGP absent → rate drops to 1. The 10^13 rate range across three substrates proves the sigma-NGP mechanism.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['III', 'IV'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Primary allylic halide (e.g., but-2-en-1-yl bromide = CH3-CH=CH-CH2-Br, Br at less hindered primary allylic C) under aqueous conditions with hydroxide (aq KOH)
valid_transformations.to: MAJOR: SN1 unrearranged product — OH at original C-Br position, pi bond unchanged (but-2-en-1-ol = CH3-CH=CH-CH2-OH); MINOR: SN1' rearranged product — OH at gamma allylic C with migrated pi bond (but-3-en-2-ol = CH3-CH(OH)-CH=CH2)
valid_transformations.conditions:
SN1 vs SN1' (SN1 PRIME) at PRIMARY ALLYLIC HALIDE under AQUEOUS CONDITIONS:

MECHANISM: C-Br ionizes → ALLYLIC CATION (delocalized): [CH3-CH+(C2)-CH=CH2] <--> [CH3-CH=CH-CH2+(C4)]. The positive charge is delocalized between C2 (secondary allylic = MORE CROWDED) and C4 (primary allylic = LESS CROWDED).

Nu (OH-) attack at C4 (LESS CROWDED) → MAJOR PRODUCT (SN1 unrearranged): CH3-CH=CH-CH2-OH (but-2-en-1-ol). Pi bond stays at C2-C3.
Nu (OH-) attack at C2 (MORE CROWDED) → MINOR PRODUCT (SN1', rearranged): CH3-CH(OH)-CH=CH2 (but-3-en-2-ol). Pi bond moved to C3-C4.

KEY RULE: 'When Nu attacks on LESS CROWDED allylic carbon atom, it forms MAJOR product.'

SN1' = SN1 reaction at allylic position which gives product with REARRANGED PI-BOND. It is MINOR for primary allylic halides in aq conditions.
SN1 (unrearranged) = MAJOR for primary allylic halide in aq conditions.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Step 1: C4-Br ionization → [CH3-CH(+)C2-CH=CH2 <--> CH3-CH=CH-CH2(+)C4] allylic cation (SN1-type, requires polar conditions to stabilize C+). Step 2a (Major, SN1): OH- attacks C4 (primary, less hindered) → CH3-CH=CH-CH2-OH. Step 2b (Minor, SN1'): OH- attacks C2 (secondary, more hindered) → CH3-CH(OH)-CH=CH2. The C4 is less sterically hindered → OH prefers C4 → unrearranged = major.
valid_transformations.notes: Carbocation intermediate: check for rearrangement (1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shift) if a more stable cation is accessible.

valid_transformations.from: Branched allylic halide (Br at the more hindered secondary or tertiary allylic carbon, Nu = harder-to-attack C-Br) treated with strong nucleophile (KCN, NaOH, etc.) under SN2-type conditions
valid_transformations.to: MAJOR: SN2' product — Nu at gamma carbon (less hindered, remote end of allylic system), pi bond migrates; MINOR: SN2 product (direct at C-Br is sterically disfavored due to hindered C-Br)
valid_transformations.conditions:
SN2 vs SN2' (SN2 PRIME) — SELECTIVITY RULE:

SN2' PRIME DEFINITION: 'SN2 reaction at allylic carbon which gives product with rearranged pi-bond is called SN2.' Nu attacks the GAMMA carbon (remote allylic end) CONCERTEDLY as Br departs from the alpha (C-Br) carbon. Pi bond migrates in the process. ALL CONCERTED (unlike SN1' which goes through a discrete cation).

SELECTIVITY RULE (same as SN1' rule): 'When Nu attacks on LESS CROWDED carbon atom, it forms MAJOR product.'

APPLICATION:
1. PRIMARY ALLYLIC C-Br (less hindered): Direct SN2 at C-Br (less crowded) = MAJOR; SN2' (gamma C more hindered) = MINOR. Example: CH3-CH=CH-CH2-Br + KCN → CH3-CH=CH-CH2-CN (SN2, MAJOR) + CH3-CH(CN)-CH=CH2 (SN2', minor).
2. SECONDARY or TERTIARY ALLYLIC C-Br (more hindered): Direct SN2 at C-Br is DISFAVORED (steric); SN2' at gamma C (primary, less crowded) = MAJOR. Example: branched allylic Br + KCN → SN2 (X, not formed) + SN2' (Major).
valid_transformations.mechanism: SN2' mechanism (CONCERTED, all arrows drawn at once): Nu:- approach from ANTI side of gamma C → Nu-Cgamma bond forms → pi bond C(gamma)=C(middle) shifts to C(middle)=C(alpha) → C(alpha)-LG breaks → LG departs. Product: Nu at gamma C, pi bond at middle-alpha C-C, LG gone. The concerted nature distinguishes SN2' from SN1' (which has a free carbocation intermediate). Stereochemistry: inversion expected at the gamma C (SN2-like anti approach).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['IV'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Allylic alcohol (pent-2-en-1-ol type = CH3-CH=CH-CH2-OH) treated with SOCl2 (thionyl chloride)
valid_transformations.to: MAJOR: SNi' product — rearranged allylic chloride (Cl at gamma C, pi bond migrated, e.g., CH3-CH(Cl)-CH=CH2 from but-2-en-1-ol) via 6-membered cyclic transition state; MINOR: SNi product — unrearranged allylic chloride (Cl at original C-OH position, retention) via 4-membered cyclic TS
valid_transformations.conditions:
SNi' PRIME (INTERNAL ALLYLIC SUBSTITUTION WITH REARRANGEMENT):

STEP 1: Allylic OH + SOCl2 → forms CHLOROSULFITE ESTER (CH3-CH=CH-CH2-O-S(=O)-Cl) in situ (quick acylation step).

STEP 2: Two possible intramolecular pathways:
(a) SNi (MINOR): 4-membered cyclic TS (LMCTS): the Cl directly attacks the adjacent C bearing O → unrearranged allylic chloride (Cl at C4, same as original OH) + SO2 released. RETENTION OF CONFIGURATION. This is the 4-membered TS (C4-O-S-Cl ring) = LMCTS. MINOR because 4-membered TS is strained.
(b) SNi' (MAJOR): 6-membered cyclic TS (6-MCTS): The Cl (at S end) swings through a 6-membered ring to attack the GAMMA C (C2, the allylic-remote carbon). The 6-member ring: Cl-S-O-C4-C3=C2. Pi bond migrates from C2-C3 to C3-C4. SO2 is expelled as the S-O-C bond breaks. Product: rearranged allylic chloride (Cl at C2, pi bond at C3-C4) = SNi'. This is MAJOR because 6-membered TS is more favorable than 4-membered TS.

CONCLUSION: Allylic alcohol + SOCl2 → predominantly REARRANGED allylic chloride (SNi') via 6-MCTS, not the unrearranged SNi product. The product has Cl at the GAMMA position relative to the original OH.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Chlorosulfite ester formed first: R-OH + SOCl2 → R-O-SO-Cl + HCl. Then intramolecular: 6-MCTS: Cl (on S) circles around the allylic chain to reach C2 (6-membered ring Cl-S-O-C4-C3=C2). In the cyclic TS: Cl forms bond with C2 (inversion-like at C2) simultaneously as C2=C3 shifts to C3=C4 and O-S breaks releasing SO2. Product: Cl at C2 + double bond at C3-C4 = SNi' (rearranged allylic chloride) + SO2.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['III', 'IV'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Cyclic allylic halide (cyclohex-2-en-1-yl bromide or similar ring allylic Br, less hindered C-Br in ring) treated with nucleophile under SN2 conditions (KCN, NaOH, etc.)
valid_transformations.to: MAJOR: direct SN2 at C-Br (less hindered in ring) = SN2 product (unrearranged); MINOR: SN2' product (at gamma C of ring = rearranged); contrast with branched allylic where SN2' may dominate
valid_transformations.conditions:
CYCLIC ALLYLIC HALIDE — SN2 vs SN2' SELECTIVITY:

For CYCLIC ALLYLIC HALIDES where the C-Br is at a LESS HINDERED position in the ring (e.g., the terminal CH-Br of cyclohex-2-en-1-yl ring = a secondary ring C but not excessively hindered):
→ Direct SN2 at C-Br = MAJOR (less crowded in the ring context)
→ SN2' (at the other allylic end in the ring) = MINOR

CONTRAST WITH BRANCHED ACYCLIC:
- Branched allylic Br (C-Br = secondary or tertiary, more hindered): SN2' is MAJOR
- Cyclic allylic Br (C-Br = ring secondary, may be less accessible from the SN2' side): SN2 is MAJOR

RULE: The LESS CROWDED allylic carbon (whether C-Br or gamma-C) gets attacked → MAJOR product. In cyclic systems the geometry determines which end is less crowded.
valid_transformations.mechanism: For cyclohex-2-en-1-yl Br + KCN: C-Br at C1 (ring, secondary but accessible). CN- attacks C1 from backside (SN2) → gives cyclohex-2-en-1-yl cyanide (SN2, direct, major) with inverted configuration at C1. Alternatively CN- attacks C3 (the gamma C of ring, also secondary, ring geometry makes it less accessible for backside SN2) → SN2' minor product with double bond moved to C1-C2.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['IV'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Acid derivative R-C(=O)-L (acyl halide, ester, anhydride, or amide) with nucleophile Nu: attacking the carbonyl carbon (SNth = nucleophilic substitution in acid derivatives)
valid_transformations.to: R-C(=O)-Nu (new acid derivative with Nu replacing L) + L- (leaving group expelled); proceeds through TETRAHEDRAL intermediate R-C(-O-)(-L)(-Nu) with two slow steps
reagents: Nu: (any nucleophile: OH-, OR-, NH3, NHR2, H2O, RS-)
valid_transformations.conditions:
SNth (NUCLEOPHILIC SUBSTITUTION IN ACID DERIVATIVES) — MECHANISM:

Parent acid: R-COOH. Four acid derivatives: ①R-C(=O)-X (acyl halide); ②R-C(=O)-OR (ester); ③R-C(=O)-O-C(=O)-R (anhydride); ④R-C(=O)-NH2 (amide).

MECHANISM (Addition-Elimination = AN + DN):
Step 1 (SLOW = Nu addition): Nu: attacks the electrophilic C=O (the acyl C, which is δ+ due to C=O polarization + electron withdrawal by L) → TETRAHEDRAL INTERMEDIATE forms: R-C(-O-)(-L)(-Nu) [sp3 carbon, four groups: R, O-, L, Nu; the former C=O is now C-O-]
Step 2 (SLOW = LG elimination): The tetrahedral intermediate expels L- (leaving group departs) → C=O reforms → product R-C(=O)-Nu.

KEY PROPERTIES:
① Addition-Elimination mechanism (NOT SN1 or SN2 — no direct substitution at acyl C!).
② IUPAC: AN + DN mechanism.
③ Rate ∝ (i) Leaving group ability of L; (ii) Electrophilicity of the acyl C (C=O carbon).
④ Rate law: Rate ∝ [R-C(=O)-L][Nu] = SECOND ORDER kinetics.

REACTIVITY ORDER (rate of SNth):
Acyl halide (R-COX) >> Anhydride (RCOOCOR) >> Ester (RCOOR) >> Amide (RCONH2)
Rationale: LG ability = X- > R-COO- > R-O- > NH2-
(Derived from conjugate acid acidity: HX > RCOOH > ROH > NH3)
valid_transformations.mechanism: Nu: attacks acyl C (C=O, the sp2 electrophilic carbon) → tetrahedral intermediate (sp3, O-/L/Nu/R attached) → L- departs → C=O reforms (sp2 restored) → R-C(=O)-Nu. BOTH steps are slow (the energy profile has two maxima and one valley = the tetrahedral intermediate). Unlike SN1/SN2 (at sp3 C), SNth occurs at the acyl C (sp2 → sp3 → sp2) and requires no inversion (because the intermediate is tetrahedral and symmetrical).
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Ester R-C(=O)-OR treated with thiolate Nu (RS-) compared to ester reacted with alkoxide (RO-); OR comparison of ester (R-C(=O)-OR) vs thioester (R-C(=O)-SR) in SNth reactivity
valid_transformations.to: Thioester (R-C(=O)-SR) undergoes SNth FASTER than ester (R-C(=O)-OR) because SR- is a better leaving group than OR- (thiols are more acidic than alcohols, making thiolate a weaker base = better LG)
valid_transformations.conditions:
THIOESTER vs ESTER REACTIVITY IN SNth:

R-C(=O)-OR < R-C(=O)-SR (rate of SNth, thioester faster)

REASON: The LEAVING GROUP determines the rate in SNth (LG ability ∝ rate).
- LG from ester: R-O- (alkoxide); conjugate acid = R-OH (pKa ≈ 16-18)
- LG from thioester: R-S- (thiolate); conjugate acid = R-SH (pKa ≈ 10-11)
- R-SH is MORE ACIDIC than R-OH (by ~5-7 pKa units) → R-S- is a WEAKER BASE → BETTER LEAVING GROUP
- Therefore: thioester (SR- LG) > ester (OR- LG) in SNth rate

This also relates to why acyl CHLORIDES are most reactive: HCl is most acidic (pKa ~ -7) → Cl- = best LG → fastest SNth.

FULL LEAVING GROUP ABILITY RANKING IN SNth:
X- (halide) > R-COO- (carboxylate) > R-S- (thiolate) > R-O- (alkoxide) > NH2- (amide)
(Note: R-COO- > R-O- because RCOOH pKa ~5 > ROH pKa ~16)

FULL REACTIVITY RANKING OF ACID DERIVATIVES:
Acyl halide > Anhydride > Thioester > Ester > Amide
valid_transformations.mechanism: The thioester has the same general SNth mechanism as the ester (addition-elimination, tetrahedral intermediate). The only difference is the LG: SR- departs more easily than OR- from the tetrahedral intermediate because RS- is more stable (less basic, larger, more polarizable) → Step 2 (LG elimination) is faster for thioester than ester → overall faster SNth.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['IV'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Acyl halide series (R-C(=O)-F, R-C(=O)-Cl, R-C(=O)-Br, R-C(=O)-I) in SNth reactions — comparing rates across the halide series
valid_transformations.to: Rate order: R-C(=O)-I > R-C(=O)-Br > R-C(=O)-Cl > R-C(=O)-F (based on leaving group ability of halide ions in the LG departure step of SNth)
valid_transformations.conditions:
ACYL HALIDE REACTIVITY ORDER IN SNth — HALIDE SERIES:

Rate: RCOF < RCOCl < RCOBr < RCOI
(Acyl fluoride LEAST reactive, acyl iodide MOST reactive)

RATIONALE BASED ON LG ABILITY (teacher's framework):
LG ability: I- > Br- > Cl- > F- (same as SN2 order)
Acidity of HX: HI > HBr > HCl >> HF
The LG departure step (step 2 in SNth): I- departs most easily → fastest for RCOI.

NOTE — COMPETING FRAMEWORK (electrophilicity of C=O):
The C=O electrophilicity increases with EWG halogen:
F (most EWG, most -I effect) → C most electrophilic → fastest Nu addition (step 1)
This gives opposite order for step 1: RCOF > RCOCl > RCOBr > RCOI
If step 1 (Nu addition) is rate-determining: F > Cl > Br > I.
If step 2 (LG departure) is rate-determining: I > Br > Cl > F.

For JEE purpose (teacher's stated order): RCOI > RCOBr > RCOCl > RCOF based on LG ability dominating.
valid_transformations.mechanism: SNth at acyl C: Nu addition (Step 1, slow) → tetrahedral intermediate → LG- departure (Step 2, slow). For the halide series, if LG departure dominates: RCOI fastest because I- is the weakest base (most acidic HI → I- = best LG in Step 2). The net rate follows I > Br > Cl > F when the LG departure step controls the rate.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['IV'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

valid_transformations.from: Benzene ring with EWG (-M group like NO2) at a specific position AND two chlorines (Ca at ortho/para to EWG, Cb at meta to EWG) treated with methoxide (CH3O- Na+, 1 equiv) — SNAr selectivity
valid_transformations.to: Selective substitution at Ca (the Cl ortho or para to EWG) by OCH3; Cb (Cl meta to EWG) remains unreacted; mechanism: Meisenheimer complex stabilized by EWG at ortho/para positions to the substituting Cl
valid_transformations.conditions:
SNAr SELECTIVITY — EWG ACTIVATES ORTHO/PARA POSITIONS:

In SNAr (nucleophilic aromatic substitution): The EWG (-M group, e.g., NO2) activates only the ORTHO and PARA positions relative to itself toward SNAr. Why: the Meisenheimer complex (anionic tetrahedral intermediate at the C where Nu attacks) is STABILIZED by EWG at ortho or para positions (EWG can delocalize the negative charge into the ring). At META positions to EWG: the negative charge in the Meisenheimer complex CANNOT be delocalized into the EWG → Meisenheimer complex is DESTABILIZED → SNAr at meta is SLOW.

SELECTIVITY RULE: With 1 equiv Nu-, ONLY the Cl ORTHO or PARA to EWG is substituted.

EXAMPLE: A ring with NO2 (EWG, -M) + two Cl groups:
- Ca = Cl at ortho to NO2: SNAr fast → OCH3 replaces Ca-Cl
- Cb = Cl at meta to NO2: SNAr slow → Cb-Cl unreacted
Product: Ring with OCH3 at Ca + Cl still at Cb (using 1 equiv CH3O-).

Note: EWG group needed for SNAr. EDG groups DEACTIVATE the ring toward SNAr.
valid_transformations.mechanism: SNAr mechanism: Nu:- attacks C-Cl (the ring C bearing Cl at ortho/para to EWG) from OUTSIDE the ring → forms Meisenheimer complex (sp3 ring C bearing: Cl, Nu, two C-C bonds, and O- charge resonating throughout the ring) → Cl- departs → aromatic ring restored. The Meisenheimer complex is stabilized by EWG ortho/para to the site of attack (negative charge in the complex can be delocalized into the EWG nitro/carbonyl). Meta EWG cannot stabilize the Meisenheimer complex → SNAr is not activated at meta.
valid_transformations.notes: EAS: product regiochemistry determined by existing substituent(s). Check for conflicting or cooperating directors before assigning major product.

valid_transformations.from: Tertiary amide R-C(=O)-N(CH3)2 (or any R-C(=O)-NR2) treated with Grignard reagent R'MgX
valid_transformations.to: Ketone R-C(=O)-R' (NOT a tertiary alcohol) after acid workup; the dimethylamine (or NR2H) is expelled on H+ workup; this is the only reagent that successfully undergoes SNth on tertiary amides
valid_transformations.conditions:
GRIGNARD + TERTIARY AMIDE → KETONE (UNIQUE SNth PRODUCT OF AMIDES):

AMIDE REACTIVITY: Tertiary amide (R-CO-NR2) is the LEAST REACTIVE acid derivative in SNth. NaCl, carboxylate, alkoxide, 2° amine, etc. CANNOT displace NR2 from the amide under normal conditions (NR2⁻/NHR⁻ is a very poor LG, pKa of amine ≈ 35-38).

HOWEVER, Grignard (a STRONG carbanion nucleophile, very reactive) CAN attack the amide C=O:
1. R'MgX (R':⁻) attacks acyl C of R-CO-NR2 → forms STABLE TETRAHEDRAL INTERMEDIATE: [R-C(-OMgX)(-NR2)(-R')] (anionic at O via OMgX; the NR2⁻ is too poor a LG to leave under basic/neutral conditions)
2. H+ WORKUP (acid, Step 2): protonates the N of NR2 → NHR2 is now protonated → NHR2 (amine) can depart → C=O reforms → KETONE R-C(=O)-R'.
3. Product: KETONE + HNR2 (the amine is expelled as the conjugate acid)

NOTE: The ketone (R-CO-R') does NOT react further with the Grignard at this stage because: (a) the reaction is done workup after 1 equiv RMgX + amide → ketone is the final product of THIS step. However if excess Grignard is added AFTER the ketone forms: the ketone would react with more RMgX → tertiary alcohol.

For acyl chloride + RMgX: The Cl⁻ leaves directly (better LG) → ketone R-CO-R' (no acid workup needed for LG departure) → if excess RMgX present → tertiary alcohol.
For tertiary amide + RMgX: NR₂ only leaves on acid workup → ketone after workup only.

CONTRAST: Nitrile (R-CN) + RMgX → imine salt → H2O workup → ketone (the nitrogen is expelled as NH3 on hydrolysis). Similar outcome but different mechanism.
valid_transformations.mechanism: R-CO-NR2 + R'MgX → [R-C(-OMgX)(-NR2)(-R')⁻] (stable, anionic tetrahedral intermediate, NR2 does NOT spontaneously leave because NR2⁻ pKa ~35) → H+ (acid workup): N gets protonated → NHR2 becomes a BETTER LG (now it's a neutral amine = leaving group as HNR2) → departs → R-C(=O)-R' (ketone) + HNR2 (amine). The acid workup step is ESSENTIAL for amide SNth with Grignard.
valid_transformations.notes: Strict anhydrous conditions required. Proton source (H₂O, ROH) destroys Grignard before reaction with substrate.

valid_transformations.from: Substrate with BOTH an acyl leaving group (C=O-L, SNth site) AND an sp3 carbon with leaving group (sp3-C-LG, SN2 site) in the same molecule, treated with limited nucleophile (1 equiv NaOH, 1 equiv Nu-)
valid_transformations.to: SNth product only (acyl C reacts, sp3 C-LG unreacted); the acyl C=O group is substituted by Nu PREFERENTIALLY over the sp3 C; this is the SNth > SN2 selectivity principle
valid_transformations.conditions:
SNth > SN2 SELECTIVITY PRINCIPLE (when both SNth and SN2 sites present):

RULE (BOXED IN TEACHER'S NOTES): SNth > SN2.
When a molecule has BOTH: (a) an acyl carbonyl group (R-C=O-L, the SNth site) AND (b) an sp3 carbon with a leaving group (R-sp3-LG, the SN2 site), the NUCLEOPHILE ATTACKS THE ACYL C (SNth) PREFERENTIALLY.

WHY SNth IS FASTER THAN SN2 (FOR THE SAME Nu):
1. Electrophilicity: The acyl C=O carbon is HIGHLY electrophilic (both C=O polarization AND the EW effect of L on the acyl C). More electrophilic than a typical sp3 C-LG.
2. Steric: Nu can approach the sp2 acyl C from EITHER face (above or below the C=O plane). No backside attack geometry required → less steric restriction.
3. The addition step in SNth is fast for reactive acid derivatives (acyl halides especially).
4. The rate law for SNth: 2nd order (Rate ∝ [substrate][Nu]) — both substrate and Nu contribute.

EXAMPLE: A substrate with -C(=O)-Cl (acyl chloride) AND -CH2-Cl (sp3 chloride) in the SAME molecule + NaOH (1 equiv):
SNth at acyl Cl: OH⁻ attacks C=O → tetrahedral intermediate → Cl⁻ departs → carboxylic acid (-COOH) formed.
SN2 at sp3 CH2Cl: OH⁻ would attack the CH2-Cl from backside → alcohol (-CH2OH).
SELECTIVITY: The acyl Cl reacts (SNth) → -COOH formed. The sp3 CH2Cl is UNCHANGED with 1 equiv NaOH.

PRACTICAL IMPLICATION: To selectively react the sp3 C-LG (SN2 site) while leaving the acyl group intact: PROTECT the acyl group or use conditions specifically for SN2 (e.g., mild alkyl-specific nucleophiles, non-basic conditions).
valid_transformations.mechanism: Nu:- + R-C(=O)-L → [R-C(-O-)(-L)(-Nu)] (th intermediate, fast for acyl halide) → L⁻ departs → R-C(=O)-Nu. The SN2 pathway (Nu attacks sp3 C-LG) is SLOWER because: (a) the sp3 C is less electrophilic, (b) backside attack requires anti geometry, (c) sp3 C-LG attack requires full inversion TS. The acyl C=O addition is kinetically preferred.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.
