valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.from: E2 product counting for complex substrates (polycyclic, bicyclic, or substrates with multiple beta-C types) — general rule application
valid_transformations.to: Total No. of products = Total number of distinct alkene structures (RULE stated by teacher: 'Total No. products = Total # alkenes'); count each alkene constitutional isomer separately AND count each E/Z stereoisomer separately; for each beta-C: if the resulting alkene has E/Z isomerism -> count 2; if no E/Z -> count 1; C+T notation (cis + trans) = 2 products from that beta-C; Saytzeff product = major; BOXED: application of all E2 rules to complex multicyclic substrates
valid_transformations.conditions:
E2 PRODUCT COUNTING — GENERAL RULE (stated by teacher, top-right of page 12):
'Total No. products = Total # alkenes'

This means: when asked 'how many products does this substrate give in E2?', count ALL distinct alkene structures:
① Each distinct β-C pathway gives a separate constitutional isomer of the alkene.
② For each constitutional isomer, check E/Z isomerism:
  - E/Z possible (both C=C carbons have 2 different substituents) → count 2 (one E, one Z)
  - No E/Z possible (terminal =CH₂, symmetric, or one C of C=C has 2 identical groups) → count 1
③ Sum all counted alkenes from all β-C pathways.

PRODUCT TYPE NOTATION (from pages 11-12):
- circled-① = 1 product (no E/Z from this β-C pathway)
- circled-② = 2 products (E + Z from this β-C pathway)
- C+T (cis + trans) in oval = 2 stereoisomers counted separately

SAYTZEFF APPLICATION:
Among all the alkenes counted, the Saytzeff product (most stable: most substituted OR resonance-stabilized) = MAJOR. But ALL the alkenes still form (just in different amounts). The total number includes both major and minor products.

FOR COMPLEX BICYCLIC SUBSTRATES:
1. Identify all distinct β-C positions adjacent to α-C(LG).
2. Check anti-periplanar accessibility for each (if rigid ring: must be trans-diaxial).
3. For each accessible β-C: draw the resulting alkene.
4. Check E/Z for each alkene: C+T = 2 products; no E/Z = 1 product.
5. Sum: total = number of E2 products.

FROM PAGE 11: complex bicyclic → products include ①, C+T, and C+T → total = 1+2+2 = 5 (or as solved by teacher). From page 12: another complex substrate → circled-② = 2 products from one β-C + other contributions.
valid_transformations.mechanism: E2 anti-periplanar: each accessible β-C contributes one alkene constitutional isomer. If the alkene from that β-C has different groups on each C of the C=C → E/Z isomers form → counted as 2 products. If one C of C=C has 2 identical groups (or is =CH₂) → no E/Z → 1 product. Summing all unique alkenes (constitutional + stereoisomeric) = total products.
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.from: Allylic bromide substrate where alpha-C-Br is adjacent to an existing ring C=C (e.g. 3-bromocyclohex-1-ene or similar allylic halide with ring double bond), treated with alc. KOH/Delta — two possible beta-H environments: one giving conjugated diene, one giving more-substituted non-conjugated alkene
valid_transformations.to: CONJUGATED DIENE (alkene in conjugation with existing ring C=C) = MAJOR product by Resonance > Saytzeff rule (BOXED by teacher in Q1 of RM lec8). The E2 product that extends the existing C=C into a conjugated system is preferred over the Saytzeff (more substituted but non-conjugated) alkene. Product shown: flat hexagonal ring with exo chain double bond extending downward = conjugated with ring C=C. The resonance-stabilized (conjugated) alkene wins even if less substituted than the Saytzeff alternative.
valid_transformations.conditions:
RESONANCE > SAYTZEFF — SPECIFIC EXAMPLE WITH ALLYLIC Br (Q1, RM lec8):

SUBSTRATE: Cyclohexene ring (one existing C=C in ring) with Br at the allylic position (C adjacent to the ring C=C). + alc. KOH/Δ.

TWO POSSIBLE E2 PRODUCTS:
(A) Eliminate toward the ring C=C side → new C=C conjugates with existing ring C=C → CONJUGATED DIENE (resonance-stabilized, extended π system)
(B) Eliminate toward the chain side → new C=C in chain, NOT conjugated with ring → isolated, possibly more substituted alkene (Saytzeff)

RESULT: Product (A) = MAJOR (Resonance > Saytzeff rule). The conjugated diene has extended π delocalization → more stable than isolated trisubstituted alkene → lower TS energy (ΔH=+ve, Hammond, TS product-like) → faster E2 rate → major.

PRODUCT DRAWN: Cyclohexene ring (hexagonal) with the new C=C extending vertically downward (from the ring carbon that was bearing Br) = the exo alkene conjugated with the ring C=C = a 1,3-diene system incorporating the ring.

BOXED: 'resonance > sytzett' (teacher's box, page 1 of RM lec8).

GENERAL APPLICATION:
Any substrate where one E2 product is conjugated (with ring C=C, aryl, carbonyl, or another C=C) and another E2 product is an isolated alkene (even if more substituted) → CONJUGATED product = major. This is why allylic halides under E2 give DIENES (not the isolated Saytzeff alkene).
valid_transformations.mechanism: E2 anti-periplanar elimination. At the β-C adjacent to the existing ring C=C: removal of β-H gives new C=C that is coplanar with and connected to the existing ring C=C → conjugation. This gives extended π MO system → stabilized product. At the other β-C (chain side): new C=C is isolated from the ring C=C → not conjugated → less stable. By Hammond (endothermic E2, product-like TS): conjugated alkene TS is more stable → faster reaction → major product.
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.from: Cyclohexyl halide with LG (Br or Cl) in EQUATORIAL position in the chair conformation, treated with alc. KOH/Delta or any strong base (E2 conditions)
valid_transformations.to: NO REACTION (No rxn). Teacher's NOTE (page 3, RM lec8): 'If leaving group in chair form present at equatorial position, E2 cannot take place bcos there is no periplanar H atom.' Equatorial LG has NO anti-periplanar (180 degree) beta-H in the chair because: the equatorial LG is at ~60 degrees to all adjacent axial H atoms (gauche, not anti-periplanar) and at ~60 degrees to equatorial H atoms. No beta-H can achieve the required 180-degree H-Cbeta-Calpha-L dihedral in the rigid chair conformation -> E2 geometrically impossible -> No reaction regardless of base strength.
valid_transformations.conditions:
EQUATORIAL LG IN CYCLOHEXYL CHAIR = NO E2 (TEACHER'S EXPLICIT NOTE, RM lec8 page 3):

TEACHER'S EXACT WORDS (underlined note): 'Note: If leaving group in chair form present at equatorial position, E2 cannot take place bcos there is no periplanar H atom.'

MOLECULAR ORBITAL EXPLANATION (from p-orbital diagram, page 3):
For E2 to occur, three bonds must be coplanar and antiperiplanar:
- The β-C-H sigma bond (breaking)
- The α-C-L sigma bond (breaking)
- The developing C=C pi bond (forming)
All three must be PARALLEL → productive MO overlap → concerted elimination.

When LG is AXIAL (correct case):
- The axial LG is anti-periplanar (180° dihedral) to the axial β-H on the adjacent ring carbon
- The C-H_axial sigma bond IS parallel to the developing C=C pi bond
- The C-L_axial sigma bond IS parallel to the developing C=C pi bond
→ All three parallel → MO overlap → E2 proceeds → trans-diaxial elimination.

When LG is EQUATORIAL (blocked case):
- Equatorial LG dihedral to all adjacent β-H: ~60° (gauche) to axial H, and ~60° or ~0° to equatorial H (neither anti-periplanar)
- NO β-H is at 180° dihedral to equatorial LG
- The C-H sigma bond at β-C CANNOT align parallel to C-L sigma bond at α-C → no MO overlap → no E2
→ NO REACTION regardless of base strength or temperature.

P-ORBITAL DIAGRAM CONFIRMATION:
Teacher draws two p-orbital diagrams:
1. ANTI-PERIPLANAR (H-Cβ-Cα-L, 180°): p-orbital lobes at H (green, C-H σ*), pi-bond forming (yellow), p-orbital at L (green, C-L σ*) → ALL PARALLEL → productive overlap → E2 possible.
2. GAUCHE (H-Cβ-Cα-L, 60°): p-orbitals at H and L are NOT parallel → no overlap → E2 IMPOSSIBLE.

EXAMPLES FROM TEACHER (page 3-6 of RM lec8):
- Cyclohexyl-Br with Br EQUATORIAL (circled by teacher) + alc. KOH → X (No reaction) — shown multiple times
- Another cyclohexyl-Br with BOTH β-C pathways blocked (equatorial or all-gauche H-to-L) → No rxn (BOXED, page 6)

AXIAL LG: E2 occurs via trans-diaxial (β-H axial anti to LG axial).
EQUATORIAL LG: E2 impossible → if under SN2-hostile conditions (3° substrate) → No rxn at all.
EQUATORIAL LG + SN1 conditions: may give substitution product via SN1/E1 through carbocation.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Molecular orbital basis: E2 requires overlap of C-H(β) σ* antibond + developing C=C π bond + C-L(α) σ* antibond. All must be parallel (anti-periplanar geometry places all three in the same plane and antiparallel). Equatorial LG places C-L at 60° to β-H C-H bonds → no productive MO overlap → concerted E2 TS cannot form.
valid_transformations.notes: This transformation is deliberately marked as a failed/blocked reaction — a common JEE trap where students predict a product when none forms.

valid_transformations.from: erythro-2-Bromo-3-deuterobutane (2-bromo-3-deuterobutane, ERYTHRO diastereomer: Br at C2-right and D at C3-right in Fischer projection = Br and D on same side in Fischer) + alc. KOH/Delta
valid_transformations.to: CIS (Z)-2-butene-3-d exclusively (labeled '(Cis)' by teacher in Q2 of RM lec8). E2 stereospecificity: anti-periplanar H removal from ERYTHRO substrate gives CIS alkene. Mechanism via Newman: in anti-periplanar conformation of erythro substrate, H(C3) is anti to Br(C2) while D(C3) is gauche to Br(C2) -> E2 removes H -> D remains on C3 of alkene -> the alkene has Me(from C2-CH3) and D(from C3) on SAME SIDE of C=C -> CIS. ERYTHRO -> CIS is the stereospecific outcome.
valid_transformations.conditions:
ERYTHRO-2-BROMO-3-DEUTEROBUTANE + alc. KOH → CIS-2-BUTENE-3-d (STEREOSPECIFIC):

FISCHER PROJECTION (Q2, RM lec8):
     CH₃
  H -||- Br    ← C2 (α-C, LG = Br on right)
  H -||- D     ← C3 (β-C, D on right)
     CH₃
ERYTHRO: Br(C2-right) and D(C3-right) are on the SAME SIDE in Fischer → Erythro isomer.

NEWMAN ANALYSIS:
Step 1: Draw Newman of C3(front) and C2(back).
Fisher → Newman: top and bottom = back bonds (going away); left and right = front bonds (coming toward viewer) AT EACH CARBON.
At C3 (front Newman): H(front-left), D(front-right), CH₃(back-bottom) [= lower CH₃]
At C2 (back Newman): H(front-left), Br(front-right), CH₃(back-top) [= upper CH₃]

Step 2: Rotate Newman to ANTI-PERIPLANAR (H at C3 anti to Br at C2, dihedral = 180°).
Conformation: H(C3) at top-front, Br(C2) at bottom-back = 180° dihedral.
In this conformation: D(C3) is at one side (gauche to Br), CH₃(C3) at other side.

Step 3: E2 removes H(C3) [anti-periplanar to Br(C2)] → base takes H, Br leaves.
Remaining groups form the alkene: C3 has (D, CH₃) and C2 has (H, CH₃) → C3=C2 alkene.

Step 4: Read the alkene stereochemistry from the Newman TS:
D(C3) is GAUCHE to Br → D is on the same side as CH₃(upper) in the Newman → in the resulting alkene:
Me(C2) and D(C3) are on the SAME SIDE of the C=C → CIS (Z) alkene.

PRODUCT: (Z)-2-butene-3-d (cis-but-2-ene-3-d). Teacher labels: '(Cis)'.

RULE: ERYTHRO diastereomer → E2 → CIS alkene.
valid_transformations.mechanism: E2 anti-periplanar: in the Newman of the erythro isomer, the anti-periplanar conformation (H-C3 anti to Br-C2 = 180°) places D on the same side as the upper Me (from C2). When H is removed and Br departs, the syn-eliminated groups (those that were on the same side as Br in the Newman) end up on the same side of the forming C=C → CIS geometry. Specifically: the groups that were NOT eliminated and were on the same face → appear on the same side of the product alkene.
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.from: threo-2-Bromo-3-deuterobutane (2-bromo-3-deuterobutane, THREO diastereomer: Br at C2-right and D at C3-LEFT in Fischer projection = Br and D on OPPOSITE sides in Fischer) + alc. KOH/Delta
valid_transformations.to: TRANS (E)-2-butene-3-d exclusively (labeled '{trans}' BOXED by teacher in Q3 of RM lec8). E2 stereospecificity: anti-periplanar H removal from THREO substrate gives TRANS alkene. Mechanism via Newman: in anti-periplanar conformation of threo substrate, H(C3) is anti to Br(C2) -> E2 removes H -> D remains -> Me(C2) and D(C3) end up on OPPOSITE sides of C=C -> TRANS. THREO -> TRANS is the stereospecific outcome. BOXED by teacher.
valid_transformations.conditions:
THREO-2-BROMO-3-DEUTEROBUTANE + alc. KOH → TRANS-2-BUTENE-3-d (STEREOSPECIFIC, BOXED):

FISCHER PROJECTION (Q3, RM lec8):
     CH₃
  H -||- Br    ← C2 (α-C, LG = Br on right)
  D -||- H     ← C3 (β-C, D on LEFT, H on right)
     CH₃
THREO: Br(C2-right) and D(C3-LEFT) are on OPPOSITE SIDES in Fischer → Threo isomer.

NEWMAN ANALYSIS:
Step 1: Draw Newman of C3(front) and C2(back).
At C3 (front Newman): D(front-left), H(front-right), CH₃(back-bottom)
At C2 (back Newman): H(front-left), Br(front-right), CH₃(back-top)

Step 2: Rotate Newman to ANTI-PERIPLANAR (H at C3-right anti to Br at C2-right → dihedral = 180°? Wait, in Fischer right bonds come toward viewer. In Newman, rotating so that H(C3) is at top-front and Br(C2) is at bottom-back.

For threo: in the anti-periplanar conformation, when H(C3) is at top-front and Br(C2) at bottom-back:
D(C3) is at a DIFFERENT position relative to Me(upper, C2) compared to erythro.
In threo anti-periplanar TS: D and Me(upper) are on OPPOSITE SIDES → Me(C2) and D(C3) end up TRANS in the product.

PRODUCT: (E)-2-butene-3-d (trans-but-2-ene-3-d). Teacher labels: '{trans}' BOXED.

RULE: THREO diastereomer → E2 → TRANS alkene.

COMPLETE E2 STEREOSPECIFICITY PAIR:
- ERYTHRO-2-bromo-3-deuterobutane → alc. KOH → CIS (Z)-2-butene-3-d
- THREO-2-bromo-3-deuterobutane → alc. KOH → TRANS (E)-2-butene-3-d
Both give 100% stereospecific outcome (not a mixture). This proves E2 is STEREOSPECIFIC.

MNEMONIC: 'Erythro gives Cis; Threo gives Trans' (for anti-periplanar E2 elimination of 2-bromo-3-deuterobutane).
valid_transformations.mechanism: E2 anti-periplanar: Newman anti-periplanar conformation of threo isomer places D(C3) and Me(C2-upper) on OPPOSITE sides of the C3-C2 bond axis. When H is removed anti-periplanar to Br, the geometry of the remaining groups (D and Me-upper) is preserved in the alkene → TRANS arrangement. The key: in threo, the anti-periplanar conformation forces D and upper-Me to be on opposite sides → trans product. In erythro, the anti-periplanar conformation forces D and upper-Me to be on same side → cis product.
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.from: Alkyl halide or alkyl substrate with two beta-H types (at different beta-C positions) treated with BULKY BASE (tert-butoxide, LDA, DBN, DBU) in E2 conditions — Hofmann Rule conditions
valid_transformations.to: LESS SUBSTITUTED (less crowded) alkene = MAJOR product (Hofmann Rule / Hofmann product). Teacher: 'less crowded alkene will be formed' (underlined). The bulky base cannot easily access the more hindered (more substituted) beta-H due to steric clash between the large base and the alkyl groups at the beta-C; it preferentially removes the LESS HINDERED (primary, terminal) beta-H -> terminal or less substituted alkene = major. Contrast: small base (CH3O-, EtO-, iPrO-, alc. KOH) -> Saytzeff (more substituted alkene). Bulky base (t-BuO-, LDA, DBN, DBU) -> Hofmann (less substituted alkene).
valid_transformations.conditions:
HOFMANN RULE IN E2 (RM lec8, pages 7-8):

DEFINITION: When a BULKY BASE is used in E2, the LESS SUBSTITUTED (less crowded) alkene is the MAJOR product. This is the HOFMANN RULE.

TEACHER'S STATEMENT: 'less crowded alkene will be formed' (underlined) — this is Hofmann Rule.

SAYTZEFF vs HOFMANN BASE CLASSIFICATION (teacher's table, page 7):

SAYTZEFF BASES (small/common = Saytzeff product = more substituted alkene):
- CH₃O⁻/Δ ≡ CH₃O⁻/CH₃OH/Δ (methoxide in methanol)
- EtO⁻/Δ (ethoxide)
- iPrO⁻/Δ (isopropoxide)
All above → E2 → Saytzeff (more substituted alkene = major)

HOFMANN BASE CUTOFF at t-BuO⁻:
- t-BuO⁻/Δ = t-BuO⁻/t-BuOH/Δ (tert-butoxide in tert-butanol) → E2 → HOFMANN

COMPLETE LIST OF 5 BULKY BASES (teacher's list, page 8):
① t-BuO⁻ (tert-butoxide, potassium tert-butoxide = KOtBu) ✓ = most common
② Large branched alkoxide (e.g. neopentoxide or similar β-branched alkoxide) ✓
③ LDA (lithium diisopropylamide = (iPr)₂N⁻Li⁺) ✓ = very hindered nitrogen base
④ DBN/Δ (1,5-diazabicyclo[3.4.0]non-5-ene) ✓
⑤ DBU/Δ (1,8-diazabicyclo[5.4.0]undec-7-ene) ✓

WHY BULKY BASE → HOFMANN:
Steric mechanism: The bulky base (large spatial footprint) cannot easily approach the CROWDED β-H at the more substituted β-C (flanked by multiple alkyl groups = more steric clash). The bulky base preferentially approaches the LESS CROWDED (primary, terminal) β-H at the less substituted β-C → removes that β-H → gives LESS SUBSTITUTED (terminal, Hofmann) alkene as major product.

EXAMPLES (teacher, page 8):
- Acyclic tertiary bromide + t-BuO⁻/Δ → Hofmann alkene (terminal, less substituted) LABELED 'Hofmann'
- Cyclohexyl substrate + t-BuOK/Δ → Hofmann product (exo/methylenecyclohexane = less substituted) LABELED 'Hofmann'

COMPARE: Same substrate with small base (alc. KOH) → Saytzeff (more substituted). Same substrate with bulky base (t-BuOK) → Hofmann (less substituted). The BASE SIZE, not the substrate, determines Saytzeff vs Hofmann.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Steric approach control: bulky base cannot approach the crowded (2° or 3°) β-C due to steric repulsion between the base's alkyl groups and the alkyl substituents at the more substituted β-C. Access to the primary (1°) β-C is unhindered → base preferentially removes 1° β-H → 1° β-C becomes the C=C → less substituted (Hofmann) alkene = major. The bulky base effectively reverses the substitution preference from Saytzeff (thermodynamic) to Hofmann (kinetic/steric).
valid_transformations.notes: EAS: product regiochemistry determined by existing substituent(s). Check for conflicting or cooperating directors before assigning major product.

valid_transformations.from: Alkyl substrate with two beta-H types and a POOR LEAVING GROUP (PLG: F, SR2+, NR3+ = sulfonium, ammonium, fluoride) treated with alc. KOH or OH- in E2 conditions — PLG gives Hofmann selectivity
valid_transformations.to: HOFMANN alkene (less substituted) = MAJOR product. Teacher's rule (page 9): 'E2 + Poor leaving group -> Follow Hofmann.' PLG rate order: 1 degree > 2 degree > 3 degree (REVERSED from GLG's 3>2>1). Quantitative data from table: SR2+ gives 30% Saytzeff / 70% Hofmann; NR3+ gives 18% Saytzeff / 82% Hofmann; extreme PLG gives 2% Saytzeff / 98% Hofmann. Mechanism: PLG makes TS carbanion-like at beta-C (E1CB-like) -> 1 degree carbanion more stable -> primary beta-H preferred -> Hofmann. BOXED YELLOW: '1 degree > 2 degree > 3 degree' for PLG E2.
valid_transformations.conditions:
E2 + POOR LEAVING GROUP → HOFMANN (RM lec8, pages 9-10):

TEACHER'S RULE (page 9, underlined):
'E2 + Good leaving group ⟹ Follow Sytzeff.'
'E2 + Poor leaving group → Follow Hofmann.'

DEFINITION — GOOD vs POOR LEAVING GROUP:
- GOOD LG (GLG): I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ (rate of E2: I fastest) — strong C-LG bond breaking desired
- POOR LG (PLG): F⁻, SR₂⁺ (sulfonium), NR₃⁺ (ammonium), NMe₃⁺ — slow or poor departure

QUANTITATIVE TABLE (teacher's page 9):
GLG (3° > 2° > 1° rate order = Saytzeff):
| LG | Saytzeff % | Hofmann % |
|---|---|---|
| -I | 80% | 20% |
| -Br | 70% | 30% |
| -Cl | 60% | 40% |

PLG (1° > 2° > 3° rate order = Hofmann, YELLOW BOXED):
| LG | Saytzeff % | Hofmann % |
|---|---|---|
| -SR₂⁺ (sulfonium) | 30% | 70% |
| -NR₃⁺ (ammonium, 1st) | 18% | 82% |
| -NR₃⁺ (ammonium, 2nd/extreme) | 2% | 98% |
YELLOW OVAL: '70% / 82% / 98%' = Hofmann % for PLG series ✓

BOXED YELLOW: '1° > 2° > 3°' = the PLG rate order (reversed from GLG 3°>2°>1°).

MECHANISM — WHY PLG → HOFMANN:
From teacher (page 10, underlined): 'Here carbanion like character will be developed in the transition state.'

With PLG: the C-LG bond is STRONG (poor at breaking) → in the E2 TS, C-LG bond is NOT significantly broken → the TS is E1CB-like (carbanion-like character at β-C, δ⁻ label shown at β-C in diagram).
Carbanion stability: 1° > 2° > 3° (primary carbanion is more stable than secondary, opposite of carbocation).
Therefore: 1° β-C (primary = terminal β-H) prefers the carbanion TS → primary β-H is preferentially removed → TERMINAL (less substituted, Hofmann) alkene = major.

GLG MECHANISM — WHY GLG → SAYTZEFF:
With GLG: C-LG bond breaks WELL in TS → cationic character at α-C (E1-like) → 3° α-C preferred → 3° substrate reacts faster → Saytzeff = more substituted alkene = major.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Two TS extremes in E2: (1) GLG: TS resembles E1 (cation at α-C) → α-C substitution matters → 3°α > 2°α > 1°α → more substituted alkene (Saytzeff); (2) PLG: TS resembles E1CB (carbanion at β-C) → β-C substitution matters inversely → 1°β > 2°β > 3°β (primary carbanion stability) → less substituted alkene (Hofmann). The % data (80:20, 70:30... 30:70, 18:82, 2:98) shows a continuous shift from Saytzeff to Hofmann as LG quality decreases.
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.from: Quaternary ammonium salt (R-CH2-CR'(NR3+)-...) = alkyl substrate with NR3+ as leaving group treated with OH-/Delta — Hofmann elimination
valid_transformations.to: HOFMANN alkene (less substituted = major) + NR3 (tertiary amine = the leaving group departs). NR3+ is a POOR LEAVING GROUP (PLG) in E2 -> Hofmann selectivity: 18% Saytzeff / 82% Hofmann to 2% Saytzeff / 98% Hofmann depending on specific ammonium. Rate order: 1 degree > 2 degree > 3 degree (carbanion TS). The leaving group NR3 (amine) departs as neutral amine. 'Hofmann elimination' = the classic name for E2 of ammonium salts. From teacher's Q (page 10): R-NMe3+ + OH-/Delta -> Hofmann alkene + NMe3.
valid_transformations.conditions:
HOFMANN ELIMINATION — E2 OF QUATERNARY AMMONIUM SALTS (RM lec8, page 10):

HISTORICAL NAME: 'Hofmann elimination' = E2 reaction of quaternary ammonium salts (R₄N⁺ where one R is H-bearing alkyl chain = the chain that undergoes elimination). The name comes from August Wilhelm von Hofmann who studied these reactions.

SUBSTRATE (teacher Q, page 10):
R-CH₂-C(NMe₃⁺)(chain)-... where NMe₃⁺ = trimethylammonium cation = the LG.
+ OH⁻/Δ (hydroxide base).

MECHANISM:
1. OH⁻ (external base) removes β-H from the less hindered (primary) β-C (Hofmann selectivity: carbanion TS, 1° > 2° > 3°).
2. C-N⁺ bond breaks: NMe₃ departs as neutral TRIMETHYLAMINE (NMe₃ = the tertiary amine LG).
3. Product alkene: the LESS SUBSTITUTED alkene (Hofmann = major because NR₃⁺ is PLG).

LEAVING GROUP: NR₃ (tertiary amine) departs as neutral molecule. This is the CLASSIC Hofmann elimination leaving group.

PRODUCT SELECTIVITY (from teacher's table, page 9):
NR₃⁺ LG → Saytzeff: 18% | Hofmann: 82% (= 82% less substituted alkene)
Extreme ammonium → Saytzeff: 2% | Hofmann: 98% (= nearly pure Hofmann)
This is because NR₃⁺ is a VERY POOR LG → very strong carbanion character at β-C in TS → very high Hofmann selectivity.

CONFORMATION REQUIREMENT:
Even for NR₃⁺ (PLG), E2 is still ANTI-PERIPLANAR (the anti requirement applies for the concerted E2 step). However, the SELECTIVITY (which β-H is removed) follows Hofmann (less hindered = 1° preferred).

BASE: OH⁻ (aq. NaOH or KOH) is commonly used for Hofmann elimination of ammonium salts. Alc. KOH can also be used.

SUMMARY:
R-CH₂-CR'(NR₃⁺)-R'' + OH⁻/Δ → R-CH=CR'-R'' (Saytzeff, minor, 18%) + R-CH₂-CR'=CH₂ (Hofmann, MAJOR, 82%) + NR₃↑
valid_transformations.mechanism: E2: OH⁻ removes β-H (less hindered 1° β-C preferred because PLG carbanion TS) → anti-periplanar arrangement → C=C forms → NR₃⁺ departs as neutral NR₃ (amine). Anti-periplanar still required for concerted E2. The Hofmann selectivity comes from carbanion TS making 1°β-C preferred (not from geometry). PLG carbanion TS: 1° carbanion (at primary β-C) is more stable than 2° or 3° → primary β-H removed → terminal Hofmann alkene = major.
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.from: Amine N-oxide (R-CH2-N+(R')2-O- = tertiary amine N-oxide, also called 'ammonium oxide') heated with Delta — Cope elimination (Ei mechanism)
valid_transformations.to: Alkene (Hofmann = less substituted, major) + hydroxylamine derivative (R'2NOH). Mechanism: Ei (internal elimination) via a 5-membered cyclic TS: N-oxide O- acts as internal base abstracting SYN beta-H (O-N-Calpha-Cbeta-H ring = 5 atoms); ANTI-PERIPLANAR IS NOT REQUIRED (syn-periplanar instead); H and O are on the SAME SIDE (syn). Rate order: 1 degree > 2 degree > 3 degree (Hofmann selectivity). This is the COPE ELIMINATION. Products: alkene + R2NOH (hydroxylamine). From teacher pages 11-12: N-oxide substrate + Δ -> alkene + N-containing byproduct (shown as N with ring).
valid_transformations.conditions:
COPE ELIMINATION (Ei MECHANISM) — AMINE N-OXIDE → ALKENE + HYDROXYLAMINE (RM lec8, pages 11-12):

SUBSTRATE: R-CH₂-N⁺(R')₂-O⁻ (= amine N-oxide = tertiary amine that has been oxidized to N-oxide)
  The N has: (1) a positive charge (N⁺), (2) an O⁻ directly bonded to N (N-oxide oxygen = the internal base), (3) two R' groups, (4) an alkyl chain with β-H available.

MECHANISM — 5-MEMBERED CYCLIC Ei TS (teacher's page 11):
  Step 1: The N-O⁻ oxygen (internal base) abstracts the β-H that is on the SAME SIDE (SYN) as the N-O group.
  Cyclic TS: O-N-Cα-Cβ-H → 5-membered ring (5 atoms in the ring: O, N, Cα, Cβ, H)
  The H is abstracted SYN to the N-O bond (SYN PERIPLANAR, NOT anti-periplanar!)
  Simultaneously: Cα-N bond breaks → N leaves with O → alkene forms.

KEY DIFFERENCE FROM E2:
- E2: ANTI-periplanar (180° dihedral H-Cβ-Cα-L)
- Cope/Ei: SYN-periplanar (0° dihedral H-Cβ-Cα-N in the cyclic TS, H and N-O on same side)
- Different stereochemical outcome from E2 vs Cope on same substrate

PRODUCTS:
  Alkene + R₂N-OH (hydroxylamine derivative = the N and O stay together)
  The amine N-oxide becomes hydroxylamine fragment after transferring H from β-C to O.

EXAMPLES (teacher pages 11-12):
  Teacher Q1 (page 11): N-oxide with two β-C positions → Cope → 'CH₂=CH₂' + N-ring (cyclic amine/piperidine derivative as hydroxylamine byproduct)
  Teacher Q2 (page 11): N-oxide substrate → Cope → box-shaped cyclic amine (pyridine type) + alkene

SELECTIVITY (Hofmann):
  1° > 2° > 3° (same as PLG E2 = carbanion-like TS at β-C in the cyclic Ei TS)
  Less substituted (Hofmann) alkene = major.

Ei MECHANISM SUMMARY:
  Ei = Elimination through an internal base (intramolecular) via CYCLIC TRANSITION STATE → syn elimination.
  Compare Ei mechanisms: Cope (amine N-oxide, 5-membered), Chugaev (xanthate ester, 6-membered), ester pyrolysis (β-elimination of esters, 6-membered). All: syn elimination, no external base, cyclic TS.

DOUBLE ELIMINATION → ALKYNE (teacher page 12, Q2):
  Substrate: Me-N⁺(iPr)(Pr)(chain)-... + OH⁻/Δ → vinyl-NR₃⁺ intermediate → second OH⁻/Δ → C≡C (ALKYNE) + amine fragment.
  First E2: removes β-H → alkene with NR₃⁺ (vinyl ammonium = vinyl-NR₃⁺ = very reactive)
  Second E2: OH⁻ removes vinylic β-H → C≡C (alkyne) + NR₃ departs.
  Product: ALKYNE + N(Me)(iPr) (amine leaving group, drawn by teacher).
valid_transformations.mechanism: Cope (Ei): N-O⁻ oxygen abstracts syn β-H in a 5-membered ring TS [O···H-Cβ-Cα-N⁺(R)₂] → synchronous: O-H bond forms (H transferred to O), Cβ-H breaks, Cα-N breaks → alkene at Cα=Cβ, and (R)₂N-OH (hydroxylamine) as byproduct. All bond changes synchronous (concerted) in the cyclic TS, but syn-periplanar (not anti). The 5-membered ring enforces the syn geometry.
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.from: Alkyl halide (C-L) dissolved in POLAR PROTIC SOLVENT heated (Delta) — E1 (Unimolecular Elimination) conditions, NO external base
valid_transformations.to: Alkene (more substituted = Saytzeff = MAJOR, BOXED) via E1 (Unimolecular Elimination). Mechanism: Step 1 (SLOW, rate-determining): C-L ionizes (polar protic solvent stabilizes carbocation and L-) -> carbocation intermediate. Step 2 (FAST): adjacent beta-H lost as H+ -> C=C forms. Rate ∝ [R-L]^1 (BOXED, first order, order = 1). Substrate rate: 3 degree >> 2 degree > 1 degree (3 degree carbocation most stable). LG order: R-F < R-Cl < R-Br < R-I (I = fastest E1). Product = Saytzeff (most substituted alkene, no Hofmann mixture). SN1 competes with E1 (same carbocation intermediate, aq. conditions favor SN1 = alcohol; alc. conditions favor E1 = alkene).
valid_transformations.conditions:
E1 (UNIMOLECULAR ELIMINATION) — FORMAL INTRODUCTION (RM lec9, page 6):

NAME: E1 = Elimination, Unimolecular. Teacher label: 'E1 (Unimolecular elimination rxn) ⟹' (circled #, underlined, in green = important).

CONDITIONS:
- Polar & protic solvent (water, aqueous alcohol, ROH)
- Heat (Δ) = provides energy for ionization
- NO external base required (unimolecular = only substrate in RDS)
- Solvent molecules (shown as circles = O's) solvate the incipient carbocation and L⁻

MECHANISM (teacher's diagram, green):
Step 1 (SLOW = rate-determining step):
  -C-C- (with L at α-C, surrounded by polar protic solvent circles) → C⊕ (carbocation) + L⁻
  Note: solvent stabilizes both the carbocation (cation stabilization) and L⁻ (anion solvation)
  This is the IONIZATION step — identical to SN1 step 1.

Step 2 (FAST):
  C⊕ (β-H present at adjacent β-C) → -H⁺ (deprotonation of β-C by solvent or L⁻) → C=C (alkene)
  The alkene formed is the MORE SUBSTITUTED one (Saytzeff) because:
  (a) the carbocation is at α-C (already substituted position),
  (b) loss of β-H gives the most stable (most substituted) alkene (thermodynamic product)
  (c) there is NO base selectivity (no bulky base → no Hofmann selectivity)
  Product: C=C = MAJOR (BOXED by teacher)

RATE LAW (BOXED by teacher):
  Rate ∝ [R-L]¹
  order = 1
  Rate = k[R-L] — only substrate concentration matters (not base, since no external base)
  This is 1st order kinetics = UNIMOLECULAR rate-determining step (only one molecule in RDS)

LG REACTIVITY ORDER (circled #, underlined):
  R-F < R-Cl < R-Br < R-I
  (I⁻ is best LG → fastest E1; F⁻ is worst LG → slowest E1)
  SAME order as SN1 (same ionization step shared between E1 and SN1)

SUBSTRATE RATE ORDER (circled #, underlined):
  3° >> 2° > 1° > (methyl = no E1)
  3° carbocation is most stable → 3° substrates ionize fastest → fastest E1
  1° carbocation is very unstable → 1° substrates essentially no E1
  (1° substrates prefer SN2 or E2 with strong base)

SN1 vs E1 COMPETITION:
Both share the same carbocation intermediate (ionization step = same).
  Aq. conditions (H₂O solvent) → SN1 (water attacks cation → alcohol) = major
  Alc. conditions (ROH at high Δ) → E1 (solvent deprotonates β-C → alkene) = major
  The ratio depends on temperature and solvent: higher T and less nucleophilic solvent → more E1.

PRODUCT SELECTIVITY IN E1:
  ONLY Saytzeff (more substituted) alkene = major (α = 100%)
  Hofmann (less substituted) alkene = NOT formed from E1 (carbocation collapses to give only most stable alkene)
  Contrast with E2: gives Saytzeff as MAJOR but Hofmann as minor (a mixture).
  Teacher's '#' note (page 2): H⁺ conditions (E1 pathway): α = 100%, ω = 0% — only one alkene.
  Therefore: E1 is more REGIOSELECTIVE than E2 (approaches regiospecific for Saytzeff).

STEREOCHEMISTRY:
  E1 is NOT stereospecific (goes through planar/sp2 carbocation → β-H can be lost from either face)
  E1 gives a mixture of E and Z alkenes (trans and cis) from same substrate.
  SN1 (same mechanism) is also NOT stereospecific.
valid_transformations.mechanism: E1 mechanism: Two-step. Step 1 (slow, RDS): heterolytic C-L cleavage assisted by polar protic solvent → R⁺ (carbocation) + L⁻. Step 2 (fast): base (solvent or L⁻) removes β-H from the most substituted available β-C → electrons from C-H shift → C=C forms → Saytzeff alkene (most substituted = most stable = major). No anti-periplanar requirement for E1 (carbocation is sp2 planar → β-H can be removed from any direction). First-order kinetics: Rate = k[R-L].
valid_transformations.notes: Carbocation intermediate: check for rearrangement (1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shift) if a more stable cation is accessible.

valid_transformations.from: Any substrate giving two possible regioisomeric alkenes in E2 (two different beta-C positions with H's) — testing whether student knows REGIOSELECTIVE vs REGIOSPECIFIC classification for E2
valid_transformations.to: E2 is REGIOSELECTIVE: gives Saytzeff (more substituted) as MAJOR + Hofmann (less substituted) as MINOR — two different regioisomers, one is major. NOT regiospecific (which would require 100% of one regioisomer). Teacher's statement (page 2): 'E2 is a regioselective rxn' (underlined). Contrast with E1 (H+ conditions): alpha = 100%, omega = 0% (via carbocation gives ONLY Saytzeff = approaches regiospecific). The ratio (alpha:omega = major:minor) depends on base size and LG quality (Saytzeff/Hofmann rules).
valid_transformations.conditions:
E2 REGIOSELECTIVITY — DEFINITION AND EXAM CLASSIFICATION (RM lec9, pages 2-3):

TEACHER'S HEADER: '→ Regioselective →' (underlined, with arrows pointing both ways on page 2)

DEFINITION OF REGIOSELECTIVE:
A reaction that gives two regioisomers (products that differ in the POSITION of the functional group) but with one as MAJOR product. The reaction is regioselective if there is a PREFERENCE (not necessarily exclusive) for one regioisomer.

DEFINITION OF REGIOSPECIFIC:
A reaction that gives ONLY ONE regioisomer (100% of one regiochemical outcome). Completely exclusive preference for one regioisomer.

E2 CLASSIFICATION = REGIOSELECTIVE:
Substrate with two beta-C positions + alc. KOH/Δ → Saytzeff alkene (BOXED 'major') + Hofmann alkene (BOXED 'minor').
Both regioisomers form, one is major → REGIOSELECTIVE (not regiospecific).

E1 via H⁺ CLASSIFICATION (teacher's '#' section, page 2):
Same substrate + H⁺ (E1 conditions) → carbocation → α-alkene (Saytzeff) = 100%, ω-alkene (Hofmann) = 0%.
Labels: α = 100%, ω = 0% (right side of page shows the two possible alkene structures separated by a vertical line).
Conclusion: E1 via H⁺ gives ONLY Saytzeff = approaches REGIOSPECIFIC for Saytzeff product.
Why: carbocation at α-C → β-H loss from most substituted β-C → most substituted alkene = Saytzeff = only product (0% from terminal = Hofmann).

COMPLETE CLASSIFICATION TABLE:
| Reaction | Regioselective/Regiospecific? | Ratio |
|---|---|---|
| E2 (alc. KOH) | Regioselective | Major (Saytzeff) + minor (Hofmann) |
| E1 (H⁺, polar protic) | Approaches regiospecific | α = 100% (Saytzeff), ω = 0% |
| SN2 | Not a regiochemistry question (no regioisomers) | 100% one product |

IMPORTANT NOTE on ALPHA/OMEGA labeling (teacher, page 2):
- 'α' (alpha) = the more substituted product (Saytzeff product, from α-position = position adjacent to LG)
- 'ω' (omega) = the terminal/less substituted product (Hofmann product, from the other end)
- For E1 via H⁺: α = 100%, ω = 0% = extremely regioselective (regiospecific) for Saytzeff
- For E2: α = major (70-80%), ω = minor (20-30%) for GLG = regioselective
valid_transformations.mechanism: Regioselective: in E2, two different beta-H's (at beta-C with different substitution) compete for base. Saytzeff beta-H (from more substituted beta-C) has more electron density available for removal (more stabilized carbanion character in TS) AND gives more stable product → preferred in small-base E2. Hofmann beta-H (from less substituted beta-C) is less preferred under small-base/GLG conditions. Result: Saytzeff major + Hofmann minor = REGIOSELECTIVE (two products, one preferred). E1: carbocation at alpha-C forms → only beta-H from adjacent C matters → most substituted alkene = ONLY product (α = 100%).
valid_transformations.notes: Carbocation intermediate: check for rearrangement (1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shift) if a more stable cation is accessible.

valid_transformations.from: Acyclic alkyl bromide with specific beta-H configurations giving trans/cis geometric isomers in E2 — testing stereoselective classification
valid_transformations.to: E2 is STEREOSELECTIVE: trans (E) alkene = MAJOR product, cis (Z) alkene = MINOR product. Trans is major because anti-periplanar transition state leads to trans alkene for acyclic substrates with most common configurations. Teacher's example (page 3): secondary bromide (zig-zag with Br) + alc. KOH -> Trans (labeled 'Trans major') + Cis (labeled 'cis', minor). Teacher's conclusion: 'E2 is a stereoselective rxn' (underlined). Definition: stereoselective = two stereoisomers produced, one is major.
valid_transformations.conditions:
E2 STEREOSELECTIVITY vs STEREOSPECIFICITY — COMPLETE FRAMEWORK (RM lec9, pages 3-5):

'STEREOSELECTIVE RXN' DEFINITION (teacher verbatim, page 3):
'The rxns in which two stereoisomers are produced and out of them one is major are called stereoselective rxn.'

E2 = STEREOSELECTIVE because:
- From ONE substrate, two geometric stereoisomers (trans + cis) can form.
- Trans (E) is MAJOR, Cis (Z) is MINOR.
- Teacher's example: secondary Br substrate + alc. KOH/Δ → Trans (major) + Cis (minor).
- Both geometric isomers form, but one predominates.
- Conclusion (teacher): '→ E2 is a stereoselective rxn.' (underlined)

WHY TRANS IS MAJOR IN E2 (acyclic substrates):
Anti-periplanar TS (180° H-Cβ-Cα-L dihedral) → for acyclic substrates where the most commonly encountered conformation has H and L anti → gives trans (E) alkene as the major product (the two larger groups end up on opposite sides = trans/E).

'STEREOSPECIFIC RXN' DEFINITION (teacher verbatim, page 4, circled #):
'When two stereoisomers on rxn with particular reagent produces different stereoisomers then it is stereospecific rxn.'

E2 = ALSO STEREOSPECIFIC because:
- DIFFERENT substrate stereoisomers (diastereomers) give DIFFERENT product stereoisomers with the SAME reagent.
- Diastereomer 1 (page 5, Q1: Me top, D left, Br right, H bottom — Fischer) + alc. KOH/Δ → TRANS (E) alkene.
- Diastereomer 2 (page 5, Q2: the diastereomer = different D position) + alc. KOH/Δ → CIS (Z) alkene, labeled '(Cis)'.
- SAME REAGENT (alc. KOH), DIFFERENT SMs → DIFFERENT products → STEREOSPECIFIC.
- Conclusion (teacher): '→ E2 is stereospecific in nature.' (underlined)

EXAMPLE FROM PAGE 5 (using D-labeled substrates from 2-bromo-3-deuterobutane):
  Q1: Me/D/Br/H arranged in one diastereomeric configuration + alc. KOH/Δ → Trans alkene (Me and D on opposite sides)
  Q2: Me/D/Br/H in diastereomeric configuration + alc. KOH/Δ → Cis alkene, labeled '·(Cis)'
  TWO DIFFERENT STARTING MATERIAL DIASTEREOMERS → TWO DIFFERENT PRODUCT GEOMETRIC ISOMERS
  → STEREOSPECIFIC by definition.

BOTH PROPERTIES SIMULTANEOUSLY:
E2 is BOTH stereoselective (Trans > Cis from a single SM) AND stereospecific (different SM diastereomers give different geometric products). These are not mutually exclusive properties.

SN2 COMPARISON (page 5, bottom):
  R-L (config R) + Nu via SN2 → R-Nu (config S) [circle R on SM, circle S on product]
  R-L (config S) + Nu via SN2 → R-Nu (config R) [circle S on SM, circle R on product]
  → SN2 is a stereospecific rxn (underlined)
  → SN2 gives 100% INVERSION = R→S and S→R = different SMs give different products.
  Also from page 3: 'SN2 is a _____ (100% + 0%)' = stereospecific [the blank = stereospecific].
valid_transformations.mechanism: Stereoselective: from one acyclic substrate, anti-periplanar TS → trans (E) product preferred because the anti-periplanar conformation (H and L at 180°) places the two remaining groups trans to each other in the alkene → trans = major. Cis requires syn-periplanar or gauche conformations → higher energy TS → minor. Stereospecific: for Diastereomer 1 with specific H-Cβ-Cα-L dihedral of 180° in the anti-periplanar conformation, the product has specific E or Z geometry determined EXACTLY by the starting configuration. Diastereomer 2 has different anti-periplanar conformation → different E/Z outcome. The product stereochemistry is DICTATED by the SM stereochemistry.
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.from: Chiral alkyl substrate R-L (with R or S configuration) reacted with nucleophile via SN2, then via SN1 — testing stereospecific vs non-stereospecific classification
valid_transformations.to: SN2: STEREOSPECIFIC (R substrate -> S product, 100% inversion; S substrate -> R product, 100% inversion; two different SMs give two different products). SN1: NOT stereospecific. 'Real SN1 is loosely stereoselective (60+40)' (teacher verbatim, page 4) = in practice gives ~60% inversion + 40% retention (not true 50:50 racemic). Reason: departing L- partially shields one face even after ionization (ion pair) -> slightly more inversion than retention. SN1 is 'not stereoselective' (teacher, page 4) in the strict sense but loosely so. SN1 is 'not stereospecific' (teacher, page 6).
valid_transformations.conditions:
SN2 vs SN1 STEREOSPECIFICITY — COMPLETE COMPARISON (RM lec9, pages 3-6):

SN2 CLASSIFICATION — STEREOSPECIFIC:
  Teacher (page 5): R-L (circle R) + Nu via SN2 → R-Nu (circle S)
                    R-L (circle S) + Nu via SN2 → R-Nu (circle R)
  Different SM enantiomers → different product enantiomers with SAME reagent (Nu, SN2 conditions).
  → '→ SN2 is a stereospecific rxn.' (underlined)
  Also from page 3: SN2 gives (100% + 0%) = 100% inversion, 0% retention.
  Mechanism: backside attack → always INVERSION → R→S and S→R (Walden inversion).

SN1 CLASSIFICATION — NOT STEREOSPECIFIC:
  Teacher (page 6): '→ SN1 is not stereospecific rxn.' (underlined)
  Mechanism: ionization → planar carbocation → Nu attacks from BOTH faces:
    Ideal: 50% inversion (from rear face) + 50% retention (from same face) = 100% racemic.
    This is NOT stereospecific (same product regardless of SM configuration).

SN1 STEREOSELECTIVITY NUANCES:
  Teacher (page 4, underlined): '→ SN1 is not stereoselective.'
  Teacher (page 4, underlined): '→ Real SN1 is loosely stereoselective (60+40).'
  'Loosely stereoselective (60+40)' = 60% inversion + 40% retention in REAL (practical) SN1.
  Why 60:40 not 50:50?
    The departing L⁻ remains associated with the carbocation (ion pair) briefly after C-L breaks.
    L⁻ partially blocks one face (the face it departed from = the retention face).
    Nu attacks more from the OTHER face (inversion face) → 60% inversion, 40% retention.
    True 50:50 racemization only if the ion pair fully dissociates to a free carbocation.
  So: 'Not stereoselective' in the strict textbook sense; 'loosely stereoselective (60+40)' in reality.
  Neither statement = stereospecific (same configuration = different products from different SMs).

COMPLETE STEREOSPECIFICITY TABLE:
| Reaction | Stereospecific? | Stereoselective? | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| SN2 | YES | YES (extreme) | 100% inversion (R→S, S→R) |
| SN1 | NO | NO (loosely: 60+40) | ~60% inv + ~40% ret |
| E2 | YES | YES (trans major) | Trans > Cis |
| E1 | NO | YES (Saytzeff major) | Saytzeff major |

SN2 is BOTH stereospecific (different SMs give different products) AND stereoselective in the extreme sense (100% + 0% = only one stereoisomeric product).
valid_transformations.mechanism: SN2: single-step backside attack → inversion of configuration at the chiral center (Walden inversion). R-configured SM → backside Nu approach → S-configured product. S-configured SM → backside Nu → R-configured product. Two different SMs give two different products = stereospecific. Mechanism enforces 100% inversion → stereoselective at 100:0 level. SN1: two-step, carbocation intermediate is sp2 planar → no face preference in ideal case → racemization (50:50). In practice: ion pair = L⁻ blocks retention face → 60% inversion (more common), 40% retention = 'loosely stereoselective.' Not stereospecific: R and S substrates both give the SAME racemic (or near-racemic) product mixture.
valid_transformations.notes: Carbocation intermediate: check for rearrangement (1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shift) if a more stable cation is accessible.

valid_transformations.from: Tertiary (or secondary) alkyl halide or substrate treated with POLAR PROTIC SOLVENT (H2O, R-OH, R-COOH, R-NH2) and heat (Delta) — E1 vs SN1 competition, temperature decides ratio
valid_transformations.to: E1 product (alkene, Saytzeff = major from E1) AND/OR SN1 product (alcohol/ether from SN1), ratio determined by TEMPERATURE. Teacher's NOTE (page 7): 'Till 60 degrees C: S > E' (= substitution > elimination below 60 degrees C). 'Above 60 degrees C: E > S' (= elimination > substitution above 60 degrees C). ΔG = ΔH - TΔS: at high T, TΔS term favors E (alkene, ΔS more positive: alkene + H2O/HX vs alcohol/ether) → E becomes thermodynamically more favorable. At low T, ΔH term dominates → SN1 (alcohol/ether product is more stable, ΔH more negative) = S > E. Polar protic reagents for E1: H2O/Δ, R-OH/Δ, R-COOH/Δ, R-NH2/Δ (all polar protic = E1/SN1 conditions). R-O- (alkoxide) = E2 conditions (NOT E1).
valid_transformations.conditions:
E1 vs SN1 TEMPERATURE COMPETITION (RM lec9, page 7):

TEACHER'S NOTE (underlined, page 7):
'Note:- Till 60°C: S > E'
'Above 60°C: E > S'

This applies to the E1 vs SN1 competition from the SAME carbocation intermediate (both share the ionization step).

THERMODYNAMIC EXPLANATION (ΔG = ΔH - TΔS):
ΔG = ΔH - TΔS (teacher writes ΔG = ΔH - TΔS (-ve))

For SUBSTITUTION (S, SN1): R⁺ + H₂O → R-OH (alcohol)
  Product = alcohol (more stable, ΔH contribution = favorable)
  ΔS is relatively small (one product formed, limited entropy gain)
  At LOW T: ΔH dominates → SN1 (S) product = thermodynamic product = major

For ELIMINATION (E, E1): R⁺ → alkene + H⁺
  Products = alkene + H⁺ (two molecules formed from one carbocation = more products)
  ΔS is LARGER (more disorder from alkene formation + solvent reorganization)
  The TΔS term INCREASES with T → at HIGH T, TΔS for E becomes larger → ΔG for E becomes more negative → E > S
  At HIGH T (>60°C): TΔS dominates → E1 (elimination) = major

TEACHER'S ENERGY DIAGRAM (page 8, bottom left):
  U-shaped energy profile: E product is at higher energy (+ve region of the curve = less stable thermodynamically)
  S product is at the MINIMUM (lower energy = more stable thermodynamically)
  BUT: higher T shifts selectivity toward E because entropy (TΔS) compensates the enthalpy gap.

REAGENTS THAT GIVE E1 CONDITIONS (teacher's '#' list, page 7):
  - H₂O/Δ
  - R-OH/Δ (alcohol solvent, protic)
  - R-COOH/Δ (carboxylic acid, protic)
  - R-NH₂/Δ (amine as protic source)
  ALL are POLAR PROTIC → stabilize carbocation → E1/SN1 conditions

CRITICAL DISTINCTION — Alkoxide vs Alcohol (teacher's table, page 9):
  R-O⁻/Δ = E2 (alkoxide = BASE → E2)
  R-O⁻/R-OH,Δ = E2 (alkoxide in its conjugate acid alcohol = still E2)
  R-OH,Δ = E1 (alcohol ONLY, no alkoxide = no base → E1/SN1)
  EVEN t-BuOH (tert-butanol) → E1, NOT E2 (t-BuO⁻ → E2, but t-BuOH → E1)

PRODUCT COUNTING (teacher's section, page 8):
  For tertiary substrates + CH₃OH/Δ: must count ALL possible products = E1 products + SN1 products.
  Teacher labels: 'All possible products: (E1 + SN1)'
  Examples from page 8: substrates giving 1, 2, or 6 total products (E1 alkenes + SN1 ethers/alcohols combined).
valid_transformations.mechanism: Shared carbocation intermediate: Substrate + polar protic/Δ → C⁺ (carbocation). From C⁺: Path E1 (fast -H⁺ from β-C → alkene, Saytzeff); Path SN1 (fast +Nu (H₂O, ROH) → alcohol/ether). Temperature controls which path dominates: Low T (<60°C): ΔH controls → SN1 (alcohol/ether more stable). High T (>60°C): TΔS controls → E1 (more entropic, more fragments). This is from ΔG = ΔH - TΔS where S product has smaller ΔS and E product has larger ΔS.
valid_transformations.notes: Carbocation intermediate: check for rearrangement (1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shift) if a more stable cation is accessible.

valid_transformations.from: Substrate with (a) at least one electron-withdrawing group (-M group: C=O, NO2, CN, SO2R, CF3) at or near beta-C AND (b) poor leaving group (PLG: F, OPh, OR, NR3+) — E1CB conditions
valid_transformations.to: Alkene via E1CB mechanism. Step 1 (FAST, equilibrium): strong base removes acidic beta-H (acidic because adjacent to EWG = -M group) -> carbanion at beta-C (= 'conjugate base' = CB, stabilized by EWG resonance). Step 2 (SLOW, RDS): L- departs (unimolecular: carbanion -> alkene + L-). Rate: first-order w.r.t. CB intermediate; OVERALL ORDER = 2 (BOXED: Overall order = 2) because CB depends on [substrate][base]. Overall Rate = K'[substrate][base]. 'E1CB' = Unimolecular w.r.t. Conjugate Base (the RDS involves only the carbanion = unimolecular in RDS). Teacher conditions: (1) at least one -M group must be present; (2) poor leaving groups should be present.
valid_transformations.conditions:
E1CB (UNIMOLECULAR ELIMINATION w.r.t. CONJUGATE BASE) — COMPLETE FORMAL INTRODUCTION (RM lec9, page 10):

TEACHER LABEL: '# E1CB (Unimolecular elimination rxn w.r.t - conjugate base)' (underlined)

NAME EXPLANATION:
  E1CB = Elimination (1) Conjugate Base
  'Unimolecular' refers to the RDS = Step 2 (carbanion → alkene + L⁻ is unimolecular, involves only the carbanion)
  'w.r.t. Conjugate Base' = the RDS involves the conjugate base (carbanion intermediate), not the original substrate
  Contrast: E1 = unimolecular w.r.t. substrate (ionization in RDS); E1CB = unimolecular w.r.t. carbanion

MECHANISM (teacher's diagram):
  -C-C- (β-C has acidic H, α-C has L = LG) in a U-shape (suggests EWG near β-C makes H acidic)
  Step 1 (FAST, ⇌ equilibrium, OVAL LABELED 'fast'):
    Strong base + H-Cβ → Carbanion (⊖) at β-C = the 'Conjugate Base (CB)'
    This is fast because the base is strong AND β-H is acidic (activated by EWG)
    The carbanion is STABILIZED by the adjacent EWG (-M group)
    This step is a FAST EQUILIBRIUM (not fast-irreversible): ⇌ not →
  Step 2 (SLOW, RDS, → not ⇌):
    ⁻Cβ-Cα-L → L⁻ departs → Cβ=Cα (alkene) formed
    'slow' label on arrow
    This is the UNIMOLECULAR step (only carbanion involved)

CONDITIONS (teacher, 'Cond'n:', left box, underlined):
  ① 'at least -M group must be present' = at least one electron-withdrawing group (-M = mesomeric withdrawing group, e.g., C=O, NO₂, CN, SO₂R, CF₃, halogens) must be present at β-C to stabilize the carbanion intermediate.
  ② 'Poor leaving groups should be present' = PLG required. If GLG (I, Br, Cl) present → E2 would occur instead (E2 is faster with GLG). PLG (F, OPh, OR, NR₃⁺, OTs in some contexts) → E1CB because PLG cannot depart in Step 1; the carbanion must form first.

RATE LAWS (teacher's numbered list):
  ① Rate ∝ [-⊖-C-C-/L]¹ → rate is first-order in the carbanion (CB) intermediate
  ② 'order = 1 w.r.t. C.B.' = unimolecular in the RDS (only carbanion in RDS → order = 1 for step 2)
  ③ K = [CB] / ([substrate][Base]ⁿ) = equilibrium constant for Step 1
     Rearranging: [CB] = K × [substrate][Base]
     Substituting into Rate₂ = k₂[CB]:
     Rate = k₂ × K × [substrate][Base] = K'[substrate][Base]

  OVERALL RATE = K'[-C-C-][Base] (teacher writes explicitly at bottom)
  OVERALL ORDER = 2 (BOXED by teacher, bottom left)
  Note: 'overall order = 2' makes E1CB look like E2 in kinetics, but the mechanism is fundamentally different!

COMPARISON TABLE — E1CB vs E1 vs E2:
| Feature | E1CB | E1 | E2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Overall order | 2 | 1 | 2 |
| Rate law | k[substrate][base] | k[substrate] | k[substrate][base] |
| RDS | Carbanion → alkene (unimolecular) | Ionization (C-L break) | Concerted |
| Intermediate | Carbanion (CB) | Carbocation | None |
| EWG needed? | YES (-M at β-C) | No | No |
| LG needed | PLG (F, OPh...) | GLG or PLG | GLG preferred |
| Stereochemistry | Not stereospecific | Not stereospecific | Stereospecific (anti) |
| D-exchange | YES (carbanion exchanges H/D before LG departs) | No | No |
| KIE | kH/kD = 1 (C-H in fast step, not RDS) | kH/kD = 1 | kH/kD ≥ 7 |

DIAGNOSTIC TEST FOR E1CB:
  D-exchange: react substrate with deuterated base/solvent (e.g. EtO⁻/EtOD).
  If E1CB: carbanion forms → exchanges H for D from EtOD → D incorporated at β-C before LG departs.
  Teacher's Q⑤ (page 12): Ph-CH₂CH₂F + EtO⁻/EtOD → Ph-CH=CH₂, and 'D exchange will be observed' (quoted).
  If E2: concerted → no carbanion intermediate → no D exchange (H goes directly to base in one step).
valid_transformations.mechanism: Two-step: Step 1 (fast ⇌): Strong base abstracts acidic β-H (activated by adjacent EWG/-M group) → carbanion at β-C (CB, stabilized by EWG resonance). This is a fast equilibrium. Step 2 (slow, RDS, unimolecular): carbanion (CB) expels PLG as L⁻ → C=C forms. Rate = k₂[CB] = k₂·K[substrate][base] = K'[substrate][base] → overall order 2. The carbanion in E1CB is the key intermediate: it is a nucleophile/carbanion = the 'conjugate base' of the β-C-H acid. PLG departs in the slow step, which is why PLG works in E1CB (whereas GLG departs easily in E2 before the carbanion can form properly).
valid_transformations.notes: EAS: product regiochemistry determined by existing substituent(s). Check for conflicting or cooperating directors before assigning major product.

valid_transformations.from: 2-Phenylethyl fluoride (Ph-CH2-CH2-F, beta-phenethyl fluoride) treated with strong base (OH-, EtO-) — E1CB example with benzylic carbanion stabilization and F as PLG
valid_transformations.to: Styrene (Ph-CH=CH2, vinylbenzene) via E1CB mechanism. Step 1 (fast): OH- or EtO- removes benzylic H (alpha to Ph = acidic by Ph resonance stabilization of carbanion) -> Ph-CH--CH2-F (benzylic carbanion, stabilized by benzene ring pi system = -M group). Step 2 (slow): F- departs (PLG: C-F strong bond, F is PLG in elimination) -> Ph-CH=CH2 (styrene). Teacher's Q3 (page 11): Ph-CH2-CH2-F + OH-/Delta -> Ph-CH=CH2. Teacher's Q5 (page 12): Same substrate + C2H5O-/C2H5OD -> Ph-CH=CH2 + 'D exchange will be observed' (quoted). D-exchange = DIAGNOSTIC FOR E1CB: carbanion (Ph-CH--CH2-F) is stable enough to abstract D from EtOD before F- departs. IUPAC: (2-fluoroethyl)benzene + hydroxide -> ethenylbenzene (styrene).
reagents: C2H5O-/Delta in C2H5OD (diagnostic: D exchange observed)
valid_transformations.conditions:
E1CB OF (2-FLUOROETHYL)BENZENE → ETHENYLBENZENE (STYRENE) (RM lec9, pages 11-12):

SUBSTRATE: Ph-CH₂-CH₂-F = (2-fluoroethyl)benzene (IUPAC)
  The Ph group (phenyl) at the β-C acts as the EWG (-M group: through resonance, carbanion at benzylic position is stabilized by delocalization into the benzene ring).
  F = poor leaving group (PLG: C-F bond is very strong = ~485 kJ/mol; F⁻ is poor LG in both E2 and SN2, but works as LG in E1CB because the carbanion forms FIRST in the slow-step).

MECHANISM:
Step 1 (fast): OH⁻ (or EtO⁻) removes the β-H at the benzylic position:
  Ph-CH₂-CH₂-F → [Ph-CH⁻-CH₂-F] (benzylic carbanion, stabilized by Ph resonance)
  Teacher's Q③ diagram: circled ⊕ on the carbanion C, adjacent to Ph and CH₂F.
Step 2 (slow, RDS): F⁻ departs from the terminal CH₂:
  [Ph-CH⁻-CH₂-F] → Ph-CH=CH₂ + F⁻
  Teacher diagram shows -F⁰ label (= -F⁻ departure, arrow down).
Product: Ph-CH=CH₂ = styrene = ethenylbenzene (IUPAC)

DIAGNOSTIC D-EXCHANGE (teacher's Q⑤, page 12):
Same substrate + C₂H₅O⁻/Δ in C₂H₅OD (deuterated ethanol):
  Step 1 forms benzylic carbanion: Ph-CH⁻-CH₂-F
  The carbanion is SUFFICIENTLY STABLE (benzylic) → it persists for some time before F⁻ departs
  During this time, it can abstract D from C₂H₅OD → Ph-CHD-CH₂-F (D incorporated at benzylic C)
  Then F⁻ departs → Ph-CD=CH₂ or Ph-CH=CH₂ (with D incorporated)
  Teacher annotation: '"D exchange will be observed"' (quoted)
  This H/D exchange is the DIAGNOSTIC TEST FOR E1CB: only possible if a carbanion intermediate forms (E1CB). Does NOT occur in E2 (concerted, no carbanion) or E1 (different intermediate).

Product (both Q③ and Q⑤): Ph-CH=CH₂ = BOXED in Q⑤ = 'Ph-(CD)=CH₂' or 'Ph-CH=CH₂' = ethenylbenzene.

EWG RATIONALE:
Ph = -M group through resonance: carbanion at benzylic C is delocalized into the benzene ring:
  Ph-CH⁻-CH₂-F ↔ [ring with delocalized negative charge] = stabilized enough for E1CB.
  CF₃ is also -M (Q④): R-CH₂-CF₃ + OH⁻ → [R-CH⁻-CF₃] (CF₃ stabilizes carbanion by induction) → R-CH=CF₂ (product = 1,1-difluoroalkene, BOXED on page 12).
  NO₂ is also -M (Q②): ring-N⁺/CH₂CH₂NO₂ substrate + OH⁻ → [CH₂⁻-CH₂-NO₂ = nitronate resonance] → CH₂=CH-NO₂ (vinyl nitro compound).
valid_transformations.mechanism: E1CB: Step 1 (fast): EtO⁻ removes benzylic H → [Ph-CH⁻-CH₂-F] (benzylic carbanion). Carbanion is stabilized by Ph (benzyl resonance). Step 2 (slow): F⁻ departs → Ph-CH=CH₂. D-exchange test: if EtOD is the solvent, the carbanion [Ph-CH⁻-CH₂-F] picks up D from EtOD before F⁻ departs → D-label appears in starting material (H/D exchange at β-C). This exchange proves the carbanion intermediate exists with a finite lifetime (long enough to exchange before LG departs = E1CB, not E2 or concerted).

valid_transformations.from: Beta-phenoxy phenyl sulfone (Ph-SO2-CH(alpha)-CH2-OPh) or beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound treated with OH- or strong base/Delta — E1CB with sulfonyl or carbonyl EWG and phenoxy/alkoxide as leaving group
valid_transformations.to: Vinyl sulfone (Ph-SO2-C=CH2) or alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl (enone) via E1CB. EWG = Ph-SO2 (sulfonyl = powerful -M group, activates alpha-C-H) or C=O (carbonyl, activates beta-C-H in beta-hydroxy carbonyls). PLG = OPh (phenoxide = relatively stable anion, better than alkoxide but still PLG under basic E1CB conditions) or OH- in beta-hydroxy carbonyl. Teacher's Q6 (page 12): Ph-SO2-CH(alpha)-CH2-OPh + OH-/Delta -> [Ph-SO2-C-(alpha)--CH2-OPh] (carbanion stabilized by SO2Ph) -> Ph-O- departs -> Ph-SO2-C=CH2 (vinyl sulfone, BOXED). Teacher's Q1 (page 11): beta-hydroxy ketone + OH-/Delta -> E1CB -> enone (alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone, dehydration under basic conditions).
valid_transformations.conditions:
E1CB WITH SULFONYL AND CARBONYL EWG (RM lec9, pages 11-12):

E1CB EXAMPLES WITH DIFFERENT EWG/-M GROUPS:

**Q① (page 11) — Beta-hydroxy carbonyl + OH⁻ → Enone (E1CB):**
Substrate: Cyclohexanone ring with -CH(M)-OH pendant (β-hydroxy ketone)
  EWG (-M group) = C=O (carbonyl): the β-H adjacent to C=O is α to the ketone = acidic (pKa ~20 for ketone α-H).
  PLG = -OH (hydroxyl/alkoxide): under basic conditions, OH is converted to O⁻ (alkoxide) = the LG.
  Mechanism: OH⁻ removes α-H → [carbanion at α-C, stabilized by C=O] → O⁻ departs (as alkoxide, E1CB step) → enone.
  Product: α,β-unsaturated ketone (enone = conjugated C=C-C=O).
  This is the ALDOL CONDENSATION PRODUCT via E1CB pathway (base-promoted dehydration of β-hydroxy carbonyl).

**Q② (page 11) — Quaternary ammonium with NO₂ chain + OH⁻ → vinyl nitro (E1CB):**
Substrate: N⁺(quaternary) ring with -CH₂-CH₂-NO₂ chain.
  EWG (-M group) = NO₂ (nitryl group, very strong -M via resonance: R-CH₂-NO₂ → R-CH=N(O)O⁻ = nitronate anion).
  PLG = N⁺ (quaternary ammonium = PLG in E1CB, similar to Hofmann elimination).
  Mechanism: OH⁻ removes H from -CH₂- adjacent to NO₂ → [carbanion = nitronate anion -CH⁻-NO₂ ↔ -CH=N(O)O⁻] → N-C bond breaks (N departs as tertiary amine) → CH₂=CH-NO₂.
  Product: CH₂=CH-NO₂ (nitroethylene = 1-nitroethene, IUPAC: nitroethene, labeled by teacher).

**Q⑥ (page 12) — β-Phenoxy phenyl sulfone + OH⁻ → vinyl sulfone (E1CB):**
Substrate: Ph-SO₂-CH(α)(H)-CH₂-OPh
  EWG (-M group) = Ph-SO₂ (phenylsulfonyl = sulfonyl group, strong -M: S=O pulls electron density strongly, pKa of α-H to sulfonyl ≈ 23-25, very acidic).
  PLG = -OPh (phenoxy = phenoxide Ph-O⁻ is more stable anion than alkoxide R-O⁻ due to Ph resonance, making it a better LG than -OR).
  Mechanism: OH⁻ removes H at α-C (adjacent to Ph-SO₂) → [Ph-SO₂-C⁻(α)-CH₂-OPh] (carbanion strongly stabilized by sulfonyl EWG) → Ph-O⁻ departs (phenoxide, shown with curved arrow) → Ph-SO₂-C(α)=CH₂.
  Product: Ph-SO₂-C(α)=CH₂ (vinyl sulfone, BOXED by teacher = Ph-S(=O)(=O)-CR=CH₂, sulfonyl vinyl compound).
  Labels: 'Ph-S-C=CH₂' with 'O' and 'b' labels on S = the two O's of sulfonyl.

EWG RANKING FOR E1CB ACTIVATION (from teacher's examples):
  NO₂ > CN > SO₂R (sulfonyl) > C=O (carbonyl) > Ph (phenyl) > CF₃
  All are -M groups. The more powerful the EWG, the more acidic the β-H, the faster the carbanion formation in Step 1.
valid_transformations.mechanism: E1CB with Ph-SO₂ EWG: Step 1 (fast): OH⁻ removes α-H (activated by sulfonyl) → [Ph-SO₂-C⁻-CH₂-OPh] (carbanion; sulfonyl resonance: Ph-SO₂-C⁻ ↔ Ph-S(O)=O...C⁻ = stabilized). Step 2 (slow): Ph-O⁻ departs → vinyl sulfone Ph-SO₂-C=CH₂. For β-hydroxy ketone: OH⁻ removes α-H (C=O activates it) → carbanion → β-O⁻ departs → enone. Both follow the same E1CB two-step: fast carbanion formation (EWG stabilized) → slow PLG departure.
valid_transformations.notes: Archetype ['I', 'III'] transformation. Verify conditions carefully; the reagent identity determines mechanism and hence product regiochemistry/stereochemistry.

SYN elimination (H and OAc must be syn-periplanar). Hofmann rule (less substituted alkene = major). Temperature: 500 degrees C (high, no solvent). Products: alkene + R-COOH (carboxylic acid). Teacher: 'Syn elimination' + 'Follow Hofmann rule' (both underlined, page 1). RESONANCE > HOFMANN also applies (Q6 page 2: boxed 'Hoff 7 Reso' = if conjugated alkene possible, that wins). valid_transformations.conditions:
ESTER PYROLYSIS (Ei MECHANISM) — COMPLETE (RM lec 10 p1, pages 1-3):

NAME: Ei = Elimination through Internal base. For esters: the C=O oxygen IS the internal base that abstracts the β-H.
PYROLYSIS = pyro (heat) + lysis (break). Thermal decomposition.

SUBSTRATE: R-C(=O)-O-CH₂-CH₂-R' (any ester with at least one β-H available = H on the C adjacent to the O of the ester, syn to the O-C=O group).

CONDITIONS:
  Temperature: Δ/500°C (very high — vapor phase pyrolysis)
  No solvent, no base, no acid needed
  Purely thermal

MECHANISM (6-MEMBERED CYCLIC TRANSITION STATE):
  The TS ring: O(of C=O)···H-Cβ-Cα-O-C(=O) = 6 atoms in ring
  Sequence: [C=O oxygen] abstacts [syn β-H] via a 6-membered ring TS
  Simultaneously: Cα-O bond breaks (the ester C-O single bond, not the C=O double bond)
  All concerted in one cyclic TS (no intermediate)

GEOMETRY REQUIREMENT:
  H (at β-C) and OC(=O)R (at α-C) must be SYN-PERIPLANAR (0° H-Cβ-Cα-O dihedral)
  The 6-membered cyclic TS enforces syn geometry
  ANTI-PERIPLANAR IS NOT REQUIRED (contrast with E2)
  → SYN ELIMINATION → SYN PERIPLANAR

PRODUCTS:
  Alkene + R-COOH (carboxylic acid)
  The acid byproduct is the carboxylate portion of the ester.
  Teacher Q①: OAc ester → alkene + CH₃COOH (acetic acid, underlined)

SELECTIVITY RULES:
  1. HOFMANN RULE (teacher underlined): less substituted alkene = major (same as bulky base E2 or Cope)
     Reason: Ei cyclic TS avoids steric strain; less hindered β-H (at 1°/terminal C) is more accessible in the 6-membered ring geometry
  2. RESONANCE > HOFMANN (teacher's Q⑥ page 2, BOXED: 'Hoff 7 Reso'):
     If a conjugated alkene is possible, it wins over the simple Hofmann product
     Same hierarchy as Cope and E2
  3. SYN GEOMETRY: the syn-periplanar β-H is removed. If a substrate has no syn-periplanar β-H available (rigid geometry), NO REACTION occurs.
     → Teacher Q⑨ (page 3): norbornyl OAc + Δ → 'No rxn' (underlined): the rigid bicyclic cage prevents any β-H from achieving syn-periplanar arrangement with OAc.

STEREOSPECIFICITY:
  Ester pyrolysis IS stereospecific (syn-specific):
  Different diastereomers give different geometric alkene products.
  Teacher Q⑧ (page 3): D-labeled diastereomer with H and OAc syn-periplanar → Trans (E) alkene labeled 'Trans.'
  The syn elimination determines whether E or Z alkene forms from a given diastereomer.

EXAMPLES (teacher pages 2-3):
  Q① acyclic OAc → acyclic alkene + CH₃COOH
  Q② cyclooctyl OAc → cyclooctene
  Q③ trans-1,4-cyclohexanediol di-OAc → 1,4-cyclohexadiene (double elimination)
  Q⑥ bicyclic di-OAc → bicyclic alkene, BOXED 'Hoff 7 Reso'
  Q⑨ norbornyl OAc + Δ → 'No rxn' (no syn β-H in rigid cage)
  Q⑩ constrained OAc → 97.5% one regioisomeric alkene

COMPARISON WITH OTHER Ei MECHANISMS:
| Feature | Ester Pyrolysis | Chugaev (Xanthate) | Cope (N-oxide) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Internal base | C=O oxygen | S of C=S | N-O⁻ oxygen |
| TS ring size | 6-membered | 6-membered | 5-membered |
| Temperature | ~500°C | ~200°C | ≥100°C |
| Syn/Anti | SYN | SYN | SYN |
| Hofmann? | YES | YES | YES |
| Byproduct | RCOOH (acid) | COS + MeSH | R₂NOH (hydroxylamine) |
| From | Ester | Xanthate ester | Amine N-oxide |
valid_transformations.mechanism: Ei (ester pyrolysis): 6-membered cyclic TS — C=O oxygen acts as internal base abstracting the syn β-H (H that is syn-periplanar = 0° dihedral relative to the ester O-C=O). Simultaneously Cα-O bond cleaves. All bonds break/form synchronously in one concerted step (no intermediate). Product: alkene (less substituted = Hofmann, unless resonance possible = then conjugated wins) + RCOOH. The 6-membered ring requires syn geometry, enforcing syn elimination.
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.from: Alcohol (R-OH) converted to methyl xanthate ester (R-O-C(=S)-S-Me) in 4 steps then heated to approximately 200 degrees C — Chugaev Reaction (Ei pyrolysis of xanthate)
valid_transformations.to: Alkene (Hofmann = less substituted = major) + COS (carbonyl sulfide = O=C=S) + MeSH (methanethiol = methyl mercaptan). Mechanism: Ei via 6-membered cyclic TS using S of C=S as internal base abstracting syn beta-H. Products: alkene + O=C=S (COS) + H-S-Me (MeSH). Temperature: approximately 200 degrees C (milder than ester pyrolysis 500 degrees C). PREPARATION: R-OH -> (1) Na -> R-ONa -> (2) CS2 -> R-O-C(=S)-SNa -> (3) Me-I/SN2 -> R-O-C(=S)-SMe (xanthate ester) -> (4) Delta/200 degrees C -> alkene + COS + MeSH. Syn elimination. Hofmann rule. Resonance > Hofmann. IUPAC of xanthate: O-alkyl S-methyl carbonodithioate. Teacher (page 4-5): 'Follow Hofmann rule' + 'It is syn elimination' + 'Hoff < Reso.' (all underlined).
valid_transformations.conditions:
CHUGAEV REACTION (PYROLYSIS OF XANTHATE) — COMPLETE (RM lec 10 p1, pages 4-5):

NAME: Chugaev Reaction = pyrolysis of an xanthate ester to give an alkene. Also a type of Ei elimination.

STEP 1 — XANTHATE PREPARATION (4 reagent steps):
  Starting material: R-OH (any secondary or primary alcohol with β-H)
  Step ①: Na (sodium metal) → R-O⁻Na⁺ (sodium alkoxide)
  Step ②: CS₂ (carbon disulfide) → R-O-C(=S)-S⁻Na⁺ (sodium xanthate salt)
    [The O-C(=S)-S⁻ unit = xanthate anion]
  Step ③: Me-I (methyl iodide) / SN2 → R-O-C(=S)-S-Me (methyl xanthate ester)
    The S⁻ alkylates on the sulfur (SN2 on Me-I)
  Step ④: Δ (~200°C) → elimination → alkene + COS + MeSH

XANTHATE STRUCTURE (teacher label 'Xanthate:'):
  R-O-C(=S)-S-Me = O-alkyl S-methyl ester of dithiocarbonic acid
  IUPAC: O-alkyl S-methyl carbonodithioate
  Key functional group: the O-C(=S)-SMe unit where: O is bonded to Cα; C= is double-bonded to S; SMe = methylthio group

STEP 2 — CHUGAEV PYROLYSIS MECHANISM (6-MEMBERED CYCLIC TS):
  Substrate: Cα(O-C(=S)-SMe)-Cβ(H)-...
  The SYN β-H (syn to the O-C=S unit) is abstracted internally.
  6-membered cyclic TS: S(of C=S)···H-Cβ-Cα-O-C(=S) = 6 atoms in ring
  [Counting: S (1), H (2), Cβ (3), Cα (4), O (5), C= (6) → 6-membered ring]
  Internal base = S of the C=S group (the sulfur abstracts the β-H)
  Simultaneously: Cα-O bond breaks (homolytically with electron pair going to C=S to generate COS)
  All concerted in one cyclic TS → syn elimination

PRODUCTS:
  Alkene (the syn elimination product, Hofmann = less substituted = major)
  + O=C=S (COS = carbonyl sulfide = the C of the xanthate becomes COS)
  + H-S-Me (MeSH = methanethiol = the SMe group picks up the β-H)
  Teacher labels at bottom: 'Mesh + O=C=S' (= MeSH + COS = two co-products)

PROPERTIES (teacher's three conclusions, page 5):
  '→ Follow Hofmann rule' (underlined)
  '→ It is syn elimination' (underlined)
  '→ Hoff < Reso.' (= Resonance > Hofmann)

TEMPERATURE COMPARISON:
  Chugaev (~200°C) < Cope (≥100°C) vs Ester pyrolysis (~500°C)
  Chugaev is preferred over ester pyrolysis when the alcohol-derived alkene is desired at milder conditions.
  The xanthate group (C=S) is a better internal H-abstracting base than ester C=O → lower activation energy → lower T.

SELECTIVITY:
  Hofmann (less substituted) = major
  If conjugated alkene possible → Resonance > Hofmann (conjugated wins)
  Syn β-H geometry required; substrates with no accessible syn β-H → no reaction

EXAMPLES (teacher pages 4-5):
  Q (double underlined): complex chain xanthate + Δ → conjugated diene + COS + SM (SMe group byproduct)
  Q2: cyclohexane-1,4-di(xanthate) + Δ → cyclohex-1,4-diene (double Chugaev elimination)

COMPARE EI MECHANISMS:
  Ester pyrolysis: 6-membered TS, O of C=O abstracts H, products = alkene + RCOOH, ~500°C
  Chugaev: 6-membered TS, S of C=S abstracts H, products = alkene + COS + MeSH, ~200°C
  Cope: 5-membered TS, O of N-O⁻ abstracts H, products = alkene + R₂NOH, ≥100°C
  ALL THREE: syn elimination, Hofmann rule, Resonance > Hofmann
valid_transformations.mechanism: Chugaev Ei: 6-membered cyclic TS [S···H-Cβ-Cα-O-C(=S)]. The thiocarboxyl S atom (of C=S) acts as internal base abstracting the syn β-H. Simultaneously, Cα-O bond breaks, releasing the O-C(=S)-SMe fragment. The electrons from Cβ-H go to form C=C (alkene). The O-C(=S)-SMe fragment reorganizes: C becomes COS (O=C=S) + H goes to SMе → MeSH. All concerted. Syn-periplanar β-H required. Products: alkene (Hofmann major) + COS + MeSH.
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.from: Tertiary amine (R3N, lone pair) treated with oxidizing agent (O3, Ag2O, MgO, H2O2, or peracid R-C(=O)-O-OH) — preparation of tertiary amine N-oxide for Cope elimination
valid_transformations.to: Tertiary amine N-oxide (R3N+-O-). The N lone pair attacks the oxidant oxygen -> N-O bond forms -> N becomes R3N+(O-) = amine N-oxide (N has +charge, O has -charge). Oxidizing agents (teacher's list, page 5): O3 (ozone); Ag2O (silver oxide); MgO (magnesium oxide); H2O2 (hydrogen peroxide = most common in lab); Peracid (R-C(=O)-O-O-H, such as mCPBA = meta-chloroperoxybenzoic acid). Teacher: '3 degree amine oxide >= 100 degrees C / Delta -> alkene + N-hydroxylamine' (underlined). Then the N-oxide undergoes Cope elimination (syn, 5-membered TS) to give alkene + hydroxylamine.
valid_transformations.conditions:
PREPARATION OF AMINE N-OXIDE AND COPE ELIMINATION (RM lec 10 p1, page 5-6):

TEACHER HEADER (page 5): '③ Copes elimination' (circled, underlined)
KEY EQUATION (underlined): '3° amine oxide ≥100°C/Δ → alkene + N-hydroxylamine'

STEP 1 — OXIDATION OF TERTIARY AMINE TO N-OXIDE:
  3° amine (R₃N:, lone pair shown) + [O] → R₃N⁺-O⁻ (tertiary amine N-oxide)

OXIDIZING AGENTS (teacher's tree diagram, page 5):
  - O₃ (ozone) — strong oxidant, converts R₃N → R₃N⁺-O⁻
  - or Ag₂O (silver oxide)
  - or MgO (magnesium oxide) = mild oxidant
  - or H₂O₂ (hydrogen peroxide) = most common practical reagent
  - or Peracid (R-C(=O)-O-O-H) = labeled with '18' by teacher = mCPBA or m-CPBA
    The peracid transfers one of its O atoms (the terminal, electrophilic O) to the N lone pair.
    R₃N: + R'-C(=O)-O-OH → R₃N⁺-O⁻ + R'-COOH (the peracid becomes carboxylate)

N-OXIDE STRUCTURE:
  R₃N⁺-O⁻ (labeled '3° amine oxide' by teacher, underlined)
  N has positive charge (+), O has negative charge (-)
  The N-O bond = coordinate/dative bond from N lone pair to O
  This is the SUBSTRATE for Cope elimination

STEP 2 — COPE ELIMINATION (from amine N-oxide, already detailed in RM lec8b):
  3° amine oxide + Δ (≥100°C) → alkene + N-hydroxylamine (R₂N-OH)
  5-membered cyclic TS: O⁻-N-Cα-Cβ-H (O abstracts syn β-H)
  SYN elimination (H and N-O on same side)
  Hofmann rule (less substituted alkene = major)
  Resonance > Hofmann (if conjugated alkene possible)

COMPLETE SEQUENCE FROM AMINE TO ALKENE:
  R₃N: → [+O₃/Ag₂O/MgO/H₂O₂/peracid] → R₃N⁺-O⁻ → [Δ ≥100°C] → alkene + R₂NOH

SELECTIVITY:
  Hofmann rule (less substituted alkene = major) because:
  - 5-membered cyclic TS avoids steric strain
  - Same Hofmann selectivity as ester pyrolysis and Chugaev (all Ei)
  Resonance > Hofmann (conjugated wins, all Ei mechanisms)
  SYN elimination (not anti-periplanar, contrast with E2)
valid_transformations.mechanism: Amine oxidation: N lone pair attacks electrophilic O of H₂O₂ (or other oxidant) → N-O bond forms → H₂O leaves → R₃N⁺-O⁻ (amine N-oxide). The N-O⁻ bond is the key: O⁻ becomes the internal base in Cope elimination. Cope mechanism (Ei, 5-membered ring): O⁻ abstracts syn β-H while N-Cα bond breaks → alkene forms at Cα-Cβ, hydroxylamine R₂NOH is released.
valid_transformations.notes: Radical mechanism: initiation required (hν or ROOR). Chain process — omitting any propagation step loses marks in mechanism questions.

valid_transformations.from: Norbornyl (bicyclo[2.2.1]heptyl) ester or similar rigid cage ester substrate heated (Delta) — testing whether Ei/ester pyrolysis occurs in rigid bicyclic systems
valid_transformations.to: NO REACTION ('No rxn', underlined by teacher). Teacher Q9 (page 3): norbornyl OAc + Delta -> 'No rxn'. Reason: in the rigid bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane (norbornane) framework, the geometry of the ring system prevents ANY beta-H from achieving a syn-periplanar (0 degree dihedral) arrangement with the OAc leaving group. Ei pyrolysis requires: H and OC(=O)R must be SYN-PERIPLANAR (0 degree dihedral, same side, for the 6-membered cyclic TS to form). In norbornyl, the C-H bonds at beta-C are all ANTI or GAUCHE to the OAc at alpha-C (constrained by the rigid cage) -> no syn-periplanar H available -> no 6-membered TS can form -> no Ei elimination -> no reaction. Compare: if E2 were attempted (anti-periplanar required), norbornyl also resists elimination because anti-periplanar H-C-C-L geometry is also very difficult in the cage. Both anti and syn requirements are problematic in norbornyl. Q10 (page 3): different norbornyl-type OAc (with one accessible syn-H) -> 97.5% one regioisomeric alkene (the specific regioisomer dictated by which H is syn-periplanar).
valid_transformations.conditions:
RIGID CAGE SUBSTRATES IN Ei ELIMINATION — NO REACTION FOR NORBORNYL (RM lec 10 p1, page 3):

TEACHER Q⑨ (page 3, bottom left):
Substrate: Norbornyl (bicyclo[2.2.1]heptyl) OAc (acetate at a ring carbon)
+ Δ → 'No rxn' (labeled and underlined by teacher)

WHY NO REACTION:
The norbornane cage (bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane) is RIGID:
  - The Cα (bearing OAc) and Cβ (adjacent to Cα) are constrained
  - The H atoms at Cβ are held at fixed dihedral angles relative to OAc at Cα
  - In the norbornane framework: the H-Cβ-Cα-OAc dihedral is NOT 0° for any β-H
  - The cage geometry prevents any β-H from achieving syn-periplanar (0°) alignment with OAc
  - Therefore: the 6-membered cyclic Ei TS [O···H-Cβ-Cα-O-C=O] CANNOT FORM
  - Result: No Ei (ester pyrolysis) occurs → 'No rxn'

CONTRAST WITH Q⑩ (page 3, bottom right):
  A different constrained ring OAc (where one β-H CAN achieve syn-periplanar with OAc)
  + Δ → One specific alkene = 97.5% (one regioisomeric alkene dominates due to unique syn-periplanar H)
  The constrained geometry LOCKS the syn-periplanar H → only one possible elimination pathway → 97.5% one product.

GENERAL RULE FOR Ei IN RIGID SYSTEMS:
  Ei (ester pyrolysis, Chugaev, Cope) requires SYN-PERIPLANAR β-H.
  In rigid ring systems: check if ANY β-H is syn to the LG.
  If YES → Ei occurs, and the product is determined by WHICH H is syn.
  If NO (all β-H's are anti or gauche, no syn available) → No Ei → 'No rxn'

COMPARE WITH E2 IN RIGID SYSTEMS (previous lectures):
  E2 requires ANTI-PERIPLANAR β-H (180°)
  If equatorial LG (chair form): no axial β-H → no E2 (teacher's 'If leaving group in chair form present at equatorial position, E2 cannot take place')
  For Ei: need SYN β-H (0°); for E2: need ANTI β-H (180°)
  Norbornyl OAc: BOTH syn-H and anti-H are geometrically restricted → no E2 AND no Ei → truly 'No rxn' for elimination.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Rigid cage prevents 6-membered cyclic Ei TS: in norbornyl, the O-C-O-Cα-Cβ-H ring cannot form because the H at Cβ cannot achieve 0° dihedral (syn-periplanar) with OAc at Cα due to the rigid bridged bicyclic framework. The concerted 6-membered TS requires all 6 atoms to be in a planar/ring conformation — impossible in norbornane geometry. Contrast: ester pyrolysis of flexible acyclic substrates easily adopts syn-periplanar conformation → Ei occurs.
valid_transformations.notes: This transformation is deliberately marked as a failed/blocked reaction — a common JEE trap where students predict a product when none forms.

valid_transformations.from: Vicinal diol (1,2-diol = pinnacol = R1-C(OH)(R2)-C(OH)(R3)(R4)) treated with H2SO4 — Pinacol-Pinacolone Rearrangement
valid_transformations.to: Pinacolone = ketone (R1-C(=O)-C(R2)(R3)(R4)) via 1,2-R shift (migration of R2 from C bearing OH to adjacent carbocation). Mechanism: (1) H2SO4 protonates one OH -> +OH2; (2) -H2O -> carbocation at alpha-C (resonance: R1-C(OH)(R2)-C+(R3)(R4) <-> R1-C(+OH)(R2)-C(R3)(R4)); (3) R2 MIGRATION (1,2-shift from beta-C to alpha-C+, teacher labels 'R2 shift / Slow'); (4) -H+ -> pinacolone (ketone product, BOXED). Substrate labeled 'Vicdiol / Pinnacol' by teacher. MIGRATION APTITUDE determines WHICH group migrates: Ar > R > H (teacher's rule, page 12b). For aryl migration: p-OMe-Ar >> p-Me-Ar > Ar > p-NO2-Ar (EDG increases aptitude, EWG decreases). Teacher example: substrate with p-NO2-Ph and p-OMe-Ph -> p-OMe-Ph migrates FAST; p-NO2-Ph migrates SLOW.
valid_transformations.conditions:
PINACOL-PINACOLONE REARRANGEMENT — COMPLETE (RM lec 10 p1, pages 12a-12b):

NAME:
  Pinacol = the vicdiol starting material (vicinal 1,2-diol)
  Pinacolone = the ketone product (after 1,2-shift)
  Pinacol-Pinacolone rearrangement = acid-catalyzed conversion of vicdiol → ketone via 1,2-shift

SUBSTRATE (teacher labels):
  R₁-C(OH)(R₂)-C(OH)(R₃)(R₄)
  'Vicdiol' (vicinal diol = 1,2-diol)
  'Pinnacol' (the classic name for vicdiol substrate)

MECHANISM (teacher's complete diagram, page 12a):
  Step 1: H₂SO₄ protonates one -OH → -⊕OH₂ (oxonium ion on one C)
    Product: R₁-C(OH)(R₂)-C(⊕OH₂)(R₃)(R₄)
    Both carbons and 'OH' and '⊕OH₂' labeled in teacher's diagram
  Step 2: -H₂O (loss of water, labeled '-H₂O' in diagram) → carbocation
    Product: R₁-C(OH)(R₂)-C⊕(R₃)(R₄) (carbocation at the C that lost OH₂)
    Resonance: R₁-C(OH)(R₂)-C⊕ ↔ R₁-C(⊕OH)(R₂)-C (oxocarbenium resonance, both drawn with ↔)
    The carbocation is STABILIZED by the adjacent OH (through lone pair donation: O lone pair → empty p orbital at C⊕)
  Step 3: R₂ MIGRATION — the key step (teacher labels 'R₂ shift / Slow'):
