    R₂ migrates from C bearing OH (beta-C) to the adjacent C⊕ (alpha-C, the carbocation)
    This is a 1,2-shift (migration to adjacent C)
    'Slow' = this is the rate-determining step or the key transformation
    After R₂ migration: the C that had OH now has a + charge (oxocarbenium): R₁-C(=⊕OH)(R₃)(R₄) at alpha-C after R₂ migrates
    OR: the O gets the + and the C=O bond forms: R₁-C(=⊕OH) which is an oxocarbenium ion
  Step 4: -H⊕ (loss of proton from ⊕OH → C=O)
    Product (BOXED): R₁-C(=O)-C(R₂)(R₃)(R₄) = PINACOLONE (ketone)
    The quaternary C adjacent to C=O has R₂, R₃, R₄ (from the original two C's after R₂ migrated)

PRODUCT = PINACOLONE:
  Pinacolone = a ketone where the carbonyl C (from original C that had OH and R₂) is next to a quaternary C (bearing R₂, R₃, R₄).
  CLASSIC EXAMPLE: Pinacol = (CH₃)₂C(OH)-C(OH)(CH₃)₂ → pinacolone = (CH₃)₃C-C(=O)-CH₃ (methyl tert-butyl ketone = 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-one IUPAC)

WHICH GROUP MIGRATES (determined by Migration Aptitude, page 12b):
  Migration aptitude: Ar > R > H (teacher's rule, different-colored chalk)
  The group with HIGHER migration aptitude migrates preferentially.
  For aryl groups: p-OMe-Ph >> p-Me-Ph > Ph > p-Cl-Ph > p-NO₂-Ph
  (Electron-donating groups on aryl: INCREASE aptitude; EWG: DECREASE aptitude)
  The more electron-rich the migrating group → more stabilization of the transition state (partial + on migrating group in TS) → faster migration.

TEACHER EXAMPLE for migration aptitude (page 12b bottom):
  Substrate: Ph-C⊕(H)-CH₂-Ph where one Ph = p-NO₂-C₆H₄ and other Ph = p-OMe-C₆H₄
  'fast' pathway: p-OMe-Ph migrates (EDG increases aptitude → fast migration)
  'slow' pathway: p-NO₂-Ph migrates (EWG decreases aptitude → slow migration)
  This shows: if two different aryl groups compete, the electron-rich aryl migrates predominantly.

APPLICATION IN PROBLEMS:
  Given vicdiol + acid → predict pinacolone:
  1. Identify which OH gets protonated (gives more stable carbocation after -H₂O)
  2. The carbocation forms preferentially at the more substituted C (more stable C⊕)
  3. The group from the adjacent C with HIGHEST migration aptitude migrates
  4. The resulting oxocarbenium → ketone after -H⁺
  Exam trap: the group migrates FROM the C bearing OH TO the adjacent carbocation C
  Result: the C that HAD OH becomes the C=O (carbonyl carbon), and the C that WAS the carbocation gets an extra substituent (R₂).
valid_transformations.mechanism: Four-step acid-catalyzed mechanism: (1) protonation of one OH; (2) -H₂O to form carbocation (stabilized by adjacent OH via resonance = oxocarbenium); (3) 1,2-shift of R₂ (aryl > alkyl > H by migration aptitude) from C-OH to C⁺ → oxocarbenium ion; (4) -H⁺ → ketone. The driving force: the carbocation is initially at C-OH (stabilized by O lone pair), and the 1,2-shift gives an even more stable oxocarbenium (C=O⁺ with delocalized charge on O) which then loses H⁺ to give the stable ketone. Net: vicdiol → ketone (rearrangement, not elimination).
valid_transformations.notes: Rearrangement step: product carbon skeleton differs from substrate. Always verify whether migration occurs before assigning product structure.

valid_transformations.from: Same secondary amine substrate (R-NMe2, with specific H and D stereochemistry at beta-C) treated via TWO DIFFERENT pathways: (A) MeI/Ag2O/Delta = Hofmann E2 (anti) vs (B) H2O2/Delta = Cope elimination (syn)
valid_transformations.to: TWO DIFFERENT alkene products from the SAME substrate depending on mechanism. Pathway A (Hofmann E2: anti-periplanar H required): anti-H removed -> specific E/Z product A. Pathway B (Cope elimination: syn-periplanar H required): syn-H removed -> OPPOSITE E/Z product B. Teacher's Q (page 9): bicyclic NMe2 substrate with H(solid wedge) and D(dashed) -> Branch 1: MeI -> N+Me3; moist Ag2O (gives OH-) -> Hofmann E2 (anti) -> Product with H label. Branch 2: H2O2 -> N-oxide (NMe2+-O-); Delta -> Cope (syn) -> Product with D label = DIFFERENT. This proves: Hofmann E2 (anti-specific) and Cope (syn-specific) are OPPOSITE in stereospecificity. The diastereomers that react in E2 are DIFFERENT from those that react in Cope.
reagents: A: (1) MeI, (2) moist Ag2O, (3) Delta = Hofmann E2 via quaternary ammonium
B: (1) H2O2, (2) Delta = Cope elimination via N-oxide
valid_transformations.conditions:
COPE vs HOFMANN E2 STEREOSPECIFICITY COMPARISON (RM lec 10 p1, pages 9-11):

SUBSTRATE: Bicyclic amine (NMe₂) with specific D-label and H at β-C (Teacher Q, page 9).

PATHWAY A — HOFMANN E2:
  Step 1: MeI (methyl iodide) methylates the NMe₂ → N⁺Me₃ (quaternary ammonium, NMe₃⁺ iodide)
  Step 2: Moist Ag₂O (silver oxide in water) converts I⁻ to OH⁻ (Ag⁺ precipitates AgI; OH⁻ is the base)
  Step 3: Δ (heat) → E2 (Hofmann elimination of quaternary ammonium)
    Mechanism: OH⁻ removes ANTI-PERIPLANAR β-H (E2 = anti requirement)
    Product A: specific geometric alkene from anti-periplanar H removal
    Labels in teacher's diagram: H labels on product (the H that was removed anti)

PATHWAY B — COPE ELIMINATION:
  Step 1: H₂O₂ (hydrogen peroxide) oxidizes NMe₂ → NMe₂⁺-O⁻ (N-oxide)
    Labeled 'OO' above N with negative charge (⁻) in teacher's diagram
  Step 2: Δ (heat ≥100°C) → Cope elimination (Ei, 5-membered cyclic TS)
    Mechanism: N-O⁻ removes SYN-PERIPLANAR β-H
    Product B: different geometric alkene from syn-periplanar H removal
    Labels in teacher's diagram: D label on product (the D that was removed syn)

KEY RESULT:
  Same substrate → Pathway A (Hofmann E2, anti) → Product A
  Same substrate → Pathway B (Cope, syn) → Product B = DIFFERENT from A
  Proves: anti (E2) and syn (Cope) are geometrically opposite → give opposite E/Z alkenes.

STEREOSPECIFICITY TABLE FOR BOTH:
| Mechanism | Periplanar requirement | Which H removed | Product E/Z |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hofmann E2 | ANTI (180°) | Anti-H | Specific E/Z (depends on SM stereo) |
| Cope (Ei) | SYN (0°) | Syn-H | OPPOSITE E/Z from E2 |

IMPLICATION FOR EXAM:
  If a question gives a chiral/meso substrate and asks 'which product from Cope?' vs 'which product from E2?':
  Draw the Newman projection → find the H that is syn (0°) to N-O for Cope, or anti (180°) to N for E2.
  The two mechanisms will often give opposite geometric isomers.
  Teacher's cyclohexyl examples (pages 10-11) with Ph groups show this: different Ph diastereomers → different Cope products → stereospecific.

MOIST Ag₂O REAGENT NOTE:
  Moist Ag₂O (= silver oxide in water or hydroxide) is used to convert R₃N⁺-I⁻ (ammonium iodide salt) to R₃N⁺-OH⁻ (ammonium hydroxide), which then undergoes E2.
  Ag⁺ + I⁻ → AgI (white precipitate, drives the reaction)
  The resulting hydroxide base then causes E2 (Hofmann) elimination.
  This is a classic step in the Hofmann exhaustive methylation sequence for amine degradation.
valid_transformations.mechanism: E2 (Hofmann): OH⁻ (from Ag₂O/H₂O) removes anti-periplanar β-H from quaternary ammonium → anti-periplanar C-H and C-N⁺ → alkene A (specific E/Z). Cope: N-O⁻ removes syn-periplanar β-H via 5-membered cyclic TS → alkene B (opposite E/Z to A). Anti vs syn = opposite geometric requirements → opposite product stereochemistry from the same substrate.
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.from: Carbocation intermediate (R3C+ or Ar2C+-CH2-) where two different aryl groups compete to migrate — testing migration aptitude in 1,2-aryl shift
valid_transformations.to: The ELECTRON-RICH aryl migrates preferentially (fast pathway). The ELECTRON-POOR aryl migrates slower or not at all. Teacher's rule: Migration aptitude = Ar > R > H. For aryl substituents: p-OMe-Ph > p-Me-Ph > Ph > p-Cl-Ph > p-NO2-Ph. Teacher example (page 12b): carbocation with p-NO2-Ph and p-OMe-Ph competing -> p-OMe-Ph migrates FAST (labeled 'fast' on arrow) -> Product A; p-NO2-Ph migrates SLOW (labeled 'slow') -> Product B = minor. REASON: In the TS of 1,2-aryl shift, partial + develops on the migrating aryl carbon. EDG (OMe, Me) stabilize this partial + via resonance -> lower TS energy -> faster migration. EWG (NO2, Cl) destabilize the partial + -> higher TS energy -> slower migration.
valid_transformations.conditions:
MIGRATION APTITUDE IN 1,2-ARYL SHIFTS — COMPLETE (RM lec 10 p1, page 12b):

TEACHER'S RULE (underlined header): 'Migration aptitude : Ar > R > H'

GENERAL ORDER:
  Aryl (Ar) > Alkyl (R) > Hydride (H)
  Within alkyl: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl (more substituted alkyl migrates better)
  Within aryl: electron-rich aryl >> electron-poor aryl

ARYL MIGRATION APTITUDE RANKING (teacher's series, decreasing left to right):
  p-OMe-C₆H₄ > p-Me-C₆H₄ > C₆H₅ > (unsubstituted) > p-Cl-C₆H₄ > p-OMe(meta)-C₆H₄ > p-NO₂-C₆H₄
  SIMPLIFIED: electron-donating substituent → higher aptitude; electron-withdrawing → lower aptitude
  ORDER (decreasing aptitude):
  p-MeO > p-Me > H (Ph) > p-Cl > p-NO₂
  [Electron-rich aryl migrates FASTER; electron-poor aryl migrates SLOWER]

MECHANISM OF ARYL 1,2-SHIFT (transition state analysis):
  In the TS of 1,2-aryl migration: the migrating aryl group bridges between the two carbons
  A partial positive charge develops on the IPSO carbon of the migrating aryl (phenonium-ion-like TS)
  EDG (OMe, Me) at p-position stabilize this partial + via resonance extension → lower ΔG‡ → faster migration
  EWG (NO₂, Cl) at p-position DESTABILIZE the partial + → higher ΔG‡ → slower migration
  This explains the aptitude order: p-OMe (strongest EDG) = fastest; p-NO₂ (strongest EWG) = slowest

TEACHER'S EXAMPLE REACTION (bottom center, page 12b):
  Substrate: Ph-C⊕(H)-CH₂-Ph where:
    - One Ph = p-NO₂-C₆H₄ (electron-poor, poor migrator)
    - Other Ph = p-OMe-C₆H₄ (electron-rich, good migrator)
  Two arrows from the carbocation:
    'fast' (top arrow): p-OMe-Ph migrates → Product A = Ph-C(⊕)(CH₂-Ph)-[migrated p-OMe-Ph]
    'slow' (bottom arrow): p-NO₂-Ph migrates → Product B = different carbocation
  Conclusion: the electron-rich aryl (p-OMe) is the preferential migrator.
  Products A and B are DIFFERENT REGIOISOMERS — determined by which aryl migrated.

APPLICATION IN PINACOL-PINACOLONE:
  If the vicdiol has one C bearing Ph and one C bearing p-OMe-Ph:
  Migration aptitude: p-OMe-Ph > Ph → p-OMe-Ph preferentially migrates
  → the pinacolone has p-OMe-Ph migrated adjacent to C=O
  → the C=O comes from the C that had the lower-aptitude group

EXAM-READY MIGRATION APTITUDE TABLE:
| Migrating group | Aptitude |
|---|---|
| p-MeO-C₆H₄ | Highest for aryl |
| p-Me-C₆H₄ | High |
| C₆H₅ (Ph) | Medium |
| p-Cl-C₆H₄ | Low |
| p-NO₂-C₆H₄ | Lowest for aryl |
| Alkyl (3°) | Lower than aryl |
| Alkyl (2°) | Even lower |
| Alkyl (1°) | Very low |
| H (hydride) | Lowest overall |
valid_transformations.mechanism: 1,2-Aryl migration TS: the aryl group bridges between the donor C (with the group migrating from it) and the acceptor C (the carbocation). The bridged 'phenonium ion' TS has a partial positive charge at the IPSO carbon of the migrating aryl. EDG substituents (OMe, Me) on the aryl ring stabilize this partial + via resonance → lower transition state energy → faster migration rate → higher migration aptitude. EWG (NO₂, Cl) destabilize → higher TS energy → slower migration. This is a KINETIC phenomenon: the group that migrates FASTER (not necessarily to the more stable product) determines the major pinacolone product.
valid_transformations.notes: Carbocation intermediate: check for rearrangement (1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shift) if a more stable cation is accessible.

valid_transformations.from: Tertiary amine (R3N) treated with peracid (RC(=O)-O-O-H, e.g., mCPBA = meta-chloroperoxybenzoic acid) — electrophilic oxygen transfer to nitrogen lone pair
valid_transformations.to: Tertiary amine N-oxide (R3N+-O-) + carboxylate (RCOO-). Mechanism: the terminal, electrophilic O of the peracid attacks the N lone pair -> N-O bond forms -> the O-O bond of the peracid breaks -> N-oxide + carboxylic acid (RCOOH). PERACID REACTIVITY ORDER (teacher, page 7, BOXED): CF3COOOH > CH3COOOH. '→ Tendency to release O' (teacher's label). MORE EWG on acyl part -> more electrophilic terminal O -> better O-transfer -> more reactive peracid. SPECIFIC PERACIDS: mCPBA (meta-chloroperoxybenzoic acid, structure m-Cl-C6H4-C(=O)-OOH, labeled on top right page 7) = most common; PBA (perbenzoic acid = Ph-C(=O)-OOH); PAA (peracetic acid = CH3-C(=O)-OOH). The N-oxide then undergoes Cope elimination at >=100 degrees C.
reagents: H2O2 (alternative, not a peracid but commonly used)
valid_transformations.conditions:
PERACID STRUCTURE AND REACTIVITY FOR AMINE N-OXIDE FORMATION (RM lec 10 p1, page 7):

PERACID GENERAL STRUCTURE: R-C(=O)-O-O-H = a carboxylic acid with an extra -O- (O-O bond = peroxide linkage)
  The terminal O (the one bonded to H) is ELECTROPHILIC = transfers to the N lone pair.

mCPBA (most common peracid, teacher page 7):
  Name: 'meta chloro perbenzoic acid' (teacher spelled out, underlined)
  Structure: m-Cl-C₆H₄-C(=O)-O-O-H
  The Cl at meta position on the benzene ring is EWG → makes the acyl group more electron-withdrawing → makes the terminal O more electrophilic → mCPBA is a good, reactive peracid.
  Top right of page: m-Cl-C₆H₄-C(=O)-O-O-H structure drawn (labeled 'α' for Cl position).

OTHER PERACIDS (teacher's list, left side page 7):
  PBA = perbenzoic acid: Ph-C(=O)-O-O-H (phenyl peracid)
  PAA = peracetic acid: CH₃-C(=O)-O-O-H = CH₃COOOH

PERACID REACTIVITY ORDER (BOXED by teacher):
  CF₃COOOH > CH₃COOOH
  '→ Tendency to release 'O'' (teacher's label, curved arrow from the box)
  CF₃ = very strong EWG → makes C=O very electron-withdrawing → makes terminal O maximally electrophilic → best O-donor
  CH₃ = weak EDG → less electrophilic O → less reactive
  FULL ORDER (derived from EWG strength on R): CF₃COOOH > mCPBA > PBA > PAA = CH₃COOOH
  (More EWG on R → more reactive peracid)

APPLICATION TO N-OXIDE FORMATION:
  R₃N: + R'-C(=O)-OOH → R₃N⁺-O⁻ + R'-COOH
  The electrophilic O of the peracid is transferred to the N lone pair.
  The O-O bond breaks (weakest bond in peracid) → N-O bond forms → peracid becomes carboxylate.

REACTIVITY CONTEXT:
  mCPBA at 0°C to RT → selective N-oxidation or alkene epoxidation
  H₂O₂ (teacher also listed) → slower but also converts R₃N → R₃N⁺-O⁻
  The N-oxide R₃N⁺-O⁻ is then heated (≥100°C) for Cope elimination.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Electrophilic O-transfer: N lone pair attacks the electrophilic terminal O of peracid (R-C(=O)-O-[O-H]). The O-O bond (weak, ~150 kJ/mol) breaks while N-O forms. Transition state: N...O...O-C(=O)R (3-center interaction). The carboxylate R-C(=O)-O⁻ departs, giving R₃N⁺-O⁻ (amine N-oxide). The more electrophilic the terminal O (from EWG on acyl), the lower the activation energy → CF₃COOOH most reactive (CF₃ = strongest EWG), CH₃COOOH least reactive (CH₃ = weakest EWG).
valid_transformations.notes: EAS: product regiochemistry determined by existing substituent(s). Check for conflicting or cooperating directors before assigning major product.

valid_transformations.from: Cyclopentyl substrate bearing N-oxide (NMe2+-O-) or xanthate (OCS2Me) with both exo and endo beta-H accessible for syn-periplanar Ei cyclic transition state — testing Hofmann vs Saytzeff in 5-membered ring
valid_transformations.to: SAYTZEFF (endocyclic, more substituted) alkene = MAJOR product. NOT Hofmann (exocyclic, less substituted). Teacher pages 1 and 5: cyclopentyl N-oxide 97.5% gives Saytzeff (endocyclic C=C in the ring). Reason: 'In the cyclic 5-membered ring which is nearly planar structure, the formation of endo cyclic double bond (Sytzebb rule) predominates' (teacher's note, page 3). Cyclopentane is nearly planar -> both exo-H (giving exocyclic C=C = Hofmann) and endo-H (giving endocyclic C=C = Saytzeff) can form the Ei cyclic TS, BUT the endo-H TS gives a planar ring TS (all atoms lie in one plane = Good TS) while the exo-H TS is less planar. Teacher also: 'Sytzebb Rule followed & cyclopentane ring hydrogen give preferred planar structure than methyl hydrogen' (page 5, double underlined). CONTRAST: Cyclohexane (chair form) = Hofmann (exocyclic) preferred because axial-equatorial alignment forces exocyclic elimination (page 3: 'in the 6-mem ring which is chair form, the exocyclic double bond (Hoffmann rule) preferred'). IUPAC example: methylcyclopentan-1-yl methyl xanthate -> 1-methylcyclopent-1-ene (endocyclic = Saytzeff, MAJOR) + methylenecyclopentane (exocyclic = Hofmann, minor).
reagents: Delta (Cope elimination, Ei, syn, no external base)
valid_transformations.conditions:
CYCLOPENTANE EI EXCEPTION — SAYTZEFF MAJOR (RM lec 10 p2, pages 1, 3, 5):

GENERAL RULE FOR EI IN RINGS:
  Cyclopentane (5-membered): SAYTZEFF (endocyclic C=C) = MAJOR
  Cyclohexane (6-membered, chair): HOFMANN (exocyclic C=C) = MAJOR
  This is the OPPOSITE of the naive Hofmann rule for Ei!

REASON FOR CYCLOPENTANE EXCEPTION:
  Teacher Note (page 3): 'In the cyclic 5-membered ring which is nearly planar structure, the formation of endo cyclic double bond (Sytzebb rule) predominates'
  Cyclopentane is NEARLY PLANAR (ring puckering is minimal, ~0.5 Å from planar)
  → Both the exo-H (on exocyclic CH₂, giving Hofmann product) AND endo-H (on ring, giving Saytzeff endocyclic C=C) are accessible for the Ei cyclic TS
  → But the endo-H TS is MORE PLANAR: all 5 (Cope) or 6 (Chugaev) atoms of the cyclic TS lie in ONE PLANE
  → Teacher page 1: 'In this case both the H (exo & endo can form T.S.) So we preferred Sytzeb t.'
  → Teacher page 5: 'Sytzebb Rule followed & cyclopentane ring hydrogen give preferred planar structure than methyl hydrogen' (double underlined)

WHY ENDO-H GIVES MORE PLANAR TS:
  In a cyclopentane ring (nearly planar), the endo-H on the ring carbon is already roughly coplanar with the ring atoms
  → The 5-membered Cope TS [O-N-Cα-Cβ-H] can form with all atoms in one plane (Good TS)
  → Teacher page 1: 'Good T.S. bcoz all atoms can lie in one plane.' (contrast with 'Bad T.S.' for other conformations)
  For the exo-H (on methyl or exocyclic CH₂): the TS is not as planar → higher activation energy → minor product

REASON FOR CYCLOHEXANE HOFMANN:
  Cyclohexane is in CHAIR FORM (rigid, not flat)
  → Axial-equatorial alignment required (see axial-equatorial rule for Cope/Chugaev below)
  → The chair geometry preferentially exposes the EXOCYCLIC H (on CH₂ outside the ring) for the axial-equatorial syn elimination
  → Endocyclic H elimination gives the more substituted C=C in the ring, but this requires a different axial-equatorial alignment
  → Teacher page 3: 'in the 6-mem ring which is chair form, the exocyclic double bond (Hoffmann rule) preferred'

EXAMPLES (teacher):
  Page 1: Spiro bicyclic NMe₂⁺-O⁻ + CH₃ + Δ → endocyclic alkene 97.5% (Saytzeff) + exocyclic CH₂= 2.5% only
  Page 5: Cyclopentyl OCS₂Me + Δ (Chugaev) → endocyclic cyclopentene (Saytzeff, MAJOR) + exocyclic methylenecyclopentane (Hofmann, minor)
  Page 5: 'Sytzebb Rule followed & cyclopentane ring hydrogen give preferred planar structure than methyl hydrogen' (double underlined)

FIRST ORDER KINETICS (teacher page 1, starred):
  '★ Both are First order kinetics 8xn' = Cope AND Chugaev are BOTH FIRST-ORDER
  Rate = k[substrate]¹ — only the substrate concentration matters
  No external base in the RDS → rate is independent of base concentration
  This is because both are INTRAMOLECULAR (internal base = no external reagent needed)
  Contrast: E2 is second-order (Rate = k[substrate][base])²; E1CB is second-order overall

GOOD vs BAD TS (teacher page 1):
  Good T.S.: 'all atoms can lie in one plane' → planar cyclic TS
  Bad T.S.: atoms cannot achieve coplanarity → non-planar ring → strain → higher activation energy
  For Cope: 5-membered ring TS is most favorable when the 5 atoms [O-N-Cα-Cβ-H] are coplanar
  For Chugaev: 6-membered ring TS is most favorable when the 6 atoms [S-C(=S)-O-Cα-Cβ-H] are coplanar
valid_transformations.mechanism: Cyclopentane Ei: both exo-H and endo-H can approach the LG (N-oxide or xanthate) in a syn-periplanar fashion because the ring is nearly planar. The ENDO-H pathway gives a more planar cyclic TS (all 5 or 6 TS atoms coplanar = 'Good TS'), minimizing torsional strain in the TS. The exo-H (methyl or CH₂ outside ring) pathway gives a less planar TS ('Bad TS' — atoms cannot all lie in one plane) → higher activation energy. Therefore: endocyclic alkene (Saytzeff, from endo-H removal) = major. This is a KINETIC preference for the more planar TS, not thermodynamic stability.
valid_transformations.notes: EAS: product regiochemistry determined by existing substituent(s). Check for conflicting or cooperating directors before assigning major product.

valid_transformations.from: Cyclohexyl substrate with N-oxide (NMe2+-O-) or xanthate axial at ring carbon, requiring axial-equatorial syn alignment of H and LG — Cope/Chugaev in cyclohexane ring
valid_transformations.to: HOFMANN (exocyclic alkene = less substituted, via CH2= exocyclic) = MAJOR product under normal conditions. For cyclohexane: axial-equatorial alignment required for Cope & Chugaev. Teacher note (page 3): 'In the cyclohexane system it requires an axial-equatorial alignment of the eliminating group. (For cope & chugaev only).' IF only ONE syn H is accessible (the axial-equatorial syn H) -> one regioisomeric alkene = major (teacher Q(a): 98% = 'only syn hydrogen'). IF BOTH exo-H AND endo-H are syn (both accessible via axial-equatorial alignment) -> Saytzeff preferred (teacher Q(b): 85%, 'Both are syn / So we preferred Sytzebb t.'). CONTRAST with cyclopentane: cyclohexane (chair) = Hofmann preferred (by default); cyclopentane (planar) = Saytzeff preferred. Teacher: 'in the 6-mem ring which is chair form, the exocyclic double bond (Hoffmann rule) preferred.' (page 3, Note 1)
reagents: Delta/200 degrees C (Chugaev, via OCS2Me xanthate)
valid_transformations.conditions:
CYCLOHEXANE EI — AXIAL-EQUATORIAL RULE (RM lec 10 p2, pages 3-4):

TEACHER NOTE (page 3): 'It is to be noted in the cyclohexane, system it requires an axial-equatorial alignment of the eliminating group. (For cope & chugaev only).'
  Labels in teacher's diagram: '← syn(upper)' and 'Anti (lower)'

AXIAL-EQUATORIAL ALIGNMENT:
  In a cyclohexane CHAIR, adjacent carbons have: axial-equatorial and axial-axial bond pairs
  For Ei (syn, 0° dihedral): we need the LG (N-oxide or xanthate) and the β-H to be on the SAME SIDE (syn)
  In chair cyclohexane, this corresponds to axial LG and equatorial β-H (or equatorial LG and axial β-H)
  = The 'axial-equatorial alignment' described by teacher = LG and β-H are on the same face (syn) but one is axial and one is equatorial
  Teacher labels: the syn pair is 'upper' (syn-upper = both pointing upward on same face)

WHEN ONLY ONE SYN H AVAILABLE (Q(a), page 3):
  If only ONE β-H is syn-periplanar to the LG (the one axial-equatorial pair with correct orientation)
  → Only ONE regioisomeric alkene can form → HIGH SELECTIVITY
  Teacher Q(a) result: 98% one alkene ('only syn hydrogen' labeled)

WHEN BOTH β-H'S ARE SYN (Q(b), page 3):
  If BOTH exo-H (giving exocyclic/Hofmann) AND endo-H (giving endocyclic/Saytzeff) are syn to the LG
  → Both TS's can form → SAYTZEFF alkene preferred (more stable product wins)
  Teacher Q(b): 85% Saytzeff alkene, label: 'Both are syn / So we preferred Sytzeb t.'

E2 AT EQUATORIAL LG → SN2 (page 4):
  When NMe₃⁺ (quaternary ammonium) is in the EQUATORIAL position of cyclohexane:
  → There is NO ANTI-PERIPLANAR (180°) β-H available (anti-periplanar in chair requires both LG and H to be axial)
  → E2 CANNOT OCCUR ('E2 not possible at eq' — teacher Q3, page 4)
  → Instead: SN2 occurs: OH⁻ attacks the N-methyl group (backside attack on CH₃-N⁺) → MeOH + tertiary amine
  Teacher label: '+ Me-OH' (methanol byproduct from SN2 demethylation)

EI COPE AT EQUATORIAL N-OXIDE IN CYCLOHEXANE (page 4):
  If NMe₂⁺-O⁻ (N-oxide) is equatorial AND the syn β-H (axial-equatorial alignment) is accessible:
  → Cope occurs (Ei does NOT require axial LG, only syn-periplanar H)
  → Product: specific alkene from the available syn-H
  Teacher Q4 (page 4): equatorial N-oxide + Δ → alkene product

COMPARISON (CYCLOHEXANE LG POSITION):
| LG position | E2 possible? | Ei (Cope/Chugaev) possible? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Axial NMe₃⁺ | YES (anti H is equatorial) | N/A | E2 gives anti elimination |
| Equatorial NMe₃⁺ | NO (no anti-axial H) | N/A | SN2 instead (+MeOH) |
| Axial NMe₂⁺-O⁻ | N/A | YES (syn H is equatorial, axial-eq alignment) | Cope: one or two syn H's → 98% or 85% |
| Equatorial NMe₂⁺-O⁻ | N/A | YES (different alignment) | Check which H is syn |

ALL EI MECHANISMS IN CYCLOHEXANE:
  The axial-equatorial rule is SPECIFIC TO COPE & CHUGAEV (teacher's note says 'For cope & chugaev only')
  Ester pyrolysis in cyclohexane is also syn (Ei) but the TS geometry varies
  E2 always needs axial LG (anti-periplanar H) = anti-elimination in ring
  Ei (Cope/Chugaev) needs syn H (axial-equatorial pair) = syn-elimination in ring
valid_transformations.mechanism: In cyclohexane chair, the syn β-H for Cope/Chugaev Ei must be in an axial-equatorial relationship with the LG: one of the pair is axial, the other equatorial, and both are on the same face of the ring (syn relationship). This is not the perfectly 0° syn-periplanar of acyclic substrates, but the 5-membered (Cope) or 6-membered (Chugaev) cyclic ring TS can accommodate the geometry. When only one such pair exists → very high regioselectivity (98%). When two such pairs exist (different β-H's both syn) → both products possible → Saytzeff preferred (more stable alkene wins). The axial-equatorial rule explains why cyclohexane gives Hofmann by DEFAULT (the exocyclic methylene CH₂= forms from the exocyclic H that is usually in the correct syn axial-equatorial relationship).
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.from: Acyclic diastereomeric substrate with Ph and D labels: erythro and threo isomers of Ph-CH(NMe2+-O-)-CH(D/H)-Ph treated with Delta — Cope elimination stereospecificity (E/Z product ratios)
valid_transformations.to: Erythro -> 89% Z (cis-stilbene type) alkene + 11% E. Threo -> 94% E (trans-stilbene type) alkene + 6% Z. Teacher page 6: 'Erythro [arrow] 89% Z' and 'Threo [arrow] 94% E.' Syn Cope elimination is STEREOSPECIFIC (like E2 which is anti-specific but OPPOSITE): erythro -> Z; threo -> E. Not 100% stereospecific for acyclic substrates because conformational flexibility allows minor amounts of the non-syn conformer to react. Rule: syn Cope/Chugaev: erythro -> Z; threo -> E. Compare E2 (anti): erythro -> E; threo -> Z (OPPOSITE assignment). So for the SAME diastereomeric substrate, Cope gives the opposite E/Z product compared to E2. Also: 5-membered Cope TS and 6-membered Chugaev TS from the SAME diastereomeric SM give DIFFERENT E/Z products (teacher Q1 vs Q2, page 2) because the different ring size changes the syn geometry.
reagents: Delta (>=100 degrees C, Cope elimination via N-oxide)
valid_transformations.conditions:
COPE/CHUGAEV SYN ELIMINATION STEREOSPECIFICITY — E/Z RATIOS (RM lec 10 p2, pages 2 and 6):

STEREOSPECIFICITY RULE FOR SYN ELIMINATION:
  For syn Cope/Chugaev elimination:
  Erythro diastereomer → Z (cis) alkene = major
  Threo diastereomer → E (trans) alkene = major
  This is because:
  In the syn conformer (H syn to LG = 0° dihedral):
    Erythro: when H is syn to LG, the two Ph groups are cis in the product → Z alkene
    Threo: when H is syn to LG, the two Ph groups are trans in the product → E alkene

COMPARE WITH E2 (ANTI):
  E2 (anti-periplanar): erythro → E; threo → Z (OPPOSITE to syn)
  So: the SAME diastereomeric substrate gives OPPOSITE E/Z products in E2 vs Cope/Chugaev.
  This is the key exam distinction.

TEACHER Q (page 6):
  Substrate: Ph-CH(NMe₂⁺-O⁻)-CH(Me/H) type
  Erythro → 89% Z (labeled by teacher)
  Threo → 94% E (labeled by teacher)
  NOT 100% because acyclic substrates have conformational flexibility → minor amounts of 'wrong' conformer react
  (If the substrate were rigid/cyclic: 99%+ stereospecificity)

COPE 5-MEMBERED TS vs CHUGAEV 6-MEMBERED TS FROM SAME SM (teacher Q1 vs Q2, page 2):
  Q1 (Cope, 5-membered TS): same Fischer cross substrate → one specific E/Z alkene (major)
  Q2 (Chugaev, 6-membered TS): SAME Fischer cross substrate but xanthate LG → DIFFERENT E/Z alkene (major)
  The different TS ring size (5 vs 6) changes the geometry of the syn elimination:
    In 5-membered Cope TS: the atoms [O-N-Cα-Cβ-H] form one ring; the H removed is the one syn to O in this TS
    In 6-membered Chugaev TS: the atoms [S-C(=S)-O-Cα-Cβ-H] form a different ring; the H syn to S in this TS may be different
  → The different β-H is removed in each case → different geometric alkene from the same SM.

CROWDED vs LESS CROWDED TS (teacher Q3, page 2):
  'If we go for H then it will be More crowded T.S. due to ph-ph same side'
  'So Main thing is staggered conformer Means less staggered conformer repulsion in T.S.'
  For the threo isomer: removing D gives a TS with Ph groups staggered (anti) = less crowded TS = preferred
  Removing H gives Ph-Ph eclipsed in the TS ring = more crowded = higher energy TS = minor pathway
  This conformational preference (less crowded TS) explains which β-H is removed even when both are syn-accessible.

CHUGAEV LONG CHAIN E/Z (page 6):
  Long chain acyclic xanthate + Δ:
  Two regioisomers: A = 33%E + 17%Z; B = 34%E + 16%Z
  Total: both regioisomers roughly 50:50; within each, E:Z ≈ 2:1 (E slightly preferred)
  Shows that Chugaev for acyclic internal substrates gives roughly equal regioisomers but E slightly > Z

SIMPLE CHAIN COPE E/Z (page 6):
  Simple chain NMe₂⁺-O⁻ substrate + Δ:
  Internal alkene (Saytzeff): 21%E + 12%Z = 33% total
  Terminal alkene (Hofmann): 67% (MAJOR, double underlined)
  Confirms: Hofmann = major for simple acyclic Cope, with E preferred within the Saytzeff fraction
valid_transformations.mechanism: Syn elimination stereospecificity: in the syn conformer (H/LG dihedral = 0°), the two groups on either side of the forming C=C are determined. For erythro substrate in syn conformer: the two large groups (Ph, Ph) end up on the SAME SIDE of the alkene C=C (cis relationship) → Z product. For threo substrate in syn conformer: Ph groups end up on OPPOSITE sides of C=C → E product. This is the OPPOSITE assignment vs E2 (anti) because E2 uses 180° dihedral (anti) while Cope uses 0° (syn) — geometrically opposite → E/Z assignments reversed for the same diastereomeric SM.
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.from: Cyclohexyl quaternary ammonium (NMe3+) with LG in equatorial position treated with OH- (E2 conditions) — testing E2 vs SN2 when E2 is geometrically blocked
valid_transformations.to: SN2 + MeOH (methanol byproduct). NOT E2 (E2 impossible). Teacher Q3 (page 4): 'E2 not possible at eq' (equatorial NMe3+ in cyclohexane). Reason: E2 requires ANTI-PERIPLANAR beta-H (180 degree dihedral H-Cbeta-Calpha-N+). In cyclohexane chair, anti-periplanar requires BOTH the LG (N+) to be AXIAL and the beta-H to be AXIAL on the adjacent C. If LG = equatorial -> there is no anti-axial H available -> E2 cannot form the anti-periplanar TS -> no E2. Alternative pathway: OH- attacks one of the N-methyl groups via SN2 (backside attack on Me-N+ bond) -> MeOH is released (labeled '+ Me-OH' by teacher) + the amine is N-demethylated to NMe2 (now tertiary amine). Teacher also: cyclooctyl NMe3+ + OH- -> bicyclic-type product = 60% (page 4) = likely trans-cyclooctene or bridged product from ring-strain-driven reaction.
valid_transformations.conditions:
E2 BLOCKED AT EQUATORIAL LG IN CYCLOHEXANE → SN2 INSTEAD (RM lec 10 p2, page 4):

TEACHER Q3 (page 4): '**E2 not possible at eq**' (explicit label)
Substrate: Cyclohexyl NMe₃⁺ (quaternary ammonium) with NMe₃⁺ in EQUATORIAL position + OH⁻/Δ

WHY E2 FAILS:
  E2 mechanism requires: H-Cβ-Cα-LG in ANTI-PERIPLANAR (180°) arrangement
  In cyclohexane CHAIR:
    Anti-periplanar requires LG (axial) and β-H (axial) on adjacent C's
    If LG = EQUATORIAL: there is no anti-axial H (the axial-axial pair is not available when LG is equatorial)
    → The 180° anti-periplanar requirement CANNOT BE SATISFIED
    → E2 does not occur: 'E2 not possible at eq'

ALTERNATIVE REACTION: SN2
  OH⁻ performs SN2 on the N-CH₃ bond (one of the methyl groups on N⁺)
  Mechanism: OH⁻ → [backside attack on N-CH₃] → MeOH (methanol leaves) + N-demethylated amine
  Teacher label: '+ Me-OH' (methanol byproduct from SN2)
  The quaternary NMe₃⁺ → tertiary NMe₂ (one methyl removed)
  This is the Hofmann degradation side reaction: when E2 is blocked, SN2 occurs at N-methyl

CYCLOOCTYL NMe₃⁺ + OH⁻ (page 4):
  Teacher: cyclooctane-NMe₃⁺ + OH⁻ → product = 60% (bicyclic/bridged structure drawn)
  In medium rings (8-membered), ring strain allows unusual geometry
  The product shown as two overlapping boxes = possibly trans-cyclooctene or a bicyclic compound
  60% yield = moderate (not clean, consistent with E2 in a geometrically constrained medium ring)

CYCLOOCTYL N-OXIDE + Δ (page 4):
  Cyclooctyl NMe₂⁺-O⁻ + Δ → cyclooctene (single ring C=C = clean product from Cope elimination)
  Cope (syn Ei) gives a clean product even in the 8-membered ring because syn alignment is achievable
  This contrasts with E2 (anti) which may be more difficult in medium rings

SUMMARY (E2 vs SN2 vs Cope in cyclohexane):
  Axial NMe₃⁺ + OH⁻/Δ → E2 (anti-periplanar, axial H removed)
  Equatorial NMe₃⁺ + OH⁻/Δ → SN2 ('+MeOH', no anti H) → amine demethylated
  N-oxide (axial or equatorial) + Δ → Cope (Ei, syn, axial-equatorial H)
  In all cases: the GEOMETRY determines the reaction pathway
valid_transformations.mechanism: Equatorial NMe₃⁺ in cyclohexane chair: the axial position on adjacent carbons is occupied by H (axial), but the LG (N⁺, equatorial) has NO anti-periplanar (180°) relationship with any H. E2 fails (no anti-H available). Instead, OH⁻ performs SN2 at the N-methyl group: OH⁻ attacks the backside of N-CH₃ bond, Mе leaves as MeOH (= the SN2 reaction is at the carbon of N-methyl, not at the ring carbon). Product: N-demethylated amine + MeOH.
valid_transformations.notes: EAS: product regiochemistry determined by existing substituent(s). Check for conflicting or cooperating directors before assigning major product.

valid_transformations.from: Vicinal 1,2-dihalide (R-CHX-CHX-R', typically X=Br or I) treated with Zn metal and heat — Zn reductive dehalogenation (Function of Zn/Delta)
valid_transformations.to: Alkene (R-CH=CH-R') + ZnX2. Teacher header: 'Function of Zn/Delta' (underlined, page 1). Mechanism: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e- (zinc is oxidized, provides 2 electrons to break both C-X bonds simultaneously). The two C-X bonds break and the C=C forms. Works for BOTH syn (cis) and anti (trans) vicinal dihalides (teacher Q1: trans-dibromocyclohexane + Zn -> cyclohexene; teacher Q3: cis-dibromocyclohexane + Zn -> cyclohexene). This is NOT stereospecific like E2 (doesn't require anti-periplanar). However, for acyclic substrates (teacher Q03, page 2): 2,3-dibromobutane + Zn/Delta -> but-2-ene; the Newman analysis shows the ANTI-PERIPLANAR Br/Br conformation reacts preferentially. Teacher Q01 (page 3): 2 molecules of CH3-CHBr2 (gem-1,1-dihalide) + Zn/Delta -> CH3-CH=CH-CH3 (but-2-ene) via bimolecular Zn-mediated reductive coupling. IUPAC: propane-2,3-diyl dibromide + Zn -> prop-2-ene (propylene) example.
reagents: Zn-Cu (zinc-copper couple for more reactive substrates)
valid_transformations.conditions:
ZN/DELTA REDUCTIVE DEHALOGENATION — FUNCTION OF Zn (RM lec 11, pages 1-3):

TEACHER HEADER: 'Funtion of Zn/Delta' (underlined, page 1)
MECHANISM: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (written explicitly by teacher)
The two electrons from Zn are used to break the two C-X bonds simultaneously.

SUBSTRATE: Any vicinal 1,2-dihalide (X on adjacent carbons = C1 and C2)
REAGENT: Zn metal (or Zn-Cu couple for more reactive substrates)
CONDITION: Δ (heat) — often done in AcOH, EtOH, or neat
PRODUCT: Alkene + ZnX₂

STEREOCHEMISTRY:
  In general: Zn/Δ dehalogenation works for BOTH cis and trans dihalides.
  Teacher Q①: trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane + Zn → cyclohexene ✓
  Teacher Q③: cis-1,2-dibromocyclohexane + Zn → cyclohexene ✓
  Both give the same alkene product regardless of starting stereochemistry.
  This CONTRASTS with E2 (which requires anti-periplanar = only works for trans/anti dihalides in ring systems).

For ACYCLIC substrates (teacher Q03, page 2):
  2,3-dibromobutane (Fischer cross: Me/H/Br//H/Br/Me) + Zn/Δ → but-2-ene
  Newman analysis shows the ANTI-PERIPLANAR Br/Br conformation reacts (anti-staggered conformer)
  The anti conformation is preferred in the TS (more stable, Br's can both reach Zn simultaneously)

CATEGORIES OF Zn ELIMINATIONS:
  1. alpha-ELIMINATION (β-elimination, 1,2-elimination): vicinal dihalide → alkene
     -CHX-CHX- + Zn → -CH=CH- + ZnX₂
  2. gamma-ELIMINATION (1,3-elimination): 1,3-dihalide + Zn(Cu) → cyclopropane
     -CHX-CH₂-CHX- + Zn → cyclopropane + ZnX₂ (see below)

BIMOLECULAR ZN COUPLING (Q01, page 3):
  2 molecules of CH₃-CHBr₂ (gem-1,1-dihalide) + 2Zn → CH₃-CH=CH-CH₃ (but-2-ene) + 2ZnBr₂
  The teacher's Newman diagram shows two CH₃-CH· radical intermediates coupling
  This is a Zn-mediated bimolecular reductive coupling of two gem-dihalides.

ALKYNE SYNTHESIS (Q18, page 6):
  1,2-Dihalide on each of two adjacent carbons (= 1,2,3,4-tetrahalide) + 2Zn → alkyne
  OR: sequential Zn treatment of 1,2-dibromide from alkene → further Zn dehalogenation of residual halogens
  Teacher Q18: zigzag-Br·Br + Zn → H≡H (alkyne labeled as 'n≡n')

ADVANTAGE OVER BASE-MEDIATED DEHALOGENATION:
  Zn works on BOTH syn and anti dihalides (no stereospecificity constraint)
  No strong base or acid needed (mild conditions)
  Works in neutral conditions (AcOH or EtOH)
  Useful when E2 is not possible (e.g., when both Br's are equatorial in cyclohexane, E2 would fail but Zn works)
valid_transformations.mechanism: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (electron-pair transfer). The two electrons reduce both C-Br bonds simultaneously: both C-Br bonds break homolytically (or via single-electron-transfer mechanism) → Zn²⁺ forms with two Br⁻ (= ZnBr₂) and the two C radicals/carbanions recombine to form the C=C double bond. This is a REDUCTIVE ELIMINATION: Zn acts as the reducing agent (electron donor). Unlike E2 (requires base attack on H, anti-periplanar) or E1CB (carbanion mechanism), Zn dehalogenation proceeds through a radical or organo-zinc intermediate. The driving force: formation of stable ZnBr₂ (very stable ionic salt).
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.

valid_transformations.from: 1,3-Dihalide (gamma-dihalide: R-CHX-CH2-CHX-R', typically X=Br or I) treated with Zn-copper couple (Zn-Cu) — gamma-elimination (1,3-elimination)
valid_transformations.to: Cyclopropane ring + ZnX2. Teacher: 'beta-elimination (1,3 elimination)' (underlined header, page 2). Teacher Q04 (page 2): Ph-CH(Br)-CH2-CH2-Br + Zn(cu)/Delta -> Ph-triangle (= phenylcyclopropane, shown as triangle with Ph). Mechanism: Zn(Cu) generates a Zn-carbenoid intermediate from the 1,3-dihalide -> the organozinc inserts into the C1-C3 bond closure intramolecularly -> 3-membered cyclopropane ring. This is specifically a 1,3-elimination (H and X on C1 and C3) generating cyclopropane. The Zn-copper couple (zinc-copper alloy) is MORE reactive than Zn alone (Cu activates the Zn surface). IUPAC: (3-bromopropyl)benzene with C1-Br -> Zn(Cu) -> phenylcyclopropane (cyclopropylbenzene). Teacher example: Ph-CH(Br)-CH2-CH2-Br -> Ph-cyclopropane (phenylcyclopropane). Also: alkylidene cyclopropane and other strained rings possible by similar intramolecular Zn-carbenoid method.
valid_transformations.conditions:
GAMMA-ELIMINATION (1,3-ELIMINATION) WITH Zn-Cu → CYCLOPROPANE (RM lec 11, page 2):

NAME: gamma-elimination = 1,3-elimination = elimination of two groups on C1 and C3 to form a 3-membered ring.
Contrast: beta-elimination = 1,2-elimination = groups on C1 and C2 → alkene.

TEACHER HEADER (page 2): 'β-elimination (1,3 elimination)' (underlined) — confusingly labeled β but it's the 1,3 type.

SUBSTRATE: 1,3-dibromide (Br on C1 and C3, with CH₂ spacer at C2)
REAGENT: Zn(cu) = Zn-copper couple
CONDITION: Δ (heat)
PRODUCT: Cyclopropane ring + ZnBr₂

TEACHER Q04 (page 2):
  Ph-CH(Br)-CH₂-CH₂-Br [= 1-bromo-3-phenyl-3-bromopropane type]
  + Zn(cu)/Δ → Ph-△ = phenylcyclopropane (triangle symbol = cyclopropyl ring)
  Mechanism (shown as Ph-CH·-CH₂-CH₂· biradical or zinc carbenoid with arrow down to cyclopropane)

MECHANISM:
  Zn-Cu reacts with one C-Br → forms R-CH(ZnBr)- (organo-zinc at C1)
  The C3-Br is then displaced INTRAMOLECULARLY by the carbanion at C1 (SN2 cyclization)
  → 3-membered ring (cyclopropane) closes with inversion at C3
  → ZnBr₂ is expelled
  Alternatively: Zn generates a Zn-carbenoid (:CH-R where carbenoid acts as C:) → inserts into CH₂-CH₂ bond → cyclopropane

WHY Zn-Cu (NOT Zn alone):
  Copper activates the zinc surface (galvanic cell effect): Cu and Zn create a short-circuit galvanic couple
  → More reactive zinc surface
  → Faster oxidative addition of Zn into C-Br bond
  → Better organo-zinc intermediate formation
  Plain Zn can do 1,2-dehalogenation (vicinal → alkene) but Zn-Cu is needed for the more reactive 1,3-cyclization.

EXAM NOTE:
  Q: 'What happens when Ph-CH(Br)-CH₂-CH₂-Br is treated with Zn-Cu?' → Phenylcyclopropane
  Q: 'Identify the reagent to convert 1,3-dibromide to cyclopropane' → Zn-Cu couple
  Q: 'What type of elimination is 1,3-elimination?' → Gamma-elimination (γ-elimination) → gives cyclopropane

COMPARE: 1,2-dihalide + Zn → alkene (β-elimination); 1,3-dihalide + Zn-Cu → cyclopropane (γ-elimination)
valid_transformations.mechanism: Zn-Cu inserts into C1-Br bond (oxidative addition) → C1-ZnBr intermediate (organo-zinc = mild carbanion at C1). C1 carbanion attacks C3-Br (intramolecular SN2 backside attack) → C1-C3 bond forms (closing the 3-membered ring) → Br⁻ leaves from C3 → cyclopropane + ZnBr₂. The 3-membered ring forms with INVERSION at C3. The driving force: relief of C1-Br and C3-Br bonds → strong ZnBr₂ formed + strained but stable cyclopropane.
valid_transformations.notes: EAS: product regiochemistry determined by existing substituent(s). Check for conflicting or cooperating directors before assigning major product.

valid_transformations.from: Amino alcohol H2N-(CH2)n-CH2-Br or similar omega-haloamine undergoing intramolecular SN2 cyclization — Baldwin's rules for ring formation (Fun Fact from teacher, page 3)
valid_transformations.to: Cyclic amine (aziridine for n=1, azetidine for n=2, pyrrolidine for n=3, piperidine for n=4, azepane for n=5) via intramolecular SN2. Rate of cyclization (teacher Fun Fact, page 3, yellow): 6-membered ring (piperidine, n=4) = FASTEST (relative rate = 100); 5-membered (pyrrolidine, n=3) = second fastest; 3-membered (aziridine, n=1) = rate 7x; 7-membered (azepane, n=5) = rate 2; 4-membered (azetidine, n=2) = SLOWEST (rate = 1, reference). RATE ORDER: 6-membered (100) > 5-membered >> 3-membered (7x) > 7-membered (2) > 4-membered (1). Teacher label: 'Rate of intramolecular cyclisation = (decreasing arrow).' The 4-membered ring is slowest because of VERY HIGH RING STRAIN in the TS (Baeyer strain in 4-membered cyclobutane-like TS). The 6-membered ring is fastest because: perfect geometry for SN2 backside attack + no ring strain in the 6-membered TS.
reagents: Base (to deprotonate NH2 to NH- if needed)
valid_transformations.conditions:
INTRAMOLECULAR CYCLIZATION RATES — RING SIZE PREFERENCE (RM lec 11, page 3):

TEACHER 'FUN FACT' (yellow, page 3): H₂N-(CH₂)ₙ-CH₂-Br → intramolecular SN2 → cyclic amine

RATES (teacher's data, directly labeled on structures):
  n=1 → 3-membered ring (aziridine): rate = 7 (circled, yellow)
  n=2 → 4-membered ring (azetidine): rate = 1 (reference, SLOWEST, circled)
  n=3 → 5-membered ring (pyrrolidine): rate not labeled (between 7 and 100, ~50-60 from literature)
  n=4 → 6-membered ring (piperidine): rate = 100 (labeled in yellow, FASTEST)
  n=5 → 7-membered ring (azepane): rate = 2 (labeled)

RATE ORDER (decreasing): **6 > 5 > 3 > 7 > 4** membered ring

WHY 4-MEMBERED IS SLOWEST:
  The TS for 4-membered ring SN2 requires a highly strained geometry (90° bond angles = Baeyer strain)
  Very high ring strain in the 4-membered cyclobutane-like TS → very high activation energy
  → Rate = 1 (lowest, reference)
  Note: 3-membered (aziridine) is faster than 4-membered despite having MORE ring strain:
    The SN2 TS for 3-membered ring is close to the BACKSIDE of the C-Br bond
    The N···C-Br geometry for a 3-membered ring TS has less entropic penalty than 4-membered
    (The geometry actually works favorably for 3-membered ring SN2 at 60° angle)

WHY 6-MEMBERED IS FASTEST:
  Perfect geometry: N···C-Br angle approaches ideal for SN2 (backside attack at ~180°)
  No ring strain in the 6-membered TS (chair-like TS = like cyclohexane chair)
  Minimal entropic penalty (not too big a ring to lose entropy)
  → Rate = 100 (highest)

WHY 3-MEMBERED (AZIRIDINE) IS FAST DESPITE STRAIN:
  Even though aziridine is very strained, the kinetics of RING FORMATION are fast (rate = 7)
  The key: the SN2 TS for 3-membered ring has N directly behind the C-Br bond at a favorable angle
  Also: the product aziridine is still kinetically accessible (small molecule, low entropy cost)
  This is the 3-exo-tet case: favorable by Baldwin's rules

BALDWIN'S RULES CONNECTION:
  All these SN2 cyclizations are X-exo-tet (where X = ring size)
  All exo-tet cyclizations are FAVORED by Baldwin's rules (regardless of ring size)
  The rate differences are KINETIC, not thermodynamic Baldwin's rule classification
  Baldwin says 'favorable' for all exo-tet; rate order tells us which is FASTEST

EXAM QUESTION TYPES:
  Q: 'Arrange these ring sizes in decreasing rate of intramolecular SN2 cyclization: 3,4,5,6,7'
  Answer: 6 > 5 > 3 > 7 > 4
  Q: 'Which ring size forms slowest in intramolecular cyclization?' → 4-membered
  Q: 'Which ring size forms fastest?' → 6-membered (rate = 100, teacher's data)
valid_transformations.mechanism: Intramolecular SN2: the nucleophile (NH₂ nitrogen) attacks the electrophilic C bearing Br from the BACKSIDE (180° or close to it). The geometry of the N···Br arrangement varies by ring size. 6-membered TS: the N and C-Br are positioned at near-ideal SN2 angle (~170°) with chair-like ring TS → lowest activation energy → fastest. 4-membered TS: the N and C-Br are at ~90° angle → very strained TS geometry → highest activation energy → slowest.
valid_transformations.notes: EAS: product regiochemistry determined by existing substituent(s). Check for conflicting or cooperating directors before assigning major product.

valid_transformations.from: 1,2,3,4-Tetrahalide (X-CHR-CHR-CHR-CHR-X, four halogens on four adjacent C's) or 1,2-dihaloalkene treated with excess Zn — double Zn dehalogenation
valid_transformations.to: Alkyne (R-C=C-R' or R-C=C-H). Teacher Q18 (page 6): 'Br-zigzag-Br -> n=n (alkyne)'. Two sequential Zn dehalogenations: first Zn removes two vicinal Br's -> alkene; second Zn removes two more Br's from what remains -> alkyne. SEQUENCE: R-CHBr-CHBr-R' (1,2-dibromide) + Zn -> R-CH=CH-R' (alkene) -> THEN if R-CH=CHBr-CHBr-R'' etc. or starting from R-CBr2-CBr2-R' (1,1,2,2-tetrahalide) + 2Zn -> R-C=C-R' (alkyne). This is the REVERSE of Br2 addition to an alkyne: adding Br2 twice to R-C=C-R' gives R-CBr2-CBr2-R' (the tetrabromide). So Zn/Delta reverses this: 1,1,2,2-tetrabromide + 2Zn -> alkyne. Teacher Q18 confirms this with the 'n=n' label for product.
valid_transformations.conditions:
ALKYNE SYNTHESIS BY DOUBLE ZN DEHALOGENATION (RM lec 11, page 6):

TEACHER Q18 (page 6): Br-chain-Br (dibromo or more) + Zn → 'n≡n' (= alkyne, H≡H type shown)

ROUTE:
  Option 1: 1,1,2,2-Tetrahalide (gem-gem dihalide on two adjacent C's) + 2Zn → alkyne
    R-CBr₂-CBr₂-R' + 2Zn → R-C≡C-R' + 2ZnBr₂
    Each Zn removes one pair of geminal Br's → generates one triple-bond component
    OR: removes both vicinal pairs in two steps
  Option 2: Sequential treatment
    Step 1: R-CBr₂-CBr₂-R' + Zn → R-CBr=CBr-R' (1,2-dihaloalkene) + ZnBr₂
    Step 2: R-CBr=CBr-R' + Zn → R-C≡C-R' + ZnBr₂
    Two separate Zn treatments → alkyne

CONTEXT IN TEACHING:
  This is the REVERSE of: alkyne + Br₂ → 1,2-dibromo alkene; then + Br₂ → 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoalkane
  Zn/Δ REVERSES both bromine additions → recovers the alkyne
  Useful for: protecting alkynes as tetrabromides, then deprotecting with Zn
  Also: making alkynes from 1,1,2-tribromides or similar multiply halogenated compounds

EXAM NOTE:
  Q: 'What product forms from CH₃-CBr₂-CBr₂-CH₃ + 2Zn/Δ?' → CH₃-C≡C-CH₃ (but-2-yne)
  Q: '1,2-Dihaloalkene + Zn → ?' → Alkyne (removes the two vinylic halogens)
  Q18 teacher test: specific Br pattern → alkyne = the double Zn dehalogenation product
valid_transformations.mechanism: Step 1: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ reduces one pair of C-Br bonds (vicinal or geminal) → one C=C double bond forms. Step 2: another Zn molecule reduces the second pair of C-Br bonds on the adjacent carbons → the second C=C π-bond forms, converting the alkene to an alkyne. Net: 2Zn + R-CX₂-CX₂-R' → R-C≡C-R' + 2ZnX₂. Each Zn provides 2 electrons to break 2 C-X bonds.
valid_transformations.notes: Elimination: specify Saytzeff (small base, more substituted) vs Hofmann (bulky base/Hofmann exhaustive/N-oxide, less substituted) product.
catalytic reforming/aromatization; also Mo2O3/delta; dehydrogenation + cyclization of alkane
valid_transformations.conditions: Al₂O₃-Cr₂O₃ catalyst (dehydrocyclisation/aromatisation); 600°C; H₂ atmosphere (or H₂ removed). Catalytic reforming (platforming): linear hexane → dehydrogenation → cyclohexane → dehydrogenation → benzene. Or: Pd/charcoal + Δ (cyclohexane → benzene, simpler). Industrial: catalytic reforming of naphtha → benzene. High temperature, metal oxide catalyst.

valid_transformations.notes: 3 HC≡CH → benzene; Berthelot reaction; cyclotrimerization of ethyne with Fe catalyst
valid_transformations.conditions: Fe catalyst (or Ni, Cr₂O₃); Δ (trimerisation, ~300°C). Three molecules of C₂H₂ → benzene (Berthelot reaction, 1866). Fe wire or Fe₂O₃ at 300°C. Also: cyclic trimer formation. Not efficient industrially (side products). Low yield; mainly of historical/mechanistic interest.

valid_transformations.notes: soda lime (NaOH+CaO) decarboxylation; PhCOOH → C6H6 + CO2; also works for naphthalene-COOH → naphthalene
valid_transformations.conditions: NaOH + CaO (soda lime); Δ (strong heat, 300–400°C); decarboxylation. PhCOONa + CaO → Ph-H + CaCO₃ (+ Na₂CO₃). Mechanism: loss of CO₂ from carboxylate anion (decarboxylation). Also: Cu powder (Ullmann decarboxylation) or Pd catalyst at lower T. Industrial decarboxylation: >200°C, base. Dry distillation of Ca salt of carboxylic acid → alkane (Kekulé synthesis equivalent for aromatic).

valid_transformations.notes: PhSO3H + dil H+ → C6H6 + SO3; REVERSIBLE sulfonation; used to temporarily block ring positions
valid_transformations.conditions: Dil H⁺ (dil H₂SO₄ or HCl); 150–250°C; aqueous; steam or pressure. Reverse of sulphonation: PhSO₃H + H₂O → Ph-H + H₂SO₄. Reversible reaction (sulphonation equilibrium). Used in synthesis to temporarily block a ring position (sulphonate → direct other EAS → desulphonate). Temperature: 150°C for activated aromatics; 250°C for deactivated.

valid_transformations.notes: kinetic control product (KCP); alpha-sulfonation at C-1; Wheland RS=7 for alpha; lower T favors kinetically preferred alpha isomer
valid_transformations.conditions: Conc H₂SO₄; ≤80°C (low temperature, kinetic control); ≤110°C. Sulphonation of naphthalene at C-1 (α-position) preferred at low temperature (kinetic product; smaller TS, α-position more reactive electrophilically). α-sulphonic acid is major below 80°C. Above 110°C → β-sulphonic acid (thermodynamic product).

valid_transformations.notes: thermodynamic control product (TCP); beta-sulfonation at C-2; reversibility of sulfonation at high T shifts to thermodynamic beta product; beta isomer more stable (less peri-H strain)
valid_transformations.conditions: Conc H₂SO₄ (or fuming H₂SO₄); >110°C (high temperature, thermodynamic control). β-sulphonic acid (2-isomer) is less sterically hindered and thermodynamically more stable than α. Equilibrium at high T favours β. Reversible sulphonation: α-product → isomerisation at high T → β. Used to make β-naphthol (via NaOH fusion of β-sulphonate).

valid_transformations.notes: beta-naphthol (2-OH): OH activates SAME ring; EAS at C-1 (ortho to OH on same ring, major); EDG directs to activated ring not the other ring
valid_transformations.conditions: EAS (electrophilic aromatic substitution); electrophile E⁺ attacks C-1 position of 2-naphthol (β-naphthol). C-1 is peri position (alpha to OH). β-Naphthol: OH activates ring toward EAS; C-1 (in same ring as OH, alpha to OH) preferred. E⁺ = Br₂ (gives 1-bromo-2-naphthol), NO₂⁺ (gives 1-nitro-2-naphthol), ArN₂⁺ (azo coupling at C-1). Lewis acid may be needed depending on E.

valid_transformations.notes: NO2 at C-1 deactivates ring-1; EAS goes to other ring (ring-2); positions 5 and 8 preferred on ring-2; EWG sends EAS to the ENTIRE other ring
valid_transformations.conditions: EAS; Lewis acid (if needed); NO₂ is meta-director in non-naphthalene EAS, but in naphthalene systems, 1-nitro at C-1 directs EAS to C-5 (peri, across the ring, in same ring or adjacent ring). C-5 substitution in 1-substituted naphthalenes is common for electron-withdrawing groups that direct to less-activated positions. Temperature and electrophile dependent.

valid_transformations.notes: phthalic anhydride (2-benzofuran-1,3-dione, C8); naphthalene C10 loses 2 carbons as CO2; intermediate = phthalic acid (benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid); classic industrial process; V2O5 = vanadium pentoxide catalyst
valid_transformations.conditions: V₂O₅ catalyst; O₂ (air); 400–500°C; gas phase; catalytic oxidation. Naphthalene + O₂ → phthalic anhydride (1,2-benzenedicarboxylic anhydride, 2-benzofuran-1,3-dione, IUPAC). Industrial: same conditions as benzene → maleic anhydride. Vanadium pentoxide on TiO₂ or Al₂O₃ support. Used in plasticiser and dye manufacture.

valid_transformations.notes: Kolbe-Schmitt reaction; NaOH → Na+ chelates O- and CO2 via 6-membered ring at ORTHO position; major = salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid); minor = 4-hydroxybenzoic acid; salicylic acid has higher bp (intramolecular H-bond, less volatile)
valid_transformations.conditions: Kolbe-Schmitt reaction: Step 1: phenol + NaOH → sodium phenoxide. Step 2: CO₂ (4–7 atm); 125–150°C; dry sodium phenoxide → sodium salicylate. Step 3: H⁺ workup → salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid). Mechanism: CO₂ electrophile attacks phenoxide at ortho C (ortho selectivity for Na salt; para for K salt). Used industrially to make aspirin precursor.

valid_transformations.notes: Reimer-Tiemann reaction; CHCl3+NaOH → :CCl2 (dichlorocarbene); :CCl2 attacks ortho carbanion of phenoxide → -Cl-/-H+ → salicylaldehyde (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde, MAJOR); ortho selectivity due to carbene attack on o-carbanion of phenoxide
valid_transformations.conditions: Reimer-Tiemann reaction: CHCl₃ + NaOH; aqueous; 60–70°C. Mechanism: CHCl₃ + NaOH → :CCl₂ (dichlorocarbene); :CCl₂ attacks phenol ring (EAS-like) → intermediate → hydrolysis → CHO group. Regioselective ortho (with trace para). Product: 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde (salicylaldehyde) + 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde. Also: Duff reaction (hexamethylenetetramine/AcOH → ortho-formylation).

valid_transformations.notes: Fries rearrangement; phenyl acetate (O-acyl) + AlCl3 → 4-hydroxyacetophenone (C-acyl, para major); O-to-C acyl migration; low T favors para product; contrast: without AlCl3, phenol+CH3COCl gives O-acylation (ester) only
valid_transformations.conditions: Fries rearrangement: AlCl₃ (Lewis acid, excess); heat (Δ, >150°C); anhydrous nitrobenzene or neat. High temperature → para product (4'-hydroxyacetophenone, 4-hydroxyphenyl ethanone). Low temperature → ortho product. AlCl₃ cleaves ester O-CO → acetyl group migrates to ring at para (high T). Used in synthesis of hydroxyphenyl ketones (sunscreen components).

valid_transformations.notes: nitration at alpha (C-1), kinetically preferred (Wheland RS=7); mild temp (25°C); alpha selectivity same as halogenation and FC alkylation with small groups
valid_transformations.conditions: Conc HNO₃ + conc H₂SO₄ (mixed acid); 25°C (RT or slightly below); NO₂⁺ electrophile. Naphthalene very reactive in EAS (like activated benzene). α-position (C-1) preferred for electrophilic attack (more stable arenium ion intermediate). Low temperature (25°C) → mono-nitration. Higher T → di-nitration. Product: 1-nitronaphthalene (major, ~95% at low T).

valid_transformations.notes: TNT synthesis: 3 successive nitrations; methyl (EDG) directs ortho/para → 1st: 2- and 4-nitrotoluene; 2nd: 2,4-dinitrotoluene; 3rd: 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene (TNT); each step requires more vigorous conditions (NO2 deactivates ring)
valid_transformations.conditions: Stepwise nitration: conc HNO₃/H₂SO₄; increasing temperature (50°C for first NO₂, 70°C for second, 100°C for third). Methyl (toluene) is EDG ortho/para director → successive nitrations at ortho and para positions. Third nitration requires higher T (ring deactivated by NO₂ groups). Product: TNT (2,4,6-trinitrotoluene = 1-methyl-2,4,6-trinitrobenzene). Three equiv mixed acid.

valid_transformations.notes: Carbylamine reaction (Abnormal Reimer-Tiemann); :CCl2 attacks N of primary amine instead of ring C; mechanism: ArNH2 + :CCl2 → ArNH-CHCl2 → -H+ → ArN-=CHCl2 → -Cl- → ArN=CCl → -Cl- → ArN≡C (isocyanobenzene); foul odor; ONLY primary amines give this test; secondary/tertiary amines do NOT
valid_transformations.conditions: Carbylamine (isocyanide) test: CHCl₃ + KOH (alc.); heat (Δ). Primary amine (PhNH₂) + CHCl₃ + base → isocyanide (PhNC, isocyanobenzene). Mechanism: CHCl₃/base → :CCl₂ (dichlorocarbene) → adds to NH₂ → N-CHCl₂ intermediate → base deprotonates → elimination of 2 HCl → isocyanide. Characteristic foul smell (carrion-like). Test for primary amines only (1°→positive; 2°, 3°→negative).

valid_transformations.notes: EAS on anthracene at meso position (C-9 or C-10); attack at C-9 gives Wheland intermediate where BOTH outer rings retain full aromaticity; maximum stabilization; C-9 >> C-1 (alpha) >> C-2 (beta); meso (9,10) positions are most reactive in anthracene EAS
valid_transformations.conditions: HNO₃/H₂SO₄ (mixed acid) or conc HNO₃ alone; RT or 0–5°C. Anthracene is very reactive in EAS (central ring most reactive; C-9 and C-10 most nucleophilic positions). Nitration very easy — mild conditions sufficient. Regioselective C-9 (meso position). If too harsh → oxidation side reactions. Dilute conditions (cold) → mono-nitration at 9-position.

valid_transformations.notes: Vanillin synthesis; 2-methoxyphenol has OCH3 occupying one ortho position → RTR :CCl2 attacks PARA instead of ortho; RTR rule: one ortho blocked → major product is PARA; 4-hydroxy-3-methoxybenzaldehyde = vanillin (flavoring, IUPAC name)
valid_transformations.conditions: Reimer-Tiemann on guaiacol (2-methoxyphenol): CHCl₃ + NaOH; 60–70°C; aqueous. :CCl₂ attacks ring → formylation at C-4 (para to OH, ortho to OMe) → 4-hydroxy-3-methoxybenzaldehyde (vanillin). Vanillin can also be made by Duff reaction or from eugenol. Reimer-Tiemann gives vanillin as major product from guaiacol.

valid_transformations.notes: Aspirin synthesis; salicylic acid phenol-OH esterifies with acetic anhydride or acetyl chloride → 2-acetoxybenzoic acid (aspirin); COOH remains free; pain killer / analgesic; one of the most important aromatic compound conversions in JEE
valid_transformations.conditions: Acetic anhydride (Ac₂O) or acetyl chloride (AcCl); pyridine (catalyst/base); RT. O-acetylation of the phenolic OH of salicylic acid → aspirin (2-acetoxybenzoic acid, 2-(acetyloxy)benzoic acid). COOH not acetylated under these conditions (less nucleophilic than phenolic OH). Commercial: salicylic acid + Ac₂O + trace H₂SO₄ (catalyst), slight heat.

valid_transformations.notes: Oil of wintergreen; methyl salicylate; main component of IODEX (topical analgesic); COOH esterified (not the phenol OH in this case); 2-hydroxybenzoic acid + MeOH/H+ → methyl 2-hydroxybenzoate (methyl salicylate)
valid_transformations.conditions: Fischer esterification: methanol (excess) + conc H₂SO₄ or HCl (cat.); reflux. COOH → COOCH₃ (not phenolic OH → esterified under these conditions since phenol is poor acyl acceptor via acid catalysis). Product: methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen). Both acid and phenol groups present but only COOH undergoes Fischer esterification.

valid_transformations.notes: Friedel-Crafts with ethylene oxide (oxirane); AlCl3 activates epoxide O → ring opens to generate PhCH2CH2+ type electrophile → benzene attacks → 2-phenylethanol; epoxide is an FC electrophile source; 2-phenylethanol is also known as rose alcohol
valid_transformations.conditions: Ethylene oxide (oxirane) + AlCl₃ (Lewis acid); anhydrous; RT to mild heat. AlCl₃ activates epoxide → electrophilic addition (EAS-type): PhH + CH₂-CH₂-O/AlCl₃ → Ph-CH₂CH₂OH (1,2-addition to opened epoxide). Product: 2-phenylethanol (phenylethyl alcohol, rose fragrance). Alternatively: benzene + CH₂=CH₂/AlCl₃ → styrene? No — oxirane gives 2-phenylethanol.

valid_transformations.notes: Claisen rearrangement; allyl phenyl ether + heat → [3,3]-sigmatropic concerted rearrangement → cyclohexadienone intermediate (ortho allylated) → 1,5-keto-enol tautomerism → 2-allylphenol; ORTHO product major; pericyclic (no catalyst needed); if BOTH ortho blocked → para product via double [3,3]; if all ortho+para blocked → No Rxn
valid_transformations.conditions: Claisen rearrangement: Δ (heat alone, 200°C); no catalyst. Phenyl allyl ether (prop-2-en-1-yloxy)benzene → [3,3]-sigmatropic → 2-allylcyclohexadienone → tautomerism → 2-allylphenol (2-(prop-2-en-1-yl)phenol). Thermal, pericyclic (concerted). Stereospecific (chair-like TS). No solvent needed; high-boiling solvents possible (DEA, PhCl).

valid_transformations.notes: Picric acid synthesis (good yield); step 1: phenol + conc H2SO4/delta → 2,4-phenoldisulfonic acid (SO3H blocks C-2 and C-4); step 2: + conc HNO3/H2SO4 → NO2 displaces SO3H at 2, 4, 6 → 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid); direct HNO3 on phenol gives LOW YIELD due to oxidation of OH by HNO3
valid_transformations.conditions: Step 1: conc H₂SO₄, Δ → sulphonation at ortho/para → 2,4-disulphophenol (blocks ring). Step 2: conc HNO₃/H₂SO₄ → nitration replaces sulphonate groups + nitrates at remaining positions → 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid). Alternative: direct fuming HNO₃ on phenol carefully. Picric acid: very acidic (pKa 0.4), yellow explosive solid (keep moist).

valid_transformations.notes: Etard reaction; methylbenzene + CrO2Cl2/CS2 → [Ph-CH(OCr(OH)Cl2)2] complex intermediate → H3O+ → benzaldehyde (Ph-CHO); SELECTIVE: stops at aldehyde (not COOH); contrast: KMnO4 goes to benzoic acid; Etard specific to benzylic CH3 → CHO
valid_transformations.conditions: Étard reaction: CrO₂Cl₂ (chromyl chloride); CS₂ or CCl₄ solvent; RT. CrO₂Cl₂ oxidises toluene (methylbenzene) selectively at benzylic position → chromium ester complex → hydrolysis → benzaldehyde. Alternatively: MnO₂/H₂SO₄, or electrolytic oxidation. Different from KMnO₄ (gives benzoic acid). CrO₂Cl₂ is selective for aldehyde without overoxidation.

valid_transformations.notes: Benzene hexachloride (BHC) synthesis; free radical addition (NOT substitution); benzene + 3 Cl2/UV → Cl adds across all 3 double bonds → C6H6Cl6 (cyclohexane hexachloride); BHC = 666 = Lindane = Gammaxene = insecticide; contrast with EAS (Cl2/FeCl3 → chlorobenzene by substitution, not addition)
valid_transformations.conditions: 3 Cl₂; UV light (hν); 500K; radical addition (not electrophilic substitution). Benzene + 3 Cl₂/hν → hexachlorocyclohexane (BHC = benzene hexachloride, lindane precursor). Anti-addition? Radical addition across all 3 double bonds. 8 possible stereoisomers; γ-BHC (lindane) is the insecticidal isomer. High Cl₂ pressure and UV needed.

valid_transformations.notes: Sandmeyer-Finkelstein for ArI; benzenediazonium + KI/Δ → iodobenzene + N2 + KCl; NO Cu catalyst needed (unlike ArCl and ArBr Sandmeyer); Cu2I2 cannot be used (cuprous iodide reduces I- back); only KI/heat gives ArI directly; KI/Δ is the UNIQUE iodine Sandmeyer route
valid_transformations.conditions: KI (potassium iodide); heat (Δ, warm, 50–80°C); aqueous. ArN₂⁺ + KI → Ar-I + N₂ + KCl. Iodination via diazonium: no Cu catalyst needed (I⁻ is good enough nucleophile/reductant). Mechanism: radical or ionic (ArN₂⁺ + I⁻ → Ar• + N₂ + I• → Ar-I). Direct method (no Sandmeyer needed for iodide). Gattermann–Sandmeyer: ArN₂⁺ + CuCN → ArCN (for nitrile).

valid_transformations.notes: Sandmeyer cyanation; benzenediazonium + NaCN (with CuCN catalyst) → benzonitrile (PhCN) + N2 + NaCl; benzonitrile = phenylcarbonitrile = masked COOH (CN can be hydrolyzed to COOH with H3O+/H+); gives ORTHO- or PARA-nitrile when starting from substituted aniline; Sandmeyer route to nitriles (cannot directly add CN to benzene without diazonium route)
valid_transformations.conditions: CuCN (copper cyanide) or NaCN/CuCN; RT to mild heat; aqueous. Sandmeyer reaction with cyanide. ArN₂⁺ + CuCN → ArCN + N₂. Mechanism: Cu(I) transfers CN• radical to Ar•. Product: benzonitrile (phenyl cyanide). Can also use Gattermann modification (Cu powder + HCN). Product used for further synthesis (hydrolysis → RCOOH; reduction → benzylamine).

valid_transformations.notes: Double bromination of nitrobenzene; NO2 is meta-director → Br goes to C-3 and C-5 (both meta positions); with 2 equiv Br2/Fe both meta positions are brominated; product = 1,3-dibromo-5-nitrobenzene (= 3,5-dibromonitrobenzene); KEY: EWG like NO2 directs to BOTH meta positions with excess electrophile; no ortho/para bromination occurs
valid_transformations.conditions: Br₂ (2 equiv) + Fe (or FeBr₃ Lewis acid); anhydrous; mild heat. Nitrobenzene: NO₂ is meta-director/EWG → EAS at meta positions (C-3 and C-5, both meta to NO₂). Two Br² added sequentially → 1,3-dibromo-5-nitrobenzene (meta-deactivated ring, need excess Br₂ and Lewis acid, higher T than for activated rings).

valid_transformations.notes: Soda lime decarboxylation; 4-aminobenzoic acid (C7) + NaOH/CaO/Δ (soda lime) → aniline (phenylamine, C6) + CO2; NH2 group NOT affected by soda lime; soda lime = NaOH + CaO (solid, high-T decarboxylation); used in long synthesis chains to remove COOH after it served as a directing group; converts ArCOOH → ArH
valid_transformations.conditions: NaOH + CaO (soda lime); strong heat (Δ, 300–400°C). Decarboxylation: 4-aminobenzoic acid → CO₂ + aniline (phenylamine). Loss of COOH group. Soda lime provides base + high melting point solid to maintain heat. Same as benzoic acid → benzene mechanism.

valid_transformations.notes: Nitrile + Grignard → ketone; benzonitrile (PhCN) + CH3MgBr → Ph-C(=N-MgBr)-CH3 (ketimine metal salt, stops here) → H3O+ → Ph-C(=NH)-CH3 (imine) → H2O → 1-phenylethan-1-one (acetophenone, PhCOCH3) + NH3; ONE Grignard adds (imine C=N less electrophilic than nitrile C≡N, second addition blocked); product is KETONE not alcohol
valid_transformations.conditions: Step 1: CH₃MgBr (methylmagnesium bromide, Grignard) + PhCN (benzonitrile) in dry ether/THF, 0°C → imine-MgBr complex (N=C of nitrile + Grignard → imine anion: Ph-C(=NMgBr)-CH₃). Step 2: H₃O⁺ workup → imine → hydrolysis → ketone (Ph-CO-CH₃, acetophenone). Net: RC≡N + RMgX → imine → ketone (one more C from Grignard). Useful for ketone synthesis from nitrile.

reagents: Pt (or Pd or Ni or Raney Ni or PtO2 or Pd-C)
valid_transformations.notes: Catalytic hydrogenation; alkene + H2/metal → alkane; SYN addition (both H delivered from same face of alkene, via adsorption on metal surface); NO rearrangement (no carbocation); exothermic (ΔH<0); catalysts: Pt, Pd, Ni, Raney Ni, PtO2 (Adam's catalyst), [Rh(PPh3)3Cl] (Wilkinson's catalyst), Pd-C, Pt-C
valid_transformations.conditions: H₂; Pt (or Pd, Ni, Raney Ni); RT to 50°C; EtOH solvent; 1–3 atm. Heterogeneous catalytic hydrogenation; syn addition of H₂ from catalyst surface. Cis and trans but-2-ene both give butane (geometry of C=C erased after full reduction). Degree of substitution: internal alkene reacts at comparable rate to terminal alkene.

valid_transformations.notes: Cyanogen (NC-CN, ethanedinitrile) + RMgX; step 1: Grignard R attacks one C of NC-CN → CN⁻ leaves as LG → R-CN (in-situ nitrile); step 2: second RMgX + R-CN → ketimine; step 3: H3O+ → R2C=O (ketone) + NH3; NET: (CN)2 + 2 CH3MgBr → propan-2-one (acetone) + NH3; only ONE ketone formed despite two CN groups
valid_transformations.conditions: Step 1: 2 CH₃MgI (methylmagnesium iodide) in dry ether + ethanedinitrile (NCCN, oxalonitrile) → double Grignard addition → diimine-Mg complex. Step 2: H₃O⁺ workup → di-imine → double hydrolysis → propan-2-one (acetone) × 2? Actually NC-CN + 2 CH₃MgX → bis(imine) → 2 × CH₃-CO-CH₃ (2 equivalents). One nitrile C with 2 × CH₃ → one ketone. Two nitrile carbons → two acetone molecules.

valid_transformations.notes: Wilkinson's catalyst [Rh(PPh3)3Cl]; homogeneous hydrogenation catalyst (soluble, reacts in solution); alkene + H2/Wilkinson's → alkane; SYN addition; selective for terminal alkenes; used when heterogeneous catalysts are too harsh (e.g., for sensitive substrates); does NOT reduce aromatic rings (unlike Ni/Pd at high pressure); contrast with Adam's catalyst PtO2 (reduced to Pt in situ, heterogeneous)
valid_transformations.conditions: H₂; [Rh(PPh₃)₃Cl] (Wilkinson's catalyst); RT; benzene or chloroform solvent; 1 atm H₂. Homogeneous catalytic hydrogenation. Wilkinson's catalyst: oxidative addition of H₂ to Rh(I) → Rh(III)(H)₂ → alkene coordinates → migratory insertion → reductive elimination → alkane. More selective than heterogeneous Pd/C.

valid_transformations.notes: Lindlar's poisonous catalytic hydrogenation; alkyne + H2/Lindlar's → CIS (Z)-alkene; syn addition of H2 from SAME face gives Z configuration; STOPS at alkene stage (poisoned catalyst cannot further reduce C=C); Lindlar's variants: H2+Pd+BaSO4+Quinoline; H2+Pt+CaCO3+Quinoline; H2+Pd+Pb(OAc)2+Quinoline; H2+Pd+BaSO4+S; P-II catalyst = Ni2B/H2 also gives CIS-alkene
valid_transformations.conditions: H₂ (1 equiv); Lindlar's catalyst (Pd/CaCO₃/Pb(OAc)₂ + quinoline) or Pd/BaSO₄/quinoline; RT; EtOH or EtOAc; 1 atm. Syn addition of H₂ → cis-but-2-ene ((Z)-but-2-ene). Stop at 1 equiv H₂ (partial reduction). Quinoline and Pb²⁺ poison reduce catalyst activity so reduction stops at alkene stage. Selectivity: alkyne > alkene.

valid_transformations.notes: Rosenmund reduction; acid chloride R-COCl + H2/Pd-BaSO4 → aldehyde R-CHO (STOPS here); poisoned Pd reduces C-Cl bond to C-H but DOES NOT further reduce C=O to alcohol; PhCOCl + H2/Pd-BaSO4 → PhCHO (benzaldehyde = benzenecarbaldehyde); works for both aryl and alkyl acid chlorides; Pd-BaSO4 = Rosenmund's poisoned Pd
valid_transformations.conditions: Rosenmund reduction: H₂; Pd/BaSO₄ (poisoned with sulphur quinoline); anhydrous xylene or toluene solvent; 50–100°C; 1 atm H₂. Selective reduction of acyl chloride to aldehyde (stops before alcohol). Pd poisoning prevents over-reduction. Alternatively: DIBALH (–78°C, dry toluene) → aldehyde. Both give benzaldehyde from benzoyl chloride.

valid_transformations.notes: SYN D2 addition to (E)-but-2-ene (trans); both D delivered from SAME face; trans-alkene (Me groups on OPPOSITE sides) + syn D addition → MESO compound (optically inactive); both faces of attack give IDENTICAL meso product (due to C2 symmetry of trans-alkene); contrast: cis-alkene + syn D2/Pt → racemic mix
valid_transformations.conditions: D₂; Pt (or Pd); RT; 1 atm; EtOH solvent. Syn addition of D₂ (both D atoms from same face of catalyst surface). (E)-but-2-ene (trans) + D₂ → syn addition → meso-2,3-dideuterobutan (both D atoms on same face = meso, has internal mirror plane). Compare: (Z)-but-2-ene + D₂ → racemic 2,3-dideuterobutan. Stereospecific proof of syn addition.

valid_transformations.notes: SYN D2 addition to (Z)-but-2-ene (cis); both D delivered from SAME face; cis-alkene (Me groups on SAME side) + syn D addition: attack from face A → (R,R) isomer; attack from face B → (S,S) isomer; equal probability → RACEMIC MIXTURE; contrast: trans-alkene + syn D2/Pt → meso compound
valid_transformations.conditions: D₂; Pt; RT; 1 atm; EtOH. Syn addition of D₂ to cis-but-2-ene → both D on same face → racemic (R,R) and (S,S) pair (two chiral centres, no plane of symmetry) = racemic mixture. Compare: trans-but-2-ene + D₂ → meso. Proof of syn addition mechanism.

valid_transformations.notes: Kolbe electrolysis; sodium ethanoate (CH3COONa) → at anode: CH3COO⁻ → -e⁻ → CH3COO• → -CO2 → CH3• → CH3• + CH3• → CH3-CH3 (ethane); at cathode: 2H2O + 2e⁻ → 2OH⁻ + H2↑ (H2 evolved, NOT Na metal); LIMITATION: CH4 cannot be prepared (HCOONa → H• → H2, methyl equivalent not possible); shortest Kolbe: sodium ethanoate → ethane (C1→C2 coupling)
valid_transformations.conditions: Kolbe electrolysis: aqueous sodium acetate solution (concentrated); 5A current; Pt anode/cathode; RT. Anode: CH₃COO⁻ → CH₃COO• → CH₃• + CO₂; 2 CH₃• → CH₃-CH₃ (ethane). Cathode: 2 H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2 OH⁻. Net: 2 CH₃COONa → C₂H₆ + 2CO₂ + 2NaOH (electrolytic). Symmetric coupling at anode.

valid_transformations.notes: Kolbe electrolysis of sodium propanoate (CH3CH2COONa); CH3CH2COO⁻ → -e⁻ → CH3CH2COO• → -CO2 → CH3CH2• (ethyl radical, 2 carbons); ethyl radical undergoes DISPROPORTIONATION (≥2 C rule) → MAJOR: ester [CH3CH2-COO-CH2CH3, ethyl propanoate, sweet smelling compound]; MINOR: ethane (CH3CH3) + ethylene (CH2=CH2); NOTE: radical with ≥2 carbons → disproportionation major over simple coupling
valid_transformations.conditions: Kolbe electrolysis cross-product? Actually: sodium propanoate (CH₃CH₂COONa) → Kolbe at anode: 2 CH₃CH₂COO⁻ → 2 CH₃CH₂• + 2CO₂ → CH₃CH₂-CH₂CH₃ (butane, not ethyl propanoate). BUT: if acetic + propionic mixed → cross-Kolbe. Ethyl propanoate would form by coupling CH₃• (from acetate) + CH₃CH₂COO⁻ → ethyl propanoate only if cross-Kolbe. Re-check: sodium propanoate electrolysis → butane (symmetric) + CO₂. Ethyl propanoate may arise from esterification side reaction at electrode.

valid_transformations.notes: Intramolecular Kolbe electrolysis; NaOOC-(CH2)3-COONa (pentanedioate, glutarate) + 5A → both carboxylates lose CO2 → •CH2-CH2-CH2• (1,3-diradical) → intramolecular coupling → cyclopropane + 2CO2; general rule: NaOOC-(CH2)n-COONa → cycloalkane with n carbons; Q11-type: n=3 → cyclopropane; n=4 → cyclobutane; n=5 → cyclopentane
valid_transformations.conditions: Kolbe intramolecular electrolysis: disodium glutarate (glutaric acid Na₂ salt); electrolysis; 5A current; Pt anode. Anode: two –COO⁻ → two carboxyl radicals → lose 2CO₂ → trimethylene diradical → ring closure → cyclopropane. Intramolecular Kolbe: adipate (n=6 dicarboxylate) → cyclobutane; glutarate (n=5) → cyclopropane; pimelate (n=7) → cyclopentane.

valid_transformations.notes: Kolbe electrolysis of sodium benzoate (PhCOONa); PhCOO⁻ → -e⁻ → PhCOO• → -CO2 → Ph• (phenyl radical) → Ph• + Ph• → Ph-Ph (1,1-biphenyl); aryl carboxylates give Kolbe coupling to biaryls; sodium triphenylacetate → Ph3C• (Gomberg's trityl radical) → Ph3C-CPh3 (hexaphenylethane, Gomberg's compound)
valid_transformations.conditions: Kolbe electrolysis: sodium benzoate (aq); 5A current; Pt anode; RT. Anode: PhCOO⁻ → PhCOO• → Ph• + CO₂; 2 Ph• → Ph-Ph (biphenyl = 1,1'-biphenyl). Coupling of phenyl radicals. Product: biphenyl. Cathode: H₂. Also called Fittig reaction when done electrochemically.

valid_transformations.notes: Fittig reaction; 2 Ar-X + Na/dry ether → Ar-Ar (biaryl) + 2 NaX; mechanism: Ar-X + Na → Ar-Na (arylsodium) + Ar-X → SN2 → Ar-Ar; Fittig = aryl version of Wurtz; gives symmetric biaryl from one aryl halide; contrast Ullmann (Cu catalyst) vs Fittig (Na); contrast Wurtz-Fittig (Ar-X + R-X + Na) which gives Ar-R (alkylbenzene)
valid_transformations.conditions: Ullmann reaction: Na metal (or Cu); dry ether (Wurtz-Fittig variation); heat. ArX + Na → Ar-Na (arylsodium) → Ar-Na + ArX → Ar-Ar + NaX. Or: 2 ArX + 2Na → Ar-Ar + 2 NaX (Fittig synthesis). Alternatively Cu/Δ (Ullmann coupling, 200–300°C): 2 ArCl + Cu → Ar-Ar + CuCl₂. Product: biphenyl (1,1'-biphenyl).

valid_transformations.notes: Wurtz-Fittig reaction; Ar-X + R-X + Na/dry ether → Ar-R (alkylbenzene) + Ar-Ar + R-R; gives THREE products as mixed Wurtz-Fittig always does; Ar-R is the desired product but is contaminated with Ar-Ar (Fittig product) and R-R (Wurtz product); Ph-Cl + C2H5-Cl + Na → ethylbenzene (major desired) + biphenyl + butane (byproducts)
valid_transformations.conditions: Wurtz-Fittig synthesis: Na metal; dry ether; heat (reflux). PhCl + Na → Ph-Na (phenylsodium); Ph-Na + EtCl (chloroethane) → Ph-Et + NaCl. Or: PhCl + Na + EtCl → Ph-Et + NaCl (mixed Wurtz-Fittig: one aryl halide + one alkyl halide + Na). Product: ethylbenzene. Side products: biphenyl (Fittig) and butane (Wurtz).

valid_transformations.notes: Corey-House synthesis; R2CuLi (Gilman reagent = lithium dialkylcuprate [R-Cu-R]⁻Li⁺) + R'-X → R-R' (CROSS-COUPLING, unsymmetric alkane); + R-X → R-R (symmetric); key advantage over Wurtz: gives ONLY the cross-coupling product without contaminating symmetric products; works best with primary alkyl halides (SN2); Gilman reagent prepared: 2RLi + CuI → R2CuLi + LiI; example: (n-Pr)2CuLi + n-BuCl → n-heptane
valid_transformations.conditions: Gilman reagent (organocuprate) with primary alkyl halide: (n-Pr)₂CuLi + 1-chlorobutane; dry ether or THF; 0°C to RT; SN2. Organocuprates couple cleanly with primary alkyl halides (no elimination, unlike Grignard). n-Pr (3C) + n-Bu (4C) → n-heptane? Wait: n-Pr = propyl (C₃), 1-chlorobutane (C₄) → C₇ (heptane), not decane. Decane (C₁₀) = two C₅ groups? (n-Bu)₂CuLi + 1-chlorohexane → C₁₀. n-Propylcuprate + 1-chloroheptane → decane (C₃+C₇).

valid_transformations.notes: Ullmann reaction; 2 Ar-I + Cu/Δ → Ar-Ar + 2CuI; requires ARYL HALIDE (Ar-I or Ar-Cl) NOT alkyl halide; Cu metal catalyst + heat; mechanism: Cu inserts into Ar-X bond → organocopper intermediate → coupling; gives SYMMETRIC biaryl from one Ar-X; CROSS Ullmann: Ar-X + Ar'-X + Cu/Δ → Ar-Ar' (unsymmetric biaryl); example: Ph-I + Ph-I + Cu/Δ → Ph-Ph (biphenyl); also: 4-NO2-Ph-Cl + Cu/Δ → 4,4'-dinitrobiphenyl; IIT-JEE standard question
valid_transformations.conditions: Ullmann coupling: Cu powder; Δ (strong heat, 200–300°C); DMF or neat. 2 PhI + Cu → Ph-Ph + CuI₂. High temperature required. Iodide more reactive than bromide or chloride. Modern: Pd-catalysed coupling (Suzuki, Negishi, Kumada) at lower T. Product: biphenyl.

valid_transformations.notes: Free radical substitution (FSR); 2-methylpropane (isobutane) + Cl2/hv → 2-chloro-2-methylpropane (major) + 1-chloro-2-methylpropane (minor); mechanism: ①initiation: Cl2+hv→2Cl•; ②propagation: (CH3)3CH + Cl• → (CH3)3C• + HCl; (CH3)3C• + Cl2 → (CH3)3CCl + Cl•; ③termination: R•+Cl•→RCl; 3° radical more stable → 3° product major; rate order: 3° > 2° > 1°
valid_transformations.conditions: Cl₂; hν (UV light); gas phase or CCl₄; RT. Radical chlorination: selectivity for tertiary C-H (3° C-H is weakest, radical most stable). 2-Methylpropane has 9 equivalent 1° H and 1 3° H; selectivity factor for Cl: 3°:1° ≈ 5:1; statistical factor: 1H×5 : 9H×1 = 5:9 = ~36% 3° product. Predominantly 2-chloro-2-methylpropane (tertiary). Compare: Br₂ gives almost exclusively 3° product (>99% selectivity at RT).
