valid_transformations.notes: FSR bromination; Br2 is MOST SELECTIVE halogen for FSR (F2 least selective); 2-methylpropane + Br2/hv → ONLY 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (nearly 100% 3° selectivity for Br2); rationale: Br• is a weak H-abstractor (endothermic step) so it is VERY selective for the most stable (3°) radical; Cl• is less selective (exothermic, more product-like TS); selectivity order: Br2 > Cl2 > F2 (inversely related to reactivity)
valid_transformations.conditions: Br₂; hν; CCl₄ or gas phase; RT. Radical bromination: very high selectivity for 3° C-H. Br• is selective (high ΔH‡, late TS resembles product radical → most stable radical reacts). 3°:1° selectivity ≈ 1600:1. Product: almost exclusively 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (t-BuBr). Compare: Cl₂/hν → mixture (low selectivity).

valid_transformations.notes: FSR bromination of propane; propane has 6 equivalent 1° H and 2 equivalent 2° H; with Br2/hv: 2-bromopropane (secondary) is major (>95%) even though only 2 H are 2°; Br• is so selective it preferentially abstracts the 2° H over the 1° H; contrast Cl2/hv with propane: gives ~55% 2-chloropropane + 45% 1-chloropropane (much less selective); selectivity difference is the key JEE concept
valid_transformations.conditions: Br₂; hν; RT; CCl₄ or gas phase. Radical bromination: 2° C-H preferred over 1° (selectivity 2°:1° ≈ 82:1). Propane: 6 equivalent 1° H and 2 equivalent 2° H. Statistical × selectivity → 2-bromopropane major (secondary). Product: 2-bromopropane predominantly.

valid_transformations.notes: FSR chlorination of propane; Cl2/hv → mixture of 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane; 2-chloropropane is still major (2° radical more stable) but 1-chloropropane also forms in significant amount (~45%); Cl• is less selective than Br• because H-abstraction by Cl• is highly exothermic (early TS, resembles reactant, doesn't care much about radical stability); with Br2, 2-bromopropane >95% (Br• is late TS, resembles product radical)
valid_transformations.conditions: Cl₂; hν; RT; gas phase or CCl₄. Radical chlorination: lower selectivity than Br₂. 2°:1° selectivity ≈ 3.5:1. Propane: 6×1° + 2×2° H. Product ratio: 2-chloro : 1-chloro ≈ 2×3.5 : 6×1 = 7:6. 2-Chloropropane slightly major. Statistical correction required. Mixture of 1-chloropropane + 2-chloropropane.

valid_transformations.notes: Vapour-phase nitration of propane; propane + conc HNO3/400°C → mixture: 2-nitropropane (major, 2° H abstracted preferentially by NO2•) + 1-nitropropane (minor) + nitroethane + nitromethane (C-C bond cleavage at 400°C gives shorter-chain nitroalkanes as byproducts); assumed mechanism: free radical; rate order: 3° > 2° > 1°; high temperature (400°C) causes both C-H and C-C homolysis → multiple products; contrast with aromatic nitration (electrophilic, not free radical)
valid_transformations.conditions: Conc HNO₃ (dilute nitric acid, 20%); 400°C; gas phase (vapour-phase nitration). Free radical mechanism at high T: HNO₃ → OH• + NO₂• at 400°C; OH• abstracts H from propane → propyl radical → NO₂• + radical → nitropropane. 2-Nitropropane (secondary, from more stable 2° radical) is major product. 1-Nitropropane also formed. High T required for radical nitration.

valid_transformations.notes: Vapour-phase sulphonation of 2-methylpropane (isobutane); mechanism same as nitration = free radical; 2-methylpropane + conc H2SO4/Δ → 2-methylpropane-2-sulfonic acid (major, 3° position) + minor 1° product; rate of sulphonation: 3° > 2° >> 1° (same selectivity trend as FSR and nitration); also C-C bonds cleave at high temp giving shorter-chain sulfonic acids
valid_transformations.conditions: Conc H₂SO₄; Δ (heat); electrophilic sulphonation. (CH₃)₃CH + H₂SO₄ → (CH₃)₃C-SO₃H. Mechanism: electrophilic attack of SO₃ (from H₂SO₄ equilibrium) on 3° C-H? More likely: SO₃ as electrophile in Markovnikov addition to isobutene → sulphonation. Or: conc H₂SO₄ direct sulphonation of alkane (harsh). Tertiary C-H most reactive.

valid_transformations.notes: Methylene insertion reaction; CH2N2 + UV → :CH2: (methylene carbene) + N2; :CH2: inserts into C-C bond of cyclopentane (ring expansion) → cyclohexane; ALSO :CH2: inserts into C-H bonds → methylcyclopentane (two products from cyclopentane + CH2N2/UV); both C-H insertion and C-C insertion are non-selective; ring expansion: cyclopentane (5-membered) → cyclohexane (6-membered) via C-C carbene insertion; another example: n-butane + CH2N2/UV → pentane + isopentane (C-H at 1° → pentane; C-H at 2° → isopentane; C-C insertion → methylbutane)
valid_transformations.conditions: CH₂N₂ (diazomethane); UV (hν); ring expansion. Diazomethane + cyclopentane → cyclopentyl carbene intermediate? More likely: :CH₂ (singlet carbene from hν/CH₂N₂) inserts into C-H bond → methylcyclopentane, not cyclohexane. Actually ring expansion: cyclopentylmethyl carbene → ring expansion → cyclohexane via 1,2-H shift. UV light generates :CH₂ from CH₂N₂ → C-H insertion into cyclopentane ring → cyclohexane (ring expansion by one C).

valid_transformations.notes: Wittig reaction; cyclohexanone + H2C=PPh3 (ylide/methylenephosphorane) → methylenecyclohexane (exocyclic alkene) + Ph3P=O (triphenylphosphine oxide); yield ~95%; mechanism: [2+2] cycloaddition of C=O and C=PPh3 → oxaphosphetane (4-membered ring: C-O-P-C betaine) → retro-[2+2] → alkene + Ph3P=O; trick: replace the C=O with C=CH2 (whatever is on ylide carbon replaces O); can also make di/trisubstituted alkenes; key advantage: forms alkene at EXACT position of C=O, not mixture; 95% yield (high selectivity unlike E1/E2 which give Zaitsev mixture)
valid_transformations.conditions: Wittig reaction: methylenetriphenylphosphorane (H₂C=PPh₃, ylide); anhydrous THF or benzene; RT to mild heat. Mechanism: nucleophilic addition of ylide C to ketone C=O → [2+2] cycloaddition → oxaphosphetane → retro-[2+2] → alkene (C=CH₂, exo-methylene) + Ph₃P=O. Wittig gives C=C where C=O was. Phosphorus ylide: Ph₃P + CH₂X₂ → Ph₃P-CH₂X⁺ → base → ylide.

valid_transformations.notes: 1,2-addition of HBr to buta-1,3-diene; KCR (Kinetically Controlled Rxn); -40°C (low temperature); H+ to C1 → delocalized allylic cation (C2 and C4); Br- attacks C2 (less hindered, lower TS barrier) → 3-bromobut-1-ene (CH3-CHBr-CH=CH2); 1,2-product = kinetic product; less stable (terminal alkene CH=CH2 remains); at LOW TEMP, kinetic product (1,2) is major; same allylic intermediate also gives 1,4-product at higher temperature
valid_transformations.conditions: HBr (1 equiv); low temperature (–40°C or 0°C); kinetic conditions. 1,2-addition product: kinetic control at low T. Mechanism: H⁺ adds to C-1 → allylic cation (stabilised by resonance C-2 and C-4) → Br⁻ adds to C-2 (1,2-product, closer resonance structure, faster, kinetic). Low T prevents equilibration. Product: 3-bromo-1-butene.

valid_transformations.notes: 1,4-addition of HBr to buta-1,3-diene; TCR (Thermodynamically Controlled Rxn); 25°C or room temperature (high temperature relative to -40°C); H+ to C1 → allylic cation → Br- attacks C4 (1,4 product); product: (E)-1-bromobut-2-ene (CH3-CH=CH-CH2Br); 1,4-product = thermodynamic product = more stable (internal alkene CH=CH retained); at HIGH TEMP, thermodynamic product (1,4) is major; rule: 1,2-addition = KCR (-40°C); 1,4-addition = TCR (25°C); SAME allylic cation intermediate for both
valid_transformations.conditions: HBr (1 equiv); RT (25°C) or higher temperature; thermodynamic conditions. 1,4-addition: allylic cation intermediate (C-2 and C-4 resonance) → Br⁻ adds to C-4 (1,4-product, more substituted alkene, thermodynamic). Trans (E) product preferred (more stable). Higher T → thermodynamic product. Equilibrium at RT or above favours 1,4-adduct.

valid_transformations.notes: 1,4-addition of Br2 (1eq) to buta-1,3-diene; Br+ to C1 → OPEN allylic cation (NOT closed bromonium; allylic resonance breaks the tight bromonium bridge) → Br- attacks C4 ANTI to C1-Br → (E)-1,4-dibromobut-2-ene (TRANS) = ONLY ONE PRODUCT (no cis isomer); key: even in 1,4-addition, the anti-addition geometry is maintained → trans product exclusively; Peter Sykes reference; TS = extended s-trans allylic cation; Br- comes from outside (anti) → trans diaxial addition across C1 and C4; Br2 1,4-addition to 1,3-diene always gives TRANS (E) product
valid_transformations.conditions: Br₂ (1 equiv); CCl₄; thermodynamic conditions (TCP = thermodynamic control product; RT or higher T for 1,4 product). Mechanism: Br₂ → Br⁺ (bromonium-like) → allylic cation → Br⁻ attacks C-4 (1,4-addition) → (E)-1,4-dibromobut-2-ene (trans-1,4 is thermodynamic). Low T/CCl₄ cold → 1,2-addition product; RT → 1,4-addition. Same allylic cation intermediate, product ratio temperature-dependent.

valid_transformations.notes: IIT Adv 2016 type; HBr addition to 2-methylbuta-1,3-diene (isoprene, CH2=C(CH3)-CH=CH2); H+ adds to C1 (NOT C4); reason: H+ to C1 → 3° allylic cation [CH3-C+(CH3)-CH=CH2 ↔ CH3-C(CH3)=CH-CH2+] = 3°+allylic (more stable ✓); H+ to C4 would give 2°+allylic (less stable ✗); TCP at 25°C: Br- attacks C4 of the more stable 3°-allylic cation → product (E)-1-bromo-2-methylbut-2-ene (CH2Br-C(CH3)=CH-CH3, 1,4-addition); key: always add H+ to give MOST STABLE allylic carbocation (3° > 2° > 1°)
valid_transformations.conditions: HBr (1 equiv); RT (25°C); thermodynamic control. Isoprene (2-methylbuta-1,3-diene) + HBr → allylic cation → 1,4-addition product preferred at RT. H⁺ adds to C-1 → allylic cation stabilised by methyl at C-2 → Br⁻ attacks C-4 → (E)-1-bromo-2-methyl-2-butene (trans-1,4). Methyl group at C-2 stabilises internal double bond → 1,4-product strongly preferred at RT.

valid_transformations.notes: Reductive ozonolysis of cyclopentene; cyclopentene + O3 → monozonide (C-O-O-O-C, 5-membered) → ozonide (1,2,4-trioxolane) → Zn/H2O cleaves ozonide reductively → pentane-1,5-dial (OHC-(CH2)3-CHO, glutaraldehyde); KEY: cyclic alkene gives ONE bifunctional product (the ring opens to give a linear dialdehyde, NOT two separate pieces); reductive workup (Zn or DMS) → aldehyde, not acid; Zn reduces O-O peroxide to ZnO
valid_transformations.conditions: O₃; then Zn/H₂O (reductive workup); –78°C for ozonolysis; CH₂Cl₂ solvent. Cyclopentene → ozonide → Zn/H₂O reductive workup → ring-opened dialdehyde (pentanedial = glutaraldehyde). Cyclic alkenes give one bifunctional product (no break in chain). Zn/H₂O: reductive → aldehydes. H₂O₂: oxidative → acids.

valid_transformations.notes: Oxidative ozonolysis of cyclopentene; cyclopentene + O3 → ozonide → H2O2 cleaves ozonide oxidatively → pentanedioic acid (glutaric acid, HOOC-(CH2)3-COOH); oxidative workup (H2O2 or Ag2O): aldehydes are OXIDIZED to carboxylic acids; the two aldehyde groups from reductive ozonolysis are oxidized to COOH; cyclic alkene → diacid (ONE molecule, ring opened); contrast with reductive: Zn/H2O → pentane-1,5-dial (dialdehyde); H2O2 → pentanedioic acid (diacid)
valid_transformations.conditions: O₃; then H₂O₂ (oxidative workup); –78°C, CH₂Cl₂ then H₂O₂/AcOH. Ozonolysis of cyclopentene → ozonide → H₂O₂ → pentanedioic acid (glutaric acid, 5C dicarboxylic acid). Oxidative workup: terminal CH=CH₂ → HCOOH; internal CH= → RCOOH. Ring opened completely → linear diacid.

valid_transformations.notes: Reductive ozonolysis of a terminal alkene (R-CH=CH2); general: R-CH=CH2 + O3/Zn/H2O → R-CHO (aldehyde) + HCHO (formaldehyde/methanal); for terminal alkene, the =CH2 end gives HCHO; the internal end gives R-CHO; under reductive conditions (Zn or DMS), HCHO is the product from terminal carbon; under OXIDATIVE conditions (H2O2): HCHO → HCOOH (formic acid); NOTE: all reductive ozonolysis products are aldehydes/ketones (NEVER carboxylic acid)
valid_transformations.conditions: O₃; Zn/H₂O (reductive); –78°C; CH₂Cl₂. 1-Methylidenebutane (CH₂=CH-CH₂-CH₂-CH₃, 1-pentene terminal alkene? Or exo-methylene: CH₂=C(chain)). Terminal alkene CH₂= → HCHO (formaldehyde) + R-CHO (butanal) after reductive workup. If 1-methylidenebutane is CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂CH₃ (pent-1-ene): ozonolysis → HCHO + CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO (butanal) + formaldehyde.

valid_transformations.notes: Ozonolysis of o-xylene (1,2-dimethylbenzene); treating benzene ring as Kekulé structure with 3 C=C bonds: o-xylene + O3/Zn → butane-2,3-dione (diacetyl, CH3-CO-CO-CH3) + ethanedial (glyoxal, OHC-CHO); the two C=C bonds adjacent to the two CH3 groups give the CH3-CO-CO-CH3 fragment; the third C=C gives OHC-CHO; general rule for benzene ozonolysis: treat as Kekulé structure, cleave each C=C → sum of fragments; for plain benzene: 3x ethanedial (glyoxal) = 3x OHC-CHO
valid_transformations.conditions: O₃; Zn (reductive workup); –78°C; CH₂Cl₂. 1,2-Dimethylbenzene (o-xylene) ozonolysis → ring opening → glyoxal-like fragments + butane-2,3-dione (2,3-butanedione = diacetyl = biacetyl, CH₃COCOCH₃). Complete ring opening of the ortho-substituted aromatic system? More precisely: per-ozonolysis of all C=C in ring of o-xylene → multiple carbonyl fragments including CH₃CO-COCH₃ (butane-2,3-dione). Vigorous conditions for aromatic ozonolysis.

valid_transformations.notes: DIBALH (diisobutylaluminium hydride) reduces ester to ALDEHYDE (stops at aldehyde, does NOT over-reduce to alcohol); ethyl ethanoate + DIBALH → ethanal (acetaldehyde); DIBALH is the MOST PREFERRED reagent for ester → aldehyde conversion; also: nitrile + DIBALH → aldehyde (after hydrolysis); amide + DIBALH → aldehyde (good yield); acyl halide + DIBALH → aldehyde; key: DIBALH stops at aldehyde stage because the aluminum alkoxide product is stable at -78°C and does not allow further reduction until workup
valid_transformations.conditions: DIBALH (diisobutylaluminium hydride, DIBAL-H); dry toluene or hexane; –78°C (very low T critical!); anhydrous. Selective reduction: ester → aldehyde (stops at aldehyde at –78°C because product aldehyde-Al complex is stable; warming → alcohol). Mechanism: H⁻ from DIBALH attacks ester C=O → tetrahedral intermediate (stable Al-O chelate at –78°C) → aqueous workup → aldehyde. At RT: ester → alcohol (2 equiv DIBALH or full reduction).

valid_transformations.notes: DIBALH reduces nitrile to aldehyde; ethanenitrile (CH3CN) + DIBALH → imine-Al intermediate → H3O+ workup → ethanal (CH3CHO); DIBALH is best for nitrile → aldehyde; contrast: LiAlH4 reduces nitrile to amine (R-CN + LiAlH4 → R-CH2-NH2); DIBALH stops at imine (which hydrolyzes to aldehyde on workup); order: DIBALH for ester/nitrile → aldehyde; LiAlH4 for nitrile → amine
valid_transformations.conditions: DIBALH; dry toluene; –78°C; anhydrous. DIBALH reduces nitrile (RC≡N) → imine-Al complex (R-CH=N-Al) → aqueous workup → aldehyde (R-CHO). Selective: stops at aldehyde (imine hydrolysis). LiAlH₄ reduces nitrile → primary amine (full reduction). DIBALH at –78°C → aldehyde (partial reduction).

valid_transformations.notes: LiAlH4 reduces carboxylic acid to primary alcohol; benzoic acid + LiAlH4/THF → benzyl alcohol; LiAlH4 ease order: Aldehyde > Ketone > Acyl Halide > Epoxide > Ester > Carboxyl > Amide > Nitrile > Nitro Alkane (most difficult) > Alkene (INERT); CARBOXYL is reduced but requires excess LiAlH4 (more sluggish than ester); ALKENE is INERT to LiAlH4 (no reaction); Nitro alkane is the MOST DIFFICULT LiAlH4 reduction (partially reduced species can form)
valid_transformations.conditions: LiAlH₄; dry ether or THF; 0°C to reflux; anhydrous; excess LiAlH₄ (2 equiv per COOH). Mechanism: H⁻ attacks COOH → acyl-O-Al complex → further H⁻ → primary alcohol (benzyl alcohol, PhCH₂OH). Aqueous workup carefully. Cannot stop at aldehyde with LiAlH₄ (must use DIBALH for that). NaBH₄ does NOT reduce carboxylic acids.

valid_transformations.notes: Borane (BH3) selectively reduces carboxylic acids; COOH is the EASIEST functional group for borane reduction; borane ease of reduction order: Carboxyl > Alkene > Ketone > Nitrile > Epoxide > Ester (most difficult) > Acyl Halide (INERT); KEY SELECTIVITY: borane reduces COOH easily but is INERT to acyl halide (completely opposite to other reagents); borane is used when you want to reduce COOH in presence of ester (borane reduces COOH, leaves ester intact); alkene IS reduced by borane (but via hydroboration, not simple reduction)
valid_transformations.conditions: BH₃ (borane, B₂H₆); THF solvent; 0°C to RT; anhydrous. BH₃ reduces carboxylic acid selectively (COOH > C=O ketones/aldehydes — actually carboxylic acid reacts fastest with BH₃ among carbonyls; ketones slower). Mechanism: BH₃ coordinates to COOH oxygen → H⁻ delivery → reduction. Aqueous H₂O₂/NaOH workup (from boron) → primary alcohol. BH₃·THF complex is more controllable than B₂H₆ gas.

valid_transformations.notes: Ozonolysis of internal alkyne gives alpha-diketone (1,2-diketone/vicinal diketone): R-C≡C-R' + O3/Zn → R-CO-CO-R'; but-2-yne (CH3-C≡C-CH3) + O3/Zn → butane-2,3-dione (CH3-CO-CO-CH3 = diacetyl); ALSO: cold KMnO4/H2O at 0°C or OsO4 + alkyne → SAME alpha-diketone (via dihydroxylation of triple bond → enediol → tautomerizes to alpha-diketone); contrast: alkene ozonolysis (O3/Zn) → aldehydes+ketones (single C=O); alkyne ozonolysis → alpha-DIKETONE (two adjacent C=O)
valid_transformations.conditions: O₃; Zn/H₂O (reductive); –78°C; CH₂Cl₂. But-2-yne (CH₃C≡CCH₃) → ozonolysis of triple bond → 2 acyl units → butane-2,3-dione (CH₃COCOCH₃, diacetyl)? Actually: ozonolysis of alkynes gives acid anhydrides or α-dicarbonyls. CH₃C≡CCH₃ + O₃ → CH₃CO-COCH₃ (butane-2,3-dione) via molozonide on triple bond → carboxylic acid fragments. Reductive workup stops at diketone.

valid_transformations.notes: Primary alcohol → aldehyde using MILD oxidants (STOPS at aldehyde, does NOT over-oxidize to acid): PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate) / PDC (pyridinium dichromate) / Collins (CrO3·2py) / Swern (oxalyl chloride+DMSO+NEt3) / Moffatt (DCC+DMSO) / Cu/Delta / X2 / NBS / MnO2 / CAN; propan-1-ol + PCC → propanal; KEY: these mild oxidants are used when you want primary alcohol → aldehyde selectively without over-oxidation; CONTRAST: strong oxidants (KMnO4/H+, K2Cr2O7/H+) over-oxidize primary alcohol → carboxylic acid (NOT useful for aldehyde synthesis); secondary alcohol + same mild oxidants → ketone (ketones are stable to over-oxidation); BEST for secondary: CrO3/pyridinium (circled in notes)
valid_transformations.conditions: PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate); CH₂Cl₂; RT; anhydrous. Selective oxidation of primary alcohol → aldehyde (stops at aldehyde, no overoxidation to acid in dry CH₂Cl₂). PCC does NOT continue to carboxylic acid. Alternatives: Swern (oxalyl chloride/DMSO/Et₃N, –78°C), Dess-Martin periodinane, MnO₂ (only allylic/benzylic).

valid_transformations.notes: Gattermann-Koch reaction: benzene + CO + HCl → benzaldehyde; catalyst: AlCl3 + CuCl (BOTH required; AlCl3 is the key Lewis acid, CuCl stabilizes CO complex; AlCl3 circled as most important in notes); mechanism: CO + HCl → [H-C≡O]+ (formyl cation, acylium) → EAS on benzene ring → benzaldehyde (PhCHO); gives ALDEHYDE directly (no methyl intermediary); ALSO: Reimer-Tiemann reaction = phenol + NaOH + CHCl3 → H+ workup → 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde (salicylaldehyde); RTR mechanism = CHCl3 + NaOH → dichlorocarbene :CCl2 → inserts into phenol ring ortho → hydrolysis → CHO
valid_transformations.conditions: Gattermann-Koch synthesis: CO + HCl (1:1) + AlCl₃/CuCl (Lewis acid catalyst); anhydrous; pressure (5–10 atm); RT to 60°C. CO/HCl + AlCl₃ → formyl cation (H-CO⁺, HAlCl₃⁻) → EAS on benzene → benzaldehyde + HCl + AlCl₃ (regenerated, catalytic). Only works for unactivated or slightly activated benzene (not alkoxy or amino-substituted — those give Duff reaction instead).

valid_transformations.notes: Vicinal diol (1,2-diol) oxidative cleavage with HIO4 (periodic acid): R-C(OH)(R1)-C(OH)(R2)-R' → R-CO-R1 + R2CO-R' (TWO SEPARATE carbonyl compounds via C-C bond cleavage); butane-2,3-diol (CH3-C(OH)H-C(OH)H-CH3) + HIO4 → 2x ethanal (CH3CHO); ALSO: Pb(OAc)4 (lead tetraacetate) gives SAME result as HIO4; RULE: the substituents on each diol carbon become the substituents on the resulting carbonyl; OH-C(R)(R1) → R-CO-R1; HIO4 ONLY works on VICINAL (adjacent, 1,2-diol) — does NOT cleave 1,3-diol or non-adjacent diols; contrast PINACOL rearrangement (H+) = gives ONE rearranged ketone (no cleavage, 1,2-shift)
valid_transformations.conditions: HIO₄ (periodic acid); aqueous; RT. Periodate cleavage of 1,2-diol (vicinal diol): CH₃CH(OH)CH(OH)CH₃ + HIO₄ → 2 CH₃CHO (ethanal) + HIO₃ + H₂O. One equiv HIO₄ per vicinal diol. Mechanism: cyclic periodate ester → oxidative cleavage. Cleaves vicinal diols specifically (not 1,3-diols). Pb(OAc)₄ is an alternative (non-aqueous). Stoichiometric: each CHOH fragment → aldehyde/ketone/HCHO.

valid_transformations.notes: Blaise ketone synthesis: nitrile + R'MgX → [R-C(=NMgX)-R' metallated imine intermediate] → H3O+ workup → R-CO-R' (KETONE); propanenitrile (CH3CH2CN) + CH3MgI → metallated aldimine intermediate → H3O+ → butan-2-one (CH3CO-CH2CH3); KEY: Grignard on NITRILE gives KETONE (not amine, not alcohol); the Grignard adds once to C≡N (adds to C) → gives C=N-MgX (imine metal complex) → acid hydrolysis → C=O (ketone); contrast: DIBALH on nitrile → ALDEHYDE (partial reduction); SnCl2/HCl (Stephens) on nitrile → ALDEHYDE; LiAlH4 on nitrile → AMINE (full reduction)
valid_transformations.conditions: Step 1: CH₃MgI (methylmagnesium iodide, Grignard) + CH₃CH₂CN (propanenitrile) in dry ether, 0°C → imine-MgI complex (CH₃CH₂-C(=NMgI)-CH₃). Step 2: H₃O⁺ → imine → ketone hydrolysis → butan-2-one (CH₃COCH₂CH₃, methyl ethyl ketone). Nitrile + Grignard → imine → ketone (one more C added). Staudinger: ketone synthesis from nitrile.

valid_transformations.notes: Kornblum oxidation: alkyl halide + DMSO/Delta → carbonyl compound; 2-bromopropane (secondary R-CHBr-R') + DMSO/Delta → propan-2-one (acetone/propan-2-one); RULES: (1) primary R-CH2-X + DMSO/Delta → R-CHO (aldehyde); (2) secondary R-CHX-R' + DMSO/Delta → R-CO-R' (ketone); (3) TERTIARY R3C-X + DMSO/Delta → NO REACTION (cannot form tertiary carbonyl = impossible, no H); MECHANISM: SN2 of DMSO on R-X → alkoxysulfonium salt → E2 beta-elimination → R-C=O (carbonyl) + DMS (dimethyl sulfide); DMSO is the oxidant (gets reduced to DMS); this is essentially the REVERSE of Swern oxidation workup
valid_transformations.conditions: Kornblum oxidation: DMSO (dimethyl sulfoxide) + heat (Δ, 100–150°C). 2° alkyl halide + DMSO → ketone (Kornblum). Mechanism: SN2 of Br by DMSO O → sulfonium ion → base or heat → elimination → ketone + dimethyl sulphide. Also: PCC/K₂Cr₂O₇ etc. (after conversion to alcohol first). Direct Kornblum: halide → ketone via DMSO oxidation.

valid_transformations.notes: Fries rearrangement: aryl ester (Ar-O-CO-R) + AlCl3/Delta → hydroxy aryl ketone (acyl group migrates from O-ester to the aromatic ring; OH is exposed on ring); phenyl ethanoate (Ph-O-CO-CH3) + AlCl3/Delta → 1-(2-hydroxyphenyl)ethan-1-one (2-hydroxyacetophenone, ortho) as MAJOR at HIGH TEMP; 4-hydroxyacetophenone (para) MAJOR at LOW TEMP; KEY TEMPERATURE RULE: LOW temp → PARA product (kinetic); HIGH temp → ORTHO product (thermodynamic, chelation stabilization); products: ortho = cyclic chelate favored thermodynamically; para = less steric, kinetically favored; RELATED: Gattermann-Koch also introduces CHO to ring (but without rearrangement)
valid_transformations.conditions: Fries rearrangement at low T (ortho product): AlCl₃; anhydrous; CS₂ or PhNO₂ solvent; RT to 100°C → ortho product (1-(2-hydroxyphenyl)ethan-1-one = 2'-hydroxyacetophenone). High T (>150°C) → para product (4'-hydroxyacetophenone). Acyl group migrates from O to ring C-ortho via intramolecular Friedel-Crafts.

valid_transformations.notes: Self-aldol condensation of ethanal (acetaldehyde, CH3CHO): (1) OH- removes α-H from CH3CHO → enolate (-CH2CHO); (2) Enolate attacks C=O of another CH3CHO → β-hydroxy aldehyde (3-hydroxybutanal, CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO = aldol product); (3) E1CB: OH- removes α-H from the β-hydroxy intermediate → carbanion → β-OH leaves → forms C=C; product = (E)-but-2-enal (trans-crotonaldehyde, CH3-CH=CH-CHO); E-geometry preferred (trans more stable); CONDITION: ≥2 α-H needed for aldol condensation (1 for enolate, 1 for E1CB); RATE ∝ [CH3CHO][OH-]^1 (first order in each)
valid_transformations.conditions: Dilute NaOH (5–10%); heat (Δ, 70–80°C); aqueous ethanol. Aldol condensation: ethanal (acetaldehyde) is both enolisable donor and electrophile acceptor. Step 1: OH⁻ + CH₃CHO → ⁻CH₂CHO (enolate) → + CH₃CHO → β-hydroxyaldehyde (aldol). Step 2: heat → dehydration → (E)-but-2-enal (crotonaldehyde, trans). Cold NaOH → aldol addition (β-hydroxy aldehyde); heat → condensation (dehydrated, conjugated).

valid_transformations.notes: Self-aldol condensation of propan-2-one (acetone): (1) OH- removes α-H → enolate CH3CO-CH2- ; (2) Enolate attacks C=O of another acetone → 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one (diacetone alcohol, β-hydroxy ketone = ALDOL PRODUCT); (3) E1CB: -H2O → 4-methylpent-3-en-2-one (mesityl oxide, CH3-CO-CH=C(CH3)2 = α,β-unsaturated ketone = ALDOL CONDENSATION product); condition: slow Δ with dilute NaOH; diacetone alcohol is the isolated product at low temp (no condensation); mesityl oxide is the product at higher temp; RATE ∝ [acetone][OH-]^1
valid_transformations.conditions: NaOH (dilute) + heat; RT first then Δ; aldol condensation. Acetone self-aldol: OH⁻ → enolate CH₂⁻COCH₃ → attacks another acetone C=O → 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one → heat → dehydration → 4-methylpent-3-en-2-one (mesityl oxide). Alternatively: mixed aldol with formaldehyde → other products. Self-condensation of acetone requires base + heat.

valid_transformations.notes: Cross-aldol condensation of propan-2-one (acetone) + ethanal (acetaldehyde) + OH-/Δ → MAJOR product = (E)-pent-3-en-2-one (CH3-CH=CH-CO-CH3, methyl vinyl ketone type); REASON MAJOR: (a) acetone has 6 α-H (generates most enolate) = nucleophile; (b) acetaldehyde C=O is more electrophilic (less hindered, more reactive) = electrophile; so cross product (acetone enolate + acetaldehyde electrophile) is major; MINOR products: crotonaldehyde (CH3CHO self-aldol) and mesityl oxide (acetone self-aldol); cross-aldol with 2 enolizable C=O compounds gives 4 possible products (A+A, A+B, B+A, B+B) = 4 condensation products theoretically; major = cross product using more reactive electrophile + more enolizable nucleophile
valid_transformations.conditions: NaOH (dilute) + acetaldehyde (ethanal); RT then heat; mixed (crossed) aldol condensation. Acetone (enolisable, acceptor and donor) + ethanal (better electrophile) → OH⁻ → acetone enolate attacks ethanal C=O → β-hydroxy ketone → heat → dehydration → (E)-pent-3-en-2-one (trans-methyl vinyl ketone analog). pH and stoichiometry control selectivity.

valid_transformations.notes: Aldol REACTION (no condensation) of acetone: (1) OH- removes α-H → enolate; (2) Enolate attacks another acetone → tetrahedral intermediate → protonation → 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one (DIACETONE ALCOHOL); NO condensation (-H2O) occurs at low temperature; DISTINCTION: Aldol RXN = β-hydroxy carbonyl product (diacetone alcohol = aldol product); Aldol CONDENSATION = α,β-unsaturated product (mesityl oxide); condition for aldol rxn only (no condensation): dilute NaOH, low temp; condition for condensation: heating/stronger base; REQUIREMENT: at least 1 α-H for aldol rxn; at least 2 α-H for aldol condensation (one for enolate, one for E1CB elimination)
valid_transformations.conditions: NaOH (dilute, 5–10%); low temperature (0–5°C or RT); aqueous. Aldol addition (not condensation): OH⁻ → acetone enolate → attacks 2nd acetone C=O → β-hydroxy ketone product (diacetone alcohol = 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one). Stop at addition product (no heat → no dehydration). Ba(OH)₂ is selective catalyst for aldol addition of acetone at RT (stops at addition, not condensation).

valid_transformations.notes: Chloral (2,2,2-trichloroacetaldehyde, CCl3CHO) + NaOH → HCOOH (or HCOONa) + CHCl3 (chloroform); this is NOT a Cannizzaro reaction; ANOMALOUS MECHANISM: OH- attacks C=O of chloral → tetrahedral adduct CCl3-C(OH)(O-)-H → the CCl3 group (trichloromethyl carbanion, CCl3-) is a good leaving group (3 Cl atoms stabilize the carbanion) → CCl3- migrates away → formate ion (HCO2-) remains → CCl3- + H2O → CHCl3 (chloroform); overall: CCl3CHO + NaOH → HCOONa + CHCl3; comparison: normal Cannizzaro (no α-C migration) = 2 RCHO → RCH2OH + RCOO-; chloral anomaly = 1 molecule reacts + CCl3- migrates out
valid_transformations.conditions: NaOH (aq); RT. Cannizzaro-type or haloform mechanism: CCl₃CHO + NaOH → CCl₃⁻ (trichloromethyl carbanion) → leaves → CHCl₃ + HCOONa. Mechanism: OH⁻ adds to aldehyde → hemiacetal anion → electron pair on O → C-CCl₃ bond breaks (CCl₃⁻ is stable carbanion, EWG effect of 3 Cl) → CHCl₃ + formate. This is the basis of the Reimer reaction and is related to chloroform synthesis from chloral hydrate.

valid_transformations.notes: Perkin reaction: benzaldehyde + acetic anhydride + sodium acetate/Δ → (E)-3-phenylprop-2-enoic acid (cinnamic acid, PhCH=CH-COOH); PERKIN REACTION ONLY FOR AROMATIC ALDEHYDES AND KETONES (not aliphatic); mechanism: (1) CH3COO- (sodium acetate, base) removes α-H from acetic anhydride → enolate -CH2-CO-O-CO-CH3; (2) Enolate attacks PhCHO → β-hydroxy adduct Ph-CH(OH)-CH2-CO-O-CO-CH3; (3) OH is acetylated by the second acetyl group → Ph-CH(OAc)-CH2-CO-O-CO-CH3 type; (4) E1CB or heat: loss of AcOH → Ph-CH=CH-CO-O-CO-CH3 (unsaturated anhydride); (5) H3O+/Δ: hydrolysis → PhCH=CH-COOH (cinnamic acid, E geometry); with propionic anhydride (CH3CH2CO)2O + AcONa → Ph-CH=C(CH3)-COOH (alpha-methylcinnamic acid)
valid_transformations.conditions: Perkin condensation: acetic anhydride (Ac₂O, 3 equiv); potassium acetate (CH₃COOK) or sodium acetate (base/catalyst); heat (Δ, 150–170°C). Mechanism: CH₃COO⁻ deprotonates Ac₂O → enolate → nucleophilic addition to PhCHO → aldol-like → acylated β-hydroxy → elimination → PhCH=CH-COOH (cinnamic acid, trans). Trans (E) preferred. Variation: propionic anhydride + NaOPr → α-methylcinnamic acid.

valid_transformations.notes: Perkin reaction Q2: 4-nitrobenzaldehyde (O2N-Ph-CHO) + acetic anhydride (Ac2O) + sodium acetate (AcO-Na+) → H3O+/Δ → (E)-3-(4-nitrophenyl)prop-2-enoic acid (4-nitrocinnamic acid); same Perkin mechanism as benzaldehyde; note that the EWG (NO2) activates the aromatic aldehyde C=O toward nucleophilic attack by the anhydride enolate → may give SLIGHTLY FASTER rate for the addition step but overall Cannizzaro rate is DECREASED by EWG (opposite for Perkin: EWG activates aldehyde toward enolate addition); Perkin works for all aromatic aldehydes (EWG or EDG on ring); product = always E (trans) geometry (more stable, thermodynamic)
valid_transformations.conditions: Perkin condensation: Ac₂O + CH₃COONa; heat (Δ, 150–170°C). Same as benzaldehyde case but EWG (NO₂) on ring makes aldehyde more electrophilic → faster condensation. Product: (E)-3-(4-nitrophenyl)prop-2-enoic acid (4-nitrocinnamic acid). Perkin works best for aldehydes lacking α-H (ArCHO) because self-condensation of the anhydride is the side reaction to avoid.

valid_transformations.notes: Perkin reaction with propionic anhydride (propanoic anhydride): PhCHO + (CH3CH2CO)2O + CH3CH2COO-Na+ → H3O+/Δ → (E)-2-methyl-3-phenylprop-2-enoic acid (alpha-methylcinnamic acid, Ph-CH=C(CH3)-COOH); the alpha-carbon of the anhydride (CH3-CH2 in propionic anhydride → the CH2 is the alpha-carbon) gets incorporated into the product; the alpha-substituent (CH3 from propionyl) ends up at the alpha-carbon of the product acid; GENERAL RULE: Perkin with (RCO)2O → Ar-CH=C(R)-COOH (R = rest of acyl group, one carbon shorter); for Ac2O (R=CH3) → one α-carbon, no substituent (R=H effectively) → Ar-CH=CH-COOH; for Pr2O (R=CH2CH3) → Ar-CH=C(CH3)-COOH
valid_transformations.conditions: Perkin with propionic anhydride: (CH₃CH₂CO)₂O + CH₃CH₂COONa (sodium propanoate); heat (Δ, 150–170°C). Propionic anhydride enolate attacks PhCHO → β-hydroxy acyl → elimination → α-methylcinnamic acid. α-Methyl substituent from propionic anhydride. E-isomer (trans) thermodynamically preferred.

valid_transformations.notes: Tischenko reaction: 2 R-CHO + Al(OR)3 → R-C(=O)-O-CH2R (ester); 2 benzaldehyde (PhCHO) + Al(OEt)3 → phenylmethyl benzoate (benzyl benzoate, Ph-C(=O)-O-CH2-Ph); TISCHENKO = Cannizzaro + esterification in one step; product = ESTER (not separate acid + alcohol); contrast Cannizzaro: 2 PhCHO + NaOH → PhCOOH + PhCH2OH (carboxylic acid + alcohol, separate); MECHANISM: Al(OR)3 coordinates to C=O (activates it as Lewis acid) → hydride transfer via cyclic 6-membered transition state from C-H of one aldehyde to C=O of another (Al coordinates both) → ester product; REQUIRES ALDEHYDE (has formyl H for hydride transfer); ketones cannot undergo Tischenko (no formyl H); also works for acrolein: CH2=CH-CHO + Al(OEt)3 → allyl acrylate (CH2=CH-CO-O-CH2-CH=CH2)
valid_transformations.conditions: Tishchenko reaction or Cannizzaro ester: Al(OEt)₃ (aluminium ethoxide) or Al(OiPr)₃ (aluminium isopropoxide); Δ; neat or dry toluene. Mechanism: Meerwein-Ponndorf-Verley/Cannizzaro variant: PhCHO + PhCHO → Ph-CH₂-OOC-Ph (phenylmethyl benzoate). Hydride transfer from one aldehyde to the other (no external H source). Tishchenko: R-CHO → R-COO-CH₂R (self-esterification via hydride transfer). Al-alkoxide catalyses.

valid_transformations.notes: Wolff-Kishner reduction: C=O → CH2 (completely removes carbonyl oxygen, replaces with H2); cyclohexanone + N2H4/H+ → cyclohexanone hydrazone (A, >C=N-NH2) → KOH/Δ → cyclohexane + N2; MECHANISM: (1) N2H4 + C=O (pH 5-7) → hydrazone (>C=N-NH2); (2) KOH/Δ: OH- removes NH2 proton → >C=N-N- → tautomerize → >C=N-NH (diazo resonance) → N2 leaves → carbanion at C → protonation by H2O → CH2 (alkane); PRODUCT: C=O → CH2 (same carbon skeleton, carbonyl removed); contrast Clemmensen reduction (Zn-Hg/HCl/Δ) = SAME product (C=O → CH2) but in ACIDIC conditions; Wolff-Kishner in BASIC; use Wolff-Kishner when substrate is acid-sensitive; use Clemmensen when substrate is base-sensitive
valid_transformations.conditions: Wolff-Kishner reduction: Step 1: NH₂NH₂ (hydrazine, EtOH, RT–reflux, H⁺ catalysis) → hydrazone (cyclohexanone hydrazone). Step 2: KOH or NaOH (excess); ethylene glycol (HOCH₂CH₂OH, high-bp solvent) or diethylene glycol; reflux (200°C). Mechanism: base deprotonates N-H of hydrazone → anion → N₂ loss → carbanion → protonation → alkane. Complementary to Clemmensen (acid/Zn). Kishner-Huang modification: use K-t-BuO/DMSO.

valid_transformations.notes: Carbonyl + NH2-G reaction: >C=O + NH2-G (pH 5-7, H+) → >C=N-G + H2O; propan-2-one (acetone) + NH2OH (hydroxylamine) → propan-2-one oxime ((CH3)2C=N-OH); MECHANISM: (1) N: of NH2-G attacks C=O → tetrahedral aminol intermediate (C with OH and NH-G); (2) protonation of OH → loss of H2O; (3) >C=N-G product; pH 5-7 is OPTIMAL: too acidic (pH<3) = amine protonated (RNH3+) → no nucleophile; too basic (pH>9) = C=O not activated → slow reaction; ALSO: G table: G=-H → NH3 → imine (>C=NH); G=-R → RNH2 (primary amine) → Schiff base (>C=NR); G=-OH → NH2OH → oxime; G=-NH2 → N2H4 → hydrazone; G=-NHPh → PhNHNH2 → phenylhydrazone; G=-NH-2,4-DNP → 2,4-DNP-hydrazone (orange precipitate, used for identification); G=-NHCONH2 → semicarbazide → semicarbazone
valid_transformations.conditions: NH₂OH·HCl (hydroxylamine hydrochloride); NaOAc (sodium acetate, buffer); aqueous-ethanolic; pH 4–5; RT. Condensation: C=O + H₂NOH → carbinolamine (C(OH)(NHOH)) → –H₂O → oxime (C=NOH). Syn and anti oximes (E/Z about C=N). Acid buffers (pH 4–5): protonates OH → facilitates dehydration step. Too acidic: protonates NH₂OH (reduces nucleophilicity). Beckmann rearrangement: oxime + H₂SO₄ → amide (anti group migrates).

valid_transformations.notes: Hydrazone formation: C=O + N2H4 (hydrazine, NH2-NH2) + H+/pH 5-7 → hydrazone (>C=N-NH2); propan-2-one (CH3COCH3) + N2H4 → propan-2-one hydrazone ((CH3)2C=N-NH2); KEY USE: hydrazone is the INTERMEDIATE in Wolff-Kishner reduction (forms at step 1); ALSO: o-phthalaldehyde + N2H4 → cyclic di-imine product (both CHO react with both NH2 of N2H4 → bicyclic ring containing N); BASICITY/REACTIVITY order for NH2-G reagents toward C=O: N2H4 (hydrazine) > PhNHNH2 (phenylhydrazine) > NH2NHCONH2 (semicarbazide) [order 1>2>3]; semicarbazide is least reactive because the CONH2 group withdraws electrons from the NH2 making it less nucleophilic; phenylhydrazone: Ph ring withdraws electrons → less nucleophilic than hydrazine; 2,4-DNP reagent (2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine) gives bright orange/red precipitate (characteristic test for C=O compounds = 2,4-DNP TEST)
valid_transformations.conditions: N₂H₄ (hydrazine, anhydrous or aq); H⁺ (mildly acidic, pH 5–7); EtOH-H₂O; RT. Condensation: C=O + N₂H₄ → hydrazone (C=N-NH₂). Same mechanism as oxime. Hydrazones: Wolff-Kishner precursor (KOH/heat → alkane); Bamford-Stevens (tosylhydrazone + base → diazo → alkene). Unsubstituted hydrazine: C=N-NH₂; phenylhydrazine → phenylhydrazone (orange-yellow).

valid_transformations.notes: Fehling test: aliphatic aldehyde (RCHO) + 5OH- + 2Cu2+ → RCOO- (carboxylate) + Cu2O↓ (brick-red/rust-red precipitate) + 3H2O; BALANCED EQUATION: R-CHO + 5OH- + 2Cu2+ → R-COO- + Cu2O(red) + 3H2O; Cu2+ (blue) → Cu2O (brick-red = positive Fehling); Fehling reagent = Fehling A (CuSO4 solution) + Fehling B (NaOH + sodium potassium tartrate, Seignette salt); the tartrate is a complexing agent that keeps Cu2+ in solution as [Cu(tartrate)]2- complex (prevents Cu(OH)2 precipitation at high pH); SELECTIVITY: aliphatic aldehydes ONLY (ethanal, propanal, butanal, methanal, etc.) give positive; aromatic aldehydes (benzaldehyde, PhCHO) give NEGATIVE Fehling; ketones (propan-2-one etc.) give NEGATIVE; also positive: α-hydroxy ketones (secondary, with H at α-C), hemiacetals of aliphatic aldehydes (R-CH(OH)(OR'), cyclic hemiacetals/lactols)
valid_transformations.conditions: Fehling's test: Fehling's A (CuSO₄ aq) + Fehling's B (NaOH + sodium potassium tartrate); mix equal volumes; heat to boiling. Cu²⁺ (blue) + RCHO → Cu₂O (brick-red precipitate) + RCOONa. Benedict's reagent (copper citrate in Na₂CO₃): same principle, stable single solution. Positive for: aliphatic aldehydes (not aromatic PhCHO), α-hydroxy ketones, reducing sugars. Negative: aromatic aldehydes, ketones (except α-hydroxy), carboxylic acids.

valid_transformations.notes: Tollens test (Silver Mirror Test): RCHO + 2[Ag(NH3)2]+ + 3OH- → RCOO- + 2Ag↓ + 4NH3 + 2H2O; silver (Ag0) deposits as silver mirror on inner surface of test tube (positive result); Tollens reagent = ammoniacal silver nitrate = [Ag(NH3)2]+NO3- OR Ag2O OR Ag+; SELECTIVITY: ALL ALDEHYDES positive (both aliphatic AND aromatic); ketones NEGATIVE; also positive: α-hydroxy ketones (secondary), hemiacetals; key stoichiometry: 1 RCHO: 2 Ag+ (2 electrons from RCHO → 2 Ag reduced); RCHO → RCOO- (oxidized 2e-); ethanal + 2[Ag(NH3)2]+ + 3OH- → ethanoate + 2Ag↓ + 4NH3 + 2H2O
valid_transformations.conditions: Tollens' test: [Ag(NH₃)₂]NO₃ (ammoniacal silver nitrate, fresh); RT or slight warmth in clean tube. RCHO + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + 3 OH⁻ → RCOO⁻ + 2 Ag⁰ (silver mirror) + 4 NH₃ + 2 H₂O. Positive: all aldehydes (aliphatic + aromatic PhCHO), formic acid, formaldehyde, α-hydroxy ketones, reducing sugars. Negative: ketones (except α-hydroxy and formaldehyde-containing). Use fresh reagent (aged → explosive silver azide).

valid_transformations.notes: Benzaldehyde (PhCHO) gives POSITIVE Tollens test (silver mirror) but NEGATIVE Fehling test (NO Cu2O precipitate); this is the KEY DISTINCTION between the two tests; ALL ALDEHYDES give positive Tollens (aliphatic AND aromatic); but ONLY ALIPHATIC ALDEHYDES give positive Fehling; benzaldehyde + 2[Ag(NH3)2]+ + 3OH- → PhCOO- (benzoate) + 2Ag↓ + 4NH3 + 2H2O (POSITIVE Tollens); benzaldehyde + Cu2+/Fehling reagent → NO Cu2O precipitate (NEGATIVE Fehling); REASON: Fehling reagent (Cu2+ in alkaline conditions) is a MILDER oxidant than Tollens (Ag+/NH3); aromatic aldehyde's C=O is deactivated by the benzene ring (resonance) → Cu2+ cannot oxidize it; Ag+ (with NH3 complex) is a stronger oxidant → can oxidize aromatic aldehydes
valid_transformations.conditions: Tollens' reagent ([Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺); RT; clean flask. Benzaldehyde (aromatic aldehyde): POSITIVE with Tollens' (forms silver mirror). NEGATIVE with Fehling's/Benedict's (aromatic aldehydes do not reduce Cu²⁺ in tartrate/citrate complex — steric or electronic reasons). This distinction is key: PhCHO positive Tollens', negative Fehling's. All aliphatic R-CHO: positive both.

valid_transformations.notes: α-Hydroxy ketone (hydroxyacetone, HOCH2-CO-CH3 = 1-hydroxypropan-2-one) gives POSITIVE Fehling AND Tollens despite being a ketone; general rule: SECONDARY α-hydroxy ketone (R-CH(OH)-CO-R, has H at α-carbon bearing OH) → positive both; TERTIARY α-hydroxy ketone (R₂C(OH)-CO-R, NO H at α-C) → negative both; REASON: secondary α-hydroxy ketone can tautomerize/enolize to an enediol → this enediol form is a strong enough reductant to reduce both Cu2+ and Ag+; the enediol (gem-diol like form at the double bond) acts as the actual reducing agent; the α-OH and α-H are both needed for enediol formation; without α-H (tertiary): no enediol possible → no reduction; examples: glucose (cyclic hemiacetal of an α-hydroxy aldehyde) → positive both; fructose (α-hydroxy ketone form) → positive both (via enediol)
valid_transformations.conditions: Fehling's or Tollens' reagent; RT to warm. 1-Hydroxypropan-2-one (acetol = hydroxyacetone, HOCH₂COCH₃) has α-hydroxy ketone functionality → positive Fehling's and Tollens' (α-hydroxy ketone is oxidised by Cu²⁺). Mechanism: α-keto-enol → reducing agent toward Cu²⁺. Fructose (α-hydroxy ketone/furanose form) also positive Fehling's.

valid_transformations.notes: Blanc Rule: butanedioic acid (succinic acid, HOOC-CH2-CH2-COOH, 4 carbons) + Δ → oxolane-2,5-dione (succinic anhydride, 5-membered cyclic anhydride) + H2O; BLANC RULE MNEMONIC: O My Son Go And Play = Oxalic, Malonic, Succinic, Glutaric, Adipic, Pimelic; for each: Oxalic (2C): CO + CO2 + H2O (decomposition); Malonic (3C): decarboxylation → acetic acid + CO2 (anhydride too strained = 4-membered ring); Succinic (4C): 5-membered anhydride (-H2O); Glutaric (5C): 6-membered anhydride (-H2O); Adipic (6C): cyclopentanone (-2CO2, -H2O); Pimelic (7C): cyclohexanone (-2CO2, -H2O); PATTERN: if anhydride ring = 5 or 6 membered → forms anhydride; if anhydride ring would be 7+ membered → forms ketone instead (Blanc ketone synthesis); anhydride dehydration: -H2O between the two COOH groups; ketone formation: double decarboxylation (-2CO2) + dehydration (-H2O)
valid_transformations.conditions: Heat (Δ) alone; 200°C; intramolecular dehydration. Butanedioic acid (succinic acid, 1,4-dicarboxylic acid) loses H₂O between the two COOH groups → oxolane-2,5-dione (succinic anhydride, 5-membered ring). Easy cyclisation (5-membered ring) — no catalyst needed. Compare: phthalic acid (1,2-dicarboxylic) → phthalic anhydride; maleic acid → maleic anhydride. 1,5-diacids form 5-membered anhydrides readily; 1,6 and longer are harder.

valid_transformations.notes: Blanc Rule: hexanedioic acid (adipic acid, HOOC-(CH2)4-COOH, 6 carbons) + Δ → cyclopentan-1-one (cyclopentanone) + 2CO2 + H2O; WHY ketone instead of anhydride: the anhydride from adipic acid would be a 7-membered ring (too large, unstable); instead: double decarboxylation (-2CO2) removes both COOH groups and ring closure forms a 5-membered KETONE; Blanc ketone synthesis: longer chain dicarboxylic acids form cyclic ketones by double decarboxylation; pimelic acid (7C, HOOC-(CH2)5-COOH) + Δ → cyclohexanone + 2CO2 + H2O (6-membered ketone); RULE SUMMARY: if heating dicarboxylic acid would give 5 or 6 membered anhydride → anhydride; if 7+ membered anhydride would form → cyclic ketone instead (one C fewer in ring = n-2 carbon ring from nC diacid); cyclopentanone from 6C = 6-2=4C ring? No: adipic C6 → cyclopentanone C5 ring (lose 1C per COOH via CO2, total 2C lost, 6-2=4 carbons in chain but the ring forms from those 4 chain C + 1 C from C=O = 5-membered ring); actually: the ring is the carbon skeleton of the chain WITHOUT the two COOH carbons + closing with C=O from the resulting chain
valid_transformations.conditions: Dry distillation of calcium/barium salt or pyrolysis; Δ (strong heat, 300–350°C). Ba or Ca salt of adipic acid (hexanedioic acid) → thermal decarboxylation of both COOH → diketone-like intermediate → ring closure → cyclopentanone + CO₂. Alternatively: adipic acid/Fe or ZnO catalyst, Δ → cyclopentanone + H₂O + CO₂. Classic industrial Reppe/Ruzicka synthesis: large ring ketones from diacid Ca salts.

valid_transformations.notes: Maleic acid ((Z)-but-2-enedioic acid, cis-HOOC-CH=CH-COOH) + Δ → maleic anhydride (furan-2,5(3H,4H)-dione, 5-membered ring anhydride with C=C inside) + H2O; the cis (Z) configuration places both COOH groups on same side of the C=C double bond → close proximity → easy dehydration → 5-membered ring anhydride; CONTRAST: fumaric acid ((E)-but-2-enedioic acid, trans) with Δ → NO rxn under normal heating conditions (trans COOH groups are far apart, C=C locks trans configuration → cannot form anhydride); HOWEVER: fumaric acid at 300°C → the C=C pi bond breaks homolytically (diradical intermediate) → allows rotation → reforms C=C in cis configuration → now maleic acid → then dehydrates → maleic anhydride; KEY: fumaric acid can give maleic anhydride BUT ONLY via prior thermal isomerization to maleic acid at 300°C
valid_transformations.conditions: Heat (Δ, 60°C or mild); maleic acid (cis-butenedioic acid) → maleic anhydride. Cis geometry of the two COOH groups allows easy intramolecular dehydration (5-membered ring) at low T. Fumaric acid (trans, IUPAC: (E)-but-2-enedioic acid) does NOT form anhydride easily (trans COOH groups far apart). Maleic anhydride: IUPAC = furan-2,5(3H,4H)-dione.

valid_transformations.notes: Phthalic acid (benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid, ortho-phthalic acid) + Δ → phthalic anhydride (2-benzofuran-1,3-dione = isobenzofuran-1,3-dione) + H2O; ortho COOH groups on adjacent ring carbons → close proximity → dehydration → 5-membered anhydride ring fused to benzene; COMPARISON: isophthalic acid (benzene-1,3-dicarboxylic acid, meta) + Δ → NO rxn (COOH too far apart for 5 or 6 membered ring); terephthalic acid (benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid, para) + Δ → NO rxn (COOH even farther); RULE: aromatic diacids → anhydride ONLY for ortho (1,2-disubstituted) isomer; meta and para give no anhydride; cis-trans analogy: ortho = like cis (close, same side); meta/para = like trans (too far)
valid_transformations.conditions: Heat (Δ, 200°C) or conc H₂SO₄; phthalic acid → phthalic anhydride (intramolecular, 5-membered ring with fused benzene). No catalyst needed for ortho-dicarboxylic acids (adjacent COOH easy to cyclise). Product: phthalic anhydride = 2-benzofuran-1,3-dione. Used in Friedel-Crafts acylation to make anthraquinone-type compounds and plasticisers (dioctyl phthalate).

valid_transformations.notes: Deformylation reaction: (2,4,6-trinitrophenyl)methanal (2,4,6-trinitrobenzaldehyde) + NaOH → 1,3,5-trinitrobenzene + HCOO⁻ (sodium formate); DEFORMYLATION = the C-CHO bond breaks, the CHO group is cleaved as HCOO⁻ (formate) and the aryl group leaves as Ar⁻ (aryl anion, stabilized by the three EWG NO₂ groups); mechanism: OH⁻ attacks C=O of ArCHO → [Ar-CH(OH)(O⁻)] tetrahedral intermediate → Ar⁻ migrates (1,2-anionic shift of Ar⁻ = aryl carbanion, stabilized by EWG) → HCOO⁻ remains → Ar⁻ + H⁺ → ArH (1,3,5-trinitrobenzene); ANALOGY: same as chloral anomaly (CCl₃⁻ migration from CCl₃CHO) but now Ar⁻ migrates instead of CCl₃⁻; GENERAL RULE: ArCHO with ≥2 EWG groups (NO₂, Cl, Br in ortho/para positions) → deformylation under NaOH; NO Cannizzaro products obtained; NOTE: single EWG (like p-NO₂-PhCHO alone) gives slow Cannizzaro (not deformylation); requires multiple or strong EWG for deformylation pathway
valid_transformations.conditions: NaOH (aq); RT; Cannizzaro reaction for aldehyde without α-H. Actually this is decarboxylation/elimination: (2,4,6-trinitrophenyl)methanal → on treatment with base, the aldehyde undergoes benzylic carbanion-type elimination → 1,3,5-trinitrobenzene + HCOO⁻? Or: Cannizzaro disproportionation → 50% alcohol + 50% acid. TNT-related aldehyde → strained system. More likely: base eliminates formyl group → TNB.

valid_transformations.notes: Deformylation of prop-2-ynal (HC≡C-CHO, propiolaldehyde/propynal) with NaOH: HC≡C-CHO + NaOH → HC≡CH (ethyne, acetylene) + HCOONa (sodium formate); mechanism: OH⁻ attacks C=O → [HC≡C-CH(OH)(O⁻)] → the HC≡C⁻ (alkynyl/propargyl carbanion) is stabilized by the sp-carbon → migrates as HC≡C⁻ → formate remains (HCOO⁻) → HC≡C⁻ + H₂O → HC≡CH (ethyne); this is DEFORMYLATION of an alkynyl aldehyde; ANALOGY: same mechanism as chloral (CCl₃⁻ migrates) and 2,4,6-trinitrobenzaldehyde (Ar⁻ migrates); all have in common: the group attached to C=O is a stabilized carbanion that can migrate; HC≡C⁻ = alkynyl anion stabilized by sp-carbon's high electronegativity; for ALL these: R-CHO + NaOH → NO Cannizzaro; instead → R⁻ + HCOO⁻; applies to: (1) CCl₃-CHO → CCl₃⁻; (2) Ar(EWG)n-CHO → Ar⁻; (3) RC≡C-CHO → RC≡C⁻
valid_transformations.conditions: NaOH (aq); RT to mild heat. Prop-2-ynal (HC≡C-CHO, propiolaldehyde) + NaOH → ethyne (HC≡CH) + HCOONa. Mechanism: Cannizzaro-type for α-keto aldehyde with alkyne. Base attacks C=O → hydride shift? Or: OH⁻ adds to C=O of conjugated aldehyde → vinyl anion (stabilised by alkyne) → β-elimination of formate → alkyne. Retro-Knoevenagel or retro-aldol type.

reagents: steric crowding prevents normal nucleophilic addition
valid_transformations.notes: Steric crowding deformylation: (2,6-dimethylphenyl)methanal (2,6-dimethylbenzaldehyde) + NaOH → 1,3-dimethylbenzene (m-xylene) + HCOONa (sodium formate); reason = STERIC CROWDING around the CHO group; the two ortho-methyl groups (2,6-positions) flank the CHO from both sides → OH⁻ cannot attack the C=O normally (too crowded, steric hindrance prevents nucleophilic approach) → instead, the aldehyde undergoes deformylation (C-CHO bond cleavage) → Ar⁻ + HCOO⁻; NOTE: this compound does NOT give Cannizzaro reaction despite having no α-H; REASON: Cannizzaro requires OH⁻ to attack C=O (step 1), which is blocked by steric crowding; deformylation is the alternative pathway; 2,6-disubstituted benzaldehyde is specifically noted as a Cannizzaro exception 'due to crowding'
valid_transformations.conditions: NaOH (aq); RT. (2,6-dimethylphenyl)methanal (2,6-dimethylbenzaldehyde) is sterically hindered → no Cannizzaro (OH⁻ cannot attack C=O easily). Instead, base causes Dakin-like or deformylation: loss of CHO group as formate → 1,3-dimethylbenzene (m-xylene). Steric crowding at C=O prevents normal nucleophilic addition → retro-Cannizzaro or deformylation mechanism.

valid_transformations.notes: 4-(Dimethylamino)benzaldehyde (p-Me₂N-C₆H₄-CHO) + NaOH → does NOT give normal Cannizzaro products; instead forms a ZWITTERION (betaine); mechanism: OH⁻ attacks C=O → tetrahedral intermediate → the dimethylamino nitrogen becomes quaternary (N⁺) and the alkoxide (O⁻) remains → ZWITTERION (Me₂N⁺=C₆H₄=CH-O⁻ quinoid/betaine form); this zwitterion is stable and does not undergo the normal Cannizzaro hydride transfer; RESULT: NO normal Cannizzaro products (no alcohol + acid); instead: zwitterionic intermediate is the final/stable product under basic conditions; similar behavior: p-hydroxybenzaldehyde (OH-Ph-CHO) + NaOH → quinoid zwitterion (⁻O=C₆H₄=CH-O⁻ type); ALL aryl aldehydes with strong ELECTRON-DONATING groups in para position (p-NR₂, p-OH) → zwitterion exception to Cannizzaro; compare to EWG aryl aldehydes → deformylation exception
valid_transformations.conditions: NaOH (aq); RT. The Me₂N group (strong EDG) makes the ring strongly electron-rich; carbonyl is push-pull activated. NaOH treatment: OH⁻ adds to C=O → tetrahedral intermediate (zwitterion with N⁺ and O⁻ or negative charge delocalised). Quinoid zwitterion form: Me₂N⁺=Ar=CH-O⁻. This is why Meisenheimer-like structures form. Not a Cannizzaro product — the aldehyde is resistant to reduction here.

valid_transformations.notes: Grignard carboxylation: RMgX + dry CO2 → R-C(=O)-OMgX (magnesium carboxylate intermediate) → H3O+ → RCOOH (carboxylic acid); ethylmagnesium bromide (CH3CH2MgBr) + CO2 → propanoic acid (CH3CH2COOH) after H3O+ workup; MECHANISM: the Grignard reagent R⁻ (carbanion) acts as nucleophile, attacks the electrophilic C of CO2 (O=C=O) → R-C(=O)OMgX; H3O+ workup gives RCOOH; GENERAL RULE: RMgX + CO2 → RCOOH (one carbon longer than R group); MUST use DRY CO2 gas (anhydrous conditions; water destroys Grignard: RMgX + H2O → RH); only ONE addition occurs (CO2 is a unique electrophile with two C=O; after first addition the magnesium carboxylate is formed, the second C=O is not as electrophilic → no second addition); PRODUCT: carboxylic acid with one MORE carbon than the Grignard alkyl group; e.g., MeMgBr + CO2 → ethanoic acid (acetic acid); EtMgBr → propanoic acid; PhMgBr → benzoic acid
valid_transformations.conditions: Step 1: dry CO₂ (gas or dry ice); dry ether/THF; 0°C; anhydrous. EtMgBr + CO₂ → Et-COO-MgBr (magnesium propanoate). Step 2: H₃O⁺ (NH₄Cl/H₂O) → propanoic acid (CH₃CH₂COOH). Mechanism: nucleophilic addition of ethyl carbanion to electrophilic C of CO₂. One C added to Grignard chain. Clean and reliable homologation to acid.

valid_transformations.notes: Nitrile acid hydrolysis: ethanenitrile (CH3CN, acetonitrile) + H3O+/Δ → ethanoic acid (CH3COOH) + NH3; MECHANISM: (1) H+ protonates N of C≡N (δ+ on C, δ- on N; H+ adds to N) → [R-C=N-H]+ (iminium); (2) H2O attacks C → [R-C(=N-H)(OH)] (hemiaminol = iminol); (3) tautomerize → R-C(=O)-NH2 (AMIDE intermediate); (4) amide + H+ → R-C(=O)-NH3+ (protonated amide); (5) H2O attacks C=O → tetrahedral intermediate; (6) -NH3 (eliminates) → R-C(OH)2 (gem-diol); (7) → R-COOH; AMIDE IS AN INTERMEDIATE under partial conditions: can isolate amide if stop early (one equivalent H3O+, gentle conditions); with excess H3O+: nitrile → amide → carboxylic acid; NH3 leaves as NH4+ in acid; CONTRAST basic: R-C≡N + OH-/H2O → R-COO- + NH3 (basic hydrolysis more direct, no acid needed for final step)
valid_transformations.conditions: H₃O⁺ (dil H₂SO₄ or HCl); excess water; heat (reflux, 100–110°C). Acid hydrolysis of nitrile: CH₃CN + H₂O/H⁺ → CH₃CONH₂ (intermediate amide) → CH₃COOH + NH₄⁺ (further hydrolysis). Full hydrolysis requires reflux; can stop at amide with partial hydrolysis. Base hydrolysis (NaOH/H₂O, reflux) → CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ → acidify → CH₃COOH.

valid_transformations.notes: Ester acid hydrolysis: ethyl ethanoate (CH3COOC2H5, ethyl acetate) + H3O+/Δ (reversible equilibrium) → ethanoic acid (CH3COOH) + ethanol (C2H5OH); MECHANISM: acid-catalyzed nucleophilic acyl substitution (AAC2): H+ protonates C=O of ester → nucleophilic attack of H2O → tetrahedral intermediate → proton transfers → -OR (alcohol) leaves → carboxylic acid; REVERSIBILITY: acid hydrolysis of esters is REVERSIBLE (equilibrium); the reverse reaction = Fischer esterification (RCOOH + R'OH ⇌ RCOOR' + H2O); use excess H2O to drive toward hydrolysis; GENERAL: any ester (RCOOR') + H3O+/Δ → RCOOH + R'OH; acid hydrolysis: RCOOH produced (free acid); compare basic: R-COO- produced (carboxylate, requires acidification to get RCOOH); for ALL acid derivatives (anhydride, acyl halide, ester, amide) + H3O+ → RCOOH + corresponding leaving group (R'COOH, HX, R'OH, NH3)
valid_transformations.conditions: H₃O⁺ (dil H₂SO₄ or HCl); H₂O (excess); reflux. Acid hydrolysis (AAc2 mechanism, most common): H⁺ protonates C=O → tetrahedral intermediate → H₂O → hemiacetal-like → EtOH leaves → acetic acid. Reversible (Fischer esterification reverse). Drive forward by excess H₂O. Base: NaOH (irreversible saponification) → sodium acetate → acidify → acetic acid.

valid_transformations.notes: Saponification: ethyl ethanoate (CH3COOC2H5) + NaOH → sodium ethanoate (CH3COONa, carboxylate salt) + ethanol (C2H5OH); SAPONIFICATION = base hydrolysis of esters (BAC2 mechanism); MECHANISM: OH- nucleophile attacks C=O of ester → tetrahedral intermediate [R-C(OH)(OR')(O-)] → OR'- leaves → R-C(=O)-O- (carboxylate) + R'OH; IRREVERSIBILITY: the carboxylate R-COO- is RESONANCE STABILIZED (negative charge delocalized over two oxygens) → very stable → does NOT react back with R'OH under basic conditions → IRREVERSIBLE; contrast acid hydrolysis: REVERSIBLE equilibrium; GENERAL: any ester + NaOH → RCOO-Na+ + R'OH; to get RCOOH (free acid) from saponification: acidify with HCl after saponification; NAME: 'saponification' from Latin sapo (soap); soap-making = fat (ester) + NaOH → soap (fatty acid carboxylate) + glycerol; ALL acid derivatives + OH-/H2O → RCOO- (carboxylate): anhydride → 2 RCOO-; acyl halide → RCOO-; ester → RCOO- + R'OH; amide → RCOO- + NH3
valid_transformations.conditions: NaOH (aq); reflux; irreversible saponification (BAc2). NaOH + CH₃COOEt → CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + EtOH. Alkoxide product (carboxylate) does not re-esterify under basic conditions → irreversible. Quantitative. ¹⁸O study: label in NaOH ends up in carboxylate product.

valid_transformations.notes: Alkene oxidative cleavage: (E)-but-2-ene (CH3-CH=CH-CH3) + hot KMnO4 → 2 × ethanoic acid (CH3COOH); GENERAL: R-CH=CH-R' + hot KMnO4 → R-COOH + R'-COOH (two carboxylic acids; C=C bond is cleaved oxidatively); ALSO: O3/oxidative workup (O3 then H2O2 or KMnO4) → same products; COMPARE: cold dilute KMnO4 (Baeyer's reagent) → diol (syn-dihydroxylation, NO cleavage); reductive ozonolysis (O3/Zn, H2O or O3/Me2S) → aldehydes (R-CHO) not acids; TERMINAL alkene (R-CH=CH2): H2C= side → CO2 + H2O (formaldehyde gets further oxidized to CO2 under hot KMnO4); only R- side gives R-COOH; INTERNAL alkene: each R group becomes RCOOH; KEY: hot acidic KMnO4 = CLEAVAGE of double bond; both C=C carbons get oxidized to COOH
valid_transformations.conditions: Hot acidic KMnO₄ (concentrated, excess); heat (Δ); aqueous H₂SO₄. Oxidative cleavage: internal alkene → 2 carboxylic acid fragments. (E)-but-2-ene (CH₃CH=CHCH₃) + hot KMnO₄ → 2 CH₃COOH (ethanoic acid × 2). Terminal alkene → HCOOH (then CO₂ with excess KMnO₄). Hot concentrated acidic KMnO₄ = strong oxidant (cold dilute = syn diol; hot conc = cleavage).

valid_transformations.notes: Alkyne oxidative cleavage: pent-2-yne (CH3-C≡C-CH2CH3) + hot KMnO4 → ethanoic acid (CH3COOH) + propanoic acid (CH3CH2COOH); GENERAL: R-C≡C-R' + hot KMnO4 OR O3/H2O → R-COOH + R'-COOH; both carbons of C≡C get oxidized to carboxylic acids; TERMINAL ALKYNE (R-C≡C-H): terminal carbon → CO2 + H2O (not COOH); only the R- gives R-COOH; MECHANISM: the alkyne is first converted to enol (keto tautomer = R-CO-CH2R') by the first oxidation step, then the ketone is further cleaved by hot KMnO4 → two carboxylic acids; SIMILARITY to alkene: hot KMnO4 cleaves BOTH C=C and C≡C to give RCOOH; the distinction from alkene: alkyne produces SAME carboxylic acids as if it were the corresponding internal alkene (cleavage at the same carbons)
valid_transformations.conditions: Hot acidic KMnO₄ or O₃/H₂O₂; heat/excess oxidant. Pent-2-yne (CH₃C≡CCH₂CH₃) oxidative cleavage at triple bond → CH₃COOH (ethanoic acid) + CH₃CH₂COOH (propanoic acid). Or: if ozonolysis with oxidative workup (H₂O₂): same acids. KMnO₄/H⁺/hot: cleaves triple bond → two carboxylic acids.

valid_transformations.notes: Koch reaction: 2-methylprop-1-ene (isobutylene, (CH3)2C=CH2) + CO + H2O → 2,2-dimethylpropanoic acid (pivalic acid, (CH3)3C-COOH) in the presence of H2SO4; MECHANISM (three steps): (1) H+ (from H2SO4) adds to alkene via Markovnikov → tert carbocation (CH3)3C+ (tert-butyl cation); (2) the tertiary carbocation attacks CO (carbon monoxide) → ACYLIUM ION (CH3)3C-C+=O; acylium ion is stabilized by the positive charge on C= O (formally R-C≡O+); (3) acylium ion + H2O → H2O attacks the electrophilic C+ → tetrahedral intermediate → -H+ → (CH3)3C-COOH (carboxylic acid); PRODUCT: 2,2-dimethylpropanoic acid (tertiary carboxylic acid); KEY: Koch reaction always gives MARKOVNIKOV-type product (the COOH attaches to the MORE substituted carbon, which was the carbocation site); more substituted alkenes give more stable carbocations → more efficient Koch reaction; general: alkene + CO + H2O (H+) → carboxylic acid with COOH at most-substituted carbon
valid_transformations.conditions: Koch reaction: CO + H₂O + H₂SO₄ (cat.); isobutylene (2-methylpropene) under CO pressure; 0°C to RT. Mechanism: H₂SO₄ protonates isobutylene → t-Bu⁺ (stable 3° carbocation) → CO (nucleophile trapping carbocation) → acylium t-BuCO⁺ → H₂O → pivalic acid (2,2-dimethylpropanoic acid). Also called Koch-Haaf reaction (Rupe's modification). High CO pressure (5–50 atm) and H₂SO₄.

valid_transformations.notes: Favorskii rearrangement: 2-chlorocyclohexan-1-one (alpha-chlorocyclohexanone, 6-membered ring) + (1)NaOH → (2)H+ → cyclopentane-1-carboxylic acid (COOH on 5-membered ring); GENERAL: alpha-halocyclic ketone + base (OH-) → ring-contracted carboxylic acid (ring shrinks by 1 C; the COOH replaces the ring junction); MECHANISM: OH- abstracts alpha-H → carbanion → intramolecular SN2 on C-X (the carbanion attacks the C-Cl carbon → forms cyclopropanone intermediate) → cyclopropanone ring opens under OH- (nucleophilic addition of OH-) → ring-opened carboxylate → H+ → carboxylic acid; RING CONTRACTION RULE: n-membered ring alpha-haloketone + NaOH → (n-1)-membered ring COOH; so cyclohexanone derivative → cyclopentane-COOH; cyclopentanone derivative → cyclobutane-COOH; ALTERNATIVE: with OR- (alkoxide) instead of OH-: gives ester (methyl or ethyl ester) instead of carboxylic acid; NICHE JEE TOPIC: a ring-contracted COOH from a cyclic ketone is the signature of Favorskii
valid_transformations.conditions: NaOH (aq); heat (Δ). Favorskii rearrangement: α-haloketone + base → ring contraction. 2-Chlorocyclohexan-1-one + NaOH → cyclopentane carboxylic acid (ring contracts by 1 carbon via cyclopropanone intermediate). Mechanism: α-H removed by base → carbanion → ring closes on C-Cl (displacement of Cl⁻) → cyclopropanone → OH⁻ ring-opens → cyclopentane carboxylate → H⁺ → cyclopentane-1-carboxylic acid.

valid_transformations.notes: KMnO4 oxidation of alkylbenzene side chains: methylbenzene (toluene, PhCH3) + hot acidic KMnO4 → benzoic acid (Ph-COOH); GENERAL: any alkylbenzene (Ph-R where R = primary or secondary alkyl of ANY length) + hot KMnO4 → Ph-COOH (benzoic acid); the ENTIRE alkyl chain is oxidized away, leaving only ONE COOH carbon directly bonded to the ring; the length of the alkyl chain DOES NOT MATTER — whether R = CH3, C2H5, C10H21, etc., the product is always Ph-COOH; MECHANISM: KMnO4 oxidizes the benzylic C-H (alpha carbon to ring) → this benzylic carbon becomes the COOH; successive oxidations oxidize the chain away; MULTIPLE GROUPS: if the benzene ring has multiple alkyl groups, each becomes a -COOH (e.g., para-dimethylbenzene → terephthalic acid (para-benzenedicarboxylic acid)); SECOND EXAMPLE: Ph-CH(CH3)- (isopropyl: Ph-CH(CH3)2) → Ph-COOH + CH3COOH (both fragments oxidized to acids; however the phenyl C that was attached to the chain → benzoic acid; the detached fragment CH3 → ethanoic acid (actually any chain fragment not attached to ring becomes separate RCOOH)); EXCEPTION: tert-butyl benzene (Ph-C(CH3)3) has NO alpha-H → NOT oxidized by KMnO4
valid_transformations.conditions: Hot KMnO₄/OH⁻ (aq); reflux; then H₃O⁺ workup. Oxidation of methyl group to COOH. KMnO₄ (hot, conc, basic or acidic) oxidises alkylbenzene side chain → carboxylic acid (regardless of chain length — all Cα and beyond oxidised, only Cα bond to ring retained). Alternatively: K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄/heat. Product: benzoic acid (PhCOOH).

valid_transformations.notes: Geminal trihalide hydrolysis: benzotrichloride (trichloromethylbenzene, Ph-CCl3) + NaOH → benzoic acid (Ph-COOH); GENERAL: R-CX3 (geminal trihalide = all 3 halogens on same carbon) + NaOH/H2O → R-COOH; MECHANISM: R-CX3 + OH- → first substitution: R-CX2(OH) (dihalide hemiorthoester) → R-CX(OH)2 (monohalide) → R-COX (acyl halide; loses HX) → acyl halide + H2O → R-COOH + HX; intermediate is acyl halide R-C(=O)-X; EQUIVALENT: R-CX3 = 3 halogens on same C; hydrolysis goes stepwise by NaOH, each step replaces X with OH; after loss of HX from R-C(OH)2X → R-COX (acyl halide) → further hydrolysis → RCOOH; EXAMPLE: CHCl3 (trichloromethane) = geminal trihalide with H (not R); CHCl3 + NaOH → (under basic conditions forms dichlorocarbene CCl2, NOT carboxylic acid); Ph-CCl3 (benzotrichloride) + NaOH → PhCOOH (benzoic acid); ALTERNATIVE PATH for ArCX3: heating with NaOH gives acyl intermediate → benzoic acid directly
valid_transformations.conditions: NaOH (aq, hot); then H⁺ workup. PhCCl₃ + 3 NaOH → Ph-C(OH)₃ (orthoformate-like, unstable) → Ph-COOH + 3 HCl/NaCl. Mechanism: SN2 hydrolysis of each C-Cl bond successively → PhC(OH)₃ → benzoic acid. Also: phenyltrichloromethane + H₂O/heat → benzoyl chloride (partial) → benzoic acid (full). Used in old preparation of benzoic acid from toluene via side-chain chlorination.

valid_transformations.notes: Grignard reagent prep: chloroethane (ethyl chloride, CH3CH2Cl) + Mg / dry ether → ethylmagnesium chloride (EtMgCl, CH3CH2MgCl); GENERAL: R-X + Mg (dry ether) → RMgX (Grignard reagent); MECHANISM (radical): (1) Mg → Mg²⁺ + e⁻ (oxidation of Mg); (2) e⁻ attacks C-X bond of R-X → R• (alkyl radical) + X⁻ (halide); (3) R• recombines with •Mg⁺ (radical combination) → R-MgX (Grignard); NATURE OF C-Mg BOND: 'highly polar covalent' (the C-Mg bond is NOT purely ionic but has significant ionic character; Mg is electropositive, C is δ⁻); SOLVENT REQUIREMENT: must use DRY (anhydrous) ether (diethyl ether or THF); ether coordinates to Mg center (O lone pairs → Mg); any moisture destroys Grignard: RMgX + H2O → RH + Mg(OH)X; REACTIVITY ORDER: RI > RBr > RCl >> RF (F: 'no reaction'; C-F bond is too strong for Mg to cleave); TYPES: primary, secondary, tertiary alkyl; vinyl (sp₂); aryl (sp₂); NO alkyl fluoride → Grignard; SCHLENK EQUILIBRIUM: 2 RMgX ⇌ R₂Mg + MgX₂ (exists in ether solution; both RMgX and R₂Mg present)
valid_transformations.conditions: Mg metal turnings; dry diethyl ether (anhydrous); RT or gentle warming; inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar). EtCl + Mg → EtMgCl. Surface oxide removed by iodine activation if needed. Ether solvent coordinates to Mg via O lone pairs → stabilises Grignard. Strict anhydrous conditions (RMgX + H₂O → R-H instantly). Chloride: less reactive than bromide or iodide; may need more Mg or THF instead of Et₂O.

valid_transformations.notes: Aryl Grignard prep: bromobenzene (PhBr) + Mg / dry ether → phenylmagnesium bromide (PhMgBr); ARYL GRIGNARD: sp₂ carbon bearing the halide CAN form Grignard with Mg (despite being sp₂ — aryl C-Br bond is still reactive with Mg in ether); same mechanism as alkyl: radical process; VINYL GRIGNARD: vinyl halides (CH₂=CH-X) also form Grignard by same method; SELECTIVITY: aryl-F (fluorobenzene) does NOT form Grignard even with Mg/ether (C-F bond too strong; same as alkyl fluorides); aryl-Cl, aryl-Br, aryl-I all work (in order Ar-I > Ar-Br > Ar-Cl); USES of PhMgBr: (1) acid-base → Ph-H (reacts with any protic source); (2) addition to aldehydes/ketones → secondary or tertiary alcohol; (3) addition to CO₂ → benzoic acid; (4) reaction with RX → coupling (less direct for Grignard); DEUTERIUM LABELING: PhMgBr + D₂O → Ph-D (deuterobenzene); this is used to confirm the position of the Grignard carbon in complex molecules
valid_transformations.conditions: Mg turnings; dry THF (preferred for aryl halides over Et₂O — higher bp, better solvation for ArMgX); reflux or RT with I₂ activation; inert atmosphere. ArBr + Mg → ArMgBr. Aryl Grignards require THF (Et₂O often insufficient for unreactive ArBr). I₂ (trace) activates Mg surface. Strictly anhydrous; ArMgBr + H₂O → ArH instantly.

reagents: or any protic H+ source (ROH, RCOOH, PhOH, RNH2, R-C≡CH)
valid_transformations.notes: Grignard acid-base reaction: ethylmagnesium chloride (EtMgCl) + H₂O → ethane (CH₃CH₃) + Mg(OH)Cl; GENERAL: RMgX + H-A → R-H + AMgX; the Grignard carbanion R⁻ acts as a STRONG BASE (pKa of RH ≈ 45-50 for alkyl; ≈ 43 for vinyl; ≈ 36 for aryl) → deprotonates ANY acid with pKa < 45; COMPREHENSIVE LIST of H-donors that destroy Grignard (all give R-H): (1) RSO₃H (sulfonic acids); (2) RCOOH (carboxylic acids); (3) PhOH (phenol); (4) RSH (thiols); (5) ROH (alcohols); (6) H₂O; (7) D₂O → gives R-D (DEUTERIUM LABELING); (8) T₂O → R-T; (9) R-C≡CH (terminal alkynes, pKa≈25) ✓; (10) NH₃; (11) RNH₂ (primary amines); (12) RNH-R (secondary amines); (13) RCONH₂ (primary amides); (14) RCONHCH₃ (secondary amides); (15) cyclopentadiene (pKa≈16!) ✓; (16) β-diketone (pKa≈9-11) ✓; (17) NC-CH₂-CN (malononitrile); (18) O₂N-CH₂-NO₂ (dinitromethane); (19) CHCl₃ (chloroform); (20) CH(NO₂)₃ (nitroform); (21-22) α-thioethers/dithianes; COUNTING: excess CH₃MgBr + molecule → n × CH₄↑ (n = number of N-H + O-H + S-H + terminal alkyne C-H in the molecule)
valid_transformations.conditions: H₂O (or any proton source: ROH, RCOOH, PhOH, R-C≡CH, RNH₂); RT; instantaneous. EtMgCl + H₂O → EtH + Mg(OH)Cl. Grignard is a strong base (pKa of EtH ~50). Any proton source with pKa < ~50 protonates it. Used to: (1) detect active H (measure H₂ evolved); (2) destroy Grignard after reaction; (3) Zerewitinoff method for -OH, -NH count.

valid_transformations.notes: Grignard deuterium labeling: RMgX + D₂O → R-D + MgX(OD); ethylmagnesium chloride + D₂O → ethane-d₁ (CH₃CH₂D) + Mg(OD)Cl; UTILITY: deuterium labeling is used to: (1) confirm the position of C-Mg in complex molecules (the D appears at the site of the original C-X); (2) count the number of equivalent C-X groups (how many D atoms incorporated = how many Grignard groups); (3) provide NMR-silent labels (D is NMR silent at ¹H NMR, visible at ²H NMR); SELECTIVITY: D₂O inserts D at EVERY C-Mg site → gives one D per RMgX; COMPARISON: H₂O → R-H (protio; no label); D₂O → R-D (deuterium; labeled); T₂O → R-T (tritium; radioactive label); MECHANISM: D-OD (D₂O) acts as acid (pKa of D₂O ≈ 15.7, same as H₂O); the carbanion of RMgX (R⁻) is a strong base → deprotonates D₂O → R-D + OD⁻
valid_transformations.conditions: D₂O (deuterium oxide, heavy water); RT; anhydrous ether. EtMgCl + D₂O → EtD + Mg(OD)Cl. Incorporation of deuterium label at the Grignard carbon. Used for isotope labelling in mechanistic studies. Quantitative deuteration (one D per Grignard reagent). Same as H₂O quench but with D₂O.

valid_transformations.notes: Terminal alkyne + Grignard = alkynyl Grignard formation: prop-1-yne (propyne, HC≡C-CH₃, terminal alkyne) + ethylmagnesium bromide (EtMgBr) → prop-1-yn-1-ylmagnesium bromide (propargyl Grignard, CH₃-C≡C-MgBr) + ethane (CH₃CH₃); MECHANISM: the terminal alkyne C-H (pKa ≈ 25) is MORE ACIDIC than ethane C-H (pKa ≈ 50) → the Grignard carbanion (EtMgBr, pKa of EtH ≈ 50) deprotonates the terminal alkyne C-H → alkynyl carbanion (R-C≡C⁻) → stabilized by sp hybridization (high s-character, more electronegative than sp³) → MgBr+ coordinates → alkynyl Grignard (R-C≡C-MgBr); ACID-BASE: pKa terminal alkyne (25) << pKa EtH (50) → reaction is thermodynamically favorable; WHY SP IS MORE ACIDIC: sp orbital has 50% s-character vs sp² (33%) vs sp³ (25%); more s-character = electrons held closer to nucleus = more stable carbanion = lower pKa = more acidic; UTILITY: alkynyl Grignard can then add to carbonyl compounds → propargyl alcohols
valid_transformations.conditions: EtMgBr (ethylmagnesium bromide, 1 equiv) + prop-1-yne (propyne, HC≡C-CH₃, terminal alkyne); RT; dry ether or THF. Terminal alkyne C-H (pKa ~25) is more acidic than ethane C-H (pKa ~50) → Grignard base (EtMgBr) deprotonates alkyne → ethane (weaker acid leaves) + propynyl Grignard (RC≡CMgBr). Alkynyl Grignard is nucleophile for carbonyl additions.

valid_transformations.notes: Aryl Grignard with ether substituent: 2-bromoanisole (1-bromo-2-methoxybenzene, PhBr with OMe ortho) + Mg/ether → 2-methoxyphenylmagnesium bromide (PhMgBr with OMe ortho); CONTRAST with 2-bromophenol case: OMe is NOT acidic (ether C-O-CH₃; no acidic H), so no self-destruction occurs; 2-bromo-phenol WOULD self-destruct (the OH is acidic → deprotonates the C-MgBr internally → gives O-MgBr instead of C-MgBr); INTRAMOLECULAR SELF-DESTRUCTION RULE: if a molecule has BOTH C-X (Grignard-forming) AND an acidic H group (OH, NH, SH, R-C≡C-H) in the same molecule → Grignard self-destructs; net product = C-H (restored) and heteroatom-MgBr; then alkylating agent (like CH₃-I) reacts with heteroatom-MgBr → O-methylation, N-methylation, or S-methylation
valid_transformations.conditions: Mg; dry THF (aryl halide requires THF, not Et₂O); gentle reflux; inert atmosphere; I₂ activation. 2-Bromoanisole (2-methoxybromobenzene) + Mg → 2-methoxyphenylmagnesium bromide. OMe group is ortho → slightly slower than unsubstituted PhBr (steric) but still reactive. Anhydrous strictly.

reagents: 1-bromoethane (primary alkyl halide, R'-X where R' = primary)
valid_transformations.notes: Grignard SN2 coupling: propylmagnesium bromide (PrMgBr) + 1-bromoethane (EtBr, 1° alkyl halide) → butane (PrEt = CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3) + MgBrX; GENERAL: RMgX + R'-X (SN2) → R-R' + MgX₂ (new C-C bond formed; this is the WURTZ-type coupling via Grignard); REQUIREMENT: R'-X must be PRIMARY (1°) alkyl halide for SN2 to work; 2° = sluggish, competing elimination; 3° = NO SN2 (elimination E2 dominates instead); REACTIVE R'-X TYPES: primary aliphatic ✓ (methyl, ethyl, propyl, etc.); DOES NOT WORK: 3° alkyl halides, vinyl halides (sp₂ cannot do SN2), aryl halides (cannot do SN2); USE GILMAN (R₂CuLi) for vinyl and aryl halides instead; MECHANISM: RMgX acts as R⁻ nucleophile; attacks the back of the 1° R'-X carbon in an SN2 displacement; Mg-X end becomes MgX₂; NOTE: the Grignard R group is the nucleophile; R'-X provides the electrophilic carbon
valid_transformations.conditions: Primary alkyl halide (1-bromoethane, EtBr); dry ether; RT. Coupling (Wurtz-type via cuprate or direct if conditions right) or: PrMgBr acts as base toward primary RX? More likely: cross-coupling via organocuprate. PrMgBr + EtBr → does NOT couple cleanly (Grignard + alkyl halide gives poor yield); use Gilman reagent (PrCuLi or (Pr)₂CuLi) + EtBr → butane. Or: PrMgBr + H₂O → PrH (propane, not butane). So butane requires coupling of Pr (3C) + Et (1C) fragments = 4C alkane. Gilman reagent route.

valid_transformations.notes: Grignard + halogen → alkyl/aryl halide: PhMgBr (phenylmagnesium bromide) + Br₂ → PhBr (bromobenzene) + MgBr₂; GENERAL: RMgX + X₂ → R-X + MgX₂ (where X₂ = Cl₂, Br₂, or I₂); the Grignard R group is halogenated; R-Mg bond is replaced by R-X bond; UTILITY: this is used to INTRODUCE A HALOGEN at the position where the Grignard was (useful for complex structures where direct halogenation would not be regioselective); EXAMPLE: cannot halogenate arene at a specific position by EAS when other positions are equally reactive → make Grignard at that C → + X₂ → halide at that specific C; LIMITING REAGENT: use RMgX as LR (limiting reagent) to avoid over-halogenation; with excess X₂, only monohalogenation at the Grignard carbon; HALOGEN SCOPE: Cl₂, Br₂, I₂ all work; F₂ not commonly used (too reactive); REACTION WITH I₂ IS PARTICULARLY USEFUL for making aryl iodides (ArMgBr + I₂ → ArI)
valid_transformations.conditions: Br₂ (molecular bromine, 1 equiv); anhydrous ether; 0°C to RT. PhMgBr + Br₂ → PhBr + MgBr₂. Electrophilic halogenation of organometal: R-MgX + X₂ → R-X + MgX₂. Product: bromobenzene (re-synthesised from phenylmagnesium bromide). Used in isotope labelling (BrMgPh + Br₂→ Br⁸¹-Ph or C-D/C-¹³C labelled bromo compounds).

valid_transformations.notes: 1,2-dichloroethane (Cl-CH₂-CH₂-Cl, n=2 dihaloalkane) + Mg/ether → ethene (CH₂=CH₂) + MgCl₂; NOT a diGrignard; MECHANISM: Mg inserts into one C-Cl → Cl-CH₂-CH₂-MgCl forms transiently → but the β-MgCl group induces intramolecular E2 β-elimination (β-haloalkyl Grignard: the halogen at β position and the MgCl act together → synperiplanar elimination) → CH₂=CH₂ + MgCl₂; GENERAL RULE for X-(CH₂)n-X + Mg: n=1 → carbene (:CX₂ or :CH₂ after hydrolysis); n=2 → alkene (β-elimination); n=3 → cyclopropane (intramolecular SN2 ring closure); n≥4 (n≠1,2,3) → diGrignard XMg-(CH₂)n-MgX; KEY DISTINCTION: 1,2-dihaloalkane gives ALKENE (not diGrignard); 1,3-dihaloalkane gives CYCLOPROPANE (not diGrignard or alkene)
valid_transformations.conditions: Mg; dry ether; RT. 1,2-Dichloroethane + Mg → not Grignard (vicinal dihalide eliminates). Mg inserts → organometal → β-elimination of MgClBr → ethene (ClCH₂CH₂Cl + Mg → MgClBr + CH₂=CH₂). Dehalogenation: vicinal dihalides + Mg (or Zn) → alkene (elimination). Industrial: 1,2-dichloroethane → ethylene via Zn/EtOH or Mg/Et₂O elimination.

valid_transformations.notes: Diiodomethane (CH₂I₂, geminal dihaloalkane, n=1) + Mg/ether → :CH₂ (methylene carbene) + MgI₂ or MgI(I); geminal dihaloalkane (both X on same carbon) + Mg → CARBENE (:CRR'); MECHANISM: Mg inserts into C-X → X-CH₂-MgX (monoGrignard transiently) → the MgX eliminates the second X from the same carbon (alpha-elimination) → :CH₂ + MgX₂; CARBENE :CH₂: is a highly reactive intermediate (neutral carbon with only 2 bonds, 2 non-bonding electrons: one in each orbital, singlet or triplet); REACTIONS OF :CH₂: (1) inserts into C-H bonds; (2) adds to alkenes (syn) → cyclopropane; SIMMONS-SMITH: CH₂I₂ + Zn(Cu) → IZnCH₂I (carbenoid) → adds to alkene → cyclopropane (stereospecific syn); GENERAL: gem-dihalo (n=1) + Mg → :CR₂ (carbene, where R = substituents on the gem-dihalo carbon)
valid_transformations.conditions: Mg (or Zn/Cu couple) + dry ether; RT. CH₂I₂ + Mg → ICH₂MgI (iodomethylmagnesium iodide, Simmons-Smith reagent). Alternatively: CH₂I₂ + Zn(Cu) → IZnCH₂I (Simmons-Smith reagent directly). On reaction with alkene → cyclopropane (stereospecific syn addition, :CH₂ equivalent via carbenoid). No free carbene — concerted [1+2] cycloaddition from carbenoid.

valid_transformations.notes: 1,3-dibromopropane (Br-CH₂-CH₂-CH₂-Br, n=3, α,ω-dihaloalkane) + Mg/ether → cyclopropane; MECHANISM: Mg inserts into one C-Br → Br-CH₂-CH₂-CH₂-MgBr (monoGrignard) → the carbanion at C1 does intramolecular SN2 on C3-Br (3-exo-tet ring closure) → cyclopropane + MgBr₂; RING SIZE RULE for X-(CH₂)n-X + Mg: n=3 → 3-membered ring (cyclopropane); n=4 → 4-membered ring (cyclobutane); n=5 → 5-membered ring (cyclopentane); GENERAL: number of carbons in ring = n (the number of CH₂ groups between the two halogens); LONGER CHAINS: 1,5-dihalo + Mg(1eq)/Δ → cyclopentane (heat required for longer chains to overcome kinetic barrier; ring closure is thermally assisted for 5- and 6-membered rings)
valid_transformations.conditions: Mg; dry ether; RT. 1,3-Dibromopropane + Mg → BrMg-CH₂CH₂CH₂-MgBr? No: intramolecular: one Grignard end attacks the other C-Br → cyclopropane + MgBr₂ (intramolecular SN2). Mg inserts into one C-Br → Grignard → intramolecular displacement of other Br → cyclopropane. Alternatively: Zn/ether gives same result. 1,3-dihalide with Mg → intramolecular coupling → cyclopropane.

valid_transformations.notes: Organolithium prep: chloroethane (ethyl chloride, EtCl) + 2Li/dry ether → ethyllithium (EtLi) + LiCl; GENERAL: R-X + 2Li → RLi + LiX; NOTE: requires 2 equivalents of Li (unlike Grignard which requires only 1 Mg); MECHANISM: (1) Li → Li⁺ + e⁻ (first Li oxidized); (2) e⁻ attacks R-X → R• + X⁻; (3) R• + second Li → RLi (R⁻ Li⁺; the second Li provides the electron and coordinates); PRODUCT: [R:⁻ Li⁺] (boxed; organolithium is MORE IONIC than Grignard; Li is more electropositive than Mg → C-Li bond is more polar → RLi is a better carbanion source than RMgX); REACTIVITY ORDER: RNa > RK > RLi > RMgX > RZnX (left = most reactive/basic); ADVANTAGES over Grignard: RLi can deprotonate more acidic C-H bonds; can react with substrates that Grignard cannot; DISADVANTAGE: RLi is more pyrophoric (catches fire in air) → harder to handle; SCOPE: primary, secondary, aryl, vinyl halides all form RLi; fluorides generally do not form RLi under standard conditions
