valid_transformations.conditions: 2 equiv Li metal; dry ether (or diethyl ether/hexane); –78°C to 0°C; strictly inert atmosphere (Ar). EtCl + 2 Li → EtLi + LiCl. Organolithiums more reactive than Grignards (stronger C-Li bond, harder Lewis acid). Use 2 Li (one for C-Li bond, one for LiCl). Organolithiums react with ether slowly → use quickly or at –78°C. EtLi used to make cuprates (EtLi + CuI → Et₂CuLi).

valid_transformations.notes: Gilman reagent prep: cyclopentyl iodide + (1)2Li → cyclopentyllithium (CpLi); CpLi + (2)CuI (0.5 eq) → dicyclopentylcuprate lithium ((Cp)₂CuLi) + LiI; GENERAL: RX + 2Li → RLi → RLi + 0.5 CuI → R₂CuLi + LiI; (OR: 2 RLi + CuI → R₂CuLi + LiI); GILMAN REAGENT (R₂CuLi) = ORGANOCUPRATE; PROPERTIES: (1) LESS REACTIVE than RLi or RMgX (C-Cu bond is less polar than C-Li or C-Mg → weaker carbanion); (2) Only ONE R group is transferred as nucleophile (the other R stays on Cu; only R⁻ attacks the electrophile); (3) the unused R is wasted (hence need R₂CuLi, not RCuLi, for 1 equivalent of R transfer); REACTS WITH: acyl halides (R'-C(=O)-Cl → R'-C(=O)-R = ketone ✓); primary alkyl halides (SN2 ✓); vinyl halides (stereospecific ✓); aryl halides ✓; DOES NOT REACT WITH: ketones ×, esters ×, nitriles ×, carboxylic acids × (too unreactive for C=O of these; only highly reactive acyl chlorides work)
valid_transformations.conditions: Step 1: cyclopentyl iodide + 2 Li → cyclopentyllithium + LiI; dry ether; –78°C; inert atmosphere. Step 2: cyclopentyllithium + CuI (0.5 equiv) → (cyclopentyl)₂CuLi·LiI (Gilman reagent). Gilman reagent used for 1,4-conjugate addition (Michael acceptors) or coupling with primary alkyl halides/acid chlorides (no 1,2-addition to ketones). More selective than RMgX or RLi.

valid_transformations.notes: Gilman reagent + acyl chloride → ketone: acetyl chloride (ethanoyl chloride, CH₃-C(=O)-Cl) + dimethylcuprate lithium (Me₂CuLi) → propan-2-one (acetone, CH₃-C(=O)-CH₃) + LiCl + CuX; GENERAL: R'-C(=O)-Cl + R₂CuLi → R'-C(=O)-R (ketone) + LiCl + CuX; this is one of the BEST methods to make KETONES via C-C bond formation; SELECTIVITY: Gilman (R₂CuLi) reacts with acyl chlorides → KETONE; UNLIKE GRIGNARD: Grignard with acyl chloride → gives over-addition (Grignard adds twice → tertiary alcohol, not ketone); Gilman stops at ketone (less reactive → does NOT add to the ketone product); MECHANISM: R₂CuLi acts as a 'soft' nucleophile → oxidative addition/transmetalation pathway (not direct SN2); the acyl chloride C=O is attacked → tetrahedral intermediate → Cl⁻ eliminated → ketone; only ONE R from R₂CuLi is transferred; SCOPE: can use complex RLi → R₂CuLi → react with R'-COCl → R'-CO-R (mixed ketone with 2 different R groups)
valid_transformations.conditions: Gilman reagent (dimethylcuprate, Me₂CuLi); dry ether; –78°C to 0°C; anhydrous. Me₂CuLi + CH₃COCl → CH₃COCH₃ (acetone). Organocuprate adds to acyl halide (1,2-addition, ketone product; no over-addition to ketone). Mechanism: transmetalation → reductive elimination. Advantage over Grignard: Grignard + RCOCl → 3° alcohol (adds twice); cuprate stops at ketone.

valid_transformations.notes: Gilman reagent + vinyl halide → stereospecific alkene: (Z)-1-bromobut-1-ene (a cis vinyl bromide with stereochemistry around C=C) + diethylcuprate lithium (Et₂CuLi) → (Z)-hex-3-ene (cis product; configuration retained); GENERAL: R₂CuLi + vinyl-X → vinyl-R (new alkene with C=C CONFIGURATION RETAINED); STEREOCHEMICAL RULE: the coupling of R₂CuLi with vinyl halides is STEREOSPECIFIC with RETENTION of the C=C geometry; (Z)-vinyl-X → (Z)-product; (E)-vinyl-X → (E)-product; WHY RETENTION: the mechanism goes through a transition state that preserves the geometry of the C=C (likely syn addition/oxidative addition at Cu preserving stereochemistry); contrast: SN2 would require back-attack at sp₂ carbon which is geometrically impossible → cannot invert; Gilman goes with retention (front-face pathway); SCOPE: also works with aryl halides (Ar-X + R₂CuLi → Ar-R); CANNOT BE DONE WITH GRIGNARD: RMgX does NOT undergo SN2 with vinyl/aryl halides → use Gilman for vinyl and aryl coupling; REFERENCE: Paula Y. Bruice textbook topic
valid_transformations.conditions: Gilman reagent (diethylcuprate, Et₂CuLi); dry ether or THF; –78°C to 0°C. Et₂CuLi + (Z)-1-bromobut-1-ene → SN2 coupling with retention? Vinyl halides normally unreactive toward SN2, but organocuprates couple efficiently via oxidative addition/reductive elimination at Cu. Stereospecific (retention of alkene geometry from vinyl halide). Product: (Z)-hex-3-ene with retention.

reagents: or PDC, Collins, Corey, Swern, Moffatt, Jones
valid_transformations.notes: Secondary alcohol → ketone: propan-2-ol (isopropanol, 2° alcohol) + PCC (or PDC, Collins, Corey, Swern, Moffatt, Jones, X₂, NBS, Cu/300°C) → propan-2-one (acetone, ketone); GENERAL: any 2° alcohol + any oxidant from the selective list → ketone; ALL oxidants (both selective and strong) oxidize 2° alcohol → ketone; KETONE CANNOT BE FURTHER OXIDIZED under normal conditions (no α-H? then completely resistant; even strong KMnO₄/H+ gives no rxn with 2° ketone product under normal conditions); under VERY HIGH TEMPERATURE and STRONG OA (hot KMnO₄, HNO₃, K₂Cr₂O₇/Δ): ketone undergoes Popoff's Rule cleavage → two carboxylic acids (C-C bonds alpha to C=O are cleaved; RCOOH formed from each fragment); TERTIARY (3°) → always NO REACTION under all standard selective oxidants
valid_transformations.conditions: PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate) in CH₂Cl₂; RT or mild Swern (oxalyl chloride/DMSO/Et₃N, –78°C); or K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄ (Jones, in acetone). 2° alcohol → ketone. PCC: mild, anhydrous, selective. Jones: aqueous, orange CrO₃/H₂SO₄/acetone. Oppenauer (Al-t-BuO/cyclohexanone, RT): 2° alcohol → ketone. All stop at ketone (no further oxidation to acid without C-C cleavage).

reagents: Jones reagent (CrO3 + H2SO4 + H2O in acetone solvent)
valid_transformations.notes: Strong oxidant oxidation of primary alcohol → carboxylic acid: propan-1-ol (1-propanol, RCH₂OH) + Jones reagent → propanoic acid (RCOOH); JONES REAGENT: CrO₃ + H₂SO₄ + H₂O + acetone (solvent); active species = H₂CrO₄ (chromic acid); MECHANISM: R-CH₂-OH + HO-Cr(=O)-OH (H₂CrO₄) → ester intermediate R-CH₂-O-Cr(=O)-OH → β-H elimination → R-CHO (aldehyde intermediate) → the aldehyde adds H₂O (in aqueous Jones) → R-CH(OH)₂ (gem-diol) → gem-diol + H₂CrO₄ → second oxidation → RCOOH; KEY: Jones goes 1° → RCOOH (all the way; NOT selective like PCC); 2° → ketone (stops at ketone; no further oxidation of ketone under Jones); 3° → NO reaction; OTHER STRONG OXIDANTS (same 1°→RCOOH): K₂Cr₂O₇/H+, KMnO₄/H+, HNO₃, H₂CrO₄, Mn⁷+ aq, Cr⁶+ aq medium; DIFFERENCE FROM PCC: PCC gives 1°→CHO (anhydrous, no water; cannot form gem-diol intermediate); Jones gives 1°→RCOOH (aqueous; gem-diol forms → second oxidation)
valid_transformations.conditions: Jones reagent (CrO₃/H₂SO₄/acetone); or K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄/heat; or KMnO₄/H⁺. Primary alcohol → carboxylic acid (via aldehyde intermediate, which is oxidised further in aqueous acidic conditions). Jones is aggressive → aldehyde → acid. PCC stops at aldehyde. Aqueous Cr(VI) or KMnO₄: 1° ROH → RCOOH.

valid_transformations.notes: MnO₂ selective oxidation: benzyl alcohol (phenylmethanol, Ph-CH₂-OH, benzylic primary alcohol) + MnO₂ → benzaldehyde (PhCHO); SELECTIVITY RULE: MnO₂ ONLY oxidizes ALLYLIC and BENZYLIC alcohols (alcohols adjacent to C=C or aromatic ring); does NOT oxidize simple aliphatic alcohols (neither primary nor secondary); EXAMPLES: PhCH₂OH (benzyl alcohol, 1°) → PhCHO ✓; Ph-CH(OH)-CH₃ (1-phenylethanol, benzylic 2°) → Ph-CO-CH₃ ✓; allylic CH₂=CH-CH₂OH (prop-2-en-1-ol) → CH₂=CH-CHO ✓; Ph-C(OH)(CH₃)₂ (dimethylphenylcarbinol, tertiary benzylic) → NO REACTION ×; simple CH₃CH₂OH → NO REACTION ×; REASON FOR SELECTIVITY: MnO₂ reacts via a radical mechanism; the benzylic/allylic C-H is weakest (lowest BDE due to resonance stabilization of the radical intermediate) → MnO₂ can abstract this H; aliphatic C-H is too strong; SYNTHETIC USE: oxidize benzyl/allyl alcohol to aldehyde in presence of aliphatic alcohol groups without affecting aliphatic ones
valid_transformations.conditions: MnO₂ (activated, freshly prepared); CH₂Cl₂; RT. MnO₂ selectively oxidises activated (allylic and benzylic) primary and secondary alcohols to aldehydes and ketones respectively, without affecting isolated C=C or other functional groups. Very mild and selective. Alternatively: PCC (but slightly less selective than MnO₂ for benzylic). Swern also works.

reagents: or K2Cr2O7/H+, HNO3, Jones reagent, H2CrO4, Tollens, Fehling (for aliphatic only), m-CPBA, H2O2, O3
valid_transformations.notes: Aldehyde oxidation to carboxylic acid: propanal (CH₃CH₂CHO) + KMnO₄/H+ → propanoic acid (CH₃CH₂COOH); COMPLETE LIST of reagents that oxidize R-CHO → RCOOH: (1) KMnO₄/H+ (acidic, hot); (2) K₂Cr₂O₇/H+; (3) HNO₃; (4) Jones reagent (CrO₃/H₂SO₄/H₂O); (5) H₂CrO₄; (6) Mn⁷+ neutral; (7) Cr⁶+ neutral; (8) O₃ (ozonolysis); (9) H₂O₂; (10) m-CPBA (meta-chloroperoxybenzoic acid); (11) Tollens (ALL aldehydes); (12) Fehling's (ALIPHATIC aldehydes only; Ar-CHO = benzaldehyde does NOT give Fehling positive); SELECTIVE REAGENTS for aldehyde (do NOT oxidize primary alcohol, only aldehyde): {O₃, H₂O₂, m-CPBA, Tollens, Fehling's} — these reagents oxidize R-CHO → RCOOH but do NOT oxidize R-CH₂-OH (primary alcohol); NON-SELECTIVE: KMnO₄, K₂Cr₂O₇, HNO₃, Jones — these oxidize BOTH primary alcohol AND aldehyde to RCOOH
valid_transformations.conditions: KMnO₄/H⁺ or K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄ (Jones) or Tollens'/Fehling's + oxidation. Aldehyde → carboxylic acid (2e⁻ oxidation). Mild oxidants: Tollens' gives silver mirror + carboxylate. Jones (CrO₃/H₂SO₄/acetone): RCHO → RCOOH cleanly. KMnO₄/acidic: RCHO → RCOOH. PCC does NOT oxidise aldehydes to acids (stops at RCHO).

valid_transformations.notes: Popoff's Rule — cyclic ketone oxidative ring opening: cyclohexanone (6-membered ring ketone) + HNO₃/Δ → hexanedioic acid (adipic acid, HOOC-(CH₂)₄-COOH); POPOFF'S RULE: ketone cleavage by hot strong oxidants (KMnO₄/H+ at high T, K₂Cr₂O₇/H+/Δ, HNO₃/Δ); RULE: the C=O carbon goes with the chain containing FEWER carbons; for CYCLIC ketones: ring is opened and BOTH fragments get COOH → diacid; MECHANISM: ketone enolizes → enol (C=C adjacent to C=O); KMnO₄ cleaves the C=C of the enol; both carbons of the former C=C become COOH; for cyclohexanone: enol of cyclohexanone has C=C in the ring → cleavage of ring → linear 6-carbon chain with COOH on each end → adipic acid; ACYCLIC EXAMPLE: pentan-2-one (CH₃-CO-CH₂CH₂CH₃) + hot KMnO₄ → CH₃COOH (acetic acid, 2C, the 'smaller' fragment containing C=O) + CH₃CH₂COOH (propanoic acid, 3C); Note: -C(=O)- goes with the chain containing fewer C atoms; DETERMINATION: count Cs on each side of ketone C=O (not counting C=O itself); fewer C side gets the C=O in the product; this is Popoff's Rule
valid_transformations.conditions: Hot concentrated HNO₃; Δ; or hot KMnO₄/H₂SO₄. Oxidative ring opening: cyclohexanone + HNO₃ (conc, fuming, 60–70°C) → ring-cleaved adipic acid (hexanedioic acid). Industrial: cyclohexanone/cyclohexanol mixture + HNO₃ (Baeyer catalyst V₂O₅/HNO₃) → adipic acid for Nylon-6,6. Vigorous acidic oxidative conditions. Commercial scale: Cu-catalysed.

reagents: (1) LiAlH4 (lithium aluminium hydride) in dry diethyl ether
valid_transformations.notes: LAH reduction of ester → TWO alcohols: ethyl propanoate (CH₃CH₂COOC₂H₅, ester) + (1)LiAlH₄ → (2)H₂O → propan-1-ol (CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, 1° alcohol from the acyl R group) + ethanol (C₂H₅OH, 1° alcohol from the OR' group); GENERAL: R-C(=O)-OR' + LiAlH₄ → R-CH₂-OH + R'-OH (TWO primary alcohols!); MECHANISM: H⁻ attacks the electrophilic C of the C=O of ester → tetrahedral intermediate → OR'⁻ (alkoxide) leaves (the OR' is a good enough leaving group in presence of Al Lewis acid) → R-CHO (aldehyde) released; excess LiAlH₄ immediately reduces R-CHO → R-CH₂-OH; the released R'O⁻ → H₂O → R'-OH; KEY: both the acyl portion (R-) and the alkoxy portion (-OR') become PRIMARY ALCOHOLS; the ester C=O becomes -CH₂OH (2 H atoms added at this C); with LiAlD₄: → R-CD₂-OH + R'-OH (D at the acyl carbon position); PRACTICAL: ester + LAH → always gives 2 alcohols; CONTRAST ESTER HYDROLYSIS: ester + NaOH → RCOO⁻ + R'-OH (only 1 alcohol + carboxylate); LAH gives BOTH as alcohols
valid_transformations.conditions: LiAlH₄; dry ether (Et₂O) or THF; 0°C to reflux; anhydrous; excess (2 equiv per ester). Ester → 2 alcohols (the acyl part → primary alcohol, the alkoxy part → ROH released). Here: ethyl propanoate → propan-1-ol (from acyl C) + ethanol (from ethoxy). The question asks for propan-1-ol: LiAlH₄ reduces ester completely → primary alcohol from the acyl C.

valid_transformations.notes: LAH reduction of amide → amine: propanamide (CH₃CH₂CONH₂, primary amide) + LiAlH₄/ether → propan-1-amine (CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂, primary amine); GENERAL (all amide types): primary amide (R-CO-NH₂) → primary amine (R-CH₂-NH₂); secondary amide (R-CO-NH-R') → secondary amine (R-CH₂-NH-R'); tertiary amide (R-CO-N(R')(R'')) → tertiary amine (R-CH₂-N(R')(R'')); KEY: C=O becomes CH₂ (oxygen is replaced by 2H; oxygen leaves); the N retains all its substituents; the nitrogen substitution TYPE is preserved (1°→1°, 2°→2°, 3°→3° amine); MECHANISM: H⁻ attacks the C of C=O of amide → tetrahedral intermediate → O⁻ (alkoxide-like) → with Al coordinating O and N → cyclic intermediate collapses → iminium ion (R-CH=N) → another H⁻ attacks the iminium C → amine (R-CH₂-N); the oxygen ends up as OAlH₂ → H₂O workup → Al(OH)₃; EXAMPLE: N-benzoyl piperidine (Ph-CO-N(CH₂)₅ ring) + LAH → N-benzyl piperidine (Ph-CH₂-N(CH₂)₅ ring; the C=O becomes -CH₂-; N stays as tertiary amine in ring); DISTINCTION from oxime/imine reduction: amide reduction goes C(=O)-N → CH₂-N (N stays same type); imine reduction: C=N-H → CH₂-NH (N becomes NH₂ if H on N)
valid_transformations.conditions: LiAlH₄; dry ether or THF; 0°C to reflux; anhydrous; excess. Amide reduction: RCONH₂ → RCH₂NH₂ (C=O → CH₂, same N). Mechanism: H⁻ delivery to amide C=O twice → amino alcohol intermediate → → primary amine. NaBH₄ does NOT reduce amides. LiAlH₄ reduces all carbonyls: amide, ester, acid (all → alcohol or amine products).

reagents: (1) LiAlH4 (lithium aluminium hydride) in dry ether
valid_transformations.notes: LAH reduction of acyl halide → primary alcohol: acetyl chloride (ethanoyl chloride, CH₃COCl) + (1)LiAlH₄ → (2)H₂O → ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH); GENERAL: R-C(=O)-Cl + LiAlH₄ → R-CH₂-OH (primary alcohol); MECHANISM: H⁻ attacks the C of acyl chloride C=O → Cl⁻ leaves (acyl chlorides are the MOST REACTIVE acid derivative; Cl⁻ is an excellent leaving group) → R-CHO (aldehyde) intermediate forms → LAH immediately reduces R-CHO → R-CH₂-OH; COMPARISON: acyl chloride + LAH is very fast (most reactive acid derivative); no isolation of intermediate possible; CONTRAST: Rosenmund reduction (H₂/Pd-BaSO₄ poisoned) selectively reduces R-COCl → R-CHO (aldehyde; stops there; the BaSO₄ poisoning of Pd slows over-reduction); LAH goes all the way to R-CH₂-OH
valid_transformations.conditions: LiAlH₄; dry ether; 0°C; anhydrous; then H₂O workup. Acid chloride is most reactive toward LiAlH₄ (even NaBH₄ reduces acid chlorides). RCOCl → RCHO (aldehyde, which is immediately reduced further by excess LiAlH₄) → RCH₂OH (primary alcohol). Alternatively: 2 equiv NaBH₄ in EtOH reduces acid chloride → alcohol. Rosenmund: DIBALH or H₂/Pd-BaSO₄ stops at aldehyde.

valid_transformations.notes: LAH reduction of cyclic anhydride → diol: butanedioic anhydride (succinic anhydride, 5-membered ring with 2 C=O and 1 O in ring) + excess LiAlH₄ → butane-1,4-diol (HO-CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂-OH, 1,4-diol); GENERAL: cyclic anhydride + LiAlH₄ → diol (ring opened, both C=O → CH₂-OH, and the ring O is released as water in workup); MECHANISM: first LiAlH₄ equivalent opens one C=O of the anhydride (ring opens: the O in ring becomes an alkoxide that is part of the chain) → forms a hydroxy acid intermediate; second LAH equivalent reduces the remaining C=O → diol; H₂O workup → diol; COMPARISON: succinic anhydride (5-membered) + LAH → 1,4-butanediol; glutaric anhydride (6-membered) + LAH → 1,5-pentanediol; PATTERN: n-membered ring anhydride → n-membered chain diol (ring opened, O in ring is removed/replaced by the chain)
valid_transformations.conditions: LiAlH₄ (excess, ≥2 equiv); dry ether; 0°C to reflux; anhydrous; then H₂O workup. Succinic anhydride reduced at both C=O → 1,4-diol (butane-1,4-diol = tetramethylene glycol). Mechanism: both anhydride carbonyls reduced → two primary alcohols. NaBH₄ also reduces anhydrides (more reactive than esters). BH₃: reduces anhydride → lactol or diol.

valid_transformations.notes: LAH (or NaBH₄) reduction of aldehyde → primary alcohol: propanal (CH₃CH₂CHO) + LiAlH₄ → propan-1-ol (CH₃CH₂CH₂OH); GENERAL: R-CHO + LiAlH₄ → R-CH₂-OH (primary alcohol, 1°); ALSO WORKS WITH NaBH₄ (sodium borohydride), H₂/Pt, H₂/Pd, H₂/Ni; MECHANISM: H⁻ from AlH₄⁻ attacks the electrophilic C of C=O (aldehyde carbon is more electrophilic than ketone due to less steric/electronic donation from R) → alkoxide intermediate R-CH₂-O⁻ (coordinated to Al) → H₂O workup → R-CH₂-OH; ALDEHYDE REDUCTION PRODUCTS: always primary alcohol (1°); KETONE REDUCTION: always secondary alcohol (2°); SELECTIVITY: LiAlH₄ reduces ALL carbonyls (aldehyde, ketone, ester, COOH, CONH₂, C≡N, C=N); NaBH₄ is SELECTIVE (reduces aldehyde and ketone ONLY; does NOT reduce ester, COOH, amide, nitrile — too mild for these)
valid_transformations.conditions: NaBH₄; EtOH or EtOH/H₂O; RT. Mild selective reduction: aldehyde → primary alcohol. NaBH₄ selective (reduces C=O not C=C). H⁻ delivers to aldehyde C → primary alcohol. Very mild: NaBH₄ + EtOH, RT, 30 min → full conversion. Workup: dilute acid or water. Alternatively: LiAlH₄/dry ether (more reactive). NaBH₄ preferred for sensitive substrates (no anhydrous condition needed).

valid_transformations.notes: LAH (or NaBH₄) reduction of ketone → secondary alcohol: propan-2-one (acetone, CH₃COCH₃) + LiAlH₄ → propan-2-ol (isopropanol, (CH₃)₂CHOH, secondary alcohol 2°); GENERAL: R-C(=O)-R' + LiAlH₄ → R-CH(OH)-R' (secondary alcohol); MECHANISM: H⁻ attacks C of ketone C=O from less hindered face → alkoxide R-CH(O⁻)-R' → H₂O → secondary alcohol; FACIAL SELECTIVITY in cyclic ketones: H⁻ (small reagent) attacks from axial direction (equatorial attack possible but depends on substrate) → can give cis or trans product; COMPARISON: LiAlH₄ (bulky) and L-Selectride (hindered LAH) give DIFFERENT facial selectivity in cyclic ketones — use to control stereochemistry; NaBH₄ also works for ketones (selective, mild); SUMMARY TABLE: aldehyde → primary alcohol; ketone → secondary alcohol; ester → two primary alcohols; RCOOH → primary alcohol; amide → amine; acyl halide → primary alcohol
valid_transformations.conditions: NaBH₄; EtOH or H₂O/EtOH; RT. Ketone → secondary alcohol. H⁻ from NaBH₄ attacks carbonyl C (less hindered face if chiral: gives mixture or facial selectivity with catalyst). Product: propan-2-ol (isopropanol). New stereocentre: racemic unless asymmetric catalyst (CBS, BINAL-H). Alternatively: LiAlH₄/ether; DIBALH; Meerwein-Ponndorf-Verley (Al-alkoxide/iPrOH).

valid_transformations.notes: SeO₂ oxidation of α-CH₃ to C=O: propan-2-one (acetone, CH₃COCH₃) + SeO₂ → 2-oxopropanal (methylglyoxal, CH₃-CO-CHO); GENERAL: SeO₂ oxidizes the -CH₂- or -CH₃ group ALPHA to an existing C=O (minimum 2 α-H required); the result is introduction of a NEW C=O at the α-carbon → α-diketone or α-ketoaldehyde; RULE 1: needs minimum 2 α-H on the carbon being oxidized; SELECTIVITY: -CH₃ > -CH₂- (methyl group is preferentially oxidized over methylene in mixed systems; boxed rule); EXAMPLES: CH₃CHO (acetaldehyde) + SeO₂ → glyoxal (OHCCHO); acetophenone (Ph-COCH₃) + SeO₂ → phenylglyoxal (Ph-CO-CHO); cyclohexanone + SeO₂ → cyclohexane-1,2-dione (1,2-diketone from ring); Ph-CH₂-Ph (diphenylmethane) + SeO₂ → Ph-CO-Ph (benzophenone; CH₂ alpha to two Ph rings → C=O); N-methylmorpholine + SeO₂ → N-formylmorpholine (N-CH₃ → N-CHO; works for N-adjacent CH₃ too); MECHANISM: SeO₂ forms an ene-type cyclic TS with the α-C-H → selenious acid intermediate → SH₂O-Se-O forms on α-C → O transferred → α-carbonyl; ALSO: for methyl ketones R-CO-CH₃ with both α-CH₃ (1C, 3H) and α-CH₂ (2C if present): CH₃ is preferentially oxidized (-CH₃ > -CH₂-)
valid_transformations.conditions: SeO₂ (selenium dioxide); dioxane or AcOH-H₂O; reflux. Riley oxidation: SeO₂ oxidises methyl ketone at α-carbon → α-diketone (2-oxopropanal = methylglyoxal = pyruvaldehyde). Mechanism: SeO₂ ene reaction with enol → [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement → → α-hydroxyl → further oxidation → diketo. Product: SeO₂ + CH₃COCH₃ → CH₃CO-CHO (methylglyoxal). SeO₂ also oxidises α-C of C=C (allylic oxidation) and secondary C=C.

valid_transformations.notes: SeO₂ oxidation of benzylic CH₂ → ketone: diphenylmethane (Ph-CH₂-Ph) + SeO₂ → diphenylmethanone (benzophenone, Ph-CO-Ph); GENERAL: benzylic CH₂ (Ph-CH₂-R) + SeO₂ → Ph-CO-R (ketone); the CH₂ between two phenyl groups is particularly reactive (both phenyl groups are electron-withdrawing at the sp₃ carbon → the α-C-H is activated); also allylic CH₂ (C=C-CH₂-) + SeO₂ → C=C-C=O (conjugated enone) or C=C-CHOH (allylic alcohol); MECHANISM: ene reaction type; SeO₂ acts as an electrophile toward the allylic/benzylic C-H via a concerted 6-membered TS (ene mechanism) → seleno intermediate → [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement → selenious acid ester → O transferred to the former C-H position → C=O
valid_transformations.conditions: SeO₂ (selenium dioxide); dioxane or glacial AcOH; reflux. Riley oxidation: Ph₂CH₂ (benzylic CH₂) → Ph₂CO (benzophenone, diphenylmethanone). Mechanism: SeO₂ ene reaction at α-C of the activated benzylic CH₂ → intermediate → → ketone. Also: CrO₂Cl₂ (Étard), MnO₂/H₂SO₄ for benzylic oxidation.

valid_transformations.notes: SeO₂ oxidation of cycloalkene → enone: cyclohex-1-ene + SeO₂ → cyclohex-2-en-1-one (2-cyclohexen-1-one); RULE 3: In cycloalkenes, the ring -CH₂- at the α-position to the double bond is oxidized to a KETONIC GROUP (C=O); the product is an enone (conjugated α,β-unsaturated ketone); RULE 4: If the cycloalkene is substituted on the double bond, the -CH₂- at α-position to the MORE SUBSTITUTED end of the double bond is oxidized → gives allylic alcohol product (R-cyclohexene + SeO₂ → allylic-OH at C adjacent to the R-substituted vinyl carbon); RULE 2 (allylic oxidation): for acyclic alkenes, SeO₂ oxidizes the -CH₂- or -CH₃ α to the MOST SUBSTITUTED end of C=C; preference order: -CH₂- > -CH₃ > -CH= (methylene > methyl > vinyl C); EXAMPLE: 2-methylbut-2-ene (CH₃-CH=C(CH₃)₂) + SeO₂ → allylic alcohol at the more-substituted end (the C with 2 CH₃ groups); one of the CH₃ → CH₂OH (allylic hydroxylation); if both CH₂ and CH₃ are present at same end: CH₂ reacts preferentially
valid_transformations.conditions: SeO₂; dioxane or EtOH-H₂O; reflux. Allylic oxidation (Riley): SeO₂ oxidises allylic C-H in cyclohexene → cyclohex-2-enol (intermediate) → cyclohex-2-en-1-one. Ene reaction mechanism: SeO₂ + alkene → [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement → allylic seleninic acid → → enone. Regioselective allylic oxidation adjacent to C=C.

valid_transformations.notes: Pb(OAc)₄ (lead tetraacetate) oxidative cleavage of vicinal diol: propane-1,2-diol (CH₃-CH(OH)-CH₂OH, 1,2-diol) + Pb(OAc)₄ → ethanal (CH₃CHO) + formaldehyde (HCHO) + Pb(OAc)₂ + 2 AcOH; GENERAL: 1,2-diol (vicinal diol) + Pb(OAc)₄ → two carbonyl compounds (one from each C of the former C-C-diol) + Pb(OAc)₂ + 2 AcOH; PRODUCT RULE: each C of the diol → C=O (aldehyde if that C had H; ketone if no H); if R-CH(OH)-CH(OH)-R' → R-CHO + R'-CHO; if R₂C(OH)-C(OH)R₂ → R₂C=O + R₂C=O (two ketones); MECHANISM: BOTH OH groups of the 1,2-diol simultaneously esterify with Pb(OAc)₄ → cyclic 5-membered Pb diester intermediate (Pb coordinated to both O) → C-C bond homolysis/heterolysis → two C=O + Pb(OAc)₂ (Pb reduced from +4 to +2); STEREOCHEMICAL REQUIREMENT: SYN (cis) diols form the cyclic 5-membered TS more readily; ANTI diols on rigid ring systems (trans-cyclohexane-1,2-diol where both OH are axial/trans) CANNOT form the cyclic Pb ester → do NOT react via the cyclic mechanism → lower reactivity; COMPARISON WITH HIO₄ (periodic acid): HIO₄ also cleaves 1,2-diols via a cyclic mechanism; both Pb(OAc)₄ and HIO₄ give same cleavage products; HIO₄ is preferred for aqueous conditions; Pb(OAc)₄ used in anhydrous (acetic acid) conditions
valid_transformations.conditions: Pb(OAc)₄ (lead tetraacetate); glacial acetic acid; RT. Periodate-equivalent: Pb(OAc)₄ cleaves vicinal diols → two carbonyls. Propane-1,2-diol (1,2-propanediol) + Pb(OAc)₄ → HCHO (formaldehyde, from primary CH₂OH) + CH₃CHO (ethanal, from secondary CHOH). One equiv Pb(OAc)₄ per diol. Non-aqueous alternative to HIO₄ (which requires water).

valid_transformations.notes: Pb(OAc)₄ cleavage of cyclic 1,2-diol → open-chain dicarbonyl: cyclopentane-1,2-diol (cis or trans, 5-membered ring with adjacent OH groups) + Pb(OAc)₄ → pentanedial (glutaraldehyde, OHC-CH₂CH₂CH₂-CHO, open chain dialdehyde); GENERAL for CYCLIC 1,2-diols: ring is OPENED and the C-C bond between the two OH-bearing carbons is CLEAVED → a linear dialdehyde (or diketone/ketoaldehyde depending on substitution); RING OPENING RULE: n-membered ring 1,2-diol → (n+1)-carbon-chain dialdehyde? No actually: for n-membered ring where adjacent C-C is cleaved: the product is a n-carbon chain with C=O at each end (e.g., cyclopentane-1,2-diol → 5C chain from cyclopentane ring = pentanedial); CEVEAT: for syn (cis) diol → cyclic mechanism works easily; trans (anti) cyclic diol → cyclic mechanism disfavored for rigid systems; ALSO WORKS WITH HIO₄ (same products); HIO₄ is the oxidant of choice for sugars (sugar vicinyl diols are cleaved to smaller fragments for determination of structure)
valid_transformations.conditions: Pb(OAc)₄ (lead tetraacetate); AcOH; RT. Or HIO₄ (periodic acid); aqueous; RT. Cyclopentane-1,2-diol (cis or trans) → oxidative cleavage → pentanedial (glutaraldehyde, OHC-(CH₂)₃-CHO). One Pb(OAc)₄ per diol → ring-opened dialdehyde. Requires vicinal (adjacent) diol. 1,3-diols: no cleavage. Used to determine diol structure.

valid_transformations.notes: SN2 at chiral centre → Walden inversion → configuration flips R→S (or S→R); GENERAL: SN2 at (R)-substrate → (S)-product (inversion); CIP R/S ASSIGNMENT PROCEDURE: (1) assign priorities a>b>c>d to 4 substituents using CIP Sequence Rules; (2) orient molecule so group d (LOWEST priority) points AWAY from viewer (into page, dash bond); (3) count a→b→c: CLOCKWISE = R; ANTI-CLOCKWISE = S; (4) if d is pointing TOWARD viewer (wedge), do step 3 then REVERSE (R↔S); CIP SEQUENCE RULE 1 (most used): higher atomic number (Z) = higher priority; tie → go to next attached atoms (outward exploration); tie broken at FIRST point of difference; SEQUENCE RULE 2 (tie-breaker for isotopes): higher mass number = higher priority (²H > ¹H); SEQUENCE RULE 3-5: for multiple bonds and stereocentres, use phantom atom rules (see phantom_atom concept)
valid_transformations.conditions: SN2 reaction conditions: nucleophile (e.g., NaOH/H₂O → alcohol intermediate → then re-bromination? Or: directly via SN2 with Br⁻ after inversion). Actually: inversion of configuration at SN2 centre. (R)-2-bromobutane + Br⁻ (Finkelstein-type: NaBr/acetone or label exchange) → (S)-2-bromobutane (net inversion). Walden inversion: SN2 gives 100% inversion at chiral centre.

valid_transformations.notes: CIP R/S assignment via diagraph (concentric circles): DIAGRAPH METHOD: draw concentric circles I, II, III, IV... starting from the stereogenic centre; each circle holds atoms at that topological distance (bonds) from the centre; compare atoms in circle I first (Sequence Rule 1: higher Z → higher priority); if a tie in circle I, proceed to circle II (compare atoms attached to tying atoms); continue outward until a decision is reached; PRECEDENCE CARRIES FORWARD: once one branch wins at any level (say 2-prime > 2-double-prime), that branch's deeper atoms (3-prime) are compared NEXT (against 3-double-prime); the LOSER branch's deeper atoms at same level (4-prime) are NEVER compared even if they have higher Z; the win is locked in and carries forward; EXAMPLES: CHBrClF → Br > Cl > F > H (immediate circle I); H₃C-CHCl-CH₂OH → at circle I: both C tie; circle II: CH₂OH gives (O,H,H) vs CH₃ gives (H,H,H); O > H → CH₂OH > CH₃; priority order: Cl > CH₂OH > CH₃ > H
valid_transformations.conditions: CIP (Cahn-Ingold-Prelog) rules; no reagent; conceptual assignment. Step 1: Assign priorities 1–4 by atomic number (higher Z = higher priority). Tie-break: compare substituents outward (next atom, etc.). Step 2: Arrange molecule with lowest priority (4) pointing away from viewer. Step 3: Trace 1→2→3: clockwise = R; anti-clockwise = S. Rules for double bonds, rings (phantom atoms), isotopes, lone pairs apply.

reagents: CIP Phantom Atom Rule for rings
valid_transformations.notes: CIP treatment of cyclopropyl (saturated ring) vs heptan-4-yl (open chain) as substituents at a chiral centre: RING OPENING RULE: to assign CIP priority to a ring substituent, open the ring into a branched chain; when the exploration of the branched chain reaches an atom ALREADY visited (ring closure point) → insert a PHANTOM ATOM (duplicate atom) with the same element symbol but ZERO atomic number (Z=0) → called 'phantom atom' or 'duplicate atom'; EXAMPLE (cyclopropyl): cyclopropyl ring opened → C branches into two paths that rejoin → at the reconnect point, insert phantom C (Z=0); in circle IV of the diagraph: phantom atoms appear; for heptan-4-yl group: in circle IV, real H atoms (Z=1) appear; since H (Z=1) > phantom C (Z=0) → heptan-4-yl group has HIGHER CIP priority than cyclopropyl group; PHANTOM ATOM RULE SUMMARY: real atoms (any Z≥1) > phantom atoms (Z=0) always
valid_transformations.conditions: CIP phantom atom rule for rings: cyclopropyl group as substituent — open the ring at the point of attachment → phantom atoms appended. Cyclopropyl (3-membered ring): at attachment C, phantom atoms added by duplicating the ring carbons. Compare to acyclic heptyl chain: at branch point, sum of atoms. Cyclopropyl may appear higher or lower depending on substituents — must apply CIP Rule 2 carefully.

reagents: CIP phantom atom rule for double bonds
valid_transformations.notes: CIP phantom atom rule for C=C double bond: RULE: a C=C double bond is treated as if each C is bonded to a PHANTOM atom of the same element; phantom C bonded to carbon of double bond replaces the second bond in CIP exploration; C=C: the two C atoms are each expanded as follows: C-1 of C=C is treated as C bonded to (C-2, phantom-C-2, real-substituents); C-2 is treated as C bonded to (C-1, phantom-C-1, real-substituents); the phantom atoms have the same Z as the real duplicated atom but do NOT have further substituents (their branches terminate at Z=0 phantom atoms); EXAMPLE: -CH=CH₂ group at a chiral centre: C-1 (=CH-) is treated as C bonded to [C-2(phantom), C-2(real), H]; C-2 (=CH₂) treated as C bonded to [C-1(phantom), C-1(real), H]; for C≡C (triple bond): each C is bonded to TWO phantom atoms of the other C, making it C bonded to (C, C, C) in CIP terms; COMPARISON: -C≡CH has CIP treatment: triple bond C bonded to (C,C,C) where two are phantoms → in circle III it contributes three C atoms; this gives alkynes very high CIP priority relative to alkenes
valid_transformations.conditions: CIP phantom atom rule for double bonds: C=C → each doubly bonded C gets a phantom duplicate of the other C (with its substituents appended as (C)(C) phantom nodes). E.g., CH₂=CH- at the vinyl C: actual = C connected to CH₂; phantom = (C) duplicate added. This phantom atom participates in CIP priority comparison. Apply recursively at each doubly-bonded atom pair.

valid_transformations.notes: R/S assignment in Fischer projections: KEY CONVENTION: in a Fischer projection, HORIZONTAL bonds point TOWARD the viewer (wedge), VERTICAL bonds point AWAY from the viewer (dash); PROCEDURE: (1) assign a>b>c>d to 4 substituents at the chiral C using CIP rules; (2) locate d (lowest priority) in the Fischer projection; CASE A: d is on a VERTICAL bond (pointing away from viewer) → count a→b→c directly; clockwise = R, counterclockwise = S; CASE B: d is on a HORIZONTAL bond (pointing toward viewer) → count a→b→c then SWAP (clockwise → S; counterclockwise → R); SHORTCUT for 3 horizontal 1 vertical: if d is horizontal, the actual configuration is the OPPOSITE of what you read; EXAMPLE (Fig. 3.89): at the asterisked C in a multi-chiral molecule, OH is on a vertical bond direction and is highest priority; H (vertical) has lowest priority → count the carbon chain arms directly; the assignment gives (S) because the carbon chain with Br > the chain with Cl at first point of difference
valid_transformations.conditions: Fischer projection CIP rules: In a Fischer projection, horizontal bonds point toward viewer; vertical bonds point away. Method: (1) Assign CIP priorities 1–4. (2) If priority 4 is on a horizontal bond (toward viewer): trace 1→2→3 and INVERT the result (R→S, S→R). (3) If priority 4 is on a vertical bond (away): trace normally. Alternatively: swap any two groups twice (even swaps = no change in R/S). D-glyceraldehyde = (R).

valid_transformations.notes: Nitrogen inversion (umbrella flip) of trialkylamine: N(sp3) pyramidal ground state → [planar sp2 N at TS] → inverted N(sp3); MECHANISM: N is sp3 (pyramidal), lone pair occupies one tetrahedral position; thermal energy drives N through a planar TS (sp2-like, lone pair in unhybridised p orbital); the three substituents pass through the same plane as N → the N is momentarily planar → then settles on the other side (lone pair now opposite) → configuration inverted; ENERGY BARRIER (ΔG#): for trimethylamine [N(CH3)3] = 7.9 kcal/mol at room temp; barriers typically 6-10 kcal/mol for simple acyclic amines → inversion is RAPID at 25°C (NMR time scale cannot resolve two conformers → apparent single species); RATE: simple amines invert ~1000 times/second at 25°C; STERIC ACCELERATION RULE: bulky substituents at N (e.g., iPr, iBu, tBu) create steric repulsion in the pyramidal GS; at the planar TS the substituents splay apart → steric strain RELIEVED → lower ΔG# → FASTER inversion; EXAMPLE: tri-isobutylamine [N(CH2CHMe2)3] inverts FASTER than trimethylamine [N(CH3)3] despite bulkier substituents; EXAMPLE: N-tBu-aziridine inverts faster than N-nBu-aziridine because t-Bu groups are compressed in pyramidal GS of the 3-membered ring
valid_transformations.conditions: Nitrogen inversion: thermal energy (kT); no reagent needed; unimolecular; RT (ultrafast, ~2×10¹¹ s⁻¹). Trialkylamine nitrogen undergoes pyramidal inversion (umbrella flipping) via planar sp² TS (lone pair in p orbital). Energy barrier ~6 kcal/mol (very low) → extremely rapid → enantiomers interconvert at RT → racemisation. Cannot isolate chiral trialkylamine enantiomers at RT. Contrast: phosphines (higher barrier ~35 kcal/mol → can be chiral, configurationally stable).

valid_transformations.notes: Nitrogen inversion in aziridine (3-membered N ring): 1-methylaziridine (N-methylaziridine) has ΔG# = 20.5 kcal/mol for nitrogen inversion (cf. 7.9 kcal/mol for trimethylamine); REASON: in the 3-membered ring, the C-N-C angle is constrained to ~60° (ring angle); at the planar TS, the N would need to be sp2 with C-N-C approaching 120°; but the ring PREVENTS the angle from opening to 120° → RING CANNOT ACCOMMODATE planar N TS → extremely high ring strain at TS → very high ΔG#; CONSEQUENCE: aziridine N chirality is PERSISTENT on the NMR time scale (unlike acyclic amines); N-substituted aziridines can be isolated as separate R and S isomers at N if the two C-substituents are also different; COMPARISON: N-methylaziridine (ΔG# = 20.5) >> N-methylpyrrolidine (ΔG# = 7.0) >> trimethylamine (ΔG# = 7.9 kcal/mol); 5-membered ring (pyrrolidine): ring is flexible enough to accommodate planar N TS → barrier similar to acyclic; STERIC ACCELERATION IN AZIRIDINES: if the N-substituent is t-Bu (bulky), the steric repulsion between t-Bu and the ring CH2 groups in the pyramidal GS is large → relief at planar TS → LOWER ΔG# for N-tBu-aziridine vs N-nBu-aziridine
valid_transformations.conditions: Thermal (kT); slow at RT; ring strain INCREASES inversion barrier. Aziridine N inversion barrier ~18–26 kcal/mol (much higher than trialkylamine ~6 kcal/mol) because ring constrains bond angles → planar sp² N in ring is very strained (ring would have to be flat in TS, requiring bond angle distortion). Therefore: aziridines are configurationally stable on chemical timescales — N-methylaziridine can exist as distinct cis/trans stereoisomers.

valid_transformations.notes: Electronic effect on nitrogen inversion: backbonding (N lone pair → adjacent pi system) → flattening of N; EXAMPLE: trivinylamine [N(CH=CH2)3]: the N lone pair is delocalized into the three vinyl C=C pi* orbital systems (allylic-type conjugation: N-p orbital conjugates with C=C pi) → the N acquires partial sp2 character → the pyramidal angle flattens toward planar; CONSEQUENCE: the 'inversion barrier' in the traditional sense decreases (N is already near planar) or the nature of the 'barrier' changes; GENERAL: any N directly bonded to a pi system (vinyl, aryl, C=O) will have partial sp2 character: amide N (R-CO-NR2): nearly planar (C-N bond has partial double bond character; restricted rotation, not inversion); aniline N (Ph-NH2): slightly pyramidal but much flatter than aliphatic amine; allylamine: intermediate; KEY RULE: the more electron-withdrawing and better pi acceptor the substituent, the more planar the N becomes; COMPARISON: N(CH=CH2)3 (ΔG# effectively decreases relative to Me3N due to flattening) vs N(CH3)3 (ΔG# = 7.9 kcal/mol); for cyclic systems with vinyl substituents at N, the combination of ring constraint + backbonding can give unusual inversion profiles
valid_transformations.conditions: Electronic orbital interaction; no reagent; inherent electronic structure. Trivinylamine: three vinyl (CH₂=CH-) groups on N → lone pair on N conjugates (backbonding) into the π* of all three C=C bonds → N becomes sp² (planar) rather than sp³ (pyramidal). The nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into conjugated vinyl groups → mesomeric effect → flat geometry. Compare: aniline (PhNH₂): partially sp² but not fully flat. Trivinylamine essentially planar N.

valid_transformations.notes: Chain isomers (skeletal isomers): same molecular formula, different carbon skeleton (backbone arrangement); DEFINITION: change the branching pattern of the C-C bonds; EXAMPLES for C5H12: (1) pentane (n-pentane, unbranched 5-carbon chain); (2) 2-methylbutane (isopentane: 4C main chain + 1C branch at C2); (3) 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane: 3C chain + 2 methyls at C2); → 3 chain isomers total for C5H12; EXAMPLES for cyclic C6H12: cyclohexane (6C ring), methylcyclopentane (5C ring + 1C side), 1,1-dimethylcyclobutane and 1,2-dimethylcyclobutane and ethylcyclobutane (4C ring variants), and cyclopropane variants (3C ring + chain); RULE: when counting chain isomers, place functional groups at the end of each carbon skeleton; KEY: chain isomers have same: (a) molecular formula MF; (b) number of C and H; different: carbon skeleton shape (linear vs branched vs ring size); COUNTING METHOD: enumerate all distinct carbon skeletons for the given total C count; for a given skeleton, the functional group must then be placed at a specific position
valid_transformations.conditions: Conceptual isomerism comparison; no actual reaction at RT (C-C bond cleavage requires >300°C). These are constitutional (structural) isomers: pentane (n-C₅H₁₂, straight chain) and 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane, branched C₅H₁₂). Both C₅H₁₂ molecular formula, different connectivity. Boiling points: pentane 36°C; neopentane 9.5°C (more branching → less surface area → lower bp). Thermodynamic stability: more branched isomer is more stable (heats of combustion: neopentane < pentane).

valid_transformations.notes: Position isomers (positional isomers): same molecular formula + same carbon skeleton + same functional group type; differ in the LOCANT (position) of the functional group or multiple bond on the chain; DEFINITION: the FG or multiple bond is placed at different carbons of the SAME skeleton; EXAMPLES: (1) pent-1-ene (C=C between C1 and C2) vs pent-2-ene (C=C between C2 and C3) — same 5C chain, different double bond position; (2) but-1-yne vs but-2-yne (same 4C chain, triple bond position differs); (3) hexan-1-ol vs hexan-2-ol vs hexan-3-ol (same 6C chain, OH at different positions); (4) cyclohex-1,3-diene vs cyclohex-1,4-diene (same ring, double bonds at different positions); (5) 1,2-dimethylcyclohexane vs 1,3 vs 1,4 — positional isomers of dimethylcyclohexane; AROMATIC POSITIONAL ISOMERS: o- (1,2-), m- (1,3-), p- (1,4-) disubstituted benzene are positional isomers; DISTINCTION from chain isomers: position isomers have the SAME carbon skeleton; chain isomers have DIFFERENT skeletons
valid_transformations.conditions: Constitutional isomers: same molecular formula C₅H₁₀, same carbon skeleton, different position of C=C double bond. Pent-1-ene (terminal) vs pent-2-ene (internal). Not interconvertible at RT (double bond rotation restricted; to interconvert must break/re-form π bond, ~60 kcal/mol). Acid-catalysed isomerisation (H⁺/heat): pent-1-ene → pent-2-ene (thermodynamic, more-substituted alkene more stable by ~1 kcal/mol per additional alkyl substituent at C=C).

valid_transformations.notes: Counting structural isomers of C3H5Cl3 (trichloropropane): propane has 3 C atoms (C1, C2, C3); C1 and C3 are equivalent (both terminal); need to place 3 Cl atoms on 3 carbons (with repetition allowed); SYSTEMATIC ENUMERATION: (1) 1,1,1-trichloropropane: Cl3C-CH2-CH3 (all three Cl on C1); (2) 1,1,2-trichloropropane: Cl2CH-CHCl-CH3 (2 Cl on C1, 1 on C2); (3) 1,1,3-trichloropropane: Cl2CH-CH2-CH2Cl (2 on C1, 1 on C3); (4) 1,2,2-trichloropropane: ClCH2-CCl2-CH3 (1 on C1, 2 on C2); (5) 1,2,3-trichloropropane: ClCH2-CHCl-CH2Cl (1 on each C) → TOTAL = 5 structural isomers; GENERAL METHOD: list all unique ways to place n identical substituents on m non-equivalent carbons; avoid duplicates by using symmetry (C1 = C3 in propane by symmetry); EXTENSION for C3H5Cl2Br (2 Cl + 1 Br on propane): since Cl and Br are DIFFERENT, each position of Br on the backbone gives additional isomers when combined with Cl placements → total = 9 structural isomers (all positional combinations of 2 Cl + 1 Br on propane skeleton, considering Cl and Br are distinct)
valid_transformations.conditions: Enumeration of constitutional isomers of C₃H₅Cl₃ (trichloropropane): systematic approach. Propane backbone: (1) 1,1,1-trichloropropane (CCl₃CH₂CH₃); (2) 1,1,2-trichloropropane (CCl₂ClCHClCH₃? i.e., CHCl₂-CHCl-CH₃); (3) 1,1,3-trichloropropane; (4) 1,2,2-trichloropropane; (5) 1,2,3-trichloropropane; (6) 1,3,3-? Actually: propane has C1, C2, C3. Place 3 Cl: (1,1,1); (1,1,2); (1,1,3); (1,2,2); (1,2,3); (2,2,2) — but 2,2,2 doesn't exist (only 2C at C2 of propane). So 5 structural isomers exist.

valid_transformations.notes: Positional isomers of disubstituted benzene (two DIFFERENT substituents X and Y): EXACTLY 3 positional isomers: (1) 1,2-XY (ortho, o-): substituents on adjacent carbons; (2) 1,3-XY (meta, m-): substituents separated by one carbon; (3) 1,4-XY (para, p-): substituents on opposite carbons; EXAMPLE: chlorobromobenzene (Cl + Br on benzene): o-chlorobromobenzene / m-chlorobromobenzene / p-chlorobromobenzene = 3 position isomers; SAME SUBSTITUENTS (X = Y, e.g., dimethylbenzene = xylene): also 3 position isomers: o-xylene (1,2), m-xylene (1,3), p-xylene (1,4); SPECIAL CASE (Ex7): 2,6-dimethylbromobenzene vs 1-methyl-2,6-dibromobenzene — the 2,6-pattern on a symmetric ring: 1-Br-2,6-di(Me) has a plane of symmetry through the 1-position → the two Me groups at 2 and 6 are EQUIVALENT (mirror images through the C1 axis) → this compound is a SINGLE compound (not two isomers); labeled 'Identical or Homomer' on the board; TRISUBSTITUTED BENZENE: 3 groups on benzene → more positional isomers depending on whether groups are same or different
valid_transformations.conditions: Benzene substitution counting: C₆H₄XY (two different substituents X and Y). Three positional isomers: ortho (1,2-; X and Y adjacent, 60° apart), meta (1,3-; two carbons apart, 120°), para (1,4-; opposite, 180°). Each is a distinct compound with different physical properties (bp, mp, dipole moment). E.g., dichlorobenzene: o-DCB (bp 180°C), m-DCB (bp 173°C), p-DCB (bp 174°C, highest mp 53°C due to centrosymmetric packing).

reagents: require bond breaking (pi bond cleavage ~65 kcal/mol)
valid_transformations.notes: Geometric isomerism (GI) in alkenes: same MF + same connectivity + different spatial arrangement about C=C; NOT interconvertible at RT (require pi bond cleavage); TWO CONDITIONS for GI to exist: (1) rotation must be RESTRICTED (C=C, ring, allene, biphenyl...); (2) each carbon of the double bond must have TWO DIFFERENT groups; if ANY carbon of the C=C has two identical groups → NO GI; EXAMPLES: 2-butene (CH3-CH=CH-CH3): C-2 has (Me, H) — different; C-3 has (Me, H) — different → GI exists; cis-2-butene (Z, both Me same side) and trans-2-butene (E, Me opposite sides) = 2 geometric isomers; 2-methylbut-2-ene (CH3-CH=C(CH3)2): C-3 has (Me, Me) — IDENTICAL → NO GI (circled X); NAMING: cis/trans (older) for simple cases; E/Z (IUPAC) for complex cases: assign CIP priority to groups on each C; if higher priority groups are on same side → Z (zusammen = together); if on opposite sides → E (entgegen = opposite); E/Z can differ from trans/cis for mixed groups (e.g., if higher Z group is on same side as longer chain, Z may correspond to trans in old nomenclature); SYSTEMS WITH RESTRICTED ROTATION (8 types): (1) double bonds C=C, C=O, C=N, N=N; (2) cycloalkane rings; (3) cycloalkenes; (4) allenes; (5) spiranes; (6) biphenyl; (7) terphenyl; (8) special cases
valid_transformations.conditions: NOT interconvertible at RT: C=C π-bond rotation barrier ~65 kcal/mol (requires breaking π bond). To interconvert: (a) acid catalyst (H⁺/Br⁻): add then eliminate — scrambles geometry; (b) radical conditions; (c) photoisomerisation (hν). Catalytic isomerisation: H₂SO₄ → protonation → free rotation of σ-bond → trans product (thermodynamic). Or NO₂/hν radical → cis→trans. Without catalyst: cis and trans are distinct isomers, stable at RT.

reagents: not interconvertible at RT (C=N rotation restricted)
valid_transformations.notes: Geometric isomerism in oximes (C=N-OH): oximes are R1R2C=N-OH; the C=N bond is restricted → GI possible IF: (1) C has two different groups R1 and R2; (2) N has two different groups (N has OH and LONE PAIR → lone pair counts as a substituent in GI analysis → ALWAYS different from OH); KEY: lone pair acts as a group on N; EXAMPLES: acetaldoxime (CH3-CH=N-OH; R1=Me, R2=H): C has (Me, H) — different; N has (OH, lone pair) — different → GI exists; SYN (Z) form: Me and OH on same side; ANTI (E) form: Me and OH on opposite sides; NAMING: syn = Me and OH same side; anti = Me and OH opposite; formaldehyde oxime (H2C=N-OH): C has (H, H) — IDENTICAL → NO GI (regardless of N having different groups, if C is symmetric → no isomers); GI IN N=N (azo compounds): Ph-N=N-Ph (azobenzene); each N has (Ph, lone pair) → different → GI exists; cis (syn): both Ph on same side of N=N; trans (anti): Ph on opposite sides; azobenzene is thermally more stable as the trans isomer; CIS RULE: N lone pair is always counted as a group for GI purposes in C=N and N=N systems
valid_transformations.conditions: E/Z isomerism about C=N double bond (geometric isomers). Syn-acetaldoxime (Z-) and anti-acetaldoxime (E-). C=N rotation barrier significant (~20–25 kcal/mol) → two distinct isolable forms. Interconversion: acid catalysis (H⁺) or heat (Δ). Beckmann rearrangement: anti-OH group migrates (group anti to OH migrates). Identification: IR, NMR, or Beckmann rearrangement product analysis.

valid_transformations.notes: Geometric isomerism in cycloalkanes: the ring is RIGID (restricted rotation about ring C-C bonds) → GI possible for substituted cycloalkanes; CONDITION: each ring carbon bearing a substituent must have TWO DIFFERENT groups (the substituent and H are different → satisfied for monosubstituted carbons in the ring); CIS = both substituents on SAME FACE of the ring plane (same side = cis); TRANS = substituents on OPPOSITE FACES of ring plane; EXAMPLES: 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane: cis-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane (both Me same face) vs trans-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane (Me on opposite faces); 1,2-cyclobutanedicarboxylic acid: cis (both COOH same side) and trans (opposite); 1,2-dimethylcyclobutane: cis and trans; KEY: for 1,1-disubstituted cycloalkanes (both substituents on same C): that C has two groups to compare → if they are the SAME (e.g., 1,1-dimethyl) → no GI (C has identical groups); if different (e.g., 1-methyl-1-ethyl) → still just one carbon with different groups → still need second substituted carbon for GI comparison; GENERAL: ring system provides rigidity; GI exists when substituents can be either syn or anti relative to ring plane
valid_transformations.conditions: Geometric isomers (cis/trans) of 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane. Ring is rigid (no free rotation about C-C in ring). Cis: both CH₃ on same face; trans: CH₃ on opposite faces. NOT interconvertible at RT (would require ring opening = breaking C-C bond, ~80 kcal/mol). Trans isomer has C₂ symmetry (chiral, two enantiomers); cis isomer has mirror plane (achiral, meso). Distinct boiling points and physical properties.

reagents: allene with different groups at both terminals
valid_transformations.notes: Pseudo-GI centre (allene with axial chirality): allenes (C=C=C: two cumulated double bonds) can show apparent geometric-like isomerism BUT it is actually AXIAL CHIRALITY (optical isomers, R/S, not cis/trans); CONDITION: each terminal sp2 carbon of allene must have TWO DIFFERENT groups; EXAMPLE: 1,3-dimethylallene (penta-2,3-diene? actually 2,3-pentadiene: CH3-CH=C=CH-CH3): C-1 has (Me, H) different; C-3 has (Me, H) different → axial chirality exists → R and S enantiomers; called PSEUDO-GI CENTRE because the system looks like it should show cis/trans but actually gives optical isomers; GEOMETRY OF ALLENE: the two terminal CH2 planes of allene are perpendicular to each other (90° dihedral); the central carbon is sp (linear); the two terminal carbons are sp2 with their substituents in perpendicular planes; when both terminal Cs have 2 different groups → the molecule is non-superimposable on its mirror image → CHIRAL (R/S, not E/Z); GENERAL RULE for cumulated dienes: even number of cumulated C=C double bonds (n=2: allene, n=4: cumulene) → AXIAL CHIRALITY (optical isomers); odd number (n=1: alkene, n=3: butatriene) → GEOMETRIC ISOMERS (E/Z)
valid_transformations.conditions: Axial chirality in allene: penta-2,3-diene (CH₃CH=C=CHCH₃). Central sp-carbon: two sets of substituents at 90° to each other. Left end: CH₃, H; right end: CH₃, H. When groups at both ends are different → axial chirality. CIP for allenes: look along axis from one end → assign priorities → R or S. R and S enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images. Allenes with same groups at each end (CH₂=C=CH₂) → achiral (Cs symmetry).

valid_transformations.notes: Optical rotation in a polarimeter: SETUP: light source → polarizer (creates plane-polarized light with all oscillations in one plane) → sample tube containing chiral compound in solution → analyzer (reads new angle of polarization plane); RESULT: a chiral (optically active) compound ROTATES the plane of polarization by angle α (alpha); DEXTROROTATORY: rotation to the RIGHT (clockwise when viewed toward the light source) → (+) or d; LEVOROTATORY: rotation to the LEFT (counterclockwise) → (-) or l; NOTE: (+)/(-) rotation is an EXPERIMENTALLY OBSERVED property; it is NOT related to R/S configuration (R doesn't always mean (+) and vice versa); SPECIFIC ROTATION [α]D = α_obs / (c × l) where c = concentration in g/mL and l = path length in decimeters (dm); standardized using sodium D-line light (589 nm); OPTICALLY INACTIVE: achiral compound → no rotation; or racemic mixture (50:50 R and S) → equal and opposite rotations cancel → net α = 0; DISTINGUISHING: observed α_obs depends on concentration, path length, temperature, solvent; [α]D is the intrinsic optical rotation of the pure compound
valid_transformations.conditions: Polarimetry: monochromatic light (Na D line, 589 nm); polarimeter with polarising filter and analyser; chiral compound in solution (usually 1 dm tube, 1 g/mL concentration). Chiral molecule (no POS, no CoS) → optical activity → rotates plane of polarised light by angle α (observed rotation). [α]ᴅ = α/(l × c): specific rotation. (+) dextrorotatory; (–) levorotatory. Racemic mixture: [α] = 0 (equal + and – cancel).

valid_transformations.notes: Chirality and optical activity — symmetry element analysis: a molecule is OPTICALLY ACTIVE (OA) = CHIRAL = RESOLVABLE if and only if it has NO POS (plane of symmetry) AND NO CoS (centre of symmetry); KEY TABLE: if POS present → optically INACTIVE (OI), regardless of CoS or AoS; if CoS present (no POS) → OI; if only AoS (Cn rotational axis; no POS, no CoS) → OA (optically ACTIVE!); if no symmetry at all (no POS, no CoS, no AoS) → OA; DEFINITIONS: ASYMMETRIC = no POS, no CoS, no AoS (all three absent); DISSYMMETRIC = no POS, no CoS, but HAS AoS (Cn rotational axis present); BOTH asymmetric and dissymmetric molecules are optically ACTIVE; EQUIVALENCES: Optically Active = Chiral = Resolvable (into enantiomers); Optically Inactive = Achiral = Non-resolvable; ALPHABET ANALOGY: letters N, S, Z have C2 rotational axis (AoS) but no POS → dissymmetric (analogous to chiral molecule with Cn axis) → would be optically active if they were molecules; letters A, B, C, D, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y have POS → achiral → optically inactive by analogy; letters E, F, G, J, K, L have no POS but also no AoS (just asymmetric shapes)
valid_transformations.conditions: No reaction — physical property. Condition for optical activity: molecule must lack (1) plane of symmetry (POS/σ), (2) centre of symmetry (CoS/i), (3) improper rotation axis (Sₙ). Sufficient condition: molecule is chiral (non-superimposable on mirror image). Asymmetric = no symmetry element at all; dissymmetric = has C-axis but no improper axis (e.g., hexahelicene). Both are optically active. Meso compounds: have internal POS → achiral despite stereocentres → NOT optically active.

valid_transformations.notes: Plane of Symmetry (POS) analysis in cyclic molecules: 1,1-dimethylcyclopropane (both CH3 on C-1): there is a plane containing C-1 and bisecting the C2-C3 bond of the ring → POS exists → achiral (OI); GENERAL RULE for 1,1-disubstituted cycloalkane: if both groups on C-1 are identical → always has POS through C-1 → always OI; 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane (one CH3 on C-2, one CH3 on C-3, same side = cis): POS exists (the plane through C-1 and perpendicular to the C2-C3 line bisects the molecule symmetrically when both CH3 are cis) → OI (meso-type); 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane (TRANS): no POS → OA (chiral pair of enantiomers); 1,2-Cl-Br-cyclopropane (different groups): no POS → OA regardless of cis/trans (since the two groups are different, even the cis version has no POS because Cl ≠ Br); oxo-containing rings with specific substitution: check if any plane bisects the molecule into two mirror-image halves; if yes → POS → OI
valid_transformations.conditions: Symmetry analysis: 1,1-dimethylcyclopropane. The C-1 carbon (two CH₃ groups) has two identical substituents (both CH₃). The ring is symmetric about the plane through C-1 and the midpoint of C-2—C-3 bond. This plane of symmetry (σ) makes the molecule achiral despite 3-membered ring. IUPAC: 1,1-dimethylcyclopropane has Cs symmetry. C-1 is not a chiral centre (two identical CH₃). Molecule is optically inactive.

valid_transformations.notes: Interchange (Swap) Method for R/S assignment: RULE: swapping ANY two groups at a chiral centre changes the configuration (R→S or S→R); each swap = one flip; ODD number of swaps = configuration flipped; EVEN number of swaps = configuration restored; PROCEDURE: when the lowest priority group (d, group 4) is NOT pointing away from the viewer (not on a dash bond), use swaps to move it to a back position; count how many swaps were needed; if ODD swaps → reverse the final reading (R becomes S or S becomes R); if EVEN swaps → keep the reading; EXAMPLE: given a wedge-dash drawing where H (group 4, lowest priority) is on a WEDGE bond (pointing toward viewer): count 1→2→3 (clockwise or anticlockwise); result say clockwise (reads R); but since H is on wedge (pointing toward viewer, opposite of required) → REVERSE → actual config = S; EQUIVALENT PROCEDURE: one swap puts H on dash → that swap changes R to S → so we need to un-do the swap → final config is the opposite of what we read after the swap; GENERAL: each group swap is equivalent to a 'transposition' in permutation theory; odd transpositions change parity (R→S); even transpositions preserve parity
valid_transformations.conditions: Interchange method: swapping any TWO groups at a CIP-assigned stereocentre → inverts configuration (R→S or S→R). Rationale: any two-group swap = odd permutation of chiral centre → changes handedness. Swapping once: R→S. Swapping twice: R→R (even permutation). Used in Fischer projection CIP assignments: each pair of swaps keeps R/S; odd number of swaps inverts. Not a chemical reaction — conceptual tool.

valid_transformations.notes: Glyceraldehyde (2,3-dihydroxypropanal) CIP assignment: structure: HOCH2-C*(H)(OH)-CHO (chiral carbon C-2); FOUR GROUPS: OH, CHO, CH2OH, H; PRIORITY ASSIGNMENT: circle I from chiral C — all four groups attach via O(OH), C(CHO), C(CH2OH), H; O(Z=8) > C(Z=6) > C(Z=6) > H(Z=1) → OH is priority 1 immediately; H is priority 4 immediately; tie between CHO and CH2OH: go to circle II; CHO-C bonded to: (O-real, O-phantom[from C=O], H) → contributes (O, O, H) at circle II; CH2OH-C bonded to: (O-real, H, H) → (O, H, H); comparing circle II: CHO gives two O at this level; CH2OH gives one O → CHO > CH2OH; FINAL PRIORITIES: OH(1) > CHO(2) > CH2OH(3) > H(4); R/S: H(4) pointing away; count OH→CHO→CH2OH; if clockwise → R; if anticlockwise → S; D-(+)-glyceraldehyde = (R)-(+)-glyceraldehyde with [α]D = +10.32 degrees; L-(-)-glyceraldehyde = (S)-(-)-glyceraldehyde with [α]D = -10.32 degrees; NOTE: D/L nomenclature (Fischer convention) for carbohydrates/amino acids is DIFFERENT from R/S (CIP); D does NOT always equal R
valid_transformations.conditions: Enantiomers: mirror image operation. D-glyceraldehyde (RCHO at C-1, OH on right in Fischer) = (R) configuration (CIP). L-glyceraldehyde (OH on left in Fischer) = (S) configuration = levorotatory (–). D = dextrorotatory (+) = (R) for glyceraldehyde (coincidence — D/L and +/– don't always correspond). Fischer conventions: D means reference compound derived from D-glyceraldehyde (historical). CIP: assign independently.

valid_transformations.notes: Serine (2-amino-3-hydroxypropanoic acid) CIP assignment: structure: HOOC-C*(H)(NH2)-CH2OH (chiral carbon); FOUR GROUPS at chiral C: COOH, NH2, CH2OH, H; PRIORITY ASSIGNMENT: circle I — NH2 (N, Z=7) > COOH (C, Z=6) ≈ CH2OH (C, Z=6) > H (Z=1); NH2(1) immediately; H(4) immediately; tie between COOH and CH2OH: circle II — COOH-C bonded to (O-real, O-phantom[from C=O], OH-oxygen); COOH-C has Rule 4 phantom O from C=O → treated as C bonded to (O, O, O) at circle II; CH2OH-C bonded to (O, H, H); COOH gives three O at circle II; CH2OH gives one O → COOH > CH2OH; FINAL PRIORITIES: NH2(1) > COOH(2) > CH2OH(3) > H(4); CONFIGURATION: natural L-serine is (S) — confirmed by counting (NH2→COOH→CH2OH counterclockwise with H pointing away → S); NOTE: L-amino acids (natural) are mostly (S), EXCEPT L-cysteine which is (R) because -CH2SH has S (Z=16) > N → changes priority order; KEY LESSON: N-containing group (NH2, NHR, NR2) gives N at circle I → always higher priority than C at circle I → amino group is ALWAYS priority 1 when compared to C-containing groups
valid_transformations.conditions: CIP assignment of L-serine: L-serine has Fischer OH on left (like L-glyceraldehyde). Substituents: NH₂ (priority 1, N highest), COOH (priority 2, C with 3 O), CH₂OH (priority 3, C with 1 O), H (priority 4). In Fischer: COOH at top (going away), NH₂ left → for CIP: NH₂ and CH₂OH horizontal (toward viewer) and COOH/H vertical. Result: (S). All L-amino acids are (S) EXCEPT L-cysteine (which is (R) because -CH₂SH has higher priority than COOH due to S).
same_molecular_formula_and_connectivity
valid_transformations.notes: B.Pt, M.Pt, density, |[alpha]_D| identical; only sign differs: (+) dextrorotatory vs (-) levorotatory; dextro=clockwise=d, laevo=counterclockwise=l

valid_transformations.conditions: resolution_via_diastereomeric_salt_formation
valid_transformations.notes: OI_reagent+A->gamma1; OI_reagent+B->gamma2; gamma1=-gamma2 (cannot separate). OA_reagent+A->gamma1; OA_reagent+B->gamma2; gamma1 != gamma2 (diastereomeric salts with different physical properties -> separable by fractional crystallisation)

valid_transformations.conditions: rotation_in_plane_of_paper_by_integer_multiple_of_180_degrees
valid_transformations.notes: n x 180 deg rotation gives IDENTICAL compound (same R/S at all centres); 90 deg rotation gives ENANTIOMER (all centres inverted); swapping ANY two groups at a chiral centre also inverts that centre

valid_transformations.conditions: (nR,nS)_configuration_pairing_internal_cancellation
valid_transformations.notes: (2R,3S)-2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic_acid (meso-tartaric_acid): internal POS bisects molecule -> [alpha]_D = 0; is diastereomer of both (2R,3R)-2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic_acid and (2S,3S)-2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic_acid

valid_transformations.conditions: same_molecular_formula_different_R_or_S_configuration_at_one_or_more_stereocentres
valid_transformations.notes: unlike enantiomers, diastereomers differ in B.Pt, M.Pt, density AND |[alpha]_D| -> separable by fractional distillation or crystallisation; meso compound is diastereomer of the optically active forms

valid_transformations.conditions: 4_different_groups_across_the_C=C=C_axis_POS_absent_CoS_absent
valid_transformations.notes: two perpendicular planes through allene eliminate any net POS; POS x, CoS x -> chiral -> OA; even cumulated double bonds give axial chirality (R/S optical isomers); allene alone with same groups on one end is achiral

valid_transformations.conditions: ortho_groups_large_enough_to_prevent_rotation_through_coplanarity_at_RT
valid_transformations.notes: example: 2-COOH,6-NO2-phenyl / 2-COOH,6-NO2-phenyl biaryl; POS x, CoS x -> chiral -> enantiomers (+) and (-) isolable at RT; no sp3 stereocentre; chiral axis is the biaryl C-C bond

valid_transformations.conditions: n_equals_number_of_optical_centres_plus_number_of_GI_centres
valid_transformations.notes: n = OC (sp3 chiral C, axial chiral axis) + GI (C=C, C=N, cycloalkane ring, etc.); no symmetry means no meso forms; formula gives TOTAL stereoisomers including all E/Z and R/S combinations

valid_transformations.conditions: molecule_has_internal_plane_of_symmetry_possible_giving_meso_forms
valid_transformations.notes: p = (n+1)/2 for odd n; p = n/2 for even n; 2^(n-1) = optically active forms; 2^(p-1) = meso forms; example n=3 p=2: 2^2+2^1=4+2=6 total; example n=2 p=1: 2^1+2^0=2+1=3 total (verified for meso case)

valid_transformations.conditions: cyclic_structure_locks_relative_configuration_of_ring_stereocentres
valid_transformations.notes: ring carbons with fixed relative configuration reduce independent n; only free exocyclic stereocentres multiply count by 2; IIT ADV 2015: spiro compound with fixed ring -> 2 stereocentres with fixed relative config -> 2 stereoisomers (one enantiomeric pair)

valid_transformations.conditions: rotation_about_C1-C2_bond_by_60_degrees
valid_transformations.notes: eclipsed: maximum VdW + maximum torsional repulsion -> highest energy, least stable; staggered: minimum repulsions -> lowest energy, most stable; barrier ethane ~12 kJ/mol (torsional only, H groups small)

valid_transformations.conditions: rotation_is_continuous_not_quantised
valid_transformations.notes: total number of conformers = infinity; net exchange of energy with surroundings = 0 at RT (interconversion too rapid); conformers are NOT isolatable unlike configurational isomers; ethane 3-fold rotational symmetry gives 3 equivalent eclipsed maxima and 3 equivalent staggered minima per 360 deg

valid_transformations.conditions: eclipsed_arrangement_of_substituents_in_Newman_projection
valid_transformations.notes: VdW repulsion proportional to group size: H/H eclipsed < H/CH3 eclipsed < CH3/CH3 eclipsed; VdW repulsion ∝ 1/r^6 (inverse sixth power of intergroup distance); applies only between GROUP electron clouds

valid_transformations.conditions: eclipse_between_any_two_bonds_regardless_of_attached_groups
valid_transformations.notes: torsional repulsion arises between bond electron clouds not group electron clouds; H-eclipsed-H = H-eclipsed-CH3 = CH3-eclipsed-CH3 in torsional contribution; independent of group size; origin: electron cloud of one sigma bond repels electron cloud of adjacent eclipsed sigma bond

valid_transformations.conditions: propane_has_C2v_symmetry_making_both_methylene_adjacent_bonds_equivalent
valid_transformations.notes: propane CH3-CH2-CH3: Newman along C1-C2 shows front=CH3,H,H; rear=CH3,H,H -> same profile as C2-C3; one unique bond rotation needed; front carbon = point, rear carbon = circle in Newman projection

valid_transformations.conditions: requires_alpha_H_on_sp3_carbon_adjacent_to_C=O
valid_transformations.notes: propan-2-one keto (99.99%) rightleftarrow prop-1-en-2-ol enol (0.01%); condition: must have alpha-H; keto>enol for simple carbonyls due to B.E.(C=O)+B.E.(C-H) > B.E.(C=C)+B.E.(O-H); triad system: O-C=O-C-H becomes O-H-C=C

valid_transformations.conditions: conjugated_system_allowing_5-atom_cyclic_transition_state_for_base_mediated_H_transfer
valid_transformations.notes: example: pent-3-en-2-one CH3-CO-CH=CH-CH3; base removes gamma-H (C5 counting O=1); carbanion delocalised across conjugated system; enol forms at multiple positions via resonance; also gives 1,7-keto-enol in longer conjugated systems (hepta-3,5-dien-2-one)

valid_transformations.conditions: stepwise_H_to_D_replacement_at_all_alpha_positions_via_repeated_enolisation
valid_transformations.notes: propan-2-one + OD-/D2O -> propan-2-one-1-d1 -> propan-2-one-1,1-d2 -> ... -> propan-2-one-d6 (CD3COCD3) over long time; cyclohexanone -> 2,2,6,6-d4-cyclohexanone (only alpha positions); conjugated enone: 1,5-enolisation also deuterates gamma positions; mechanism: OD- removes alpha-H -> enolate anion -> D2O donates D+ at alpha-C

valid_transformations.conditions: intramolecular_O-H---O_hydrogen_bond_stabilisation_plus_C=C_resonance
valid_transformations.notes: pentan-2,4-dione: ~80% enol in CCl4 (non-polar); enol stabilised by: (i) chelation (intramolecular O-H...O=C H-bond forms 6-membered ring); (ii) conjugation of C=C with second C=O; (iii) less steric strain in enol than keto; polar protic solvents reduce enol% by competing H-bond

valid_transformations.conditions: aromaticity_of_benzene_ring_provides_extraordinary_thermodynamic_stabilisation
valid_transformations.notes: phenol is the enol tautomer of cyclohexa-2,4-dien-1-one; aromaticity adds ~150 kJ/mol stabilisation -> enol ~100%; extreme exception to keto>enol rule; Saytzeff rule: more substituted C=C is more stable (applies to enol stability too)

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_2013_recommendations
valid_transformations.notes: steps: (1) identify longest carbon chain as parent (2) number from end giving lowest locant set to substituents (3) name substituents alphabetically ignoring di/tri/tetra prefixes (4) cite locants before each substituent name; common groups: methyl isopropyl n-butyl sec-butyl tert-butyl isobutyl; if two locant sets tied compare first point of difference choosing lower

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_nomenclature_cycloalkane_rules
valid_transformations.notes: cyclo- prefix + number of ring carbons + -ane; single substituent -> locant 1 by default (eg 1-methylcyclohexane but just methylcyclohexane); multiple substituents: number ring to give lowest locant set; then alphabetical order; eg 1-ethyl-3-methylcyclohexane not 1-methyl-3-ethylcyclohexane

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_bicycloalkane_nomenclature
valid_transformations.notes: bicyclo[m.n.p]alkane: m >= n >= p; m,n,p = number of carbons in each bridge between the two bridgehead carbons; total carbons = m+n+p+2; numbering: start at one bridgehead, traverse longest bridge first then second longest then shortest; example: bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane (norbornane) has bridges of 2,2,1 carbons; total = 2+2+1+2 = 7 C

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_spiro_nomenclature
valid_transformations.notes: spiro[m.n]alkane: m < n; m = number of C in smaller ring minus spiro C; n = number of C in larger ring minus spiro C; total C = m+n+1 (the +1 is the shared spiro carbon); numbering: start adjacent to spiro C in smaller ring, go around smaller ring, through spiro C, then around larger ring; spiro C gets highest number of smaller ring as its locant

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_suffix_prefix_hierarchy
valid_transformations.notes: principal FG dictates suffix: -ane (alkane) -ene (alkene) -yne (alkyne) -ol (alcohol) -al (aldehyde) -one (ketone) -oic_acid (carboxylic acid) -oate (ester) -amide (amide) -amine (amine); parent chain must be longest chain CONTAINING the principal FG; FG always gets lowest possible locant overriding substituent numbering direction

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_complex_substituent_nomenclature
valid_transformations.notes: C1 of substituent = the carbon directly bonded to parent chain; number substituent chain from C1 outward; apply IUPAC to substituent; enclose in parentheses with locants; example: isopropyl = (1-methylethyl); sec-butyl = (1-methylpropyl); tert-butyl = (1,1-dimethylethyl); isobutyl = (2-methylpropyl); isopentyl = (3-methylbutyl); sec-pentyl = (1-methylbutyl); neopentyl = (2,2-dimethylpropyl)

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_preferred_systematic_substituent_names
valid_transformations.notes: sec-butyl = (1-methylpropyl); tert-butyl = (1,1-dimethylethyl); isobutyl = (2-methylpropyl); n-butyl = butyl; isopropyl = (1-methylethyl); both common and systematic names acceptable for simple groups; complex groups MUST use parenthetical systematic names

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_ring_vs_chain_parent_selection
valid_transformations.notes: if ring_C >= chain_C: ring is parent; cycloalkane + name; example: cyclopropane (3C) + propyl (3C) -> 1-propylcyclopropane (ring parent); if chain_C > ring_C: chain is parent; ring becomes cycloalkyl substituent; example: cyclopropyl (3C) + butane (4C) -> 1-cyclopropylbutane (chain parent); rule: chain beats ring only when strictly longer

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_cycloalkane_substituent_numbering
valid_transformations.notes: number ring to give lowest locant set; if two numbering directions give same lowest locant set, choose direction that gives first substituent listed alphabetically the lower locant; example: cyclohexane with methyl at C1 and ethyl at C2 or C6: count to give (1,2) not (1,6) -> 1-ethyl-2-methylcyclohexane (ethyl alphabetically first gets direction)

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_nomenclature_allows_either_common_or_systematic_substituent_names
valid_transformations.notes: example: tridecane with isopentyl at C6 and sec-pentyl at C8 -> valid: 6-isopentyl-8-sec-pentyltridecane OR 6-(3-methylbutyl)-8-(1-methylbutyl)tridecane; complex example: decane with two sec-pentyl groups at C5 and methyls at C3 -> 3,3-dimethyl-5,5-di(1-methylbutyl)decane; alphabetise by first letter of substituent name (ignoring di/tri)

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_amine_nomenclature_1_degree
valid_transformations.notes: parent chain = longest chain containing the C bonded to N; N-bearing C gets lowest possible locant; suffix -amine appended to parent alkane name minus final -e; examples: CH3CH2CH2CH2NH2 = butanamine (no locant needed since N at C1); CH3CH(NH2)CH2CH2CH3 = pentan-2-amine; prefix amino- used when amine is secondary FG

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_N-substituted_amine_nomenclature
valid_transformations.notes: N-substituents cited as N-alkyl before the parent name; parent = longest chain on N; multiple different N-subs: list alphabetically with N- locator each; example: (CH3)(C2H5)NH-propyl = N-ethyl-N-methylpropanamine; if two same N-subs: N,N-dimethyl...; ring on N: N-cyclohexyl... example N,2-diethyl-N-propylcyclohexanamine

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_aldehyde_nomenclature_and_prefix
valid_transformations.notes: aldehyde as PRINCIPAL FG: suffix -al; CHO carbon = C1 always; parent chain includes CHO carbon; as SECONDARY FG (when COOH or amide is principal): prefix formyl- cited with locant in chain; example: HOOC-CH2-CH2-CH2-CHO = 5-formylpentanoic acid (COOH = C1, CHO = C5) OR 6-oxohexanoic acid; both acceptable

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_ketone_nomenclature_and_dual_prefix_options
valid_transformations.notes: ketone as PRINCIPAL FG: suffix -one; as SECONDARY FG: prefix keto- OR oxo- both acceptable; oxo- is IUPAC preferred; keto- is older but accepted at JEE level; example: OHC-CH2-CO-CH3 = 3-oxobutanal = 3-ketobutanal (both correct); internal C=O gets keto/oxo prefix; terminal CHO gets formyl prefix

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_amide_nomenclature
valid_transformations.notes: amide = -C(=O)-N<; suffix -amide; prefix carbamoyl-; carbonyl C = C1 (gets highest priority, lowest locant); N-substituents: N-alkyl- prefix before parent; 1=primary RCONH2; 2=secondary RCONHR; 3=tertiary RCONR2; example: CH3CH2CH2CO-NH-CH3 = N-methylbutanamide; complex: 3-bromo-N-ethyl-N-methylbutanamide; mega: 3-bromo-6-cyano-N-(2-cyclopentylbutyl)-2-cyclopropyl-5-formyl-4-ketooctanamide

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_ester_substituent_prefix_rules
valid_transformations.notes: alkoxycarbonyl = -C(=O)-OR: the carbonyl C is on the substituent side; e.g. methoxycarbonyl = -COOCH3; ethoxycarbonyl = -COOC2H5; alkanoyloxy = -O-C(=O)-R: the oxygen of the substituent leads; e.g. ethanoyloxy (acetoxy) = -OCOCH3; propanoyloxy = -OCOC2H5; example: 3-ethanoyloxy-4-methoxycarbonylcyclohexanecarboxylic acid

valid_transformations.conditions: Hantzsch-Widman_replacement_nomenclature
valid_transformations.notes: oxa = O replacing CH2; aza = NH replacing CH2; bora = B replacing CH2; locant = position of heteroatom; 2-oxacyclohexan-1-one = delta-valerolactone (O at ring C2, C=O at C1); 2-azacyclohexan-1-one = delta-valerolactam (lactam); open chain: HOOC-CH2-CH2-O-CH2-NH-CH2-B-CH2-CH3 = 7-aza-9-bora-5-oxadecanoic acid (heteroatoms listed with locants in ascending order)

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_epoxide_bridging_oxygen_nomenclature
valid_transformations.notes: x,y-epoxy prefix: x and y = locants of two C atoms bridged by O; 1,2-epoxyethane = oxirane (common name); 1,2-epoxypropane = methyloxirane (common); 1,3-epoxypropane = oxetane (4-membered ring); 3,4-epoxycyclohexanone (O bridges C3-C4 of cyclohexanone ring); 3,5-epoxycyclohexanone (O bridges C3-C5 making bicyclic); 1,2,4,5-diepoxypentane (two epoxide groups)

valid_transformations.conditions: dicarboxylic_acid_nomenclature
valid_transformations.notes: mnemonic O My Son Go And Play: O=Oxalic_acid=ethanedioic_acid (HOOC-COOH, 2C); My=Malonic_acid=propanedioic_acid (3C); Son=Succinic_acid=butanedioic_acid (4C); Go=Glutaric_acid=pentanedioic_acid (5C); And=Adipic_acid=hexanedioic_acid (6C); Play=Pimelic_acid=heptanedioic_acid (7C); both common and IUPAC names acceptable

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_amide_derived_substituent_nomenclature
valid_transformations.notes: -NH-CHO = formylamino prefix (N-formylamino or formamido); example: 3-formylaminocyclohexanecarboxylic acid = cyclohexanecarboxylic acid with -NH-CHO at C3; analogous: acetylamino = -NH-COCH3 = acetamido

valid_transformations.conditions: DU_formula_method_M-III
valid_transformations.notes: DU = (C+1) - [(H+X-N)/2]; C=carbon count; H=hydrogen count; X=halogen count (treated like H, monovalent); N=nitrogen count (trivalent, reduces denominator); O and S (divalent) are COMPLETELY IGNORED; examples: C8H8 -> (8+1)-(8+0-0)/2 = 9-4 = 5; C4H8O -> (4+1)-(8+0-0)/2 = 5-4 = 1 (O ignored); C6H12N4 -> (6+1)-(12+0-4)/2 = 7-4 = 3; C8H8Cl2N -> (8+1)-(8+2-1)/2 = 9-9/2 = 9-4.5 = 4.5? no: (8+2-1)=9/2=4.5; if DU non-integer: check formula

valid_transformations.conditions: DU_direct_count_method_M-I
valid_transformations.notes: DU = number_of_pi_bonds + number_of_rings; each C=C counts as 1 DU; each C=O counts as 1 DU; each C=N counts as 1 DU; C-triple-C or C-triple-N counts as 2 DU (two pi bonds); each ring closure = 1 DU regardless of ring size; benzene = 3 (pi) + 1 (ring) = 4 DU; complex example: compound with COOH + CN + 3 rings = 1 (COOH pi) + 2 (CN triple) + 3 (rings) + 3 (benzene pi) = 9 DU; cubane C8H8 = 0 pi + 5 rings = 5 DU

valid_transformations.conditions: DU_hydrogen_saturation_method_M-II
valid_transformations.notes: M-II: DU = (H_saturated - H_actual) / 2; H_saturated = 2C+2 for alkane CnH(2n+2); example: C8H8 -> saturated analog C8H18 -> DU = (18-8)/2 = 5; for cycloalkanes formula is CnH2n (DU=1 per ring); for ring+alkene formula is CnH(2n-2) (DU=2); when N present: add N to chain, each N contributes +1 to saturated H count; when halogens present: replace X with H for saturation count

valid_transformations.conditions: Greek_letter_position_nomenclature_for_carbon_positions
valid_transformations.notes: counting from COOH or C=O carbon (position-0/functional-group-C): alpha (alpha) = 1st C bonded to COOH/C=O; beta = 2nd; gamma = 3rd; delta = 4th; epsilon = 5th; for ketone R-CO-R: both sides have alpha,beta,gamma independently; alpha-H = H on alpha carbon = enolisable H; for COOH: alpha-C is the C bonded to the carboxyl C, not the carboxyl C itself; no-alpha-H example: (COOH)2C< = quaternary C bearing two COOH has no alpha-H

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_heteroatom_functional_group_prefix_nomenclature
valid_transformations.notes: imine = -CH=NH (imino- prefix); thioether = -S- bridge (thio- replaces O in ether naming; e.g., dimethyl thioether = methylsulfanylmethane or dimethyl sulfide); thioester = -C(=O)-S- linkage (acylthio- or thiocarbonyloxy-); primed locants (1-prime, 2-prime, 3-prime) used when substituents on a substituent have their own ring carbons; cyclohexa-1,3-diene (conjugated) vs cyclohexa-1,4-diene (non-conjugated) distinction in locants

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_common_to_systematic_aromatic_names
valid_transformations.notes: toluene=methylbenzene; anisole=methoxybenzene; phenol=hydroxybenzene; aniline=benzenamine; cumene=(1-methylethyl)benzene=isopropylbenzene; styrene=ethenylbenzene=vinylbenzene; o-xylene=1,2-dimethylbenzene; m-xylene=1,3-dimethylbenzene; p-xylene=1,4-dimethylbenzene; o-cresol=2-methylphenol; m-cresol=3-methylphenol; p-cresol=4-methylphenol; mesitylene=1,3,5-trimethylbenzene; isooctane=2,2,4-trimethylpentane; acetone=propan-2-one (NOT IUPAC: crossed out in notes)

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_aromatic_acid_common_name_conversion
