valid_transformations.notes: benzoic_acid=benzenecarboxylic_acid; phthalic_acid=benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic_acid (ortho); isophthalic_acid=benzene-1,3-dicarboxylic_acid (meta); terephthalic_acid=benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic_acid (para, used in PET polyester with ethylene glycol); salicylic_acid=2-hydroxybenzoic_acid; salicylaldehyde=2-hydroxybenzaldehyde; aspirin=2-(ethanoyloxy)benzoic_acid; anthranilic_acid=2-aminobenzoic_acid; o-toluic_acid=2-methylbenzoic_acid; m-toluic_acid=3-methylbenzoic_acid; p-toluic_acid=4-methylbenzoic_acid; benzamide=benzenecarboxamide; phthalimide=isoindole-1,3(2H)-dione; phthalic_anhydride=isobenzofuran-1,3-dione

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_aliphatic_acid_common_name_conversion
valid_transformations.notes: lactic_acid=2-hydroxypropanoic_acid (alpha-hydroxypropionic); tartaric_acid=2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic_acid; citric_acid=2-hydroxypropane-1,2,3-tricarboxylic_acid; pyruvic_acid=2-oxopropanoic_acid (alpha-ketopropionic); glyoxalic_acid=2-oxoacetic_acid (OHC-COOH); mandelic_acid=2-hydroxy-2-phenylacetic_acid; carbamic_acid=aminocarbonyl_acid=H2N-COOH; acetoacetic_ester=ethyl_3-oxobutanoate (CH3COCH2COOEt); glycol=ethane-1,2-diol; glycerol=propane-1,2,3-triol; glyceraldehyde=2,3-dihydroxypropanal; glyoxal=ethanedial; pivaldehyde=2,2-dimethylpropanal

valid_transformations.conditions: IUPAC_heterocyclic_common_name_conversion
valid_transformations.notes: furan=oxolane_(saturated:_tetrahydrofuran=THF=oxolane_IUPAC); pyrrole=1H-pyrrole_(azacyclopenta-2,4-diene); thiophene=thiacyclopenta-2,4-diene; pyridine=azabenzene_(azinane_saturated=piperidine); indole=1H-benzo[b]pyrrole (benzene_fused_with_pyrrole); morpholine=1-oxa-4-azacyclohexane_(6-membered_with_O_and_NH); piperidine=azinane=hexahydropyridine; oxirane=ethylene_oxide=1,2-epoxyethane; oxetane=1,3-epoxypropane; aziridine=1H-aziridine_(3-membered_with_NH); THF=oxolane; coumarin=2H-chromen-2-one_(benzolactone); furfural=furan-2-carbaldehyde; tropone=cyclohept-2-en-1-one; tropolone=2-hydroxycyclohept-2-en-1-one; phloroglucinol=benzene-1,3,5-triol

valid_transformations.conditions: mild_oxidation_at_room_temperature_only_aldehyde_oxidised_not_primary_alcohol
valid_transformations.notes: CHO-(CHOH)4-CH2OH + Br2/H2O -> COOH-(CHOH)4-CH2OH (gluconic acid); Br2/H2O = mild oxidant; oxidises ONLY the aldehyde CHO to COOH; does NOT oxidise the primary alcohol CH2OH at C6; product is a monocarboxylic acid (6C, one COOH); this PROVES the carbonyl is at C1 as an ALDEHYDE (not ketone C=O, which would not be oxidised by Br2/H2O); contrasted with HNO3 which oxidises both CHO and CH2OH to give saccharic acid (dicarboxylic)

valid_transformations.conditions: intramolecular_hemiacetal_formation_C5-OH_attacks_C1-CHO_in_aqueous_solution
valid_transformations.notes: C5-OH (circled in Fischer) attacks C1-CHO intramolecularly -> forms 6-membered pyranose ring (like tetrahydropyran skeleton); two new configurations at C1 (anomeric C): alpha-form (OH at C1 axial in Haworth) vs beta-form (OH at C1 equatorial); Haworth conversion rules: right in Fischer = DOWN in Haworth; left in Fischer = UP; C6 (CH2OH) always UP; alpha-D(+)-glucopyranose = less stable (axial anomeric OH); beta-D(+)-glucopyranose = more stable (equatorial anomeric OH); cold conc. recrystallisation -> alpha (mp 146 C); hot dilute -> beta (mp 153 C)

valid_transformations.conditions: spontaneous_ring_opening_and_ring_closure_via_open_chain_intermediate
valid_transformations.notes: mutarotation: when pure alpha-glucose ([alpha]D = +112 degrees) or pure beta-glucose ([alpha]D = +18.7 degrees) is dissolved in water the specific rotation changes over time until reaching equilibrium at +52.5 degrees; mechanism: cyclic form opens to give open-chain aldehyde intermediate (0.02%) then ring closes to give either alpha or beta; equilibrium composition: alpha ~36%, open chain ~0.02%, beta ~64%; beta predominates because equatorial OH at anomeric C is more stable

valid_transformations.conditions: mild_reduction_selective_for_aldehyde_or_ketone
valid_transformations.notes: CHO-(CHOH)4-CH2OH + NaBH4 -> CH2OH-(CHOH)4-CH2OH (glucitol=sorbitol=alditol); the C1 aldehyde is reduced to a primary alcohol; product has CH2OH at BOTH ends; glucitol/sorbitol is a sugar alcohol used as sweetener; reduction of glucose confirms one terminal CHO

valid_transformations.conditions: esterification_of_all_free_OH_groups
valid_transformations.notes: CHO-(CHOH)4-CH2OH + 5 Ac2O -> CHO-(CH-OAc)4-CH2-OAc (glucose pentaacetate); 5 OH groups acetylated at C2,C3,C4,C5,C6; stable compound (not 2 on same C) -> all 5 OH on DIFFERENT carbons; CHO at C1 does NOT react (not an OH group in open chain) but DOES react in cyclic form; when glucose pentaacetate (cyclic) is tested with NH2OH -> no oxime -> confirms CHO now tied up in hemiacetal ring

valid_transformations.conditions: D_L_configuration_from_penultimate_asymmetric_carbon_OH_right_D_left_L
valid_transformations.notes: generic name = aldehyde/ketone prefix + carbon count suffix; C3=triose, C4=tetrose, C5=pentose, C6=hexose; D/L = configuration at HIGHEST-NUMBERED asymmetric carbon (penultimate carbon, second from bottom in Fischer with C1 at top as CHO); OH on RIGHT at penultimate C = D; OH on LEFT = L; reference compound: D-glyceraldehyde (C2-OH on right when C1=CHO at top); examples: glucose = D-aldohexose; fructose = D-ketohexose; D-erythrose and D-threose are both D-aldotetroses (same generic name but different C2 configuration = diastereomers)

valid_transformations.conditions: acid_or_enzyme_hydrolysis_of_glycosidic_bond
valid_transformations.notes: sucrose = alpha-D-glucopyranose linked to beta-D-fructofuranose via C1(glucose)-C2(fructose) glycosidic bond; BOTH anomeric carbons involved in bond -> no free anomeric OH -> non-reducing sugar; hydrolysis gives D-glucose (dextrorotatory +52.5) + D-fructose (laevorotatory -92); invert sugar: sucrose [alpha]=+66 -> mixture [alpha]=negative (fructose rotation dominates because |[alpha]_fructose| > |[alpha]_glucose|)

valid_transformations.conditions: acid_or_enzyme_hydrolysis
valid_transformations.notes: maltose = C12H22O11; two alpha-D-glucose units linked C1(glucose1)-C4(glucose2) alpha-1,4-glycosidic bond; C1 of second glucose is FREE (anomeric OH free) -> reducing sugar; lactose = milk sugar C12H22O11; beta-D-galactose linked C1(galactose)-C4(glucose) beta-1,4-glycosidic bond; C1 of glucose free -> reducing sugar; raffinose = trisaccharide C18H32O16 -> glucose + fructose + galactose on hydrolysis

valid_transformations.conditions: alkaline_conditions_TIFB_test_for_reducing_sugars
valid_transformations.notes: TIFB-positive structures: (1) free aldehyde -CHO; (2) alpha-hydroxy ketone R-CO-CH(OH)- (can tautomerise to enol->aldehyde); (3) hemiacetal with free anomeric OH (can ring-open to give trace free C=O); TIFB-negative: ketone without adjacent OH; acetal (full glycoside, both anomeric OHs replaced by OR); all monosaccharides are reducing (free anomeric OH); maltose and lactose are reducing (one anomeric OH free); sucrose is non-reducing (both anomeric C in glycosidic bond)

valid_transformations.conditions: both_anomeric_carbons_occupied_in_alpha_1_beta_2_glycosidic_linkage
valid_transformations.notes: sucrose has alpha-1,beta-2-glycosidic bond between C1(alpha-glucose) and C2(beta-fructose); both C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose are tied in the bond as full acetal; neither can ring-open to give free carbonyl; sucrose does not reduce Tollens or Fehling; sucrose CANNOT mutarotate (no free anomeric OH to exchange); upon hydrolysis the released monosaccharides (glucose and fructose) ARE individually reducing

valid_transformations.conditions: SN2_at_alpha_carbon_bearing_halogen_excess_NH3_prevents_dialkylation
valid_transformations.notes: step 1: R-CH2-COOH + X2/PX3 (HVZ reaction) -> R-CH(X)-COOH (alpha-haloacid); step 2: R-CH(X)-COOH + NH3(excess) -> R-CH(NH2)-COO-NH4+ (ammonium salt, SN2 at alpha-C, excess NH3 prevents N-dialkylation); step 3: H3O+ -> R-CH(NH2)-COOH (amino acid); note: excess NH3 is essential to get primary amine product; if stoichiometric NH3, secondary or tertiary amines form; this gives racemic amino acid (DL mixture) so optical resolution needed to get pure L-form

valid_transformations.conditions: sequential_amide_formation_then_dehydration_to_cyclic_imide
valid_transformations.notes: phthalic acid (o-HOOC-C6H4-COOH) + NH3 -> o-(H2NOC)-C6H4-(CONH2) (phthalamide diamide) -> heat -> phthalimide (cyclic imide with NH, benzene fused 5-membered ring CO-NH-CO) + H2O; phthalimide has acidic NH (pKa ~8.3) that can be deprotonated by NaOH/KOH to give potassium phthalimide (Gabriel reagent) used as masked NH2 equivalent in synthesis

valid_transformations.conditions: SN2_at_alpha_halo_ester_then_acid_hydrolysis_of_N_C_bond_and_ester
valid_transformations.notes: step 1: phthalimide + NaOH -> potassium/sodium phthalimide (N-anion); step 2: phthalimide anion + R-CHX-COOR' (alpha-haloester, SN2 at alpha-C) -> N-alkylated phthalimide R-CH(CO2R')-N-phthalimide; step 3: H3O+ -> phthalic acid + R-CH(NH2)-COOH (amino acid); ester also hydrolysed; advantage: avoids over-alkylation (NH3 gives multiple substitution); gives primary amine only; example: phthalimide + (1)NaOH (2)PhCH2Cl (3)H3O+ -> phenylalanine (Ph-CH2-CH(NH2)-COOH)

valid_transformations.conditions: Fischer_projection_D_L_configuration_convention_for_amino_acids
valid_transformations.notes: convention: draw alpha-amino acid in Fischer with COOH at top (C1) and R group at bottom; NH2 on LEFT = L-amino acid (matches L-glyceraldehyde with OH on left when CHO at top); NH2 on RIGHT = D-amino acid; KEY: all 20 natural amino acids found in proteins are L-amino acids (only exception: D-amino acids in some bacterial cell walls and certain antibiotics); glycine is neither D nor L (optically inactive, no chiral centre at alpha-C since R=H)

valid_transformations.conditions: classification_by_relative_number_of_acidic_and_basic_groups
valid_transformations.notes: neutral amino acids: equal COOH and NH2 count (one each for most); acidic amino acids: extra COOH in side chain -> Aspartic acid (Asp, D): HOOC-CH2-CH(NH2)-COOH; Glutamic acid (Glu, E): HOOC-(CH2)2-CH(NH2)-COOH; basic amino acids: extra NH2 in side chain -> Lysine (Lys, K): H2N-(CH2)4-CH(NH2)-COOH (epsilon-amino); Arginine (Arg, R): guanidino group; Histidine (His, H): imidazole ring; proline (Pro, P) is unique: secondary amino (N in pyrrolidine ring), not primary NH2

valid_transformations.from: aminobenzene (aniline) — N lone pair adjacent to benzene ring
valid_transformations.to: 5 canonical structures via +M donation; electron density increased at ortho and para positions
valid_transformations.conditions: N must be sp2; lone pair in p-orbital parallel to ring π-system
valid_transformations.notes: 5 structures: neutral + 2 Kekulé + N⁺=ring with ⁻ at ortho-2, ortho-6, and para-4. N lone pair less available for protonation → aniline (aminobenzene) is 10⁶× less basic than cyclohexylamine. -NR₂ > -NHR > -NH₂ in +M strength.

valid_transformations.to: 6 canonical structures via -M withdrawal; electron density decreased at ortho and para
valid_transformations.conditions: -M effect: π-electrons of C=O conjugate with ring, pulling electron density FROM ring INTO C=O
valid_transformations.notes: 6 structures: neutral + 2 Kekulé of ring + 3 from -CHO withdrawal (⁻ on O, ⁺ on ring at ortho-2, ortho-6, para-4). Polarity: C⁺=O⁻ in CHO. CHO is -M and -I → strong EWG, meta-director for electrophilic aromatic substitution.

valid_transformations.conditions: -M effect of NO₂: N⊕ draws π-electrons from ring at ortho and para; NO₂ itself resonates: N⁺(-O⁻)=O ↔ N⁺(=O)O⁻
valid_transformations.notes: Ring canonicals: neutral + 2 Kekulé + ⁺ at ortho + ⁺ at para (with ⁻ on N). NO₂ has dual resonance: ring interaction + internal O-N-O. Net: ring extremely electron-deficient at ortho/para → strong deactivator and meta-director.

valid_transformations.notes: Resonance hybrid has partial + character on terminal CH₂ and partial - on O. This explains 1,4-addition (Michael addition) to α,β-unsaturated carbonyl: nucleophile attacks terminal carbon (δ⁺). IUPAC: prop-2-enal; α-carbon = C2, β-carbon = C3 (terminal CH₂).

valid_transformations.from: +M donor group attached to benzene ring
valid_transformations.to: ring activation ordered by +M power: O⁻ > NH₂ > NHR > NR₂ > OH > OR > NHC(=O)R > OC(=O)R > Ph > F > Cl > Br > I
valid_transformations.conditions: +M power determined by: lone pair availability + orbital size match with ring p-orbital. F 2p-2p (best overlap); Cl 2p-3p; Br 2p-4p; I 2p-5p (worst). Amide N has lower +M than NH₂ because lone pair already donated into C=O.
valid_transformations.notes: Key: anionic groups (O⁻, NH⁻) are strongest +M; acylated heteroatoms (NHAc, OAc) weaker because resonance with acyl C=O competes; halogens +M decreases down group despite increasing lone pair polarisability.

valid_transformations.from: -M acceptor group (polar multiple bond) attached to benzene ring
valid_transformations.to: ring deactivation ordered by -M power: NO₂ > C≡N > CHO > C(=O)R > anhydride > COOR > COOH > CONH₂ > COO⁻
valid_transformations.conditions: -M power determined by: electrophilicity of carbonyl/sp carbon + stabilisation of negative charge in -M structure. Anhydride has two C=O competing for electrons. Carboxylate (COO⁻) weakest because negative charge already stabilised.

valid_transformations.to: 5 canonical structures via -M withdrawal of C≡N: ⁺ at ortho-2, ortho-6, para-4 with ⁻ on N of CN

valid_transformations.from: benzenesulfonic acid (Ph-SO₃H) — sulfonyl group attached to benzene

valid_transformations.from: set of canonical (resonating) structures of a molecule
valid_transformations.to: most stable canonical structure identified by Rule I: complete octet is highest priority
valid_transformations.conditions: Rule I: neutral structure (complete octet, no charge) > charged structure with octet. F/O/N cannot bear +ve charge with incomplete octet — such canonical structures are forbidden and must not be drawn.
valid_transformations.notes: Priority I overrides all other rules. Example: for prop-2-enal resonance, structure O=CH-CH=CH2 (neutral, all octets complete) is most stable contributor. A canonical showing O⁺ with 3 bonds and no lone pair on O is forbidden (O would have only 6 electrons).

meta_tags.semantic_obfuscation: IUPAC: prop-2-enal (acrolein); canonical structure stability hierarchy

valid_transformations.from: two canonical structures with complete octets
valid_transformations.to: more stable canonical identified by Rules II-IV: π-bonds > charge number > charge position > charge distance
valid_transformations.conditions: After Rule I (octet) is satisfied, apply: II=more π-bonds preferred; III=−ve on more electronegative atom + +ve on less EN atom preferred; IV=less distance between opposite charges preferred
valid_transformations.notes: Full priority order (boxed in notes): Octet > π-bond count > number of charges > position of charge > distance between charges > stability of charged centre. Example: phenol canonical structures stability: neutral (1=5) > O⁺H with adjacent ⁻ (2=4) > O⁺H with ⁻ far from O (3, greatest charge separation).

valid_transformations.from: canonical structure with positive charge on oxygen/nitrogen/fluorine with incomplete octet
valid_transformations.to: FORBIDDEN — this canonical structure cannot exist
valid_transformations.conditions: F, O, N are Period 2 elements with no d orbitals — they CANNOT expand octet; therefore a +ve charge with incomplete octet on F/O/N is physically impossible
valid_transformations.notes: Valid: O⁺ with complete octet (O has 4 bonds + 0 lone pairs OR 3 bonds + 1 lone pair = 8 electrons). Invalid: O⁺ with only 6 electrons (3 bonds, 0 lone pairs = incomplete). This restricts which enolate/enal resonance structures can be drawn.

valid_transformations.to: only 2 canonical structures (Kekulé pair); no +M effect; ring strongly deactivated

valid_transformations.notes: LDPE: high pressure (1000–2000 atm), 350–570K, radical mechanism → branched chains (branching prevents close packing → low density). HDPE: Ziegler-Natta, low pressure, 333–343K → linear chains → high crystallinity → high density. PVC thermoplastic, can be plasticised. Teflon = poly(tetrafluoroethene): most chemically inert polymer known; non-stick surface.

valid_transformations.from: synthetic rubber monomers — addition copolymerisation (BUNA-N, BUNA-S, Neoprene)
valid_transformations.to: BUNA-N [-CH₂-CH=CH-CH₂-CH₂-CH(CN)-]ₙ (from buta-1,3-diene + acrylonitrile); BUNA-S [-CH₂-CH=CH-CH₂-CH₂-CH(Ph)-]ₙ (from buta-1,3-diene + phenylethene/styrene); Neoprene [-CH₂-C(Cl)=CH-CH₂-]ₙ (from 2-chlorobuta-1,3-diene = chloroprene)
valid_transformations.conditions: BUNA-N: oil-resistant rubber (nitrile rubber); BUNA-S: general purpose synthetic rubber; Neoprene (polychloroprene): oil and flame resistant, homo-polymer of 2-chloro-1,3-butadiene (chloroprene); all are addition polymers and elastomers
valid_transformations.notes: BUNA = butadiene + Na (sodium, early catalyst). -N = acrylonitrile; -S = styrene. Neoprene monomer: 2-chlorobuta-1,3-diene (IUPAC: 2-chloro-1,3-butadiene); polymer is polychloroprene. Neoprene is a HOMO-polymer (one monomer type). BUNA-N and BUNA-S are both copolymers. All are elastomers held by weak van der Waals forces.

valid_transformations.from: ethane-1,2-diol (ethylene glycol, HO-CH₂-CH₂-OH) + benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid (terephthalic acid, p-HOOC-C₆H₄-COOH) — condensation polymerisation
valid_transformations.to: poly(ethylene terephthalate) PET [Terylene] — polyester [-O-CH₂-CH₂-O-C(=O)-C₆H₄-C(=O)-]ₙ + n H₂O
valid_transformations.conditions: condensation polymer; copolymer (two different monomers); polyester (ester linkages -COO-); fibre-forming (held by H-bonds in crystalline domains); PET used as Terylene (fibre), Dacron (USA name)
valid_transformations.notes: PET properties: high tensile strength (crystalline fibre), used in clothing, bottles, films. Both monomers are bifunctional: diol gives -OH and dicarboxylic acid gives -COOH; ester bond forms between them with H₂O lost. Classified as: condensation + copolymer + polyester + fibre. Compare Nylon-6,6 (polyamide, also fibre, but amide bonds not ester bonds).

valid_transformations.from: hexane-1,6-diamine (hexamethylenediamine, H₂N-(CH₂)₆-NH₂) + hexanedioic acid (adipic acid, HOOC-(CH₂)₄-COOH) — condensation; OR azepan-2-one (caprolactam) — ring-opening polymerisation
valid_transformations.to: Nylon-6,6 [-NH-(CH₂)₆-NH-C(=O)-(CH₂)₄-C(=O)-]ₙ (copolymer, polyamide); OR Nylon-6 [-NH-(CH₂)₅-C(=O)-]ₙ (homo-polymer, polyamide via ring-opening of caprolactam at Δ)
valid_transformations.conditions: Nylon-6,6: two bifunctional monomers each with 6 carbons → co-polymer; 6,6 means 6C diamine + 6C diacid. Nylon-6: single monomer caprolactam (6-membered cyclic lactam) → homo-polymer via ring-opening at Δ. Both form amide bonds (-CO-NH-).
valid_transformations.notes: Key differences: Nylon-6,6 = copolymer; Nylon-6 = homo-polymer. Both = condensation polymers, polyamides, fibres. Amide linkage is same in both but arrangement differs (Nylon-6,6: alternating 6C+6C; Nylon-6: uniform 6C). Properties: high tensile strength (H-bonding between amide groups → crystalline). Nylon-6 melting point lower than Nylon-6,6 (430°C vs 455°C) because of different H-bond geometry.

valid_transformations.from: phenol (hydroxybenzene) + methanal (formaldehyde, HCHO) — condensation polymerisation, H⁺ or OH⁻ catalyst
valid_transformations.to: Novolac (linear phenol-formaldehyde polymer, acid conditions, used in paints) OR Bakelite (cross-linked 3D network, excess HCHO/base conditions; thermosetting)
valid_transformations.conditions: Step 1 (both): phenol + HCHO → 2-hydroxybenzyl alcohol (ortho-methylol phenol). Step 2 acid: further condensation → linear Novolac chain. Step 2 base/excess HCHO: 3D cross-linking at ortho and para positions → thermosetting Bakelite. Bakelite = hard, infusible, network polymer (thermosetting).
valid_transformations.notes: Novolac: linear polymer [-Ph(OH)-CH₂-]ₙ; soluble, used in paints and lacquers; requires hardener (e.g. hexamethylenetetramine) to cure to Bakelite. Bakelite: once cross-linked, CANNOT be remelted (thermosetting). Melamine-formaldehyde resin: melamine (2,4,6-triamino-1,3,5-triazine) + HCHO → methylol intermediate → cross-linked melamine polymer (crockery, laminates). Classified: condensation + copolymer + network polymer + thermosetting.

meta_tags.semantic_obfuscation: IUPAC: hydroxybenzene (phenol); methanal (formaldehyde); Novolac linear; Bakelite cross-linked network thermosetting; melamine = 2,4,6-triamino-1,3,5-triazine

valid_transformations.from: 2-methylpropene (isobutylene, H₂C=C(CH₃)₂) + Lewis acid (BF₃, AlCl₃, FeBr₃, SnCl₄) + trace H₂O — cationic polymerisation
valid_transformations.to: poly(2-methylpropene) [polyisobutylene, PIB] [-CH₂-C(CH₃)₂-]ₙ via tertiary carbocation chain mechanism
reagents: Lewis acid (BF₃, AlCl₃, FeBr₃, SnCl₄) + trace H₂O
valid_transformations.conditions: Step 1 Initiation: BF₃ + H₂O → H⁺[BF₃OH]⁻; H⁺ adds to CH₂ (Markovnikov) → tertiary (CH₃)₂C⁺-CH₃. Step 2 Propagation: (CH₃)₂C⁺ + n isobutylene → growing tertiary carbocation chain. Step 3 Termination: carbocation + counter-ion → neutral polymer chain.
valid_transformations.notes: Cationic polymerisation requires: (1) electron-rich alkene (stabilises carbocation intermediate); (2) Lewis acid catalyst. Works for: polystyrene (H₂C=CHPh → tertiary-benzylic), polyvinyl ethers (H₂C=CH-OR), polyisobutylene. Contrast with anionic (electron-poor monomers) and radical (any alkene). Cationic: rate of propagation >> termination → high MW but broad distribution.

meta_tags.semantic_obfuscation: IUPAC: 2-methylpropene; poly(2-methylpropene) = polyisobutylene; Lewis acid-catalysed cationic chain-growth polymerisation; tertiary carbocation propagation

valid_transformations.from: propenenitrile (acrylonitrile, CH₂=CH-CN) + organolithium initiator (R-Li) or potassium amide (KNH₂) — anionic polymerisation
valid_transformations.to: poly(propenenitrile) [polyacrylonitrile, PAN] [-CH₂-CH(CN)-]ₙ via carbanion chain mechanism; NO chain termination → living polymer
valid_transformations.conditions: Step 1 Initiation: R-Li → R:⁻ Li⁺; R:⁻ + CH₂=CHCN → R-CH₂-CH⁻(CN) Li⁺. Step 2 Propagation: growing carbanion adds to more monomer; CN groups stabilise carbanion (EWG). No termination step in pure anionic polymerisation → living polymer chain remains active until quenched.
valid_transformations.notes: Anionic polymerisation key feature: NO spontaneous chain termination → called 'living polymerisation'. The chain keeps growing as long as monomer is available. On addition of new monomer (even different type) → block copolymers can be formed. Examples: Buna-type synthetic rubbers, polyacrylonitrile, polyisoprene (anionic). Requires electron-poor monomers (C=C adjacent to EWG like -CN, -CHO, -COOR) to stabilise the carbanion intermediate.

meta_tags.semantic_obfuscation: IUPAC: propenenitrile (acrylonitrile); poly(propenenitrile); anionic living polymerisation; carbanion propagation; no chain termination

valid_transformations.from: ethene (H₂C=CH₂) + benzoyl peroxide initiator [PhC(=O)-O-O-C(=O)Ph] — free radical polymerisation
valid_transformations.to: poly(ethene) [-CH₂-CH₂-]ₙ (LDPE) via phenyl radical chain mechanism; three distinct steps: initiation, propagation, termination
valid_transformations.conditions: Step 1 Initiation: Ph-CO-O-O-CO-Ph → Δ/hν → 2 Ph-CO-O• → 2 Ph• + 2 CO₂; Ph• + CH₂=CH₂ → Ph-CH₂-CH₂•. Step 2 Propagation: Ph-CH₂-CH₂• + n CH₂=CH₂ → growing radical chain. Step 3 Termination: two radical chains combine (coupling) or disproportionate (H-transfer → one saturated + one unsaturated end).
valid_transformations.notes: Free radical polymerisation used for LDPE (high pressure, radical mechanism → branched). Termination modes: (a) combination: R• + R• → R-R; (b) disproportionation: one chain gives H to another → one saturated + one with terminal alkene. Explains why NOT all ethylene converts to polymer (side reactions, termination). Initiator is NOT the same as catalyst — it is consumed. AIBN (azobisisobutyronitrile) is another common initiator.

valid_transformations.from: 1,2-dichloroethane (ethylene dichloride, Cl-CH₂-CH₂-Cl) + sodium disulphide (Na₂S₂) — condensation copolymerisation
valid_transformations.to: Thiokol (thiocol) [-CH₂-CH₂-S-S-]ₙ + 2n NaCl (sodium chloride eliminated); condensation polymer
valid_transformations.conditions: Each step: one -Cl replaced by -S₂-S⁻Na⁺; second -Cl of adjacent molecule closes chain. NaCl eliminated. Polysulphide rubber (Thiokol) — resistant to organic solvents, oils, jet fuels. Condensation + copolymer (two different monomers) + addition of sulphide links.
valid_transformations.notes: Thiokol uses SN2 on the primary C-Cl bonds. Product is a polysulphide elastomer (rubber-like) with alternating C₂H₄ and S₂ units. Used as fuel hose, gasket material. Not to be confused with natural rubber — Thiokol has sulphur in main chain (not as cross-link). Question: Is it addition or condensation? Condensation (because NaCl small molecule is eliminated).

meta_tags.semantic_obfuscation: IUPAC: 1,2-dichloroethane; sodium disulphide; Thiokol = polysulphide rubber; NaCl elimination; condensation copolymer

valid_transformations.from: natural rubber (cis-1,4-polyisoprene) + elemental sulphur (S₈) at 373–415K — vulcanisation
valid_transformations.to: vulcanised rubber: cross-linked network with polysulphide bridges (-Sx-) at double bond positions or allylic CH₂ sites; improved elasticity, tensile strength, and chemical resistance
valid_transformations.conditions: Sulphur forms cross-links (-Sx- bridges, x = 1–8) between polyisoprene chains at double bond C=C or adjacent allylic CH₂ groups; prevents chain slipping → improved mechanical properties. Temperature 373–415K. Higher %S → more cross-links → harder rubber.
valid_transformations.notes: Properties of vulcanised rubber vs raw: BETTER elasticity (optimal cross-links), BETTER tensile strength, BETTER chemical resistance, LESS absorption of water, LESS solubility in organic solvents, NOT brittle at low T or sticky at high T. Ebonite (40–50% S) = very hard, non-elastic (excessive cross-linking removes elasticity entirely). Vulcanisation also involves thiazole accelerators to speed process. Natural rubber = cis-1,4-polyisoprene; gutta percha = trans-1,4-polyisoprene (non-elastic, different geometry).

valid_transformations.from: pinacol (2,3-dimethylbutane-2,3-diol or vicinal diol Ph₂C(OH)-C(OH)Ph₂) + H⁺ — Pinnacol-Pinacolone rearrangement
valid_transformations.to: pinacolone (ketone) via 1,2-aryl or 1,2-alkyl shift; migration aptitude :Ar > R > H (within Ar: p-OMe > p-Me > Ph > p-Cl > p-NO₂; within R: 3° > 2° > 1°)
valid_transformations.conditions: Step 1: Protonation of one OH → oxonium → loss of H₂O → tertiary carbocation. Step 2: 1,2-migration of adjacent group (Ar, R, or H) to carbocation → new oxocarbenium ion. Step 3: deprotonation → ketone. Migration aptitude order for Pinnacol-Pinacolone is :Ar > R > H — aryl migrates MOST (reversed vs SN1 where H migrates most). Within Ar: EDG-substituted Ar migrates faster; EWG-substituted Ar migrates slower.
valid_transformations.notes: Key distinction: Pinnacol-Pinacolone (:Ar > R > H) vs SN1 (H > R > Ar). The aryl group migrates best in Pinnacol because it stabilises the bridging transition state (phenonium-like) with its π-electrons. For the aryl ranking: p-OMe (EDG) > p-Me > Ph (unsubstituted) > p-Cl > p-NO₂ (EWG). For alkyl ranking within R: 3° > 2° > 1° (as per carbocation stability). The group that migrates is ANTI-PERIPLANAR to the departing OH₂.

meta_tags.semantic_obfuscation: IUPAC: 2,3-dimethylbutane-2,3-diol (pinacol); Pinnacol-Pinacolone = 1,2-diol rearrangement; migration aptitude :Ar > R > H; EDG on aryl accelerates migration; phenonium-like bridged TS

valid_transformations.from: ketone (R₁-C(=O)-R₂) + meta-chloroperoxybenzoic acid (mCPBA) or H₂O₂/BF₃ — Baeyer-Villiger oxidation
valid_transformations.to: ester (R₂-O-C(=O)-R₁ or R₁-O-C(=O)-R₂) where the HIGHER-migrating group migrates; migration aptitude: H > 3° alkyl > 2° alkyl > cyclohexyl > phenyl (Ar) > 1° alkyl > cyclopropyl > methyl (CH₃)
valid_transformations.conditions: Mechanism: Nucleophilic addition of peroxyacid O-OH to C=O → tetrahedral intermediate (Criegee intermediate). Then 1,2-migration of R group anti-periplanar to the O-O bond → loss of carboxylate → ester. The group that migrates is retained with its configuration (suprafacial migration). For cyclic ketones → lactone (ring expansion). O is inserted between C=O carbon and the migrating group.
valid_transformations.notes: Full Baeyer-Villiger migration order: H > 3° > 2° > cyclohexyl > Ph > 1° > cyclopropyl > CH₃. Key exceptions: (1) H migrates FASTER than 3° alkyl — opposite to carbocation stability; (2) cyclopropyl migrates SLOWER than 1° alkyl (unlike SN1 where cyclopropylcarbinyl is exceptionally fast); (3) Ph (aryl) migrates less readily than secondary alkyl. Regioselectivity rule: more substituted/electron-rich C migrates → O goes between carbonyl C and the migrating group → ester C-O forms on side of migrating group.

valid_transformations.from: 4,4-disubstituted cyclohexa-2,5-dien-1-one (dienone with two R groups at C-4) + H⁺ — Dienone-Phenol rearrangement
valid_transformations.to: 4-monosubstituted phenol (ArOH) + one R migrates from C-4 to C-3 (1,2-shift); migration aptitude: COOEt > Ph > Me (most stabilising anion migrates fastest)
valid_transformations.conditions: Mechanism: H⁺ protonates enone → allylic carbocation at C-4 → 1,2-migration of the better-migrating group (COOEt > Ph > Me) from C-4 to the adjacent C-3 → dienyl cation → loss of proton → phenol (aromatization). The group that MIGRATES is the one with better migratory aptitude; the remaining group stays at C-4 of the phenol product.
valid_transformations.notes: Migration aptitude in Dienone-Phenol: COOEt (ethoxycarbonyl) > Ph (phenyl) > Me (methyl). The migrating group moves with its bonding electrons (nucleophilic migration). EWG-containing group (COOEt) migrates fastest because it stabilises the developing carbanion character at the migration terminus. Contrast with SN1 where EDG-Ar migrates fastest. Product is a phenol (thermodynamically stable aromatic compound drives rearrangement).

meta_tags.semantic_obfuscation: IUPAC: cyclohexa-2,5-dien-1-one (dienone); dienone-phenol rearrangement; 1,2-shift; migration aptitude COOEt > Ph > Me; aromatization driving force

valid_transformations.from: benzil (1,2-diphenylethanedione, Ar-CO-CO-Ar) + NaOH/H₂O — Benzil-Benzilic acid rearrangement
valid_transformations.to: benzilic acid salt (2-hydroxy-2,2-diphenylacetate, Ar₂C(OH)-COO⁻Na⁺) via 1,2-aryl shift; rate order for aryl substituent effect: EWG-Ar > unsubstituted-Ph > EDG-Ar (controlled by INITIAL ATTACK, not migration); Ph > Ph(Cl) > Ph(OMe)
valid_transformations.conditions: Mechanism: OH⁻ attacks the C=O of benzil → tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate. Then 1,2-aryl migration (with electrons) from one carbon to the adjacent carbon → carboxylate product. RDS = initial nucleophilic addition (OH⁻ attack at C=O). EWG on aryl makes C=O more electrophilic → faster OH⁻ attack → faster reaction. This is therefore INVERSE to Hofmann/Pinnacol/SN1 where EDG on aryl increases rate.
valid_transformations.notes: Key: unlike most 1,2-aryl shifts where EDG on Ar = faster, Benzil-Benzilic rate is determined by INITIAL ATTACK step (nucleophilic addition to carbonyl). EWG on aryl → more electrophilic C=O → faster OH⁻ attack → faster overall. Teacher's sequence: Ph > Ph-Cl > Ph-OMe (from notes). This is the ONE rearrangement where EWG on Ar accelerates (due to initial attack being RDS). Hofmann degradation also uses aryl migration but migration is RDS → EDG = faster (opposite). Benzil-Benzilic is self-oxidation-reduction: one Ar oxidised (COO⁻), one reduced (C-OH).

meta_tags.semantic_obfuscation: IUPAC: 1,2-diphenylethanedione (benzil); 2-hydroxy-2,2-diphenylacetic acid (benzilic acid); initial attack RDS; EWG accelerates benzil-benzilic; inverse of Hofmann/SN1 aryl aptitude

valid_transformations.from: ketone (R₁-C(=O)-R₂) + diazomethane (CH₂N₂) — homologation ring expansion or chain extension
valid_transformations.to: homologated ketone (R₁-C(=O)-CH₂-R₂ or ring-expanded lactone if cyclic) via 1,2-migration; migration aptitude: H > Ph (phenyl) > R (alkyl) [H migrates MOST readily, alkyl LEAST]
valid_transformations.conditions: Mechanism: CH₂N₂ adds to C=O as nucleophile → diazonium zwitterion intermediate (R₁-C(-O⁻)(-CH₂N₂⁺)-R₂). Loss of N₂ → 1,2-shift of group anti-periplanar to N₂ → chain-elongated ketone. Migration aptitude H > Ph > R. Examples: Ph-CO-CH₃ + CH₂N₂ → CH₃-CO-CH₂-Ph (Ph migrates); RCHO (aldehyde, H on C=O) + CH₂N₂ → R-CO-CH₃ (H migrates → methyl ketone). For cyclic ketones: ring expansion by one CH₂.
valid_transformations.notes: In the diazonium intermediate, the group ANTI-PERIPLANAR to N₂ migrates (like Beckmann rearrangement where anti group migrates). Priority: H > Ph > R — H migrates fastest because C-H bond is most easily donated (hyperconjugation-like). Ph > R because Ph can delocalize the developing positive charge. Contrast with Baeyer-Villiger where H also migrates fastest, but phenyl migrates LESS than 2° alkyl in BV (different mechanisms). CH₂N₂ + ketone is NOT the same as Arndt-Eistert (which uses acyl halide + CH₂N₂ → ketene → homologated acid).

conceptual_fragility.description: Introduces historically low-solve-rate concepts. Difficulty weight is archetype-normalised — a concept fragile in one archetype may be routine in another.

concepts.name: Anti-Markovnikov addition (peroxide effect)
concepts.explanation: HBr adds anti-Markovnikov in presence of peroxides via free-radical mechanism. Applies ONLY to HBr, not HCl or HI.
concepts.definition: HBr adds anti-Markovnikov in presence of peroxides via free-radical mechanism. Applies ONLY to HBr, not HCl or HI.
concepts.why_fragile: The rule is counterintuitive: HBr normally follows Markovnikov, but peroxide completely reverses this. The condition 'peroxide' or 'ROOR' must be spotted immediately; students often miss it if buried in the question.
concepts.common_error: Applying Markovnikov's rule even when 'peroxides' or 'hν' conditions are given. Giving 2-bromopropane from propene + HBr/ROOR instead of 1-bromopropane. Also: forgetting that anti-Markovnikov applies only to HBr (not HCl or HI in radicals).

concepts.name: Saytzeff vs Hofmann product selectivity
concepts.explanation: Strong, small base (KOH/alc) gives Saytzeff (more substituted alkene). Bulky base (t-BuOK) gives Hofmann (less substituted). Quaternary ammonium gives Hofmann exclusively.
concepts.definition: Strong, small base (KOH/alc) gives Saytzeff (more substituted alkene). Bulky base (t-BuOK) gives Hofmann (less substituted). Quaternary ammonium gives Hofmann exclusively.
concepts.why_fragile: Students memorise Saytzeff as 'the rule' and forget the exceptions. Bulky base, quaternary ammonium (Hofmann exhaustive), and amine N-oxide all give Hofmann product — three different triggers, all equally testable.
concepts.common_error: Predicting Saytzeff (more substituted alkene) from every elimination. Failing to identify t-BuOK as bulky base. Confusing Hofmann exhaustive methylation product with Saytzeff; forgetting that cyclic systems under N-oxide give endocyclic (Saytzeff-like) product.

concepts.name: SN1 vs SN2 competition
concepts.explanation: SN2: primary substrates, strong nucleophile, polar aprotic solvent, inversion. SN1: tertiary substrates, weak nucleophile, polar protic solvent, racemisation. Secondary: solvent and nucleophile decide.
concepts.definition: SN2: primary substrates, strong nucleophile, polar aprotic solvent, inversion. SN1: tertiary substrates, weak nucleophile, polar protic solvent, racemisation. Secondary: solvent and nucleophile decide.
concepts.why_fragile: Four variables determine SN1 vs SN2: substrate class, nucleophile strength, solvent type, and temperature. Students typically check substrate class and stop, ignoring solvent polarity (polar protic stabilises SN1) and nucleophile bulk (bulky Nu → E2 instead).
concepts.common_error: Saying secondary substrates 'always do SN2.' Ignoring that secondary + polar protic + weak Nu → SN1 is equally valid. Also: predicting pure product when competition gives mixture; failing to note that tertiary CANNOT do SN2.

concepts.name: Stereospecific epoxide ring opening
concepts.explanation: Acid-catalysed: attack at more substituted carbon (Markovnikov), anti addition. Base-catalysed: attack at less substituted carbon (anti-Markovnikov), anti addition. Both give anti product.
concepts.definition: Acid-catalysed: attack at more substituted carbon (Markovnikov), anti addition. Base-catalysed: attack at less substituted carbon (anti-Markovnikov), anti addition. Both give anti product.
concepts.why_fragile: The rule is counterintuitive: HBr normally follows Markovnikov, but peroxide completely reverses this. The condition 'peroxide' or 'ROOR' must be spotted immediately; students often miss it if buried in the question.
concepts.common_error: Applying Markovnikov's rule even when 'peroxides' or 'hν' conditions are given. Giving 2-bromopropane from propene + HBr/ROOR instead of 1-bromopropane. Also: forgetting that anti-Markovnikov applies only to HBr (not HCl or HI in radicals).

concepts.name: Carbocation rearrangement during SN1 and dehydration
concepts.explanation: 1,2-hydride or methyl shift converts a less stable carbocation to a more stable one before nucleophilic attack. Neopentyl and 2-methylpropan-1-ol are classic traps.
concepts.definition: 1,2-hydride or methyl shift converts a less stable carbocation to a more stable one before nucleophilic attack. Neopentyl and 2-methylpropan-1-ol are classic traps.
concepts.why_fragile: Students must proactively ask 'is there a more stable cation available?' at every carbocation intermediate. Rearrangement is NOT automatic — it only occurs if it leads to a more stable cation. Multiple rearrangements can occur sequentially.
concepts.common_error: Missing the rearrangement entirely and predicting the unrearranged product. Performing the rearrangement in the wrong direction (less stable → more stable, never reverse). Forgetting that neopentyl and cyclobutylcarbinyl systems rearrange almost exclusively.

concepts.name: Regioselectivity in unsymmetrical epoxide opening
concepts.explanation: Nucleophile attacks from the backside. Under acidic conditions, attack at the more substituted (more electrophilic) carbon; under basic conditions, attack at the less hindered carbon.
concepts.definition: Nucleophile attacks from the backside. Under acidic conditions, attack at the more substituted (more electrophilic) carbon; under basic conditions, attack at the less hindered carbon.
concepts.why_fragile: Two rules apply depending on conditions: acid opens at more-substituted carbon (Markovnikov-like); base opens at less-substituted carbon (SN2). Additionally, both conditions give overall anti (trans) addition — students often forget the stereo outcome or mix the two conditions.
concepts.common_error: Opening at the wrong carbon (applying acid rule under basic conditions or vice versa). Predicting syn addition product instead of anti. Forgetting that cyclopentene oxide + base → trans-cyclopentane-1,2-diol.

concepts.name: Keto-enol tautomerism and enolisation
concepts.explanation: Alpha-hydrogens are acidic (pKa ~20). Base gives enolate; acid gives enol. Reactivity: enolate attacks electrophiles at carbon. Asymmetric ketones give kinetic vs thermodynamic enolate.
concepts.definition: Alpha-hydrogens are acidic (pKa ~20). Base gives enolate; acid gives enol. Reactivity: enolate attacks electrophiles at carbon. Asymmetric ketones give kinetic vs thermodynamic enolate.
concepts.why_fragile: The keto form is thermodynamically favoured for simple ketones/aldehydes, but the enol form is preferred for phenols (aromaticity) and β-diketones (chelation). Students apply the 'keto preferred' rule universally.
concepts.common_error: Predicting keto form of phenol (destroys aromaticity → incorrect). Underestimating enol content of β-diketones (up to 80–90%). Forgetting that enolisation requires α-hydrogen — carbonyl with no α-H cannot enolise.

concepts.name: Aldol condensation: crossed and intramolecular
concepts.explanation: Requires α-hydrogen. Crossed aldol is complicated by four possible products unless one component has no α-H (e.g., formaldehyde, benzaldehyde, acetone). Intramolecular gives rings.
concepts.definition: Requires α-hydrogen. Crossed aldol is complicated by four possible products unless one component has no α-H (e.g., formaldehyde, benzaldehyde, acetone). Intramolecular gives rings.
concepts.why_fragile: Crossed aldol gives four possible products when both reactants have α-hydrogens — students forget this and predict one clean product. Intramolecular aldol (cyclisation) has ring-size constraints. Acid-catalysed aldol mechanism differs from base-catalysed.
concepts.common_error: Predicting clean crossed aldol from two different aldehydes with α-H (gives intractable mixture). Forgetting that intramolecular aldol at 5 or 6-membered ring transition state is favoured. Not recognising that β-hydroxy carbonyl dehydrates on heating.

concepts.name: Cannizzaro reaction requirement
concepts.explanation: Disproportionation of aldehydes having NO α-hydrogen (HCHO, C₆H₅CHO, (CH₃)₃CCHO) under conc. NaOH. One molecule oxidised to acid, other reduced to alcohol.
concepts.definition: Disproportionation of aldehydes having NO α-hydrogen (HCHO, C₆H₅CHO, (CH₃)₃CCHO) under conc. NaOH. One molecule oxidised to acid, other reduced to alcohol.
concepts.why_fragile: The Cannizzaro reaction only works for aldehydes WITHOUT α-H. Students apply it to all aldehydes. The disproportionation gives exactly 50% alcohol + 50% acid — students often write a different ratio.
concepts.common_error: Applying Cannizzaro to acetaldehyde or other aldehydes with α-H (those undergo aldol condensation instead). Getting the ratio wrong (it is always 1:1 alcohol:acid). Forgetting that crossed Cannizzaro uses HCHO preferentially as the hydride donor.

concepts.name: Acidity order: carboxylic acids > phenols > water > alcohols > terminal alkynes
concepts.explanation: Counterintuitive because phenol (aromatic) is more acidic than alcohol despite both having OH. Resonance stabilisation of phenoxide ion. Effect of EWG/EDG on acid strength.
concepts.definition: Counterintuitive because phenol (aromatic) is more acidic than alcohol despite both having OH. Resonance stabilisation of phenoxide ion. Effect of EWG/EDG on acid strength.
concepts.why_fragile: The acidity order is counterintuitive at multiple points: (1) phenol more acidic than water despite being 'carbon compound'; (2) terminal alkyne (pKa~25) more acidic than NH₃ (pKa~38); (3) carboxylic acids ionise in water but phenols barely do.
concepts.common_error: Placing alcohols more acidic than water. Placing alkyne less acidic than NH₃. Forgetting that picric acid (phenol with 3 NO₂) is as acidic as HCl and reacts with NaHCO₃. Neglecting inductive vs resonance effects on substituted carboxylic acids.

concepts.name: Basicity order of amines: aliphatic > ammonia > aromatic
concepts.explanation: Electron-donating alkyl groups increase basicity. Lone pair delocalised into ring in aniline reduces basicity. Among aromatic amines, meta-substitution with EWG decreases basicity most.
concepts.definition: Electron-donating alkyl groups increase basicity. Lone pair delocalised into ring in aniline reduces basicity. Among aromatic amines, meta-substitution with EWG decreases basicity most.
concepts.why_fragile: Amine basicity has multiple competing factors: electron donation increases basicity, but aromatic conjugation donates lone pair into ring (decreasing basicity). Aqueous vs gas phase basicity reverses the order for methylamines due to solvation effects.
concepts.common_error: Ranking aromatic amines higher than aliphatic amines. Placing tertiary aliphatic amine as most basic in water (it is in gas phase, but in water secondary amine is often most basic due to solvation). Forgetting that amide N is essentially non-basic.

concepts.name: Hofmann bromamide degradation
concepts.explanation: Converts primary amide RCONH₂ to primary amine RNH₂ — the product has one fewer carbon. Often tested by asking for carbon count of product.
concepts.definition: Converts primary amide RCONH₂ to primary amine RNH₂ — the product has one fewer carbon. Often tested by asking for carbon count of product.
concepts.why_fragile: Students memorise Saytzeff as 'the rule' and forget the exceptions. Bulky base, quaternary ammonium (Hofmann exhaustive), and amine N-oxide all give Hofmann product — three different triggers, all equally testable.
concepts.common_error: Predicting Saytzeff (more substituted alkene) from every elimination. Failing to identify t-BuOK as bulky base. Confusing Hofmann exhaustive methylation product with Saytzeff; forgetting that cyclic systems under N-oxide give endocyclic (Saytzeff-like) product.

concepts.name: Hydroboration-oxidation stereoselectivity
concepts.explanation: Syn addition of BH₃, then H₂O₂/NaOH with retention of configuration. Net result: anti-Markovnikov, syn addition, giving opposite face alcohol to mCPBA epoxidation-opening.
concepts.definition: Syn addition of BH₃, then H₂O₂/NaOH with retention of configuration. Net result: anti-Markovnikov, syn addition, giving opposite face alcohol to mCPBA epoxidation-opening.
concepts.why_fragile: The rule is counterintuitive: HBr normally follows Markovnikov, but peroxide completely reverses this. The condition 'peroxide' or 'ROOR' must be spotted immediately; students often miss it if buried in the question.
concepts.common_error: Applying Markovnikov's rule even when 'peroxides' or 'hν' conditions are given. Giving 2-bromopropane from propene + HBr/ROOR instead of 1-bromopropane. Also: forgetting that anti-Markovnikov applies only to HBr (not HCl or HI in radicals).

concepts.name: Rearrangement during elimination (ring expansion/contraction)
concepts.explanation: Cyclobutyl → cyclopentyl and related ring changes when carbocation intermediate can relieve ring strain by methyl/hydride shift before elimination.
concepts.definition: Cyclobutyl → cyclopentyl and related ring changes when carbocation intermediate can relieve ring strain by methyl/hydride shift before elimination.
concepts.why_fragile: E2 requires anti-periplanar H and LG (180° dihedral). In cyclohexane, only trans-diaxial arrangement satisfies this. Students forget this geometric constraint and predict E2 from equatorial LG substrates.
concepts.common_error: Predicting E2 from equatorial LG in cyclohexane ring (need axial LG and anti-axial H). Predicting Saytzeff from bulky base (gives Hofmann). Forgetting that E2 is 2nd-order (bimolecular). Predicting E2 from norbornyl tosylate (geometrically impossible in rigid bicyclic).

concepts.name: Directing effects in multiply-substituted benzenes
concepts.explanation: Two substituents may cooperate (ortho/para directors → same position) or conflict. In conflict, stronger activator wins. Halogen: deactivating but ortho/para directing.
concepts.definition: Two substituents may cooperate (ortho/para directors → same position) or conflict. In conflict, stronger activator wins. Halogen: deactivating but ortho/para directing.
concepts.why_fragile: This concept appears simple but has hidden exceptions or conditions that modify the expected outcome. The rule breaks down under specific substrate structures, reagent choices, or reaction conditions that JEE Advanced specifically tests.
concepts.common_error: Applying the standard rule without checking whether the exceptional condition is present. Not recognising the specific structural feature or reagent variant that triggers the different behaviour. Giving only one product when the question has special conditions producing a different outcome.

concepts.name: Iodoform test scope
concepts.explanation: Positive for CH₃CHO, CH₃COR (methyl ketones), and alcohols CH₃CH(OH)R. NOT for other ketones or aldehydes. Ethanol also positive. Useful distinction in structure elucidation.
concepts.definition: Positive for CH₃CHO, CH₃COR (methyl ketones), and alcohols CH₃CH(OH)R. NOT for other ketones or aldehydes. Ethanol also positive. Useful distinction in structure elucidation.
concepts.why_fragile: Haloform reaction requires a specific structural motif: CH₃CO- group (methyl ketone) or CH₃CH(OH)- (which oxidises to CH₃CO-). Students apply it to all ketones or forget that secondary alcohols with methyl group also give iodoform.
concepts.common_error: Testing 2-pentanone with iodoform test (negative — no CH₃CO-). Forgetting that ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃CHO under oxidative conditions in I₂/NaOH) gives iodoform. Predicting iodoform from formaldehyde (gives iodoform only partially, then HCOO⁻).

concepts.name: Tollens vs Fehling selectivity
concepts.explanation: Both detect aldehydes. Fehling fails with aromatic aldehydes (e.g., benzaldehyde). Tollens works with all aldehydes. Formic acid (HCOOH) also reduces Tollens. Glucose reduces both.
concepts.definition: Both detect aldehydes. Fehling fails with aromatic aldehydes (e.g., benzaldehyde). Tollens works with all aldehydes. Formic acid (HCOOH) also reduces Tollens. Glucose reduces both.
concepts.why_fragile: Aromaticity criteria (Hückel rule: 4n+2 π electrons, cyclic, planar, conjugated) must all be satisfied. Students forget the planarity requirement or miscalculate π electron count (e.g., in charged species, the charge changes the electron count).
concepts.common_error: Applying Hückel rule without checking planarity (COT is planar in tub conformation → not aromatic despite 8π → antiaromatic). Forgetting that a lone pair on ring atom counts as π electrons when in a p-orbital (pyrrole N: 2 electrons in ring). Not recognising charged aromatic species (cyclopentadienyl anion = 6π = aromatic).

concepts.name: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis scope
concepts.explanation: Gives only primary amines; 2° and 3° amines cannot be made. Cannot be used with aryl halides (no SN2 on arene). Clean alternative to ammonolysis which gives mixtures.
concepts.definition: Gives only primary amines; 2° and 3° amines cannot be made. Cannot be used with aryl halides (no SN2 on arene). Clean alternative to ammonolysis which gives mixtures.
concepts.why_fragile: Gabriel synthesis gives ONLY primary amines. Students forget this limitation and try to make secondary or tertiary amines. Also: the synthesis requires two steps (phthalimide alkylation then hydrazine hydrolysis or KOH hydrolysis).
concepts.common_error: Attempting Gabriel synthesis to make secondary amine. Forgetting that the last step (hydrolysis) requires either hydrazine or alkaline conditions — the N-alkyl phthalimide does not hydrolyse in dilute acid. Confusing Gabriel (1° amine) with Hofmann (1° amine, different route).

concepts.name: Basicity order depends on alkyl group size
concepts.explanation: The standard order 2° > 1° > 3° > NH3 only holds for small R groups (R=Me). For R=Et: 2° > 3° > 1° > NH3. For R=iPr: 1° > NH3 > 2° > 3°. For R=tBu: NH3 > 1° > 2° > 3° — steric hindrance completely inverts the order. In water, solvation stabilises smaller amines more, pulling 3° down; in gas phase, inductive effect dominates.
concepts.definition: The standard order 2° > 1° > 3° > NH3 only holds for small R groups (R=Me). For R=Et: 2° > 3° > 1° > NH3. For R=iPr: 1° > NH3 > 2° > 3°. For R=tBu: NH3 > 1° > 2° > 3° — steric hindrance completely inverts the order. In water, solvation stabilises smaller amines more, pulling 3° down; in gas phase, inductive effect dominates.

concepts.name: LAH reduction of amide preserves carbon count; Hofmann degradation loses one carbon
concepts.explanation: RCONH2 + LAH → R-CH2-NH2 (same number of C, amide C becomes CH2). RCONH2 + KOH/Br2 → R-NH2 (loses the carbonyl C, Hofmann degradation). Students commonly expect both give the same amine. Critical consequence: benzamide + LAH = benzylamine (Ph-CH2-NH2), NOT aniline.
concepts.definition: RCONH2 + LAH → R-CH2-NH2 (same number of C, amide C becomes CH2). RCONH2 + KOH/Br2 → R-NH2 (loses the carbonyl C, Hofmann degradation). Students commonly expect both give the same amine. Critical consequence: benzamide + LAH = benzylamine (Ph-CH2-NH2), NOT aniline.

concepts.name: Selective reduction with (NH4)2S reduces the LESS electron-deficient NO2
concepts.explanation: In polynitro aromatics, mild reagents like (NH4)2S or NH4SH selectively reduce the NO2 group that is LESS electron-deficient (i.e., less activated toward reduction). Counter-intuitive: stronger EWG neighbours make a NO2 harder to reduce with mild agents. Example: in 2,4-dinitrotoluene with OCH3, the NO2 ortho to OCH3 (EDG) is reduced first.
concepts.definition: In polynitro aromatics, mild reagents like (NH4)2S or NH4SH selectively reduce the NO2 group that is LESS electron-deficient (i.e., less activated toward reduction). Counter-intuitive: stronger EWG neighbours make a NO2 harder to reduce with mild agents. Example: in 2,4-dinitrotoluene with OCH3, the NO2 ortho to OCH3 (EDG) is reduced first.
concepts.why_fragile: Inductive effect decays rapidly with distance (1/r³ approximately). Students apply inductive effect at 3 or 4 bonds away as if it were as strong as at 1 bond. Also: halogens have -I (destabilise cation, stabilise anion) but +M (donate into ring) — two opposing effects.
concepts.common_error: Applying full inductive effect at the γ-position. Ranking halogens as electron-donating by inductive effect (they are electron-withdrawing inductively). Forgetting that NR₂ is +M but very weakly -I, so overall it is strongly electron-donating.

concepts.name: Condition-dependent reduction of ArNO2
concepts.explanation: Acidic (Sn/HCl, Fe/HCl, Zn/AcOH, H2/Pt): → ArNH2. Neutral (Zn/NH4Cl/H2O): → ArNHOH (phenylhydroxylamine). Basic (Zn/NaOH, 1 mol): → Ar-N=N-Ar (azobenzene). Strongly basic (Zn/NaOH, 2 mol or LAH): → ArNH-NHAr (hydrazobenzene). Excess basic (Zn/NaOH 3+ mol): → azoxybenzene.
concepts.definition: Acidic (Sn/HCl, Fe/HCl, Zn/AcOH, H2/Pt): → ArNH2. Neutral (Zn/NH4Cl/H2O): → ArNHOH (phenylhydroxylamine). Basic (Zn/NaOH, 1 mol): → Ar-N=N-Ar (azobenzene). Strongly basic (Zn/NaOH, 2 mol or LAH): → ArNH-NHAr (hydrazobenzene). Excess basic (Zn/NaOH 3+ mol): → azoxybenzene.

concepts.name: Isocyanide (R-NC) vs cyanide (R-CN) on reduction give different amine classes
concepts.explanation: R-CN + H2/Pt or LAH → R-CH2-NH2 (primary amine, one extra C inserted). R-NC + H2/Pt or LAH → R-NH-CH3 (secondary amine, the isocyanide C becomes CH3). Students often assume both give 1° amine.
concepts.definition: R-CN + H2/Pt or LAH → R-CH2-NH2 (primary amine, one extra C inserted). R-NC + H2/Pt or LAH → R-NH-CH3 (secondary amine, the isocyanide C becomes CH3). Students often assume both give 1° amine.

concepts.name: Gabriel synthesis limitations: no ArX, no 2° or 3° products
concepts.explanation: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis only works with primary alkyl halides (SN2). ArX cannot be used (aryl halides don't undergo SN2 without activation). Product is exclusively 1° amine — cannot make 2° or 3°. This is often tested as 'which of these cannot be made by Gabriel synthesis?'

concepts.name: Hofmann exhaustive methylation gives mixture, not selective product
concepts.explanation: NH3 + excess RX + heat → statistical mixture of 1°, 2°, 3° amines AND quaternary ammonium salt. Each successive alkylation is less selective. This is NOT a way to make a pure higher amine.

concepts.name: Benzidine rearrangement: major product is 4,4' not 2,4'
concepts.explanation: Hydrazobenzene + HCl/heat → Benzidine (4,4'-diaminobiphenyl) is MAJOR (~70%). 2,4'-diaminobiphenyl (diphenyline) is the minor product (~30%). The [3,3]-sigmatropic-type rearrangement through a cyclic transition state favours the para-para (4,4') connectivity.

concepts.name: Carbylamine test uses dichlorocarbene as reactive intermediate
concepts.explanation: CHCl3 + 3KOH → :CCl2 (dichlorocarbene) + KCl + H2O. x=3 equivalents of KOH are needed. Carbene reacts with R-NH2 (must be 1° amine) → R-N=C (isocyanide, foul smell). 2° and 3° amines do NOT give this test.

concepts.name: Oxidation of aniline: KMnO4 gives benzoquinone, Caro's acid gives nitrobenzene
concepts.explanation: PhNH2 + KMnO4/heat → para-benzoquinone (ring C-H oxidation dominates). PhNH2 + Caro's acid (H2SO5) → nitrobenzene (N oxidation only). Students expect KMnO4 to give nitrobenzene (which would require N oxidation only). The reagent determines which bond is oxidised.

concepts.name: Solubility in water order for amines inverted from boiling point order
concepts.explanation: Water solubility: NH3 > 1° > 2° > 3° (more H-bonds = more soluble). Boiling point: 1° > 2° > 3° (same reasoning — more H-bonding = higher bp). 3° amines cannot H-bond with each other (no N-H) so lowest bp and solubility.

concepts.name: Dow's process: product is sodium phenoxide, not phenol directly
concepts.explanation: PhCl + NaOH at 623K/300 atm → sodium phenoxide (Ph-O⁻Na⁺). Acidification (H⁺) is a SEPARATE step to get phenol. Students assume phenol forms directly and forget the acidification step.

concepts.name: Cumene process: phenol + acetone (not phenol alone)
concepts.explanation: Cumene (isopropylbenzene) → CHP → dil H₂SO₄ → phenol + acetone (1:1 molar, 58g acetone per 94g phenol). Migration order: Ar > R > H (phenyl migrates, not methyl). Students drop the acetone co-product from products.

concepts.name: Diarylmethane peroxide: electron-rich Ar migrates selectively
concepts.explanation: In Ar-CH(OOH)-Ar' rearrangement, the MORE electron-rich aryl ring migrates preferentially. OMe-phenyl migrates over NO₂-phenyl → gives OMe-phenol + NO₂-benzaldehyde. Reversed from what students expect based on stability.
concepts.definition: In Ar-CH(OOH)-Ar' rearrangement, the MORE electron-rich aryl ring migrates preferentially. OMe-phenyl migrates over NO₂-phenyl → gives OMe-phenol + NO₂-benzaldehyde. Reversed from what students expect based on stability.

concepts.name: Dienone-phenol rearrangement: migration order is -COO⁻ > R > Ar
concepts.explanation: In acid-catalysed dienone-phenol rearrangement, esters and carboxylates migrate BETTER than R groups, which migrate better than Ar. This is opposite to the Ar > R > H order in carbocation rearrangements. The anchimerically-assisted nature differs.
concepts.definition: In acid-catalysed dienone-phenol rearrangement, esters and carboxylates migrate BETTER than R groups, which migrate better than Ar. This is opposite to the Ar > R > H order in carbocation rearrangements. The anchimerically-assisted nature differs.
concepts.why_fragile: Students must proactively ask 'is there a more stable cation available?' at every carbocation intermediate. Rearrangement is NOT automatic — it only occurs if it leads to a more stable cation. Multiple rearrangements can occur sequentially.
concepts.common_error: Missing the rearrangement entirely and predicting the unrearranged product. Performing the rearrangement in the wrong direction (less stable → more stable, never reverse). Forgetting that neopentyl and cyclobutylcarbinyl systems rearrange almost exclusively.

concepts.name: Fries rearrangement vs Claisen rearrangement — different substrates and mechanisms
concepts.explanation: Fries: Ph-O-CO-R + AlCl₃/Δ → hydroxy aryl ketone (acyl migrates from O to C-ring via acylium; Lewis acid catalysed). Claisen: Ph-O-CH₂-CH=CH₂ + heat → 2-allylphenol (thermal [3,3]-sigmatropic; no catalyst). Different bonds form and break. Students conflate them.
concepts.definition: Fries: Ph-O-CO-R + AlCl₃/Δ → hydroxy aryl ketone (acyl migrates from O to C-ring via acylium; Lewis acid catalysed). Claisen: Ph-O-CH₂-CH=CH₂ + heat → 2-allylphenol (thermal [3,3]-sigmatropic; no catalyst). Different bonds form and break. Students conflate them.

concepts.name: Claisen rearrangement: allyl migrates to ortho with inversion of allyl terminus
concepts.explanation: The gamma-carbon (far end) of the allyl group bonds to the ortho position of the ring. The double bond inverts: allyl was CH₂-CH=CH₂, new bond forms at CH₂ (was terminal). If ortho blocked, double migration can place it para.

concepts.why_fragile: Stereochemical outcomes require tracking configuration through each step. Students who do not draw the mechanism or use a 3D representation frequently get inversion/retention/racemisation wrong. SN2 → inversion, SN1 → racemisation, SNi → retention — all three are tested.
concepts.common_error: Predicting inversion in SN1 (gives racemisation). Predicting retention in SN2 (gives inversion). Missing double inversion (net retention via tosylate → inversion then SN2 → second inversion). Forgetting that E2 is stereospecific (anti-periplanar) while E1 is not.

concepts.name: FeCl₃ test: violet with phenol/enols only, NOT all -OH compounds
concepts.explanation: FeCl₃ gives violet/purple complex with phenols and enolizable carbonyls (β-keto esters, cyclopentane-1,3-dione, acetoacetic ester) because these form enolate-Fe complexes. Simple ketones without enol give NEGATIVE. Acetate → blood red. Formate → similar. Students confuse -OH type: enol-OH positive, alcohol-OH negative.

concepts.name: Phenol acidity: reacts with Na and NaOH but NOT Na₂CO₃
concepts.explanation: Phenol pKa ~10. Na₂CO₃ (pKa2 ~10.3) — equilibrium barely favours right; effectively no visible reaction. NaHCO₃ (pKa ~6.4): even more acidic than CO₂, definitely no reaction. Students assume all acids react with carbonate. Phenol IS more acidic than alcohol but less acidic than carboxylic acid.

concepts.why_fragile: The acidity order is counterintuitive at multiple points: (1) phenol more acidic than water despite being 'carbon compound'; (2) terminal alkyne (pKa~25) more acidic than NH₃ (pKa~38); (3) carboxylic acids ionise in water but phenols barely do.
concepts.common_error: Placing alcohols more acidic than water. Placing alkyne less acidic than NH₃. Forgetting that picric acid (phenol with 3 NO₂) is as acidic as HCl and reacts with NaHCO₃. Neglecting inductive vs resonance effects on substituted carboxylic acids.

concepts.name: Phenol bromination: Br₂/H₂O gives 2,4,6-tribromination without catalyst
concepts.explanation: Phenol's ring is so activated that aqueous Br₂ gives IMMEDIATE white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol without any Lewis acid. To get monobromination (4-Br), must use non-polar solvent (Br₂/CS₂ or CCl₄) which prevents ionisation. Students assume mono-substitution like benzene.

concepts.name: Phenol does NOT react with Lucas, PCl₃, SOCl₂, or HX like an aliphatic alcohol
concepts.explanation: Lucas reagent (conc HCl/ZnCl₂): NO reaction with phenol (no SN1/SN2 at sp² carbon). PCl₃, SOCl₂: NO reaction. HX: NO reaction. Only PCl₅ reacts (slow) to give PhCl. Phenol behaves as an acid (forms phenoxide) rather than as an alcohol in substitution chemistry.

concepts.why_fragile: Four variables determine SN1 vs SN2: substrate class, nucleophile strength, solvent type, and temperature. Students typically check substrate class and stop, ignoring solvent polarity (polar protic stabilises SN1) and nucleophile bulk (bulky Nu → E2 instead).
concepts.common_error: Saying secondary substrates 'always do SN2.' Ignoring that secondary + polar protic + weak Nu → SN1 is equally valid. Also: predicting pure product when competition gives mixture; failing to note that tertiary CANNOT do SN2.

concepts.name: Williamson synthesis: 3° alkyl halide gives elimination, not ether
concepts.explanation: RO⁻ is a strong base. With 3° R'X, E2 dominates over SN2 → alkene + ROH. Rule: use 1° (or methyl) R'X with any alkoxide. Use the hindered alcohol as the alkoxide and the unhindered one as the halide. Never use tertiary halide in Williamson.

concepts.why_fragile: E2 requires anti-periplanar H and LG (180° dihedral). In cyclohexane, only trans-diaxial arrangement satisfies this. Students forget this geometric constraint and predict E2 from equatorial LG substrates.
concepts.common_error: Predicting E2 from equatorial LG in cyclohexane ring (need axial LG and anti-axial H). Predicting Saytzeff from bulky base (gives Hofmann). Forgetting that E2 is 2nd-order (bimolecular). Predicting E2 from norbornyl tosylate (geometrically impossible in rigid bicyclic).

concepts.name: Liebermann-Nitroso test detects phenol AND secondary amine with 3-colour sequence
concepts.explanation: Phenol + NaNO₂/HCl → 4-nitrosophenol (green-blue) ↔ tautomer. + conc H₂SO₄/Δ → indophenol (RED). + NaOH → dark BLUE (Na-indophenolate). 2° amine similarly gives colour. Students know one colour; the 3-step sequence is the trap.

concepts.why_fragile: The keto form is thermodynamically favoured for simple ketones/aldehydes, but the enol form is preferred for phenols (aromaticity) and β-diketones (chelation). Students apply the 'keto preferred' rule universally.
concepts.common_error: Predicting keto form of phenol (destroys aromaticity → incorrect). Underestimating enol content of β-diketones (up to 80–90%). Forgetting that enolisation requires α-hydrogen — carbonyl with no α-H cannot enolise.

concepts.name: Phenolphthalein: colorless at BOTH low AND very high pH
concepts.explanation: Phenolphthalein: colorless at pH < 8.3 AND at pH > 10 (excess NaOH deprotonates both phenolic OH groups, giving colorless trianion). Pink ONLY at pH 8.3-10. Students think 'add NaOH → pink' always works, but excess NaOH decolorises it.

concepts.name: Mixed ether (ArOR) cleavage: ArO-C bond breaks, NOT the Ar-O bond
concepts.explanation: In ArO-R + conc HX: the alkyl-O bond breaks (C-O where C is sp3) to give ArOH + RX. The Ar-O bond is stronger due to lone pair delocalization into ring. Products: phenol + alkyl halide. Students predict PhX + ROH.

concepts.why_fragile: Resonance structures are not real species — they are mental constructs. Students draw resonance structures as if they are equilibrium species. Major resonance contributor (most bonds, neutral atoms, complete octets) determines actual properties of the molecule.
concepts.common_error: Treating resonance structures as interconverting species (they are not). Ignoring the weight of resonance contributors (a minor contributor with charge separation does not equally contribute to hybrid). Forgetting that resonance delocalisation determines reactivity site.

concepts.name: Ether peroxide: forms at alpha-C of ether, explosive when heated
concepts.explanation: Stored diethyl ether slowly forms Et-O-CH(OOH)-CH₃ at the alpha-C-H via radical chain with O₂. This peroxide accumulates and is explosive when ether is distilled. Never heat or concentrate old ether without first testing for peroxides (e.g., KI/starch paper).

concepts.why_fragile: The rule is counterintuitive: HBr normally follows Markovnikov, but peroxide completely reverses this. The condition 'peroxide' or 'ROOR' must be spotted immediately; students often miss it if buried in the question.
concepts.common_error: Applying Markovnikov's rule even when 'peroxides' or 'hν' conditions are given. Giving 2-bromopropane from propene + HBr/ROOR instead of 1-bromopropane. Also: forgetting that anti-Markovnikov applies only to HBr (not HCl or HI in radicals).

concepts.name: YG protonation priority rule: -OH protonates first only if C⁺ is resonance-stabilized
concepts.explanation: If protonating the -OH group gives a resonance-stabilized carbocation (benzylic, allylic, tertiary), then -OH is protonated first. Otherwise, the less electronegative system (alkene C=C or alkyne C≡C) is protonated first because it's a weaker base. Key for dehydration and acid-catalysed cyclisation problems.

concepts.name: Phenol cannot be esterified directly with carboxylic acid (Fischer esterification fails)
concepts.explanation: Fischer esterification (RCOOH + ROH → acid cat) works for aliphatic alcohols. Phenol is too weakly nucleophilic (lone pair delocalized into ring) for direct esterification. Must use more reactive acyl chloride or anhydride instead. Students try to make phenyl esters with RCOOH/H⁺ and get no reaction.

concepts.name: H₂SO₄ dehydration temperature windows
concepts.explanation: Three distinct temperature ranges give three products: T<110°C → alkyl sulfate (R-OSO₂OH); 110-170°C → ether (R-O-R, intermolecular); T>170°C → alkene (E1, Saytzeff). Exact cutoffs are exam-tested.

concepts.why_fragile: Students memorise Saytzeff as 'the rule' and forget the exceptions. Bulky base, quaternary ammonium (Hofmann exhaustive), and amine N-oxide all give Hofmann product — three different triggers, all equally testable.
concepts.common_error: Predicting Saytzeff (more substituted alkene) from every elimination. Failing to identify t-BuOK as bulky base. Confusing Hofmann exhaustive methylation product with Saytzeff; forgetting that cyclic systems under N-oxide give endocyclic (Saytzeff-like) product.

concepts.name: ThO₂ gives Hofmann product (anti-Saytzeff) uniquely
concepts.explanation: All dehydrating agents (H₂SO₄, Al₂O₃, POCl₃, KHSO₄, ZnCl₂, H₃PO₄) give Saytzeff (E1 or E2) EXCEPT ThO₂/Δ which gives E1cb → Hofmann (least substituted alkene). Students always include ThO₂ with other agents.

concepts.name: AAc2 acyl-O cleavage vs AAL alkyl-O cleavage
concepts.explanation: In AAc2 (most common), the nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon → acyl-O bond breaks. In AAL1/BAL1, the alkyl-O bond breaks (SN1 on the alkyl part). ¹⁸O labeling distinguishes: in AAc2 the ¹⁸O from acid OH goes to water; in AAL1 it goes to the tert-alcohol product.

concepts.name: Rate of esterification ∝ 1/steric hindrance
concepts.explanation: Both acid AND alcohol steric bulk independently reduce rate. Alcohol order: MeOH > EtOH > i-PrOH > t-BuOH (t-BuOH barely reacts). Acid order: H-COOH > Me-COOH > Et-COOH >> iso-COOH > t-COOH. Phenol < aliphatic alcohol (PhO⁻ poor nucleophile). Acyl-Cl > anhydride > acid as electrophile.

concepts.name: CH₂N₂ reactivity selectivity: R-COOH > Ph-OH > R-OH
concepts.explanation: Diazomethane (CH₂N₂) reacts with acidic O-H first. Order matches acidity. In a molecule with both COOH and OH, 1 eq CH₂N₂ methylates COOH selectively. Alcohol reacts last (needs excess CH₂N₂).

concepts.name: Glycerol + KHSO₄/Δ gives Acrolein (not a simple diol product)
concepts.explanation: Glycerol dehydration under KHSO₄ or H₂SO₄ eliminates 2 H₂O to give acrolein (CH₂=CH-CHO), an α,β-unsaturated aldehyde. The 1,2-diol portion of glycerol dehydrates first, then the vinyl alcohol tautomerizes. Classic JEE detection reaction — acrolein has pungent smell.

concepts.name: AAc1 trap: pivalic acid + MeOH/H₂SO₄ → t-BuOMe (not ester)
concepts.explanation: Pivalic acid (Me₃C-COOH) under H₂SO₄ + MeOH goes AAc1: protonation → acylium (Me₃C-CO⁺) → loses CO → t-Bu⁺ → MeOH → t-BuOMe (ether). Product is an ETHER, not an ester. The CO loss is the trap. D.U. counting on product confirms.

concepts.name: BAc1 and AAL2 are the two mechanisms that NEVER happen
concepts.explanation: Of 8 possible ester hydrolysis mechanisms (A/B × Ac/Al × 1/2), exactly two never occur: BAc1 (acylium in base = impossible) and AAL2 (H₂O is too weak a nucleophile for SN2 on alkyl-O in acid). Students must remember which 2 of 8 are forbidden.

concepts.name: CAN test color depends on alcohol degree
concepts.explanation: CAN = (NH₄)₂[Ce(NO₃)₆]. 1° and 2° alcohols give RED complex (positive). 3° alcohol and phenol give BROWN/GREEN (NOT red). In JEE Mains, phenol is considered CAN-negative; in JEE Advanced context, phenol may be tested as brown/green. The Ce⁴⁺→Ce³⁺ reduction drives the test.

concepts.name: Victor Meyer: 3° nitroalkane gives COLORLESS (no reaction with HNO₂)
concepts.explanation: Victor Meyer test: 3° nitroalkane has no α-H → cannot react with HNO₂ → no nitroso-nitronate formed → no color change → COLORLESS. 1° gives RED (aci-form, NaOH-soluble). 2° gives BLUE/insoluble. All 3 must be memorized. The α-H requirement is the mechanistic key.

concepts.name: Saponification (BAc2) is irreversible; acid hydrolysis (AAc2) is reversible
concepts.explanation: Acid hydrolysis of esters (AAc2, H₃O⁺) is an equilibrium — you need excess water or remove product to drive it forward. Saponification (NaOH) is irreversible because the carboxylate product (RCOO⁻) cannot react back with R'OH under basic conditions. Irreversibility is a JEE IV-type comparative question.

concepts.name: Acidity ordering for Na/NaOH/NaHCO₃ reactivity
concepts.explanation: Full acidity order: R-SO₃H > picric acid > squaric acid > RCOOH > phenol > H₂O > R-OH > R-C≡CH > R-NH₂ > R-H. Na metal reacts with all from R-OH upward. NaOH reacts from phenol upward. NaHCO₃ reacts from RCOOH upward. Exception: 2,4-dinitrophenol + NaHCO₃ reacts (super-acidic phenol).

concepts.name: Birnbaum-Simonini ratio rule (ester vs R-I)
concepts.explanation: 1 mol RCOOAg + 1 mol I2 → R-I (major). But 2 mol RCOOAg (excess Ag) + 1 mol I2 → R-COO-R (ester, major). The MORE Ag salt you add, the MORE ester you get — counterintuitive.

concepts.why_fragile: Inductive effect decays rapidly with distance (1/r³ approximately). Students apply inductive effect at 3 or 4 bonds away as if it were as strong as at 1 bond. Also: halogens have -I (destabilise cation, stabilise anion) but +M (donate into ring) — two opposing effects.
concepts.common_error: Applying full inductive effect at the γ-position. Ranking halogens as electron-donating by inductive effect (they are electron-withdrawing inductively). Forgetting that NR₂ is +M but very weakly -I, so overall it is strongly electron-donating.

concepts.name: Dipole moment order of methyl halides (CH3Cl maximum)
concepts.explanation: CH3F < CH3Cl > CH3Br > CH3I. CH3Cl has the HIGHEST dipole, not CH3F. Reason: μ = q × d; q (electronegativity) decreases F→I, but d (bond length) increases F→I; the product q×d peaks at Cl.

concepts.name: Haloform rate reversal in acidic vs basic medium
concepts.explanation: Basic medium: γ1 < γ2 < γ3 (successive halogenations get faster; CX3 more acidic). Acidic medium (X2/CH3COONa): γ1 >> γ2 >> γ3 (first halogenation fastest; enol mechanism, X on alpha makes enol formation slower). Acid gives mono, base gives trihalide.

concepts.name: Kinetic isotope effect proves haloform RDS
concepts.explanation: R-CO-CD3 reacts slower than R-CO-CH3 in haloform. Proves rate-determining step involves C-H (not C-D) bond breaking (alpha deprotonation). Also: F2 = Cl2 = Br2 = I2 same rate → halogen is NOT in the RDS.

concepts.name: Borodine-Hunsdiecker rate order (1° fastest)
concepts.explanation: Rate of Hunsdiecker: 1° > 2° > 3°. This is OPPOSITE to carbocation stability. Mechanism is radical (R-COO•→ R• + CO2 → R-Br); the radical prefers less hindered R•, not more stable.

concepts.name: Beta-keto ester haloform rule
concepts.explanation: β-keto esters (R-CO-CH2-COOEt) do NOT give haloform. The alpha-H between two EWG is most acidic and gets iodinated FIRST, but this position's triiodination does not give haloform cleavage (wrong carbon). Rule: 'All β-keto esters are haloform negative.'

concepts.name: Acid and acid derivatives are haloform negative
concepts.explanation: CH3COOH, CH3COCl, CH3COOMe, (CH3CO)2O, CH3CONH2, CH3CONHMe, CH3CONMe2 — ALL negative for haloform despite containing CH3-C(=O) group. Reason: lack of enolizable proton (acid) or the electron-withdrawal from X makes base-assisted alpha-iodination impossible.

concepts.why_fragile: E2 requires anti-periplanar H and LG (180° dihedral). In cyclohexane, only trans-diaxial arrangement satisfies this. Students forget this geometric constraint and predict E2 from equatorial LG substrates.
concepts.common_error: Predicting E2 from equatorial LG in cyclohexane ring (need axial LG and anti-axial H). Predicting Saytzeff from bulky base (gives Hofmann). Forgetting that E2 is 2nd-order (bimolecular). Predicting E2 from norbornyl tosylate (geometrically impossible in rigid bicyclic).

concepts.name: Swart reaction as best method for R-F
concepts.explanation: R-Cl/Br/I + AgF/Hg2F2/CaF2/CoF3/SbF3/heat → R-F. SN2 mechanism → inversion. This is the BEST method for making alkyl fluorides. Direct F2 addition is explosive; HF is corrosive and poor nucleophile.

concepts.why_fragile: Stereochemical outcomes require tracking configuration through each step. Students who do not draw the mechanism or use a 3D representation frequently get inversion/retention/racemisation wrong. SN2 → inversion, SN1 → racemisation, SNi → retention — all three are tested.

concepts.name: Chloroform phosgene oxidation and storage
concepts.explanation: CHCl3 + O2/hv → COCl2 (phosgene, extremely poisonous war gas). Stored in dark bottles filled to brim (minimize air exposure) + 1% EtOH (scavenges phosgene: COCl2 + 2 EtOH → EtO-CO-OEt diethyl carbonate, harmless).

concepts.name: Mixed haloform from pre-halogenated ketones
concepts.explanation: If alpha-C already has a halogen, the product is a MIXED trihalomethane: CH3COCH2Cl + I2/NaOH → CHClI2 (not CHI3). CH3CO-CHBr2 + I2/NaOH → CHBr2I. The existing halogen stays on the haloform carbon.

concepts.name: Iodoform test scope for alcohols
concepts.explanation: Only alcohols that can be oxidized to a methyl ketone (or acetaldehyde) give iodoform: EtOH → CH3CHO ✓; iPrOH → acetone ✓; sBuOH → MEK ✓. MeOH→HCHO (no CH3CO) ✗; nPrOH→propanal (no CH3CO) ✗; tBuOH cannot be oxidized to methyl ketone ✗.

concepts.name: Steric crowding blocks haloform (2,6-disubstituted aryl ketone)
concepts.explanation: A methyl aryl ketone where both ortho positions are substituted (2,6-dihalogenated aryl methyl ketone) gives NO haloform reaction. Steric crowding around the alpha-C or the C=O prevents the required base/I2 approach.

concepts.why_fragile: Steric effect is non-intuitive: it slows reactions even when the electronic effect is favourable. Students rank reaction rates purely on electronic grounds and ignore the geometric factor.
concepts.common_error: Predicting fast SN2 on a neopentyl system (very slow due to steric hindrance despite primary substrate). Ignoring ortho substitution rate reduction vs para in EAS. Underestimating the steric effect of t-Bu group on pKa of carboxylic acids (electron-donating increases pKa).

concepts.name: SOCl2 retention vs inversion (pyridine dependent)
concepts.explanation: R-OH + SOCl2 (no pyridine) → R-Cl with RETENTION (SNi: intramolecular Cl delivery from chlorosulfite intermediate). R-OH + SOCl2 + pyridine → R-Cl with INVERSION (pyridine acts as base, deprotonates; now external Cl⁻ attacks via SN2).

concepts.name: Acidic vs basic alpha-bromination regiochemistry
concepts.explanation: Unsymmetric ketone + Br2/OH⁻ → bromination at MORE substituted alpha-C (thermodynamic enolate, more stable). Unsymmetric ketone + Br2/H⁺ → bromination at LESS substituted alpha-C (kinetic enol, less substituted forms faster). Regiochemistry is controllable by pH.
