concepts.name: SN NGP (Neighbouring Group Participation = Anchimeric Assistance): full list of NGP groups, double-inversion = retention, ring size rules for -OR, quantitative rate effects (600x, 4x slower, 4000x)
concepts.description:
SN NGP (NEIGHBOURING GROUP PARTICIPATION) = ANCHIMERIC ASSISTANCE:

DEFINITION: A neighboring group Y (on the carbon adjacent to the LG-bearing C) acts as an INTERNAL nucleophile, displacing the LG intramolecularly → forms a bridged cyclic intermediate → external Nu opens the bridge → product.

GROUPS THAT CAN SHOW NGP (complete list):
1. -COO- (carboxylate), -COOR (ester)
2. -C-Ar (aryl / aryl-C= nearby π system)
3. -O-C(=O)-R (acyloxy, ester, forms cyclic acyloxonium)
4. -OR, -OH, -O- (ethers and alkoxides — see ring size rules below!)
5. -NH2, -NHR, -NR2 (primary, secondary, tertiary amines)
6. -NH-C(=O)-R (amide NH)
7. -SH, -SR, -S- (thiols and sulfides = EXCELLENT NGP, forms episulfonium)
8. -I, -Br, -Cl (halogen lone pairs! YES, halogens can do NGP)
9. -C=C (alkene, forms a cyclopropylcarbinyl-like bridged cation)
10. Benzene ring (aromatic π, forms 'phenonium ion' bridged cation)
11. Cyclopropane ring (bent bonds can participate)
12. C=C=C (allene)
13. Epoxide (can participate)

RING SIZE RULES FOR -OR (OXYGEN) NGP:
- 3 mem: XXX (very bad — oxiranium from O is too strained)
- 4 mem: X (bad)
- 5 mem: ✓ (good — tetrahydrofuranium)
- 6 mem: ✓ (good — tetrahydropyranium)
- 7 mem: X (bad — entropy too costly)

NOTE: Sulfur (S) can form 3-membered episulfonium (3 mem = OK for S, because C-S bond is longer → less angle strain). This is why PhS-NGP gives 600× rate enhancement even with 3-membered ring.

QUANTITATIVE NGP RATE EFFECTS:
1. PhS-CH2CH2-Cl vs CH2CH2-Cl: 600× FASTER (PhS NGP, 3-membered episulfonium, S is large)
2. MeO-CH2CH2-Cl vs CH2CH2-Cl: 4× SLOWER (O NGP not possible for 3-membered ring; -I inductive effect of O slows SN2)
3. Beta-OMe with OTs (forming 5 or 6-membered ring): 4000× FASTER than simple OTs without NGP

STEREOCHEMICAL OUTCOME OF NGP:
- REQUIREMENT: Y and LG must be ANTI (trans, anti-periplanar) for NGP to occur (allows backside intramolecular SN2)
- Step 1: Y attacks from ANTI face of LG → 1st INVERSION at C-LG
- Step 2: External Nu attacks bridged intermediate from ANTI → 2nd INVERSION
- NET: RETENTION OF CONFIGURATION at the original reaction site (double inversion)
- If bridged intermediate is symmetric: Nu attacks either C equally → two ENANTIOMERS

NGP PRODUCTS VS SIMPLE SN2:
- NGP: RETENTION at original LG-C (unusual for SN-type!)
- Simple SN2: INVERSION at LG-C
concepts.why_fragile: Multiple interconnected failure modes: (1) Students don't recognize which groups can show NGP (especially halides and aryl groups are often missed). (2) Students don't know the ring size rules for -OR (3 and 4-membered O rings = bad; 5 and 6 = good). (3) The double-inversion = RETENTION is counterintuitive: students expect SN reactions to always give inversion, but NGP gives retention (two inversions). (4) The quantitative rates (600× for PhS, 4× SLOWER for MeO, 4000× for beta-OMe with 5/6 ring) are frequently tested directly in JEE. (5) Students may confuse NGP with normal SN2 and not recognize when the outcome is retention vs. inversion.

concepts.description:
EPOXIDE RING OPENING — COMPLETE ACID vs. BASE COMPARISON:

┌─────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Condition       │ Acidic                  │ Basic/Neutral           │
├─────────────────┼─────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
│ Mechanism       │ SN1-type                │ SN2                     │
│ First step      │ H+ protonates O         │ Nu- attacks directly    │
│ Nu attacks      │ MORE substituted C (3°) │ LESS substituted C (1°) │
│ Anti addition?  │ Yes (anti still)        │ Yes (strict anti)       │
│ Regiochemistry  │ Markovnikov for Nu      │ Anti-Markovnikov for Nu │
│ Rearrangement?  │ NO (ring constrains)    │ NO                      │
│ Stereo at Nu-C  │ Some inversion (less    │ Strict inversion (SN2)  │
│                 │ clean due to SN1 char.) │                         │
└─────────────────┴─────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────┘

BOTH ACIDIC AND BASIC: ANTI ADDITION (Nu and OH are TRANS in the product)

SELECTED EXAMPLES:
1. Propylene oxide + H2O/H+ → 1-propan-2-ol (OH at 1°, H2O adds at 2°) — acid: more substituted
2. Propylene oxide + NaOH → 2-propan-1-ol derivative (OH at 2°, NaOH at 1°) — base: less substituted
3. Cyclohexene oxide + HBr/acid → trans-2-bromocyclohexanol (Br at more subst. C, OH at less subst.)
4. Cyclohexene oxide + NaOCH3 → trans-2-methoxycyclohexanol (OMe at less subst., OH at more subst.)

SPECIAL CASE — SYMMETRICAL EPOXIDES:
For symmetric epoxides (e.g., cyclohexene oxide), both C's of the epoxide are equivalent: acid and base opening give the SAME connectivity (trans product) but the mechanism differs. With 18O-labeled symmetric epoxide: 2 enantiomers formed (18O can be on either C in the product).
concepts.why_fragile: The regiochemistry reversal between acidic (Nu → more substituted C) and basic (Nu → less substituted C) on the SAME epoxide is the most tested concept. Students: (1) Apply SN2 rule ('less hindered = less substituted') universally, including for acidic conditions → predict Nu at 1° even in acid → wrong. (2) Confuse the stereochemistry: even though ACID gives SN1-like mechanism, the product is STILL anti-addition (not mixture) because the protonated epoxide still constrains approach to one face. (3) In 18O labeling: don't correctly track which product is the enantiomer of which, leading to wrong count of products.

concepts.name: Episulfonium from PhS-NGP: 600x faster than alkyl chloride, 3-membered ring OK for S (not O), double inversion = retention; MeO-NGP impossible (3 mem), 4x SLOWER than reference
concepts.description:
EPISULFONIUM ION FROM THIOETHER NGP:

FORMATION: PhS-CH2-CH2-Cl → [PhS forms 3-membered ring by attacking C-Cl from anti] → episulfonium ion (C-S+(Ph)-C, 3-membered ring) + Cl-

WHY 3-MEMBERED RING IS OK FOR S (unlike O):
- C-S bond length: ~1.82 Å (longer than C-O at ~1.43 Å)
- Longer bond = SMALLER internal angle in 3-membered ring for S vs. O
- LESS RING STRAIN in 3-membered ring for S compared to O
- Therefore: 3-membered episulfonium (C-S+-C) forms readily
- 3-membered oxiranium (C-O+-C from alcohol/ether NGP): too strained → does NOT form

QUANTITATIVE RATE: PhS-NGP = 600× faster than no-NGP. The episulfonium is a particularly good bridged intermediate because: (a) S is large and polarizable (excellent donor), (b) 3-membered ring is not too strained for S.

CONTRAST — MeO-NGP:
- MeO-CH2-CH2-Cl: O would need to form a 3-membered ring (oxiranium) → 3 mem = XXX for O → NGP not possible
- Plus -I inductive effect of MeO group slows SN2 slightly
- Net result: MeO-β-chloride is 4× SLOWER than simple alkyl chloride (NO rate enhancement; actually inhibited)
- KEY: S does NGP via 3-membered ring; O does NOT

RATEBOOK:
| Group     | Ring size | Rate vs. reference  |
|-----------|-----------|---------------------|
| PhS (β)  | 3-mem     | 600× FASTER         |
| MeO (β)  | 3-mem (X) | 4× SLOWER           |
| O-5-ring  | 5-mem     | up to 4000× FASTER  |
| O-6-ring  | 6-mem     | fast                |
| Aryl (β)  | 3-mem     | depends on sub.     |

- PhS-CH2-CH2-Cl + H2O → (episulfonium) → 2-phenylthioethanol OR 2-chloro-1-phenylthioethanol depending on which C is attacked

concepts.name: NGP stereochemistry: Y and LG must be ANTI for NGP to occur; double inversion = retention at LG-carbon; symmetric bridged intermediate gives enantiomers (not retention + racemization, but BOTH enantiomers from two faces of attack)
concepts.description:
NGP STEREOCHEMICAL ANALYSIS (DETAILED):

REQUIREMENT FOR NGP: Y and LG must be ANTI (anti-periplanar, 180° dihedral) for the intramolecular SN2 (step 1) to occur efficiently. This is the same requirement as for normal SN2: backside attack requires anti geometry. In a cyclohexane: Y and LG must be BOTH AXIAL (trans-diaxial) for anti relationship.

STEP-BY-STEP STEREOCHEMISTRY:
Substrate: Y at Cα (configuation S), LG at Cβ (configuration S or R)
Step 1: Y lone pair → attacks Cβ from ANTI of LG (SN2, INVERSION at Cβ) → LG departs → bridged intermediate [Cα-Y(+)-Cβ] with specific geometry
Step 2: External Nu:- → attacks either Cα or Cβ from ANTI of Y (SN2, INVERSION at the attacked C) → Y-C bond breaks

CASE A — Nu attacks Cβ (original LG carbon):
- Two inversions at Cβ (once from Y attack, once from Nu attack) → RETENTION of configuration at Cβ
- Y migrated from Cα to bridged intermediate → after Nu opens bridge, Y stays on Cα (its original position)

CASE B — Nu attacks Cα (original Y carbon) in symmetric intermediate:
- Y migrates functionally: end up with Y on Cβ (where LG was originally) and Nu on Cα (where Y was)
- Overall: walking substitution (Y moves, Nu in Y's place, product has Y where LG was)

FOR SYMMETRIC EPISULFONIUM (or any symmetric bridged intermediate):
- Nu can attack EITHER Cα or Cβ with equal probability
- Product 1: Nu at Cβ (retention at Cβ) + Y at Cα (original)
- Product 2: Nu at Cα (walking inversion at Cα) + Y migrated to Cβ
- In a symmetric substrate: Product 1 and Product 2 are ENANTIOMERS
- 'en' (enantiomers) in the boxed notation = the two enantiomers from symmetric episulfonium
- NOT 'racemization': the ratio is 1:1 (equal prob.) for symmetric intermediates, giving a racemate, but the mechanism is distinct from true SN1 racemization

EXAMPLE (SMe on cyclohexane + aq KOH):
Substrate: trans-2-(methylthio)cyclohexyl chloride [SMe and Cl trans = anti in diaxial position]
SMe (S lone pair) attacks C-Cl from anti → episulfonium (3-mem ring, S+ bridging) → OH- attacks either C → two enantiomeric products (trans-2-(methylthio)cyclohexanol, racemic).
concepts.why_fragile: The 'double inversion = retention' argument requires step-by-step tracking through two separate SN2 events at the same carbon. Students often: (1) Apply 'NGP = normal SN2 = inversion' (wrong; it's TWO inversions = retention). (2) Confuse 'enantiomers formed' with 'no stereochemistry' — the two enantiomers are formed for a specific reason (symmetric intermediate, not loss of stereocontrol). (3) Miss that the REQUIREMENT is anti-periplanar Y and LG — if the substrate has syn/gauche Y-LG geometry, NGP cannot occur and simple SN2 dominates.

concepts.name: Non-classical norbornyl cation (exo-norbornyl 140,000x faster than endo): sigma-NGP from C1-C6 bridge bond anti to exo-OTs; EWG (CF3) kills sigma-NGP; pi-NGP Hammett: OMe(30x) > Me(11x) > H(1x) > Cl(0.3x)
concepts.description:
QUANTITATIVE NGP RATE EFFECTS (THREE KEY SYSTEMS):

1. NORBORNYL SIGMA-NGP (exo vs endo, 140,000x):
   exo-NorbornylOTs reacts 140,000x FASTER than endo-NorbornylOTs in AcOH.
   Reason: The C1-C6 sigma bond (norbornane bridge) is ANTI to the exo-OTs → sigma-NGP occurs → bridged non-classical norbornyl cation (delocalized C+ between C1 and C2 via C1-C6-C2 bridge = the Winstein non-classical carbocation).
   Endo-OTs: C1-C6 bond is NOT anti to endo face → no sigma-NGP → slower normal SN1.
   Rate ratio: exo/endo = 140,000 (some sources: ~350; from Winstein's work, 140,000 is for specific derivatives).

2. CF3 SUBSTITUENT EFFECT ON SIGMA-NGP (rate = 14x10^12 to 1):
   Bicyclic compound with OAr sulfonate LG + sigma-NGP from C-C bond:
   - R1=R2=H: rate = 14 x 10^12 (max sigma-NGP, C-C sigma bond electron-rich)
   - R1=H, R2=CF3: rate = 15 x 10^6 (partially inhibited sigma-NGP)
   - R1=R2=CF3: rate = 1 (sigma-NGP eliminated; only normal pathway)
   The 10^13-fold rate range proves sigma-NGP is real and quantifiable.

3. PI-NGP FROM PHENYL (PHENONIUM) — HAMMETT CORRELATION:
   G-substituted phenyl ring at beta-C doing pi-NGP → phenonium ion formation:
   G: -OMe (30x) > -Me (11x) > H (1.0x) > -Cl (0.3x)
   Trend: EDG → more electron-rich ring → better pi-donor for NGP → faster.
   EWG → depleted ring → worse pi-NGP → slower.
   This is a rho-negative correlation (positive charge develops in aromatic ring = EDG stabilizes TS).

4. SIGMA vs PI vs LONE PAIR NGP COMPARISON (from earlier rates):
   Lone pair (PhS, 3-mem): 600x faster
   Lone pair (O, 5-6 mem): 4000x faster
   Pi-NGP (phenyl, H sub): ~1x (relative, depending on substrate)
   Sigma-NGP (C-C bond): up to 10^12x faster for norbornyl-type systems
   IMPORTANT: Sigma-NGP is quantitatively the most powerful in appropriate geometries (norbornyl).
concepts.why_fragile: Four independent rate numbers that must be memorized with their physical basis: (1) 140,000x exo/endo norbornyl — students often forget which is faster (exo = faster, sigma-NGP; endo = slower). (2) CF3 killing sigma-NGP (14x10^12 → 1): students may not connect CF3 at the sigma-donor C with NGP rate. (3) Hammett for pi-NGP: students confuse EDG/EWG effects on pi-NGP (which should be EDG=faster, EWG=slower, confirmed by OMe>H>Cl sequence). (4) The comparison across different NGP types (sigma-NGP in norbornyl is the strongest in favorable geometry). All four facts are tested in JEE Advanced rate-comparison problems.

concepts.name: Carboxylate NGP (COO- as NGP group) in alpha-bromo acids: Ag2O/H2O/NaOH gives RETENTION (NGP via cyclic lactone, double inversion); conc NaOH alone gives INVERSION (direct SN2)
concepts.description:
CARBOXYLATE (COO-) AS NGP GROUP IN ALPHA-BROMO ACIDS:

SUBSTRATE: 2-bromoalkanoic acid (COOH-CHBr-R or similar; Br and COOH on adjacent C's or beta relationship).

TWO PATHWAYS:

1. CONC. NaOH (SIMPLE SN2):
   OH- attacks C-Br directly from backside → SINGLE INVERSION → alpha-hydroxy acid with INVERTED config.
   Example: (S)-2-bromopropionic acid + conc NaOH → (R)-lactic acid [inversion at C2]

2. Ag2O/H2O/NaOH (SN NGP PATH):
   (a) NaOH deprotonates COOH → COO- (the NGP group is now ready)
   (b) Ag+ (from Ag2O) coordinates to Br → AgBr precipitates (assists ionization)
   (c) COO- oxygen attacks C-Br from ANTI face (intramolecular SN2, 1st INVERSION) → forms strained lactone (cyclic ester: alpha-lactone = 3-membered if alpha-bromo, or beta-lactone = 4-membered if beta-bromo)
   (d) H2O (nucleophile) attacks the strained lactone from anti (2nd INVERSION) → opens lactone → OH is installed with retention
   NET: two inversions = RETENTION of config. at the C that bore Br.
   Example: (S)-2-bromopropionic acid + Ag2O/H2O/NaOH → (S)-lactic acid [RETENTION at C2]

KEY: Same starting material (e.g., (S)-2-bromopropionic acid) → conc NaOH → (R)-lactic acid (inversion) vs. Ag2O/NaOH → (S)-lactic acid (retention). The TWO CONDITIONS give OPPOSITE STEREOCHEMICAL OUTCOMES.

COO- IS AN EXCELLENT NGP GROUP because: carboxylate has two oxygen lone pairs, is planar (sp2), and the intramolecular SN2 geometry is favorable when COOH and LG are appropriately positioned.
concepts.why_fragile: Students often assume 'NaOH always gives inversion (SN2)' and don't realize Ag2O changes the mechanism to NGP (giving retention). The Ag2O role is not obvious: Ag+ assists Br removal AND enables the COO- NGP by providing conditions for ionization. The product stereochemistry (retention vs. inversion from the same substrate) is directly tested in JEE Advanced questions about reaction conditions and stereochemistry.

concepts.description:
PHENONIUM ION (PI-NGP FROM ARYL RING) — COMPLETE ANALYSIS:

FORMATION: When a phenyl group is at the beta-position to a leaving group (Ar-C1H-C2H-LG), the phenyl pi electrons act as a neighboring group. The aromatic C-C bond donates into the sigma* of C2-LG (backside approach from the pi system) → LG departs → PHENONIUM ION forms.

STRUCTURE OF PHENONIUM ION:
A SPIROCYCLIC/BRIDGED BICYCLIC CATION:
- The phenyl ring becomes part of a 3-membered ring (the two carbons + one ring carbon form a cyclopropane-like bridge)
- Or more accurately: the phenyl group bridges C1 and C2 via the ipso carbon → C1-C(ipso)-C2 bridge = benzene ring fused into a cyclopropane ring
- The positive charge is delocalized in the bridged ring (shown as two resonance structures with + on different positions of the ring)

PRODUCTS FROM PHENONIUM:
- Nu attacks C1: retention-like product at C1
- Nu attacks C2 (original LG C): rearranged product (phenyl migrated effectively)
- If aromatic ring has substituents: products may involve ring attack at ortho/para positions too

HAMMETT CORRELATION (substituent G on phenyl ring):
- G=-OMe (p-methoxyphenyl/anisyl): 30x faster than G=H
- G=-Me (p-tolyl): 11x faster
- G=H (phenyl): 1x (reference)
- G=-Cl (p-chlorophenyl): 0.3x slower
- This is rho-negative (EDG stabilize the developing C+ in phenonium) = electrophilic aromatic mechanism

RATEBOOK:
| G | Rate (relative) |
|---|------------------|
| p-OMe | 30 |
| p-Me | 11 |
| H | 1 |
| p-Cl | 0.3 |
| p-CF3 | << 0.3 |

NOTE: Phenonium = non-classical (bridged, delocalized) cation, not a 'regular' spiro compound. It can be trapped by nucleophiles at both C1 and C2.
concepts.why_fragile: Students may know 'NGP from phenyl gives phenonium' but confuse the STRUCTURE (spiro-bicyclic vs planar) and the PRODUCTS (Nu at C1 vs C2 give different products). The Hammett correlation (OMe=30x, Me=11x, H=1x, Cl=0.3x) requires understanding that EDG accelerate phenonium formation (pi-NGP builds + charge in ring = EDG stabilize it). EWG slow it. This is the opposite of electrophilic substitution (where EDG also help, so students sometimes confuse direction). The specific numbers (30, 11, 1, 0.3) are testable and require precise recall.

concepts.description:
AMINE (N) AND THIOETHER (S) NGP — SPECIFIC EXAMPLES:

1. AMINO-NGP (NHMe or NR2):
Substrate: A compound with -NHMe at Calpha and -Br at Cbeta (in anti relationship).
Mechanism: N lone pair (from -NHMe) attacks C-Br from ANTI → forms AZIRIDINIUM (3-membered ring with N+Me bridging Calpha and Cbeta) + Br-.
Opening: OH- (from KOH) attacks aziridinium at either C from outside → ring opens → product with NHMe and OH.
STEREOCHEMISTRY: Double inversion = NET RETENTION at the original C-Br.
Product: If symmetric aziridinium → 2 enantiomers. If the aziridinium can only be opened at one C (sterically or geometrically constrained) → single product with retention.

2. SMe-NGP → EPISULFONIUM → NaSH OPENS → THIOL PRODUCT:
Substrate: Cyclopentane ring with SMe (methylthio) and I (iodide) in anti relationship + NaSH (sodium hydrogen sulfide, Na+SH-).
Step 1: SMe lone pair attacks C-I from ANTI → episulfonium (3-membered S+Me bridge, 1st inversion at C-I).
Step 2: HS- (from NaSH) attacks episulfonium at C bearing I (or the other C of the bridge) → S-H bond forms (2nd inversion) → opens episulfonium.
Product: The SH group replaces I at the specific position (retention at the I-C if HS- attacks that C; inversion at the SMe-C if HS- attacks the SMe-C).
LABEL: '[SN NGP by -SMe]'
Product: cyclopentyl compound with SH (where I was) + SMe (retained on adjacent C) + OCH3 (unchanged).

GENERAL RULE: ALL HETEROATOM GROUPS (N, O, S, halogen) with lone pairs can do NGP if: (a) ANTI geometry between Y and LG, (b) favorable ring size for intermediate (S: 3 mem = OK; N: 3 mem = OK; O: 3 mem = XX, 5 or 6 = OK).

Students may not recognize that -NHMe can act as NGP (confusing NGP groups with only S or O). concepts.name: SN1' vs SN2' vs SNi' prime reactions: definitions, selectivity rule (Nu at LESS CROWDED allylic C = MAJOR), and comparison: SN1' minor for primary allylic; SN2' major for hindered allylic; SNi' major for allylic OH + SOCl2
concepts.description:
FIVE ALLYLIC SUBSTITUTION TYPES IN RM lec6:
①SN1' (SN1 Prime)
②SN2' (SN2 Prime)
③SNi' (SNi Prime)
④SNth
⑤SNAr

═══ UNIFIED SELECTIVITY RULE ═══
'When Nu attacks on LESS CROWDED allylic carbon atom, it forms MAJOR product.'

① SN1' PRIME:
DEFINITION: SN1 rxn at allylic position giving product with REARRANGED π-bond.
MECHANISM: C-LG ionizes → allylic cation (delocalized) → Nu attacks ONE OF THE TWO ALLYLIC C's.
PRODUCT A (SN1, unrearranged): Nu at less-crowded allylic C = MAJOR (same-side product, pi bond stays).
PRODUCT B (SN1', rearranged): Nu at more-crowded end = MINOR (pi bond moved, rearranged).
For PRIMARY allylic Br in aq conditions: SN1 (unrearranged) = Major; SN1' (rearranged) = Minor.
For cyclic allylic: depends on ring geometry; SN1' can be major when rearranged end is less hindered.

② SN2' PRIME:
DEFINITION: SN2 rxn at allylic carbon giving product with REARRANGED π-bond (CONCERTED mechanism!).
MECHANISM: Nu attacks GAMMA C (remote allylic end) simultaneously as LG departs from ALPHA C, pi bond migrates. ALL IN ONE STEP (no carbocation intermediate — this distinguishes it from SN1').
SELECTIVITY:
- C-LG at PRIMARY (less hindered): SN2 direct = MAJOR; SN2' = MINOR.
- C-LG at SECONDARY/TERTIARY (more hindered): SN2 disfavored; SN2' (at gamma = less hindered) = MAJOR.

③ SNi' PRIME (ALLYLIC SOCl2 REACTION):
Substrate: Allylic alcohol + SOCl2.
MECHANISM: (a) Forms chlorosulfite ester (C-O-SO-Cl). (b) 6-MCTS (6-membered cyclic TS): Cl attacks GAMMA C through ring → rearranged allylic chloride (SNi') + SO2 = MAJOR (6-mem TS preferred). (c) 4-MCTS (SNi): Cl attacks ALPHA C directly → unrearranged allylic chloride = MINOR (4-mem TS strained).
SNi' (6-MCTS) >> SNi (4-MCTS) in preference.

COMPARISON TABLE:
| Type | Mechanism | Intermediate | Rearranged product major when... |
|------|-----------|-------------|----------------------------------|
| SN1' | Stepwise (C+ first) | Allylic cation | Cyclic systems or crowded alpha C |
| SN2' | Concerted | None | Alpha C is hindered (2° or 3°) |
| SNi' | Concerted cyclic TS | None (cyclic TS) | Always major (6-MCTS preferred) |
concepts.why_fragile: Students frequently confuse SN1' and SN2' mechanisms (one has a cation, one is concerted), and apply the 'major product rule' (less crowded = major) incorrectly. Common errors: (1) Thinking SN1' is ALWAYS the major product of allylic ionization — wrong: for primary allylic, SN1 (unrearranged) = major. (2) Thinking SN2' is the major for all allylic Br compounds — wrong: only when C-Br is hindered (secondary/tertiary). (3) Missing that SNi' (via 6-MCTS with SOCl2) gives the REARRANGED allylic chloride as major — students expect the unrearranged retention product from SOCl2 (the normal SNi, but for allylic systems the 6-MCTS dominates). (4) Confusing the 'prime' reactions with NGP or other named mechanisms.

concepts.name: SNi' mechanism detail: allylic alcohol + SOCl2 → chlorosulfite ester → 6-MCTS (6-membered cyclic TS, major, rearranged SNi' product) vs 4-MCTS (minor, unrearranged SNi product); SO2 expelled in both
concepts.description:
SNi' (SNi PRIME) MECHANISM — DETAILED:

STARTING MATERIAL: Allylic alcohol R-CH=CH-CH2-OH + SOCl2.

STEP 1 (fast): ROH + SOCl2 → R-CH=CH-CH2-O-S(=O)-Cl + HCl (CHLOROSULFITE ESTER formation).
This is the intermediate for both SNi and SNi' pathways.

STEP 2 — TWO COMPETING CYCLIC PATHWAYS:

PATH A: SNi (4-MCTS, MINOR):
4-membered cyclic TS: Cl-S-O-Cα (the C that was bonded to O). In this TS: Cl bonds to Cα from the SAME FACE as O (syn delivery of Cl, RETENTION of configuration). Double bond does NOT migrate. Product: R-CH=CH-CH2-Cl (same connectivity as OH, just OH→Cl; retention at C-OH) + SO2.
Why minor: 4-membered TS = strained (4-membered ring = unfavorable entropy and angle strain).

PATH B: SNi' (6-MCTS, MAJOR):
6-membered cyclic TS: Cl(on S)...S-O-Cα-C=Cγ ring (with Cl reaching around to Cγ). Atoms in the 6-membered ring: Cl—S—O—Cα—C=Cγ (6 atoms). In this TS: Cl attacks Cγ (the gamma/distal allylic C), the pi bond shifts from Cα=Cβ to Cβ=Cγ, and S-O bond breaks (SO2 expelled). REARRANGED ALLYLIC CHLORIDE is formed (Cl at gamma C, pi bond migrated). Why MAJOR: 6-membered TS is highly favored (chair-like TS, minimal strain, no ring strain like in 4-membered).

FINAL PRODUCTS AND RATIO:
- SNi' (rearranged, 6-MCTS): MAJOR (e.g., from but-2-en-1-ol: gives 1-chlorobut-2-ene → wait: gives CH3-CH(Cl)-CH=CH2 = but-3-en-2-yl chloride, which is the rearranged product)
- SNi (unrearranged, 4-MCTS): MINOR (e.g., gives CH3-CH=CH-CH2-Cl = but-2-en-1-yl chloride, unrearranged)

BOTH PATHS EXPEL SO2 (the sulfur dioxide is the byproduct that drives the reaction forward thermodynamically).
concepts.why_fragile: Students know 'SOCl2 gives allylic chloride via SNi' but don't realize that for ALLYLIC alcohols, the SNi' (rearranged, via 6-MCTS) is the MAJOR product, not the SNi (retention, unrearranged). In normal non-allylic alcohols (e.g., 2-propanol + SOCl2): only SNi possible (direct Cl delivery with retention, 4-MCTS). But in allylic alcohols: the 6-MCTS (SNi') wins. The 4-MCTS vs 6-MCTS distinction and the resulting regiochemistry (Cl at original C = minor vs Cl at gamma C = major) is the key testable concept.

concepts.name: SN2' concerted mechanism: Nu attacks gamma C (anti to LG) simultaneously with LG departure from alpha C, pi bond migrates; stereochemistry: anti addition of Nu at gamma relative to LG departure at alpha
concepts.description:
SN2' (SN2 PRIME) — MECHANISM AND STEREOCHEMISTRY:

KEY DISTINCTION FROM SN1': SN2' is CONCERTED (single step, no carbocation). SN1' is STEPWISE (carbocation intermediate).

CONCERTED SN2' MECHANISM:
1. Nu:- approaches gamma C (Cgamma = the allylic C remote from LG) from ANTI side (backside approach)
2. SIMULTANEOUSLY: Cgamma-Cbeta pi bond shifts → Cbeta-Calpha new pi bond forms
3. SIMULTANEOUSLY: Calpha-LG breaks (LG departs)
All three arrow-pushing events happen at once = TRUE concerted mechanism.

STEREOCHEMISTRY OF SN2':
- Since it is SN2-like: INVERSION at the gamma C (where Nu adds)
- The nu arrives ANTI to the departing LG (anti addition geometry)
- 'Anti-SN2' pathway = Nu and LG are anti to each other across the allylic system
- In practice: there is also an energetically accessible 'syn' SN2' in some cases (Nu comes from same side as LG), but anti SN2' is preferred in polar solvents.

MECHANISM ARROWS (e.g., CH3-CH=CH-CH2-Br + KCN for SN2'):
1. CN- (approaching C2 from anti side of the allylic system relative to Br at C4)
2. C2=C3 pi bond: curved arrow C2=C3 → C3-C4 (migrate the pi bond)
3. C4-Br: curved arrow showing Br departure
→ Product: CH3-CH(CN)-CH=CH2 (SN2' product) + Br-

SELECTIVITY SUMMARY:
- C4 (primary, less crowded): direct SN2 preferred → SN2 = major
- C2 (secondary, less crowded? No wait: C2 is the one with Me adjacent = more crowded): SN2' = minor for this substrate
- For BRANCHED substrate where C-Br (the alpha C) is hindered: gamma C is now the less crowded → SN2' major

DISTINGUISHING SN2' FROM SN1':
| Feature | SN2' | SN1' |
|---------|------|------|
| Mechanism | Concerted | Stepwise |
| Intermediate | None | Allylic C+ |
| Conditions | Strong Nu, SN2 solvents | Polar solvent, ionizing |
| Stereospecificity | Yes (inversion at gamma C) | No (both faces of C+) |
| Product ratio | Depends on crowding | Depends on crowding |
concepts.why_fragile: The concerted nature of SN2' is frequently tested (vs. the stepwise SN1'). Students draw an intermediate for SN2' (wrong: no intermediate) or miss that ALL THREE events (Nu-C bond forming, pi migration, C-LG bond breaking) are simultaneous. The stereochemistry (anti SN2') is also tested: inversion at gamma C (backside SN2 attack at gamma C) while the pi bond migrates. This is distinct from SN1' where the allylic cation has no stereochemical memory.

concepts.name: Five special allylic substitution types: SN1', SN2', SNi', SNth, SNAr — complete taxonomy introduced in RM lec6
concepts.description:
FIVE SPECIAL SUBSTITUTION REACTIONS COVERED IN RM LEC6:

① SN1' (SN1 PRIME): SN1 at allylic position with pi bond rearrangement. Via allylic C+ intermediate. Minor in simple aq conditions when C-LG is primary (less hindered). Major when the rearranged product's C is less hindered.

② SN2' (SN2 PRIME): SN2 at gamma allylic C with pi bond rearrangement. Concerted. Major when C-LG is hindered (secondary/tertiary allylic). Minor when C-LG is primary (direct SN2 is easier).

③ SNi' (SNi PRIME): Internal allylic substitution via 6-MCTS. Triggered by SOCl2 on allylic OH. Major because 6-MCTS preferred over 4-MCTS. Gives rearranged allylic chloride (Cl at gamma C) as major + SO2 byproduct.

④ SNth: [Not yet covered in detail in pages 1-6 of lec6 — will be covered in later pages]

⑤ SNAr: [Nucleophilic aromatic substitution — not yet covered in pages 1-6 of lec6; will be covered later]

COMMON THREAD ACROSS SN1', SN2', SNi':
- All involve ALLYLIC substrates
- All give a REARRANGED product (pi bond position changes)
- All follow the rule: 'Nu attacks LESS CROWDED allylic C → MAJOR product'
- The UNREARRANGED product is the 'normal' reaction (SN1, SN2, SNi respectively)
- The REARRANGED product is the 'prime' reaction (SN1', SN2', SNi' respectively)
concepts.why_fragile: Students mix up which 'prime' reaction applies in which context. The taxonomy (SN1' = stepwise via C+; SN2' = concerted; SNi' = intramolecular cyclic TS) requires clear mapping of mechanism to named reaction type. The shared rule ('less crowded = major') helps but can be misapplied if students don't correctly identify which allylic carbon is 'less crowded' for each substrate.

concepts.name: SNth (nucleophilic acyl substitution): addition-elimination mechanism via tetrahedral intermediate; rate order acyl halide > anhydride > ester > amide; LG ability X- > RCOO- > RO- > NH2-; thioester > ester; acyl halide series I > Br > Cl > F
concepts.description:
SNth — NUCLEOPHILIC SUBSTITUTION IN ACID DERIVATIVES: COMPLETE SUMMARY

DEFINITION: Nucleophilic substitution at the acyl carbonyl carbon (sp2 C=O) of acid derivatives (R-COX, RCOOR, RCOOCOR, RCONH2).

MECHANISM:
Step 1 (SLOW, AN): Nu: + R-C(=O)-L → [R-C(-O-)(-L)(-Nu)(-R)] = TETRAHEDRAL INTERMEDIATE (sp3 acyl C)
Step 2 (SLOW, DN): Tetrahedral intermediate → R-C(=O)-Nu + L-
Type: Addition-Elimination = AN + DN. TWO slow steps (two energy barriers, one tetrahedral intermediate valley).
Kinetics: Rate ∝ [R-CO-L][Nu] = 2nd order.
Rate also depends on: (i) LG ability of L; (ii) electrophilicity of acyl C.

LEAVING GROUPS AND THEIR ABILITIES:
| Derivative | LG | Conjugate acid | Acidity | LG ability |
|------------|-----|----------------|---------|------------|
| Acyl halide (R-COX) | X- | HX | Very high | Best |
| Anhydride (RCOOCOR) | RCOO- | RCOOH | pKa ~5 | Good |
| Thioester (RCOSR) | RS- | RSH | pKa ~10 | Good |
| Ester (RCOOR) | RO- | ROH | pKa ~16 | Poor |
| Amide (RCONH2) | NH2- | NH3 | pKa ~38 | Very poor |

FULL REACTIVITY ORDER:
R-COX (acyl halide) > RCOOCOR (anhydride) > RCOSR (thioester) > RCOOR (ester) > RCONH2 (amide)

ACYL HALIDE SUB-ORDER (based on LG ability dominance):
RCOI > RCOBr > RCOCl > RCOF (I- = best LG, F- = worst)

THIOESTER vs ESTER: RCOSR > RCOOR (SR- = thiolate, better LG than OR- = alkoxide; RSH pKa ~10 vs ROH pKa ~16)

ADDITIONAL NOTES:
- NO inversion of stereochemistry (unlike SN2): the tetrahedral intermediate is sp3 but the geometry at acyl C is not as stereochemically sensitive as SN2 at sp3 C.
- The mechanism is called 'addition-elimination' not 'direct substitution' — there IS a tetrahedral intermediate (detectable in principle).
- Rate depends on BOTH Nu and substrate (2nd order) — unlike SN1 which is independent of Nu.
concepts.why_fragile: Multiple failure modes: (1) Students confuse SNth mechanism with SN2 (which has no intermediate at sp3 C, just a TS). SNth HAS a real tetrahedral intermediate. (2) Reactivity order requires knowing LG ability order AND the acid acidity reasoning: the most acidic conjugate acid = the best LG = the most reactive acid derivative. (3) The thioester position (between anhydride and ester) is often missed. (4) The acyl halide series (I > Br > Cl > F in LG ability framework) is the REVERSE of the C electrophilicity-based order (F > Cl > Br > I) — two competing frameworks give opposite predictions, and JEE questions test which framework to use. (5) The rate is 2nd order (∝ [substrate][Nu]) — students may predict 1st order or 0th order in Nu.

concepts.name: SNth AN+DN mechanism: tetrahedral intermediate is real (NOT a transition state); two distinct slow steps; second-order kinetics; rate controlled by both LG ability and C=O electrophilicity
concepts.description:
SNth MECHANISM — DETAILED MECHANISTIC ANALYSIS:

THE TETRAHEDRAL INTERMEDIATE:
- The key intermediate in SNth is the TETRAHEDRAL INTERMEDIATE (abbreviated 'th').
- It is a TRUE INTERMEDIATE (local energy minimum on the PES), NOT a transition state.
- Structure: R-C(-O-)(-L)(-Nu) — the former C=O becomes C-O- (anionic oxygen), the acyl C is now sp3 with 4 bonds: R, O-, L, Nu.
- It can (in principle) be detected/trapped in some reactions.
- After the th forms: it collapses by expelling L- → product R-C(=O)-Nu.

ENERGY PROFILE:
- TWO slow steps = TWO energy maxima in the reaction coordinate.
- TS1: for Nu addition to C=O (AN step).
- Tetrahedral intermediate (valley between the two maxima).
- TS2: for LG departure from the tetrahedral intermediate (DN step).
- Compare: SN1 = one maximum (ionization) + carbocation intermediate. SN2 = one maximum (inversion TS), no intermediate. SNth = two maxima + tetrahedral intermediate.

RATE LAW: Rate = k[R-CO-L][Nu]
- 2nd order: rate depends on BOTH substrate and nucleophile.
- This distinguishes it from SN1 (rate = k[substrate], independent of Nu).

WHICH STEP IS RATE-LIMITING?
- If Step 1 (Nu addition) is slower: rate depends on Nu nucleophilicity AND electrophilicity of C. The more electrophilic the C (more EWG on R or L), the faster Step 1.
- If Step 2 (LG departure) is slower: rate depends on LG ability. The better the LG (X- > RCOO- > RO- > NH2-), the faster Step 2.
- In practice: for acyl halides with strong Nu: often Step 2 (LG departure) is the overall 'bottleneck' when considering LG differences within the halide series (I- > F- in LG ability).

ADDITION-ELIMINATION vs ELIMINATION-ADDITION (contrast):
- SNth = ADDITION-ELIMINATION: Nu adds first, then LG leaves (tetrahedral intermediate).
- SNAr uses the SAME type of mechanism (addition-elimination, Meisenheimer complex is the 'th' equivalent for aromatic systems).
concepts.why_fragile: The distinction between 'tetrahedral intermediate' (real, detectable, local minimum) and 'transition state' (not detectable, saddle point) is critical. Students often draw the tetrahedral 'th' as a TS instead of an intermediate. The two-barrier energy profile (two slow steps) is also frequently misunderstood: students may draw only ONE barrier (treating SNth as a one-step process). The 2nd-order kinetics (rate depends on [Nu]) is important for distinguishing SNth from SN1 (rate independent of Nu) in kinetics-based JEE problems.

concepts.name: SNAr (nucleophilic aromatic substitution): Meisenheimer complex intermediate; requires EWG ortho/para to the leaving Cl; meta EWG does NOT activate SNAr; EDG deactivates; selectivity with 1 equiv Nu
concepts.description:
SNAr (NUCLEOPHILIC AROMATIC SUBSTITUTION) — INTRODUCTION:

DEFINITION: Nucleophilic substitution on an AROMATIC RING, replacing a halide (Cl, F, Br, NO2, etc.) with a nucleophile. Requires activation by electron-withdrawing groups (EWG).

MECHANISM (ADDITION-ELIMINATION, same general type as SNth):
Step 1: Nu:- attacks the ring carbon bearing LG (Cl) from OUTSIDE the ring → forms MEISENHEIMER COMPLEX (an sp3 carbon in the ring with O-/negative charge delocalized in the ring; the ring is no longer aromatic).
Step 2: LG (Cl-) departs → ring rearomatizes → product ArNu.
Meisenheimer complex = the 'tetrahedral intermediate' equivalent for aromatic systems.

ACTIVATION REQUIREMENT:
EWG (-M groups: NO2, CN, C=O, CF3, etc.) at ORTHO or PARA to the C-Cl stabilize the Meisenheimer complex by delocalizing the negative charge into the EWG.
META EWG cannot stabilize the Meisenheimer complex → no activation at meta positions.
EDG (+M groups: OMe, NR2, OH) DEACTIVATE SNAr (they destabilize the anionic Meisenheimer complex by donating electrons = more negative charge, more destabilizing).

SELECTIVITY RULE:
With LIMITED Nu (1 equiv): the Cl at the position most activated by EWG (ortho or para to EWG) is substituted first.
With excess Nu: can substitute all activated positions.

EXAMPLE Q3 (from teacher's notes):
Ring with EWG (NO2-type, -M) + two Cl (Ca ortho to EWG, Cb meta to EWG) + CH3O- (1 equiv):
Ca-Cl → OCH3 (ortho to EWG = activated toward SNAr)
Cb-Cl → unchanged (meta to EWG = NOT activated)
Product: ring with OCH3 at Ca, Cl at Cb.

CONTRAST WITH EAS (electrophilic aromatic substitution):
- EAS: EDG activates (electrons donated into ring = ring is electron-rich = reacts with E+); EWG deactivates.
- SNAr: EWG activates (electrons withdrawn from ring = ring accepts Nu:- more easily); EDG deactivates.
- EAS: ortho/para director = EDG; meta director = EWG.
- SNAr: activated by EWG ortho/para to LG; not activated by EWG meta; EDG at ortho/para DEACTIVATES.
concepts.why_fragile: Students confuse EAS (activated by EDG, ortho/para to EDG = major) with SNAr (activated by EWG, ortho/para to EWG = major). The positional requirement is the SAME (ortho/para to the directing group), but the TYPE OF GROUP (EDG vs EWG) is OPPOSITE. This causes systematic errors: students predict EDG activates SNAr (wrong) or that EWG activates ortho/para for BOTH EAS and SNAr (partially right but for wrong reasons). The Meisenheimer complex mechanism (two slow steps, anionic intermediate) mirrors SNth's tetrahedral intermediate concept.

concepts.name: SNth selectivity when two acyl chlorides on same ring with EDG (MeO): the acyl C less affected by EDG (meta to MeO, more electrophilic) reacts faster with Nu; acyl C ortho/para to MeO is less electrophilic = reacts slower
concepts.description:
SNth CHEMOSELECTIVITY — TWO ACYL GROUPS ON A RING WITH EDG:

PROBLEM (Q4 from teacher's notes):
A benzene ring with MeO (EDG, +M donor) and TWO acyl chloride groups at different positions + CH3S- Na+ (1 equiv, thiolate = good Nu for SNth).

SELECTIVITY: The acyl chloride at the POSITION LESS AFFECTED BY MeO'S RESONANCE DONATION reacts faster.

REASONING:
- MeO (+M, EDG) donates electrons by resonance into the ORTHO and PARA positions of the ring.
- An acyl chloride C(=O)-Cl at the ORTHO or PARA position to MeO: the ring C bearing C(=O)-Cl receives electron density from MeO resonance → the carbonyl C (C=O) of that acyl group is LESS ELECTROPHILIC (ring C has more electron density → less δ+ at the C=O).
- An acyl chloride at META to MeO: MeO resonance cannot reach the meta ring C → that ring C is NOT electron-enriched by MeO → the C=O at meta is MORE ELECTROPHILIC (normal, unaffected).
- SNth: Nu attacks the MORE ELECTROPHILIC C=O first → FASTER reaction at meta acyl group.

CONCLUSION: With 1 equiv Nu (CH3S-), the acyl chloride at META position to MeO is selectively converted to thioester (C(=O)-SMe). The ortho or para acyl chloride is unchanged.

GENERAL PRINCIPLE: In SNth selectivity on aromatic rings, EDG on the ring REDUCE electrophilicity of acyl groups at ortho/para positions. The LESS ELECTRON-DONATED acyl carbon (meta to EDG) is MORE ELECTROPHILIC and reacts faster with nucleophiles.
concepts.why_fragile: Students know 'EDG donates into ortho/para' but don't apply it to the ELECTROPHILICITY of an attached acyl C=O. The key step: EDG at ortho to a C(=O)-Cl → ring C gets more electrons → the attached C=O C gets slightly more electrons via conjugation → less electrophilic → slower SNth at that site. Students often predict the ortho acyl group reacts faster (wrong) because 'EDG is nearby = reacts easily' — but for SNth it's the OPPOSITE (EDG reduces electrophilicity = slower).

concepts.name: SNAr two mechanisms: (1) Addition-Elimination via Meisenheimer complex (slow addition, fast elimination, EWG required ortho/para); (2) Elimination-Addition = Benzyne mechanism (strong base, no EWG needed)
concepts.description:
SNAr — COMPLETE MECHANISTIC TAXONOMY:

TWO MECHANISMS:
①Addition-Elimination (common, for activated arenes)
②Elimination-Addition = BENZYNE MECHANISM (for unactivated or special cases)

① ADDITION-ELIMINATION (Meisenheimer mechanism):
- Nu:- attacks ipso C bearing L → MEISENHEIMER COMPLEX (non-aromatic sp3 ring C, anionic) → L- departs → ArNu
- REQUIRES: EWG at ortho or para to L (to stabilize the Meisenheimer anion by resonance)
- SLOW step: Addition (Nu attacks ring, ring loses aromaticity)
- FAST step: Elimination (L departs, ring rearomatizes)
- CONDITIONS: Can work at room T with strongly activated rings (multiple EWG); otherwise needs high T/P
- INTERMEDIATE: Meisenheimer complex [Ar(Nu)(L)]⁻ (detectable for some activated systems!)
- PRODUCT PREDICTION: Nu replaces L at the activated position (ortho/para to EWG)

② ELIMINATION-ADDITION (Benzyne mechanism):
- Base (typically NaNH2 or strong base) removes H adjacent to the C-L → BENZYNE (1,2-didehydrobenzene = a cyclic alkyne-like species, highly strained)
- Then Nu:- adds across the benzyne triple bond
- REQUIRES: Very strong base (NaNH2, typically), no EWG needed
- PRODUCTS: Nu can appear at C1 (where L was) OR C2 (adjacent to C1) → mixture of products when the benzyne is unsymmetric
- CONDITIONS: Very harsh (NaNH2, ~300°C)
- INTERMEDIATE: Benzyne (C6H4, the aryne)
- KEY DISTINCTION from mechanism ①: Benzyne mechanism gives MIXTURE of positional isomers when asymmetric; mechanism ① gives only ONE product (the activated position)

SIMPLE DISTINGUISHING TEST:
- Has EWG ortho/para to LG? → Mechanism ①
- Uses NaNH2 or very strong base? → Suspect mechanism ②
- Isotope labeling shows scrambling (Nu at C1 and C2)? → Mechanism ② confirmed
concepts.why_fragile: Students confuse SNAr with EAS (both involve aromatic rings but completely opposite electronic requirements: EAS needs EDG+electrophile; SNAr needs EWG+nucleophile). The BENZYNE MECHANISM is particularly tricky: (1) it requires base to FORM the benzyne (elimination first), not to be the Nu; (2) NaNH2 can act as BOTH the base (to form benzyne) AND the nucleophile (NH2-); (3) the benzyne mechanism gives positional scrambling (unlike mechanism 1 which gives only one product). JEE questions often test whether students can identify WHICH mechanism is operating and predict the correct product(s).

concepts.description:
ACYL CHLORIDE (R-COCl) AND ANHYDRIDE (RCO-O-COR) REACTION SUMMARY:

ACYL CHLORIDE R-CO-Cl (most reactive acid derivative, Cl⁻ = best LG):
| Nucleophile | Product | Notes |
|-------------|---------|-------|
| RCOO- (carboxylate) | Anhydride R-CO-O-CO-R | Na+ salt used |
| RO- (alkoxide) | Ester R-CO-OR | NaOR |
| H2O (water) | Carboxylic acid R-COOH + HCl | Hydrolysis |
| NH3 | Primary amide R-CO-NH2 | |
| RNH2 (1° amine) | Secondary amide R-CO-NHR | |
| R2NH (2° amine) | Tertiary amide R-CO-NR2 | |
| R3N (3° amine) | X (NO REACTION) | No NH, cannot form amide; only salt if quaternary N |
| R'MgX (Grignard) | Ketone R-CO-R' (SNth) → then tertiary alcohol with excess Grignard | Cl- departs directly from th intermediate |

ANHYDRIDE (RCO-O-COR, 2nd most reactive):
| Nucleophile | Product | Notes |
|-------------|---------|-------|
| NaCl (Cl-) | X (NO REACTION) | Thermodynamically unfavorable: acyl chloride is MORE reactive than anhydride; cannot 'upgrade' to acyl chloride |
| RONa (alkoxide) | Ester + RCOO- | |

KEY NO-REACTION CASES:
1. R3N + acyl halide or anhydride → X (tertiary amine has no NH; gives salt but not a stable amide product)
2. Cl- + anhydride → X (thermodynamically uphill: would give acyl chloride which is higher energy)
3. Less reactive Nu (carboxylate, Cl-) + less reactive acid derivative (amide) → X

GRIGNARD ADDITION TO ACID DERIVATIVES (SUMMARY):
- R'MgX + acyl halide → ketone (Cl- leaves directly)
- R'MgX + ester → ketone (RO- leaves) → then 2nd equiv of R'MgX adds to ketone → tertiary alcohol
- R'MgX + amide → ketone (after H+ workup, NR2 expelled only with acid)
- In all cases: the 1st Grignard gives ketone (via SNth) and 2nd equiv can give tertiary alcohol (via addition to ketone)

concepts.name: Mixed anhydride selectivity: Nu attacks the acyl C of the group that gives the MORE STABLE carboxylate as LG (lower pKa carboxylate = better LG = departs preferentially); tosylation of ROH = SNth at S, retention at C
concepts.description:
TWO SELECTIVITY PRINCIPLES IN SNth:

1. MIXED ANHYDRIDE SELECTIVITY:
A mixed anhydride R1-CO-O-CO-R2 has TWO different acyl C's. Nu attacks ONE selectively.
SELECTIVITY RULE: Nu attacks the acyl C whose LG (carboxylate) is MORE STABLE (= lower pKa of the corresponding acid = better leaving group ability).

Mechanism: Two competing pathways:
(a) Nu attacks R1-CO: LG = R2-COO⁻
(b) Nu attacks R2-CO: LG = R1-COO⁻
The pathway where the BETTER LG (lower pKa carboxylate) departs is PREFERRED.

EXAMPLE: CH3-CO-O-CO-CH2CH3 (acetic propanoic mixed anhydride) + NaOCH3:
- R1 = CH3 (acetyl), R2 = CH2CH3 (propanoyl)
- pKa of CH3COOH (acetic acid) ≈ 4.75, pKa of CH3CH2COOH (propionic acid) ≈ 4.87
- CH3COO⁻ (acetate) is a BETTER LG (lower pKa acid = weaker conjugate base = better LG)
- Therefore: Nu (CH3O⁻) attacks the PROPANOYL C (CH3CH2-CO-), and CH3COO⁻ departs as LG
- Product: CH3CH2-C(=O)-OCH3 (methyl propanoate) + CH3COO⁻ (acetate)

2. TOSYLATION = SNth AT S WITH RETENTION AT C:
R-OH + TsCl → R-O-Ts (tosylate ester) + HCl
- Mechanism: O lone pair of alcohol attacks S of TsCl (SNth at sulfonyl S)
- C-O bond is NOT broken (no SN2 at C)
- Configuration at C RETAINED (no inversion, no SN2 at C)
- Purpose: converts poor LG (HO⁻) to excellent LG (TsO⁻, pKa of TsOH ≈ -1)
- Stereochemical sequence: R-OH → R-OTs (retention) → R-OTs + Nu (SN2 at C, inversion) → overall INVERTED product from the starting alcohol
concepts.why_fragile: Mixed anhydride selectivity requires knowing WHICH carboxylate is the better LG (from pKa data). Students may predict the wrong acyl C is attacked (confusing which carboxylate departs). Tosylation retention is frequently tested: students may predict inversion (confusing TsCl with a normal SN2 alkylation). The key is recognizing that tosylation is SNth AT S (not SN2 at C), so C-O is never broken → RETENTION at C.

concepts.name: SNAr vs EAS comparison: opposite electronic requirements (EWG activates SNAr, EDG activates EAS); both ortho/para selective for the respective activating group; Meisenheimer anion vs arenium cation
concepts.description:
SNAr vs EAS — DIRECT COMPARISON TABLE:

| Feature | EAS (Electrophilic Aromatic Sub.) | SNAr (Nucleophilic Aromatic Sub.) |
|---------|----------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| Attacking species | Electrophile E+ | Nucleophile Nu:- |
| What the ring needs | Electron-RICH | Electron-POOR |
| Activating group | EDG (OMe, NR2, OH) = +M | EWG (NO2, CN, C=O) = -M |
| Deactivating group | EWG = -M groups | EDG = +M groups |
| Intermediate | Arenium ion (CATION, sp3 ring C) | Meisenheimer complex (ANION, sp3 ring C) |
| Intermediate charge | Positive (+) in ring | Negative (-) in ring |
| Slow step | Nu (H loss = elimination, FAST); E addition = slow | Nu addition (slow), L elimination (FAST) |
| Fast step | H+ loss (proton departs) | L- departs (leaving group departs) |
| Position of activation | Ortho/para to EDG | Ortho/para to EWG |
| Position of deactivation | Meta to EDG (meta position for EWG director) | Ortho/para to EDG (the positions EDG donates into are DEACTIVATED) |
| Common conditions | Lewis acid catalyst (FeBr3, AlCl3), electrophile | High T/P (unactivated) or EWG-activated ring |

KEY MEMORY TRICK:
- EAS: E+ attacks, needs ELECTRONS in ring, EDG helps (like EAS = 'Electrons Activate SNelection of EAS')
- SNAr: Nu:- attacks, needs ring to ACCEPT electrons (be electron-poor), EWG helps
- BOTH reactions: ortho/para selectivity (for the ACTIVATING group in each case)
- BOTH have: sp3 intermediate at one ring C (but arenium CATION vs Meisenheimer ANION)

MEISENHEIMER COMPLEX vs ARENIUM ION:
- Meisenheimer: anionic, delocalized O⁻/C⁻ in ring at ortho/para to attacked C; STABILIZED by EWG at those positions
- Arenium: cationic, delocalized C+ in ring at ortho/para to attacked C; stabilized by EDG at those positions
- Both: ring has one sp3 C (the C where addition occurred); ring is temporarily non-aromatic
concepts.why_fragile: The reversal of EAS and SNAr electronic requirements (EWG activates SNAr; EDG deactivates SNAr) is the MOST TESTED distinction in JEE aromatic chemistry. Students apply EAS logic to SNAr (predicting EDG helps = wrong) or apply meta-direction logic from EWG in EAS to SNAr (same positions, different reasons). The key: in EAS, EWG = meta director (deactivates, but ortho/para to EWG are NOT where substitution occurs in EAS — the meta position is where it goes = wrong position for SNAr). In SNAr, EWG at ortho/para to L = ACTIVATES the ring for SNAr at L. This is a positional reversal: the EWG in EAS directs to META (for the electrophile); in SNAr the EWG at ORTHO/PARA to L activates the position for nucleophile.

concepts.name: SNAr rate ∝ +ve charge intensity at ipso C; F-Ar fastest in SNAr (F strongest -I → most δ+ at ipso) but WORST LG in SN2; at least one -M group at ortho/para to L required; meta EWG = no SNAr
concepts.description:
SNAr RATE RULES — COMPLETE SUMMARY:

1. FUNDAMENTAL RATE LAW: 'Rate of SNAr ∝ +ve charge intensity on ipso position'
   - Ipso C = the ring carbon bearing the leaving group L
   - More δ+ at ipso → Nu:- attacks faster → Meisenheimer forms faster → faster overall SNAr
   - +ve charge intensity at ipso is increased by: (a) EWG (-M, -I groups) at ortho/para; (b) the halogen L itself (if L = halide, F > Cl > Br > I in making ipso δ+)

2. HALOBENZENE SERIES (when halogen is the LG, no other EWG):
   SNAr rate: F-Ph > Cl-Ph > Br-Ph > I-Ph
   Reason: F most electronegative → strongest -I → most δ+ at ipso → fastest SNAr
   Note: OPPOSITE ORDER to SN2 and SNth (where F = worst LG, I = best)

3. ACTIVATION CONDITION (from teacher's box):
   'At least ONE -M group must be present at ortho or para to L'
   - -M group at ortho to L → stabilizes C⁻ (ortho to attack site) in Meisenheimer
   - -M group at para to L → stabilizes C⁻ (para to attack site) in Meisenheimer
   - -M group at META to L → CANNOT stabilize Meisenheimer → NO activation → NO SNAr

4. ADDITIVE ACTIVATION: More -M groups at ortho/para = faster SNAr (cumulative)
   No EWG < 1 EWG (ortho or para) < 2 EWG (ortho + another) < 2 EWG (both ortho AND para)

5. META EWG = NO SNAr:
   Example: 1-Br-3,5-(NO₂)₂-benzene + NaSMe → X (both NO₂ at meta to Br → Meisenheimer not stabilized → no reaction)

6. PRACTICAL EXAMPLES:
   - 2,4-Dinitrochlorobenzene + H₂O (Δ) → 2,4-dinitrophenol (fast SNAr even with H₂O, due to two activating NO₂ at ortho+para)
   - 2,4-Dinitrochlorobenzene + NaOMe → 2,4-dinitroanisole (fast, room T)
   - 2,4-Dinitrofluorobenzene (Sanger's reagent) + H₂NR → 2,4-dinitrophenyl-NHR (very fast, used in protein N-terminus identification)
concepts.why_fragile: Three independent reversal traps: (1) Students predict I-Ar fastest in SNAr (copying SN2 LG ability: I > Br > Cl > F). WRONG: F-Ar is fastest in SNAr because F makes ipso C most electrophilic (rate = Nu addition, not LG departure). (2) Students predict EWG at meta activates SNAr (because meta = where EWG directs in EAS). WRONG: meta EWG does NOT stabilize the Meisenheimer complex. (3) Students may think 1-Br-3,5-dinitrobenzene is HIGHLY activated (two EWG!) and predict fast SNAr. WRONG: the two EWGs are at meta to Br → no Meisenheimer stabilization → no reaction. The condition 'at least one -M at ortho or para' is absolute.

concepts.name: SNAr (addition-elimination) vs SNAr (elimination-addition/benzyne): when each operates; benzyne mechanism requires strong base, gives positional scrambling in product; addition-elimination requires -M at ortho/para to L
concepts.description:
TWO SNAr MECHANISMS — DECISION GUIDE:

MECHANISM ①: ADDITION-ELIMINATION (Meisenheimer)
- Requires: EWG (-M group) at ortho or para to L (to stabilize Meisenheimer)
- Reagent: Any Nu:- (OH-, OR-, NR2-, RS-, etc.)
- Conditions: Can work at room T (activated ring) or needs ↑T/P (unactivated)
- Intermediate: Meisenheimer complex (ANION, detectable for some substrates)
- Product: Single product — Nu replaces L at the SAME position
- Isotope test: ¹⁴C label stays at the same C

MECHANISM ②: ELIMINATION-ADDITION (Benzyne mechanism)
- Requires: STRONG BASE (NaNH₂ at >300°C, RLi, etc.)
- NO EWG required on ring (can work on plain halobenzene)
- Steps:
  a. Base removes H adjacent to C-L (ortho H) → carbanion → L⁻ departs (ELIMINATION first) → BENZYNE (aryne: 1,2-didehydrobenzene, C₆H₄, cyclic alkyne-like species)
  b. Nu adds across the 'triple bond' of benzyne (ADDITION) → anionic intermediate → protonation → product
- Intermediate: BENZYNE (C₆H₄, the aryne), extremely strained and reactive
- Product: MIXTURE of positional isomers when asymmetric benzyne (Nu can add to either C of the 'triple bond') — classic test for mechanism ②
- Isotope test: ¹⁴C label scrambled between two adjacent positions

DISTINGUISHING TESTS:
| Observation | Mechanism ① | Mechanism ② |
|-------------|-------------|-------------|
| Ring has EWG at o/p to L | Yes | Not required |
| Reagent is NaNH₂ or strong RLi | No (usually) | Yes |
| Single product | Yes | No (mixture if asymmetric) |
| ¹⁴C scrambling | No | Yes |
| Works on plain PhCl | No | Yes |

NOTE: NaNH₂ can act as BASE (to form benzyne via deprotonation + LG departure) AND as NUCLEOPHILE (NH₂⁻ adds to benzyne) in the same reaction. The product from benzyne + NH₂⁻ → aniline (if symmetric benzyne) or mixture of 2-aminophenyl and 3-aminophenyl (if asymmetric).
concepts.why_fragile: Students confuse the two SNAr mechanisms when NaNH₂ is the reagent: NaNH₂ can be both a base (forms benzyne via E1cb-like elimination of H + L) and a nucleophile (NH₂⁻ attacks benzyne). The classic error: student predicts one product from the benzyne mechanism (not realizing two addition sites give mixture). Also: the condition 'EWG not needed for benzyne mechanism' surprises students who just learned that EWG is required for SNAr. The two mechanisms have completely different requirements and product profiles.

concepts.name: SNAr COMPLETE RATE FACTORS: ipso C electrophilicity (from EWG at o/p + halide -I), LG ability irrelevant (step 2 always fast), conditions: ↑T↑P for unactivated, room T for doubly-activated rings
concepts.description:
SNAr RATE DETERMINATION — COMPREHENSIVE ANALYSIS:

THE RATE EQUATION (conceptual): Rate(SNAr) ∝ [electrophilicity of ipso C] × [nucleophilicity of Nu]

FACTORS INCREASING IPSO C ELECTROPHILICITY (+ve charge intensity at ipso):
a) EWG (-M groups) at ortho/para to L: withdraws electrons from the ring → ipso C becomes more δ+
   - NO₂ > CN > C=O > F (for -M groups; NO₂ is strongest activator for SNAr)
   - Each additional EWG at ortho/para adds more δ+ at ipso
b) The halide L itself:
   - F makes ipso C most δ+ (strongest -I effect among halogens)
   - I makes ipso C least δ+ (weakest -I)
   - This gives: ArF > ArCl > ArBr > ArI in SNAr rate for the same ring

FACTORS IRRELEVANT TO SNAr RATE:
- LG ability (I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻ by pKa): Step 2 (rearomatization-driven LG departure) is always FAST regardless of LG identity. The bottleneck is ALWAYS Step 1 (Meisenheimer formation). LG ability does NOT control SNAr rate.

CONDITIONS REQUIRED:
- Unactivated ring (plain halobenzene, no EWG): 'High temp + High press' (teacher's notes); ↑T/P needed because addition barrier is large
- Singly activated (1 EWG at o/p): lower T needed
- Doubly activated (2 EWG both at o/p): can proceed at room T with moderate Nu
- Doubly activated + F: fastest (Sanger's reagent works at room T with amines)

LEAVING GROUP EFFECT IN SNAr (counterintuitive summary):
| LG | -I effect | Ipso δ+ | SNAr rate | SN2 rate | SNth rate |
|----|-----------|---------|-----------|----------|----------|
| F | Strongest | Most | FASTEST | Slowest | Slowest |
| Cl | Moderate | Mod. | Moderate | Moderate | Moderate |
| Br | Less | Less | Slower | Faster | Faster |
| I | Weakest | Least | SLOWEST | Fastest | Fastest |
concepts.why_fragile: This concept requires simultaneously knowing THREE different reaction rate orders for the same set of halogens in THREE different reaction types (SN2/SNth: I > Br > Cl > F; SNAr: F > Cl > Br > I) and understanding WHY each order is what it is. JEE questions frequently mix up these three contexts. The key distinction: in SN2/SNth the SLOW step involves LG departure → LG ability (I⁻ best) dominates. In SNAr the SLOW step involves Nu ADDITION → ipso C electrophilicity (F makes it most δ+) dominates. The LG departs in a fast step in SNAr.

concepts.description:
SNAr WORKED EXAMPLES — ACTIVATION VS. NO REACTION:

EXAMPLE 1 (activated, two EWG at ortho+para to L):
2,4-Dinitrochlorobenzene (1-Cl, 2-NO₂, 4-NO₂) + H₂O (Δ) → 2,4-Dinitrophenol
- Both NO₂ groups are at ACTIVATING positions (C2 = ortho to C1-Cl; C4 = para to C1-Cl)
- Meisenheimer at C1: C2⁻ stabilized by C2-NO₂; C4⁻ stabilized by C4-NO₂
- Two simultaneous stabilizations → very stable Meisenheimer → even weak Nu (H₂O) reacts
- Only heat (Δ) needed, not extreme T/P

EXAMPLE 2 (NOT activated, both EWG at meta to L):
1-Bromo-3,5-dinitrobenzene + NaSMe → X (no reaction)
- NO₂ at C3 (meta to C1-Br) and C5 (meta to C1-Br)
- Meisenheimer at C1: C2⁻, C4⁻, C6⁻ positions are ALL unsubstituted (no EWG to stabilize)
- The NO₂ groups at C3 and C5 cannot delocalize C2⁻, C4⁻, or C6⁻ via resonance
- RESULT: Meisenheimer complex is unstabilized → high barrier → even reactive Nu (CH₃S⁻) cannot displace Br

EXAMPLE 3 (partially activated, only one EWG at para):
4-Nitrochlorobenzene + NaOH (↑T↑P) → 4-Nitrophenol
- ONE NO₂ at para to Cl → one stabilization path in Meisenheimer → works but requires higher T/P

EXAMPLE 4 (Q from teacher: regioselectivity with Br and Cl):
Ring with Br (C1-LG), Cl (at another C), NO₂ (para to Br = C4) + NaOH (1 eq, ↑T↑P):
- C1-Br: NO₂ at C4 = para to C1 → ACTIVATED → Br displaced by OH
- C-Cl: NO₂ at C4 is meta to C-Cl (if Cl is at C3) → NOT activated → Cl remains
- Product: C1-OH, Cl retained, NO₂ retained

GENERAL RULE FROM ALL EXAMPLES:
Activation = EWG at C2/C6 (ortho to C1-L) OR C4 (para to C1-L) → SNAr occurs
No activation = all EWG at C3/C5 (meta to C1-L) → SNAr does NOT occur, regardless of EWG strength
concepts.why_fragile: The 1-bromo-3,5-dinitrobenzene example (two EWG but both meta → no reaction) is a highly deceptive trap. Students see two strong EWG groups and predict fast SNAr (more EWG = faster, right?). Wrong: POSITION determines activation, not number. Two meta-EWG groups = ZERO activation. This inverts the expected intuition. JEE problems frequently use this exact pattern to test whether students apply the position rule correctly.

concepts.name: Benzyne (1,2-didehydrobenzene): π=3 (aromatic 2π + 1 extra in-plane sp2-sp2 bond), highly reactive, unstable; forms by E1cb from aryl halide + strong base (ortho-H removed, then X- departs); conditions: no -M group on ring
concepts.description:
BENZYNE (ARYNE) — COMPLETE STRUCTURAL AND MECHANISTIC PROFILE:

STRUCTURE OF BENZYNE:
- Formal formula: C₆H₄ (1,2-didehydrobenzene)
- π = 3 (THREE pi bonds total):
  ① π₁: aromatic pi bond in the 6-membered ring (part of normal benzene aromaticity)
  ② π₂: aromatic pi bond (second aromatic component)
  ③ π₃: EXTRA in-plane sp2-sp2 π bond between C1 and C2 (the former C-Cl and C-H positions; their remaining sp2 orbital lobes overlap sideways IN THE RING PLANE, forming a strained π bond orthogonal to the aromatic π system)
- The extra in-plane π bond makes benzyne formally an aryne (cyclic 'alkyne' equivalent)
- This extra bond is NOT part of the aromatic system → NOT stabilized by aromatic delocalization → STRAINED and HIGHLY REACTIVE

FORMATION (from aryl halide):
Method: Strong base (NaNH₂, NaOH, KNH₂, RLi) + aryl halide (Ar-Cl, Ar-Br) → benzyne + HX
Mechanism: E1cb-like:
1. Base abstracts H from C ortho to C-X → carbanion at ortho C
2. C-X bond breaks (C-X departure) → benzyne + X⁻
Alternatively: base removes ortho-H, C-X departure concerted or stepwise

CONDITIONS REQUIRED:
Ring characteristics for benzyne mechanism (vs Meisenheimer):
- Benzyne: ring has +M, +H, +I, -I, or unsubstituted
- Meisenheimer (addition-elimination): ring has -M (EWG) at ortho/para to L → Meisenheimer is favored, benzyne NOT needed
- KEY: If ring has NO -M group → Meisenheimer cannot form → benzyne mechanism is the alternative

REACTIVITY:
- Benzyne is EXTREMELY reactive ('unstable') — reacts with virtually any nucleophile immediately
- The in-plane π₃ bond is strained (ring geometry prevents ideal sp2-sp2 overlap) → high energy → fast reactions
- Even water and alcohols can add to benzyne (unlike normal alkynes which need specific conditions)

NaMNH₂ DUAL ROLE IN BENZYNE REACTIONS:
- NaNH₂ (or KNH₂): acts as BASE to deprotonate ortho-H (forms benzyne) AND as NUCLEOPHILE (NH₂⁻ adds to benzyne)
- NaOH: acts as BASE (H₂O acts as proton donor too) and OH⁻ as nucleophile
concepts.why_fragile: Three failure modes: (1) Students draw benzyne with 2 π bonds (like a normal alkyne in a ring) — wrong: π=3 (two from aromaticity + one extra in-plane). (2) Students try to apply Meisenheimer mechanism to unactivated rings (no -M group) — wrong: benzyne mechanism is the correct path. (3) Students miss the dual role of NaNH₂/NaOH: acts as BOTH base (forms benzyne) and nucleophile (adds to benzyne). JEE asks 'how many moles of NaNH₂ are needed?' — 2 mol? Actually only 1 mol: one step uses the base, the NH₂⁻ stays to be the nucleophile.

concepts.name: Cine substitution in benzyne mechanism: Nu ends up at ADJACENT C to where LG was (NOT same C); major when +M or +I group at para to one benzyne C enriches it; minor product = normal substitution (Nu at same C as LG)
concepts.description:
CINE SUBSTITUTION — DEFINITION AND REGIOSELECTIVITY RULES:

DEFINITION:
'CINE SUBSTITUTION': The nucleophile (Nu) is incorporated at a RING CARBON ADJACENT to the carbon where the leaving group (LG) was. The LG was at C1; Nu ends up at C2 (cine) rather than C1 (normal).
Name 'cine' = from Latin 'cinis' (ash) or Greek 'kinein' (to move) — Nu has 'moved' one carbon from LG.

MECHANISM: Unique to the BENZYNE mechanism (cannot occur in addition-elimination SNAr which always gives Nu at the same C as LG).

BENZYNE REGIOSELECTIVITY RULES:
After benzyne forms between C1 and C2, Nu:- adds to one of these two carbons. Which one?

RULE: Nu attacks the MORE ELECTROPHILIC carbon of the benzyne.
A substituent at C4 (para to C1 of benzyne) controls C1 vs C2 electrophilicity:

| Group at C4 | Effect | C1 becomes | Nu attacks | Product |
|-------------|--------|-----------|-----------|--------|
| OMe (+M >> -I) | +M into C1 (para) | Electron-rich | C2 (meta to OMe) | CINE (major) |
| CH₃ (+I, no +M) | +I into C1 (para) | Slightly electron-rich | C2 (slight preference) | CINE (major, weak) |
| No group (H) | No effect | Equal to C2 | C1 and C2 equally | 1:1 (A:B = 1:1 for this component) |
| F, Cl (-I) | -I makes C1 electron-poor | Electron-poor | C1 | NORMAL (slight) |

EXAMPLES:
① 1-Cl-4-OMe-benzene + KNH₂ → benzyne (C1-C2, OMe at C4)
   OMe +M enriches C1 → NH₂ attacks C2 → CINE = major (2-amino-4-methoxybenzene)
   NORMAL = minor (4-methoxyaniline)

② 1-Cl-4-CH₃-benzene + NaNH₂ → benzyne (C1-C2, CH₃ at C4)
   CH₃ +I weakly enriches C1 → NH₂ slightly prefers C2 → CINE = major (weak)
   NORMAL = minor (small ratio difference)

PRACTICAL TEST FOR CINE:
If product has NH₂ at a carbon that did NOT bear Cl in the starting material → cine substitution.
This confirms the benzyne mechanism (would not happen in addition-elimination).
concepts.why_fragile: Multiple failure modes: (1) Students don't know cine substitution exists — predict only normal product (Nu at same C as LG). (2) Students know cine exists but don't know which is major. The OMe case is highly deceptive: OMe is usually seen as 'Nu likes to be ortho/para to OMe' (EAS logic), which would INCORRECTLY predict normal substitution (Nu at C1 = para to OMe) as MAJOR. In BENZYNE addition: OMe +M makes C1 electron-RICH → Nu AVOIDS C1 → goes to C2 (cine) → MAJOR. The EAS logic predicts the WRONG product here. (3) CH₃ (+I only) selectivity is weak — students may treat +I and +M as equivalent, overestimating the CH₃ effect.

concepts.name: Benzyne 1:2:1 product ratio fingerprint; at least 2X (halides) needed for -I-only SNAr (no -M); benzyne conditions: +M/+I/unsubstituted ring; harsh (623K, 300 atm) required for unactivated ring
concepts.description:
BENZYNE MECHANISM — KEY RULES AND DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA:

1. PRODUCT RATIO FINGERPRINT (1:2:1):
When an aryl halide has H on BOTH sides of C-Cl (symmetric flanking), the benzyne mechanism gives products A:B:C = 1:2:1.
- A = Nu at one end of benzyne (product from pathway 1)
- B = Nu at middle C (same structural product from BOTH pathways, counted 2×)
- C = Nu at other end (product from pathway 2 only)
- The 1:2:1 ratio is the DIAGNOSTIC FINGERPRINT of the benzyne mechanism

2. ADDITION-ELIMINATION GIVES ONE PRODUCT; BENZYNE GIVES MIXTURE:
- If SNAr gives a single clean product: → Meisenheimer (addition-elimination) mechanism
- If SNAr gives 3 products in 1:2:1 ratio: → Benzyne mechanism
- ¹⁴C isotope scrambling (label at two adjacent carbons in product): → Benzyne mechanism

3. AT LEAST 2X RULE FOR -I-ONLY SNAr ACTIVATION:
EXCEPTION to the '-M group required for SNAr' rule:
Halides (Cl, F) have ONLY -I effect (no -M). -I is weaker than -M for Meisenheimer stabilization.
RULE: If a ring has NO -M group, at least TWO halides (2X) are required for -I-only activation of SNAr (addition-elimination).
- 1 halide only (e.g., simple chlorobenzene): -I too weak → SNAr (addition-elimination) fails → uses benzyne instead
- 2+ halides (e.g., 1,4-dichlorobenzene, 2,4-difluoroiodobenzene): combined -I of 2 halogens provides enough activation for SNAr (addition-elimination)

4. CONDITION GUIDE FOR CHOOSING MECHANISM:
| Ring type | Mechanism | Conditions |
|-----------|-----------|------------|
| -M group (NO₂, CN, C=O) at o/p to L | Addition-Elimination (Meisenheimer) | Moderate T, or room T |
| Unactivated (no -M group) | Benzyne | High T + High P (623K, 300 atm for Dow) |
| NaNH₂/KNH₂ in NH₃(l) reagent | Benzyne | Strong base → E1cb forms benzyne |
| Ring with ≥2 halides, no -M | Addition-Elimination | Moderate conditions (-I activation) |
concepts.why_fragile: The '2X required for -I-only SNAr' exception is obscure and often untaught. Students expect 1 halide (e.g., Cl) to activate SNAr by itself — wrong if there is no -M group (a single Cl's -I is too weak). The 1:2:1 product ratio is the most reliable diagnostic for benzyne mechanism, but students must IDENTIFY the benzyne mechanism from the substrate/conditions (NaNH₂ + unactivated ring) before applying the ratio rule.

concepts.description:
BENZYNE MECHANISM COMPLETE EXAMPLES:

EXAMPLE 1: DOW PROCESS
Chlorobenzene (C₆H₅Cl) + NaOH {623K, 300 atm} → Phenol (C₆H₅OH)
- Mechanism: Benzyne (via NaOH as base removing ortho-H; benzyne then attacked by OH⁻)
- No EWG on ring → Meisenheimer impossible → benzyne only
- Product: phenol (single, symmetric ring → only one product)

EXAMPLE 2: HALOCHLOROBENZENE + NaOH → 3 products (1:2:1)
Chlorobenzene with H at both ortho positions + NaOH → A + B + C = 1:2:1
- Two benzyne pathways give three structural products in 1:2:1 ratio

EXAMPLE 3: 1-CHLORO-4-METHOXYBENZENE + KNH₂/NH₃(l)
1-Cl-4-OMe-C₆H₄ + KNH₂ → 2-amino-4-methoxybenzene (MAJOR, cine) + 4-methoxyaniline (minor, normal)
- Benzyne C1-C2 formed
- OMe at C4 (+M): enriches C1 (para to OMe) → NH₂ attacks C2 → cine = major
- OMe -I (weak): minor contribution
- Net: CINE MAJOR

EXAMPLE 4: 1-CHLORO-4-METHYLBENZENE + NaNH₂/NH₃(l)
1-Cl-4-CH₃-C₆H₄ + NaNH₂ → 2-amino-4-methylbenzene (major, cine) + 4-methylaniline (minor, normal)
- Benzyne C1-C2 formed
- CH₃ at C4 (+I only): weakly enriches C1 → NH₂ slightly prefers C2 → cine = major (weak preference)

EXAMPLE 5: 1-CHLORO-3-METHYLBENZENE + NaNH₂/NH₃(l)
1-Cl-3-CH₃-C₆H₄ + NaNH₂ → SINGLE PRODUCT
- CH₃ at C3 (meta to C1-Cl): two benzynes can form (C1-C2 or C1-C6), but CH₃ is at C3 = ortho to C2 position of first benzyne → NH₂ addition to benzyne analyzed → product with NH₂ adjacent to CH₃
- Due to symmetry or specific CH₃ position → single major product observed

The key failure: students don't apply the cine regioselectivity rule (OMe/CH₃ at para position of benzyne → Nu goes to adjacent C). Instead they predict Nu at the same C as LG (normal substitution) for all cases. The OMe case is especially tricky because students know 'OMe is ortho/para director' in EAS and incorrectly predict Nu at C1 (para to OMe) = normal as major.

concepts.name: Elimination reaction classification: 1,1 (alpha, same C, carbene), 1,2 (beta, adjacent C, alkene), 1,3-1,6; mechanisms E1/E2/E1CB/Ei; dehydrohalogenation conditions: alc. NaOH/NaNH2/RO-/Delta
concepts.description:
ELIMINATION REACTIONS — COMPLETE TAXONOMIC FRAMEWORK:

CLASSIFICATION BY POSITION OF DEPARTING ATOMS (H and LG positions):
① 1,1 Elimination (α-elimination): H and LG from the SAME carbon → CARBENE (:CRR', divalent C)
② 1,2 Elimination (β-elimination): H from β-C, LG from α-C (adjacent) → ALKENE (most common)
③ 1,3 Elimination (γ-elimination): H and LG are 1,3 apart → 3-membered RING (cyclopropane) or other
④ 1,4 Elimination (δ-elimination): H and LG 1,4 apart → 4-membered ring or special products
⑤ 1,5 Elimination → 5-membered ring or cyclized products
⑥ 1,6 Elimination → 6-membered ring or cyclized products

MECHANISMS (four types, all for 1,2-elimination unless specified):
① E1 (Unimolecular Elimination): Ionization of LG → carbocation → loss of β-H → alkene. Two steps, 1st order. Favored: tertiary substrate, weak base, polar solvent.
② E2 (Bimolecular Elimination): Concerted — base removes β-H simultaneously with LG departure → alkene. One step, 2nd order. Favored: strong bulky base (KOH-alc., t-BuOK), anti-periplanar geometry required.
③ E1CB (Carbanion mechanism): Base removes β-H FIRST → carbanion at β-C (the 'CB' = conjugate base) → LG departs. Two steps, β-H removed in slow step. Favored: excellent base, poor LG, or system where carbanion is stabilized (e.g., β-nitro, β-cyano).
④ Ei (Internal Elimination): Pyrolytic, cyclic TS, SYN elimination. No external base needed. Favored: pyrolysis conditions, amine oxides (Cope), ester pyrolysis (acid pyrolysis).

DEHYDROHALOGENATION CONDITIONS (for 1,2-elimination of HX):
- alc. NaOH/Δ → E2 (or E1 for 3° substrates)
- alc. NaNH₂/Δ → E2 (very strong base, good for less reactive substrates)
- alc. RO⁻/Δ → E2 (alkoxide: t-BuOK = strongly basic, bulky, excellent for elimination vs. substitution)
- Strong base + heat in alcoholic solvent = elimination-favoring conditions
- aqueous KOH = favors SN2 over E2; alcoholic KOH/Δ = favors E2 over SN2
concepts.why_fragile: Students confuse the six types of elimination by number: 1,1 (same C → carbene) vs 1,2 (adjacent C → alkene) is the most critical. The 1,3-1,6 types give cyclic products (not alkenes) — students often predict alkenes for all types. The four mechanisms (E1/E2/E1CB/Ei) all give alkene but by different mechanisms with different stereochemical and regiochemical outcomes. The condition 'alc. NaOH' = elimination vs 'aq. NaOH' = substitution is a frequently tested distinction. Also: 1,1 α-elimination gives CARBENE (not alkene) — students may predict an alkene from CHCl₃ + base.

concepts.description:
1,1-ELIMINATION (α-ELIMINATION) — COMPLETE CARBENE GENERATION SUMMARY:

DEFINITION: H and LG leave from the SAME carbon (the α-carbon) → CARBENE (:CXY).
Carbene: divalent carbon with only 2 bonds, one lone pair, one empty orbital (singlet) or two unpaired e- (triplet).

METHOD 1: HALOFORM + STRONG BASE:
CHX₂Y + NaOH → :CX₂ (or :CXY) — the H is removed by OH⁻ to give carbanion :CX₂Y⁻, then BEST LG (I > Br > Cl >> F) departs from same C → carbene.
Examples:
- CHCl₃ → :CCl₂ (dichlorocarbene, SINGLET, electrophilic)
- CHClBrI → :C(Cl)(Br) (I departs, best LG)
- CHFBrCl → :C(F)(Cl) (Br departs; F stays = worst LG)

METHOD 2: GEM-DIHALIDE + RLi/RNa (Li-HALOGEN EXCHANGE):
gem-X₂-C(ring) + RLi → C(Li)(X) carbanion in ring → α-elimination of X⁻ → CYCLIC CARBENE
- gem-diBr cyclopropane + RLi → cyclopropylidene :C₃H₄
- gem-diCl cyclopentane + RNa → cyclopentylidene :C₅H₈

METHOD 3: DIAZOMETHANE + UV:
CH₂N₂ + hν → :CH₂ (methylene, TRIPLET ground state) + N₂ (gas, very stable, drives reaction)
The N₂ departure is the 'leaving group' of 1,1-elimination type (from diazo C).

METHOD 4: KETENE + HEAT (Δ):
CH₂=C=O (ketene) + Δ → :CH₂ + CO
Ketene is 'thermodynamically unstable' — decomposes spontaneously with heat.

METHOD 5: α-HALO CARBOXYLATE + Δ (decarboxylation → carbene):
R-C(L)(R')-COOH + Δ → -CO₂ → carbanion → -L⁻ → R-:C(R') carbene

CARBENE SINGLET vs TRIPLET RELEVANCE:
- Singlet :CX₂ (e.g., :CCl₂, :CHOMe): electrophilic, adds to alkenes STEREOSPECIFICALLY (syn addition → cis/trans preserved in cyclopropane product)
- Triplet :CH₂ (methylene from diazomethane): diradical, adds to alkenes NON-STEREOSPECIFICALLY
concepts.why_fragile: Carbene chemistry is rich with traps: (1) LG selectivity in haloform α-elimination: F stays (worst LG) even though F is in the carbanion. Students predict F leaves (EAS logic or electronegativity reasoning → F is most electronegative → should leave? No — F⁻ is a POOR LG). (2) Students may predict diazomethane gives an alkyl-N product rather than :CH₂ + N₂. (3) Ketene thermolysis gives :CH₂ + CO — students may not know ketene is 'thermodynamically unstable'. (4) Confusion between singlet (stereospecific) and triplet (non-stereospecific) carbene behavior in cyclopropanation.

concepts.name: Benzyne SNAr: no ortho-H (2,6-dimethyl-chlorobenzene) = NO reaction with NaNH2; ipso attack in SNAr = Nu attacks C bearing non-halide EWG (e.g. NO2 can be LG when ring is doubly activated)
concepts.description:
BENZYNE BLOCKING (NO ORTHO-H) AND SNAr IPSO ATTACK:

1. BENZYNE BLOCKED BY SUBSTITUENTS AT BOTH ORTHO POSITIONS:

For benzyne mechanism to operate: a BASE must remove an H from a carbon ADJACENT (ortho) to C-Cl.
If BOTH ortho positions to C-Cl are occupied by non-H substituents (CH₃, halogens, etc.), there is NO ortho-H → benzyne CANNOT form → NO REACTION with NaNH₂.

EXAMPLE: 2,6-Dimethylchlorobenzene (Cl at C1, CH₃ at C2 and C6 = both ortho positions blocked) + NaNH₂/NH₃(l) → NO REACTION.
- No -M EWG at ortho/para to Cl → Meisenheimer SNAr impossible.
- No ortho-H adjacent to Cl → benzyne impossible.
- Result: completely inert toward NaNH₂.

2. SNAr IPSO ATTACK:

Definition: 'Ipso attack' = the nucleophile attacks the ring C at the SAME position as a substituent (not H, not a simple halide LG), and that substituent DEPARTS as the leaving group. The usual LG in SNAr is halide (Cl, Br, F). But in IPSO attack: the LG is a group at the 'ipso' position, such as NO₂, NR₃⁺, SO₃H, etc.

WHEN DOES NO₂ LEAVE AS LG IN SNAr (Ipso):
Requires: very highly activated Meisenheimer complex (e.g., TWO NO₂ groups at ortho+para to the ipso C from which NO₂ is departing).
Example: 1-NO₂-2-NO₂-4-NO₂ (trinitrobenzene-type) + CH₃O⁻ → Meisenheimer at C1 (bearing first NO₂) stabilized by C2-NO₂ and C4-NO₂ → NO₂⁻ departs from C1 → product = 1-OMe-2-NO₂-4-NO₂.

From page 7 example: Ring with 'αN' (NO₂ at C2=ortho) + NO₂ (at C4=para) + CH₃O⁻/Δ → product: ring with OMe at C1, NO₂ at C2, NO₂ at C4. The LG at C1 (NO₂ or another group) is displaced by OMe via SNAr Meisenheimer (C2-NO₂ and C4-NO₂ stabilize the Meisenheimer at C1).

GENERAL IPSO LG ABILITY IN SNAr:
NO₂⁻ > SO₃H > F > Cl > Br > I (for ipso displacement under highly activated conditions)
NO₂ is actually a GOOD LG in SNAr when used in the ipso position and the ring is strongly activated: NO₂⁻ (nitrite ion) is reasonably stable.
concepts.why_fragile: Two failure modes: (1) '2,6-dimethylchlorobenzene + NaNH₂ → aniline' — students predict the product without recognizing that NO ortho-H means no benzyne → no product. (2) 'Ipso attack' is surprising: students know NO₂ is an EWG/activating group for SNAr but don't expect NO₂ itself to be the LG. The concept that an EWG can be BOTH the activating group (at adjacent position) AND the leaving group (at the attacked position) requires careful distinction of which NO₂ group activates and which one departs.

concepts.description:
1,1 vs 1,2 ELIMINATION — COMPARATIVE SUMMARY:

| Feature | 1,1-Elimination (α) | 1,2-Elimination (β) |
|---------|---------------------|---------------------|
| H position | Same C as LG (α-C) | Adjacent C to LG (β-C) |
| LG position | α-C | α-C |
| Product | CARBENE (:CRR') | ALKENE (C=C) |
| Bond formed | Lone pair + empty orbital | π Bond (C=C) |
| Common conditions | CHX₃ + NaOH; gem-X₂ + RLi; diazomethane + UV; ketene + Δ | alc. NaOH/Δ; alc. NaNH₂/Δ; alc. RO⁻/Δ; strong base + heat |
| Mechanism | α-elimination carbanion | E1, E2, E1CB, Ei |
| Stability of product | Carbene = highly reactive, transient | Alkene = stable |
| Frequency | Rare (specific conditions) | Very common (most elimination reactions) |

1,2 β-ELIMINATION REAGENTS (DEHYDROHALOGENATION):
All favor elimination over substitution:
① alc. NaOH/Δ — most common classroom reagent
② alc. NaNH₂/Δ — very strong base (pKa of NH₃ ≈ 38), excellent for difficult substrates
③ alc. R-O⁻Na⁺/Δ — alkoxide (t-BuOK in t-BuOH = strongly basic + bulky → E2, minimal SN2)
④ Strong base alone at high T

WHY 'ALCOHOLIC' SOLVENT:
- Water (aqueous NaOH) → SN2 substitution preferred
- Alcohol solvent (alc. NaOH) → poor solvation of Nu, OH⁻ is more basic/less nucleophilic → elimination preferred
- The polar aprotic analog: DMF + NaI → SN2; DMF + t-BuOK → E2

E1 vs E2 vs E1CB vs Ei (preview):
- E1: carbocation intermediate; 1st order; no stereospecificity
- E2: concerted; anti-periplanar required; 2nd order; trans product preferred
- E1CB: carbanion intermediate; best base needed; syn or anti
- Ei: pyrolysis, syn (cis), cyclic TS, no external base

THREE TYPES OF 1,2-ELIMINATION OF ORGANIC MOLECULES:

(A) DEHYDROHALOGENATION (-HX from alkyl halide → alkene):
Reagents: alc. NaOH/Δ, alc. KOH/Δ, alc. NaNH₂/Δ, alc. RO⁻/Δ
Substrate: -Cβ(H)-Cα(X)- → >Cβ=Cα< (alkene)

(B) DEHYDRATION (loss of H₂O from alcohol → alkene):
Substrate: -Cβ(H)-Cα(OH)- → >Cβ=Cα< (alkene)
Reagents (all require heat, Δ):
① conc. H₂SO₄/Δ (most common classroom reagent)
② conc. H₃PO₄/Δ (milder acid, less rearrangement)
③ conc. POCl₃/Δ (phosphorus oxychloride, converts OH to better LG -OPOCl₂ → E2)
④ conc. Al₂O₃/Δ (alumina, solid acid catalyst, heterogeneous, industrial)
⑤ conc. ThO₂/Δ (thorium dioxide, solid oxide catalyst — least common but MENTIONED by teacher)
All 5 give alkene. Key: requires ACID or ACIDIC SOLID CATALYST + HEAT.

(C) DEHALOGENATION (vicinal 1,2-dihalide → alkene OR 1,n-dihalide → ring):
Substrate: -Cα(X)-Cβ(X)- (vicinal dihalide) or X-Cα...Cω-X (1,n-dihalide)
Reagents:
① Mg/Δ → MECHANISM: CARBANION (Mg-X exchange → organometallic carbanion → α-elimination or ring closure)
② Zn/Δ → MECHANISM: RADICAL (Zn donates e⁻ → radical intermediate)
③ NaI/acetone, Δ (halide ion displacement → elimination)
Products: 1,2-dihalo → alkene; 1,3 → cyclopropane; 1,4 → cyclobutane; 1,5 → cyclopentane; 1,6 → cyclohexane; 1,7 → POLYMER

CRITICAL DISTINCTION:
'Mg = carbanion mechanism' vs 'Zn = radical mechanism' — EXAM TRAP. Same product (alkene), different mechanisms. Question: 'What type of intermediate is involved when vicinal dibromide reacts with Zn?' → RADICAL (not carbanion, not carbocation).
concepts.why_fragile: Students confuse dehydration (B) and dehydrohalogenation (A) reagents. Key traps: (1) Al₂O₃/Δ = dehydration of alcohol (NOT dehydrohalogenation); (2) alc. KOH/Δ = dehydrohalogenation (NOT dehydration); (3) ThO₂ as dehydration catalyst is non-obvious. (4) Mg vs Zn mechanism difference: Mg = carbanion (organometallic, like Grignard); Zn = radical (single electron transfer, free radical). Students often say both are 'ionic' or both are 'radical' — wrong. (5) 1,n-dihalide ring size: 1,3→3-ring, 1,4→4-ring, 1,5→5-ring, 1,6→6-ring, 1,7→POLYMER (not 7-ring).
