concepts.description:
E2 REACTION — COMPLETE MECHANISTIC AND KINETIC PROFILE:

BOX HEADING: [E2 Rxn]

FIVE KEY PROPERTIES OF E2:

① LEAVING GROUP RATE ORDER:
R-F < R-Cl < R-Br < R-I (E2 rate)
F = slowest LG (C-F bond strong, F⁻ poor LG), I = fastest. Same as SN2 LG order.

② RATE LAW — BIMOLECULAR (2nd order):
Rate ∝ [R-L]¹[Base]¹ → Order = 2.
Rate = k[substrate][base]. Depends on BOTH substrate AND base concentrations simultaneously → rate doubles if either doubles.

③ ENERGY PROFILE — CONCERTED, ONE TS, ΔH = +Ve:
- ONE TS‡ maximum, NO intermediate (not E1 which has carbocation intermediate)
- ΔH = +Ve (ENDOTHERMIC): alkene product is at HIGHER energy than starting alkyl halide + base
- '#TS looks like product' (HAMMOND'S POSTULATE): endothermic reaction → LATE TS → TS is PRODUCT-LIKE → the TS resembles the alkene product → stability of alkene ∝ stability of TS → Saytzeff product (more stable alkene) is kinetically preferred

④ RATE ORDER BY SUBSTRATE CLASS:
E2: 3° > 2° > 1° (BOXED)
→ Gives MORE CROWDED ALKENE (Saytzeff): tertiary substrate → most substituted alkene
Comparison:
- SN1 = 3° > 2° > 1° (carbocation stability)
- SN2 = 3° < 2° < 1° (steric access)
- E1 = 3° > 2° > 1° (carbocation stability)
- E2 = 3° > 2° > 1° (product-like TS: stability of alkene product determines TS)

⑤ ANTI-PERIPLANAR GEOMETRY (checkmark = REQUIRED):
Elimination tree: syn → syn-periplanar (dihedral=0°) | Anti ✓ → anti-periplanar (dihedral=180°)
E2 requires H-Cβ-Cα-L dihedral = 180° (anti-periplanar).
Reason: maximum orbital overlap for developing π bond → the breaking C-H σ* and breaking C-L σ* must align with the forming Cβ=Cα π bond → anti arrangement of H and L maximizes this overlap.
Consequence: Cyclic systems must be in the TRANS-DIAXIAL conformation (for chair) to undergo E2. Cis-diaxial or equatorial-axial cannot go E2.

TRANSITION STATE STRUCTURE:
[B⊖⋯Hβ⋯Cβ⋯⋯Cα⋯Lˉ]‡ — all in one bracket. Partial bonds: B⋯H (forming), H-Cβ (breaking), Cβ=Cα (forming π), Cα-L (breaking). All SIMULTANEOUS = concerted.
concepts.why_fragile: E2 has the most testable properties in all of JEE elimination chemistry. Failure modes: (1) Students predict E2 rate order = 3°<2°<1° (confusing with SN2). E2 = 3°>2°>1°, same as E1. (2) Students say E2 requires syn-periplanar TS (Ei requires syn, not E2). (3) Students predict ΔH for E2 is -ve (exothermic) — wrong, ΔH = +ve (endothermic) means TS is product-like. (4) Students don't know the TS looks like product (Hammond) → can't explain why E2 gives Saytzeff product. (5) LG order in E2: R-F is SLOWEST (worst LG), not fastest. (6) Order = 2 means it depends on both [substrate] AND [base] — students sometimes say 'E2 depends only on base'.

concepts.description:
1,n-ELIMINATION RING SIZE PRODUCTS:

SUBSTRATE: X-C₁-C₂-...-Cₙ-X (alpha,omega-dihaloalkane, halide at each end)
REAGENTS: Mg/Δ (carbanion) or Zn/Δ (radical)

PRODUCTS BY RING SIZE n:
| n (chain length) | Ring formed | Ring type |
|---|---|---|
| 3 (1,3-dihalo) | 3-membered | Cyclopropane △ |
| 4 (1,4-dihalo) | 4-membered | Cyclobutane □ |
| 5 (1,5-dihalo) | 5-membered | Cyclopentane ⬠ |
| 6 (1,6-dihalo) | 6-membered | Cyclohexane ⬡ |
| 7 (1,7-dihalo) | POLYMER | Polymerization |

General formula: 1,n-dihalo → (n-1)-membered ring (for n = 3,4,5,6)
For n ≥ 7: POLYMERIZATION (intramolecular ring closure fails, intermolecular dominates)

RING STABILITY (governs which rings form readily):
Most stable: 5-membered and 6-membered rings (cyclopentane, cyclohexane)
3-membered (cyclopropane): strain but forms by metal dehalogenation
4-membered (cyclobutane): strain but forms with Mg/Zn
7-membered: TOO LARGE for efficient ring closure under these conditions → polymer

MECHANISM FOR RING CLOSURE (Mg example for 1,3-dichloro):
1. Mg inserts into C1-Cl → C1-MgCl (carbanion at C1 + MgCl attached)
2. C1 carbanion (intramolecular SN2) attacks C3-Cl → 3-membered ring + MgCl₂
→ CYCLOPROPANE

FOR 1,7: C1 carbanion cannot reach C7 of SAME molecule (too low probability) → attacks C7-X of ANOTHER molecule intermolecularly → polymer.

REAGENT MECHANISTIC DISTINCTION (exam critical):
- Mg/Δ → 'Think CARBANION' (organometallic, nucleophilic carbon, carbanion character)
- Zn/Δ → 'Think RADICAL' (single electron transfer, radical intermediates)
- NaI/acetone/Δ → SN2-like exchange (Finkelstein on each halide) → eventual elimination
concepts.why_fragile: Ring size prediction from 1,n-dihalo + Mg/Zn is a classic JEE question. Failure modes: (1) Predicting 7-membered ring from 1,7-dihalo → polymer is the correct answer. Students who don't know this predict cycloheptane. (2) Getting the ring size wrong: 1,3-dihalo gives 3-ring (cyclopropane, not ethylene). Formula: n carbon chain with X at C1 and Cn → (n-1) membered ring from C2 to Cn, plus new C1-Cn bond → n-membered ring? Actually: C1 attacks Cn → C1-Cn bond forms + X₂ lost → ring contains C1,C2,...,Cn = n-membered ring. Wait: 1,3-dihalo is Cl-C1-C2-C3-Cl, n=3 → C1 attacks C3 → C1-C2-C3 ring = 3-membered (cyclopropane). Yes, n atoms in chain → n-membered ring. (3) Confusing Mg=carbanion vs Zn=radical.

concepts.description:
HAMMOND'S POSTULATE APPLIED TO E2 + STEREOCHEMICAL REQUIREMENT:

HAMMOND'S POSTULATE:
For endothermic reactions (ΔH = +ve): the TS is PRODUCT-LIKE (late TS).
For exothermic reactions (ΔH = -ve): the TS is REACTANT-LIKE (early TS).

APPLICATION TO E2:
E2 ΔH = +ve (endothermic, confirmed by teacher: 'ΔH = +Ve' BOXED). Therefore:
→ E2 TS is PRODUCT-LIKE (resembles the alkene product, as stated: '#TS looks like product')
→ The stability of the ALKENE PRODUCT ≈ stability of the TS
→ More stable alkene = more stable TS = lower activation energy = FASTER pathway
→ MORE SUBSTITUTED (more stable) alkene = MAJOR PRODUCT (Saytzeff/Zaitsev rule)
This is WHY Saytzeff product is major in E2: the product-like TS makes the pathway leading to more stable alkene kinetically preferred.

STEREOCHEMICAL REQUIREMENT:
E2 geometry TREE (from teacher's diagram):
• syn-periplanar (dihedral H-Cβ-Cα-L = 0°): H and L on SAME FACE
  - NOT preferred for E2 (no checkmark)
  - When E2 does go syn (very rare): called 'syn-E2' or attributed to Ei in some frameworks
• Anti-periplanar (dihedral H-Cβ-Cα-L = 180°): H and L on OPPOSITE FACES ✓
  - REQUIRED for E2 (checkmark)
  - Allows developing p-orbitals at Cβ and Cα to be anti → maximum overlap → π bond forms

Ei vs E2 STEREOCHEMISTRY DISTINCTION:
- E2: ANTI-periplanar (dihedral = 180°) → generally anti elimination
- Ei (internal, pyrolysis): SYN-periplanar (dihedral = 0°) → cyclic TS, always SYN

CONSEQUENCES OF ANTI-PERIPLANAR REQUIREMENT:
① Cyclohexane substrates: E2 requires TRANS-DIAXIAL arrangement of H and LG
  → cis-4-tert-butylchlorocyclohexane (with Cl equatorial, H on the same face) cannot go E2 easily
  → trans-4-tert-butylchlorocyclohexane (with Cl axial, H axial on opposite face) undergoes E2 readily
② Acyclic substrates: the ANTI conformation (H and L anti) must be achievable → usually no problem for acyclic
③ Vinyl halides and other systems where anti-periplanar is geometrically constrained → modified E2
concepts.why_fragile: Hammond postulate is subtle: students often can't explain WHY E2 gives Saytzeff product — they just memorize 'more substituted = major' without understanding the thermodynamic basis (ΔH = +ve → product-like TS → stability of alkene product ≈ stability of TS). The anti vs syn periplanar distinction is another frequent trap: E2 = anti-periplanar (Ei = syn-periplanar). Students sometimes say 'E2 has syn elimination' (wrong: that's Ei/pyrolysis). Newman projection analysis of which conformer undergoes E2 is a direct exam question.

concepts.name: Anti-elimination > Saytzeff (BOXED rule): in cyclic/rigid substrates, E2 product is the alkene from the beta-H that is ANTI-PERIPLANAR (trans-diaxial) to LG, not the most substituted; acyclic = Saytzeff applies normally
concepts.description:
ANTI-ELIMINATION > SAYTZEFF — BOXED RULE FROM TEACHER:

SAYTZEFF RULE (Zaitsev rule): More substituted alkene = major product of E2 (applies in ACYCLIC systems).

ANTI-PERIPLANAR RULE: E2 TS requires dihedral H-Cβ-Cα-L = 180° (anti-periplanar). In RIGID systems, this geometry is fixed — only the β-H that is anti-periplanar to LG can be eliminated.

CONFLICT: In some rigid/cyclic systems, the β-H that is anti-periplanar to LG is NOT on the carbon that would give the more substituted alkene (Saytzeff). In this case:
BOX: 'Anti-elimination > Saytzeff' → THE PRODUCT IS DETERMINED BY ANTI-PERIPLANAR GEOMETRY, NOT BY SAYTZEFF.

EXAMPLES:
① Cyclohexane with CH₃ at one ring position and Cl at α-C (axial): the specific β-H trans-diaxial to Cl gives a specific alkene. If the trans-diaxial H is on the carbon adjacent to CH₃ (more substituted side), Saytzeff and anti-periplanar agree. If trans-diaxial H is on the LESS substituted side, anti-periplanar wins → less substituted alkene is the actual product.
② Rigid bicyclic systems: the dihedral angles are completely fixed → only ONE possible E2 product (no choice of β-H) → anti-periplanar determines the product uniquely.
③ Adamantyl or norbornyl systems: famous examples where anti-periplanar geometry overrides all other predictions.

WHEN SAYTZEFF APPLIES NORMALLY: Acyclic substrates (free rotation → any dihedral accessible → anti-periplanar always achievable for any β-H → the more substituted β-H pathway has more stable product-like TS → Saytzeff wins by kinetics via Hammond).

SUMMARY TABLE:
| Substrate type | Primary factor for product selectivity |
|---|---|
| Acyclic | Saytzeff (more substituted = major) |
| Cyclic/rigid | Anti-periplanar (trans-diaxial β-H → product) |
| Conflict | Anti-periplanar > Saytzeff (ALWAYS) |
concepts.why_fragile: This is one of the most heavily tested E2 concepts in JEE. Students memorize 'E2 = Saytzeff product' from acyclic examples and apply it blindly to cyclohexane chair problems. Wrong: in cyclohexane E2, the trans-diaxial arrangement determines the product. A question like 'What is the major E2 product of menthyl chloride?' tests exactly this — the trans-diaxial β-H (which may be on the LESS substituted side in the chair) determines the product, NOT the most substituted alkene from Saytzeff. The boxed rule 'Anti-elimination > Saytzeff' is the overriding principle the teacher boxed for a reason.

concepts.name: E2 on cyclohexyl halides: rate depends on LG ability (I>Br>Cl) AND axial vs equatorial position (axial=fast, equatorial=slow); rate order Q7: 2>1>3>4 (I-axial > Br-axial > Br-equatorial > Cl); bridgehead LG = no rxn (no anti-periplanar H possible)
concepts.description:
E2 RATE ON CYCLOHEXYL HALIDES — TWO FACTORS:

FACTOR 1 — LEAVING GROUP ABILITY: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ (same as for all E2, weaker C-LG bond = better LG)
FACTOR 2 — CONFORMATIONAL ACCESSIBILITY: axial LG >> equatorial LG for E2 rate

WHY AXIAL > EQUATORIAL:
- LG AXIAL on cyclohexane: the LG is already in anti-periplanar relationship with β-H at the AXIAL position on BOTH adjacent carbons (trans-diaxial). No conformational change needed → E2 TS directly accessible → FAST.
- LG EQUATORIAL on cyclohexane: the LG is gauche (≈60°) to all β-H atoms (the axial β-H is gauche; the equatorial β-H is gauche from the other direction). Must RING-FLIP (chair flip) to put the LG in axial position first, THEN the anti-periplanar arrangement is accessible → requires extra activation energy for ring flip → SLOW.

Q7 RATE ORDER (BOXED: 2>1>3>4):
1. Compound 1 (Br, axial position): Br is good LG AND axial → second fastest
2. Compound 2 (I, axial position): I is BEST LG AND axial → FASTEST
3. Compound 3 (Br, equatorial or geometrically disadvantaged): Br good LG but equatorial → must flip → slower than Br-axial
4. Compound 4 (Cl, any position): Cl = worst LG → SLOWEST
Combined: 2 > 1 > 3 > 4

BRIDGEHEAD CASES (from Q4):
For some rigid bicyclic systems, ALL β-H atoms are locked at gauche (not anti-periplanar) to the LG, regardless of conformation (no ring flip possible) → No E2 reaction at all.

PRACTICAL RULE:
For any cyclohexyl system: (1) Draw the chair. (2) Put LG axial (flip if needed). (3) Identify trans-diaxial β-H on adjacent carbons. (4) Apply E2 there → that β-H determines the product. (5) Rate ∝ LG ability × (axial LG avoids ring flip cost).
concepts.why_fragile: Students often know E2 requires anti-periplanar but fail to connect this to the RATE DIFFERENCE between axial and equatorial substrates. The Q7 rate order question (2>1>3>4) requires simultaneously applying LG ability AND conformation effects. A common error: ranking purely by LG ability (I > Br > Cl) → gives I > Br > Cl which would be 2>1=3>4, missing the conformation effect that separates Br-axial (1) from Br-equatorial (3). Also: many students don't know that equatorial LG needs a ring flip → extra activation energy → slower E2.

concepts.name: Kinetic Isotope Effect (KIE) in E2: kH/kD > 1 (BOXED), C-H bond breaking in rate-determining TS; E2 (concerted) shows KIE; E1 shows NO KIE (C-H breaking not in RDS); E1CB shows KIE (C-H breaking is RDS)
concepts.description:
KINETIC ISOTOPE EFFECT (KIE) IN ELIMINATION MECHANISMS:

Q8 SETUP: CH₂-CH₂Cl (r₁) vs CD₂-CH₂Cl (r₂) + alc. KOH/Δ
BOX: r₁ > r₂ → KIE is observed → kH/kD > 1 (BOXED)

PRIMARY KIE:
Definition: When the isotopically labeled bond (C-H vs C-D) is the bond that BREAKS in the rate-determining step → primary KIE.
Typical value: kH/kD = 2-7 at 25°C (or kH/kD ≈ 6-7 for fully concerted, approaches theoretical max at 25°C).
Cause: C-D has lower zero-point energy (ZPE) than C-H (ZPE ∝ 1/√reduced_mass → D heavier → lower ZPE → C-D bond effectively stronger → harder to break → slower rate → kH/kD > 1).

KIE AS MECHANISTIC PROBE (KEY TABLE):
| Mechanism | C-H breaking step | KIE observed? |
|---|---|---|
| E2 (concerted) | In the ONLY step (TS): C-H + C-L break together | YES: kH/kD > 1 |
| E1 (carbocation) | In the FAST step (after RDS = C-L break → carbocation) | NO: kH/kD ≈ 1 |
| E1CB (carbanion) | In the FIRST step (RDS = base removes β-H) | YES: kH/kD > 1 |

DISTINGUISHING E2 FROM E1 BY KIE:
- E2: KIE observed (kH/kD > 1) — C-H breaking in TS
- E1: NO KIE for β-H (kH/kD ≈ 1) — C-H breaking is a fast step after carbocation forms
- Both E2 and E1CB show KIE, but they differ in: rate order (E2 = 2nd order; E1CB = 2nd order), stereochemistry (E2 = anti; E1CB = variable), and whether rate depends on base (E2: yes; E1: no)

KIE SECONDARY (minor): isotope NOT at the breaking bond but nearby → kH/kD ≈ 1.0-1.3 (weak effect, not diagnostic).
concepts.why_fragile: KIE is a subtle mechanistic concept rarely encountered in standard JEE preparation but present in advanced questions. Key failure modes: (1) Students say 'E2 is concerted = all bonds break at same time = no KIE' — wrong; concerted means C-H IS breaking in the TS → PRIMARY KIE. (2) Students confuse primary KIE (kH/kD = 2-7, diagnostic) with secondary KIE (kH/kD ≈ 1.1, non-diagnostic). (3) Students don't know E1 shows NO KIE for β-H: they predict KIE for E1 too. The mechanistic distinction: E1 RDS = ionization (C-L break), NOT proton loss → β-H breaking is fast step → no KIE in E1. The teacher's Q8 uses KIE to confirm E2 mechanism.

concepts.description:
E2 PRODUCT COUNT DETERMINATION:

RULE: Each DISTINCT β-carbon (adjacent to α-C bearing LG) that has a β-H in anti-periplanar position gives ONE SET of alkene products. Count the distinct β-carbons/positions.

FROM TEACHER'S QUESTIONS:
Q1 (acyclic, secondary+ substrate): BOX 'No. of product = 3' — three distinct E2 pathways give three alkenes. The major ('CT7' = central circled) is the Saytzeff (more substituted) product.
Q2 (cyclohexane with CH₃ and Cl-axial): ONE major product (anti-diaxial β-H → specific alkene). Anti-elimination > Saytzeff applies.
Q3 (bicyclic): ONE specific alkene from the fixed anti-periplanar β-H in the rigid framework.
Q4 (rigid bicyclic, NO anti-periplanar H): BOX 'No rxn' = 0 products.
Q5 (substituted cyclohexyl halide): BOX 'No. of P = 2' — two anti-periplanar β-H positions (ring β-H and exocyclic β-H) → two products; endocyclic alkene = MAJOR (more substituted, Saytzeff and anti-periplanar agree here).
Q6 (simple cyclohexyl chloride): ONE product (cyclohexene) — all ring β-H are equivalent by symmetry.

HOW TO COUNT PRODUCTS:
1. For each distinct β-C adjacent to α-C: does it have a β-H anti-periplanar to LG?
   - Acyclic: rotate freely → all β-H are accessible → count all β-C types
   - Cyclic: only trans-diaxial β-H qualifies
2. If β-H accessible: draw the resulting alkene. Count unique alkene structures (including E/Z isomers as separate products).
3. Total = number of distinct anti-periplanar pathways.

FOR 2-HALOBUTANE (a 3-product substrate):
α-C = C2 (bearing halide). β-Carbons: C1 (gives 1-butene, minor) and C3 (gives 2-butene cis + 2-butene trans). 1-butene + cis-2-butene + trans-2-butene = 3 products. Major = trans-2-butene (most substituted AND most stable = Saytzeff AND anti-periplanar, since anti-conformer of 2-halobutane gives trans-alkene preferentially).
concepts.why_fragile: Counting E2 products is a direct JEE question type. Students often undercounted (miss cis/trans isomers) or overcounted (count both enantiomers of a single constitutional isomer). Key insight: E/Z isomers are different products; enantiomers are NOT. The 'No. of products = 3' from Q1 likely comes from: 2 constitutional isomers (1-alkene + 2-alkene), where the 2-alkene gives 2 stereoisomers (cis + trans) = 3 total. The 'No. of P = 2' from Q5 comes from 2 constitutional isomers (endocyclic + exocyclic). Students who don't count E/Z isomers would say 2 for Q1 (wrong) and 1 for Q5 (wrong).

concepts.name: E2 product counting with Ha/Hb at same beta-C: diastereotopic beta-H atoms give different E/Z stereoisomers; 2-halobutane type gives 3 products (1 terminal + 2 internal E/Z); each geometric isomer counts separately
concepts.description:
E2 PRODUCT COUNTING — Ha/Hb DISTINCTION AND E/Z STEREOISOMERS:

Q8 (teacher): Secondary bromide with Ha and Hb LABELED at β-C. + alc. KOH/Δ → OVAL: 'No of P = 3'.

DIASTEREOTOPIC β-H ATOMS:
On an sp3 β-C with two H atoms (Ha and Hb), these H's may be DIASTEREOTOPIC (chemically inequivalent) if the molecule lacks a plane of symmetry. In E2:
- Anti-periplanar elimination with Ha → one face of the forming π bond → E alkene
- Anti-periplanar elimination with Hb → opposite face → Z alkene
These are DISTINCT PRODUCTS (different compounds), both counted separately.

GENERAL COUNTING ALGORITHM FOR E2:
① Identify each distinct β-carbon (adjacent to α-C bearing LG).
② For each β-C: draw the alkene formed.
③ Check if E/Z isomerism is possible in that alkene:
  - Terminal alkene (=CH₂): NO E/Z → count as 1 product
  - Internal alkene (both sides of C=C substituted, DIFFERENT groups): E/Z possible → count as 2 products (E + Z)
  - Internal alkene (symmetric): NO E/Z → count as 1 product
④ Sum up all distinct alkene species (constitutional × stereochemical)

EXAMPLE — 2-BROMOBUTANE:
α-C = C2 (CHBr). Two β-carbons:
- β-C = C1 (CH₃): eliminates → 1-butene (CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃, terminal → NO E/Z) → 1 product
- β-C = C3 (CH₂CH₃): eliminates → 2-butene (CH₃CH=CHCH₃, internal + different groups on each C → E/Z possible) → E-2-butene + Z-2-butene → 2 products
Total = 1 + 2 = 3 products. ✓ (Matches 'No of P = 3' from Q8)
Saytzeff major = E-2-butene (most substituted + most stable E isomer).

HA/HB EXPLANATION:
At β-C3 of 2-bromobutane: the two H's (call them Ha and Hb) are diastereotopic (the molecule has a chiral center at C2). Anti-periplanar elimination with Ha gives one of the 2-butene isomers; with Hb gives the other. This is WHY one β-C gives 2 products (E + Z), not just 1.
concepts.why_fragile: Product counting is heavily tested in JEE. Failure modes: (1) Students say '2-bromobutane gives 2 products' (1-butene + 2-butene) by counting structural isomers, ignoring E/Z → wrong, it gives 3 products. (2) Students count E and Z alkene as one product ('2-butene') → wrong for JEE product counting (cis-2-butene ≠ trans-2-butene = 2 distinct compounds). (3) Students don't understand why Ha and Hb at the same β-C give different products — the diastereotopic nature of H atoms in a chiral substrate explains this. The teacher's oval 'No of P = 3' specifically uses Q8 to emphasize this counting.

concepts.description:
SAYTZEFF PRODUCT FOR SUBSTRATES WITH CYCLOALKYL RING + CHAIN:

Q9 (teacher): Substrate = α-C(Br) bearing: (1) cyclopentane ring attached, (2) aliphatic chain attached. Three E2 pathways:

PATHWAY A — Elimination toward RING:
The β-H on the ring carbon adjacent to α-C is removed → C=C bond forms IN the ring (endocyclic C=C) → cyclopentene-type product with the chain substituent. This alkene is MORE SUBSTITUTED because the ring C=C is flanked by ring carbons on both sides (one having the chain = two alkyl groups on each C of the double bond) → SAYTZEFF PRODUCT. Teacher labels this circled-① = 'S' (Saytzeff). ONE structural isomer from this pathway (endocyclic, no E/Z possible at ring-junction C=C in this type of substrate).

PATHWAY B — Elimination toward CHAIN:
The β-H on the chain carbon adjacent to α-C is removed → C=C bond forms in the chain → chain alkene (less substituted than endocyclic because the chain C=C has fewer alkyl substituents). Two geometric isomers (E and Z) → circled-② and circled-② (each '②' = one stereoisomer).

COUNTING: ① (Saytzeff endocyclic, major) + ② (E-chain) + ② (Z-chain) = 3 PRODUCTS.

GENERAL RULE — CYCLOALKYL RING AT α-C:
Endocyclic alkene (C=C inside the ring) > exo/chain alkene in terms of substitution → endocyclic = Saytzeff = major.
For cyclopentane attached at α-C: cyclopentene = 1 structural product from ring pathway; chain alkene = 2 products (E+Z) from chain pathway.

THE 'S' LABEL (teacher's notation):
In Q9, the endocyclic product is labeled 'circled-① = S' where S = Saytzeff. This notation convention: the number in circle = how many STRUCTURAL isomers from that β-C pathway; S = Saytzeff = major. The chain pathway gives 2 structural isomers (circled-②) but is MINOR compared to the Saytzeff endocyclic.
concepts.why_fragile: Students see '① endocyclic' vs '② chain (2 isomers)' and predict the chain alkene is major because 'more products from chain side' (wrong logic). The product COUNT from each β-C is not the same as the SELECTIVITY toward each product. The Saytzeff principle: more substituted alkene = major (kinetically, via product-like TS). Endocyclic (more substituted) = major despite giving only 1 structural type. Chain (less substituted) = minor despite giving 2 stereoisomers. Also: students may think 'endocyclic means fewer substituents' — wrong for cyclopentyl: the ring junction C=C has both ring C's as substituents = trisubstituted or tetrasubstituted → very stable.

concepts.name: 1,3-dihaloalkane + Mg/Delta mechanism: Mg insertion -> C1-MgCl carbanion -> intramolecular SN2 at C3 -> cyclopropane + MgCl2 byproduct; confirms Mg=carbanion mechanism for 1,n-dihalide ring closure
concepts.description:
1,3-DIHALO + Mg MECHANISM — DETAILED (FROM TEACHER PAGE 1):

SUBSTRATE: Cl-C₁-C₂-C₃-Cl (1,3-dichloropropane or homolog, zigzag with 'cl' at C1 and C3)

MECHANISM:
Step 1 — Mg insertion: Mg(0) + C1-Cl → C1-MgCl
  (Mg metal inserts into the C1-Cl bond, oxidizing Mg from 0 to +2; C1 gains organometallic character = carbanion behavior → 'Think carbanion')
Step 2 — Intramolecular SN2 ring closure: C1 (nucleophile, carbanion) attacks C3 (electrophile, still bearing Cl) in an intramolecular SN2 reaction → the C1-C3 bond forms, the C3-Cl bond breaks, Cl⁻ departs as the leaving group.
Products: CYCLOPROPANE (triangle, 3-membered ring: C1-C2-C3) + MgCl₂ (byproduct, shown explicitly and underlined by teacher).

BYPRODUCT MgCl₂: The Mg²⁺ collects both Cl atoms (one from step 1 = C1-Cl, one from step 2 = C3-Cl departure) → forms MgCl₂.

WHY 'THINK CARBANION' FOR Mg:
The C1-MgCl organometallic has significant CARBANION character at C1 (the C-Mg bond is polarized C⁻ because Mg is electropositive). This carbanion then acts as the nucleophile in the intramolecular SN2 at C3.

CONTRAST Mg vs Zn:
- Mg/Δ: 'Think carbanion' → organometallic intermediate → SN2-type ring closure
- Zn/Δ: 'Think radical' → single-electron transfer → radical intermediate → ring closure
BOTH give cyclopropane as product but by fundamentally different mechanisms.

CHAIN LENGTH → RING SIZE:
1,3-dihalo (3-C chain between Cl's) → 3-ring
1,4-dihalo → 4-ring
1,5-dihalo → 5-ring
1,6-dihalo → 6-ring
1,7-dihalo → POLYMER (labeled with circled-cross by teacher = special exception)
concepts.why_fragile: The mechanism detail (Mg→C1-MgCl→SN2 at C3) is tested in 'name the intermediate' questions. Students know 'Mg + dihalide → ring' but don't know the intermediate is an ORGANOMETALLIC CARBANION that does intramolecular SN2. The MgCl₂ byproduct is also tested (students might say the byproduct is MgCl or MgCl₃ — wrong). The 'Think carbanion' vs 'Think radical' labels are exact exam targets for Mg vs Zn mechanism discrimination.

concepts.description:
E2 ELIMINATION — COMPLETE 5-PROPERTY SUMMARY (FROM TEACHER PAGES 3-4):

SUBSTRATE: -C_β(H)-C_α(X)- + strong base(B⊖)/Δ, alc. KOH/Δ, alc. NaNH₂/Δ, or R-O⊖/Δ → [E2 elimination TS] → -C=C- (alkene)

TRANSITION STATE STRUCTURE (from teacher's TS bracket diagram):
[B⊖⋯H⁺⋯C_β-C_α⋯L⁻]‡
- Base⊖ at top approaching β-H
- H⁺ (H is PARTIALLY POSITIVE in TS — it's being removed by base, gaining partial positive character as C-H bond weakens)
- C_β-C_α bond developing π character
- L departing downward from C_α
All CONCERTED (one bracket = one TS).

① LG RATE ORDER: R-F < R-Cl < R-Br < R-I (rate of E2)
('rate of E2' label below the inequality)

② SUBSTRATE CLASS RATE ORDER: 3° > 2° > 1° (Saytzeff Rule)
('R-L: 3°>2°>1° (Saytzeff Rule)' — the substrate rate order for R-L AND the Saytzeff rule are linked: 3° gives faster E2 AND gives more substituted Saytzeff alkene)

③ ENERGY PROFILE:
- Single peak at T.S. (no intermediate, concerted mechanism)
- BOXED: 'ΔH = +ve, endothermic' (ΔH is positive = E2 is endothermic)
- Reactant at lower left, TS at peak, product (>C=C<) at HIGHER LEVEL than reactant
→ 'In E2 Rxn Transition state will look like product.' (Hammond's postulate: endothermic → late TS → TS resembles alkene product)

KEY CORRELATIONS (Hammond applied to E2):
- ΔH=+ve → late TS → TS resembles the ALKENE PRODUCT
- More stable alkene = more stable product-like TS = lower Ea = FASTER rate
- Therefore: more substituted alkene (Saytzeff) = major product
- Therefore: 3° substrate gives more substituted alkene → faster E2 (3°>2°>1°)

ALL 5 PROPERTIES TOGETHER (exam-ready):
1. Reagents: alc. strong base + Δ
2. TS: concerted anti-periplanar [B⊖⋯H⁺⋯Cβ-Cα⋯L⁻]‡
3. Kinetics: 2nd order, Rate = k[R-L][Base]
4. Thermodynamics: ΔH = +ve (endothermic)
5. Product: Saytzeff (more substituted alkene), major
concepts.why_fragile: The TS structure detail ('H is partially positive in TS') is an advanced mechanistic point — H is transferred to the base, so it acquires partial + charge as the C-H bond is BREAKING (H is being lost from C, becoming more like H⁺ en route to B-H). Students may think H is partially negative (being removed by base = taking H as H⁻). Actually: the base removes it as H⁺ in a proton transfer sense — the H develops partial + charge as it's being transferred to the electronegative base. This TS detail helps explain the concerted nature and why stronger bases give faster E2.

concepts.name: Resonance > Saytzeff (BOXED): when one E2 product is conjugated/resonance-stabilized, it is major over the more-substituted Saytzeff product; complete hierarchy: Anti-periplanar > Resonance > Saytzeff
concepts.description:
RESONANCE > SAYTZEFF — BOXED RULE FROM TEACHER (page 7 of RM lec7 p2):

COMPLETE E2 PRODUCT SELECTIVITY HIERARCHY (all rules together):
1. Anti-periplanar requirement → determines WHICH β-H CAN react (geometry gate)
   If no anti-periplanar β-H available → No reaction.
   'Anti-elimination > Saytzeff'
2. Among geometrically accessible β-H's:
   If one gives CONJUGATED/RESONANCE-STABILIZED alkene → RESONANCE > SAYTZEFF → conjugated alkene = major
   'Resonance > Sytzeff' (BOXED)
3. If no resonance factor → Saytzeff (more substituted) = major.
   '3°>2°>1° and Saytzeff Rule'

WHEN RESONANCE > SAYTZEFF APPLIES:
Substrate has two types of β-H: one giving a conjugated alkene, one giving a more substituted but non-conjugated alkene. The CONJUGATED product is major.

TYPICAL EXAMPLES:
① Alkyl halide adjacent to a ring double bond: elimination toward the ring → conjugated alkene (diene or triene) = major; elimination away from ring → isolated more-substituted alkene = minor.
② Bicyclic substrate where one β-C gives endocyclic alkene conjugated with another ring → major product.
③ Allylic halide where one pathway gives a conjugated diene → major.

WHY (HAMMOND'S POSTULATE):
ΔH E2 = +ve → TS resembles product → stability of product ∝ stability of TS.
Conjugated alkene is stabilized by: (a) π-π overlap/extended conjugation, (b) resonance delocalization of electrons → LOWER energy than a more substituted non-conjugated alkene → more stable TS → lower Ea → faster E2 → MAJOR.
Quantitatively: conjugation stabilization per double bond ≈ 15 kJ/mol; each methyl substituent on C=C ≈ 5-7 kJ/mol. For a conjugated alkene, 15 kJ/mol >> 5 kJ/mol per methyl → conjugation wins for moderate substitution differences.

SUMMARY TABLE OF E2 MAJOR PRODUCT RULES:
| Priority | Condition | Winner |
|---|---|---|
| 1 (absolute) | Anti-periplanar not available | No reaction |
| 2 (overrides Saytzeff) | Resonance-stabilized alkene possible | Conjugated alkene = major |
| 3 (default) | No special effects | Saytzeff (most substituted) = major |
concepts.why_fragile: Resonance > Saytzeff is a hidden rule that most students don't know because textbooks often only teach 'Saytzeff = major in E2.' The full hierarchy (Anti-periplanar > Resonance > Saytzeff) is tested in JEE Advanced when the substrate has a conjugated product possibility. Students who apply Saytzeff blindly predict the wrong major product. The correct logic: check anti-periplanar first, then check resonance, then apply Saytzeff. The teacher's boxed rule 'Resonance > Sytzeff' is an explicit exam target.

concepts.name: E2 stereospecificity: different diastereomers give different alkene stereochemistry; anti-periplanar requirement -> substrate stereoconfig determines product alkene config (diastereomer 1 -> trans E2 product; diastereomer 2 -> cis E2 product); E2 is STEREOSPECIFIC not just stereoselective
concepts.description:
E2 STEREOSPECIFICITY — SUBSTRATE CONFIG DETERMINES PRODUCT CONFIG:

FROM TEACHER (pages 9-10, Fischer/Newman analysis):

SUBSTRATE: CHD at β-C (one H and one D at same β-carbon), α-C bears Br.

DIASTEREOMER 1 (first Fischer projection): specific relative configuration of H, D, Br, CH₃.
→ The anti-periplanar conformation has H (not D) anti to Br.
→ E2 removes H (H is anti-periplanar to Br in the most stable anti-periplanar conformation) → D remains on the alkene carbon.
→ The remaining groups arrange in a TRANS configuration on the C=C.
→ Product: TRANS (E) ALKENE (labeled 'Trans', underlined by teacher).

DIASTEREOMER 2 (second Fischer projection): DIFFERENT relative configuration at the chiral centers.
→ In the anti-periplanar conformation of THIS diastereomer: H is also anti to Br but on the OPPOSITE face.
→ E2 removes H from this face → D remains → the groups arrange in CIS configuration.
→ Product: CIS (Z) ALKENE (labeled 'Cis', BOXED by teacher).

KEY CONCLUSION: E2 IS STEREOSPECIFIC.
- Diastereomer 1 → TRANS alkene (exclusively, by anti-periplanar mechanism)
- Diastereomer 2 → CIS alkene (exclusively, same mechanism but different substrate config)
Both substrates give the SAME constitutional alkene (same C=C position) but with OPPOSITE GEOMETRIC STEREOCHEMISTRY.

DEFINITION: STEREOSPECIFIC vs STEREOSELECTIVE:
- Stereospecific: different stereoisomers of SUBSTRATE give different stereoisomers of PRODUCT
- Stereoselective: reaction gives predominantly one stereoisomer of PRODUCT (regardless of substrate sterics)
E2 is STEREOSPECIFIC: the substrate diastereomer determines the product alkene geometry with complete fidelity.

MECHANISM EXPLANATION (Newman):
For each diastereomer: rotate the Fischer projection into a Newman (about Cβ-Cα). Find the anti-periplanar conformation (H front, Br back, 180° dihedral). The substituents NOT involved in elimination (on front C: D, CH₃; on back C: CH₃, etc.) become the substituents of the C=C product. Their relative position in the Newman → their cis/trans relationship in the alkene:
- Front substituents across from back substituents in anti-Newman → trans in product.
- Front substituents on same side as back substituents → cis in product.
concepts.why_fragile: E2 stereospecificity (not just stereoselectivity) is an advanced JEE concept. Failure modes: (1) Students predict the same product from both diastereomers (just different yields) — wrong: completely different stereochemistry. (2) Students apply Saytzeff to determine stereochemistry (wrong: Saytzeff determines regiochemistry, not geometric isomer). (3) Newman projection analysis of E2 stereospecificity requires drawing the anti-periplanar conformation and tracking ALL substituents simultaneously — a multi-step 3D analysis that students find difficult. (4) Confusion with E1 (which gives a mixture of E/Z from the carbocation intermediate) vs E2 (which gives stereospecific product from the anti-periplanar TS).

concepts.name: KIE definition and magnitude: 'if rate is affected by isotopes -> kinetic isotopic effect is observed' (teacher definition, underlined); kH/kD >= 7 stated by teacher; primary KIE max ~7 at 25 degrees C; tunneling can give kH/kD > 7
concepts.description:
KINETIC ISOTOPE EFFECT (KIE) — DEFINITION AND MAGNITUDE:

TEACHER'S DEFINITION (underlined, from page 8): 'If rate is affected by isotopes then it is called that kinetic isotopic effect is observed.'

FROM Q (page 8):
Reaction 1: CH₃-CH₂-α-Cl → alc. KOH → rate r₁
Reaction 2: CD₃-CH₂-α-Cl → alc. KOH → rate r₂
BOXED: r₁ > r₂
BOXED: kH/kD ≥ 7 (the ratio is stated as ≥ 7)

WHY kH/kD ≥ 7 IS SIGNIFICANT:
Classical primary KIE upper limit at 25°C (based on zero-point energy difference for C-H vs C-D): kH/kD_max ≈ 6-7.
Theoretically: kH/kD = exp[(ZPE_CD - ZPE_CH)/kT] where ZPE = zero-point energy.
For C-H: ZPE ≈ 18 kJ/mol; for C-D: ZPE ≈ 13 kJ/mol → ΔΔG‡ ≈ 5 kJ/mol → kH/kD ≈ e^(5000/8.314×298) ≈ 7.7.
Values exceeding 7 indicate TUNNELING: quantum mechanical tunneling of H (lighter) through the activation barrier — tunneling is much more probable for H than D → further enhances kH/kD beyond the classical limit.

TYPES OF KIE:
- PRIMARY KIE (kH/kD = 2-7, or >7 with tunneling): the ISOTOPICALLY LABELED BOND is the one BREAKING in the rate-determining step. Most diagnostic.
- SECONDARY KIE (kH/kD = 1.0-1.3): isotope is near but not at the breaking bond. Less diagnostic.

E2 GIVES PRIMARY KIE: β-C-H (or β-C-D) bond breaks in the concerted TS → PRIMARY KIE → kH/kD = 2-7+ → confirms C-H bond breaking in rate-determining step.

DIAGNOSTIC VALUE:
- Observed KIE → mechanism has C-H/C-D breaking in RDS → E2 or E1CB
- No KIE → C-H breaking is in fast step after RDS → E1
Teacher's Q: r₁ > r₂ (KIE observed) + kH/kD ≥ 7 → confirms E2 mechanism.
concepts.why_fragile: The kH/kD ≥ 7 value is specific and testable. Students may think 'KIE is just kH/kD > 1' without knowing the specific magnitude range. Values > 7 indicate tunneling — this is a JEE Advanced level concept. Also: the teacher's definition ('if rate is AFFECTED BY isotopes → KIE is observed') is exact and has a specific meaning: not just any rate difference, but specifically due to the isotopic substitution being in the RDS. Students confuse 'KIE observed' with 'D substrate gives no reaction' — wrong, D substrate still reacts, just slower.

concepts.name: E1 ring expansion: cyclobutyl cation -> cyclopentyl cation (Wagner-Meerwein 1,2-alkyl shift, ring strain relief); alc. KOH = E2 no rearrangement; aq. KOH = E1/SN1 = ring expansion possible; cyclobutyl+ more strained than cyclopentyl+
concepts.description:
CYCLOBUTYL CATION → CYCLOPENTYL CATION (RING EXPANSION IN E1):

FROM TEACHER PAGE 7 (top Q): Cyclobutyl bromide under different conditions:

CONDITION 1: alc. KOH/Δ (E2 conditions):
E2 = concerted, NO carbocation intermediate → NO rearrangement → exocyclic alkene (methylenecyclobutane) = direct E2 product (cyclobutane ring intact).

CONDITION 2: aq. KOH / ionizing conditions (E1/SN1):
Step 1: Br⁻ departs (ionization) → CYCLOBUTYL CATION (⊕ on cyclobutane ring, 4-membered ring)
Step 2: RING EXPANSION — 1,2-alkyl shift (Wagner-Meerwein): one ring C-C bond of cyclobutyl cation migrates to the adjacent cationic C → ring expands from 4 to 5 → CYCLOPENTYL CATION (⊕ on cyclopentane ring, 5-membered ring)
Step 3: OH⁻ (or H₂O) attacks cyclopentyl⁺ → CYCLOPENTANOL (5-membered ring with OH)

DRIVING FORCE FOR RING EXPANSION:
Cyclobutane ring strain ≈ 115 kJ/mol >> cyclopentane ring strain ≈ 27 kJ/mol. The ring expansion from cyclobutyl⁺ → cyclopentyl⁺ relieves substantial ring strain → THERMODYNAMICALLY favorable.

CARBOCATION STABILITY: Cyclopentyl⁺ (secondary, 5-membered ring, low strain) > Cyclobutyl⁺ (secondary, 4-membered ring, high strain) → ring expansion is also driven by carbocation stability.

GENERAL PRINCIPLE — RING EXPANSION UNDER E1/SN1:
- Small ring cations (cyclopropyl⁺, cyclobutyl⁺) are prone to ring expansion (1,2-shift to larger ring)
- Only under E1/SN1 conditions (cation intermediate forms)
- Under E2: concerted → no cation → no rearrangement → ring size unchanged

COMPARISON:
| Condition | Intermediate | Product | Ring expansion? |
|---|---|---|---|
| alc. KOH/Δ (E2) | None (concerted) | Exo alkene (4-membered ring intact) | NO |
| aq. KOH or ionizing (E1) | Cyclobutyl⁺ → Cyclopentyl⁺ | Cyclopentanol | YES |

Failure modes: (1) Students predict cyclobutanol as SN1 product (wrong: ring expansion happens → cyclopentanol). (2) Students predict ring expansion under E2 conditions (wrong: E2 is concerted, no cation → no rearrangement). (3) Students don't recognize that 'alc. KOH = E2 = no rearrangement' vs 'aq. KOH = E1/SN1 = rearrangement possible.' The two conditions give ENTIRELY DIFFERENT product types: alkene with 4-ring (E2) vs alcohol with 5-ring (E1 + rearrangement).

concepts.description:
TEACHER'S VERBATIM NOTE ON EQUATORIAL LG (RM lec8, page 3, underlined):
'Note: If leaving group in chair form present at equatorial position, E2 cannot take place bcos there is no periplanar H atom.'

THIS IS AN ABSOLUTE BLOCK, NOT JUST SLOW:
Equatorial LG in cyclohexyl chair → E2 is IMPOSSIBLE (not just slower). The word 'cannot' (not 'will not readily') makes this an absolute geometric statement.

REASON — CHAIR GEOMETRY:
In a cyclohexane chair:
- Equatorial C-L bond angle to adjacent axial C-H: ~60° (gauche dihedral, NOT 180°)
- Equatorial C-L bond angle to adjacent equatorial C-H: ~60° (also gauche/synclinal)
NO β-H in the chair exists at 180° dihedral to an equatorial LG.

AXIAL LG FOR COMPARISON:
- Axial C-L bond to adjacent axial C-H on adjacent ring carbon: 180° (trans-diaxial = anti-periplanar)
→ Axial LG: E2 proceeds via trans-diaxial β-H removal.
→ Equatorial LG: NO trans-diaxial β-H possible → E2 CANNOT OCCUR.

IMPLICATION FOR CYCLOHEXYL RINGS:
Conformational analysis is REQUIRED before predicting E2 products:
Step 1: Draw the chair conformation of the substrate.
Step 2: Identify the position of LG — AXIAL or EQUATORIAL?
If EQUATORIAL: No E2 reaction (check whether SN1/E1 is possible instead).
If AXIAL: E2 proceeds via the trans-diaxial β-H.

FROM TEACHER'S EXAMPLES (RM lec8, pages 3-6):
- Br equatorial + alc. KOH → X (No reaction) — confirmed multiple times across pages 3,4,5,6
- 'No rxn' BOXED on page 6 when BOTH β-C pathways are geometrically blocked (equatorial Br + no accessible anti-periplanar H from either β-C)
- Br axial → E2 occurs → specific product from trans-diaxial elimination

MEMORY AID: 'Equatorial LG = E2 dead end.' Only AXIAL LG allows trans-diaxial E2 in chair.

This is the single most tested cyclohexyl E2 application. The teacher's verbatim note ('E2 CANNOT take place bcos there is no periplanar H atom') is an exact exam statement. Students who say 'equatorial LG gives slower E2' instead of 'equatorial LG gives NO E2' will consistently get cyclohexyl E2 problems wrong. The note explicitly uses 'cannot' — absolute, not graded.

concepts.name: p-orbital MO basis for anti-periplanar requirement in E2: C-H sigma bond at beta-C must be PARALLEL to C-L sigma bond at alpha-C (both parallel to forming C=C pi bond); 180 degrees = perfect overlap; 60 degrees (gauche) = no overlap = no E2; teacher draws p-orbital diagram comparing anti vs gauche
concepts.description:
p-ORBITAL MOLECULAR ORBITAL EXPLANATION FOR ANTI-PERIPLANAR REQUIREMENT (RM lec8, page 3):

TEACHER'S p-ORBITAL DIAGRAM:
Two structures shown with colored p-orbital lobes (green = C-H and C-L sigma* bonds; yellow = forming C=C pi bond).

STRUCTURE 1 — ANTI-PERIPLANAR (H and L at 180°):
- Backbone: H-Cβ-Cα-L in anti-periplanar zig-zag (all in one plane, H and L on opposite sides)
- GREEN p-orbital lobe at H (= the C-H sigma antibond/sigma bond being broken at β-C)
- YELLOW p-orbitals at Cβ-Cα (= the forming C=C pi bond)
- GREEN p-orbital lobe at L (= the C-L sigma bond breaking at α-C)
- ALL THREE ARE PARALLEL AND COPLANAR → productive MO overlap:
  (a) C-H(β) σ* overlaps with forming C=C π → weakens C-H bond concertedly
  (b) C-L(α) σ* overlaps with forming C=C π → weakens C-L bond concertedly
  → Concerted E2 TS forms → elimination proceeds.

STRUCTURE 2 — GAUCHE (H and L at 60°):
- H-Cβ-Cα-L with 60° dihedral (H and L not coplanar with the C-C bond)
- p-orbital at H is NOT parallel to p-orbital at L
- Neither is aligned with the forming C=C π bond
- NO productive MO overlap → concerted E2 TS cannot form → no E2

KEY PRINCIPLE:
E2 requires orbital symmetry-allowed concerted overlap of three bonds simultaneously:
1. C(β)-H σ bond (breaking: H transferred to base)
2. C(β)-C(α) bond (becoming π bond: new double bond forms)
3. C(α)-L σ bond (breaking: LG departs)
All three bonds must be in the same plane (coplanar) and in anti arrangement → the C-H and C-L bonds must be ANTIPERIPLANAR (parallel, antiparallel to each other = 180° dihedral).

WHY ANTI (180°) AND NOT SYN (0°):
Both syn-periplanar (0°) and anti-periplanar (180°) have coplanar C-H and C-L bonds (σ bonds parallel to forming π bond). However:
- Anti-periplanar (180°, staggered): C-H and C-L are antiparallel → each σ* faces the other → PERFECT ANTI ORBITAL OVERLAP → strongly favored
- Syn-periplanar (0°, eclipsed): C-H and C-L are parallel in same direction → less favorable orbital overlap + severe torsional strain in TS → disfavored
Conclusion: ANTI-periplanar is preferred over SYN-periplanar by both orbital overlap and TS strain.

FOR CYCLOHEXYL CHAIRS:
- AXIAL LG + AXIAL β-H (trans-diaxial): dihedral = 180° → anti-periplanar → E2 proceeds
- EQUATORIAL LG + any β-H: dihedral = 60° → gauche → no E2 (teacher's note)
- AXIAL LG + EQUATORIAL β-H: dihedral = 60° → gauche → no E2 from that specific β-H
concepts.why_fragile: The p-orbital MO explanation is tested in 'EXPLAIN WHY anti-periplanar is required for E2' questions. Students who only memorize the geometric requirement (180°) without understanding the orbital basis give incomplete answers. The colored p-orbital diagrams (green/yellow) explicitly show: parallel = productive overlap = E2 possible; 60° = no overlap = no E2. This MO basis also explains why syn-periplanar (0°) is disfavored despite being coplanar — the anti arrangement gives better σ* to π* orbital alignment.

concepts.name: Erythro -> CIS alkene and Threo -> TRANS alkene in E2 stereospecificity of 2-bromo-3-deuterobutane: complete mnemonic established from Newman analysis (Q2 and Q3 of RM lec8); both results confirmed with Fischer projection + Newman + product structure
concepts.description:
ERYTHRO/THREO → CIS/TRANS STEREOSPECIFICITY IN E2 (COMPLETE, RM lec8 Qs 2-3):

THE TWO RESULTS (teacher explicitly labeled):
- Q2 (Erythro): Fischer [H,Br at C2; H,D at C3 both on RIGHT side] → E2 → '(Cis)' (CIS alkene)
- Q3 (Threo): Fischer [H,Br at C2; D,H at C3 with D on LEFT] → E2 → '{trans}' BOXED (TRANS alkene)

MNEMONIC: ERYTHRO → CIS; THREO → TRANS (for anti-periplanar E2)

HOW TO DETERMINE (Newman analysis steps):
1. Draw Fischer projection of the substrate.
2. Identify β-C and α-C (β-C has D and H; α-C has Br and H for 2-bromo-3-deuterobutane).
3. Convert Fischer → Newman (β-C front, α-C back):
   - In Fischer: left and right bonds come TOWARD viewer → these become front branches in Newman
   - Top and bottom bonds go AWAY from viewer → these become the C-C backbone in Newman
4. Rotate Newman to anti-periplanar: place H(β-C) at top-front, Br(α-C) at bottom-back (180°).
5. Note the positions of D(β-C) and Me(α-C upper) in this Newman:
   - Same side → CIS product (erythro substrate)
   - Opposite sides → TRANS product (threo substrate)
6. Identify cis/trans: groups that are ON THE SAME SIDE in the anti-periplanar Newman → same side of product C=C.

INTUITION (why this works):
E2 removes H(β-C) and Br(α-C). The remaining groups: D(β-C) and Me(upper, α-C) stay in their positions. Their spatial relationship in the ANTI-PERIPLANAR TS is directly mapped onto the alkene geometry:
- If D and Me(upper) are on same side of the C-C bond axis in the anti-periplanar Newman → they will be on the same side of the C=C in the product → CIS.
- If D and Me(upper) are on opposite sides in the anti-periplanar Newman → opposite sides of C=C → TRANS.

FOR ERYTHRO:
- Br(C2,right) and D(C3,right) in Fischer → same right side
- In anti-periplanar Newman: D(C3) and Me(C2-upper) on same side → CIS product
FOR THREO:
- Br(C2,right) and D(C3,left) in Fischer → opposite sides
- In anti-periplanar Newman: D(C3) and Me(C2-upper) on opposite sides → TRANS product

GENERAL APPLICATION:
This method extends to any substrate with two chiral centers where one center has the LG and the other has a specific labeled atom (D, CD₃, halo, etc.). The Fischer → Newman → anti-periplanar → read geometry method always gives the correct E2 product stereochemistry.
concepts.why_fragile: This is the highest-difficulty E2 analysis: three-dimensional stereochemical outcome requiring Fischer → Newman → E2 → alkene geometry tracking in one problem. Failure modes: (1) Students draw the wrong Newman from Fischer (most common error: not correctly placing left/right Fischer bonds as front Newman branches). (2) Students incorrectly identify which groups stay and which leave. (3) Students don't know the ERYTHRO → CIS, THREO → TRANS mnemonic and attempt to re-derive each time (prone to errors under exam pressure). (4) Students confuse erythro/threo with R/S or with cis/trans of the starting material rather than of the product. The teacher explicitly labels both outcomes (Q2: '(Cis)'; Q3: '{trans}' BOXED) to establish the mnemonic.

concepts.description:
CYCLOHEXYL E2 ANALYSIS — COMPLETE DECISION TREE (RM lec8, pages 3-6):

STEP-BY-STEP ANALYSIS (from teacher's multiple examples):

Step 1: Draw the CHAIR CONFORMATION of the cyclohexyl substrate.
Step 2: Identify LG position: AXIAL or EQUATORIAL?
  If EQUATORIAL: 'No rxn' (No E2 — teacher's note applies). STOP.
  If AXIAL: Continue.
Step 3: Draw Newman projection of α-C to β-C bond(s).
Step 4: In the Newman, find the β-H that is TRANS-DIAXIAL to the axial LG (180° dihedral = axial β-H).
Step 5: That specific β-H is REMOVED in E2 → determine the alkene product regiochemistry.
Step 6: Apply ANTI-ELIMINATION > SAYTZEFF if the anti-periplanar product conflicts with the Saytzeff product.

FROM TEACHER'S EXAMPLES (pages 4-5 of RM lec8):
- Cyclohexyl-Br (axial Br) with CH₃ at various ring positions → Newman analysis → label '6' or similar pointing to the specific anti-diaxial β-H → product = specific cyclohexene or methylcyclohexene.
- ONE of the β-C pathways may be BLOCKED (labeled X in Newman, meaning no axial β-H at that β-C because the β-C has only equatorial H or no H).
- The PRODUCT is from whichever β-C has an axial β-H anti-diaxial to axial LG.

MULTIPLE 'No rxn' CONFIRMATIONS (pages 3-6):
- Cyclohexyl-Br equatorial + alc. KOH → X (circled, page 3)
- Another equatorial Br + alc. KOH → X (page 4)
- Complex substrate where BOTH β-C's are blocked → No rxn (BOXED, page 6)
- Some substrates show ONE β-C blocked (X in Newman) but another β-C accessible → product from accessible pathway only

NEWMAN NOTATION:
- 'X' in Newman = that β-C pathway is blocked (no accessible anti-periplanar H) → skip
- 'n' in Newman = H atom available at that position → accessible for E2
- Circle around β-H in Newman = the specific H that will be removed in E2

concepts.description:
HOFMANN RULE — COMPLETE FRAMEWORK (RM lec8, pages 7-8):

TEACHER'S DEFINITION (underlined): 'less crowded alkene will be formed' = Hofmann Rule = when bulky base is used in E2, the LESS SUBSTITUTED alkene is the major product.

E2 PRODUCT RULE BY BASE SIZE:
                 Base           Product
                 CH₃O⁻         Saytzeff (more substituted)
                 EtO⁻          Saytzeff
                 iPrO⁻         Saytzeff
            [CUTOFF]
                 t-BuO⁻        Hofmann (less substituted) ← BULKY BASE START
                 LDA            Hofmann
                 DBN            Hofmann
                 DBU            Hofmann

THE 5 BULKY BASES (teacher's list, RM lec8 page 8):
① t-BuO⁻ / t-BuOK (tert-butoxide = potassium tert-butoxide) ✓ — most common bulky base
② Large branched alkoxide (β-branched alkoxide, very hindered) ✓
③ LDA = lithium diisopropylamide = (iPr)₂N⁻Li⁺ ✓ — the most commonly tested after t-BuO⁻
   Structure: two isopropyl groups on N, Li⁺ counter-ion; 'lithium diisopropylamide' spelled out
④ DBN/Δ = 1,5-diazabicyclo[3.4.0]non-5-ene
⑤ DBU/Δ = 1,8-diazabicyclo[5.4.0]undec-7-ene

EQUIVALENCES FROM TEACHER (page 7):
'CH₃O⁻/Δ ≡ CH₃-O⁻/CH₃-OH/Δ' — methoxide in methanol = same as alc. conditions with CH₃OH
't-O⁻/Δ = t-O⁻/t-OH, Δ' — tert-butoxide in tert-butanol = most common bulky base setup

STERIC MECHANISM:
Bulky base → cannot access hindered 2°/3° β-C → approaches only 1°/terminal β-C → removes 1° β-H → less substituted alkene = major.
Small base → can access all β-C's → preferentially removes β-H at 2°/3° β-C (more acidic, more available) → more substituted alkene (Saytzeff) = major.

COMPLETE E2 HIERARCHY (all rules combined):
1. Anti-periplanar geometry check (absolute requirement)
2. Resonance > Saytzeff (if conjugation possible)
3. Saytzeff (default, small base, GLG)
4. Hofmann (bulky base OR PLG → replaces step 3)
5. Anti-elimination > Saytzeff (in rigid cyclic systems)
concepts.why_fragile: Hofmann Rule is a major exam target in JEE. Students know Saytzeff as the 'default' and forget to check base size. The key exam scenarios: (1) Same substrate, two conditions: alc. KOH (Saytzeff) vs t-BuOK (Hofmann) — completely different products. (2) LDA is frequently tested as a bulky base alongside t-BuOK. (3) The 5-base list (t-BuO⁻, LDA, DBN, DBU, and one more) must be memorized. (4) The 'cutoff': iPrO⁻ = still Saytzeff; t-BuO⁻ = Hofmann — this borderline is explicitly tested.

concepts.description:
E2 + GLG vs PLG — QUANTITATIVE HOFMANN/SAYTZEFF TABLE (RM lec8, page 9):

TEACHER'S RULES (two lines, underlined):
'E2 + Good leaving group ⟹ Follow Sytzeff.'
'E2 + Poor leaving group → Follow Hofmann.'

FULL QUANTITATIVE TABLE:

GOOD LEAVING GROUPS (GLG: I, Br, Cl) — rate order: 3° > 2° > 1° (normal E2):
| LG | % Saytzeff | % Hofmann | Trend |
|---|---|---|---|
| −I | 80% | 20% | Saytzeff dominant |
| −Br | 70% | 30% | Saytzeff dominant |
| −Cl | 60% | 40% | Saytzeff still majority |

POOR LEAVING GROUPS (PLG: F, SR₂⁺, NR₃⁺) — BOXED YELLOW RATE ORDER: 1° > 2° > 3° (reversed!):
| LG | % Saytzeff | % Hofmann | Trend |
|---|---|---|---|
| −F | ~0% | ~100% | nearly pure Hofmann |
| −SR₂⁺ (sulfonium) | 30% | 70% | Hofmann dominant |
| −NR₃⁺ (ammonium) | 18% | 82% | Hofmann strongly dominant |
| −NR₃⁺ (extreme) | 2% | 98% | almost pure Hofmann |

YELLOW OVAL on right: '70% / 82% / 98%' = the Hofmann % values for the PLG series ✓

MECHANISM FOR REVERSED ORDER WITH PLG:
Teacher (page 10, underlined): 'Here carbanion like character will be developed in the transition state.'

For PLG (poor LG): the C-LG bond does NOT break easily in the TS (PLG = strong bond, reluctant departure). The TS is E1CB-like: β-C develops δ⁻ (partial negative/carbanion character, labeled δ⁻ at β-C in diagram). Carbanion stability: 1° > 2° > 3° (primary carbanion = more stable, opposite of carbocation!). Therefore: 1° β-C prefers the carbanion TS → 1° β-H preferentially removed → terminal Hofmann alkene = major.

For GLG (good LG): C-LG bond breaks readily → TS is E1-like (cationic character at α-C) → 3° substrate faster (3° α-C stabilizes the cationic character) → more substituted β-C preferred → Saytzeff.

NUMERIC RELATIONSHIPS:
- As LG ability decreases (I→Br→Cl→F→SR₂⁺→NR₃⁺): % Hofmann increases (20→30→40→~100→70→82→98%)
- As LG ability increases: % Saytzeff increases (80→70→60→...)
- The PLG numbers (70, 82, 98) are circled in yellow oval as key exam numbers

concepts.name: Cope elimination (Ei): amine N-oxide as substrate -> SYN periplanar elimination via 5-membered cyclic TS; product = Hofmann alkene + hydroxylamine; no external base needed; contrast with E2 (anti-periplanar, external base)
concepts.description:
COPE ELIMINATION (Ei MECHANISM) — COMPLETE (RM lec8, pages 11-12):

SUBSTRATE: R-CH₂-N⁺(R')₂-O⁻ (= amine N-oxide = tertiary amine oxidized with H₂O₂ or mCPBA)

5-MEMBERED CYCLIC TRANSITION STATE (teacher's mechanism diagram):
          O⁻
          |
     H---N⁺---R'
     |         |
    Cβ---Cα
In the cyclic TS: O (on N) abstracts H from Cβ while Cα-N breaks.
Atoms in ring: O-H-Cβ-Cα-N⁺ → 5 atoms = 5-membered ring.
Geometry: H and O are on the SAME SIDE of the Cβ-Cα bond → SYN PERIPLANAR (0° dihedral H-Cβ-Cα-N).

KEY CONTRAST:
| Feature | E2 | Cope (Ei) |
|---|---|---|
| Periplanar geometry | ANTI (180°) | SYN (0°) |
| Base | External (alc. KOH) | Internal (N-O⁻) |
| TS ring | No cyclic TS | 5-membered ring |
| Substrate LG | Halide, etc. | N-oxide O⁻ |
| Product stereochemistry | Depends on substrate stereo (E2 stereospecific) | Depends on syn TS geometry |
| Product | Alkene + X⁻ | Alkene + R₂NOH |

SELECTIVITY: Hofmann (1° > 2° > 3°) — same as PLG E2 — because the Ei TS also has carbanion character at β-C.

PRODUCTS:
- Alkene (major = less substituted = Hofmann)
- R₂N-OH (hydroxylamine derivative = the N-oxide fragment after H transfer)

TEACHER'S EXAMPLES:
Q1 (page 11): N-oxide substrate (β at two positions) + Δ → 'CH₂=CH₂' + N-ring (the N-oxide converts to ethylene + piperidine-type hydroxylamine or pyrrolidine-type product)
Q2 (page 11): N-oxide + Δ → cyclic amine product + alkene
Q1 (page 12): Complex N-oxide + Δ → large cyclic amine product + specific alkene

DOUBLE ELIMINATION → ALKYNE (page 12 Q2):
Substrate: Me-N⁺(iPr)(Pr)(chain) + OH⁻/Δ → [first E2: NR₃⁺ LG] → vinyl-N⁺ (vinyl ammonium) → [second OH⁻/Δ: second E2] → C≡C (ALKYNE) + N(Me)(iPr) (amine)
The 'C≡C' (alkyne) product and N(Me)(iPr) amine are explicitly drawn by teacher.

Ei GENERAL PATTERN:
Ei = 'Elimination through Internal base.' The internal base is part of the leaving group → intramolecular H-transfer via cyclic TS. Types:
- Cope (amine N-oxide) — 5-membered ring, syn
- Chugaev (xanthate ester) — 6-membered ring, syn
- Ester pyrolysis (carboxylate β-elimination) — 6-membered ring, syn
All: syn elimination, no external base, cyclic TS.
concepts.why_fragile: Cope elimination is tested in JEE in the form: 'What product forms when an amine N-oxide is heated?' Students often forget the N-oxide is a specific substrate and that the elimination is SYN (not anti like E2). The 5-membered cyclic TS is the key identifying feature. Product is HYDROXYLAMINE (not just amine), and the alkene is HOFMANN (less substituted). The contrast with E2 (syn vs anti) is an exam-favorite comparison question.

concepts.description:
COMPLETE E2 SELECTIVITY MATRIX (synthesized from RM lec7-8):

FACTOR HIERARCHY (apply in order):
1. ANTI-PERIPLANAR (ABSOLUTE): No anti-periplanar β-H → No reaction. Check this first always.
2. RESONANCE > SAYTZEFF: If one product is conjugated → conjugated alkene = major (regardless of substitution).
3. BASE SIZE: Bulky base → HOFMANN (less substituted). Small/medium base → continue to #4.
4. LG QUALITY: PLG → HOFMANN (1°>2°>3°). GLG → SAYTZEFF (3°>2°>1°).

QUANTITATIVE DATA (exam-ready):

SMALL BASE + GLG:
Base: CH₃O⁻/EtO⁻/iPrO⁻/alc.KOH → Saytzeff (3°>2°>1°)
I:  80% Saytzeff, 20% Hofmann
Br: 70% Saytzeff, 30% Hofmann
Cl: 60% Saytzeff, 40% Hofmann

BULKY BASE:
t-BuO⁻/LDA/DBN/DBU → Hofmann (less substituted) regardless of LG

SMALL BASE + PLG (1°>2°>3°, carbanion TS):
SR₂⁺:  30% Saytzeff, 70% Hofmann
NR₃⁺:  18% Saytzeff, 82% Hofmann
extreme NR₃⁺: 2% Saytzeff, 98% Hofmann

MEMORY TABLE:
| LG | Base | Selectivity | Major |
|---|---|---|---|
| I, Br, Cl | Small | Saytzeff | More substituted |
| I, Br, Cl | Bulky | Hofmann | Less substituted |
| F, SR₂⁺, NR₃⁺ | Small | Hofmann | Less substituted |
| F, SR₂⁺, NR₃⁺ | Bulky | Hofmann | Less substituted |

SELECTIVITY MECHANISMS:
- Saytzeff: thermodynamic (more stable alkene product, product-like TS, Hammond)
- Hofmann (bulky base): steric approach control (bulky base avoids hindered β-C)
- Hofmann (PLG): E1CB-like TS (carbanion at β-C, 1° most stable)

EXAM APPLICATION FLOWCHART:
① Draw substrate → identify all β-C positions → check anti-periplanar availability
② Any β-C giving conjugated alkene? → Yes: that pathway = major (Resonance > Saytzeff)
③ Is base BULKY? (t-BuO⁻, LDA, DBN, DBU) → Yes: less substituted = major (Hofmann)
④ Is LG POOR? (F, SR₂⁺, NR₃⁺) → Yes: 1°β-C = major pathway (Hofmann)
⑤ Default: more substituted = major (Saytzeff, I/Br/Cl LG, small base)
concepts.why_fragile: The complete matrix (GLG+small→Saytzeff; GLG+bulky→Hofmann; PLG+any→Hofmann; resonance overrides all) is the most complex E2 concept. JEE Advanced tests whether students can apply ALL FOUR factors simultaneously: e.g., 'substrate with NR₃⁺ LG and t-BuOK base — what is the major product and why?' Both PLG and bulky base independently predict Hofmann, so the answer is unambiguous Hofmann (but the student needs to know BOTH reasons). Memorizing just one factor (e.g., only Saytzeff) will fail on ~50% of E2 selectivity questions.

concepts.name: E1 (Unimolecular Elimination) formal introduction: Rate ∝ [R-L]^1 (BOXED, order = 1), polar protic + Delta, ionization -> carbocation -> -H+ (fast) -> Saytzeff alkene; LG order F<Cl<Br<I; substrate rate 3 degree >> 2 degree > 1 degree
concepts.description:
E1 UNIMOLECULAR ELIMINATION — COMPLETE FORMAL INTRODUCTION (RM lec9, page 6):

TEACHER LABEL: '⊕ E1 (Unimolecular elimination rxn) ⟹' (circled # = important, underlined, green)

CONDITIONS:
  - Polar & protic solvent (H₂O, ROH = alcohols, DMSO-water mixtures)
  - Heat (Δ)
  - NO external base (the solvent itself can deprotonate; base is not in the rate-determining step)
  - Substrate must be 2° or 3° (1° = no E1, carbocation too unstable)
  - Solvent molecules shown as circles around C-L bond = polar protic stabilizes the carbocation.

MECHANISM (teacher's two-step diagram, green):
  1. -C-C- (with L, surrounded by solvent circles 'OOOOO') + Polar protic/Δ
     → -C-C⊕- (carbocation) + L⁻ [SLOW, rate-determining]
  2. -H⁺ / FAST (label 'fast' written by teacher) → C=C (alkene) [MAJOR, BOXED]
  Both steps go through the carbocation — same intermediate as SN1.

RATE LAW (BOXED by teacher, two-line box):
  Rate ∝ [R-L]¹
  order = 1
  = First-order kinetics; only substrate concentration appears in the rate law.
  No base in the rate law (unlike E2 which is second-order: Rate = k[R-L][base]).
  This is the KEY DISTINCTION: E1 rate is INDEPENDENT of base concentration.

LG REACTIVITY ORDER (teacher, circled #, underlined):
  R-F < R-Cl < R-Br < R-I
  (Increasing LG ability: I >> Br > Cl >> F)
  Same order as SN1 because both share the same ionization step.
  R-I = fastest E1/SN1; R-F = slowest.

SUBSTRATE RATE ORDER (teacher, circled #, underlined):
  3° >> 2° > 1°
  3° carbocation: most stable (3 alkyl groups stabilize by hyperconjugation) → fastest ionization → fastest E1
  2° carbocation: moderate → E1 possible
  1° carbocation: very unstable → E1 essentially does NOT occur
  Methyl cation: no E1 (primary + no β-H from carbocation on methyl)

PRODUCT (teacher): C=C alkene = MAJOR (BOXED). Always SAYTZEFF (most substituted) because:
  The carbocation intermediate collapses by losing β-H from the most substituted β-C → most stable alkene.
  No Hofmann product from E1 (carbocation doesn't select for less substituted alkene).
  Teacher '#' note (page 2): E1 (H⁺) gives α = 100% (Saytzeff), ω = 0% (Hofmann).

COMPARISON TABLE — E1 vs E2:
| Feature | E1 | E2 |
|---|---|---|
| Order | 1st order (Rate = k[R-L]) | 2nd order (Rate = k[R-L][base]) |
| Intermediate | Carbocation | No intermediate (concerted) |
| Base needed | No (solvent acts as base) | Yes (alc. KOH, t-BuOK, etc.) |
| Condition | Polar protic, Δ | Alc. KOH, Δ |
| Stereoselectivity | Not stereospecific | Stereospecific |
| Regiochemistry | Only Saytzeff (α=100%) | Saytzeff major + Hofmann minor |
| Substrate rate | 3° >> 2° > 1° | 3° > 2° > 1° (same direction but E2 faster for 1°) |
| KIE | NO KIE (C-H not broken in RDS) | YES KIE (kH/kD ≥ 7, C-H broken in RDS) |
concepts.why_fragile: E1 vs E2 is one of the most tested comparisons in JEE Advanced. Key exam traps: (1) E1 is first-order (Rate = k[R-L]) while E2 is second-order (Rate = k[R-L][base]). Students confuse the rate laws. (2) E1 gives ONLY Saytzeff (α=100%, no Hofmann) while E2 gives both major+minor. (3) E1 is NOT stereospecific; E2 IS stereospecific. (4) E1 has NO KIE (C-H not broken in RDS = ionization); E2 HAS KIE (C-H broken in RDS = concerted). (5) The substrate rate order 3°>>2°>1° for E1 vs E2 both have the same order but for different reasons: E1 = carbocation stability, E2 = steric effects on TS.

concepts.name: Stereoselective vs Stereospecific definitions (teacher verbatim): Stereoselective = two stereoisomers produced, one is major; Stereospecific = two different SM stereoisomers + same reagent = two different product stereoisomers; E2 is BOTH; SN2 is stereospecific; SN1 is NOT stereospecific ('loosely stereoselective 60+40')
concepts.description:
STEREOSELECTIVE vs STEREOSPECIFIC — DEFINITIONS AND CLASSIFICATIONS (RM lec9, pages 3-5):

STEREOSELECTIVE REACTION — DEFINITION (teacher verbatim, page 3):
'The rxns in which two stereoisomers are produced and out of them one is major are called stereoselective rxn.'

Key elements:
- Two (or more) stereoisomers are formed
- One stereoisomer is the MAJOR product (not necessarily 100%)
- SAME starting material, SAME reagent → two products, one major

STEREOSPECIFIC REACTION — DEFINITION (teacher verbatim, page 4, circled #):
'When two stereoisomers on rxn with particular reagent produces different stereoisomers then it is stereospecific rxn.'

Key elements:
- TWO DIFFERENT STEREOISOMERIC STARTING MATERIALS reacted with the SAME REAGENT
- Each SM gives a DIFFERENT stereoisomeric PRODUCT
- The product stereochemistry is DICTATED by the SM stereochemistry
- The two SMs give two different products (not the same product)

COMPARISON:
| Term | What varies | What's observed | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stereoselective | Fixed SM → two products | One stereoisomeric product is major | E2: Trans major + Cis minor |
| Stereospecific | Two different SMs + same reagent | Each SM gives different stereoisomeric product | E2: Dia-1 → Trans; Dia-2 → Cis |

NOTE: These are NOT mutually exclusive. E2 is BOTH simultaneously.

CLASSIFICATION OF EACH REACTION:

E2: BOTH stereoselective AND stereospecific:
- Stereoselective: from one substrate, Trans (E) is major, Cis (Z) is minor (page 3)
- Stereospecific: Diastereomer 1 + alc. KOH → Trans; Diastereomer 2 + alc. KOH → Cis (page 5)
  Teacher: '→ E2 is stereospecific in nature.' (underlined)

SN2: Stereospecific (and stereoselective in the extreme):
- R-L + Nu → S product (100%); S-L + Nu → R product (100%)
- '→ SN2 is a stereospecific rxn' (page 5, underlined)
- 100%+0% = only one stereoisomeric product → also perfectly stereoselective

SN1: NOT stereospecific; loosely stereoselective:
- '→ SN1 is not stereoselective.' (page 4, underlined)
- '→ Real SN1 is loosely stereoselective (60+40).' (page 4, underlined)
  = 60% inversion + 40% retention (ion pair effect, departing L⁻ shields one face)
  In theory: 50:50 racemic (if free carbocation). In practice: 60:40 (ion pair)
- '→ SN1 is not stereospecific rxn.' (page 6, underlined)
  R and S substrates of SN1 both give essentially racemic mixture = same product from different SMs.

E1: NOT stereospecific (not explicitly stated but follows from carbocation mechanism):
- Carbocation intermediate is sp2 planar → β-H lost from either face → no stereospecificity
- E1 gives mixture of E and Z alkenes with no fixed ratio determined by SM configuration

MEMORY AID (exam-ready classification table):
| Reaction | Stereoselective? | Stereospecific? |
|---|---|---|
| E2 | YES (Trans major) | YES (Dia-1→Trans, Dia-2→Cis) |
| E1 | YES (Saytzeff major) | NO |
| SN2 | YES (100% inversion) | YES (R→S, S→R) |
| SN1 | 'loosely' (60+40) | NO |
concepts.why_fragile: Stereoselective vs stereospecific is one of the highest-difficulty conceptual distinctions in JEE Advanced organic chemistry. Students conflate the two terms constantly. The critical exam points: (1) Stereoselective = two products, one major (about the PRODUCT ratio from one SM). Stereospecific = different SMs give different products with same reagent (about how SM stereochemistry controls product stereochemistry). These are independent properties. (2) E2 is BOTH simultaneously — can be asked about E2 as stereoselective (Trans major) AND as stereospecific (Diastereomer 1 → Trans, Diastereomer 2 → Cis). (3) 'Real SN1 is loosely stereoselective (60+40)' is a teacher-verbatim nuance that distinguishes textbook (50:50 racemic) from real SN1 — an exam trap.

concepts.name: Regioselective vs Regiospecific: E2 is regioselective (Saytzeff major + Hofmann minor, two regioisomers); E1 via H+ gives alpha = 100% (Saytzeff only), omega = 0% (approaches regiospecific); definitions and comparison
concepts.description:
REGIOSELECTIVE vs REGIOSPECIFIC — E2 AND E1 (RM lec9, pages 2-3):

TEACHER HEADER (page 2): '→ Regioselective →' (underlined, with arrows)

REGIOSELECTIVE DEFINITION:
A reaction that gives two or more REGIOISOMERS (products differing in position of the functional group / bond connectivity) but with ONE as major. The reaction shows a PREFERENCE for one positional isomer but does not give 100% of it.

REGIOSPECIFIC DEFINITION:
A reaction that gives ONLY ONE regioisomer (100%, no other regioisomers). Completely position-specific.

E2 CLASSIFICATION = REGIOSELECTIVE (teacher, page 2):
  Substrate (branched bromide) + alc. KOH/Δ → Saytzeff alkene (BOXED 'major') + Hofmann alkene (BOXED 'minor')
  → '→ E2 is a regioselective rxn' (underlined)
  Both regioisomers form; Saytzeff is major but Hofmann is also present.
  Quantitatively: for Br (GLG): Saytzeff = 70%, Hofmann = 30%.

E1 VIA H⁺ (teacher '#' note, page 2) = APPROACHES REGIOSPECIFIC for Saytzeff:
  Same substrate + H⁺ (acid, E1 conditions) → carbocation → two possible alkenes:
  TOP PATHWAY: β-H loss from more substituted β-C → Saytzeff alkene, 'α = 100%'
  BOTTOM PATHWAY: β-H loss from less substituted β-C → Hofmann alkene, 'ω = 0%'
  RIGHT SIDE of page: vertical line separating two alkene structures (α and ω)
  Conclusion: E1 via H⁺ gives ONLY Saytzeff (α = 100%), ZERO Hofmann (ω = 0%)
  Mechanism: carbocation (from H⁺ addition or from ionization) forms at α-C → only one β-H pathway available (the more substituted one gives more stable Saytzeff product → 100%)

ALPHA/OMEGA NOTATION (teacher, page 2):
  'α' (alpha) = Saytzeff alkene (the more substituted product, from the position adjacent to the original LG)
  'ω' (omega) = Hofmann alkene (the terminal/less substituted product)
  For E1: α = 100%, ω = 0%
  For E2: α = Saytzeff% (major, 60-80%), ω = Hofmann% (minor, 20-40%)

COMPLETE REGIOCHEMISTRY TABLE:
| Reaction | Classification | α (Saytzeff) | ω (Hofmann) |
|---|---|---|---|
| E2 (small base, GLG) | REGIOSELECTIVE | Major (70-80%) | Minor (20-30%) |
| E1 (H⁺ or polar protic) | Approaches regiospecific | ~100% (α = 100%) | ~0% (ω = 0%) |
| E2 (bulky base or PLG) | REGIOSELECTIVE (reversed) | Minor | Major |

NOTE: 'Regioselective' does NOT mean 'only one product forms.' It means one is PREFERRED (major). E2 is regioselective = two products, one major. Contrast with 'regiospecific' = only one product (100%). E1 is more regiospecific (for Saytzeff) than E2.
concepts.why_fragile: JEE Advanced asks students to classify reactions as regioselective or regiospecific. E2 is regioselective (two products, one major) — students often confuse this with 'regiospecific.' The alpha=100%, omega=0% for E1 (teacher's exact notation from page 2) is an exam-favorite data point. Students may incorrectly say E2 is 'regiospecific' because 'Saytzeff is always major' — but major is not the same as exclusive (100%). Both products form in E2; only in E1 (via carbocation) is Saytzeff exclusive.

concepts.name: E1 KIE: E1 has NO kinetic isotope effect (C-H bond NOT broken in rate-determining step = ionization step); contrast with E2 (kH/kD >= 7, C-H broken in RDS); this distinguishes E1 from E2 experimentally
concepts.description:
E1 KIE vs E2 KIE — MECHANISTIC DISTINCTION (RM lec9 + RM lec7/8 synthesis):

E1 — NO KIE:
In E1, the rate-determining step (RDS) is IONIZATION of C-L bond (Step 1: C-L → C⁺ + L⁻).
C-H bond is NOT BROKEN in the RDS — it is broken in Step 2 (fast step: -H⁺).
KIE measures whether C-H (or C-D) bond breaking is in the RDS.
Since C-H is broken in the FAST step (not RDS): replacing H with D (deuterium) does NOT change the rate of E1.
kH/kD ≈ 1 for E1 (no KIE, or very small secondary KIE).
Teacher (from RM lec7): 'If rate is affected by isotopes then it is called that kinetic isotopic effect is observed' — E1 rate is NOT affected by H→D isotope change.

E2 — YES KIE (kH/kD ≥ 7):
In E2, the mechanism is CONCERTED: C-H bond is broken IN THE SAME STEP as C-L bond breaks (the single rate-determining step).
C-H (or C-D) is broken in the RDS → deuterium substitution (D heavier than H, C-D bond stronger) slows E2.
kH/kD ≥ 7 (teacher's BOXED value from RM lec7) = significant primary KIE.
'r₁ > r₂' (rate with H > rate with D) BOXED by teacher.
Experimentally: if kH/kD ≥ 7 → E2 mechanism. If kH/kD ≈ 1 → E1 (or SN1 if nucleophile present).

COMPLETE KIE TABLE:
| Mechanism | RDS | C-H in RDS? | KIE? | kH/kD |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E1 | Ionization (C-L breaks) | NO | NO KIE | ≈1 |
| E2 | Concerted (C-H + C-L break together) | YES | YES KIE | ≥7 (BOXED) |
| SN1 | Ionization (C-L breaks) | NO | NO KIE | ≈1 |
| SN2 | Backside attack (C-L breaks) | NO | NO KIE for C-H | ≈1 |

EXAM APPLICATION:
If a question says 'the reaction rate of R-CHBr-CH₃ is 7 times faster than R-CDBr-CH₃' → kH/kD = 7 → E2 mechanism.
If 'the rate is the same for R-CHBr-CH₃ and R-CDBr-CH₃' → kH/kD = 1 → E1 (or SN1/SN2) mechanism.
KIE is the definitive experimental test to DISTINGUISH E2 from E1.
concepts.why_fragile: KIE is a high-difficulty JEE Advanced mechanistic topic. The trap: students know 'KIE ≥ 7 means E2' but forget 'KIE = 1 means E1 (NOT E2).' The key logic: KIE measures C-H bond breaking in the RDS. E2 has C-H broken in RDS (concerted) → KIE ≥ 7. E1 has C-H broken in the FAST step (not RDS) → KIE ≈ 1. This is the experimental method to distinguish E1 from E2 without knowing the order. Also: E1 is first-order (independent of base) while E2 is second-order (dependent on base) — another experimental distinction. KIE alone identifies whether C-H is in RDS.

concepts.name: E1CB complete mechanism: FAST carbanion formation (EWG activates beta-H; strong base; fast equilibrium) -> SLOW L- departure (PLG; RDS; unimolecular); OVERALL ORDER = 2 (BOXED); D-exchange diagnostic; conditions: -M group + PLG
concepts.description:
E1CB MECHANISM — COMPLETE (RM lec9, pages 10-12):

NAME: E1CB = Elimination, Unimolecular, Conjugate Base. 'Unimolecular w.r.t. Conjugate Base' = the rate-determining step (RDS) is unimolecular and involves the conjugate base (carbanion).

TWO-STEP MECHANISM:

Step 1 — FAST EQUILIBRIUM (teacher labels 'fast', double arrow ⇌):
  Substrate + Strong Base ⇌ Carbanion (CB) + BH
  - The β-H is ACIDIC because of adjacent -M group (EWG: C=O, NO₂, CN, SO₂R, CF₃, Ph)
  - Strong base removes this acidic H quickly (fast) → carbanion at β-C
  - The carbanion is STABILIZED by the -M group (resonance delocalization into EWG)
  - This step is REVERSIBLE (equilibrium, not irreversible)

Step 2 — SLOW (teacher labels 'slow', single →, RDS):
  Carbanion (CB) → alkene + L⁻
  - The PLG (L) departs in this step
  - This is unimolecular: only the carbanion involved (no base needed in this step)
  - PLG departure is SLOW because PLG = poor leaving group (C-F, C-OPh, C-OAr strong bonds)
  - Drives the equilibrium of Step 1 forward (Le Chatelier)

RATE DERIVATION (teacher's rate law section):
  Rate = k₂[CB] (from RDS, Step 2)
  K_eq (Step 1) = [CB]/([substrate][base]) → [CB] = K_eq × [substrate][base]
  Substituting: Rate = k₂ × K_eq × [substrate][base] = K'[substrate][base]
  → OVERALL RATE = K'[substrate][base]
  → OVERALL ORDER = 2 (BOXED by teacher)
  Note: 'order = 1 w.r.t. C.B.' (the RDS alone is first-order) but overall = 2.

CONDITIONS (teacher's two requirements, page 10):
  ① 'at least -M group must be present' = EWG at β-C (to acidify β-H and stabilize carbanion)
  ② 'Poor leaving groups should be present' = PLG required (F, OPh, OR, NR₃⁺, OTs occasionally)
     Reason: with GLG (Br, I), E2 would be faster (GLG departs well in concerted E2)
             with PLG, E2 is slow → carbanion mechanism (E1CB) takes over

EWG (-M GROUP) EXAMPLES FOR E1CB:
  - C=O (carbonyl) → β-hydroxy ketone + base → enone (aldol dehydration, Q①)
  - NO₂ (nitro) → -CH₂CH₂NO₂ substrate → CH₂=CH-NO₂ (nitroethene, Q②)
  - Ph (phenyl) → benzylic H acidified → Ph-CH₂CH₂F + base → styrene (Q③, Q⑤)
  - CF₃ (trifluoromethyl) → R-CH₂CF₃ + base → R-CH=CF₂ (Q④)
  - SO₂Ph (sulfonyl) → Ph-SO₂-CHα-CH₂OPh + base → Ph-SO₂-C=CH₂ (Q⑥)

PLG EXAMPLES FOR E1CB (teacher's examples):
  - F (fluoride): C-F is PLG → Ph-CH₂CH₂F E1CB
  - OPh (phenoxide): C-OPh used as LG → Ph-SO₂-CH-CH₂-OPh E1CB
  - OH/O⁻ (alkoxide in β-hydroxy carbonyl) → E1CB
  - NR₃⁺ (ammonium) → E1CB with NO₂ substrate

DIAGNOSTIC H/D EXCHANGE TEST (teacher Q⑤, page 12):
  Ph-CH₂CH₂F + C₂H₅O⁻/C₂H₅OD → Ph-CH=CH₂ + 'D exchange will be observed'
  Mechanism: carbanion Ph-CH⁻-CH₂F (stable, benzylic) lives long enough to:
    - Abstract D from C₂H₅OD: Ph-CHD-CH₂F → then F⁻ departs → Ph-CHD-CH=CH₂ (D-label incorporated)
  This exchange PROVES the carbanion intermediate (E1CB). E2 gives NO D-exchange (concerted, no carbanion).
concepts.why_fragile: E1CB is among the hardest topics in JEE Advanced organic chemistry. Multiple traps: (1) Despite being called 'unimolecular,' overall order = 2 (like E2). Students confuse 'unimolecular RDS' with 'first-order overall.' (2) The two conditions (EWG + PLG) are both required — miss either one and E1CB doesn't work. (3) The D-exchange test is the definitive experimental proof: E1CB shows D-exchange (carbanion exchanges H/D before LG departs); E2 does NOT (concerted, no carbanion). (4) The EWG is at the β-C (not the α-C where LG is). (5) The carbanion stability (not carbocation stability) determines E1CB reactivity — opposite of E1.

concepts.name: Temperature controls E1 vs SN1 ratio: Till 60 degrees C = S > E (substitution major); Above 60 degrees C = E > S (elimination major); ΔG = ΔH - TΔS: E has larger ΔS, high T favors E; E1 reagents: H2O, R-OH, R-COOH, R-NH2 (all polar protic)
concepts.description:
TEMPERATURE EFFECT ON E1 vs SN1 COMPETITION (RM lec9, pages 7-8):

TEACHER'S TEMPERATURE NOTE (page 7, underlined):
  'Note:- Till 60°C: S > E'
  'Above 60°C: E > S'

This is for E1 vs SN1 competition (both proceed through the same carbocation intermediate; temperature determines which pathway from the carbocation is favored).

THERMODYNAMIC BASIS (ΔG = ΔH - TΔS, teacher page 8 bottom):
  For SUBSTITUTION (SN1): carbocation + Nu (H₂O, ROH) → alcohol/ether (R-OH or R-OR')
    ΔH = more negative (product = alcohol, thermodynamically more stable)
    ΔS = smaller (one product from one intermediate, minor entropy change)
  For ELIMINATION (E1): carbocation → alkene + H⁺
    ΔH = less negative (alkene is less stable than alcohol)
    ΔS = LARGER (more products, more degrees of freedom = more disorder)
    TΔS term grows with T → at high T, TΔS dominates → ΔG for E becomes more negative than ΔG for S
    Teacher's energy diagram: S product at energy minimum (more stable, ΔH favored), E product at higher energy (+ve region = less ΔH stable, but more ΔS favorable).

TEACHER'S ENERGY DIAGRAM (page 8, bottom left):
  ΔG = ΔH - TΔS ((-ve)) annotation — E is labeled at +ve energy level, S is at minimum.
  At LOW T: TΔS small → ΔH controls → S (alcohol) is product = S > E
  At HIGH T: TΔS large for E → ΔG(E) < ΔG(S) → E1 (alkene) is product = E > S
  CUTOFF = 60°C (teacher's empirical value)

E1 POLAR PROTIC REAGENTS (teacher's list, '#' section, page 7):
  - H₂O/Δ (water + heat = classic SN1 + E1)
  - R-OH/Δ (alcohol + heat = same carbocation intermediate, E1 or SN1)
  - R-COOH/Δ (carboxylic acid + heat = proton source)
  - R-NH₂/Δ (amine = protic; less common but listed)
  All are POLAR PROTIC SOLVENTS → promote ionization of C-L → carbocation → E1/SN1.

CRITICAL DISTINCTION: R-O⁻ (alkoxide) vs R-OH (alcohol):
  R-O⁻/Δ = E2 (alkoxide = BASE → bimolecular E2)
  R-OH/Δ = E1 (alcohol = protic solvent, no base → unimolecular E1/SN1)
  This applies even to t-BuOH: t-BuOH = E1 (protic, no base); t-BuO⁻ = E2 (bulky base, Hofmann).
  TEACHER'S TABLE (page 9, boxed):
    R-O⁻/Δ → E2
    R-O⁻/R-OH,Δ → E2
    R-OH,Δ → E1

ALL POSSIBLE PRODUCTS FROM E1 + SN1 (teacher page 8):
  When substrate + CH₃OH/Δ → count ALL products = E1 alkenes + SN1 ethers/alcohols.
  Teacher's examples: substrates give 1, 2, or 6 total products (labeled in product tree).
  'All possible products: (E1 + SN1)' = teacher's label for this type of question.
concepts.why_fragile: The 60°C temperature cutoff (S>E below 60°C; E>S above 60°C) is a quantitative teacher-stated rule that JEE explicitly tests. Students may know 'high T favors E2' from E2 vs SN2 but don't know the temperature threshold for E1 vs SN1. Also: the thermodynamic explanation (ΔG = ΔH - TΔS, larger ΔS for E product) is exam-testable reasoning. The t-BuOH → E1 distinction (not E2) is a critical trap: many students see 't-Bu' and automatically predict E2/Hofmann, but the OH vs O⁻ distinction is decisive.
