distractors.surface_reading: E2 elimination shows NO kinetic isotope effect (kH/kD ≈ 1) because E2 is CONCERTED — all bonds break simultaneously in one step, so no single step is rate-determining in the way that would show a KIE. A KIE requires a two-step mechanism where one step is slow.
distractors.correct_answer: E2 shows a PRIMARY KINETIC ISOTOPE EFFECT (kH/kD > 1, BOXED by teacher: Q8 'KIE is observed'). 'Concerted' means there is ONE TS, but C-H breaking still contributes to the activation energy of that TS → C-D bond requires higher energy to break in the TS → D-substrate has higher Ea → slower rate → kH/kD > 1. Teacher's Q8: r₁(H-substrate) > r₂(D-substrate); kH/kD > 1. KIE does NOT require a two-step mechanism — it only requires that the isotopically substituted bond is being broken in the rate-determining step (or contributing to the TS energy). For E2, the concerted TS includes C-H breaking → primary KIE. It is E1 (not E2) that shows NO β-H KIE, because in E1 the RDS is C-L ionization (not C-H breaking).
distractors.example: Comparison: CH₃CH₂Br + KOH-alc. → r₁; CD₃CH₂Br + KOH-alc. → r₂; r₁/r₂ = kH/kD ≈ 5 (primary KIE, large). This LARGE KIE confirms E2 mechanism (C-H breaking in TS). If the mechanism were E1: r₁/r₂ ≈ 1.0 (no primary KIE at β-D).

distractors.surface_reading: Bridgehead bicyclic halides (LG at bridgehead or at a position where beta-H atoms are gauche to LG) react slowly in E2 under standard conditions but will eventually react under forcing conditions (excess t-BuOK, very high temperature). The anti-periplanar requirement increases the activation energy but does not make E2 impossible.
distractors.correct_answer: For certain rigid bicyclic systems where ALL β-H are gauche (dihedral ≠ 180°) to the LG, E2 gives NO REACTION (not just slow reaction). Teacher's Q4: rigid bicyclic + alc. KOH/Δ → 'No rxn' (underlined = ABSOLUTE). Anti-periplanar geometry is NOT about activation energy — it is a GEOMETRIC requirement for the orbital overlap that allows the concerted TS to form. No orbital overlap = no TS = no reaction, period. This is analogous to how a bridgehead double bond (Bredt's rule violation) cannot form regardless of conditions — geometry is not a kinetic barrier, it is a topological impossibility for E2. The substrate would need to undergo a different mechanism entirely (e.g., radical or ionic substitution, not E2).
distractors.example: 1-Chloronorbornane (LG at bridgehead C1 of norbornane): NO E2 product even with t-BuOK at high temperature. The bridgehead position has NO anti-periplanar β-H possible in the rigid bicyclo[2.2.1] framework. The observation of 'no alkene product' under strong base conditions is diagnostic for this type of substrate.

distractors.surface_reading: For E2 on cyclohexyl halides, axial and equatorial substrates react at the same rate because chair flip equilibrium is fast — the substrate rapidly equilibrates between axial and equatorial conformers, so both conformations are equally available as reactive species.
distractors.correct_answer: Axial LG reacts FASTER in E2 than equatorial LG (same substrate, LG in different positions). Teacher's Q7 rate order 2>1>3>4 includes this effect. Reason: E2 specifically requires the AXIAL conformer (LG axial = trans-diaxial with β-H at adjacent carbons = anti-periplanar). While chair flip is fast (equilibrium), the EQUILIBRIUM RATIO matters: if LG is more stable equatorial (favored 90:10 over axial), only 10% of the substrate is in the reactive conformation at any time. E2 rate = k₂[reactive conformer] ∝ fraction with LG axial × [total substrate]. More axial-preferring LG (bulky, less) → higher fraction in reactive conformer → faster effective E2. Less axial-preferring LG (small, 'equatorial-preferred') → lower fraction in reactive conformer → slower effective E2.
distractors.example: 4-tert-butylchlorocyclohexane: the tert-butyl group locks the ring (axial t-Bu is very unfavorable) → if Cl is trans to t-Bu (both equatorial in stable conformer, Cl axial in minor conformer), E2 proceeds slowly. If Cl is cis to t-Bu (Cl axial in stable conformer), E2 proceeds rapidly. Same LG (Cl), same ring size, same base — but >10× rate difference due to axial vs equatorial conformer populations.

distractors.surface_reading: 2-Bromobutane (CH₃CHBrCH₂CH₃) + alc. KOH gives 2 products from E2: 1-butene (from C1 β-H elimination) and 2-butene (from C3 β-H elimination). Total = 2 alkenes.
distractors.correct_answer: 2-Bromobutane + alc. KOH gives 3 products (OVAL in teacher's Q8 equivalent: 'No of P = 3'). The two constitutional isomers are: 1-butene (terminal, no E/Z possible = 1 product) and 2-butene (internal). BUT 2-butene exists as TWO stereoisomers: cis-2-butene (Z) and trans-2-butene (E). Teacher explicitly marks these as 'C+T.' (cis + trans = 2 products from C3 β-C). Each stereoisomer of 2-butene is a distinct compound → counted separately. Total: 1-butene + cis-2-butene + trans-2-butene = 3 products. Saytzeff major = trans-2-butene (most substituted AND more stable E isomer).
distractors.example: Q8 from teacher: acyclic secondary bromide with Ha and Hb at β-C + alc. KOH/Δ → OVAL 'No of P = 3'. The Ha gives E-alkene and Hb gives Z-alkene from the same β-C. This is why one β-C yields 2 products (E + Z). If JEE asks 'how many alkenes can be obtained by E2 of 2-bromobutane?', the answer is 3, not 2.
distractors.description: Distractor example: 2 bromobutane e2 gives 2 products forgetting ez isomers. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.

distractors.surface_reading: When a secondary bromide has a cyclopentyl group and an alkyl chain at the alpha-C, the chain alkene (exocyclic) is the more substituted product because the chain has more carbon substituents extending from the double bond, whereas the endocyclic alkene is confined within the ring.
distractors.correct_answer: The ENDOCYCLIC alkene (C=C bond within the cyclopentyl ring) is MORE SUBSTITUTED than the chain alkene — endocyclic = Saytzeff product. Reason: the endocyclic C=C is flanked by ring carbons on both sides (each C of the C=C has TWO other ring carbons plus possibly the chain/LG as substituents = trisubstituted or tetrasubstituted alkene). The chain alkene typically has fewer alkyl substituents at the double bond. Teacher Q9: the endocyclic product is labeled '① = S' (Saytzeff = circled-1 = major). The two chain alkenes (E+Z) are labeled circled-② = minor. Endocyclic more stable = lower Ea via product-like TS = major.
distractors.example: Substrate: 1-bromo-1-cyclopentylpropane (cyclopentyl + ethyl chain at C1-Br). E2: endocyclic pathway → cyclopentene with chain substituent at C1 (trisubstituted alkene, C=C flanked by ring C's and the chain). Chain pathway → 1-pentene-like with cyclopentyl pendant (less substituted at C=C). Endocyclic = Saytzeff = major (labeled S by teacher).

distractors.surface_reading: In the Mg-mediated ring closure of 1,3-dichloropropane to cyclopropane, the Mg byproduct is MgCl (magnesium monochloride) because only one C-Cl bond is involved in the Mg insertion step that initiates the reaction.
distractors.correct_answer: The byproduct is MgCl₂ (magnesium DICHLORIDE), not MgCl. Teacher explicitly writes and underlines 'MgCl₂' as the byproduct in the 1,3-elimination mechanism diagram. Reason: Mg(0) is oxidized to Mg(II) in the reaction, collecting TWO Cl atoms total — one from the Mg insertion step at C1-Cl → C1-MgCl (first Cl onto Mg), and one from the intramolecular SN2 step at C3-Cl (second Cl departs from C3 → goes to Mg) → MgCl₂ forms. Two chlorides, one Mg(II) → MgCl₂. Charge balance: Mg(0) → Mg(2+) + 2e⁻; each C-Cl + e⁻ → C⁻ + Cl⁻; overall: Mg(0) + 2 C-Cl → C-C (ring) + MgCl₂.
distractors.example: 1,3-dichloropropane + Mg/Δ → cyclopropane + MgCl₂. Teacher's mechanism diagram: Mg inserts into C1-Cl → [C1-MgCl + •• arrows] → intramolecular SN2 at C3 → cyclopropane (triangle) + MgCl₂ (underlined at right). The full mechanism shows both Cl atoms ending up on the same Mg atom. MgCl₂ is a white solid ionic compound (soluble in THF/ether) and is the classic byproduct of Grignard-type reactions.

distractors.surface_reading: 1,n-dihaloalkane + Mg/Delta undergoes E2 elimination where the Mg-generated carbanion acts as a base, removing a beta-H from adjacent to one of the C-Cl positions and causing the other C-Cl to lose Cl- to form an alkene with a double bond in the chain.
distractors.correct_answer: 1,n-dihaloalkane + Mg/Δ undergoes INTRAMOLECULAR SN2 (ring closure), NOT E2 elimination. The mechanism (teacher's page 1 detail): Mg inserts into C1-Cl → C1-MgCl (carbanion at C1) → C1 carbanion acts as NUCLEOPHILE (not base) and attacks C_n (the other C bearing Cl) in an intramolecular SN2 → C1-C_n bond forms → ring closes → cycloalkane. The product is a RING (cyclopropane/cyclobutane/cyclopentane/cyclohexane), not an alkene. E2 would give an alkene by removal of β-H; intramolecular SN2 gives a ring by C-C bond formation. The carbanion from Mg is a nucleophile here, not a base.
distractors.example: 1,4-dibromobutane + Mg/Δ → cyclobutane (□) + MgBr₂. The C1 carbanion attacks C4 → 4-membered ring. If E2 occurred instead: would give 3-bromobutene or similar alkene (one C-Br remaining in product) — that is NOT the observed product. Confirmed: Mg on 1,n-dihalide → cycloalkane (ring) via intramolecular SN2 mechanism.
distractors.description: Distractor example: 1 n dihalide ring closure goes via e2 not intramolecular sn2. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.
distractors.why_attractive: SN2 is the first-taught substitution mechanism. Students default to it for all C-X situations without checking substrate class, nucleophile, or solvent constraints.
distractors.correct_resolution: SN2 requires: (1) primary or methyl substrate (3° essentially impossible); (2) strong nucleophile; (3) polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMSO, DMF). For secondary: check whether SN1 or E2 might compete. For vinyl/aryl: SN2 is impossible (use SNAr or benzyne).

distractors.surface_reading: The 'Resonance > Saytzeff' principle is just a specific application of Saytzeff rule: resonance-stabilized alkenes are more stable, and Saytzeff predicts that the more stable alkene is major. Therefore, these two rules always agree with each other and 'Resonance > Saytzeff' is just saying the same thing as Saytzeff.
distractors.correct_answer: Resonance > Saytzeff is a SEPARATE OVERRIDE RULE, not a restatement of Saytzeff. Saytzeff specifically refers to alkyl SUBSTITUTION at the C=C — more alkyl groups → more stable. Resonance refers to CONJUGATION with adjacent π systems — extended π delocalization → more stable. These two effects can CONFLICT: a disubstituted conjugated alkene can be MORE STABLE than a trisubstituted non-conjugated alkene (when conjugation stabilization > extra substitution stabilization). In that conflict: 'Resonance > Saytzeff' means the conjugated (less substituted) alkene is MAJOR. If the two rules always agreed, there would be no need for a separate 'Resonance > Saytzeff' rule — the teacher explicitly BOXED this rule separately because it overrides Saytzeff in specific cases.
distractors.example: Substrate where β-C1 gives butadiene-type conjugated alkene (disubstituted, resonance stabilized) and β-C2 gives a trisubstituted alkene (Saytzeff). Saytzeff predicts trisubstituted = major. Resonance > Saytzeff predicts conjugated = major. JEE question tests knowing this hierarchy: conjugated = major wins over trisubstituted.
distractors.description: Distractor example: Resonance and saytzeff are the same rule in e2. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.
distractors.why_attractive: Elimination reactions are often forgotten as a competing pathway. Students predict substitution products even when bulky base and high temperature should favour elimination.
distractors.correct_resolution: Check: (1) if strong, bulky base → E2 preferred over SN2; (2) if high temperature → elimination favoured over substitution; (3) if 3° substrate → E1/E2 or SN1 (not SN2). Anti-periplanar requirement for E2: check geometry before predicting product.

distractors.surface_reading: When two diastereomers of 2-bromobutane-3-d (with D at C3) undergo E2, both give the same mixture of cis-2-butene and trans-2-butene, just in different proportions — one diastereomer gives more trans and the other gives more cis, but both give some of each.
distractors.correct_answer: Diastereomer 1 gives ONLY TRANS alkene (stereospecifically), not a mixture with cis as minor. Diastereomer 2 gives ONLY CIS alkene (stereospecifically), not a mixture. Teacher explicitly shows: Fischer → Newman analysis confirms each diastereomer gives only ONE geometric isomer (Diastereomer 1: 'Trans' underlined; Diastereomer 2: 'Cis' BOXED). E2 is STEREOSPECIFIC: the anti-periplanar requirement means exactly ONE spatial arrangement of H and Br is viable (180° dihedral), and this gives one specific product alkene geometry with complete stereocontrol. No mixture — purely trans from one diastereomer, purely cis from the other. (The KIE makes D removal slower than H, but the GEOMETRY determines which geometric isomer forms, not the KIE).
distractors.example: erythro-2-bromo-3-deuterobutane → E2 → cis-2-butene (only). threo-2-bromo-3-deuterobutane → E2 → trans-2-butene (only). The naming (erythro/threo) of the substrate diastereomers determines (cis/trans) the product alkene geometry with 100% specificity. This is the textbook E2 stereospecificity proof.
distractors.description: Distractor example: E2 on different diastereomers gives different amounts of same e z mixture. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.

distractors.surface_reading: Cyclobutyl bromide treated with alc. KOH and aq. KOH give the same products (cyclobutene and cyclobutanol) because KOH is KOH — it doesn't matter whether the solvent is water or alcohol, both provide OH⁻ as the nucleophile/base.
distractors.correct_answer: Cyclobutyl bromide + alc. KOH → E2 → exo alkene (methylenecyclobutane, 4-membered ring intact, NO ring expansion). Cyclobutyl bromide + aq. KOH → E1 → cyclobutyl cation → RING EXPANSION → cyclopentyl cation → cyclopentanol (5-membered ring, NOT 4-membered). Completely DIFFERENT products from the two conditions: (1) 4-membered ring alkene vs (2) 5-membered ring alcohol. The solvent determines the mechanism: alcoholic solvent → base acts as base (E2, concerted, no cation, no rearrangement); aqueous solvent → OH⁻ less basic due to hydration, SN1/E1 pathway opens → carbocation forms → ring expansion occurs → larger ring product. Teacher's page 7 explicitly shows the two pathway comparison (top Q).
distractors.example: Cyclobutyl bromide: alc. KOH = E2 = methylenecyclobutane (4-ring alkene). Cyclobutyl bromide: aq. KOH = E1/SN1 = cyclobutyl⁺ → cyclopentyl⁺ (ring expansion) → cyclopentanol. Same substrate, same formula of reagent (KOH), different solvent → different mechanism → different ring size → completely different products.

distractors.surface_reading: The kinetic isotope effect (KIE) for C-H vs C-D bond breaking in E2 is small, with kH/kD between 1 and 2, because deuterium is only slightly heavier than hydrogen and the effect on reaction rate is minimal.
distractors.correct_answer: The primary KIE for C-H vs C-D bond breaking in E2 is kH/kD = 2 to 7 (or ≥7 with tunneling). Teacher explicitly boxes: 'k₁/k₂ ≥ 7' in Q8 of RM lec7 p2. This is a LARGE KIE effect (not small). Reason: the ZPE difference between C-H and C-D bonds is significant (≈5 kJ/mol difference in ZPE) → at 25°C, kH/kD can reach 6-7 (classical limit) and exceed 7 with quantum tunneling. A value of kH/kD = 2-7 indicates STRONG primary KIE, confirming C-H bond breaking in the rate-determining step. Values kH/kD = 1.0-1.3 would indicate secondary KIE (isotope not at breaking bond). For E2, the primary KIE (2-7+) is observed because β-C-H breaks directly in the TS.
distractors.example: CH₃CH₂-CHBrCH₃ → alc. KOH: r₁. CD₃CH₂-CHBrCH₃ → alc. KOH: r₂. Teacher: r₁ > r₂ (BOXED), kH/kD ≥ 7. This magnitude (≥7) is at the high end of primary KIE, suggesting possible tunneling contribution. JEE may ask: 'What is the approximate kH/kD for E2?' Answer: 2-7 (or ≥7 per teacher). NOT close to 1 (which would mean E1 or no KIE).

distractors.surface_reading: A cyclohexyl bromide with Br in the equatorial position undergoes E2 more slowly than the axial-Br conformer, because the equatorial Br is 60 degrees (gauche) from the beta-H atoms. E2 can still occur but proceeds through the gauche conformation at a much slower rate.
distractors.correct_answer: E2 with equatorial Br gives NO REACTION (not just slow). Teacher's note: 'E2 CANNOT take place bcos there is no periplanar H atom.' The 60° gauche dihedral has zero productive MO overlap (p-orbital diagram shows: gauche p-orbital geometry → no overlap → no E2 TS possible). The required 180° anti-periplanar is a geometric necessity, not an energetic preference. Only the anti-periplanar conformation gives the productive MO overlap needed for concerted E2. Equatorial Br cannot achieve 180° dihedral with any beta-H in the rigid chair → E2 is geometrically impossible → rate = 0, not just slow.
distractors.example: Methylcyclohexyl bromide with Br equatorial + alc. KOH → X (No reaction) — shown with circled Br and X mark by teacher (pages 3-4, RM lec8). Compare with the same substrate after chair flip (Br becomes axial) → E2 proceeds. So the AXIAL conformer reacts; the EQUATORIAL conformer cannot react in E2. For freely-flipping rings, always draw the Br-axial conformer for E2 analysis.

distractors.surface_reading: In E2 elimination, both syn-periplanar (0 degrees, H and L on same side) and anti-periplanar (180 degrees, H and L on opposite sides) arrangements should give E2 products with equal facility, since in both cases the C-H, C-C, and C-L bonds are all coplanar. The teacher's p-orbital diagram showing anti-periplanar as correct applies equally to syn-periplanar.
distractors.correct_answer: Anti-periplanar (180°) is the required geometry for concerted E2; syn-periplanar (0°) does NOT give normal E2. Reasons: (1) Orbital: at anti (180°), C-H and C-L sigma bonds are ANTIPARALLEL → their sigma* orbitals overlap optimally with the forming C=C pi bond; at syn (0°), they are parallel in SAME direction → less favorable orbital overlap. (2) Conformational: anti-periplanar TS is staggered (low torsional strain); syn-periplanar TS is fully eclipsed (high torsional strain → raises TS energy). Syn-periplanar E2 ONLY occurs in special Ei mechanisms (ester pyrolysis, Chugaev reaction, xanthate pyrolysis) which proceed via a 6-membered cyclic TS using a different intramolecular base — completely distinct from E2. Teacher's p-orbital diagram specifically compares anti (180°) vs gauche (60°) — both anti-periplanar (coplanar, anti) and non-periplanar (gauche, not coplanar) cases. The correct one (180°) allows productive overlap; 60° does not.
distractors.example: In ester pyrolysis (Ei mechanism): the C=O oxygen acts as intramolecular base, H is removed SYN to the LG (OAc group) via a cyclic 6-membered TS → syn elimination. This is NOT the same as E2. E2 reactions: always anti-periplanar (180°). Ei reactions (Cope elimination, Chugaev): syn-periplanar (0°) via cyclic TS. The two mechanisms produce DIFFERENT alkene stereoisomers from the same substrate.
distractors.description: Distractor example: Syn periplanar e2 equivalent to anti periplanar since both coplanar. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.

distractors.surface_reading: The erythro and threo diastereomers of 2-bromo-3-deuterobutane both give a mixture of (E)-2-butene-3-d and (Z)-2-butene-3-d from E2. The erythro isomer gives more Z (cis) and the threo gives more E (trans), but both give some of each isomer because there are multiple conformations available.
distractors.correct_answer: Each diastereomer gives ONLY ONE geometric isomer from E2 — it is STEREOSPECIFIC, not just stereoselective. Teacher Q2: erythro → ONLY '(Cis)'. Teacher Q3: threo → ONLY '{trans}' (BOXED). The anti-periplanar requirement means only one conformation per diastereomer is reactive in E2 → one stereospecific product only. From a pure erythro substrate: 100% cis alkene, 0% trans. From a pure threo substrate: 100% trans alkene, 0% cis. This is why E2 is called STEREOSPECIFIC (not stereoselective). If you observe a mixture of E and Z from E2 of a 'single' substrate, it means your substrate was not a pure diastereomer (it was a mixture of erythro + threo = racemic mixture or mixture of diastereomers).
distractors.example: erythro-2-bromo-3-deuterobutane (pure) + alc. KOH → (Z)-2-butene-3-d (100%, pure cis). threo-2-bromo-3-deuterobutane (pure) + alc. KOH → (E)-2-butene-3-d (100%, pure trans). No mixture from each pure diastereomer. This is proven by teacher's Newman analysis in Q2 and Q3 of RM lec8 showing the complete conversion to single geometric isomers.

distractors.surface_reading: An allylic halide (Br at carbon adjacent to existing C=C in the ring) undergoes E2 to give the Saytzeff product — the most substituted alkene. The conjugation of the new C=C with the existing ring C=C is an additional stabilization factor, but Saytzeff still predicts the most substituted alkene regardless of whether the less substituted alkene happens to be conjugated.
distractors.correct_answer: For allylic halides where one E2 product is CONJUGATED (diene, extending existing ring C=C) and another is the Saytzeff (more substituted, isolated) alkene: RESONANCE > SAYTZEFF → CONJUGATED DIENE = MAJOR. Teacher's Q1 (RM lec8): cyclohexenyl-Br + alc. KOH → conjugated alkene (product with exo chain C=C conjugated with ring C=C) = major. BOX: 'resonance > sytzett.' Conjugation provides ca. 15 kJ/mol stabilization per diene overlap, which exceeds the ca. 5-7 kJ/mol per methyl group (Saytzeff stability). Since E2 TS is product-like (Hammond, ΔH=+ve), the more stable (conjugated) product gives a more stable TS → faster rate → major. Resonance > Saytzeff is a SEPARATE OVERRIDING RULE above Saytzeff in the hierarchy.
distractors.example: 3-Bromocyclohex-1-ene + alc. KOH: two options: (A) eliminate toward C1=C2 (existing ring double bond) → 1,3-cyclohexadiene (conjugated diene) = major [Resonance > Saytzeff]; (B) eliminate toward C4 → 3-methylenecyclohexene (more substituted ring, isolated) = minor [would be Saytzeff but loses to resonance]. Product: 1,3-cyclohexadiene (conjugated). Teacher's boxed rule: 'resonance > sytzett' applies here.
distractors.description: Distractor example: Allylic halide e2 always gives saytzeff not conjugated diene. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.

distractors.surface_reading: For E2 elimination of alkyl halides (I, Br, Cl substrates), the Saytzeff product (more substituted alkene) is always the major product, regardless of what base is used. Saytzeff rule applies universally to E2 of halides.
distractors.correct_answer: Saytzeff is the major product ONLY when a NON-BULKY base is used (CH₃O⁻, EtO⁻, iPrO⁻, alc. KOH). When a BULKY base (t-BuO⁻, t-BuOK, LDA, DBN, DBU) is used, the HOFMANN product (less substituted alkene) becomes major, even for I, Br, or Cl substrates. Teacher's examples (page 8): alkyl bromide + t-BuO⁻/Δ → Hofmann (labeled). The base size overrides the substrate preference. For ANY substrate: bulky base = Hofmann = 'less crowded alkene will be formed' (teacher's verbatim). JEE will give the same substrate with two bases and ask for both products — knowing the base-size cutoff (iPrO⁻ = Saytzeff; t-BuO⁻ = Hofmann) is essential.
distractors.example: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane: + alc. KOH → 2-methylbut-2-ene (Saytzeff = more substituted, trisubstituted, MAJOR); + t-BuOK → 2-methylbut-1-ene (Hofmann = less substituted, terminal, MAJOR). Same substrate, same halide (Br), different base → completely different major products.
distractors.description: Distractor example: All alkyl halides give saytzeff in e2 regardless of base. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.

distractors.correct_resolution: Check: (1) if strong, bulky base → E2 preferred over SN2; (2) if high temperature → elimination favoured over substitution; (3) if 3° substrate → E1/E2 or SN1 (not SN2). Anti-periplanar requirement for E2: check geometry before predicting product.

distractors.surface_reading: Poor leaving groups (F, SR2+, NR3+) simply make E2 slower overall but do not change WHICH alkene is the major product — the Saytzeff/Hofmann ratio stays the same as for good LG, just the overall rate decreases.
distractors.correct_answer: PLG completely CHANGES THE SELECTIVITY from Saytzeff to Hofmann, not just the rate. Teacher's table (page 9): Br (GLG) → 70% Saytzeff / 30% Hofmann; NR₃⁺ (PLG) → 18% Saytzeff / 82% Hofmann. This is a COMPLETE REVERSAL of major product, not just a rate effect. The mechanism changes: PLG = carbanion-like TS at β-C → 1°>2°>3° rate order (reversed from GLG's 3°>2°>1°). The BOXED rule: '1° > 2° > 3°' for PLG (teacher's yellow box). The selectivity shift from Saytzeff to Hofmann is the primary effect of PLG; the slower overall rate is a secondary observation.
distractors.example: Substrate: R-CH₂-CR'(NR₃⁺)-CH(R'')(CH₃) with two β-C options: primary (CH₂) and secondary (CH(R'')(CH₃)). GLG: primary β-C gives 30%, secondary gives 70% (Saytzeff from secondary wins). PLG (NR₃⁺): primary β-C gives 82%, secondary gives 18% (Hofmann from primary wins). Complete selectivity reversal. The PLG doesn't just slow things down — it redirects the base to the less hindered position via carbanion TS.
distractors.description: Distractor example: Plg poor lg gives slower e2 overall not different selectivity. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.

distractors.surface_reading: Cope elimination (from amine N-oxide substrate) requires anti-periplanar geometry just like E2 — the N-O group must be anti to the beta-H for the 5-membered cyclic transition state to form. Therefore, Cope elimination gives the same stereochemical product as E2 from the same substrate.
distractors.correct_answer: Cope elimination (Ei) requires SYN periplanar geometry (0°), NOT anti-periplanar. The N-O⁻ oxygen must abstract the β-H that is on the SAME SIDE as the N-O bond — this is required by the 5-membered ring TS geometry (ring: O-N-Cα-Cβ-H, all five atoms in a ring → the H must be syn to O). Anti-periplanar H atoms CANNOT react in Cope because they cannot reach the N-O oxygen (it's on the other side). Cope gives SYN elimination product; E2 gives ANTI elimination product. From the same substrate: different diastereomers react in Cope vs E2, and the product alkene has OPPOSITE geometric isomer compared to E2. Teacher's pages 11-12: the N-oxide mechanism shows H abstraction syn to N-O via 5-membered ring — this is the defining feature of Cope/Ei.
distractors.example: For threo-R-CHD-CHR'-N⁺R₂-O⁻: E2 with external base → anti-periplanar → trans (E) alkene. Cope (same substrate, internal O⁻ base) → syn-periplanar → cis (Z) alkene. The stereochemical outcome is completely different because one uses anti (E2) and the other uses syn (Cope) geometry.
distractors.description: Distractor example: Cope elimination requires anti periplanar geometry like e2. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.

distractors.surface_reading: LDA (lithium diisopropylamide) is an extremely strong base (pKa of conjugate acid ~36) and because strong bases favor E2 over SN2, LDA with a substrate gives the SAYTZEFF product (more substituted alkene) because strong base = more E2 character. Base STRENGTH determines product, not base SIZE.
distractors.correct_answer: LDA gives HOFMANN (less substituted) alkene as major product — NOT Saytzeff — because LDA is both STRONG AND BULKY (two isopropyl groups create a very hindered base). Teacher's bulky base list (page 8): ③ LDA (lithium diisopropylamide = (iPr)₂N⁻Li⁺) ✓ = explicitly listed as bulky base giving Hofmann. Distinction: base STRENGTH (pKa-based) determines E2 vs SN2 competition (stronger base = more E2). Base SIZE (steric bulk) determines Saytzeff vs Hofmann in E2 (larger base = Hofmann). LDA is both strong (pKa~36) AND bulky → it strongly favors E2 AND gives Hofmann product (less substituted). t-BuOK is also both strong (pKa~19) AND bulky → both give Hofmann. Alc. KOH is moderate strength and small → Saytzeff. Strong + bulky = Hofmann. Moderate + small = Saytzeff.
distractors.example: Secondary alkyl halide: + alc. KOH/Δ → E2 + SN2 mixture, Saytzeff E2 product. + LDA/Δ → E2 major (LDA is too bulky/strong for SN2), Hofmann alkene (LDA is too bulky for Saytzeff). + t-BuOK/Δ → E2 major, Hofmann alkene. Both LDA and t-BuOK: (1) strongly favor E2 over SN2 due to steric bulk avoiding SN2 backside attack, (2) give Hofmann E2 product due to steric approach control.

distractors.surface_reading: Stereoselective and stereospecific both describe reactions where one particular stereoisomeric product is formed preferentially. They are essentially synonymous terms with stereospecific being the stronger form (more selective). A reaction that gives only one stereoisomeric product is both stereoselective and stereospecific.
distractors.correct_answer: Stereoselective and stereospecific describe DIFFERENT concepts. Stereoselective (teacher definition, page 3): 'The rxns in which two stereoisomers are produced and out of them one is major are called stereoselective rxn.' = from ONE SM, two stereoisomeric products form but one is major. Stereospecific (teacher definition, page 4, circled #): 'When two stereoisomers on rxn with particular reagent produces different stereoisomers then it is stereospecific rxn.' = two DIFFERENT SM stereoisomers react with the SAME reagent to give TWO DIFFERENT PRODUCT stereoisomers. The KEY DIFFERENCE: stereoselective is about the PRODUCT RATIO from ONE SM; stereospecific is about the SM→PRODUCT RELATIONSHIP (different SMs give different products). E2 is BOTH simultaneously: stereoselective (Trans major from one SM) AND stereospecific (Diastereomer 1 → Trans; Diastereomer 2 → Cis).
distractors.example: E2 with alc. KOH: From ONE secondary bromide → Trans (major) + Cis (minor) = STEREOSELECTIVE. From Diastereomer 1 (one 2-bromo-3-deuterobutane) → Trans; from Diastereomer 2 → Cis = STEREOSPECIFIC. SN1 gives 60% inversion + 40% retention = 'loosely stereoselective' (one product slightly major) but is NOT stereospecific (R and S SN1 substrates give the same near-racemic mixture = NOT different products from different SMs).

distractors.surface_reading: E1, like E2, gives a mixture of Saytzeff (major) and Hofmann (minor) alkenes because the carbocation intermediate can lose any beta-H — from the more substituted beta-C (Saytzeff) or the less substituted beta-C (Hofmann). The ratio is different from E2 but both elimination mechanisms give both regioisomers.
distractors.correct_answer: E1 gives ONLY Saytzeff: α = 100%, ω = 0% (teacher's '#' section, page 2). The carbocation mechanism does NOT give Hofmann product because: the carbocation at α-C is sp2 and β-H is lost from the most accessible and energetically preferred position (more substituted β-C → more stable alkene). No base is involved in E1 to create steric selectivity, but the thermodynamic preference for the most stable alkene means ONLY Saytzeff forms. There is no mechanism in E1 for the Hofmann (less substituted) alkene to become the major or even minor product under standard conditions. This makes E1 'α = 100%, ω = 0%' — essentially regiospecific for Saytzeff. Contrast: E2 gives Saytzeff = 70% (major) + Hofmann = 30% (minor) for Br LG with small base.
distractors.example: Secondary bromide: + H⁺/Δ (E1 conditions) → carbocation → ONLY 2-methylbut-2-ene (Saytzeff, α = 100%), ZERO 2-methylbut-1-ene (Hofmann, ω = 0%). + alc. KOH/Δ (E2) → 2-methylbut-2-ene (70%, Saytzeff MAJOR) + 2-methylbut-1-ene (30%, Hofmann minor). E2 gives both; E1 gives only Saytzeff.
distractors.description: Distractor example: E1 gives saytzeff plus hofmann mixture like e2 because carbocation can lose any beta h. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.

distractors.surface_reading: E2 is regiospecific (gives only ONE specific regioisomeric alkene) because the anti-periplanar geometry requirement restricts which beta-H can be removed — only the beta-H that is perfectly anti-periplanar (180 degrees) to the leaving group can be eliminated, so only one alkene product forms.
distractors.correct_answer: E2 is REGIOSELECTIVE (not regiospecific): it gives Saytzeff (major) + Hofmann (minor) = a mixture of two regioisomers. The anti-periplanar requirement restricts GEOMETRY (which conformation is active), not REGIOCHEMISTRY (which regioisomer forms). For acyclic substrates, different rotational conformers with anti-periplanar H at different beta-C positions are both accessible → both regioisomers can form from anti-periplanar removal of H at beta-C1 (Saytzeff) and anti-periplanar H at beta-C2 (Hofmann). The Saytzeff product is simply more preferred (more acidic β-H at more substituted position, more stable product). Teacher's label (page 2): 'E2 is a regioselective rxn' (underlined, = clearly NOT regiospecific). It is E1 (via carbocation) that approaches regiospecific: α = 100%, ω = 0% (page 2).
distractors.example: 2-Bromobutane + alc. KOH: beta-C2 has 3H's (primary beta-C, Hofmann side) and beta-C4 position doesn't exist but C2 adjacent: Removing Hb from C1 (adjacent) → but-1-ene (Hofmann, less substituted, minor); Removing Ha from C3 (adjacent) → but-2-ene (Saytzeff, more substituted, major). Both are anti-periplanar accessible → both form (70:30 Saytzeff:Hofmann for Br LG, small base) = REGIOSELECTIVE. Not regiospecific.
distractors.description: Distractor example: E2 is regiospecific not regioselective because the anti periplanar requirement limits which beta h is removed. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.

distractors.surface_reading: SN1 reactions always produce exactly 50:50 racemic product (equal amounts of R and S enantiomers) because the planar carbocation intermediate has no face preference — the nucleophile attacks from both faces of the flat sp2 carbocation with equal probability.
distractors.correct_answer: SN1 does NOT always give exactly 50:50 racemic. Teacher's statement (page 4): 'Real SN1 is loosely stereoselective (60+40).' Real SN1 gives approximately 60% inversion + 40% retention because: the departing L⁻ forms an ION PAIR with the nascent carbocation — L⁻ transiently blocks the face it departed from (the retention face). Nucleophile has somewhat less access to the blocked face → more attack from the inversion face → 60% inversion, 40% retention. True 50:50 racemization only occurs if the carbocation is fully dissociated from L⁻ (rarely achieved even in highly polar solvents). Teacher also notes: 'SN1 is not stereoselective' (strict definition) because 60:40 is a weak selectivity, AND 'SN1 is not stereospecific' — both statements are correct. The 60:40 ratio is the exam-expected answer for 'real SN1 stereochemistry.'
distractors.example: (R)-2-bromobutane + H₂O (SN1 conditions) → NOT exactly 50% (S)-butan-2-ol + 50% (R)-butan-2-ol. ACTUAL: ~60% (S)-butan-2-ol (inversion) + ~40% (R)-butan-2-ol (retention) = 'loosely stereoselective (60+40).' The departing Br⁻ shields the retention face (R-face) briefly → more attack on the inversion face (S-product). JEE answer: Real SN1 = 60:40 inversion:retention (teacher's exact wording).

distractors.surface_reading: E1CB is a first-order reaction because the name 'E1CB' contains 'E1' (unimolecular elimination), just like E1 is first order. Both E1 and E1CB are unimolecular eliminations, so both should have Rate = k[substrate] (first order overall).
distractors.correct_answer: E1CB is SECOND ORDER overall, not first order. Teacher explicitly boxes: 'Overall order = 2' and writes 'Overall Rate = K'[substrate][Base].' The 'unimolecular' in E1CB refers ONLY to the rate-determining step (Step 2: carbanion → alkene + L⁻ is unimolecular — no base in this step). Step 1 is a fast equilibrium involving the base: [CB] = K_eq × [substrate][base]. Substituting: Rate = k₂[CB] = K'[substrate][base] → OVERALL = 2nd order. E1 is the mechanism with Rate = k[R-L]¹ (first order): 'Rate ∝ [R-L]¹, order = 1' BOXED on page 6. E1CB and E2 have the SAME form of rate law (both 2nd order) — this is why they cannot be distinguished by kinetics alone.
distractors.example: Substrate + strong base: Rate = k[substrate][base]. E2 also: Rate = k[substrate][base]. Same rate law. To distinguish: D-exchange test (E1CB yes; E2 no) or KIE (E1CB kH/kD ≈ 1; E2 kH/kD ≥ 7). Pure kinetics cannot tell E1CB from E2.

distractors.surface_reading: High temperature always favors elimination over substitution in any substrate-reagent combination. Whether the elimination is E1 or E2, and whether the substitution is SN1 or SN2, high temperature always shifts the ratio toward elimination. The 'high T = more elimination' rule applies universally.
distractors.correct_answer: The 'high T favors E' rule applies but with SPECIFIC CONTEXT: (1) For E1 vs SN1 (polar protic conditions): 'Till 60°C: S>E; Above 60°C: E>S' (teacher's exact rule, page 7). The 60°C threshold is the quantitative exam answer. (2) For E2 vs SN2 (R-O⁻ conditions): higher T also generally favors E2, but the specific threshold/ratio depends on the substrate class and base. The ΔG = ΔH - TΔS logic: elimination products (alkene) have LARGER ΔS than substitution products (alcohol/ether) because alkene formation gives more independent molecules and more entropy. As T increases, TΔS term for elimination grows → ΔG for E becomes more negative → E > S. Teacher's energy diagram (page 8): E product at higher energy (+ve = less ΔH stable), S product at minimum (more ΔH stable). At low T: ΔH controls → S major. At high T: TΔS controls → E major. The 60°C cutoff is the JEE exam answer for E1 vs SN1 competition specifically.
distractors.example: Tertiary bromide + H₂O (aqueous): 40°C → SN1 major (S>E, below 60°C). 80°C → E1 major (E>S, above 60°C). Same substrate + alc. KOH (R-O⁻): temperature increase also shifts E2 vs SN2 ratio toward E2, but the threshold and ratio depend on base concentration and substrate.
distractors.description: Distractor example: High temperature always favors e2 over sn2 in all elimination competition scenarios. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.
distractors.why_attractive: SN2 is the first-taught substitution mechanism. Students default to it for all C-X situations without checking substrate class, nucleophile, or solvent constraints.
distractors.correct_resolution: SN2 requires: (1) primary or methyl substrate (3° essentially impossible); (2) strong nucleophile; (3) polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMSO, DMF). For secondary: check whether SN1 or E2 might compete. For vinyl/aryl: SN2 is impossible (use SNAr or benzyne).

distractors.surface_reading: E1CB (Elimination Unimolecular Conjugate Base) is just another elimination mechanism and can occur with any leaving group including good leaving groups like bromide (Br) or iodide (I) as long as a strong base is present. The key factor is the strong base, not the leaving group quality.
distractors.correct_answer: E1CB specifically requires POOR LEAVING GROUPS (PLG). Teacher's condition ② (page 10): 'Poor leaving groups should be present.' With GLG (I, Br, Cl), E2 would compete and usually dominate because GLG departs readily in the concerted E2 step. PLG (F, OPh, NR₃⁺, OR) cannot depart easily in E2's concerted step → the carbanion mechanism (E1CB) takes over: base removes β-H first (fast, carbanion formed) → PLG departs in the slow step. All teacher's E1CB examples use F (Q③, Q④, Q⑤) or OPh (Q⑥) or NR₃⁺ (Q②) as the leaving group — never I, Br, or Cl. The combination EWG at β-C + PLG at α-C is the DUAL REQUIREMENT for E1CB. Remove either condition → E1CB does not operate.
distractors.example: Ph-CH₂-CH₂-F + OH⁻ → E1CB (benzylic EWG + F as PLG → carbanion → F⁻ departs slowly). Ph-CH₂-CH₂-Br + OH⁻ → E2 (Br is GLG → concerted anti-periplanar elimination dominates over E1CB). Ph-CH₂-CH₂-F + OH⁻: F is PLG → cannot do E2 easily → E1CB takes over. F being the worst LG (strongest C-F bond) ensures the carbanion forms first before F can depart.
distractors.description: Distractor example: E1cb works with any substrate including those with good leaving groups like bromide. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.

distractors.surface_reading: When a substrate reacts with EtO- base in EtOD (deuterated ethanol) and D-incorporation is observed in the product, this proves the E2 mechanism because E2 involves the base removing the beta-H — in EtOD solvent, the base would incorporate D from EtOD into the substrate as it removes H.
distractors.correct_answer: D-exchange PROVES E1CB, NOT E2. Teacher's direct annotation (Q⑤, page 12): substrate + EtO⁻/EtOD → product + '"D exchange will be observed"' — this is an E1CB substrate (Ph-CH₂CH₂F with Ph as EWG and F as PLG). In E2 (concerted): the base removes β-H and the LG departs SIMULTANEOUSLY in one step → the H goes directly to the base (EtO⁻ + H → EtOH) without any carbanion intermediate → NO D-exchange into the substrate occurs. In E1CB: Step 1 (fast) base removes β-H → carbanion intermediate with finite lifetime. The carbanion can then react with EtOD (the deuterated solvent) to get D back → H/D exchange at β-C. This is observable because D appears in the product alkene (e.g., Ph-CD=CH₂) or back in the recovered starting material. D-exchange = carbanion existed = E1CB proven. No D-exchange = concerted = E2.
distractors.example: Ph-CH₂CH₂F + EtO⁻ in EtOD: E1CB → [Ph-CH⁻-CH₂F] (carbanion, stable benzylic) → EtOD donates D to carbanion → Ph-CHD-CH₂F → F⁻ departs → Ph-CHD-CH=CH₂ (D in vinyl position). D-exchange observed = E1CB confirmed. If it were E2: H → EtO⁻ in concerted step → EtOH (H goes to ethoxide directly, not recycled back to substrate) → Ph-CH=CH₂ (no D in product) → no D-exchange = no E1CB.

distractors.surface_reading: Ester pyrolysis at 500 degrees C is a high-temperature reaction. High temperature always favors thermodynamic products. The thermodynamic alkene product is the more substituted (Saytzeff) alkene because it is more stable (more hyperconjugation). Therefore, ester pyrolysis gives Saytzeff (more substituted) alkene as the major product.
distractors.correct_answer: Ester pyrolysis gives HOFMANN (LESS substituted) alkene = major product. Teacher: '→ Follow Hofmann rule' (underlined, page 1). The Ei mechanism (6-membered cyclic TS with internal base C=O abstracting syn β-H) gives Hofmann selectivity because the less hindered (terminal/primary) β-H is more accessible in the 6-membered ring geometry. This is a KINETIC selectivity, not thermodynamic. The 'high temperature = Saytzeff' rule applies to E1 vs SN1 competition (substitution vs elimination ratio), NOT to the regiochemical selectivity within elimination. For ester pyrolysis: Hofmann always (unless Resonance overrides to give conjugated product). ALL three Ei mechanisms (ester, Chugaev, Cope) give Hofmann as major = less substituted. None give Saytzeff.
distractors.example: sec-Butyl acetate + Δ/500°C: → but-1-ene (Hofmann, terminal, MAJOR) + but-2-ene (Saytzeff, internal, minor). The terminal alkene dominates despite being less stable, because the 6-membered Ei TS preferentially removes the syn terminal β-H (less hindered). Same substrate + alc. KOH/Δ (E2, small base) → but-2-ene (Saytzeff, more substituted, MAJOR).
distractors.description: Distractor example: Ei ester pyrolysis gives saytzeff alkene because high temperature favors thermodynamic product. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.

distractors.surface_reading: The Chugaev reaction (xanthate pyrolysis) and ester pyrolysis both proceed through a 6-membered Ei cyclic TS and both give alkene as the main product. Since the mechanisms are analogous, the byproducts should also be analogous. Ester pyrolysis gives RCOOH (carboxylic acid), so Chugaev also gives a carboxylic acid-like byproduct.
distractors.correct_answer: Chugaev gives COMPLETELY DIFFERENT byproducts: COS (carbonyl sulfide = O=C=S) + MeSH (methanethiol = H-S-Me), NOT a carboxylic acid. Teacher labels explicitly (page 4): 'Mesh + O=C=S' (= MeSH + COS). Ester pyrolysis gives RCOOH because the ester group R-C(=O)-O- contains an oxygen acid fragment. Chugaev substrate R-O-C(=S)-SMe contains S-based fragments: after elimination, the O-C(=S)-SMe piece becomes O=C=S (COS, isoelectronic with CO₂) and H-SMe (MeSH, from the β-H transferred to the SMe sulfur). The 'analogous mechanism' gives analogous ALKENE product, but the byproducts are determined by the STRUCTURE of the non-alkene fragment, not by the TS shape.
distractors.example: Xanthate R-O-C(=S)-SMe + Δ/200°C → R' (alkene) + O=C=S (COS) + H-SMe (MeSH). Three products total. Ester R-O-C(=O)-R' + Δ/500°C → alkene + R'-COOH. Two products total. COS (O=C=S) is an inorganic gas; MeSH (methanethiol) smells strongly — both are exam-testable byproducts of Chugaev.

distractors.surface_reading: The Cope elimination converts a tertiary amine directly to an alkene when treated with H2O2. H2O2 oxidizes the amine AND the oxidized product immediately eliminates in a one-step process to give the alkene directly. There is no separate N-oxide intermediate.
distractors.correct_answer: Cope elimination is a TWO-STEP process. Step 1: 3° amine + [O] (H₂O₂, O₃, peracid, etc.) → 3° amine N-oxide (R₃N⁺-O⁻). Step 2 (separate): 3° amine N-oxide + Δ (≥100°C) → alkene + N-hydroxylamine (R₂NOH). The N-OXIDE is the key intermediate — it must form first (Step 1) before elimination can occur (Step 2). Teacher's diagram (page 5): 3° amine → [oxidant tree] → R₃N⁺-O⁻ (labeled '3° amine oxide', underlined) → Δ/≥100°C → alkene + N-hydroxylamine. The N-oxide IS the substrate for Cope elimination — without it, the 5-membered cyclic TS [O-N-Cα-Cβ-H] cannot form. H₂O₂ is listed as one of the oxidants for Step 1 (along with O₃, Ag₂O, MgO, and peracid), but it does NOT cause direct elimination — it only makes the N-oxide.
distractors.example: Trimethylamine N-oxide (Me₃N⁺-O⁻) made from trimethylamine + H₂O₂ → then heated at ≥100°C → ethylene (if one Me has β-H? Only if N has an ethyl or larger group) + Me₂NOH (N,N-dimethylhydroxylamine). The two steps are separate: oxidation (Room T to mild heat) then elimination (≥100°C). The N-oxide can be isolated between the two steps.
distractors.description: Distractor example: Cope elimination uses h2o2 oxidation of amine to give alkene directly in one step. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.

distractors.surface_reading: All three Ei mechanisms (ester pyrolysis, Chugaev, Cope) are essentially the same reaction: internal base in a cyclic TS removes the syn beta-H to give alkene. Since they are the same type of mechanism, they give the same byproducts and require the same temperature and conditions.
distractors.correct_answer: All three Ei mechanisms share the same syn elimination principle and give Hofmann alkene as major product, but they DIFFER in: (1) TS ring size (ester = 6-membered; Chugaev = 6-membered; Cope = 5-membered); (2) Temperature (ester = ~500°C; Chugaev = ~200°C; Cope = ≥100°C); (3) Internal base atom (ester: O of C=O; Chugaev: S of C=S; Cope: O of N-O⁻); (4) Byproducts (ester: RCOOH; Chugaev: COS + MeSH; Cope: R₂NOH = N-hydroxylamine); (5) Substrate type (ester vs xanthate vs amine N-oxide). The COMMON features are: syn elimination, Hofmann rule, Resonance > Hofmann, no external base, no reaction if no syn β-H available. Teacher's page-level distinction: page 1 (ester), pages 4-5 (Chugaev), pages 5-6 (Cope) — three separate topics in the same lecture.
distractors.example: Cyclohexyl acetate + Δ/500°C → cyclohexene + CH₃COOH (acid byproduct, ester Ei). Cyclohexyl methyl xanthate (OCSMe) + Δ/200°C → cyclohexene + COS + MeSH (Chugaev byproducts). N-methylcyclohexylamine N-oxide + Δ/100°C → cyclohexene + MeNHOH (N-methylhydroxylamine, Cope byproduct). All give cyclohexene but with completely different byproducts and temperatures.

distractors.surface_reading: In the Pinacol-Pinacolone rearrangement, the hydride (H) migrates preferentially because it is the smallest group — it has no steric barriers and can squeeze through the transition state most easily compared to bulkier aryl or alkyl groups. Smallest group = fastest migration.
distractors.correct_answer: H (hydride) has the LOWEST migration aptitude: Ar > R > H. Hydride is the WORST migrator in 1,2-shifts in cationic rearrangements, not the best. The migration aptitude is determined by ELECTRONIC FACTORS (how well the migrating group stabilizes the partial positive charge in the bridged TS), not steric size. Aryl migrates best because it can stabilize δ+ through its π-system (aromatic resonance). Alkyl migrates better than H because alkyl can hyperconjugate to stabilize δ+. Hydride has no π-system and no hyperconjugation available → lowest aptitude. The steric argument (smaller = faster) is wrong for 1,2-shifts in carbocations. Teacher's rule: 'Migration aptitude: Ar > R > H' (underlined). If H migrated best, all pinacol rearrangements would give aldehyde products (RCHO, from H migration) rather than ketones (R₂C=O, from R migration). In practice, ketones form (R or Ar migrates, not H).
distractors.example: Pinacol (CH₃)₂C(OH)-C(OH)(CH₃)₂ + H₂SO₄: Four groups on the donor C are CH₃, CH₃ (and the OH becomes C=O). The CH₃ (methyl) groups migrate preferentially over H (Ar>R>H means any alkyl > H). Product: (CH₃)₃C-C(=O)-CH₃ (pinacolone). NO aldehyde forms from H migration.
distractors.description: Distractor example: In pinacol rearrangement h hydride migrates preferentially because it is the smallest group and can migrate most easily through space. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.
distractors.why_attractive: Rearrangements are unexpected: the product has a different carbon skeleton than the starting material. Students predict the unrearranged product by default.
distractors.correct_resolution: Check for rearrangement at every carbocation intermediate: (1) Is a 1,2-shift possible? (2) Does it give a more stable cation? (3) Can a ring expand? Always evaluate stability of rearranged vs unrearranged cation before predicting product.

distractors.surface_reading: If a secondary amine R-NMe-R' undergoes Cope elimination (via N-oxide) or Hofmann E2 (via quaternary ammonium), both reactions remove a beta-H adjacent to the N-bearing carbon and form an alkene. The geometry of removal (syn vs anti) doesn't matter for the final product identity — only which beta-C the H comes from matters. So both give the same alkene.
distractors.correct_answer: Cope (syn) and Hofmann E2 (anti) from the SAME substrate give DIFFERENT alkene products when there are diastereomeric β-H's (H and D with different configurations). Teacher Q (page 9): same NMe₂ substrate → Pathway ①MeI/Ag₂O/Δ (Hofmann E2, ANTI) → Product with H label. Pathway ①H₂O₂/②Δ (Cope, SYN) → Product with D label = DIFFERENT alkene. The syn vs anti requirement removes DIFFERENT β-H's: Cope removes the syn-H (same face as N-O); Hofmann E2 removes the anti-H (opposite face from N). When the syn-H and anti-H are different substituents (e.g., one is H and one is D at a stereogenic β-carbon), the two products are different geometric isomers (different E/Z or different regioisomers in the alkene). This is the key proof that Cope is stereospecifically SYN while E2 is stereospecifically ANTI.
distractors.example: Bicyclic NMe₂ substrate (page 9): H (solid wedge, axial) and D (dashed, equatorial) at β-C. Cope (H₂O₂/Δ): syn-D is removed (if D is syn to N-O) → alkene retains H at C=C. Hofmann E2 (MeI/Ag₂O/Δ): anti-H is removed (H anti to N) → alkene retains D at C=C. Two different alkene structures (H-labeled vs D-labeled at different positions).
distractors.description: Distractor example: Cope elimination and hofmann e2 from the same secondary amine substrate give the same alkene product because both remove a beta h adjacent to nitrogen. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.
distractors.why_attractive: Elimination reactions are often forgotten as a competing pathway. Students predict substitution products even when bulky base and high temperature should favour elimination.
distractors.correct_resolution: Check: (1) if strong, bulky base → E2 preferred over SN2; (2) if high temperature → elimination favoured over substitution; (3) if 3° substrate → E1/E2 or SN1 (not SN2). Anti-periplanar requirement for E2: check geometry before predicting product.

distractors.surface_reading: In the migration aptitude ranking for aryl 1,2-shifts, a p-NO2-phenyl group should migrate FASTER than unsubstituted phenyl because NO2 makes the aryl ring electron-poor and therefore the carbon can better accept the positive charge during migration (electron-poor carbon is more cationic character in the TS = better for migration into a cation).
distractors.correct_answer: p-NO₂-Ph migrates SLOWER than Ph (unsubstituted). In the migration TS, a partial POSITIVE charge develops on the IPSO carbon of the MIGRATING aryl (the bridged 'phenonium ion' TS). NO₂ (EWG) DESTABILIZES this partial + at the ipso carbon because EWG withdraw electrons → reduce electron density at ipso → cannot stabilize δ+. EDG (OMe, Me) DONATE electrons to the migrating aryl → stabilize the partial + → lower TS energy → faster migration. The aryl group itself is the NUCLEOPHILE in the migration (its π-electrons attack the adjacent carbocation). An electron-RICH aryl (EDG) is a better nucleophile → migrates faster. An electron-POOR aryl (NO₂) is a worse nucleophile → migrates slower. Teacher's example (page 12b): p-NO₂-Ph = 'slow' migrator; p-OMe-Ph = 'fast' migrator from the same substrate.
distractors.example: Substrate with p-NO₂-Ph and p-OMe-Ph both attached to the same C adjacent to a carbocation: Teacher shows 'fast' arrow for p-OMe-Ph migration, 'slow' arrow for p-NO₂-Ph migration. Full ranking: p-OMe-Ph > p-Me-Ph > Ph > p-Cl-Ph > p-NO₂-Ph (decreasing migration aptitude).
distractors.description: Distractor example: Migration aptitude ranking places no2 substituted aryl above unsubstituted phenyl because no2 makes the aryl electron poor and more electrophilic at carbon. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.

distractors.correct_resolution: Identify the specific condition or structural feature that makes the standard rule invalid here. Trace the mechanism step-by-step rather than applying a memorised rule. Check whether electronic and steric factors both support the predicted outcome.

distractors.surface_reading: In Pinacol-Pinacolone rearrangement, when one of the two carbons bearing OH is a primary carbon (RCH(OH)-C(OH)R'R''), the carbocation forms at the primary C (weaker C+ but forms because the other OH activates it), and then a hydride shifts from the adjacent secondary C to the primary C+ to give an aldehyde (from the remaining C=O at the secondary C after H migrated).
distractors.correct_answer: In Pinacol-Pinacolone rearrangement, protonation occurs at the OH that gives the MORE STABLE carbocation. A primary carbocation (at 1° C) is so unstable it essentially does NOT form under standard conditions. Instead, the OH at the MORE SUBSTITUTED C is protonated and that C becomes the C⊕ (more stable 2° or 3° carbocation). Then the group with highest migration aptitude migrates FROM the OTHER C (the one still bearing OH) TO the C⊕. The product is a KETONE (from 2° or 3° original C), not an aldehyde. Aldehydes form only when there is no alkyl or aryl group available to migrate (pure H shift) — but H has lowest migration aptitude (Ar > R > H), so in practice H rarely migrates when R or Ar are available. Only in specific cases where H is the only option does aldehyde form.
distractors.example: 2-methylpropane-1,2-diol (Me₂C(OH)-CH₂-OH): The 2° C (bearing 2 methyls and OH) loses OH to give the 3° carbocation Me₂C⁺-CH₂OH (more stable). Then methyl migrates from 3°-C to... wait, this would give Me₂C(=O)... Simpler: for glycol (HO-CH₂-CH₂-OH), carbocation at either C would be 1° → very unfavorable → glycol doesn't undergo classic Pinacol rearrangement easily. Classic Pinacol works best with 2,3-substituted diols where a tertiary carbocation can form.
distractors.description: Distractor example: Pinacol pinacolone rearrangement produces an aldehyde when the vicinal diol has one primary carbon bearing the oh. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.
distractors.why_attractive: Carbonyl reactions (addition, condensation, reduction) are among the most tested in JEE. The many named reactions and their conditions create confusion between similar-looking transformations.
distractors.correct_resolution: Key decision tree: identify the carbonyl type (aldehyde/ketone/ester/acid/amide/acyl halide) → identify the reagent class → determine mechanism → predict product, stereochemistry, and any competing pathways.

distractors.surface_reading: Cope elimination (Ei, syn) always gives Hofmann (less substituted) as major product. Cyclopentyl N-oxide + Δ → major product is methylenecyclopentane (= exocyclic CH2= = Hofmann = less substituted) because Ei = Hofmann rule.
distractors.correct_answer: Cyclopentyl N-oxide + Δ → SAYTZEFF (endocyclic cyclopentene = more substituted) = MAJOR. NOT Hofmann. Teacher data (page 1): 97.5% Saytzeff, only 2.5% Hofmann. Teacher note (page 3): 'In the cyclic 5-membered ring which is nearly planar structure, the formation of endo cyclic double bond (Sytzebb rule) predominates.' The cyclopentane ring is nearly planar → both exo-H and endo-H can access the Cope TS, but the ENDO-H gives a planar 5-membered TS ('Good T.S. bcoz all atoms can lie in one plane' — teacher) → Saytzeff major. The Hofmann rule applies to ACYCLIC substrates and CYCLOHEXANE (chair) substrates but is OVERRIDDEN in cyclopentane by the planarity preference. Teacher page 5: 'Sytzebb Rule followed & cyclopentane ring hydrogen give preferred planar structure than methyl hydrogen' (double underlined).
distractors.example: 1-methylcyclopentyl N-oxide (NMe₂⁺-O⁻ on the ring C, with CH₃ group) + Δ: → 1-methylcyclopent-1-ene (endocyclic = Saytzeff, MAJOR, 97.5%) + methylenecyclopentane (exocyclic = Hofmann, MINOR, 2.5%). Same substrate type in cyclohexane would give Hofmann (exocyclic) as major. The ring size changes the selectivity.
distractors.description: Distractor example: Cope elimination from cyclopentyl n oxide gives hofmann exocyclic methylenecyclopentane as major product because all ei mechanisms give hofmann less substituted. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.
distractors.why_attractive: Elimination reactions are often forgotten as a competing pathway. Students predict substitution products even when bulky base and high temperature should favour elimination.
distractors.correct_resolution: Check: (1) if strong, bulky base → E2 preferred over SN2; (2) if high temperature → elimination favoured over substitution; (3) if 3° substrate → E1/E2 or SN1 (not SN2). Anti-periplanar requirement for E2: check geometry before predicting product.

distractors.surface_reading: When NMe₃⁺ is equatorial in cyclohexane, E2 cannot occur (no anti-periplanar H). Ei (Cope) also requires a specific periplanar arrangement. If neither E2 nor Ei can proceed due to geometric constraints, no elimination occurs and the substrate is unreactive.
distractors.correct_answer: When E2 is blocked (equatorial NMe₃⁺, no anti-H), SN2 OCCURS INSTEAD: OH⁻ attacks the N-methyl group → MeOH + demethylated amine. Teacher Q3 (page 4): 'E2 not possible at eq / so SN2 / + Me-OH.' This is NOT 'no reaction' — a productive SN2 pathway opens up. Furthermore: Ei (Cope) does NOT require anti-periplanar geometry. Ei (Cope/Chugaev) requires SYN-PERIPLANAR (0°) geometry, not anti (180°). So even if E2 is blocked (no anti-H), Cope (syn-H) might still be possible IF the substrate is an N-oxide (not quaternary ammonium). For the specific case of EQUATORIAL NMe₃⁺ + OH⁻: E2 blocked → SN2 on methyl group → MeOH product. The SN2 pathway (demethylation) is the productive reaction, not 'no reaction.'
distractors.example: Equatorial-NMe₃⁺ cyclohexane + KOH/Δ: → Teacher: SN2 gives N-demethylation + MeOH ('+Me-OH' label). COMPARE: if the same cyclohexyl amine were treated with H₂O₂ first to make the N-oxide, then Δ: → Cope (syn, axial-equatorial alignment) → alkene. Two different reagent pathways → two different reactions.
distractors.description: Distractor example: For e2 from cyclohexyl nme3 equatorial position no reaction occurs because there is no anti periplanar h and ei also requires anti periplanar geometry. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.

distractors.correct_resolution: Check: (1) if strong, bulky base → E2 preferred over SN2; (2) if high temperature → elimination favoured over substitution; (3) if 3° substrate → E1/E2 or SN1 (not SN2). Anti-periplanar requirement for E2: check geometry before predicting product.

distractors.surface_reading: For erythro substrate Ph-CH(NMe₂⁺O⁻)-CHD-Ph, Cope syn elimination removes the syn-D. In the syn conformer, the two Ph groups are on the same face → they end up trans (E) in the alkene. So erythro → E alkene by Cope.
distractors.correct_answer: Erythro substrate → Cope (syn) → Z (cis) alkene = MAJOR. NOT E. Teacher (page 6): 'Erythro → 89% Z.' The reasoning: erythro = same groups on same side (Fischer convention). In the syn conformer where H/D is syn to N-O⁻: the two Ph groups end up on the SAME SIDE of the forming C=C → Z (cis) alkene. Students who apply anti-elimination logic (where erythro → E) get it backwards for syn elimination. RULE: SYN elimination (Cope/Chugaev): erythro → Z; threo → E. ANTI elimination (E2): erythro → E; threo → Z. These are OPPOSITE. The 89% (not 100%) reflects conformational flexibility in acyclic substrates. The E2 rule (erythro→E) is the 'intuitive' rule many students know; the Cope reversal (erythro→Z) requires understanding that syn and anti removal give opposite geometries.
distractors.example: Erythro-Ph-CH(NMe₂⁺O⁻)-CH(Me)-Ph + Δ (Cope): teacher gives 89% Z. Same substrate + KOH/Δ (E2 if NMe₃⁺ instead): would give primarily E (trans) alkene. The SAME erythro substrate gives Z from Cope and E from E2 — opposite E/Z from opposite geometric requirements.
distractors.description: Distractor example: Erythro substrate undergoes cope syn elimination to give e trans alkene because in the syn periplanar conformation the groups on the same face give trans geometry. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.

distractors.surface_reading: Cope elimination uses N-O⁻ as a base to abstract β-H, while E2 uses OH⁻ as a base. Both are base-mediated β-elimination reactions. Both break C-H and C-LG bonds in the TS. Therefore, both should be second-order kinetics: Rate = k[substrate][base] for E2, and Rate = k[N-oxide][base] for Cope. Similarly, Chugaev uses the S-sulfur as a base — but it's still a base-mediated elimination → second order.
distractors.correct_answer: Cope and Chugaev are FIRST ORDER, NOT second order. Teacher (page 1, starred): '★ Both are First order kinetics 8xn.' Rate = k[substrate]¹. The key difference: in Cope and Chugaev, the BASE IS PART OF THE SUBSTRATE (intramolecular = internal base). The N-O⁻ oxygen and the C=S sulfur are WITHIN THE SAME MOLECULE as the β-H they abstract. → No external base is needed in the TS → the rate depends only on [substrate]. → First order. In E2: the base (OH⁻, t-BuO⁻) is EXTERNAL (intermolecular) → rate depends on both [substrate] AND [base] → second order. The distinction: INTRAMOLECULAR base = first order; INTERMOLECULAR base = second order. Cope/Chugaev: intramolecular → 1st order. E2: intermolecular → 2nd order. E1CB: 2nd order (base deprotonates β-H in Step 1: Rate = K'[substrate][base]).
distractors.example: Rate experiment: double [Cope substrate] → rate doubles (1st order in substrate). Double [base] → rate unchanged (no base added in Cope elimination step). Contrast E2: double [KOH] → rate doubles (1st order in [base] too). Rate law test distinguishes Cope (1st order) from E2 (2nd order). Teacher's star (★) on page 1 marks this as an exam fact.
distractors.description: Distractor example: Cope and chugaev are second order reactions like e2 because both involve a base abstracting a beta h and a leaving group departing simultaneously. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.

distractors.correct_resolution: Check: (1) if strong, bulky base → E2 preferred over SN2; (2) if high temperature → elimination favoured over substitution; (3) if 3° substrate → E1/E2 or SN1 (not SN2). Anti-periplanar requirement for E2: check geometry before predicting product.

distractors.surface_reading: Zn/Δ dehalogenation removes vicinal dihalides to give alkenes via an anti-periplanar mechanism (similar to E2). Since E2 requires anti-periplanar geometry, Zn should also require anti geometry. Therefore, cis-1,2-dibromocyclohexane (where both Br's are equatorial = anti to each other? No — both equatorial = gauche not anti) should NOT react with Zn/Δ.
distractors.correct_answer: Zn/Δ dehalogenation works for BOTH cis and trans 1,2-dihalides. Teacher Q① and Q③ (page 1): both trans- AND cis-1,2-dibromocyclohexane give cyclohexene when treated with Zn/Δ. Zn mechanism = ELECTRON TRANSFER (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻) that simultaneously reduces both C-Br bonds. There is NO requirement for anti-periplanar geometry (unlike E2 which requires H and LG at 180°). For acyclic substrates (Q03 Newman, page 2), the anti-periplanar Br/Br conformer REACTS PREFERENTIALLY (it's more stable and accessible), but this is a PREFERENCE not a strict requirement. The key difference: E2 = base removes H (needs anti geometry); Zn = removes BOTH Br's via electron transfer (no geometry constraint for the Br/Br pair).
distractors.example: cis-1,2-Dibromocyclohexane + Zn/Δ → cyclohexene (teacher Q③, works). Same compound + KOH/EtOH (E2): E2 would need anti-diaxial H/Br arrangement — for cis Br's in cyclohexane, the geometry depends on conformation, but E2 removes H-Br not Br-Br. These are completely different reactions. Zn removes both Br's; KOH removes H+Br.
distractors.description: Distractor example: Zn dehalogenation requires anti periplanar br br arrangement like e2 anti elimination so cis dihalides do not react with zn. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.

distractors.surface_reading: Ring strain decreases with increasing ring size (3 > 4 > 5 ≈ 6 > 7 in ring strain). Therefore, cyclization rate follows ring stability: 6 > 5 > 7 > 4 > 3 (most strained = slowest to form). The 3-membered aziridine forms SLOWEST because it has maximum ring strain.
distractors.correct_answer: The 4-membered ring (azetidine) is the SLOWEST, NOT the 3-membered ring (aziridine). Teacher's Fun Fact data (page 3, yellow): 3-membered ring rate = 7; 4-membered ring rate = 1 (MINIMUM). Aziridine (3-membered) forms FASTER than azetidine (4-membered) despite having more ring strain. The rate order is: 6(100) > 5 > 3(7) > 7(2) > 4(1). The reason: the TS geometry for 3-exo-tet cyclization is actually favorable (N can approach C-Br from a near-ideal backside angle even in a 3-membered ring), while 4-exo-tet is geometrically and energetically very disfavorable (extreme Baeyer strain at ~90° angles in the TS). Ring strain of the PRODUCT ≠ activation energy of the TS. 4-membered ring formation has maximum TS strain, not 3-membered.
distractors.example: H₂N-CH₂-CH₂-Br (n=1) → aziridine: rate = 7 (faster). H₂N-CH₂-CH₂-CH₂-Br (n=2) → azetidine: rate = 1 (slowest). H₂N-(CH₂)₄-CH₂-Br (n=4) → piperidine (6-membered): rate = 100 (fastest). The 4-membered ring is uniquely slow due to the special geometry problem in the TS.
distractors.description: Distractor example: The fastest intramolecular cyclization to form a 3 membered ring aziridine is slower than forming a 6 membered ring only because of ring strain and 3 membered rings form slower than 4 membered rings. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.

distractors.surface_reading: Zn removes C-X bonds to give alkenes. Whether the halides are at 1,2 positions or 1,3 positions, Zn eliminates them to give the most stable alkene. So Ph-CH(Br)-CH₂-CH₂-Br (1,3-dibromide) + Zn → Ph-CH=CH-CH₃ (the most stable Saytzeff alkene).
distractors.correct_answer: 1,3-Dihalide + Zn-Cu → CYCLOPROPANE, NOT alkene. Teacher Q04 (page 2): Ph-CH(Br)-CH₂-CH₂-Br + Zn(cu)/Δ → phenylcyclopropane (triangle symbol = cyclopropane). This is γ-ELIMINATION (1,3-elimination): C1 and C3 both lose their Br's, and C2 bridges them to close a 3-membered ring. The product is CYCLOPROPANE, not an alkene. The reagent is ZN-CU COUPLE (more reactive than plain Zn). Plain Zn + 1,2-dihalide → alkene (1,2-elimination). Zn-Cu + 1,3-dihalide → cyclopropane (1,3-elimination). These are fundamentally different products from different starting materials.
distractors.example: 1,2-Dibromopropane + Zn → prop-1-ene (alkene, 1,2-elimination). 1,3-Dibromopropane + Zn-Cu → cyclopropane (3-membered ring, 1,3-elimination). Same elements added/removed, completely different product! The key is the RELATIVE POSITIONS of the two halogens (adjacent = 1,2 → alkene; with one C spacer = 1,3 → cyclopropane).

distractors.surface_reading: Copper (Cu) in the Zn-Cu couple simply makes Zn more reactive by creating a galvanic cell (Cu/Zn bimetallic). Since the reactivity increase is only kinetic (makes it faster), the PRODUCTS should be the same regardless of whether plain Zn or Zn-Cu is used. Zn and Zn-Cu both give alkenes from dihalides — they just differ in rate.
distractors.correct_answer: Zn-Cu can give DIFFERENT PRODUCTS from plain Zn for certain substrates. Specifically: 1,3-dihalides + Zn-Cu → cyclopropane (γ-elimination); 1,3-dihalides + plain Zn → may not react efficiently or gives a different product. Teacher Q04 uses ZN-CU specifically for the cyclopropane product from Ph-CH(Br)-CH₂-CH₂-Br. The Zn-Cu couple is more reactive and specifically enables the INTRAMOLECULAR RING-CLOSING STEP (the organo-zinc attacks C3-Br intramolecularly = SN2 ring closure). Plain Zn may not generate the organo-zinc intermediate effectively enough for this intramolecular step. So: for 1,2-dihalide: Zn alone → alkene; for 1,3-dihalide: Zn-Cu needed → cyclopropane. The choice of Zn vs Zn-Cu CHANGES THE PRODUCT in certain substrate classes.
distractors.example: Ph-CH(Br)-CH₂-CH₂-Br + Zn alone: may give incomplete reaction or mixture. Ph-CH(Br)-CH₂-CH₂-Br + Zn-Cu/Δ: clean cyclopropane formation. Teacher specifically labels 'Zn(cu)' (zinc-copper) for Q04, emphasizing it's NOT plain Zn for this substrate. The copper activation is necessary for the reactive organo-zinc intermediate needed for cyclopropane ring closure.

distractors.description: Students predict beta (C-2) is preferred for EAS on naphthalene because C-1 is at the ring junction (sterically hindered); actually alpha (C-1) is kinetically preferred because its Wheland intermediate has RS=7 vs RS=5 for beta
distractors.why_plausible: Steric hindrance logic: C-1 is flanked by two ring carbons, C-2 is only flanked by one; students apply steric argument (which works for many reactions) incorrectly here
distractors.correct_reasoning: Electronic stability of Wheland intermediate determines regioselectivity; alpha attack (RS=7) > beta attack (RS=5); steric argument is secondary to electronic stabilization of intermediate

distractors.correct_reasoning: Sulfonation is reversible; <=110°C → alpha (KCP); >110°C → beta (TCP); temperature switches the product; not memorizing this leads to wrong answers on JEE

distractors.correct_reasoning: In naphthalene, EWG deactivates its ring so completely that EAS occurs on the other ring; no EAS at 'meta' on the EWG-bearing ring; cross-ring effect is unique to polycyclic aromatics

distractors.description: Students think CHCl3 itself directly attacks phenol as electrophile in Reimer-Tiemann; actually CHCl3+NaOH first generates :CCl2 (dichlorocarbene) which is the real electrophile
distractors.why_plausible: CHCl3 is the named reagent; students assume it reacts directly like CH3I does in alkylation; the intermediate carbene is not obvious from the reagent names
distractors.correct_reasoning: CHCl3 + NaOH → CCl3⁻ → :CCl2 (dichlorocarbene); :CCl2 is electrophilic carbene that attacks ortho of phenoxide; CHCl3 is a carbene precursor, not the electrophile

distractors.description: Students predict naphthalene + V2O5/O2 gives naphthalene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid (C10, adding COOH groups without ring loss); actually gives phthalic anhydride (C8, one ring opens, 2 carbons lost)
distractors.why_plausible: Methylbenzene → benzoic acid shows oxidation of methyl without ring loss; students apply this analogy incorrectly to naphthalene ring oxidation
distractors.correct_reasoning: V2O5/O2/500°C is aggressive; completely oxidizes one ring of naphthalene; 2 terminal carbons lost as CO2; phthalic acid cyclizes to phthalic anhydride (C8 product total)
distractors.why_attractive: Oxidising and reducing agents have different selectivities that are easily confused. Students apply a uniform 'strong oxidant → complete oxidation' rule.
distractors.correct_resolution: Selectivity determines product: PCC → aldehyde from 1° alcohol (no over-oxidation); KMnO₄ cold → syn diol; KMnO₄ hot → C-C cleavage; LiAlH₄ → complete reduction; NaBH₄ → aldehyde/ketone only; DIBALH at −78°C → aldehyde from ester. Always specify conditions.

distractors.description: Students predict phenol + RCOCl/AlCl3 gives O-acylation (phenyl ester) because AlCl3 'just activates' the acyl chloride for esterification; actually gives C-acylation (hydroxyaryl ketone, para major) via Fries mechanism
distractors.why_plausible: O-acylation of phenols is the expected reaction; AlCl3 is seen as a catalyst for esterification, not something that changes the reaction site from O to C
distractors.correct_reasoning: Without AlCl3 → O-acylation (ester); with AlCl3 → Fries/C-acylation (ketone, para major); AlCl3 generates acylium species → intramolecular EAS gives ring C-acylation at para
distractors.why_attractive: Carbonyl reactions (addition, condensation, reduction) are among the most tested in JEE. The many named reactions and their conditions create confusion between similar-looking transformations.
distractors.correct_resolution: Key decision tree: identify the carbonyl type (aldehyde/ketone/ester/acid/amide/acyl halide) → identify the reagent class → determine mechanism → predict product, stereochemistry, and any competing pathways.

distractors.description: Students predict anthracene EAS at alpha (C-1) by analogy with naphthalene (where C-1 is preferred); actually anthracene EAS occurs at meso C-9 because both outer rings preserve aromaticity in the intermediate
distractors.why_plausible: Naphthalene alpha preference is well-known; students extrapolate it to anthracene without considering the meso position's unique stabilization from two preserved aromatic rings
distractors.correct_reasoning: Anthracene meso (C-9) attack → Wheland with both outer rings aromatic; alpha attack → only one ring aromatic; two rings preserved >> one ring preserved in stabilization
distractors.why_attractive: Aromaticity criteria must all be satisfied simultaneously (cyclic, planar, conjugated, 4n+2 π electrons). Students apply Hückel count without checking planarity or conjugation.
distractors.correct_resolution: All four Hückel criteria required: (1) cyclic; (2) planar; (3) every ring atom has a p-orbital (fully conjugated); (4) 4n+2 π electrons. If any criterion fails → not aromatic. Check each criterion explicitly before assigning aromaticity.

distractors.description: Students predict all amines (primary, secondary, tertiary) give carbylamine test (foul isocyanide smell) with NaOH/CHCl3; actually only PRIMARY amines give positive carbylamine test
distractors.why_plausible: All amines have nitrogen and can react with electrophiles; students don't know that the N-H proton is essential for the mechanism of isocyanide formation
distractors.correct_reasoning: Carbylamine requires R-NH2 (N-H available for deprotonation after :CCl2 attack); secondary amines have only one N-H so cannot complete deprotonation to give N=CCl; only primary amines give isocyanide
distractors.why_attractive: Amine reactions are diverse and condition-dependent. The same amine class (1°, 2°, 3°) gives different products with different reagents. Students apply a single rule to all amines.
distractors.correct_resolution: Classify amine (1°/2°/3°, aliphatic/aromatic) first. Then apply reagent-specific rules. Key distinctions: carbylamine test (+ve only for 1°); Hinsberg test (sulfonyl chloride + base); Nitrous acid (1° aromatic → diazonium; 2° → nitrosamine; 3° aliphatic → no reaction; 3° aromatic → ring nitroso).

distractors.description: Students predict bulky alkyl groups go to alpha (C-1) in naphthalene FC alkylation because RS=7 argument always favors alpha over beta; actually bulky groups (iPr, tBu) give beta (C-2) as major due to peri-H steric clash at C-1
distractors.why_plausible: The RS=7 vs RS=5 argument correctly predicts alpha for small groups; students apply it universally without considering steric override for large substituents
distractors.correct_reasoning: Small R (Me, Et): electronic wins (RS=7 at alpha) → alpha; Bulky R (iPr, tBu): steric wins (peri-H at C-8 clashes with large group at C-1) → beta; the RS argument assumes negligible steric difference, invalid for large groups

distractors.description: Students predict TNT has NO2 groups at 2,3,4 positions (ortho to each other) or 2,4,5 or other arrangements; actually TNT = 1-methyl-2,4,6-trinitrobenzene with NO2 at 2,4,6 (all ortho/para to CH3)
