distractors.description: Students predict RTR always gives ortho product even when one ortho is blocked (e.g., 2-methoxyphenol → 2-OH-6-CHO product); actually blocked ortho → para major (vanillin at C-4 for guaiacol)
distractors.why_plausible: Ortho is the standard RTR product (for unsubstituted phenol); students apply this rule universally without the 'blocked ortho → para' modification
distractors.correct_reasoning: RTR: normally ortho (both available); one ortho blocked → para major; both ortho blocked → 100% para; this rule is essential for predicting RTR products of substituted phenols
distractors.why_attractive: SN2 is the first-taught substitution mechanism. Students default to it for all C-X situations without checking substrate class, nucleophile, or solvent constraints.
distractors.correct_resolution: SN2 requires: (1) primary or methyl substrate (3° essentially impossible); (2) strong nucleophile; (3) polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMSO, DMF). For secondary: check whether SN1 or E2 might compete. For vinyl/aryl: SN2 is impossible (use SNAr or benzyne).

distractors.description: Students confuse salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid) with aspirin (2-acetoxybenzoic acid); these are different compounds; salicylic acid is the precursor to aspirin (via acetylation of phenol OH)
distractors.why_plausible: Both have similar names and both are pain-related compounds; students may remember 'salicylate = aspirin' without knowing the structural difference
distractors.correct_reasoning: Salicylic acid = 2-hydroxybenzoic acid (free phenol-OH and free COOH); aspirin = 2-(acetyloxy)benzoic acid (phenol-OH esterified as acetate, COOH free); aspirin is made FROM salicylic acid by acetylation

distractors.description: Students think oil of wintergreen is salicylic acid or phenol, not an ester; actually oil of wintergreen = methyl 2-hydroxybenzoate (methyl salicylate, ester of salicylic acid with methanol) = main component of IODEX

distractors.description: Students use ZnCl2 as an effective Friedel-Crafts catalyst (like AlCl3); actually ZnCl2 is the WEAKEST Lewis acid for FC (order: AlCl3 > BF3 > SbCl5 > FeCl3 > SnCl4 > ZnCl2); ZnCl2 is used for Clemmensen reduction, not FC EAS
distractors.why_plausible: ZnCl2 is a Lewis acid (zinc is electron-deficient); students know it catalyzes some reactions (Lucas test, Blanc reaction) and overgeneralize to FC
distractors.correct_reasoning: AlCl3 is the strongest and most effective FC Lewis acid; ZnCl2 is too weak to effectively ionize alkyl halides or activate acyl compounds for FC EAS; use AlCl3 (or BF3/FeCl3 for milder) for FC reactions

distractors.description: Students predict Fries rearrangement at high temperature (160°C) still gives para as major (less sterically hindered); actually high T Fries → ortho is MAJOR (thermodynamic product, stabilized by intramolecular H-bonding)
distractors.why_plausible: Para is generally the major EAS product for steric reasons; students apply this logic to Fries without knowing the thermodynamic inversion at high T
distractors.correct_reasoning: Fries: 60°C → para major (kinetic); 160°C → ortho major (thermodynamic); intramolecular H-bond stabilizes the ortho product, making it thermodynamically more stable despite steric disadvantage
distractors.why_attractive: Rearrangements are unexpected: the product has a different carbon skeleton than the starting material. Students predict the unrearranged product by default.
distractors.correct_resolution: Check for rearrangement at every carbocation intermediate: (1) Is a 1,2-shift possible? (2) Does it give a more stable cation? (3) Can a ring expand? Always evaluate stability of rearranged vs unrearranged cation before predicting product.

distractors.description: Students predict Claisen rearrangement gives para product (less hindered than ortho) or arbitrary position; actually Claisen gives ORTHO product as major via [3,3] sigmatropic (only if ortho blocked does it go to para)
distractors.why_plausible: Para is less hindered; students don't know the [3,3] TS geometry requires ortho attack; the pericyclic nature of the reaction is not obvious
distractors.correct_reasoning: Claisen [3,3] sigmatropic: 6-membered TS has C-1 of allyl bonded to C-ortho of ring; geometry requires ortho attack → 2-allylphenol is the normal product; para only when BOTH ortho positions are blocked (double [3,3] mechanism)
distractors.why_attractive: Rearrangements are unexpected: the product has a different carbon skeleton than the starting material. Students predict the unrearranged product by default.
distractors.correct_resolution: Check for rearrangement at every carbocation intermediate: (1) Is a 1,2-shift possible? (2) Does it give a more stable cation? (3) Can a ring expand? Always evaluate stability of rearranged vs unrearranged cation before predicting product.

distractors.description: Students think phenol + excess HNO3/H2SO4 gives picric acid in good yield because NH2 (or OH) strongly activates ring for multiple nitrations; actually gives LOW yield due to HNO3 oxidizing the phenol ring
distractors.why_plausible: OH is a very strong activating group; students expect trinitration to work well since each step should be faster; they don't account for HNO3 oxidizing the phenol
distractors.correct_reasoning: HNO3 is an oxidant, not just a nitrating agent; activated phenol ring is oxidized (not selectively nitrated 3 times); sulfonation blocking strategy protects from oxidation and gives picric acid in good yield

distractors.description: Students predict secondary and tertiary aromatic amines also give positive azo dye test (foul-smelling or colored product) since they also have nitrogen; actually ONLY primary aromatic amines give positive azo dye test
distractors.why_plausible: All aromatic amines have N; students don't know that diazonium formation requires R-NH2 (primary N-H2); secondary and tertiary have no free N-H2 for diazotization
distractors.correct_reasoning: Azo dye test = diazotization (needs ArNH2, primary amine) + azo coupling; secondary amines (ArNHR) give N-nitroso compounds, not diazonium; tertiary amines (ArNR2) give N-nitroso salts; neither gives the colored azo dye

distractors.description: Students predict ArI Sandmeyer needs Cu2I2 catalyst by analogy with ArCl (Cu2Cl2) and ArBr (Cu2Br2); actually ArI uses KI/Δ directly — NO Cu catalyst; Cu2I2 is thermodynamically unstable
distractors.why_plausible: The Sandmeyer pattern for Cl and Br uses Cu(I) halide; students systematically apply this to iodine without knowing the cuprous iodide stability exception
distractors.correct_reasoning: ArCl and ArBr Sandmeyer: need Cu2Cl2 and Cu2Br2 respectively; ArI Sandmeyer: KI + Δ (no Cu); Cu2I2 is unstable (disproportionates); the iodide exception must be memorized explicitly

distractors.description: Students predict meta-directing EWG group always gives monosubstitution at C-3 only, even with excess electrophile; actually both meta positions (C-3 and C-5) can be brominated with 2 equiv Br2/Fe
distractors.why_plausible: Most benzene EAS problems involve monosubstitution; students don't think about the symmetry that makes C-3 and C-5 equivalent and both available for EWG meta-direction with excess reagent
distractors.correct_reasoning: Nitrobenzene + 1 Br2/Fe → 3-bromonitrobenzene (mono); + 2 Br2/Fe → 1,3-dibromo-5-nitrobenzene (di, both meta); excess electrophile fills both equivalent meta positions

distractors.description: Students predict ArCN + H2/Ni → ArCHO (benzaldehyde, thinking N is lost and C becomes CHO); actually H2/Ni fully reduces CN to CH2NH2 (benzylamine); benzaldehyde from benzonitrile needs DIBAL-H at -78°C
distractors.why_plausible: Students think of CN as a C with N attached; they expect reduction to remove N and give CHO; they don't know that H2/Ni is too strong and adds all 4H to give amine
distractors.correct_reasoning: H2/Ni is a non-selective heterogeneous catalyst that fully reduces CN → CH2NH2; for selective reduction to aldehyde: use DIBAL-H at -78°C → imine intermediate → hydrolysis → ArCHO

distractors.description: Students confuse soda lime (NaOH+CaO, solid, high T) with NaOH/H2O (aqueous) reactions; soda lime causes decarboxylation (ArCOOH → ArH); NaOH/H2O causes saponification or hydrolysis but NOT decarboxylation
distractors.why_plausible: Both involve NaOH; students don't know that CaO and high temperature are essential for decarboxylation; they apply NaOH/H2O hydrolysis rules to soda lime conditions
distractors.correct_reasoning: NaOH/H2O (aqueous, low T): ester saponification, salt formation; NaOH/CaO (soda lime, fused, high T): decarboxylation of sodium carboxylates → ArH + Na2CO3; different conditions = fundamentally different reaction

distractors.description: Students predict nitrile + excess RMgX → tertiary alcohol (two additions, by analogy with ketone → tertiary alcohol); actually nitrile + RMgX → ketone (only ONE addition; imine blocks second Grignard)

distractors.correct_reasoning: Nitrile + 1 RMgX → ketimine (blocked for second addition) → H3O+ → ketone (not alcohol); only alcohol-forming pathway is: nitrile → ketone → then SEPARATE Grignard addition to that ketone

distractors.description: Students predict HCN + RMgX → aldehyde (RCHO) after H3O+ workup, thinking Grignard adds to C of HCN like with other nitriles/carbonyls; actually HCN protonates the Grignard → R-H (no carbonyl product)

distractors.description: Students predict cyanogen (NC-CN) + 2 RMgX → diketone (OC-CO type, alpha-diketone) since each CN reacts with one Grignard; actually CN- leaves as LG after first Grignard attack → only one ketone formed

distractors.correct_reasoning: First Grignard attacks one C of NC-CN → CN- leaves as LG → R-CN (mononitile) formed; second Grignard adds to R-CN → ketimine → H3O+ → one ketone; only ONE ketone from (CN)2 + 2 RMgX

distractors.description: Students predict Lindlar's catalyst gives TRANS (E)-alkene from alkyne (thinking 'hindered catalyst = bulky groups go anti = trans'); actually Lindlar's gives CIS (Z)-alkene via syn addition
distractors.why_plausible: Anti-Markovnikov and anti-addition are known; students may expect bulky Pd/BaSO4 to give anti/trans addition; they don't know that the poisoned catalyst gives syn (same-face) addition
distractors.correct_reasoning: Lindlar's: syn addition (both H from same metal surface face) → CIS (Z) alkene; for TRANS alkene from alkyne: use Na/NH3 (dissolving metal reduction, anti addition = trans product)

distractors.description: Students predict acid chloride + H2/Pd-BaSO4 (Rosenmund) → primary alcohol (R-CH2OH), thinking H2 is a 'strong reductant' that fully reduces acyl chloride to alcohol; actually Rosenmund STOPS at aldehyde (RCHO)
distractors.why_plausible: LiAlH4 reduces acid chloride to alcohol (R-CH2OH); students apply this expectation to H2/Pd-BaSO4; they don't know the poisoned Pd is selective for C-Cl reduction over C=O reduction
distractors.correct_reasoning: Rosenmund: R-COCl + H2/Pd-BaSO4 → R-CHO (aldehyde, stops here); for alcohol from acid chloride: use LiAlH4 (reduces C=O completely); LiAlH4 and Rosenmund give OPPOSITE levels of reduction

distractors.description: Students predict trans (E) alkene + syn addition → RACEMIC MIXTURE (just like cis + syn); actually trans + syn → MESO compound (optically inactive for a different reason)

distractors.description: Students predict H2/Pt reduces ketone C=O as easily as alkene C=C (both are reducible by H2); actually H2/metal selectively reduces C=C; 'ketones are difficult to reduce' by catalytic hydrogenation

distractors.description: Students predict sodium propanoate Kolbe → butane (CH3CH2-CH2CH3) as major product (two ethyl radicals couple like methyl radicals give ethane); actually major is ethyl propanoate (ESTER) not butane
distractors.why_plausible: CH3COONa → ethane (CH3•+CH3• coupling); students extrapolate to CH3CH2COONa → butane (CH3CH2•+CH3CH2• coupling); they don't know ≥2C radicals preferentially disproportionate/form ester

distractors.why_attractive: Radical reactions are less intuitive than ionic. Students forget chain propagation steps and apply Markovnikov's rule (ionic) to radical conditions.
distractors.correct_resolution: Radical mechanism: identify the initiator (hν, ROOR, heat). Write initiation (radical generation), propagation (two steps: H-abstraction then halogen abstraction), termination (combination of any two radicals). Anti-Markovnikov product from radical HBr. Selectivity: Br > Cl; 3° > 2° > 1° C-H.

distractors.description: Students predict alkane nitration at 400°C gives only C-H substitution products (same carbon count as starting alkane); actually C-C bond also cleaves at 400°C giving shorter-chain nitroalkanes as additional products
distractors.why_plausible: Nitration conceptually = replace H with NO2; students count distinct H environments and predict that many products; they don't know 400°C causes C-C homolysis too, adding more products than C-H substitution alone
distractors.correct_reasoning: Propane + conc HNO3/400°C → 1-nitropropane + 2-nitropropane (C-H) + nitroethane + nitromethane (C-C cleavage at 400°C); actual product count > expected from C-H substitution alone
distractors.why_attractive: SN2 is the first-taught substitution mechanism. Students default to it for all C-X situations without checking substrate class, nucleophile, or solvent constraints.
distractors.correct_resolution: SN2 requires: (1) primary or methyl substrate (3° essentially impossible); (2) strong nucleophile; (3) polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMSO, DMF). For secondary: check whether SN1 or E2 might compete. For vinyl/aryl: SN2 is impossible (use SNAr or benzyne).

distractors.description: Students predict methylene insertion (CH2N2/UV) only inserts :CH2: into C-H bonds (more common bond for substitution); actually :CH2: also inserts into C-C bonds → ring expansion of cycloalkanes
distractors.why_plausible: C-H insertion = common for carbenes; students don't know C-C insertion is also possible; they would predict only methylcyclopentane from cyclopentane + CH2N2 (C-H insertion only)
distractors.correct_reasoning: Cyclopentane + CH2N2/UV → cyclohexane (C-C insertion, ring expansion) + methylcyclopentane (C-H insertion); both pathways occur; :CH2: is non-selective and inserts into whatever bond it encounters

distractors.description: Students predict Wittig reaction gives a mixture of alkene isomers (like E2 elimination) or that the double bond can form at multiple positions; actually Wittig forms double bond at EXACTLY the C=O position, no regioisomers, 95% yield
distractors.why_plausible: E2 elimination gives Zaitsev product and often multiple alkene isomers; students generalize all alkene-forming reactions as giving mixtures
distractors.correct_reasoning: Wittig: C=O + ylide → replaces C=O with C=C at EXACT same position; no migration of double bond possible; trick: just replace O with =CR2 (ylide carbon substituents); gives single regioisomeric alkene in 95% yield
distractors.why_attractive: Elimination reactions are often forgotten as a competing pathway. Students predict substitution products even when bulky base and high temperature should favour elimination.
distractors.correct_resolution: Check: (1) if strong, bulky base → E2 preferred over SN2; (2) if high temperature → elimination favoured over substitution; (3) if 3° substrate → E1/E2 or SN1 (not SN2). Anti-periplanar requirement for E2: check geometry before predicting product.

distractors.description: Students predict tertiary alkyl halide + PPh3 → phosphonium salt → ylide (reasoning: PPh3 is a good nucleophile so it can attack even 3° C-X); actually 3° R-X gives NO reaction with PPh3 (SN2 impossible at tertiary carbon)
distractors.why_plausible: PPh3 is an excellent nucleophile (phosphorus donor, much better than water or alcohols); students assume a good nucleophile can overcome steric hindrance of 3° carbon
distractors.correct_reasoning: SN2 mechanism requires backside attack; 3° carbon is too hindered → no SN2 → no phosphonium salt → no ylide; Wittig only works with ylides derived from 1° or 2° alkyl halides; for ketone Wittig (disubstituted ylide), use 2° R-X

distractors.description: Students predict 1,4-addition (to 1,3-diene + HBr) is the kinetic product; actually 1,2-addition is kinetic (at -40°C) and 1,4-addition is thermodynamic (at 25°C)
distractors.why_plausible: 1,4-addition = the 'extended' or 'conjugated' addition = sounds more 'complex' = students assume complex = slower = kinetic product; or they think longer-range Nu attack = slower = not kinetic; intuition is wrong
distractors.correct_reasoning: 1,2-addition = KCR at -40°C (lower TS barrier, shorter-range Nu attack); 1,4-addition = TCR at 25°C (more stable product, but higher TS barrier); temperature is the key diagnostic: -40°C → 1,2; 25°C → 1,4

distractors.description: Students predict isoprene + HBr: H+ adds to C4 (by Markovnikov, more substituted carbon gets H from the isolated C3=C4 alkene) giving 2°+allylic cation; actually H+ to C1 gives 3°+allylic (more stable, preferred)

distractors.description: Students predict 1,4-addition as major for 1,3,5-hexatriene (by analogy with 1,3-diene where 1,4 is thermodynamic); actually 1,6-addition is major for trienes under thermodynamic control

distractors.description: Students predict DMS in O3/DMS workup is an oxidant (since DMSO is a common oxidant in Swern oxidation); actually DMS is the REDUCTANT in ozonolysis (gets oxidized to DMSO; reduces the ozonide peroxide)
distractors.why_plausible: In Swern oxidation: DMSO IS the oxidant; students reverse the role, thinking DMS (reduced form of DMSO) would act as an oxidant in ozonolysis too
distractors.correct_reasoning: In ozonolysis: O3/DMS = REDUCTIVE ozonolysis; DMS (S in reduced state) gets oxidized to DMSO; the ozonide's peroxide oxygen is transferred to DMS → reductive workup; same product as O3/Zn/H2O; contrast Swern: DMSO is activated to be the oxidant of alcohols
distractors.why_attractive: Oxidising and reducing agents have different selectivities that are easily confused. Students apply a uniform 'strong oxidant → complete oxidation' rule.
distractors.correct_resolution: Selectivity determines product: PCC → aldehyde from 1° alcohol (no over-oxidation); KMnO₄ cold → syn diol; KMnO₄ hot → C-C cleavage; LiAlH₄ → complete reduction; NaBH₄ → aldehyde/ketone only; DIBALH at −78°C → aldehyde from ester. Always specify conditions.

distractors.description: Students predict cyclopentene ozonolysis gives two separate aldehyde molecules (pentanal split into 2 pieces); actually gives ONE bifunctional molecule: pentane-1,5-dial
distractors.why_plausible: Acyclic alkene ozonolysis gives 2 pieces; students apply the same logic to cyclic alkenes without recognizing the ring carbons stay connected
distractors.correct_reasoning: Cyclic alkene: ring C=C bond breaks, ring opens, but the two carbons remain connected through the rest of the ring → ONE linear dialdehyde; cyclopentene (5C ring) → pentane-1,5-dial (OHC-(CH2)3-CHO, 5C chain); never two separate molecules from monocyclic alkene

distractors.description: Students predict Fries rearrangement at high temperature gives para product (generalizing that para is preferred for activated aromatic rings); actually high temp gives ORTHO, low temp gives PARA
distractors.why_plausible: In standard EAS, para is often the major product (less steric strain than ortho); students apply the same rule to Fries rearrangement; they don't know the thermodynamic product (high temp) is the chelation-stabilized ortho isomer
distractors.correct_reasoning: Fries rearrangement: HIGH TEMP → ORTHO (thermodynamic; ortho hydroxy aryl ketone forms intramolecular H-bond between OH and C=O → stabilized chelate ring → thermodynamically favorable); LOW TEMP → PARA (kinetic; less steric, faster formation); summary: high = ortho; low = para; this is opposite to what students expect from normal EAS temperature effects
distractors.why_attractive: Aromaticity criteria must all be satisfied simultaneously (cyclic, planar, conjugated, 4n+2 π electrons). Students apply Hückel count without checking planarity or conjugation.

distractors.description: Students predict Stephens reduction (R-CN + SnCl2/HCl) gives amine (R-CH2NH2) since SnCl2 is a reductant and full reduction of nitrile would give amine; actually gives ALDEHYDE (R-CHO)

distractors.description: Students predict aldol condensation dehydration is E2 (concerted base-removes-H and OH leaves simultaneously); actually E1CB (base removes α-H first to give stabilized carbanion, then β-OH leaves)
distractors.why_plausible: Most dehydrations in organic chemistry are E2 or E1; students apply the default E2 mechanism; they don't know E1CB is special here because the α-H is much more acidic (α to C=O) and gives a stabilized carbanion
distractors.correct_reasoning: E1CB: (1) OH- removes α-H → stabilized carbanion (enolate); (2) β-OH leaves; base removes α-H (NOT β-H) because α-H is more acidic (adjacent to C=O, pKa~20); the carbanion intermediate is real (not transition state); contrast E2: base removes H while X/OH leaves simultaneously; contrast E1: ionization first then base removes H
distractors.why_attractive: Elimination reactions are often forgotten as a competing pathway. Students predict substitution products even when bulky base and high temperature should favour elimination.
distractors.correct_resolution: Check: (1) if strong, bulky base → E2 preferred over SN2; (2) if high temperature → elimination favoured over substitution; (3) if 3° substrate → E1/E2 or SN1 (not SN2). Anti-periplanar requirement for E2: check geometry before predicting product.

distractors.description: Students predict formaldehyde (HCHO) can form an enolate and self-condense like acetaldehyde (since it has H atoms); actually HCHO has NO α-H (no carbon adjacent to C=O) and CANNOT self-condense

distractors.description: Students predict cross-aldol of two different enolizable carbonyl compounds (A and B) gives only 2 products (cross A+B and cross B+A); actually gives 4 products (A+A, B+B self-condensations + two cross-condensations)

distractors.description: Students predict Cannizzaro is always second order (rate ∝ [RCHO][OH-]) regardless of base concentration; actually under highly basic conditions (conc. NaOH), order becomes 4 (rate ∝ [HCHO]²[OH-]²)

distractors.description: Students predict reactions of C=O with NH2OH or N2H4 are fastest in strongly acidic conditions (pH<3) since acid protonates C=O making it more electrophilic; actually optimal pH = 5-7 (strongly acidic conditions give no reaction because amine gets protonated)
distractors.why_plausible: Students know Lewis/Brønsted acids activate C=O toward nucleophilic attack; they extrapolate: 'more acidic = more activated C=O = faster'; they don't know the amine nucleophile is also deactivated by the same acid (protonated to ammonium)
distractors.correct_reasoning: pH 5-7 is optimal: acid moderately activates C=O while keeping amine unprotonated (nucleophilic); at pH<3: amine is fully protonated (NH3+, no lone pair) → no nucleophile → no reaction; at pH>9: C=O activation lost → slow; the pH-rate profile shows a bell-shaped curve with maximum at pH 5-7; this is why NH2OH, N2H4, semicarbazide reactions are done in acetate buffer (pH 4-5) or dilute HCl (pH 5-6)
distractors.why_attractive: Amine reactions are diverse and condition-dependent. The same amine class (1°, 2°, 3°) gives different products with different reagents. Students apply a single rule to all amines.
distractors.correct_resolution: Classify amine (1°/2°/3°, aliphatic/aromatic) first. Then apply reagent-specific rules. Key distinctions: carbylamine test (+ve only for 1°); Hinsberg test (sulfonyl chloride + base); Nitrous acid (1° aromatic → diazonium; 2° → nitrosamine; 3° aliphatic → no reaction; 3° aromatic → ring nitroso).

distractors.description: Students predict Wolff-Kishner (N2H4/KOH/Δ) reduces both C=O and C=C (since the conditions are harsh — high temperature, strong base); actually Wolff-Kishner ONLY reduces C=O, not C=C
distractors.why_plausible: KOH at high temperature is a strong base; Δ provides high temperature; students think these harsh conditions would reduce any unsaturation; they don't know hydrazone formation is specific to C=O compounds
distractors.correct_reasoning: Wolff-Kishner mechanism is SPECIFIC to C=O: step 1 requires C=O + N2H4 → hydrazone (N2H4 does NOT react with C=C alkenes); since alkenes don't form hydrazones, they are unaffected by KOH/Δ step 2; selectivity: in a molecule with both C=C and C=O, Wolff-Kishner reduces only C=O → CH2, C=C remains; to also reduce C=C: use H2/Pd (hydrogenation) separately

distractors.description: Students predict benzaldehyde gives positive Fehling test (Cu2O precipitate) since benzaldehyde IS an aldehyde and aldehydes give positive Fehling; actually benzaldehyde gives NEGATIVE Fehling but POSITIVE Tollens
distractors.why_plausible: Students learn 'aldehydes give positive Fehling, ketones do not'; they apply this to benzaldehyde; they don't know the rule is specifically for ALIPHATIC aldehydes and aromatic aldehydes are exceptional
distractors.correct_reasoning: Fehling positive = aliphatic aldehydes ONLY; Tollens positive = ALL aldehydes; PhCHO = Fehling ✗ (negative), Tollens ✓ (positive); the oxidizing power of Fehling Cu2+ is too weak to oxidize aromatic aldehydes (benzene ring resonance stabilizes the ArC=O); to distinguish PhCHO from aliphatic RCHO: run BOTH Fehling and Tollens; if Fehling ✗ and Tollens ✓ → aromatic aldehyde; if both ✓ → aliphatic aldehyde

distractors.description: Students predict ALL ketones give negative Fehling and Tollens; actually α-hydroxy ketones (secondary) give POSITIVE both tests
distractors.why_plausible: Students learn 'Fehling and Tollens distinguish aldehydes from ketones: aldehydes positive, ketones negative'; they apply this universally to all ketones; they don't know α-hydroxy ketones (which have OH adjacent to C=O) are exceptions that can form enediol and reduce Cu2+/Ag+

distractors.description: Students predict hemiacetal and acetal give the same Fehling/Tollens result (both negative, since both have the carbonyl C=O blocked by OR groups); actually hemiacetal gives positive, acetal gives negative

distractors.description: Students predict benzaldehyde gives NEGATIVE Tollens test (similar to Fehling negative) because aromatic C=O is deactivated by the benzene ring; actually Tollens is POSITIVE for ALL aldehydes including benzaldehyde
distractors.why_plausible: If students know Fehling is negative for PhCHO, they might incorrectly apply the same reasoning to Tollens ('aromatic aldehyde C=O is deactivated by resonance → cannot be oxidized'); they don't know Tollens Ag+ is a STRONGER oxidant than Fehling Cu2+
distractors.correct_reasoning: Tollens reagent ([Ag(NH3)2]+) is a stronger oxidant than Fehling Cu2+ (in alkaline tartrate); while Cu2+/Fehling cannot oxidize aromatic aldehyde C=O (too mild), Ag+/Tollens CAN (strong enough); therefore Tollens = ALL aldehydes positive (both aliphatic and aromatic); for JEE: ALWAYS PhCHO → Fehling ✗, Tollens ✓ (this combination of results identifies an aromatic aldehyde)
distractors.why_attractive: Aromaticity criteria must all be satisfied simultaneously (cyclic, planar, conjugated, 4n+2 π electrons). Students apply Hückel count without checking planarity or conjugation.
distractors.correct_resolution: All four Hückel criteria required: (1) cyclic; (2) planar; (3) every ring atom has a p-orbital (fully conjugated); (4) 4n+2 π electrons. If any criterion fails → not aromatic. Check each criterion explicitly before assigning aromaticity.

distractors.description: Students predict glutaric acid (5C) gives cyclopentanone on heating (by analogy with adipic acid = cyclopentanone); actually glutaric acid gives 6-membered anhydride on heating, NOT cyclopentanone (cyclopentanone comes from adipic acid, 6C)

distractors.description: Students predict trans-cyclohexane-1,2-dicarboxylic acid gives NO rxn on heating (because it's a trans diacid and trans means COOH groups apart → no anhydride); actually trans-cyclohexane-1,2-diacid DOES give anhydride (ring flip makes it accessible)

distractors.description: Students predict fumaric acid gives maleic anhydride on ordinary heating (same as maleic acid) because both are butenedioic acids with the same formula; actually fumaric gives NO anhydride at ordinary T and requires 300°C + prior isomerization to maleic

distractors.description: Students predict isophthalic acid (1,3-benzene-dicarboxylic) or terephthalic acid (1,4-benzene-dicarboxylic) give cyclic anhydrides on heating, just like ortho phthalic acid; actually only ORTHO phthalic acid gives phthalic anhydride; meta and para give no anhydride

distractors.description: Students predict 2,4,6-trinitrobenzaldehyde gives Cannizzaro (very fast, since EWG makes C=O very electrophilic); actually gives DEFORMYLATION: 2,4,6-trinitrobenzene + HCOONa

distractors.description: Students predict 2,6-dimethylbenzaldehyde gives Cannizzaro (still an aryl aldehyde without α-H, just has methyl groups); actually gives deformylation due to steric crowding of CHO

distractors.description: Students predict p-aminobenzaldehyde (4-H2N-C6H4-CHO) undergoes Cannizzaro with NaOH: 2 p-NH2-PhCHO → p-NH2-PhCH2OH + p-NH2-PhCOOH; actually forms a zwitterion (no Cannizzaro products)

distractors.description: Students predict amide (RCONH2) hydrolyzes faster than ester (RCOOR') because the N-H bonds in amide are more polar/reactive and NH2 is a better leaving group than OR'; actually ester hydrolyzes MUCH faster than amide
distractors.why_plausible: Students might think NH2 is a better leaving group than OR' (since NH3 is a weaker acid than alcohol → NH2- is a stronger base... wait that would make NH2 a WORSE leaving group); or they think the N-H polarity facilitates hydrolysis; the resonance argument is rarely taught clearly

distractors.description: Students predict that carboxylic acids with longer alkyl chains are stronger acids (more groups = more electron withdrawal = more stabilization of RCOO-); actually longer alkyl chains = WEAKER acids

distractors.description: Students treat Grignard (RMgX) as a fully ionic salt R⁻(MgX)⁺ — a 'naked carbanion' — and predict it will react with ALL electrophiles just like a carbanion would, including with ether solvent or other very weak electrophiles
distractors.why_plausible: RMgX is described as having 'carbanion character' and the R group acts as R⁻ in many reactions; students equate 'carbanion character' with 'fully ionic'; they also expect it to react with the ether solvent
distractors.correct_reasoning: RMgX is 'highly polar covalent' (NOT purely ionic); it has significant carbanion CHARACTER but is not a free carbanion; it requires specific electrophiles (carbonyl C, protic acids, CO₂) to react; it does NOT react with: (1) ether solvent (stable in ether; that's why ether is the solvent); (2) nitrogen gas; (3) alkenes (unless activated); the 'carbanion' approximation is useful for PREDICTING PRODUCTS but overstates the reactivity

distractors.description: Students predict cyclopentadiene C-H (the sp3 CH₂ between two double bonds) is not acidic enough to react with Grignard (RMgX), since sp³ C-H is very weak acid
distractors.why_plausible: sp³ C-H typically has pKa ≈ 45-50; students expect cyclopentadiene to be similar; they don't know about the aromatic stabilization of the cyclopentadienyl anion
distractors.correct_reasoning: Cyclopentadiene (cyclopenta-1,3-diene) C-H at the sp³ carbon (C-5, between the two double bonds) has pKa ≈ 16 — as acidic as water! The reason: deprotonation gives the cyclopentadienyl anion (Cp⁻) which is AROMATIC (6 π-electrons, Hückel: n=1, 4n+2=6); aromatic anion is extremely stable → dramatically lowers pKa; pKa 16 means cyclopentadiene readily reacts with RMgX (pKa of RH ≈ 50 >> 16 → favorable); in counting CH₄ problems, the cyclopentadienyl C-H MUST be counted

distractors.description: Students predict the C-Grignard (C-MgX) survives even when the same molecule also contains an OH or NH group; they expect both functional groups to coexist, or they expect the Grignard to selectively ignore the OH/NH

distractors.description: Students predict RMgX + 3° R'-X → R-R' (C-C bond coupling via SN2); actually 3° alkyl halide + Grignard → E2 elimination (alkene + R-H), NOT coupling
distractors.why_plausible: The general Grignard SN2 rule 'RMgX + R'X → R-R'' seems to apply to all alkyl halides; students may not know the SN2 fails at 3° carbon or that Grignard is basic enough to do E2
distractors.correct_reasoning: 3° R'-X + RMgX → E2 elimination product (alkene from R'-X) + R-H; the carbanion of RMgX acts as BASE (not nucleophile) at 3° C because SN2 is sterically blocked; JEE: if asked what forms from (CH₃)₃CBr + EtMgBr → isobutylene (elimination) + ethane (from E2), NOT 2,2-dimethylbutane (coupling); use only 1° alkyl halides for Grignard SN2 coupling
distractors.why_attractive: SN2 is the first-taught substitution mechanism. Students default to it for all C-X situations without checking substrate class, nucleophile, or solvent constraints.
distractors.correct_resolution: SN2 requires: (1) primary or methyl substrate (3° essentially impossible); (2) strong nucleophile; (3) polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMSO, DMF). For secondary: check whether SN1 or E2 might compete. For vinyl/aryl: SN2 is impossible (use SNAr or benzyne).

distractors.description: Students predict Gilman reagent (R₂CuLi) adds to ketones to give tertiary alcohols, since Grignard does this and Gilman is 'similar'
distractors.why_plausible: Both Grignard and Gilman are organometallic nucleophiles that transfer R⁻; students generalize from Grignard's reactivity to Gilman without knowing about HSAB selectivity
distractors.correct_reasoning: Gilman (R₂CuLi) does NOT react with ketones (too unreactive; C-Cu bond is weakly polar = soft nucleophile; ketone C=O = hard electrophile); Gilman SELECTIVELY reacts with: acyl chlorides → ketone; vinyl/aryl halides → coupled product; alkyl halides → R-R'; JEE tests: 'which of these does NOT react with R₂CuLi?' → ketone; 'to make a ketone from an acyl chloride, use ___?' → Gilman (NOT Grignard, which over-adds to give alcohol)
distractors.why_attractive: Carbonyl reactions (addition, condensation, reduction) are among the most tested in JEE. The many named reactions and their conditions create confusion between similar-looking transformations.
distractors.correct_resolution: Key decision tree: identify the carbonyl type (aldehyde/ketone/ester/acid/amide/acyl halide) → identify the reagent class → determine mechanism → predict product, stereochemistry, and any competing pathways.

distractors.description: Students predict RMgX can couple with vinyl bromide (CH₂=CH-Br) via SN2 to give an allyl product (just like it couples with 1° alkyl halide)
distractors.why_plausible: SN2 coupling works for 1° alkyl halides + Grignard; students assume it should also work for vinyl halides since Br is a good leaving group
distractors.correct_reasoning: SN2 at an sp₂ carbon (vinyl or aryl) is GEOMETRICALLY IMPOSSIBLE (backside attack requires a 180° trajectory through the π system, which is sterically and orbitally forbidden); Grignard CANNOT couple with vinyl or aryl halides via SN2; use GILMAN REAGENT (R₂CuLi) for vinyl and aryl halide coupling (stereospecific, retention of C=C geometry); for vinyl halide + Grignard → no reaction or scrambled product; JEE: 'coupling with retention of geometry at C=C requires ___?' → R₂CuLi (Gilman reagent)

distractors.description: Students predict 1,2-dihaloalkane (ClCH₂CH₂Cl) + Mg → 1,2-diGrignard (ClMg-CH₂-CH₂-MgCl), since both carbons have leaving groups and Mg can insert into each C-X
distractors.why_plausible: The general rule 'Mg inserts into C-X bonds' seems to apply to both C-X bonds of a dihaloalkane; students expect diGrignard formation for ANY dihaloalkane

distractors.description: Students predict PCC oxidizes primary alcohol all the way to carboxylic acid (since PCC contains Cr which is a strong oxidant, same as Jones reagent)

distractors.description: Students predict that concentrated/hot KMnO₄ or Jones reagent can oxidize tertiary alcohols (since 'strong oxidant' should react with everything)
distractors.why_plausible: KMnO₄ and Jones are described as 'strong oxidizing agents'; students think 'strong' means 'reacts with all alcohols regardless of substitution'; the mechanism-based limitation (no α-H in 3°) is not intuitively obvious

distractors.description: Students predict LiAlH₄ reduces carboxylic acid (RCOOH) to aldehyde (RCHO), stopping at that partial reduction stage

distractors.description: Students predict ester + LiAlH₄ gives ONE primary alcohol (R-CH₂OH from the acyl R part only), treating the OR' group as a leaving group that is discarded

distractors.description: Students predict amide + LiAlH₄ → carboxylic acid + amine (breaking the C-N bond like acid hydrolysis does)
distractors.why_plausible: Students know amide hydrolysis (H₃O+ or OH-) breaks the C-N bond → RCOOH + NH₃ (or amine); they may assume LAH does the same; they confuse hydrolysis (aqueous C-N cleavage) with LAH reduction (anhydrous C=O reduction)
distractors.correct_reasoning: Amide + LiAlH₄ → AMINE only (R-CH₂-NR'R''); the C-N bond is NOT broken; only the C=O is reduced to CH₂; no carboxylic acid is produced; LAH converts amide → amine by: C=O removed as water (from workup) → C-N bond stays; result: one carbon less in the original chain but N stays attached; JEE: 'N,N-dimethylbenzamide + LiAlH₄ →?' → N,N-dimethylbenzylamine (Ph-CH₂-N(CH₃)₂); the C=O (acyl) becomes CH₂; N-dimethyl stays

distractors.correct_resolution: Classify amine (1°/2°/3°, aliphatic/aromatic) first. Then apply reagent-specific rules. Key distinctions: carbylamine test (+ve only for 1°); Hinsberg test (sulfonyl chloride + base); Nitrous acid (1° aromatic → diazonium; 2° → nitrosamine; 3° aliphatic → no reaction; 3° aromatic → ring nitroso).

distractors.description: Students predict NaBH₄ (sodium borohydride) can reduce esters to primary alcohols, just like LiAlH₄ (since 'both are hydride reducing agents')

distractors.description: Students predict SeO₂ allylic oxidation targets the LESS substituted end of the C=C double bond (like hydroboration which is anti-Markovnikov)
distractors.why_plausible: Students confuse SeO₂ allylic oxidation selectivity with hydroboration-oxidation (BH₃/H₂O₂), which is anti-Markovnikov; they apply the anti-Markovnikov rule incorrectly to SeO₂
distractors.correct_reasoning: SeO₂ targets the MORE substituted end (Markovnikov-like in the allylic position); for 2-methylbut-2-ene: the C with 2 methyl groups is more substituted → SeO₂ oxidizes one of those CH₃ groups → allylic alcohol at the more-substituted end; JEE: 'SeO₂ reacts with (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃ → which carbon is oxidized?' → the (CH₃)₂C end (more substituted); one of the CH₃ groups → CH₂OH; selectivity: -CH₂- > -CH₃ at that end
distractors.why_attractive: Oxidising and reducing agents have different selectivities that are easily confused. Students apply a uniform 'strong oxidant → complete oxidation' rule.
distractors.correct_resolution: Selectivity determines product: PCC → aldehyde from 1° alcohol (no over-oxidation); KMnO₄ cold → syn diol; KMnO₄ hot → C-C cleavage; LiAlH₄ → complete reduction; NaBH₄ → aldehyde/ketone only; DIBALH at −78°C → aldehyde from ester. Always specify conditions.

distractors.description: Students predict Pb(OAc)₄ (or HIO₄) cleaves 1,3-diols (or any diol) to carbonyl compounds

distractors.description: Students predict SeO₂ can oxidize any secondary aliphatic CH₂ group (like a general mild oxidant), not just allylic or α-carbonyl positions

distractors.description: Student assigns R/S without reversing when the lowest-priority group (d) is on the WEDGE bond (pointing toward viewer) — giving the opposite configuration
distractors.why_plausible: Students memorize 'clockwise = R, counterclockwise = S' but forget this only applies when d points AWAY; if d is in a wedge (toward viewer), the apparent rotation direction is the MIRROR of the actual direction, requiring a swap

distractors.description: Student assigns CIP priority based on length of carbon chain (longer chain = higher priority) instead of atomic number at first point of difference
distractors.why_plausible: In IUPAC nomenclature, the principal chain is the LONGEST chain; students confuse IUPAC chain selection (longest = main) with CIP priority (highest Z = highest priority); these are completely different criteria

NO: -CH₂OH (O at circle II, Z=8) > -CH₂CH₂CH₃ = -CH₂CH₃ at circle II both give C(Z=6) → then circle III: -CH₂CH₂CH₃ gives C vs -CH₂CH₃ gives H → C>H → propyl > ethyl; FINAL: -CH₂OH > -CH₂CH₂CH₃ > -CH₂CH₃

distractors.description: Student treats phantom atoms (duplicate atoms for double bonds or rings) as having full atomic number equal to real atoms — giving alkenes or cycloalkyl groups incorrectly high priority
distractors.why_plausible: The phantom atom has the same Z as the atom it duplicates (phantom C has Z=6 same as real C); students assume the phantom C counts the same as a real C in priority comparison and don't know that phantom atoms have no further substituents and terminate further exploration
distractors.correct_reasoning: Phantom atoms have the SAME Z as the real atom (phantom C: Z=6) so in the first circle where they appear, they count the same as real C; BUT phantom atoms carry NO further substituents (their branches terminate in Z=0 phantom atoms); so at the NEXT deeper circle, a real atom (even H, Z=1) beats the phantom atom's branch (Z=0); the net effect: phantom atoms boost priority at the first circle but lose to any real atom at the second circle; for ring CIP: the phantom atom at the reconnect has the same Z as real ring atoms at that circle, but its branch is empty (Z=0) → any real branch wins at the next level; for C=C phantom atoms: they contribute one extra 'virtual C' at the attached circle; JEE: '-CH=CH₂ vs -CH₂CH₃ at circle I: both C; circle II: =CH- (C=C) contributes (C-real, C-phantom, H) vs -CH₂- contributes (C, H, H); comparing highest: C(phantom) vs C → tie; comparing next: H vs H → tie; next: H vs H... actually both are C at circle II; circle III of =CH₂ branch gives (C-phantom, C-phantom) while circle III of -CH₂CH₃ is H; C-phantom(6) > H(1) → -CH=CH₂ wins

distractors.description: Student predicts that bulkier N-substituents always give SLOWER inversion (higher ΔG#) because larger groups take more energy to squeeze past each other in the planar TS
distractors.why_plausible: The common intuition is that steric bulk makes reactions harder; students apply this to the transition state (planar N) without considering that the bulky groups also DESTABILIZE the pyramidal ground state; the barrier is a difference (TS - GS), not just the TS energy alone
distractors.correct_reasoning: Steric acceleration: very bulky groups (iPr, iBu, tBu) compress each other at ~109° in the pyramidal GS; at the planar ~120° TS they are farther apart; ΔG# = (TS energy) - (GS energy); since GS is raised MORE by bulk than the TS → ΔG# DECREASES; JEE: 'Compare inversion rate of i-Bu3N vs Me3N' → i-Bu3N inverts FASTER (steric acceleration; lower ΔG#)
