distractors.why_plausible: students_know_that_one_mole_of_NH3_reacts_with_one_mole_of_the_haloacid_to_replace_X_with_NH2; they_see_no_reason_for_excess; but_with_stoichiometric_NH3_the_product_alpha-amino_acid_(which_still_contains_NH2)_will_react_FURTHER_with_more_haloacid_giving_N-alkylated_secondary_and_tertiary_amines; excess_NH3_ensures_that_NH3_(present_in_large_excess)_competes_effectively_with_the_product_amine_for_the_remaining_haloacid_keeping_product_as_primary_amine
distractors.description: Distractor example: Excess ammonia unnecessary in alpha halo acid to amino acid conversion. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.
distractors.why_attractive: This distractor mimics a correct reasoning step but misapplies it to a situation where the standard rule does not hold. The surface-level similarity to a correct argument makes it convincing.
distractors.correct_resolution: Identify the specific condition or structural feature that makes the standard rule invalid here. Trace the mechanism step-by-step rather than applying a memorised rule. Check whether electronic and steric factors both support the predicted outcome.

distractors.why_plausible: students_know_amines_are_basic_due_to_nitrogen_and_extend_this_to_classify_amino-group-containing_compounds_as_basic; in_amino_acid_classification_however_aspartic_acid_(Asp_D)_and_glutamic_acid_(Glu_E)_are_ACIDIC_amino_acids_because_their_side_chains_contain_an_EXTRA_COOH_group_making_them_net_acidic_at_physiological_pH; basic_amino_acids_are_those_with_EXTRA_amino_groups:_Lysine_(epsilon_NH2)_Arginine_(guanidino)_Histidine_(imidazole)
distractors.description: Distractor example: Aspartic acid and glutamic acid are basic amino acids because they contain nitrogen. Student incorrectly applies this reasoning, leading to an incorrect answer.
distractors.why_attractive: Amine reactions are diverse and condition-dependent. The same amine class (1°, 2°, 3°) gives different products with different reagents. Students apply a single rule to all amines.
distractors.correct_resolution: Classify amine (1°/2°/3°, aliphatic/aromatic) first. Then apply reagent-specific rules. Key distinctions: carbylamine test (+ve only for 1°); Hinsberg test (sulfonyl chloride + base); Nitrous acid (1° aromatic → diazonium; 2° → nitrosamine; 3° aliphatic → no reaction; 3° aromatic → ring nitroso).

distractors.description: Inductive (I), Mesomeric (M), and Hyperconjugation (H) are PERMANENT effects — present in ground state without attacking reagent. Electromeric (E) and Inductomeric (IM) are TEMPORARY — require an attacking reagent and disappear when reagent leaves.
distractors.why_attractive: All are called 'electron displacement effects', so students assume all operate similarly in ground state
distractors.correct_resolution: Check if the effect requires an incoming electrophile/nucleophile to be present. If yes → temporary (E/IM); if no → permanent (I/M/H).

distractors.type: acidity of 2,2,2-trichloroethanoic acid attributed to resonance
distractors.description: 2,2,2-trichloroethanoic acid (CCl3COOH, pKa ≈ 0.66) is far more acidic than ethanoic acid. Distractor: students attribute this to resonance of Cl lone pairs with C=O. Correct: three chloro groups exert cumulative −I effect through σ-bonds, each withdrawing electron density additively.
distractors.why_attractive: Cl does participate in +M resonance with benzene ring, so students generalise this to aliphatic systems
distractors.correct_resolution: In aliphatic (non-conjugated) systems, inductive effect dominates; resonance (M/R) requires π-system conjugation.

distractors.description: Distractor: C−D (deuterium) bond is stronger (higher zero-point energy), so students assume CD3 is less electron-donating. Correct: C−T > C−D > C−H in +I effect because the heavier isotope pulls the σ-bond electrons slightly less effectively toward the substituent, leaving more electron density on carbon.
distractors.why_attractive: Bond dissociation energy trend (C−T > C−D > C−H) is confused with electron-donation direction
distractors.correct_resolution: Isotope effect on +I: CT3 > CD3 > CH3 (tritiated > deuterated > protiated methyl).

distractors.type: resonance structures treated as real equilibrating species
distractors.description: Students write resonance contributors as if the molecule oscillates between them (like tautomers). Canonical structures (e.g. the two Kekulé structures of benzene) are fictitious; the actual benzene molecule is the hybrid with all C-C bonds equal at 1.40Å. Arrow: ↔ (resonance), NOT ⇌ (equilibrium).
distractors.why_attractive: Resonance arrow ↔ visually resembles equilibrium arrow ⇌; textbooks draw multiple canonical structures side-by-side which looks like a list of real forms
distractors.correct_resolution: Resonance hybrid is the ONLY real structure; canonical structures are bookkeeping fictions. The molecule does NOT flip between them.

distractors.type: UV light assumed to always cause ionic (heterolytic) products
distractors.description: Distractor: UV breaks bonds by giving energy → ions (H⁺ + Cl⁻). Correct: UV (photolysis) gives HOMOLYTIC fission → radicals (Cl• + Cl•). Ionic (heterolytic) products require stabilisation by polar solvents, not UV energy alone.
distractors.why_attractive: Students associate high-energy UV with 'complete bond breaking' and ionic products, confusing photochemical energy with electrochemical bond polarisation
distractors.correct_resolution: hν/UV → homolytic → radicals; polar solvent/base → heterolytic → ions. Both break bonds, but the electron-sharing mode differs.

distractors.type: N lone pair in aniline (aminobenzene) fully available for protonation (same as aliphatic amine)
distractors.description: Distractor: aniline (aminobenzene) has -NH2 like methylamine, so it should have similar basicity. Correct: in aniline, N lone pair is donated into the benzene ring π-system (+M effect) via p-π resonance, making it LESS available for protonation → aniline pKaH = 4.6 vs methylamine pKaH = 10.6.
distractors.why_attractive: Both have -NH2 group; students focus on lone pair presence rather than its availability after resonance delocalisation
distractors.correct_resolution: Resonance donation of N lone pair reduces its basicity; more resonance structures involving N lone pair → lower Kb/higher pKaH for the amine.

distractors.description: Students often count only 3 structures for phenol (2 Kekulé + 1 with O donating). Correct total = 5: neutral phenol + Kekulé-2 + O⁺=ring/⁻ at ortho-2 + O⁺=ring/⁻ at ortho-6 + O⁺=ring/⁻ at para-4. The two ortho positions contribute SEPARATELY as distinct canonical structures.
distractors.why_attractive: Ortho-2 and ortho-6 look identical by symmetry in drawing, leading students to count them as one structure
distractors.correct_resolution: They are chemically distinct canonical structures even if symmetry-equivalent — both must be counted. Total canonical structures for phenol = 5.

distractors.type: -NH₂ on benzene ring increases electron density at meta positions
distractors.description: Distractor: since NH₂ is electron-donating, it increases electron density everywhere including meta. Correct: +M effect of −NH₂ specifically increases density at ortho (2, 6) and para (4) positions. Meta (3, 5) positions are actually relatively electron-POOR compared to ortho/para in aminobenzene.
distractors.why_attractive: General statement 'EDG adds electrons to ring' is conflated with 'adds to all positions equally'
distractors.correct_resolution: Resonance canonical structures show ⁻ charge at ortho and para only, never at meta. Meta remains electron-neutral relative to para/ortho → electrophilic attack occurs at ortho/para, NOT meta.

distractors.type: -COOH group on benzene is EDG because it attaches via carbon
distractors.description: Distractor: -COOH is attached to ring via carbon (like methyl); methyl is +I EDG, so -COOH should also be EDG. Correct: -COOH has a polar C=O that conjugates with ring via -M effect; the -M electron withdrawal DOMINATES over any +I. -COOH is net EWG, deactivates ring, and directs to meta.
distractors.why_attractive: Methyl (−CH₃) and carboxyl (−COOH) both attach via carbon; students apply the same reasoning ignoring the polar C=O in COOH
distractors.correct_resolution: The C=O double bond in -COOH creates -M effect that overwhelms any weak +I from the C-C bond. Always check for polar π-bonds adjacent to the point of ring attachment before classifying EDG/EWG.

distractors.type: iodine strongest +M halogen because largest and most polarisable
distractors.description: Distractor: I has the most polarisable lone pairs and largest size → best +M donor. Correct: +M requires ORBITAL OVERLAP, not polarisability. F (2p lone pair) overlaps perfectly with ring 2p → strongest +M. I (5p lone pair) has worst 2p-5p mismatch → weakest +M. Fluorobenzene is the most activated halobenzene ring despite F being most electronegative.
distractors.why_attractive: Polarisability is used for Van der Waals forces and some nucleophilicity arguments; students mistakenly apply it to resonance overlap
distractors.correct_resolution: +M power for halogens: F > Cl > Br > I (orbital size match); +I and polarisability: I > Br > Cl > F (both opposite trends).

distractors.type: N-acetylamino (NHAc) group is as activating as -NH₂ for benzene ring
distractors.description: Distractor: both -NH₂ and -NHAc have nitrogen with lone pair → both donate equally into ring. Correct: in -NHC(=O)R (acetanilide/acetamido group), the N lone pair is strongly donated into the adjacent C=O via amide resonance (N-C(=O) resonance keeps N in sp2, lone pair in p used for amide bond). Only residual lone pair density reaches ring. -NHAc is much WEAKER +M donor than -NH₂.
distractors.why_attractive: Both have 'N with lone pair adjacent to ring'; students ignore amide resonance that pre-empts lone pair availability
distractors.correct_resolution: +M ranking: -NR₂ > -NHR > -NH₂ >> -NHC(=O)R >> -NC(=O)R₂. Amide N lone pair is largely tied up in amide bond, not available for ring donation.

distractors.type: anhydride is weaker EWG than ester because it has two oxygens donating into carbonyl
distractors.description: Distractor: anhydride has two oxygen donors per carbonyl → each C=O is less electrophilic → weaker -M. Correct: the anhydride oxygen BETWEEN the two carbonyls must donate simultaneously to both; each C=O gets LESS donation from this bridging O than an ester C=O gets from its dedicated O-R. Hence anhydride carbonyls are MORE electrophilic than ester carbonyl → anhydride has stronger -M than ester.
distractors.why_attractive: More oxygens = more donation seems intuitive; students don't account for the competing withdrawal from both sides of the bridging oxygen
distractors.correct_resolution: -M power: anhydride (-C(=O)-O-C(=O)-) > ester (-COOR) > acid (-COOH) > amide (-CONH₂). Anhydride is also more reactive toward nucleophiles (acyl substitution) for the same reason.

distractors.type: more canonical structures = more stable molecule in all cases
distractors.description: Distractor: phenol (5 canonical structures) must be more stable than cyclohexanol (1 structure). While resonance stabilisation IS real, the key is the QUALITY of canonical structures, not just quantity. Five charged canonical structures contribute less than two neutral ones. The actual resonance energy depends on the energy of individual canonical structures and their weights.
distractors.why_attractive: More structures → more delocalization → more stable is a valid principle, but only for similarly-weighted structures (e.g. benzene 2 Kekulé). When structures are very unequal in stability, minor structures contribute negligibly.
distractors.correct_resolution: Compare canonical structures by quality first (Rule I: octet), then quantity. Benzene is more stable than butadiene per π-bond not because of more structures, but because all 6 carbon structures are equally weighted.

distractors.type: canonical structure showing O+ with only 6 electrons is valid for enol resonance
distractors.description: Distractor: in enol resonance (CH2=C-OH), students draw the cationic form with O⁺ having only 3 bonds and 1 lone pair (=6 electrons, incomplete octet) as a canonical structure. This is INVALID. O can bear +ve charge only with complete octet (4 bonds or 3 bonds + 1 lone pair that still gives 8 electrons). The valid structure has O⁺ with one lone pair remaining: ⁺O(H)=C-CH2⁻.
distractors.why_attractive: Drawing resonance arrows mechanically from O lone pair to C=C gives O⁺ as 'destination'; students don't count electrons on the resulting O
distractors.correct_resolution: After drawing resonance arrow, COUNT electrons on every atom. O⁺ must still have 8 electrons (4 bonds = 8, or 3 bonds + 1 LP = 8). If O ends up with 6, redraw — that canonical is forbidden.

distractors.type: canonical structure stability solely determined by charge position (Rule III alone)
distractors.description: Distractor: the canonical with ⁻ on O and ⁺ on C is always most stable because O is most electronegative. Correct: Rule III (charge position) is LOWER priority than Rules I and II. A structure with complete octet (Rule I) and neutral charge outranks even the best charge-positioned structure. A charged structure with more π-bonds (Rule II) may outrank one with fewer π-bonds even if charge positions are worse.
distractors.why_attractive: The charge-on-electronegative-atom rule is memorable and often decisive; students overuse it while ignoring octet completeness and π-bond count
distractors.correct_resolution: Always apply rules in priority order: Octet → π-bonds → charge count → charge position → charge distance → charge stability. Only use charge position rule when higher priority rules give a tie.

distractors.type: KOH absorbs water in Liebig's method apparatus
distractors.description: Distractor: students write 'KOH absorbs H₂O, CaCl₂ absorbs CO₂' — reversed from the actual roles. Correct: anhydrous CaCl₂ absorbs H₂O (first in path); KOH solution absorbs CO₂ (second in path). Weight increase of CaCl₂ = H₂O collected; weight increase of KOH = CO₂ collected.
distractors.why_attractive: KOH is a strong base and a desiccant (hygroscopic); students know KOH absorbs water in general lab use and apply this to Liebig's setup incorrectly.
distractors.correct_resolution: In Liebig's apparatus: CaCl₂ → H₂O; KOH → CO₂. The sequence ensures water is removed before the gas reaches KOH, so KOH weight increase = CO₂ only.

distractors.type: Volume collected in nitrometer used directly as V at STP
distractors.description: Distractor: students use V₁ (volume of N₂ collected at experimental T₁, P₁) directly in the %N formula. Correct: must first correct for aqueous tension (P_N₂ = P₁ − P_H₂O), then convert to STP using combined gas law: V₂ = P_N₂V₁T₂/(T₁P₂). Only V₂ (at STP, 273K, 760 mmHg) goes into the %N formula.
distractors.why_attractive: The PV/T conversion step is often skipped under time pressure; students go directly from collected volume to percentage.
distractors.correct_resolution: Always: (1) subtract aqueous tension → get P_N₂; (2) convert to STP → get V₂; (3) use V₂ in %N = 28V₂×100/(22400×w₁).

distractors.type: %O calculated as (CO₂ mass × 32/44) in combustion analysis
distractors.description: Distractor: students try to extract %O from the CO₂ data — since CO₂ has 2 oxygen atoms, they compute the oxygen content of CO₂ and claim it comes from the organic compound. Wrong — the oxygen in CO₂ comes from BOTH the organic compound AND the excess O₂ used for combustion. Impossible to separate sources.
distractors.why_attractive: CO₂ contains oxygen; students reason 'oxygen must come from the compound' and ignore the supplied O₂.
distractors.correct_resolution: %O = 100 − %C − %H − %N − %S − %X. Oxygen content is always determined by subtraction, never from combustion gas oxygen directly.

distractors.type: phenylalanine gives positive Xanthoproteic test because it contains a benzene ring
distractors.description: Distractor: phenylalanine has a benzene ring → aromatic amino acid → Xanthoproteic positive. Correct: phenylalanine gives NEGATIVE. Only tyrosine and tryptophan are positive. Phenylalanine's benzene ring has no activating substituent (no -OH, no -NH on ring) → insufficient EAS reactivity for Xanthoproteic nitration conditions.
distractors.why_attractive: Textbooks list phenylalanine as an 'aromatic amino acid' alongside tyrosine and tryptophan; students infer that all three give the same biochemical tests. The distinction requires understanding which rings are activated for EAS.
distractors.correct_resolution: Xanthoproteic positive: tyrosine (phenolic -OH activates ring) and tryptophan (indolic N-H activates ring). Phenylalanine (plain benzene, no activating group) → negative.

distractors.type: ninhydrin gives purple with all amino acids including proline
distractors.description: Distractor: ninhydrin reacts with amino acids → always purple (Ruhemann's purple). Correct: proline and hydroxyproline give YELLOW-ORANGE with ninhydrin. They are secondary amines (imino acids — N is in a pyrrolidine ring, no free -NH₂). The Ruhemann's purple mechanism requires free primary -NH₂ to release NH₃. Proline cannot release NH₃ → different yellow condensation product forms instead.
distractors.why_attractive: The ninhydrin test is taught as a universal amino acid test; students memorise 'ninhydrin = purple' without learning the proline/hydroxyproline exception.
distractors.correct_resolution: Ninhydrin colours: purple = primary α-amino acids, ammonia, primary amines; yellow-orange = proline, hydroxyproline; brown = asparagine. Use colour to identify amino acid type in unknown mixture.

distractors.type: Seliwanoff's test negative for sucrose because sucrose is a non-reducing sugar
distractors.description: Distractor: sucrose is non-reducing → cannot open ring → Seliwanoff's negative. Correct: sucrose gives POSITIVE Seliwanoff's test. The 6M HCl in Seliwanoff's reagent is strong enough to hydrolyse the sucrose glycosidic bond → free fructose + glucose released. Fructose (a ketose) reacts to give the deep red colour. Note: Fehling's / Tollens' reagent is alkaline and mild → does NOT hydrolyse sucrose → sucrose negative there.
distractors.why_attractive: Non-reducing sugar → negative carbohydrate tests is a valid rule for Fehling's/Tollens'/Benedict's, but students incorrectly extend it to Seliwanoff's (which uses strongly acidic conditions that cause hydrolysis first).
distractors.correct_resolution: Seliwanoff's uses 6M HCl → hydrolyses disaccharides (including sucrose) before colour test. Any disaccharide or oligosaccharide containing a ketose unit will give positive Seliwanoff's after acid hydrolysis.

distractors.type: NaBH₄ reduces carboxylic acid to primary alcohol like LAH
distractors.description: Distractor: both NaBH₄ (SBH) and LAH are hydride donors, so both should reduce -COOH to -CH₂OH. Correct: NaBH₄ does NOT reduce carboxylic acids. Only LAH, BH₃·THF, or H₂/Ru-C achieve COOH → CH₂OH. NaBH₄ reduces aldehydes and ketones only (and sometimes esters with difficulty). The COOH group is too electron-rich (resonance stabilised carboxylate) for the mild NaBH₄ hydride.
distractors.why_attractive: Both LAH and NaBH₄ are named 'hydride reducing agents'; students assume they have the same substrate scope and apply LAH reactions to NaBH₄.
distractors.correct_resolution: LAH reduces: RCOOH, RCOOR, RCONH₂, RCHO, RCOR, RCOCl. NaBH₄ reduces: RCHO, RCOR only (ketones and aldehydes). Key selectivity: NaBH₄ cannot touch RCOOH, RCOOR, RCONH₂.

distractors.type: ether has higher boiling point than alcohol of similar molecular weight due to symmetry
distractors.description: Distractor: diethyl ether (MW=74) is a 'symmetric' molecule with C-O-C dipole → high BP. Correct: ethanol (MW=46) boils at 78°C while diethyl ether (MW=74) boils at only 35°C. Alcohols have MUCH higher BP than ethers of similar MW because alcohols have O-H···O hydrogen bonding (strong); ethers can only accept H-bonds (no O-H donor) → no intermolecular H-bonding between ether molecules. General BP: carboxylic acid > alcohol >> ketone > aldehyde > ether > hydrocarbon.
distractors.why_attractive: Ethers have higher MW than alcohols of same carbon number, making the comparison seem unfair; students also know ethers have lone pairs (can accept H-bond) and assume this is similar to alcohol H-bonding.
distractors.correct_resolution: H-bond strength requires both DONOR (O-H or N-H) and acceptor. Ether has only acceptor (lone pair on O) but no donor → cannot H-bond with itself → low BP. Alcohol has both donor (O-H) and acceptor (lone pair on O) → strong H-bonds → high BP.

distractors.type: more chain branching in alcohols decreases solubility in water (same as hydrocarbons)
distractors.description: Distractor: branching makes alcohol more 'hydrocarbon-like', less polar → lower solubility. Correct: for alcohols, branching INCREASES solubility because it makes the molecule more compact, reducing hydrophobic alkyl surface exposed to water; the polar -OH group becomes relatively more dominant. n-pentan-1-ol < 2-methylbutan-2-ol in water solubility. But branching DOES lower BP (less London force surface area). So branching has OPPOSITE effects on solubility (increases) and boiling point (decreases).
distractors.why_attractive: For pure hydrocarbons, branching also affects London forces similarly; students extrapolate this to alcohols and predict lower solubility with branching.
distractors.correct_resolution: For alcohols: branching ↑ → solubility ↑ (compact, less hydrophobic surface, -OH dominates); branching ↑ → BP ↓ (less surface area for London dispersion). These are two different phenomena governed by different intermolecular forces.

distractors.type: Victor Meyer test: 2° alcohol gives red colour (same as 1°)
distractors.description: Distractor: 2° alcohol contains α-H and reacts with HNO₂ → some colour. Red is the visible colour of the test → 2° must also give red. Correct: 2° gives BLUE pseudonitrole (insoluble in NaOH). 1° gives RED nitrolic acid (soluble in NaOH → red solution). 3° gives COLOURLESS (no reaction). The mnemonic RBC (Red-Blue-Colourless) maps to 1°-2°-3°.
distractors.why_attractive: Both 1° and 2° nitroalkanes react with HNO₂; students assume both give the same coloured product. The crucial difference is whether the product dissolves in NaOH (1° does → red) or remains as a blue liquid (2° does not → blue).
distractors.correct_resolution: 1° → nitrolic acid (has -NOH, acidic, dissolves in NaOH → RED solution). 2° → pseudonitrole (no acidic H, insoluble in NaOH → BLUE liquid). 3° → no reaction → COLOURLESS.

distractors.type: phenol gives positive CAN test because it has a hydroxyl group like alcohols
distractors.description: Distractor: CAN test detects -OH compounds → phenol (which has -OH) should give red CAN colour. Correct: phenol gives NEGATIVE CAN test. CAN specifically detects ALIPHATIC alcohols. Phenol does not coordinate with Ce⁴⁺ to give the characteristic red complex. This makes CAN useful for distinguishing aliphatic alcohol from phenol in a mixture.
distractors.why_attractive: Phenol contains -OH, which is the structural basis of CAN test for alcohols; students assume all -OH compounds respond to CAN the same way.
distractors.correct_resolution: CAN test: aliphatic 1°/2° alcohol → RED. 3° alcohol → brown/green. Phenol → NEGATIVE. Ether → NEGATIVE. CAN is the characteristic test ONLY for aliphatic alcohols.

distractors.type: para-nitrophenol reacts with NaHCO₃ to give CO₂ because nitro group increases acidity
distractors.description: Distractor: -NO₂ is EWG → it increases phenol acidity significantly → phenol pKa goes from 10 to ~7 → should react with NaHCO₃. Correct: para-nitrophenol pKa ~7.1 is STILL less acidic than H₂CO₃ (pKa ~6.3) → does NOT react with NaHCO₃. Minimum requirement for NaHCO₃ reaction: compound pKa < 6.3. Para-nitrophenol fails this threshold. 2,4-dinitrophenol (pKa ~4.1) and picric acid (pKa ~0.7) both react.
distractors.why_attractive: The -NO₂ group's strong -I and -M effect clearly increases acidity; students extrapolate that one -NO₂ group is enough to cross the NaHCO₃ threshold. The exact pKa values needed to verify this are not intuitively obvious.
distractors.correct_resolution: NaHCO₃ threshold: pKa < 6.3. Para-NO₂-phenol pKa ~7.1 → NO reaction. 2,4-dinitrophenol pKa ~4.1 → YES. Picric acid pKa ~0.7 → YES. Need ≥2 nitro groups on phenol to cross the NaHCO₃ threshold.

distractors.type: higher temperature during alcohol dehydration gives more ether (more nucleophilic substitution at higher energy)
distractors.description: Distractor: higher temperature → more reaction energy → more intermolecular substitution → more ether. Correct: higher temperature FAVOURS ELIMINATION over substitution. T > 170°C → alkene (E1 predominates); 110–170°C → ether (SN1-type). Increasing temperature shifts the product FROM ether TOWARD alkene, not the other way. Entropy drives elimination at high T (two molecules → one product + one small molecule).
distractors.why_attractive: Higher energy 'drives more reaction' is a valid heuristic, but the regiochemical preference shifts from substitution to elimination as temperature rises — a nuance students miss.
distractors.correct_resolution: Temperature + conc. H₂SO₄ product: <110°C → sulphate ester; 110–170°C → ether; >170°C → alkene. Higher T → elimination NOT substitution.

distractors.type: ThO₂ dehydration gives Zaitsev product (same as other dehydrating agents)
distractors.description: Distractor: ThO₂ is a dehydrating agent like Al₂O₃ and H₂SO₄ → should give more substituted (Zaitsev) alkene. Correct: ThO₂ is the exception — it gives the LESS substituted (Hofmann/anti-Zaitsev) alkene via a surface-catalysed mechanism that preferentially removes the less hindered β-H. All other common agents (H₂SO₄, Al₂O₃, POCl₃, KHSO₄, H₃PO₄) give Zaitsev.
distractors.why_attractive: ThO₂ is grouped with other metal oxide dehydrating agents (like Al₂O₃ → Zaitsev); students apply the same rule to all oxide catalysts.
distractors.correct_resolution: Zaitsev: H₂SO₄, Al₂O₃, POCl₃, KHSO₄, H₃PO₄. Anti-Zaitsev (Hofmann): ThO₂ ONLY. Memorise as a standalone exception.

distractors.type: number of -OH groups in a polyol = MW increase on acetylation / 43
distractors.description: Distractor: acetylation adds -C(=O)-CH₃ (MW = 43) per -OH; so n = ΔMW/43. Correct: each acetylation replaces -H (MW 1) with -C(=O)CH₃ (MW 43); NET increase per OH = 43 − 1 = 42. Therefore n = ΔMW/42. The lost hydrogen (MW 1) is always subtracted. Calculation: C(12) + O(16) + CH₃(15) − H(1) = 42.
distractors.why_attractive: Students add the acetyl group MW directly (43) without subtracting the H that leaves; or confuse the MW of acetyl group itself with the net MW change.
distractors.correct_resolution: ΔMW per OH = 42 (not 43). n(OH) = total ΔMW / 42. For amines (-NH₂): n(NH₂) = ΔMW/42 (same calculation — -NH₂ → -NHC(=O)CH₃, replaces one H by C(=O)CH₃).

distractors.type: PET (Terylene) is a homo-polymer because it has one repeating unit
distractors.description: Distractor: PET has one repeating unit in the chain → homo-polymer. Correct: PET (polyethylene terephthalate / Terylene) is a COPOLYMER. It is made from TWO different monomers: ethane-1,2-diol (ethylene glycol) and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid (terephthalic acid). Having one repeating unit in the polymer chain does not make it a homo-polymer — what matters is whether one or two different monomers are used in synthesis.
distractors.why_attractive: The polymer chain has a regular repeating unit, and 'homo' suggests 'same/uniform' — students conclude it's a homo-polymer because the chain looks uniform.
distractors.correct_resolution: Homo-polymer: one monomer type. Copolymer: two or more monomer types. PET uses two (diol + diacid) → copolymer. Nylon-6,6 uses two (diamine + diacid) → copolymer. Nylon-6 uses one (caprolactam) → homo-polymer. Polystyrene, polyethene → homo-polymers.

distractors.type: thermosetting polymers can be re-melted at very high temperatures unlike thermoplastics
distractors.description: Distractor: thermosetting polymers are just 'heat-stable' thermoplastics — at very high temperatures they will melt. Correct: thermosetting polymers CANNOT be remelted. When heated, the cross-links become stronger (more cross-linking occurs) → the polymer becomes more rigid and eventually chars/decomposes without ever melting or flowing. This is the fundamental difference from thermoplastics, which melt reversibly. Bakelite, once set, is permanently infusible.
distractors.why_attractive: Students reason: 'high enough temperature melts everything' — true for simple substances but incorrect for thermosetting network polymers where covalent crosslinks throughout the material prevent chain movement.
distractors.correct_resolution: Thermoplastic: reversible soften (heat) ↔ harden (cool). Thermosetting: on heating → MORE crosslinks → irreversibly infusible → eventually chars. No melting point exists for thermosetting polymers.

distractors.type: Neoprene, BUNA-N, and BUNA-S are all copolymers because they are both synthetic rubbers
distractors.description: Distractor: all synthetic rubbers made from butadiene-based chemistry are copolymers. Correct: Neoprene (polychloroprene) is a HOMO-polymer — its monomer is 2-chlorobuta-1,3-diene (chloroprene) and only ONE monomer is used. BUNA-N (butadiene + acrylonitrile = 2 monomers → copolymer) and BUNA-S (butadiene + styrene = 2 monomers → copolymer) are copolymers.
distractors.why_attractive: Neoprene is always listed alongside BUNA-N and BUNA-S; all are grouped as synthetic rubbers. Students assume similar reactions mean similar monomer count. The key difference: Neoprene's monomer (chloroprene) already carries the halogen substituent on a single diene — no second monomer needed.
distractors.correct_resolution: Homo-polymers among rubbers: natural rubber (polyisoprene from 2-methylbuta-1,3-diene), Neoprene (polychloroprene from chloroprene). Copolymers: BUNA-N, BUNA-S. Test: how many distinct monomers? One → homo; two or more → co.

distractors.type: gutta percha and natural rubber have similar mechanical properties since both are polyisoprene
distractors.description: Distractor: gutta percha and natural rubber both have formula (C₅H₈)ₙ and both are poly(2-methylbuta-1,3-diene) → same structure → same properties. Correct: they are geometric isomers — CIS (natural rubber, elastic) vs TRANS (gutta percha, non-elastic). The cis configuration forces chain coiling → elastic; trans allows chain extension → crystalline, rigid. Gutta percha is used to erase pencil marks (non-elastic); natural rubber is used for tyres (elastic after vulcanisation).
distractors.why_attractive: Same name (polyisoprene), same empirical formula, same repeat unit — students conclude same properties.
distractors.correct_resolution: cis-1,4-polyisoprene = natural rubber = elastic. trans-1,4-polyisoprene = gutta percha = non-elastic. Geometric isomerism of polymer internal double bonds controls chain geometry and crystallinity.

distractors.type: anionic polymerisation has faster termination than cationic because anions are more reactive
distractors.description: Distractor: anions are highly reactive → they react with everything including the chain → faster termination. Correct: anionic polymerisation has NO spontaneous termination — it is a living polymerisation. Carbanions stabilised by adjacent EWG (CN, etc.) persist at the chain end. The chain continues growing until a proton source is deliberately added. Cationic polymerisation DOES have spontaneous termination (carbocations rearrange, react with counter-ion). Free radical DOES have termination (radical combination/disproportionation).
distractors.why_attractive: Anions are nucleophilic and reactive → students assume they react with everything → rapid termination. The specific stability of carbanions adjacent to EWG is not obvious.
distractors.correct_resolution: Termination: anionic = NONE (living polymer). Cationic = spontaneous. Free radical = spontaneous (combination or disproportionation). Living polymerisation → block copolymers possible by sequential monomer addition.

distractors.type: Thiokol is a cross-linked polysulphide addition polymer like vulcanised rubber
distractors.description: Distractor: Thiokol has S-S bonds similar to vulcanised rubber cross-links → it must be made by adding sulphur to a polymer (addition, like vulcanisation). Correct: Thiokol is a CONDENSATION POLYMER (not addition). It is made by condensation of 1,2-dichloroethane with Na₂S₂ → -Sx- in the MAIN CHAIN (not as cross-links). NaCl is the eliminated small molecule. Unlike vulcanised rubber where sulphur bridges are cross-links between polyisoprene chains, in Thiokol the sulphur is PART OF the main chain in every repeat unit.
distractors.why_attractive: Both Thiokol and vulcanised rubber contain C-S-S-C bonds; students confuse the structural role of sulphur (main chain in Thiokol vs cross-link in vulcanised rubber).
distractors.correct_resolution: Vulcanised rubber: polyisoprene chains + S cross-links between chains (not in main chain). Thiokol: [-CH₂-CH₂-S₂-]ₙ = sulphide in main chain; condensation of 2-carbon dihalo + disulphide; NaCl eliminated per step.

distractors.type: applying SN1 migration aptitude (H > R > Ar) to Pinnacol-Pinacolone rearrangement
distractors.description: Distractor: SN1 and Pinnacol-Pinacolone both involve 1,2-shifts, so the migration order must be the same: H > R > Ar. Correct: Pinnacol-Pinacolone has :Ar > R > H. Aryl migrates MOST (not least) in Pinnacol. H migrates LEAST (not most). The reversal of H vs Ar is the critical distinction. Within each class, EDG-Ar > EWG-Ar in BOTH reactions, but the H-vs-Ar order completely reverses.
distractors.why_attractive: Both are 1,2-shift reactions occurring at carbocations. Students apply one universal order without distinguishing the mechanistic origin of the preference. The EDG-Ar trend is the same, which reinforces the false assumption that everything is the same.
distractors.correct_resolution: SN1/E1: H > R > Ar. Pinnacol-Pinacolone: :Ar > R > H. Baeyer-Villiger: H > 3° > 2° > ... > Me. Each reaction has a DIFFERENT order based on which step is RDS and what stabilises the TS.

distractors.type: in Baeyer-Villiger oxidation, tertiary alkyl migrates faster than H because tertiary carbocations are most stable
distractors.description: Distractor: Baeyer-Villiger involves a 1,2-shift, and tertiary carbocations are most stable in SN1, so in BV the order should be 3° > 2° > 1° > H > Me. Correct: BV migration order is H > 3° > 2° > cyclohexyl > Ph > 1° > cyclopropyl > Me. H migrates FASTEST, not 3° alkyl. BV is a CONCERTED migration (Criegee mechanism) toward the O-O bond, NOT a carbocation. Carbocation stability does not predict BV migratory aptitude.
distractors.why_attractive: The analogy to SN1 (where 3° is most reactive) is compelling. Students forget BV is a different mechanism (concerted, no discrete carbocation). The word 'migration' triggers the SN1 order by association.
distractors.correct_resolution: BV migratory aptitude is determined by the ability of the C-X bond to donate electrons into the O-O σ*. C-H has excellent hyperconjugation → H migrates best. For cyclic ketones, the substituent trans to C=O occupies the anti-periplanar position and migrates (trans selectivity in cyclic BV).

distractors.type: EDG on aryl accelerates all aryl-migrating rearrangements including Benzil-Benzilic acid
distractors.description: Distractor: In SN1, Pinnacol-Pinacolone, Hofmann degradation, and O₂ reactions, EDG on aryl increases migration rate. Therefore in Benzil-Benzilic, EDG on aryl should also accelerate the reaction. Correct: Benzil-Benzilic is the ONE exception where EWG on aryl accelerates the reaction and EDG (OMe) slows it. The teacher explicitly notes: 'This is due to initial attack' — the RDS in Benzil-Benzilic is OH⁻ nucleophilic addition to C=O, not aryl migration. EWG → more electrophilic C=O → faster initial attack → faster overall.
distractors.why_attractive: The EDG-Ar rule holds across 5+ different rearrangements. Benzil-Benzilic is the unique exception. Without knowing which step is RDS, students apply the universal EDG rule to all reactions.
distractors.correct_resolution: Hofmann: migration is RDS → EDG on Ar → faster (migration of EDG-Ar is easier). Benzil-Benzilic: initial OH⁻ attack is RDS → EWG on Ar → more electrophilic C=O → faster OH⁻ attack → faster. The RDS determines which electronic effect dominates.
